1

Module 1·Revise fast · about 1 weekMust

Basics and syntax

13 topics · about 2 h of reading

This module is the foundation of everything else in these notes. You already know some Java, so treat it as a fast but careful revision: the goal is to fill the small gaps that cause real bugs and that interviewers love to probe — Integer == Integer, 0.1 + 0.2, "Java is pass-by-value", why String is immutable, and the nextInt() + nextLine() trap.

It starts with how Java code actually runs (JDK, JVM, bytecode), then data types, operators, control flow, methods, arrays and strings, and ends with console input and output. Later modules build on it: objects and classes in Module 2, collections in Module 4, and what happens in memory in Module 7.

After this module you will be able to:

  • explain the roles of the JDK, JRE and JVM, and what javac and java do;
  • choose the right primitive type, predict overflow, casting and promotion results, and use BigDecimal for money;
  • write if, switch (old and new style) and loops without fall-through or off-by-one mistakes;
  • explain pass-by-value correctly, overload methods, and write varargs and recursive methods;
  • work with 1D and 2D arrays and the Arrays class;
  • explain the String pool, immutability and StringBuilder, and use the common String methods;
  • read input with Scanner and BufferedReader, and format output with printf;
  • solve the 30 basic practice programs (patterns, primes, palindromes, matrices) without looking anything up.

JDK, JRE and JVM: how Java code runs

You write source code, javac compiles it to platform-neutral bytecode, and the JVM on each machine loads, verifies and runs that bytecode — interpreting it first and compiling the hot parts to machine code.

Java is both compiled and interpreted. That is the reason one Java program runs on Windows, Linux and macOS without changes. Three names are confused again and again, so learn them precisely.

JVM (Java Virtual Machine)
The program that runs bytecode. It loads classes, checks them, manages memory (including garbage collection) and executes your code. There is a different JVM build for each operating system and CPU, but they all run the same bytecode. When you type java Main, you start a JVM.
JRE (Java Runtime Environment)
The JVM plus the standard class library (java.lang, java.util, java.io, …) — everything needed to run a Java program, but not to compile one.
JDK (Java Development Kit)
The JRE plus the developer tools: the compiler javac, jar, javadoc, jshell, javap, jcmd and more. As a developer, you install a JDK.

Think of it as nesting: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM. Since Java 11, vendors such as Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Oracle and Microsoft ship only a JDK; a separate JRE download is rare now. To build a small runtime for deployment you can use the jlink tool.

From source to running program

  1. Compile. javac Main.java checks syntax and types, then writes Main.class. This file holds bytecode — instructions for an imaginary machine (the JVM), not for your real CPU. If there is a compile error, no .class file is produced.
  2. Load. The class loader finds Main.class and brings it into memory when it is first needed (details in Class loading).
  3. Verify. The bytecode verifier checks that the bytecode is safe: valid instructions, correct types on the stack, no jumping into the middle of an instruction. This is one reason Java is safer than languages that run raw machine code.
  4. Execute. The interpreter starts running bytecode immediately, one instruction at a time. It is slow but starts fast. The JVM counts how often each method and loop runs.
  5. Optimise. Hot code is handed to the JIT (just-in-time) compiler, which turns it into machine code and keeps it in memory. This is why Java programs get faster after a short warm-up. More in JVM architecture.

Platform independence — "write once, run anywhere"

Bytecode is the same on every platform; only the JVM differs. A .class file compiled on your Windows laptop runs on the Linux server in the cloud, as long as the server has a JVM that is new enough. This is why you can build with Maven on a laptop and deploy a .jar inside a Docker image. Note the limit: the language is portable, but your program can still be non-portable if it hard-codes paths such as C:\data or uses native libraries.

Your first compile-and-run

public class Hello {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Namaste, Java!");
    }
}
$ javac Hello.java          # produces Hello.class
$ java Hello                # note: the class name, not Hello.class
Namaste, Java!
$ java Hello.java           # Java 11+: compile in memory and run in one step
Namaste, Java!

The last form is the single-file source launcher (Java 11). It compiles in memory and runs; no .class file is written. It is perfect for small experiments and practice programs.

JShell — a Java calculator (Java 9)

JShell is a REPL (read-eval-print loop). You type a statement or expression and see the result at once. No class or main is needed. Use it to test a string method or an operator rule in ten seconds.

$ jshell
jshell> 7 / 2
$1 ==> 3
jshell> 7 / 2.0
$2 ==> 3.5
jshell> "java".toUpperCase()
$3 ==> "JAVA"
jshell> /exit

Tools that come with the JDK

ToolPurpose
javacCompiles .java to .class
javaStarts a JVM and runs a class, a .jar or a single source file
jarPacks classes into a .jar archive
javadocGenerates HTML documentation from /** */ comments
javapShows the contents of a class file (javap -c Hello prints the bytecode)
jshellInteractive Java prompt
jcmd, jstack, jmapInspect a running JVM (see tools)

Versions you will meet

Oracle ships a new Java every six months; some releases are LTS (long-term support) and are the ones companies use in production: Java 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25. Java 25 is the latest LTS, Java 21 is the most common in new Spring Boot projects, and many older systems still run Java 8 or 11. Check yours with java -version and javac -version. If they differ, your PATH or JAVA_HOME points to different JDKs — a common setup problem.

Rule: the JVM version must be at least the version you compiled for

Code compiled by a newer javac may fail on an older JVM with UnsupportedClassVersionError ("class file version 65.0, this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 61.0"). Use javac --release 17 (or Maven's maven.compiler.release) to target an older version safely.

Edge cases and errors

  • 'javac' is not recognized (Windows) means only a JRE is installed or the JDK's bin folder is not on PATH.
  • Error: Could not find or load main class Hello — wrong class name, wrong folder, or you typed java Hello.class.
  • The JVM is not "interpreted only": hot code is compiled to machine code, and that code can even be faster than static C++ for some workloads because the JIT knows the real runtime behaviour.
  • Java is not 100 % platform independent: file separators, line endings and native libraries differ.

Tip: use the single-file launcher and JShell for practice

For the 30 practice programs at the end of this module you do not need a project. A file Prime.java and the command java Prime.java is enough, and IntelliJ's Run button does the same.

Interview: "Explain JDK, JRE and JVM. How is Java platform independent?"

  • JVM runs bytecode; JRE = JVM + class libraries; JDK = JRE + tools like javac.
  • javac turns source into bytecode, which is platform neutral; each OS has its own JVM that understands the same bytecode. So bytecode is portable, and the JVM is not.
  • Walk through the pipeline: compile → class loader → verifier → interpreter + JIT → machine code.
  • Mention JIT warm-up and that "Java is compiled and interpreted".

Structure of a Java program, naming and keywords

A Java file holds a package declaration, imports and one or more classes; execution starts at public static void main(String[] args), and every word in that line has a reason.

Java source code is organised into classes, and classes into packages. A typical file has this order: package line, import lines, then the class.

package com.shop;                 // 1. where this class lives (folder: com/shop)

import java.util.List;            // 2. bring other classes into scope
import java.util.ArrayList;

/** Prints a small order summary. */   // 3. documentation comment
public class OrderApp {           // 4. class name = file name (OrderApp.java)

    static final double GST = 0.18;    // a constant (see naming below)

    public static void main(String[] args) {    // 5. program entry point
        List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();
        items.add("Pen");
        items.add("Notebook");
        System.out.println("Items: " + items + ", GST rate: " + GST);
    }
}
Items: [Pen, Notebook], GST rate: 0.18

public static void main(String[] args) — word by word

public
The JVM must be able to call the method from outside the class, so it must be visible everywhere.
static
The method belongs to the class, not to an object. The JVM has no object yet when the program starts, so it must be able to call main without creating one.
void
It returns nothing. To report an exit status, call System.exit(code); 0 means success.
main
The exact name the JVM looks for. Main or MAIN will not work.
String[] args
The command-line arguments as an array of strings. The name args is only a convention; String... args (varargs) also works.

The method does not return a value to the JVM and has no throws restriction: you may write main(String[] args) throws Exception. When main ends and no non-daemon threads are still running, the JVM exits.

Command-line arguments

public class Greet {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        if (args.length == 0) {
            System.out.println("Usage: java Greet.java <name> [city]");
            return;
        }
        String city = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "India";
        System.out.println("Hello " + args[0] + " from " + city);
    }
}
$ java Greet.java Asha Pune
Hello Asha from Pune
$ java Greet.java
Usage: java Greet.java <name> [city]

Arguments always arrive as Strings. To use a number, convert it: int age = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);, which throws NumberFormatException for input like "abc". Reading args[0] when no argument was given throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException — always check args.length.

Rules for files and classes

  • A file may contain many classes, but at most one public top-level class, and the file must be named after it. public class OrderApp in Order.java fails with class OrderApp is public, should be declared in a file named OrderApp.java.
  • The package line, if present, must be the first statement. The folder structure should match: package com.shop lives in com/shop/.
  • Classes in java.lang (String, Math, Integer, System) are imported automatically. Everything else needs an import or the full name.
  • import java.util.*; imports all classes of that package (not sub-packages). It is legal, but professional code prefers explicit imports, and IntelliJ manages them for you (Ctrl+Alt+O).
  • import static java.lang.Math.*; imports static members so you can write sqrt(x). Use it sparingly.

Comments

// single-line comment
/* multi-line
   comment */
/** Javadoc comment: describes the class or method below; see the Javadoc article. */

Naming conventions

ElementStyleExamples
Class, interface, record, enumPascalCase, nounsOrderService, PaymentGateway, Status
MethodcamelCase, verbscalculateTotal, isActive, getName
Variable, parameter, fieldcamelCaseorderCount, customerName
Constant (static final)UPPER_SNAKE_CASEMAX_RETRIES, GST_RATE
Packageall lower case, reversed domaincom.flipkart.cart, in.gov.irctc
Generic type parameterOne capital letterT, E, K, V

Identifiers (names) may contain letters, digits, _ and $, cannot start with a digit, are case-sensitive, and cannot be a keyword. Booleans read well as questions: isPaid, hasStock.

Keywords

Java reserves about fifty words. You do not need to memorise them, but know the groups: primitive types (int, boolean, …); control flow (if, else, switch, for, while, do, break, continue, return); OOP (class, interface, extends, implements, new, this, super, abstract, final, static, enum); access (public, protected, private); exceptions (try, catch, finally, throw, throws); others (synchronized, volatile, transient, instanceof, package, import).

  • true, false and null are literals, not keywords, but you cannot use them as names either.
  • goto and const are reserved but unused.
  • var, record, yield, sealed and permits are contextual keywords: special only in certain places, so old code with a variable named record still compiles. var is a reserved type name, not a keyword (rules).

Version note: Java 25 and simpler first programs

Java 25 finalised compact source files and instance main methods: a source file can contain just void main() { ... } without a class declaration, public or static, to make the first program easier for beginners. Older JVMs (8, 11, 17, 21) do not support this as a standard feature, and real projects, Spring Boot included, still use the classic form above. Learn the classic main; you will see it everywhere.

Mistakes with main and file names

  • Writing public void main(String[] args) (no static) or static public void Main. With older Java: Error: Main method not found in class Hello. (static public is fine; only the name, parameter and static matter.)
  • Running java Hello.class instead of java Hello.
  • Naming a class like a library class (String, List) in your package and then wondering why List<String> breaks.

Conventions professionals follow

  • One top-level class per file, named after the file.
  • Names say what a thing is, not how it is stored: customers, not customerList2. Avoid one-letter names except for loop indexes (i, j).
  • Keep main thin: it should create objects and call them. In Spring Boot, main is one line: SpringApplication.run(App.class, args);.

Interview: "Why is main static? Can we overload or omit main?"

  • It is static so the JVM can call it without creating an object of the class.
  • You can overload main (for example main(int x)), but the JVM starts only the String[] version.
  • A class without main compiles fine; it just cannot be started directly (a library class).
  • You can declare main as final or synchronized, and add throws.

Data types, variables, wrappers and var

Java has eight primitive types that hold plain values, reference types that point to objects, wrapper classes (Integer, Double) that bridge the two, and var to let the compiler infer a local variable's type.

Java is statically typed: every variable has a type fixed at compile time, and the compiler checks that you use it correctly. There are two families:

  • Primitive types — eight built-in types that store the value itself (a number, a character, a true/false). They are not objects and have no methods.
  • Reference types — classes, interfaces, arrays, enums, records. The variable stores a reference (an address-like handle) to an object on the heap. null means "no object".

The eight primitive types

TypeSizeRangeDefault (field)Literal examples
byte8 bit−128 to 1270(byte) 100
short16 bit−32,768 to 32,7670(short) 1000
int32 bit−2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (about ±2.1 billion)042, 1_000_000, 0xFF, 0b1010, 017
long64 bitabout ±9.22 × 10180L42L, 9_000_000_000L
float32 bitabout 7 decimal digits of precision0.0f3.14f
double64 bitabout 15–16 decimal digits of precision0.03.14, 1e-3, 2.5d
char16 bit0 to 65,535 (unsigned UTF-16 code unit)'\u0000''A', '\n', '\u20B9'
booleannot specified (JVM-dependent)true or falsefalsetrue

Key facts to remember:

  • Whole-number literals are int by default, decimals are double. Add L for long and f for float: long big = 3_000_000_000L; — without the L the compiler says integer number too large.
  • Underscores make numbers readable (1_00_00_000 is fine). 0x is hex, 0b is binary, a leading 0 is octal — so int x = 010; is 8!
  • Ranges: Integer.MAX_VALUE, Integer.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE are constants you can print.
  • Defaults apply only to fields (instance and static) and array elements. A local variable has no default: reading it before assigning is a compile error — variable x might not have been initialized.
  • A char is really a number, so 'A' + 1 is 66. Characters outside the basic range (many emoji) need two chars (a surrogate pair), so "😀".length() is 2.
public class Types {
    static int fieldDefault;          // fields get default values
    static boolean flagDefault;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int views = 1_250_000;
        long population = 1_400_000_000L;
        double price = 499.50;
        float rating = 4.5f;
        char grade = 'A';
        boolean paid = true;
        int mask = 0b1010;            // 10
        int hex = 0xFF;               // 255

        System.out.println(views + " " + population + " " + price + " " + rating);
        System.out.println(grade + " " + paid + " " + mask + " " + hex);
        System.out.println(fieldDefault + " " + flagDefault);
        System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE + " " + Long.MAX_VALUE);
        System.out.println(Byte.MIN_VALUE + " " + Byte.MAX_VALUE);
    }
}
1250000 1400000000 499.5 4.5
A true 10 255
0 false
2147483647 9223372036854775807
-128 127

Variables and scope

A variable is a named storage location. Declare it with a type, optionally assign a value: int count = 0;. Declared inside a method it is a local variable, alive only in its block { }. Declared in a class it is a field. Use final to forbid reassignment: final int MAX = 5;. You cannot declare two locals with the same name in overlapping scopes — Java does not allow shadowing a local with another local.

Wrapper classes, autoboxing and unboxing

Collections such as List hold objects only, so each primitive has an object twin, a wrapper class in java.lang:

PrimitiveWrapperPrimitiveWrapper
byteBytelongLong
shortShortfloat / doubleFloat / Double
intIntegerchar / booleanCharacter / Boolean

Wrappers are immutable, can be null, and carry useful static methods: Integer.parseInt("42"), Integer.valueOf(42), Integer.toBinaryString(10), Integer.compare(a, b), Double.parseDouble, Character.isDigit(c), Character.isLetter(c), Boolean.parseBoolean. Autoboxing is the compiler converting a primitive to its wrapper automatically; unboxing is the reverse:

List<Integer> marks = new ArrayList<>();
marks.add(85);                 // autoboxing: int -> Integer.valueOf(85)
int first = marks.get(0);      // unboxing:   Integer -> first.intValue()
Integer boxed = 10;            // boxing
int sum = boxed + 5;           // unboxing happens, then int addition

The Integer cache and the == trap

Boxing calls Integer.valueOf(int), which returns a cached object for values from −128 to 127 and creates a new object for others. So == (which compares references for objects) gives surprising answers:

Integer a = 127, b = 127;
Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(a == b);        // true  (same cached object)
System.out.println(c == d);        // false (two different objects)
System.out.println(c.equals(d));   // true  (compares the values)
System.out.println(c == 128);      // true  (one side is primitive: c is unboxed)

Integer e = new Integer(5);        // deprecated for removal: do not use
Long l = 10L;
System.out.println(l.equals(10));  // false: 10 is an Integer, not a Long
true
false
true
true
false

Rule: compare wrapper objects with equals() (or unbox first), never with ==. The cache exists for Byte, Short, Integer, Long (−128 to 127), Character (0 to 127) and Boolean; Float and Double are not cached. The upper bound of the Integer cache can be raised with a JVM option, so never depend on it.

NullPointerException from unboxing

Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();
stock.put("pen", 10);
int pens = stock.get("pen");        // fine: 10
int pencils = stock.get("pencil");  // get returns null -> unboxing null
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException:
  Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because the return value of
  "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null

The fix is to use getOrDefault("pencil", 0) or to keep the value as Integer and check for null. The same happens in a ternary such as cond ? nullInteger : 0, and when a database column that allows NULL is mapped to a primitive int field — use Integer for nullable columns.

var — local variable type inference (Java 10)

With var the compiler infers the type from the right-hand side. The variable is still statically typed; it is not like JavaScript's var.

var count = 10;                       // int
var name = "Ravi";                    // String
var items = new ArrayList<String>();  // ArrayList<String>
for (var item : items) { }            // fine in loops

var x;                                // error: cannot infer type (no initializer)
var n = null;                         // error: cannot infer type for null
var arr = {1, 2, 3};                  // error: array initializer needs an explicit type
var lambda = () -> 5;                 // error: no target type
count = "text";                       // error: count is an int
  • var works only for local variables (also loop variables and try-with-resources), never for fields, parameters or return types.
  • It needs an initializer that gives a clear type. var is not a keyword: you can still name a variable var, but not a class.
  • var x = 10; is int; if you want long write 10L.

Convention: when to use var

Use it when the type is obvious from the right side (var users = new ArrayList<User>();) or very long. Avoid it when it hides information: var result = service.process(request); forces the reader to look up what result is.

Rules to remember

  • Money, IDs and counters that can pass 2.1 billion need long (or BigDecimal for money). Never store money in double.
  • Use int by default for whole numbers, double for decimals, boolean for flags. byte, short and float are for special cases like binary data and large arrays.
  • Local variables must be initialised before use; fields and array elements have defaults.

Common mistakes

  • float f = 3.14; fails: the literal is a double (possible lossy conversion from double to float). Write 3.14f.
  • long big = 3000000000; fails because the literal is read as int first. Write 3000000000L.
  • Using == on Integer or Long values from collections or method results.
  • Using wrappers in hot loops (Long sum = 0L; sum += i; creates millions of objects). Use long.

Interview: "Why does Integer 127 == 127 give true but 128 == 128 give false?"

  • Autoboxing calls Integer.valueOf, which returns cached objects for −128…127. Within the cache both references point to the same object; outside it, two new objects are created.
  • == compares references for objects, so use equals().
  • Related questions: primitive vs wrapper, autoboxing cost, NPE on unboxing null, why collections cannot hold primitives (generics work with objects).

Operators, precedence and expressions

Operators combine values into expressions; knowing precedence, short-circuiting, i++ vs ++i, integer division and the hidden cast in += removes a whole group of classic bugs.

Operator groups

GroupOperatorsNotes
Arithmetic+ - * / %+ also joins strings
Unary+ - ++ -- ! ~! is boolean NOT, ~ flips bits
Relational< <= > >= == != instanceofGive a boolean
Logical&& || !Short-circuit
Bitwise& | ^ ~Work on bits; on booleans they do not short-circuit
Shift<< >> >>>Move bits left or right
Assignment= += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>= >>>=Compound forms include a cast
Ternarycond ? a : bThe only three-operand operator

Precedence (highest first)

Precedence decides which operator is applied first. When two operators have the same precedence, associativity decides: most go left to right; assignment, ternary and unary operators go right to left.

LevelOperatorsAssociativity
1() [] ., postfix i++ i--left to right
2prefix ++i --i, unary + - ! ~, cast, newright to left
3* / %left to right
4+ - (and string +)left to right
5<< >> >>>left to right
6< <= > >= instanceofleft to right
7== !=left to right
8–10&, then ^, then |left to right
11–12&&, then ||left to right
13? :right to left
14= += -= … (all assignments)right to left

You do not need to memorise the table. Use parentheses whenever the order is not obvious: a + b * c is fine, but a & b == c is a bug (it means a & (b == c)), so write (a & b) == c.

Integer arithmetic gotchas

System.out.println(7 / 2);           // 3     integer division drops the fraction
System.out.println(7 / 2.0);         // 3.5   one double operand -> double division
System.out.println(1 / 2 * 3.0);     // 0.0   (1/2) is 0 first
System.out.println(7 % 3);           // 1
System.out.println(-7 % 3);          // -1    sign follows the dividend (left operand)
System.out.println(7 % -3);          // 1
System.out.println(Math.floorMod(-7, 3));   // 2   always non-negative for a positive divisor
System.out.println(5.5 % 2);         // 1.5   % works on decimals too

System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1);          // -2147483648  overflow wraps around
System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1L);         // 2147483648   long arithmetic
System.out.println(Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE));    // -2147483648  no positive counterpart

System.out.println(5 / 0.0);         // Infinity
System.out.println(0.0 / 0.0);       // NaN
System.out.println(5 / 0);           // throws ArithmeticException
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
  • Integer division truncates toward zero. int percent = marks / total * 100; is almost always wrong (it is 0 unless marks equals total). Multiply first or use a double: marks * 100 / total.
  • Overflow is silent. Integer arithmetic wraps around with no exception. When it matters, use Math.addExact, multiplyExact, toIntExact, which throw ArithmeticException: integer overflow.
  • % is "remainder", not "modulo": the result has the sign of the left operand. For array-index wrap-around use Math.floorMod(index, length).
  • Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException; floating-point division by zero gives Infinity or NaN. NaN != NaN, so use Double.isNaN(x).

i++ vs ++i

Both add 1 to i. The difference is the value of the expression: i++ (post-increment) gives the old value, then increments; ++i (pre-increment) increments, then gives the new value. As a standalone statement (i++;) they are identical.

int i = 5;
int a = i++;          // a = 5, i = 6
int b = ++i;          // i = 7, b = 7
int j = 5;
int k = j++ + ++j;    // 5 + 7 = 12, j = 7
int x = 5;
x = x++;              // x stays 5: the old value is assigned back
System.out.println(a + " " + b + " " + j + " " + k + " " + x);
5 7 7 12 5

Do not write code like j++ + ++j in real projects — it is only an interview puzzle.

Short-circuit && and || vs & and |

&& stops as soon as the result is known: if the left side is false, the right side is not evaluated. || stops when the left side is true. The single & and | always evaluate both sides.

String name = null;
if (name != null && name.length() > 3) {      // safe: length() is never called
    System.out.println("long name");
}
if (name != null & name.length() > 3) {       // NullPointerException: both sides run
    System.out.println("long name");
}

int calls = 0;
boolean r1 = (calls++ > 0) && (calls++ > 0);   // second part skipped
System.out.println(calls);                         // 1

Use short-circuit to guard: list != null && !list.isEmpty(), divisor != 0 && total / divisor > 5. Put cheap checks first.

Ternary operator

String status = marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail"; It is an expression (it produces a value), so it can be used inside a println or a return. Nesting is allowed but quickly hard to read. A subtle trap is numeric promotion: both branches are converted to a common type.

System.out.println(true ? 1 : 2.0);        // 1.0   int is promoted to double
Integer n = null;
int r = true ? n : 0;                       // NullPointerException: n is unboxed

Bitwise and shift operators

System.out.println(5 & 3);       // 1    0101 & 0011 = 0001
System.out.println(5 | 3);       // 7    0101 | 0011 = 0111
System.out.println(5 ^ 3);       // 6    XOR: 1 where bits differ = 0110
System.out.println(~5);          // -6   flips all bits: -(5) - 1
System.out.println(5 << 2);      // 20   shift left = multiply by 2^2
System.out.println(-16 >> 2);    // -4   signed shift keeps the sign bit
System.out.println(-16 >>> 28);  // 15   unsigned shift fills with 0
System.out.println(1 << 33);     // 2    int shift count uses only the low 5 bits (33 & 31 = 1)
boolean even = (7 & 1) == 0;     // false: lowest bit tells odd/even

Common uses: checking odd/even (n & 1), flags and permissions packed into one int, fast multiplication by powers of two, and the XOR trick in puzzles ("find the single non-duplicate number": XOR all numbers, pairs cancel out).

Compound assignment has a hidden cast

a += b means a = (T)(a + b) where T is the type of a. The cast is added for you and silently drops information.

byte b = 127;
b += 1;                    // OK: b = (byte)(b + 1)  -> -128, wraps around
b = b + 1;                 // error: incompatible types: possible lossy conversion
                           //        from int to byte

int total = 10;
total += 3.7;              // total = (int)(10 + 3.7) = 13, decimals lost
char c = 'a';
c += 1;                    // 'b'
String s = "Rs ";
s += 500;                  // "Rs 500"

The same rule applies to ++ and --: b++ on a byte compiles. It is a favourite interview question because it looks like it should not compile.

String + and evaluation order

System.out.println(1 + 2 + "A");       // 3A    (1 + 2) first, then join
System.out.println("A" + 1 + 2);       // A12   left to right, already a String
System.out.println("A" + (1 + 2));     // A3
System.out.println('a' + 'b');         // 195   char + char = int
System.out.println("" + 'a' + 'b');    // ab

Rule: operands are evaluated left to right

Java guarantees left-to-right evaluation of operands, unlike C. So i + i++ is well defined. Precedence only says how operands group, not the order in which side effects happen.

Common mistakes

  • Using = instead of == in a condition. if (x = 5) does not compile for int (good), but if (flag = true) compiles for boolean and always passes.
  • Comparing strings and objects with == (see Strings).
  • Computing an average with integer division: sum / count when both are int.
  • Forgetting that && binds tighter than ||: a || b && c is a || (b && c).

Interview: operator puzzles

  • "What does int x = 5; x = x++ + ++x; give?" — 5 + 7 = 12. Explain post vs pre increment and left-to-right evaluation.
  • "Why does byte b = 10; b += 5; compile but b = b + 5; not?" — compound assignment includes an implicit cast; b + 5 is an int.
  • "&& vs &?" — short-circuit vs always evaluate both; & also works bitwise on integers.
  • "What is -7 % 3?" — -1; the result takes the sign of the dividend.

Type casting, numeric promotion and floating-point precision

Widening conversions are automatic and safe, narrowing casts can lose data silently, arithmetic on small types is promoted to int, and double cannot store 0.1 exactly — so money belongs in BigDecimal.

Widening and narrowing

Java converts between numeric types in two directions. Widening (small to big) is implicit because no information is lost. Narrowing (big to small) needs an explicit cast — your promise to the compiler that you accept the loss.

long to float is allowed implicitly even though a float has only about 7 digits of precision, so it can lose accuracy without any error. boolean cannot be converted to or from any other type.

int i = 100;
long l = i;                    // widening, automatic
double d = i;                  // 100.0

double pi = 3.99;
System.out.println((int) pi);          // 3     truncates, does not round
System.out.println((int) -3.99);       // -3    truncates toward zero
System.out.println((int) Math.round(pi));  // 4  round first if you want rounding
System.out.println((byte) 130);        // -126  130 - 256: only the low 8 bits are kept
System.out.println((int) 3_000_000_000L);  // -1294967296  low 32 bits
System.out.println((int) 1e20);        // 2147483647  saturates at Integer.MAX_VALUE
System.out.println((int) Double.NaN);  // 0

int big = 123456789;
float f = big;                         // allowed, but loses precision
System.out.println((int) f);           // 123456792

Casting an object reference is different: it never changes the object, it only tells the compiler to treat the reference as another type. A wrong cast throws ClassCastException at runtime (see Module 2).

char and int

char c = 'A';
int code = c;                       // 65  (widening)
char next = (char) (c + 1);         // 'B' (c + 1 is an int, so cast back)
char lower = (char) (c + 32);       // 'a'
int digit = '7' - '0';              // 7   classic digit conversion
char fromInt = (char) 97;           // 'a'
c++;                                // 'B' (++ and += include the cast)
System.out.println(code + " " + next + " " + lower + " " + digit + " " + fromInt + " " + c);
65 B a 7 a B

For letters, prefer Character.toUpperCase(c) and Character.isLetter(c) over manual arithmetic.

Numeric promotion in expressions

Before an arithmetic operator runs, Java promotes operands:

  1. If either operand is double, the other becomes double.
  2. Otherwise, if either is float, the other becomes float.
  3. Otherwise, if either is long, the other becomes long.
  4. Otherwise, both become int — including byte, short and char.

The last rule surprises beginners: the result of byte + byte is an int.

byte x = 10, y = 20;
byte z = x + y;            // error: incompatible types: possible lossy conversion
                           //        from int to byte
byte z2 = (byte) (x + y);  // OK
byte k = 10;               // OK: 10 is a constant that fits into byte
final int LIMIT = 50;
byte m = LIMIT;            // OK: LIMIT is a compile-time constant that fits
int a = 5;
byte n = a;                // error: a is not a constant

long total = 1000000 * 1000000;     // -727379968: int * int overflows BEFORE widening
long right = 1000000L * 1000000;    // 1000000000000: one long operand is enough

The last two lines are a famous bug: the multiplication is done in int, overflows, and only the wrong result is widened to long.

Why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3

float and double store numbers in binary (IEEE 754). Just as 1/3 has no exact decimal form (0.3333…), 0.1 has no exact binary form (it repeats forever in base 2). The computer stores the nearest value, and tiny errors appear:

System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);             // 0.30000000000000004
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);      // false
System.out.println(1.1 * 3);               // 3.3000000000000003
System.out.println(new java.math.BigDecimal(0.1));
System.out.println(0.5 + 0.25);            // 0.75  (exact in binary)

double a = 0.1 + 0.2, b = 0.3;
System.out.println(Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9);   // true: compare with a tolerance
0.30000000000000004
false
3.3000000000000003
0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
0.75
true

Floating point is fine for science, graphics and statistics, where tiny errors do not matter. It is wrong for money, where every paisa must add up. Never compare doubles with ==; compare with a tolerance. Also remember Math.round(2.5) is 3 but Math.round(-2.5) is −2 (it rounds half up toward positive infinity), and it returns a long for a double argument.

BigDecimal for money

java.math.BigDecimal stores an exact decimal number as an unscaled integer plus a scale (digits after the point). It is immutable, so every operation returns a new object.

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;

public class Invoice {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("499.99");       // from a String, never a double
        BigDecimal total = price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(3));      // 1499.97
        BigDecimal gst = total.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.18"));       // 269.9946
        BigDecimal gstRounded = gst.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP); // 269.99
        BigDecimal grand = total.add(gstRounded);

        System.out.println(total + " " + gst + " " + gstRounded + " " + grand);

        BigDecimal third = BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal("3"), 4, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
        System.out.println(third);                          // 0.3333

        System.out.println(new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")));    // false
        System.out.println(new BigDecimal("2.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.00"))); // 0
        System.out.println(BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal("3")));  // throws
    }
}
1499.97 269.9946 269.99 1769.96
0.3333
false
0
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: Non-terminating decimal expansion;
  no exact representable decimal result.
  • Construct from a String (new BigDecimal("0.1")) or BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1). new BigDecimal(0.1) keeps the double's error, as shown above.
  • Methods: add, subtract, multiply, divide, negate, abs, pow(int), compareTo, signum, setScale, scale, stripTrailingZeros.
  • Always pass a scale and RoundingMode to divide unless the result is certainly finite.
  • Use compareTo for numeric equality; equals also compares scale (2.0 and 2.00 differ). This matters when BigDecimal is a key in a HashMap or in a HashSet.
  • RoundingMode.HALF_UP is the school rule (2.5 → 3). HALF_EVEN ("banker's rounding") reduces bias and is common in finance.
  • Alternative: store money as a long number of paise (₹499.99 = 49999). Fast and exact; you must format it yourself. In databases use NUMERIC(12,2), not FLOAT.

Rule: narrowing needs a cast, and promotion happens before the operator runs

Assigning a bigger type to a smaller one without a cast is a compile error — except for constants that fit (byte b = 10;). Arithmetic on byte, short and char always produces an int.

Edge cases

  • (int) Double.NaN is 0 and out-of-range values saturate; no exception is thrown.
  • Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative; Math.toIntExact(long) throws ArithmeticException if the value does not fit.
  • float keeps about 7 digits: 16777217f prints as 1.6777216E7. Prefer double unless memory forces float.
  • 0.0 == -0.0 is true, but Double.valueOf(0.0).equals(-0.0) is false.

Wrong: money in double

double price = 0.10;
double total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) total += price;
System.out.println(total);   // 0.9999999999999999

Right: BigDecimal from strings

BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("0.10");
BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO;
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) total = total.add(price);
System.out.println(total);   // 1.00

Interview: "Why not use double for money?" and "What is the output of 0.1 + 0.2?"

  • Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so errors accumulate; 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004.
  • Use BigDecimal built from Strings, with an explicit scale and RoundingMode; or use integer paise.
  • Mention equals vs compareTo on BigDecimal and the divide exception for non-terminating results.
  • Also expect: "byte + byte gives which type?" (int) and "what does (int) 3.99 return?" (3).

Control flow: if, switch, switch expressions and loops

Use if/else for decisions, arrow-form switch for choosing among values, and for, enhanced for, while and do-while for repetition, with labeled break/continue to leave nested loops.

if / else if / else

int marks = 72;
if (marks >= 90) {
    System.out.println("Distinction");
} else if (marks >= 60) {
    System.out.println("First class");
} else if (marks >= 40) {
    System.out.println("Pass");
} else {
    System.out.println("Fail");
}                                   // prints: First class

The condition must be a boolean — Java has no "truthy" values, so if (count) with an int is a compile error. Conditions are checked top to bottom and the first true branch runs; order your ranges from most to least specific. Always use braces, even for one line: a missing brace is the cause of the famous "goto fail" style bugs. Also avoid a stray semicolon: if (x > 5); ends the if with an empty statement.

The classic switch and fall-through

int day = 3;
switch (day) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("Mon");
        break;
    case 2:
    case 3:                         // 2 and 3 share this code
        System.out.println("Tue or Wed");
    case 4:
        System.out.println("falls into Thu");   // no break above -> also runs
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("Other");
}
Tue or Wed
falls into Thu

In the colon form, execution continues into the next case until a break — this is fall-through. It is occasionally useful (grouping cases) but mostly a bug source. The switch selector can be byte, short, char, int (and their wrappers), String (Java 7), or an enum — not long, float, double or boolean. Case labels must be constants and unique. A String switch uses equals, is case-sensitive, and throws NullPointerException if the selector is null.

Arrow-form switch and switch expressions (Java 14)

The arrow form case X -> has no fall-through and needs no break. A switch can also be an expression that produces a value; then it must cover all cases (add default, or list every enum constant).

enum Status { PENDING, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }

public class SwitchExpr {
    static int daysIn(String month) {
        return switch (month) {
            case "Feb" -> 28;
            case "Apr", "Jun", "Sep", "Nov" -> 30;    // several labels in one case
            default -> 31;
        };
    }

    static String describe(Status s) {
        return switch (s) {                            // no default needed: all constants covered
            case PENDING -> "Packing your order";
            case SHIPPED -> "On the way";
            case DELIVERED -> "Delivered";
            case CANCELLED -> "Cancelled";
        };
    }

    static String fee(int amount) {
        return switch (amount / 1000) {
            case 0 -> "Free";
            case 1, 2 -> "Rs 5";
            default -> {                                // block: compute, then yield a value
                int fee = amount / 1000 * 2;
                if (fee > 50) {
                    yield "Rs 50 (capped)";
                }
                yield "Rs " + fee;
            }
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(daysIn("Apr") + " " + daysIn("Jan"));
        System.out.println(describe(Status.SHIPPED));
        System.out.println(fee(500) + ", " + fee(1500) + ", " + fee(8000) + ", " + fee(40000));
    }
}
30 31
On the way
Free, Rs 5, Rs 16, Rs 50 (capped)
  • yield returns a value from a block inside a switch expression; return is not allowed there.
  • An enum switch expression without default is checked by the compiler. If you later add an enum constant, every such switch fails to compile — a benefit, because you cannot forget a case.
  • A switch statement may use arrows too (case 1 -> System.out.println("one");). The old colon form can also be used in an expression with yield, but you will rarely see it.
  • Pattern matching in switch (case Circle c ->, guards with when) is covered in Module 5.

Loops

LoopUse whenChecks condition
for (init; cond; update)You know the count or need an indexBefore each pass
enhanced for (T x : items)Visit every element of an array or Iterable—
while (cond)Repeat until something changesBefore each pass (may run 0 times)
do { } while (cond);Body must run at least once (menus, input retry)After each pass
 
// for: sum 1..5
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    sum += i;
}
System.out.println(sum);                       // 15

// enhanced for over an array and a list
String[] cities = {"Pune", "Delhi", "Chennai"};
for (String city : cities) {
    System.out.print(city + " ");
}
System.out.println();

// while: count digits of a number
int n = 12345, digits = 0;
while (n > 0) {
    n /= 10;
    digits++;
}
System.out.println(digits);                    // 5

// do-while: runs once even though the condition is false
int tries = 10;
do {
    System.out.println("tries = " + tries);
} while (tries < 5);

// several variables in a for header; infinite loop forms
for (int i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i += 3, j -= 3) {
    System.out.print(i + "-" + j + " ");       // 0-10 3-7
}
System.out.println();
15
Pune Delhi Chennai
5
tries = 10
0-10 3-7

Every part of the for header is optional: for (;;) and while (true) loop forever until a break or return. The loop variable declared in the header exists only inside the loop.

With the enhanced for, assigning to the loop variable does not change the array (it is a copy of the value or reference), and you must not add or remove elements of a collection while looping over it — that throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use an Iterator, removeIf, or an index loop instead (Module 4).

break, continue and labels

break leaves the nearest loop (or switch). continue skips the rest of the current pass and goes to the next one. In nested loops, a label lets you name the loop to leave or continue.

// find the first pair (a, b) with a * b == 24 and a < b
outer:
for (int a = 1; a < 10; a++) {
    for (int b = a + 1; b < 10; b++) {
        if (a * b == 24) {
            System.out.println(a + " x " + b);
            break outer;                 // leaves BOTH loops
        }
    }
}

for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) {
        continue;                        // skip even numbers
    }
    System.out.print(i + " ");           // 1 3 5
}
System.out.println();
3 x 8
1 3 5

Labels are rare; if you need one often, move the nested loops into a method and use return.

Two small programs every interview asks

public class FizzBuzzPrime {
    static boolean isPrime(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        for (int i = 2; (long) i * i <= n; i++) {   // only up to the square root
            if (n % i == 0) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 15; i++) {
            if (i % 15 == 0) System.out.print("FizzBuzz ");
            else if (i % 3 == 0) System.out.print("Fizz ");
            else if (i % 5 == 0) System.out.print("Buzz ");
            else System.out.print(i + " ");
        }
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println(isPrime(29) + " " + isPrime(91));
    }
}
1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz Fizz 7 8 Fizz Buzz 11 Fizz 13 14 FizzBuzz
true false

Rules

  • An if/while condition must be boolean.
  • Switch case labels must be compile-time constants and unique; a switch expression must be exhaustive and every arm must produce a value (or throw).
  • Code after break, continue, return or throw in the same block is unreachable and does not compile.
  • A variable declared in one case of a colon-style switch is visible in the following cases (one shared block) — another reason to prefer arrows.

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one: i <= arr.length instead of i < arr.length throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
  • Missing break in an old-style switch, so later cases run too.
  • Semicolon after the header: for (...); or while (x < 5); makes an empty loop body, and a following { } block runs once.
  • Infinite loop because the variable that the condition checks is never updated.
  • Modifying the list inside a for-each loop (ConcurrentModificationException).
  • Comparing strings in a condition with == instead of equals.

Conventions

  • Prefer arrow-form switch (Java 14+) for new code; use default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(...) to reject unknown values.
  • Prefer the enhanced for when you do not need the index; use streams for filtering and mapping (Module 5).
  • Use early return/continue (guard clauses) to avoid deep nesting.

Interview: "Switch vs if-else? Old switch vs switch expression?"

  • Switch is for one value compared with constants; if-else handles ranges and complex conditions.
  • Old switch falls through without break; arrow switch does not; a switch expression returns a value, is exhaustive and uses yield in blocks.
  • Allowed selector types: integral types up to int and their wrappers, String, enum.
  • "while vs do-while" — the second runs the body at least once.

Methods: parameters, return types, overloading, varargs and recursion

A method is a named, reusable block of code with parameters and a return type; Java picks between overloaded methods at compile time using an order — exact match, widening, boxing, varargs.

A method groups statements under a name so you can call them again and again. It is the basic unit of reuse. Syntax:

//  modifiers   return-type  name   (parameters)         throws
    public static  double    price  (double base, int qty) throws IllegalArgumentException {
        if (qty <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive");
        }
        return base * qty;          // a method with a return type must return on every path
    }
  • The signature is the name plus the parameter types (order matters). The return type and parameter names are not part of it.
  • Parameters are the variables in the declaration; arguments are the values you pass in the call.
  • A void method returns nothing; return; exits early. Any other method must return a value of a compatible type on every path or compilation fails (missing return statement).
  • Calling a method that returns a value and ignoring it is legal but often a bug (for example, calling s.toUpperCase() without using the result).

Static and instance methods (intro)

public class Counter {
    private int count;                          // instance field: one per object

    public void increment() {                   // instance method: works on one object
        count++;
    }

    public static int square(int x) {           // static method: belongs to the class
        return x * x;                           // cannot use count (no object)
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Counter.square(5));  // 25: call through the class name
        Counter c = new Counter();
        c.increment();                          // instance method needs an object
        // increment();                         // error: non-static method cannot be
                                                //        referenced from a static context
    }
}

A static method cannot use this or instance fields directly. Use static methods for utilities that need no object state (Math.max, Integer.parseInt). Objects are explained fully in Module 2.

Overloading

Overloading means several methods with the same name but different parameter lists (count, types or order) in the same class. It is resolved at compile time from the declared types of the arguments. Changing only the return type is not overloading: it is a compile error (method already defined). Overloading is different from overriding, which is a runtime concept for subclasses (Module 2).

How Java picks the overload

The compiler tries three phases in order and stops at the first phase that finds a match:

  1. Exact match or widening of primitives and references (no boxing): int → long → float → double, or a subclass to its superclass.
  2. Boxing or unboxing: int ↔ Integer, then widening of the result.
  3. Varargs methods.

Within a phase, the most specific method wins. If none is more specific, the call is ambiguous and does not compile.

public class Overloads {
    static void show(int x)       { System.out.println("int"); }
    static void show(long x)      { System.out.println("long"); }
    static void show(Integer x)   { System.out.println("Integer"); }
    static void show(Object x)    { System.out.println("Object"); }
    static void show(int... x)    { System.out.println("varargs"); }

    static void text(String s)        { System.out.println("String"); }
    static void text(Object o)        { System.out.println("Object"); }
    static void both(String s)        { System.out.println("String"); }
    static void both(StringBuilder s) { System.out.println("StringBuilder"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        show(5);                       // int      exact match
        show(5L);                      // long
        show((short) 5);               // int      short widens to int (closest type)
        show('a');                     // int      char widens to int
        show(Integer.valueOf(5));      // Integer  exact reference match
        show(5.5);                     // Object   double is boxed to Double, then widened
        show("hi");                    // Object
        show(1, 2);                    // varargs
        show();                        // varargs
        text(null);                    // String   most specific of String and Object
        // both(null);                 // error: reference to both is ambiguous
    }
}
int
long
int
int
Integer
Object
Object
varargs
varargs
String

Varargs

Varargs (type... name) lets a method accept zero or more arguments. Inside, it is just an array. Rules: it must be the last parameter, and a method has only one.

static int sum(int... nums) {          // nums is an int[]
    int total = 0;
    for (int n : nums) total += n;
    return total;
}

static String label(String prefix, Object... parts) {
    return prefix + ": " + parts.length + " parts";
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(sum());                 // 0
    System.out.println(sum(4));                // 4
    System.out.println(sum(1, 2, 3));          // 6
    System.out.println(sum(new int[]{5, 5}));  // 10: you may pass an array directly
    System.out.println(label("order"));        // order: 0 parts
}

Varargs allocates an array on each call, so avoid it in hot code. Familiar varargs methods: String.format, List.of, Arrays.asList, printf.

Recursion (intro)

Recursion is a method calling itself. Every recursive method needs a base case (where it stops) and a step that moves toward it. Each call gets its own stack frame; too many frames cause StackOverflowError (Stack and heap).

static long factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;                 // base case
    return n * factorial(n - 1);          // smaller problem
}

static int sumDigits(int n) {
    return n == 0 ? 0 : n % 10 + sumDigits(n / 10);
}

static long fibSlow(int n) {              // correct, but exponential time
    return n < 2 ? n : fibSlow(n - 1) + fibSlow(n - 2);
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(factorial(5));     // 120
    System.out.println(sumDigits(4821));  // 15
    System.out.println(fibSlow(10));      // 55
    System.out.println(factorial(21));    // -4249290049419214848 (long overflow)
}

Many recursive solutions can also be written with a loop, which is faster and cannot overflow the stack. Java does not optimise tail calls. Recursion shines for trees, graphs and divide-and-conquer (see DSA · Module 2).

Rules

  • Overloads must differ in the number, types or order of parameters, not just in return type or parameter names.
  • Overload resolution uses the compile-time (declared) types: Object o = "hi"; show(o); picks the Object version.
  • A varargs parameter must be last; at most one per method.
  • A method must return a value on every path if its return type is not void.

Conventions

  • Methods are verbs (calculateFee), booleans start with is/has/can.
  • Keep a method short and focused: one job, ideally under 20–30 lines, three or four parameters at most. If you need more, group them in a record or object.
  • Validate arguments at the start and throw IllegalArgumentException for bad input.
  • Do not overload with confusing, nearly identical signatures like remove(int) and remove(Object) — List.remove has exactly this trap.

Common mistakes

  • Missing base case or a step that never reaches it: StackOverflowError.
  • Ignoring a return value: name.trim(); does nothing useful because strings are immutable.
  • Calling an instance method from static main without creating an object.
  • Expecting a method to change the caller's variable — see the next article.

Interview: "What is method overloading? How does the compiler choose?"

  • Same name, different parameter lists; resolved at compile time (static polymorphism); return type alone is not enough.
  • Order: exact/widening → boxing → varargs; the most specific candidate wins; otherwise ambiguity error.
  • Give the example show(5) with show(long) and show(Integer): long is chosen because widening beats boxing.
  • Overloading vs overriding: compile-time vs runtime, same class vs parent-child.

Pass-by-value: why Java never passes by reference

Java always passes a copy of the argument: for primitives it copies the value, for objects it copies the reference — so a method can change the object the caller sees, but can never re-point the caller's variable.

This is the most misunderstood point in Java, and interviewers ask it constantly. The statement is simple: Java is always pass-by-value. There is no pass-by-reference in the language. What confuses people is that the value being copied for an object variable is a reference.

Primitives: the method gets a copy of the number

static void addTen(int x) {
    x = x + 10;                     // changes only the method's own copy
    System.out.println("inside: " + x);
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int amount = 100;
    addTen(amount);
    System.out.println("outside: " + amount);
}
inside: 110
outside: 100

Objects: the method gets a copy of the reference

A variable of an object type holds a reference to an object on the heap, not the object itself. When you call a method, the parameter becomes a second variable holding a copy of that reference. Both variables now point to the same object.

Two things can happen with that copied reference, and they behave differently:

static void mutate(StringBuilder s) {
    s.append(" world");              // follows the reference, changes the SHARED object
}

static void reassign(StringBuilder s) {
    s = new StringBuilder("other");  // changes only the local copy of the reference
}

static void tryChangeString(String s) {
    s = s + "!";                     // strings are immutable: a new object, local only
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("hello");
    mutate(sb);
    System.out.println(sb);          // hello world   (caller sees the change)
    reassign(sb);
    System.out.println(sb);          // hello world   (caller's reference unchanged)

    String name = "Ravi";
    tryChangeString(name);
    System.out.println(name);        // Ravi

    int[] marks = {50, 60};
    changeFirst(marks);
    System.out.println(marks[0]);    // 99: arrays are objects too
}

static void changeFirst(int[] a) { a[0] = 99; }
hello world
hello world
Ravi
99

So: using the copied reference (calling methods, changing fields, array elements) affects the shared object. Reassigning the parameter affects nothing outside. That one fact answers almost every question.

The swap test

If Java had pass-by-reference, a swap method would work. It does not:

static void swap(int a, int b) {
    int temp = a;
    a = b;
    b = temp;                         // swaps the copies only
}

static void swapNames(StringBuilder a, StringBuilder b) {
    StringBuilder temp = a;
    a = b;
    b = temp;                         // swaps the copied references only
}

static void swapInArray(int[] arr, int i, int j) {
    int temp = arr[i];
    arr[i] = arr[j];                  // modifies the shared array: this one works
    arr[j] = temp;
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int x = 1, y = 2;
    swap(x, y);
    System.out.println(x + " " + y);              // 1 2

    StringBuilder p = new StringBuilder("P"), q = new StringBuilder("Q");
    swapNames(p, q);
    System.out.println(p + " " + q);              // P Q

    int[] nums = {1, 2};
    swapInArray(nums, 0, 1);
    System.out.println(nums[0] + " " + nums[1]);  // 2 1
}

To swap two variables you do it inline, or you return values (a record or array holding both), or you swap elements inside a shared container as in swapInArray — as Collections.swap(list, i, j) does.

Pass-by-value vs pass-by-reference

QuestionPass-by-value (Java)True pass-by-reference (C++ &)
What does the method receive?A copy of the variable's content (number or reference)An alias of the caller's variable itself
Can the method change the caller's primitive?NoYes
Can the method change the object's fields?Yes, through the copied referenceYes
Can the method make the caller's variable point to a new object?NoYes

Practical consequences

  • A method that receives a List can add to the caller's list. If that is not what you want, copy it first (new ArrayList<>(list) or List.copyOf).
  • To return more than one result, return a record: record MinMax(int min, int max) {}.
  • Marking a parameter final stops the method from reassigning it, but does not stop it from changing the object.
  • The same copying rule applies to assignment: b = a; copies the reference, so a and b share one object (aliasing), unless you make a real copy.

Rule: you can change the object, not the caller's variable

Inside a method, param.something() can change the shared object. param = ... only changes the local copy. Java has no way to modify a caller's local variable from another method.

Edge cases

  • null is passed as a null reference; calling a method on it throws NullPointerException, but assigning a new object to the parameter is still invisible to the caller.
  • Immutable arguments (String, Integer, BigDecimal, records of immutables) cannot be modified through a reference, so they behave "like values" in practice.
  • Arrays are objects: int[] passed to a method can be modified in place; its length cannot change.

Common mistakes

  • Saying "primitives are passed by value, objects by reference". Wrong: both by value; for objects the value is the reference.
  • Writing a void normalize(String s) that "fixes" the string; since String is immutable it must return the new string.
  • Storing a caller's mutable list inside your object without copying, so later changes by the caller silently alter your state.

Interview: "Is Java pass by value or pass by reference?"

  • Always pass by value. For objects the value copied is the reference.
  • Prove it with the swap example: a method cannot swap two caller variables, because only copies are swapped.
  • A method can mutate a passed object (list.add) but reassigning the parameter has no effect on the caller.
  • Follow-up: "What is printed after reassign(sb)?" Use the diagram to answer: the local reference moved; the caller's did not.

Arrays (1D and 2D) and the Arrays class

An array is a fixed-size, zero-indexed block of same-typed elements stored as an object; the java.util.Arrays class provides sort, search, fill, copy, compare and print helpers.

An array stores a fixed number of values of one type in contiguous memory. It is an object (it lives on the heap), its size is fixed when created, and it is indexed from 0 to length - 1. Access by index is O(1).

Declaring and creating

int[] marks = new int[5];                  // five zeros: default values
int[] scores = {90, 85, 70};               // literal, size from the values
int[] more = new int[]{1, 2, 3};           // also valid, needed in some places
String[] names = new String[3];            // [null, null, null]
int legacy[] = new int[2];                 // C-style declaration: legal, avoid it

marks[0] = 50;
System.out.println(marks.length);          // 5   (a field, not a method: no parentheses)
System.out.println(scores[scores.length - 1]);   // 70: the last element
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(names));
5
70
[null, null, null]
  • Default values: 0 for numbers, false for boolean, '\u0000' for char, null for objects.
  • The size is fixed. To "grow" an array, create a bigger one and copy (Arrays.copyOf), or use ArrayList, which does this for you.
  • Printing an array directly shows a useless identity like [I@1b6d3586. Use Arrays.toString.
  • int[] b = a; does not copy; both variables refer to the same array.

Errors you will meet

int[] a = new int[5];
a[5] = 1;
  java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 5
int[] n = new int[-1];
  java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException: -1
int[] x = null;
x[0] = 1;
  java.lang.NullPointerException

Looping and common operations

int[] a = {4, 9, 2, 7};

int max = a[0], sum = 0;
for (int v : a) {                       // enhanced for: read-only walk
    if (v > max) max = v;
    sum += v;
}
System.out.println("max=" + max + " sum=" + sum + " avg=" + (double) sum / a.length);

// reverse in place with two pointers
for (int i = 0, j = a.length - 1; i < j; i++, j--) {
    int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;
}
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(a));
max=9 sum=22 avg=5.5
[7, 2, 9, 4]

Two-dimensional and jagged arrays

Java has no true matrix: a 2D array is an array of arrays. Each row is its own array object, so rows can have different lengths (a jagged array).

import java.util.Arrays;

public class Matrix {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] grid = new int[2][3];                  // 2 rows, 3 columns, all zeros
        int[][] m = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 6}};          // 3 rows, 2 columns
        int[][] jagged = new int[3][];                 // rows not created yet
        for (int i = 0; i < jagged.length; i++) {
            jagged[i] = new int[i + 1];                // lengths 1, 2, 3
            Arrays.fill(jagged[i], i + 1);
        }

        System.out.println(m.length + " rows, " + m[0].length + " columns");
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(m[1]));     // [3, 4]
        System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(jagged));

        // matrix multiplication: (2x3) * (3x2) = (2x2)
        int[][] a = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};
        int[][] b = {{7, 8}, {9, 10}, {11, 12}};
        int[][] c = new int[a.length][b[0].length];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < b[0].length; j++) {
                for (int k = 0; k < b.length; k++) {
                    c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
                }
            }
        }
        System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(c));
    }
}
3 rows, 2 columns
[3, 4]
[[1], [2, 2], [3, 3, 3]]
[[58, 64], [139, 154]]

Printing a 2D array with Arrays.toString shows the row identities; use deepToString. A loop over int[][] is two nested loops; the outer loop variable is a row (int[]).

The java.util.Arrays class

MethodWhat it does
Arrays.toString(a)Readable text [1, 2, 3]
Arrays.deepToString(a)Same for nested arrays
Arrays.sort(a)Sorts in place, ascending; also sort(a, from, to) and sort(T[], Comparator)
Arrays.binarySearch(a, key)Index of key in a sorted array, else -(insertionPoint) - 1
Arrays.fill(a, v)Sets all elements to v
Arrays.copyOf(a, n)New array of length n (pads with zeros/null or truncates)
Arrays.copyOfRange(a, from, to)New array of [from, to) — to is exclusive
Arrays.equals(a, b)Same length and equal elements; deepEquals for nested arrays
Arrays.hashCode(a)Hash from the contents
Arrays.asList(T... a)Fixed-size List view backed by the array
Arrays.stream(a)A stream over the elements (IntStream for int[])
 
import java.util.*;

public class ArraysClass {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] a = {5, 3, 9, 1, 7};
        int[] copy = Arrays.copyOf(a, 7);               // [5, 3, 9, 1, 7, 0, 0]
        int[] part = Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 1, 4);       // [3, 9, 1]
        int[] same = a.clone();                         // shallow copy, same length

        Arrays.sort(a);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a));         // [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
        System.out.println(Arrays.binarySearch(a, 7));  // 3
        System.out.println(Arrays.binarySearch(a, 4));  // -3  (insertion point 2)
        System.out.println(Arrays.equals(a, same));     // false: a is sorted now
        System.out.println(a == same);                  // false: different objects
        System.out.println(Arrays.stream(a).sum() + " " + Arrays.stream(a).max().getAsInt());
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(copy) + " " + Arrays.toString(part));

        int[] zeros = new int[4];
        Arrays.fill(zeros, -1);                         // [-1, -1, -1, -1]

        Integer[] boxed = {3, 1, 2};
        Arrays.sort(boxed, Collections.reverseOrder()); // descending needs objects
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(boxed));     // [3, 2, 1]

        String[] words = {"pear", "fig", "banana"};
        Arrays.sort(words, Comparator.comparing(String::length));
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(words));     // [fig, pear, banana]

        List<String> fixed = Arrays.asList("a", "b", "c");
        fixed.set(0, "z");                              // allowed: writes through
        System.out.println(fixed);                      // [z, b, c]
        fixed.add("d");                                 // UnsupportedOperationException
    }
}
  • Arrays.sort on primitives uses a dual-pivot quicksort; on objects it uses a stable merge sort (TimSort). Both are O(n log n); sort an array once and then use binarySearch for O(log n) lookups.
  • binarySearch on an unsorted array gives an undefined result.
  • Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3) returns a List<Integer>, but Arrays.asList(intArray) returns a List<int[]> with a single element — a classic trap. It is fixed-size (add/remove throw UnsupportedOperationException); wrap it with new ArrayList<>(...) to get a growable list, or use List.of.
  • Copies: clone(), copyOf and System.arraycopy(src, srcPos, dest, destPos, length) are shallow — an array of objects copies the references, not the objects. For a 2D array, each row must be copied separately.
  • array.equals(other) is identity comparison (inherited from Object). Use Arrays.equals.

Array covariance and ArrayStoreException

Arrays are covariant: a String[] is also an Object[]. The compiler therefore allows an unsafe store, and the JVM checks the real element type at runtime:

Object[] objects = new String[2];
objects[0] = "ok";
objects[1] = 42;           // compiles, but fails at runtime
java.lang.ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer

Generic collections are invariant (List<String> is not a List<Object>), so the same mistake is caught at compile time — one of the reasons to prefer collections to arrays (Module 4).

Rules

  • Array size is fixed at creation and cannot be changed; valid indexes are 0..length-1.
  • length is a field for arrays, length() a method for strings, size() a method for collections.
  • Arrays are objects: passed by value (the reference is copied), compared by identity with ==, and shared on assignment.

Common mistakes

  • for (int i = 0; i <= a.length; i++) — off by one, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
  • Printing System.out.println(arr) and getting [I@....
  • Thinking int[] copy = original; makes a copy.
  • Creating an array of objects and calling a method on an element before filling it: new Person[3] holds three nulls.
  • Using Arrays.sort(int[], Collections.reverseOrder()) — it does not compile; use Integer[] or sort and reverse.

Interview: array questions

  • "Array vs ArrayList?" — fixed vs resizable, primitives allowed vs objects only, faster and lighter vs more features (Module 4).
  • "Can you change the size of an array?" — no; create a new one and copy.
  • "What does binarySearch return when the key is missing?" — -(insertion point) - 1.
  • Coding warm-ups: reverse an array, find the second largest, rotate by k, remove duplicates from a sorted array, merge two sorted arrays, matrix transpose.

Strings: immutability, the String pool and common methods

A String is an immutable sequence of characters; literals are shared through the String pool, so compare contents with equals(), never ==, and remember that every "change" creates a new object.

A String is an object (not a primitive) that holds text. You create it with a literal: String city = "Pune";. Strings are used everywhere — names, JSON, SQL, URLs, log lines — so it is worth understanding exactly how they behave.

Immutability

Immutable means the object cannot change after creation. Methods such as toUpperCase(), replace() and trim() do not modify the string; they return a new one.

String name = "ravi";
name.toUpperCase();                 // result thrown away: name is unchanged
System.out.println(name);           // ravi
name = name.toUpperCase();          // now name points to a NEW string "RAVI"
System.out.println(name);           // RAVI

Why Java made String immutable:

  • String pool sharing. Many variables can safely point to one shared "java" object, because nobody can change it. If strings were mutable, changing one would change all.
  • Security. Strings carry file paths, class names, database URLs and user names. If a path could change after a security check passed, the check would be meaningless.
  • Thread safety. Immutable objects can be shared between threads with no locks.
  • Hash code caching. A string's hashCode() is computed once and stored, which makes String an excellent HashMap key. This only works because the content cannot change.
  • Class loading. Class names are strings; they must not change between lookup and load.

The price: many temporary objects when you build text in a loop. That is the job of StringBuilder.

The String pool

The String pool (string constant pool or intern pool) is a special area inside the heap (since Java 7; before that it was in PermGen) where the JVM keeps one copy of each distinct string literal. When you write a literal, the JVM first looks in the pool; if the text already exists it reuses that object, otherwise it adds it.

String a = "java";
String b = "java";
String c = new String("java");      // always creates a new object on the heap
String d = c.intern();              // returns the pooled "java"

System.out.println(a == b);         // true   same pooled object
System.out.println(a == c);         // false  different objects
System.out.println(a.equals(c));    // true   same characters
System.out.println(a == d);         // true   intern() gives the pooled copy

String e = "ja" + "va";             // joined by the compiler: constant expression
System.out.println(a == e);         // true

String part = "ja";
String f = part + "va";             // computed at runtime: new object
System.out.println(a == f);         // false

final String fixed = "ja";
String g = fixed + "va";            // final variable with a constant: compile-time constant
System.out.println(a == g);         // true
System.out.println(a == f.intern());// true
  • new String("java") creates one new heap object, and the literal "java" inside the parentheses is in the pool (created the first time that line is loaded, if not already there). A common interview question: "How many objects does new String("abc") create?" — answer: one on the heap, plus the pooled literal if it did not exist yet (so one or two).
  • The compiler joins constant expressions at compile time, so "ja" + "va" is stored as "java". Concatenation that involves a non-final variable or a method call happens at runtime and creates a new object.
  • intern() returns the pooled instance of equal content. It is rarely needed in application code; do not use it to avoid writing equals.
  • Strings produced at runtime (from Scanner, files, JSON, the network, substring) are not in the pool, which is another reason == fails on real data.

== vs equals vs equalsIgnoreCase vs compareTo

ExpressionComparesResult type
a == bReferences: are they the same object?boolean
a.equals(b)Characters, case-sensitiveboolean
a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)Characters, ignoring caseboolean
a.compareTo(b)Dictionary order by Unicode value; 0 if equal, negative if a is firstint

Write "admin".equals(role), with the literal first. It never throws NullPointerException if role is null, while role.equals("admin") does. "apple".compareTo("banana") is -1 (the difference between 'a' and 'b'), and "apple".compareTo("apricot") is -2.

Common methods

MethodPurpose and example
length()Number of chars: "Java".length() is 4
charAt(i)The char at index i; invalid index throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException
substring(from), substring(from, to)Part of the string; to is exclusive: "Hello".substring(1, 3) is "el"
indexOf(x), lastIndexOf(x)Position of the first/last match, or -1
contains(s), startsWith(s), endsWith(s)Boolean checks
replace(a, b)Replaces every literal occurrence (char or text)
replaceAll(regex, s)Replaces by regular expression
split(regex)Splits into a String[] (the argument is a regex)
String.join(sep, parts...)Joins strings or an Iterable with a separator
trim() / strip()Remove surrounding whitespace (see below)
isEmpty() / isBlank()Length zero / empty or only whitespace (isBlank is Java 11)
repeat(n)"ab".repeat(3) is "ababab" (Java 11)
toUpperCase(), toLowerCase()Change case
toCharArray()Copy into a char[]
chars()An IntStream of the characters
String.valueOf(x)Converts a number, char, boolean or object to a String
formatted(args...)"%s has %d".formatted(a, b), same as String.format (Java 15)
lines()Stream of lines (Java 11)
concat(s)Same as + for two strings
 
String raw = "  Hello, Java World  ";
String s = raw.strip();                          // "Hello, Java World"

System.out.println(raw.length() + " " + s.length());          // 21 17
System.out.println(s.charAt(0) + " " + s.indexOf("Java"));    // H 7
System.out.println(s.lastIndexOf('o') + " " + s.indexOf("xyz"));   // 13 -1
System.out.println(s.substring(7, 11) + "|" + s.substring(7)); // Java|Java World
System.out.println(s.contains("Java") + " " + s.startsWith("Hello") + " " + s.endsWith("d"));
System.out.println(s.replace('l', 'L'));                      // HeLLo, Java WorLd
System.out.println(s.replaceAll("\\s+", "_"));                // Hello,_Java_World
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(s.split(" ")));            // [Hello,, Java, World]
System.out.println(String.join("-", "UPI", "NEFT", "IMPS"));  // UPI-NEFT-IMPS
System.out.println("ab".repeat(3) + " " + "  ".isBlank() + " " + "".isEmpty());
System.out.println("banana".chars().filter(ch -> ch == 'a').count());   // 3
System.out.println("Hi %s, you are %d".formatted("Asha", 25));
System.out.println(String.valueOf(42) + String.valueOf(true));  // 42true

char[] letters = "hello".toCharArray();
Arrays.sort(letters);
System.out.println(new String(letters));                      // ehllo

split takes a regex

System.out.println("a.b.c".split(".").length);          // 0   "." matches ANY char
System.out.println(Arrays.toString("a.b.c".split("\\.")));        // [a, b, c]
System.out.println(Arrays.toString("a|b|c".split("\\|")));        // [a, b, c]
System.out.println(Arrays.toString("a,b,,".split(",")));          // [a, b]   trailing empties dropped
System.out.println(Arrays.toString("a,b,,".split(",", -1)));      // [a, b, , ]  keep them
System.out.println(Arrays.toString("  a  b ".trim().split("\\s+")));  // [a, b]
System.out.println(Arrays.toString("a1b22c".split("\\d+")));      // [a, b, c]

Characters like . | * + ? ( ) [ ] \ $ ^ have special meaning in a regex. Escape them with \\ (a backslash in a Java string literal is written \\) or use Pattern.quote(".").

trim vs strip, isEmpty vs isBlank
