  • trim() (old) removes characters up to code point ' ' (space, tab, newline and control characters). It does not remove Unicode spaces such as the non-breaking space.
  • strip() (Java 11) uses Character.isWhitespace and understands Unicode. Prefer it in new code. stripLeading() and stripTrailing() exist too.
  • isEmpty() is true only for length 0. isBlank() is true for length 0 or whitespace only. For form input, isBlank() is usually what you want.

Immutability trap in a loop

String result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    result += i;                // creates a new String each time
}
System.out.println(result);     // 01234

Each pass copies the whole text so far. For five items this is nothing; for 100,000 it is slow and creates a lot of garbage. See the next article.

Rules

  • Compare string contents with equals/equalsIgnoreCase; == compares references.
  • String methods return new strings; assign the result.
  • String indexes start at 0; substring(from, to) includes from and excludes to.
  • switch on a String uses equals and throws NullPointerException for null.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • StringIndexOutOfBoundsException from charAt or substring when an index is negative or too large (the message wording differs between Java versions).
  • NullPointerException on s.length() when s is null. The text "null" appears if you concatenate a null: "x" + null is "xnull".
  • NumberFormatException from Integer.parseInt("12a") or parseInt("").
  • length() counts UTF-16 units, so an emoji can count as 2. For true characters use codePointCount.
  • Case conversion depends on locale for some languages (Turkish dotted i). Use toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) for identifiers and keys.

Common mistakes

  • if (name == "Ravi") — works in a quick demo because of the pool, then fails with real input.
  • Calling str.toUpperCase() and ignoring the result.
  • Using split(".") or split("|") without escaping.
  • Using new String("text") for no reason; it wastes memory and breaks == expectations.
  • Putting a password in a String: it stays in memory until garbage collected, so Java APIs for passwords use char[], which can be wiped.

Interview: "Why is String immutable? What is the String pool? == vs equals?"

  • Immutable for pool sharing, security, thread safety, cached hash code and class loading.
  • The pool is a region of the heap that stores one copy of each literal; intern() adds or fetches a string from it; new String("a") bypasses it.
  • == compares references, equals compares characters; give the example a == c false, a.equals(c) true.
  • Compile-time constant folding: "ja" + "va" == "java" is true; with a non-final variable it is false.
  • Related: String is final (cannot be subclassed), implements Comparable, CharSequence and Serializable.

StringBuilder, StringBuffer and building text efficiently

Use StringBuilder to build text in a loop because it changes one internal buffer instead of creating a new String each time; StringBuffer is its old synchronized twin.

StringBuilder (Java 5) is a mutable sequence of characters. It keeps an internal array that grows when needed (the default capacity is 16, and it grows automatically), so append is cheap on average.

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.append("Order #").append(1042).append(" total: ").append(499.5);   // chaining
sb.insert(0, "[NEW] ");
System.out.println(sb);                    // [NEW] Order #1042 total: 499.5
System.out.println(sb.length());           // 31

sb.setLength(0);                           // clear and reuse the builder
sb.append("racecar");
System.out.println(sb.reverse());          // racecar  (reverse changes sb in place)

StringBuilder b2 = new StringBuilder("Hello");
b2.append(' ').append("World");
b2.replace(0, 5, "HELLO");                 // [0, 5) replaced
b2.deleteCharAt(b2.length() - 1);          // remove last char
b2.setCharAt(0, 'J');
System.out.println(b2);                    // JELLO Worl
System.out.println(b2.indexOf("W") + " " + b2.charAt(2));   // 6 L
String finished = b2.toString();           // turn into an immutable String when done

Common StringBuilder methods

MethodPurpose
append(x)Adds any type at the end; returns the builder (chainable)
insert(i, x)Inserts at index i
delete(from, to), deleteCharAt(i)Removes characters
replace(from, to, s)Replaces a range
reverse()Reverses in place
setCharAt(i, c), charAt(i)Write/read one char
setLength(n)Truncates or pads with '\0'
length(), capacity()Characters stored / buffer size
indexOf, lastIndexOf, substringLike String
toString()Creates the final String

String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer

PointStringStringBuilderStringBuffer
Mutable?NoYesYes
Thread-safe?Yes (immutable)NoYes (methods are synchronized)
Speed in loopsSlow (new object each time)FastestSlower than StringBuilder (locking)
Since1.01.51.0
Use forConstants, keys, valuesBuilding text in one threadLegacy code; rarely needed

A StringBuilder is normally a local variable used by one thread, so locking in StringBuffer is wasted effort. Sharing one builder between threads is almost always a design smell anyway.

Why + in a loop is slow

// Slow: O(n^2) work. Pass k copies all the k characters built so far.
String s = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
    s += "x";
}

// Fast: O(n). One buffer, appended in place.
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(100_000);   // optional: pre-size the capacity
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
    sb.append("x");
}
String t = sb.toString();

A single expression such as "a" + b + "c" + d is fine: the compiler turns it into one efficient concatenation (since Java 9 through invokedynamic; before it used a hidden StringBuilder). The problem is only repeated concatenation across loop passes, where each pass creates a new intermediate string. For one-off joins prefer String.join, StringJoiner, String.format or stream.collect(Collectors.joining(", ")).

Typical uses

// 1. Palindrome check
static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
    String clean = s.toLowerCase().replaceAll("[^a-z0-9]", "");
    return clean.contentEquals(new StringBuilder(clean).reverse());
}

// 2. Build a comma-separated list without a trailing comma
static String csv(int[] values) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        if (i > 0) sb.append(", ");
        sb.append(values[i]);
    }
    return sb.toString();
}

// 3. Count characters, then rebuild
static String compress(String s) {          // "aaabbc" -> "a3b2c1"
    StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
    int i = 0;
    while (i < s.length()) {
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        int j = i;
        while (j < s.length() && s.charAt(j) == c) j++;
        out.append(c).append(j - i);
        i = j;
    }
    return out.toString();
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"));   // true
    System.out.println(csv(new int[]{3, 5, 8}));                         // 3, 5, 8
    System.out.println(compress("aaabbc"));                              // a3b2c1
}

Rule: StringBuilder does not override equals() or hashCode()

sb1.equals(sb2) compares references, and a builder is a bad HashMap key because its content can change. Compare with sb1.compareTo(sb2) == 0 (Java 11), or convert with toString() first. String.contentEquals(CharSequence) compares a string to a builder.

Common mistakes

  • Passing a char where an int is expected: new StringBuilder('A') sets the capacity to 65, it does not add "A". Use new StringBuilder("A").
  • Appending 'a' + 'b' (which is the int 195) instead of "a" + "b".
  • Calling sb.reverse() and forgetting that it changed sb itself.
  • Concatenating strings in a loop and wondering why a report takes minutes.

How a StringBuilder works inside

A StringBuilder owns one array of characters (a compact byte array since Java 9) and a counter called count. length() is that counter; capacity() is the size of the array. append copies the new characters into the free space. Only when the array is full does the builder allocate a bigger array (about double the old size plus 2) and copy the old content once. Because the size doubles, the copying cost over many appends adds up to O(n) in total, so each append is amortised O(1).

StringBuilder a = new StringBuilder();
System.out.println(a.capacity());            // 16 (the default)
a.append("12345678901234567");               // 17 characters do not fit in 16
System.out.println(a.length() + " " + a.capacity());   // 17 34

StringBuilder b = new StringBuilder("Hello");
System.out.println(b.capacity());            // 21 = 16 + length of the initial text

StringBuilder c = new StringBuilder(1000);   // you choose the capacity
c.ensureCapacity(5000);                      // grow once, up front
c.append("short");
c.trimToSize();                              // give back the unused space
System.out.println(c.length() + " " + c.capacity());   // 5 5

Pre-sizing with new StringBuilder(expectedLength) avoids the repeated growth. It is a small gain; correct use of a builder matters far more than the exact capacity.

Ways to build text: which one when?

WayBest forWatch out
a + bA short, one-line joinSlow when repeated in a loop (see above)
StringBuilderLoops, conditional pieces, editing in placeNot thread-safe; remember toString()
String.join(sep, items)Joining an existing collection or arrayNo prefix or suffix
StringJoinerDelimiter plus prefix and suffix: [a, b, c]Slightly more code than join
Collectors.joiningJoining the result of a streamElements must already be CharSequence; map them first
String.format, formattedTemplates with numbers and paddingSlowest of the group; fine outside hot loops
Text blockFixed multi-line text (SQL, JSON)Still a constant, not a builder

StringBuffer: what "synchronized" really gives you

Each StringBuffer method locks the object while it runs, so two threads calling append at the same time never corrupt the buffer. That protects only single calls. A sequence such as "check length(), then append" is still a race, because another thread can run between the two calls. If threads must build one text together, hold your own lock around the whole sequence, or let each thread build its own StringBuilder and merge the results. In new code StringBuffer is almost never the answer.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • StringIndexOutOfBoundsException — charAt, setCharAt, deleteCharAt, insert or substring with an index outside 0..length. Also thrown by delete(start, end) when start is negative or greater than end; an end past the length is silently clamped.
  • NegativeArraySizeException — new StringBuilder(-1).
  • NullPointerException — new StringBuilder((String) null). But append((String) null) does not throw: it appends the four letters null.
  • OutOfMemoryError — the buffer cannot grow beyond about 2 billion characters, and a huge builder can exhaust the heap sooner.
  • reverse() treats a surrogate pair (an emoji or a rare script character) as one unit, so it does not break such characters.

Wrong: a builder defeated by + inside append

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String name : names) {
    sb.append(name + ", ");        // creates a temporary String every pass
}

Right: append each piece

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String name : names) {
    sb.append(name).append(", ");
}
// or simply: String.join(", ", names)

Conventions

  • Keep the builder a local variable, build, call toString() once, and return the String. Do not store builders in fields or pass them between threads.
  • Declare the variable as StringBuilder (it has no useful interface); take CharSequence in method parameters that only read text.
  • Do not rewrite a simple a + b + c into a builder; it is no faster and harder to read.
  • For a trailing separator, either test i > 0 before appending (as above) or call setLength(sb.length() - 2) at the end.

In real projects

Builders appear in report and CSV export code, custom toString() methods, log messages built in loops, and code generators. For SQL do not glue user input into a builder: that opens the door to SQL injection. Build the statement text with a builder if you must, but pass the values as ? parameters to a PreparedStatement.

Interview: "String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer"

  • String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and not thread-safe; StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized.
  • Loop concatenation with + is O(n²) because of repeated copying; builder appends are amortised O(1).
  • Default capacity 16; the buffer grows (roughly doubling) when it is full — pre-size when you know the size.
  • Mention that a single-line + expression is already optimised by the compiler.

Input and output: Scanner, BufferedReader, printf and text blocks

Read console input with Scanner (easy) or BufferedReader (fast), watch the nextInt() + nextLine() pitfall, and format output with printf or String.format.

Output basics

  • System.out.println(x) prints and adds a line break; print(x) does not.
  • System.out.printf(format, args...) formats like C's printf; System.out.format is the same.
  • System.err is the error stream: it can be redirected separately (2>errors.txt). In real applications you use a logger instead (Logging).

Scanner

java.util.Scanner splits input into tokens (separated by whitespace) and converts them for you.

import java.util.Scanner;

public class ScannerDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.print("Enter age: ");
        int age = sc.nextInt();
        System.out.print("Enter price: ");
        double price = sc.nextDouble();
        System.out.print("Enter first word: ");
        String word = sc.next();                 // one token
        sc.nextLine();                           // consume the rest of that line
        System.out.print("Enter full name: ");
        String fullName = sc.nextLine();         // whole line, spaces allowed
        System.out.println(age + " " + price + " " + word + " [" + fullName + "]");
        sc.close();
    }
}
Enter age: 25
Enter price: 99.5
Enter first word: hello
Enter full name: Asha Rao
25 99.5 hello [Asha Rao]
MethodReads
nextInt(), nextLong(), nextDouble(), nextBoolean()The next token, converted; leaves the line break in the buffer
next()The next token as a String (stops at whitespace)
nextLine()The rest of the current line (can be empty), and consumes the line break
hasNext(), hasNextInt(), hasNextLine()Whether another token/line is available; use these for loops and validation

The nextInt() + nextLine() pitfall

If the user types 5 and presses Enter, the input buffer contains 5\n. nextInt() reads 5 and stops, leaving \n. The next nextLine() immediately reads the rest of that line — which is empty — and returns "", so your program seems to skip the question.

Wrong: the name is always empty

int n = sc.nextInt();
String name = sc.nextLine();   // reads the leftover "\n" -> ""

Right: consume the line break first

int n = Integer.parseInt(sc.nextLine().trim());
String name = sc.nextLine();   // reads the real line

Two safe approaches: read everything with nextLine() and parse yourself (shown above), or call an extra sc.nextLine() after nextInt(). Invalid input such as abc for nextInt() throws InputMismatchException and leaves the bad token in the buffer, so loops must call sc.next() to discard it. Reading when nothing is left throws NoSuchElementException.

static int readInt(Scanner sc, String prompt) {
    while (true) {
        System.out.print(prompt);
        if (sc.hasNextInt()) {
            int value = sc.nextInt();
            sc.nextLine();                 // clear the line break
            return value;
        }
        System.out.println("Please enter a whole number.");
        sc.next();                         // discard the bad token
    }
}

A Scanner can also parse a string or file: new Scanner("10 20 30"). Closing a Scanner on System.in closes the standard input for the whole program, so create one Scanner for System.in and close it once, at the end.

BufferedReader — fast input

Scanner is convenient but slow for large input (it uses regular expressions). BufferedReader reads whole lines through a buffer and is the usual choice when input has many lines — competitive programming, big files. It reads text only; you convert it yourself.

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStreamReader;
import java.util.StringTokenizer;

public class FastInput {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in))) {
            int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine().trim());        // first line: count
            StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer(br.readLine()); // second line: numbers
            long sum = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                sum += Long.parseLong(st.nextToken());
            }
            System.out.println("Sum = " + sum);
        }
    }
}
3
10 20 30
Sum = 60
  • readLine() returns null at the end of input, so loops read until null.
  • readLine() throws the checked IOException: declare throws IOException or catch it.
  • Instead of StringTokenizer you can use line.split(" ") — simpler, slightly slower.
PointScannerBufferedReader
ParsingBuilt in (nextInt, …)Manual (Integer.parseInt)
Speed on large inputSlowFast
Checked exceptionsNone for System.inIOException
Best forSmall console programs, menusLarge input, files, performance

Formatted output with printf and String.format

System.out.printf("%-10s|%8d|%8.2f%n", "Pen", 12, 5.5);
System.out.printf("%-10s|%8d|%8.2f%n", "Notebook", 3, 45.0);
System.out.println(String.format("%05d", 42));            // 00042
System.out.println(String.format("%,d", 1234567));        // 1,234,567
System.out.println(String.format("%x %X %o", 255, 255, 8));   // ff FF 10
System.out.println(String.format("%b %c %e", true, 'A', 12345.678));
System.out.println(String.format("%+d and 100%%", 5));    // +5 and 100%
String line = String.format("%s paid Rs %.2f", "Asha", 1499.5);
System.out.println(line);
Pen       |      12|    5.50
Notebook  |       3|   45.00
00042
1,234,567
ff FF 10
true A 1.234568e+04
+5 and 100%
Asha paid Rs 1499.50
SpecifierMeaning
%dInteger (byte, short, int, long, BigInteger)
%f, %.2fDecimal number; .2 is digits after the point (rounds half up)
%sAny value as text (calls toString())
%c, %bCharacter, boolean
%x, %X, %o, %eHex, uppercase hex, octal, scientific
%nPlatform line separator (prefer to \n in format strings)
%%A literal percent sign
%10d, %-10sWidth 10, right-aligned / left-aligned with -
%05d, %+d, %,dZero-padded, with sign, with thousands separator

A mismatch throws an exception at runtime: String.format("%d", 3.5) gives IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Double, and a missing argument gives MissingFormatArgumentException. The thousands separator and decimal mark follow the default Locale; for lakh/crore grouping (12,34,567) use NumberFormat with the en-IN locale (Locale.forLanguageTag("en-IN")).

Text blocks (Java 15)

A text block is a multi-line string between triple quotes. It keeps line breaks, needs no \n or escaped quotes, and removes the common indentation. It is ideal for JSON, SQL and HTML. More about it in Module 5.

String sql = """
        SELECT id, name
        FROM customers
        WHERE city = 'Pune'
        ORDER BY name
        """;
System.out.print(sql);
SELECT id, name
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'Pune'
ORDER BY name

Rules

  • The opening """ must be followed by a line break; the closing """ position decides the indentation that is removed.
  • Every printf specifier must match its argument type; the count of arguments must match the count of specifiers.
  • Create one Scanner per input source; do not close System.in early.

Common mistakes

  • The nextInt() / nextLine() skip (above).
  • Using %d for a double or %f for an int.
  • Using \n in printf for a platform-correct newline; use %n.
  • Forgetting to trim() before Integer.parseInt(line): a trailing space causes NumberFormatException.
  • Creating a new Scanner(System.in) in every method: buffered input is lost between scanners.

Interview: "Scanner vs BufferedReader? Why does nextLine() seem to be skipped?"

  • Scanner tokenises and parses (convenient, slower); BufferedReader reads lines (fast, manual parsing, throws IOException).
  • nextInt() leaves the line break in the buffer; the following nextLine() consumes that empty remainder.
  • Fix: read lines and parse, or add one extra nextLine().
  • Mention hasNextInt() for validation and InputMismatchException.

The Math class, Random and ThreadLocalRandom

Math offers static methods for everyday arithmetic (pow, sqrt, floorMod, addExact); use ThreadLocalRandom for quick random numbers and SecureRandom when the value protects something.

Math essentials

MethodResult and notes
abs(x), max(a, b), min(a, b)Same type as the arguments; abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) stays negative
pow(a, b), sqrt(x), cbrt(x)Always return double; sqrt(-1) is NaN
floor(x), ceil(x)Round down / up, as a double
round(x)Nearest whole number (half rounds up); long for double, int for float
floorDiv(a, b), floorMod(a, b)Division and remainder that round toward negative infinity
addExact, subtractExact, multiplyExact, toIntExactThrow ArithmeticException on overflow
hypot(a, b), signum(x)sqrt(a²+b²) without overflow; −1, 0 or 1
log(x), log10(x), exp(x)Natural log, base-10 log, ex
sin, cos, toRadians, PI, ETrigonometry works in radians
clamp(value, min, max)Keeps a value inside a range (Java 21)
 
System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 10));            // 1024.0
System.out.println((int) Math.pow(2, 10));      // 1024
System.out.println(Math.sqrt(144));             // 12.0
System.out.println(Math.ceil(7 / 2));           // 3.0   7/2 is already 3 (int division)
System.out.println(Math.ceil(7 / 2.0));         // 4.0
System.out.println(Math.floor(-1.5) + " " + Math.ceil(-1.5));   // -2.0 -1.0
System.out.println(Math.round(2.5) + " " + Math.round(-2.5) + " " + Math.round(2.4));  // 3 -2 2
System.out.println(Math.floorDiv(-7, 2) + " " + (-7 / 2));       // -4 -3
System.out.println(Math.floorMod(-7, 5) + " " + (-7 % 5));        // 3 -2
System.out.println(Math.hypot(3, 4));           // 5.0
System.out.println(Math.addExact(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1));         // throws
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: integer overflow

To round a price to two decimals with double people write Math.round(x * 100) / 100.0. It is acceptable for display, but use BigDecimal.setScale for real money. Use pow only when you need powers of non-integers or large powers; for squares write x * x, which is faster and exact for integers.

Random numbers

ToolUse it forNotes
Math.random()Quick demosA double in [0.0, 1.0)
java.util.RandomReproducible sequences (tests, simulations)new Random(42) gives the same numbers each run; thread-safe but contended
ThreadLocalRandomEveryday random numbers, especially from many threadsThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 7) — upper bound exclusive; do not share the object between threads, and it cannot be seeded
java.security.SecureRandomOTPs, tokens, passwords, keysCryptographically strong; slower. Never use Random for security
 
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.Random;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;

public class RandomDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Random seeded = new Random(42);              // same seed -> same sequence every run
        int fromRandom = seeded.nextInt(100);        // 0..99
        double d = seeded.nextDouble();              // [0.0, 1.0)

        int dice = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 7);   // 1..6

        int otp = new SecureRandom().nextInt(900_000) + 100_000; // 6-digit OTP: 100000..999999
        System.out.println("dice=" + dice + " otp-length=" + String.valueOf(otp).length());

        int min = 10, max = 20;                      // random int in [min, max]
        int inRange = min + (int) (Math.random() * (max - min + 1));
        System.out.println(inRange >= min && inRange <= max);   // true
    }
}
dice=4 otp-length=6
true

The dice and OTP values change on each run. nextInt(bound) returns 0 to bound - 1 and throws IllegalArgumentException if bound is zero or negative.

Common mistakes

  • Math.random() * 10 cast to int gives 0–9, not 1–10: add 1 for 1–10.
  • Creating a new Random() inside a loop — create it once.
  • Using Random for OTPs or session tokens: it is predictable. Use SecureRandom.
  • Assuming Math.round returns an int: it returns long for a double, so int r = Math.round(x); does not compile.

Interview: Random vs ThreadLocalRandom vs SecureRandom

  • Random: seedable, reproducible, shared state; ThreadLocalRandom: one instance per thread, no contention, not seedable; SecureRandom: unpredictable, for security.
  • Math.floorMod vs % with negatives; Math.round(-2.5) is −2.

Interview questions — Basics and syntax

What are the JDK, JRE and JVM? How is Java platform independent?

The JVM runs bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the standard libraries. The JDK is the JRE plus development tools such as javac. javac compiles source to platform-neutral bytecode in .class files; each operating system has its own JVM that executes the same bytecode. So the bytecode is portable and the JVM is platform specific. At runtime the class loader loads classes, the verifier checks them, and the interpreter and JIT compiler run them.

Why is main declared public static void?

public so the JVM can call it from outside; static so no object is needed to start the program; void because it returns nothing to the JVM (use System.exit(code) for a status). The parameter String[] args carries the command-line arguments. A different signature compiles but will not be started as the entry point.

Why does Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b give true, but 128 gives false?

Autoboxing calls Integer.valueOf, which returns cached objects for values from −128 to 127. Inside that range both variables share one object; outside it, two different objects are created, and == compares references. Always use equals() for wrapper objects.

Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

Always pass-by-value. For primitives the value is copied. For objects the reference is copied, so the method and the caller share one object: calling list.add(x) in the method changes what the caller sees. But assigning a new object to the parameter only changes the local copy. That is why a swap(a, b) method cannot swap the caller's variables.

Why is String immutable, and what is the String pool?

Immutability allows safe sharing of literals in the pool, protects security-sensitive values like paths and class names, makes strings thread-safe, and lets hashCode() be cached, which is ideal for HashMap keys. The String pool is a heap area that keeps one instance for each distinct literal. new String("a") creates a separate heap object; intern() returns the pooled one.

What does this print? String a = "java"; String b = new String("java"); System.out.println(a == b); System.out.println(a.equals(b));

false then true. a points to the pooled literal and b to a new heap object, so the references differ, but the characters are equal. "ja" + "va" == "java" would be true because the compiler folds constants, while part + "va" == "java" with a non-final variable part is false.

String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?

String is immutable. StringBuilder is mutable and not thread-safe, so it is the fastest for building text. StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized, so it is thread-safe but slower, and rarely needed. Concatenating with + in a loop is O(n²) because every pass copies the text; use a StringBuilder there.

Why can't you use double for money? What do you use instead?

Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, and errors accumulate. Use BigDecimal created from Strings (new BigDecimal("0.10")), set the scale and a RoundingMode explicitly, and compare with compareTo. Or keep the amount as a long in paise. In the database use NUMERIC(p, s).

Why does byte b = 10; b += 5; compile but b = b + 5; does not?

b + 5 is promoted to int, and assigning an int to a byte needs a cast. A compound assignment b += 5 is defined as b = (byte)(b + 5), so the compiler adds the cast for you. The same hidden cast silently truncates in int i = 10; i += 3.7; (result 13).

What is the output of int x = 5; x = x++ + ++x;?

12. x++ yields 5 and sets x to 6; ++x sets x to 7 and yields 7; the sum 12 is then assigned to x. Java evaluates operands left to right. Also remember that x = x++; leaves x unchanged.

How does Java choose between overloaded methods?

At compile time, in three phases: first exact match or widening without boxing, then boxing/unboxing, then varargs. The most specific method wins; if none is more specific, the call is ambiguous. So with show(int), show(long) and show(Integer), the call show(5) picks int, and without show(int) it picks long (widening beats boxing). Return type is not part of the signature.

Why does Scanner.nextLine() sometimes return an empty string after nextInt()?

nextInt() reads only the number and leaves the line break in the buffer. The next nextLine() reads the rest of that line, which is empty. Fix it by reading all input with nextLine() and parsing with Integer.parseInt, or by calling one extra nextLine() after nextInt().

What can a switch be used on, and what is a switch expression?

The selector may be byte, short, char, int (and wrappers), String or an enum — not long, double or boolean. In the old colon form, missing break causes fall-through. Since Java 14 the arrow form has no fall-through, and a switch expression produces a value (int days = switch (m) { case "Feb" -> 28; default -> 31; };), must be exhaustive, and uses yield inside a block.

What does Arrays.asList return, and what are its traps?

A fixed-size list backed by the array: set works and writes through to the array, but add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. With a primitive array like int[] you get a List<int[]> of size 1. Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(...) for a normal list, or use List.of for an immutable one.

What exceptions can arrays and strings throw at runtime?

ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for a bad array index, NegativeArraySizeException for a negative size, ArrayStoreException when storing the wrong type into a covariant array, StringIndexOutOfBoundsException for charAt/substring, NullPointerException for a null array or string, NumberFormatException for bad numeric text, and ArithmeticException: / by zero for integer division by zero.

Cheat sheet — Basics and syntax

  • JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM JDK has the tools, JRE the libraries, JVM runs bytecode.
  • Run javac A.java then java A; or java A.java (Java 11+); jshell for experiments.
  • main public static void main(String[] args); one public class per file, file name = class name.
  • Primitives byte 8, short 16, int 32, long 64, float 32, double 64, char 16 (unsigned), boolean.
  • Literals 10L, 3.14f, 1_000_000, 0xFF, 0b101; decimals default to double, integers to int.
  • Defaults fields and array elements: 0 / false / null; locals have none.
  • Integer cache −128…127; compare wrappers with equals.
  • Unboxing null throws NullPointerException.
  • var local variables only; needs an initializer; still statically typed.
  • Division int / int drops the fraction; -7 % 3 == -1; use Math.floorMod for wrap-around.
  • Overflow wraps silently; Math.addExact throws; use 1000000L * 1000000 for long maths.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004; money → BigDecimal("0.10") + setScale + RoundingMode.
  • Promotion byte/short/char arithmetic gives int; b += 1 has a hidden cast, b = b + 1 does not compile.
  • Casting narrowing truncates: (int) 3.99 == 3, (byte) 130 == -126.
  • i++ / ++i old value then add / add then new value.
  • && and || short-circuit; & and | evaluate both sides.
  • switch arrow form has no fall-through; switch expressions return a value and use yield.
  • Loops for, enhanced for, while, do-while; break outer; leaves a labeled loop.
  • Pass-by-value always; object references are copied; reassigning a parameter never changes the caller.
  • Overload order exact/widening → boxing → varargs; most specific wins.
  • Arrays fixed size, length field; Arrays.toString, deepToString, sort, copyOf, fill, equals.
  • Arrays.asList fixed-size view; List.of immutable; new ArrayList<>(…) growable.
  • Strings immutable; literals pooled; equals for content, "x".equals(s) avoids null.
  • split takes a regex: split("\\."), split("\\s+"); trailing empty strings dropped.
  • Builders StringBuilder for loops (not thread-safe), StringBuffer synchronized.
  • Input Scanner for small programs, BufferedReader for speed; beware nextInt() then nextLine().
  • printf %d %s %.2f %n %5d %-10s %05d %,d.
  • Random ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(1, 7) for everyday use; SecureRandom for secrets.

Practice — Basics and syntax

  1. Warm-up: types and operators (easy). In JShell or a single file, predict and then check: 7 / 2, -7 % 3, (byte) 200, 0.1 + 0.2, 'a' + 1, 1 + 2 + "x", Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1. Done when all seven guesses match the output and you can explain each.
  2. Star and number patterns (easy). Print a right triangle, an inverted triangle, a pyramid, a diamond, a hollow square, Floyd's triangle and Pascal's triangle of height n. Done when each prints correctly for n = 1, 5 and 9.
  3. Number programs (easy). Write: even/odd, prime check (up to √n), primes up to N, factorial (iterative and recursive), Fibonacci (first N), GCD and LCM, Armstrong number, perfect number, sum of digits, reverse a number, palindrome number, binary to decimal and back. Done when each handles 0, 1 and a large int without errors.
  4. String programs (easy to medium). Write: reverse a string, palindrome (ignoring case and punctuation), count vowels and consonants, anagram check (sort the chars, then a count array), first non-repeating character, remove duplicates, count words, capitalise each word, run-length compression. Done when each works on empty strings and on strings with spaces.
  5. Array programs (medium). Write: reverse an array, largest and second largest, sum and average, remove duplicates from a sorted array, merge two sorted arrays, rotate by k, linear and binary search, bubble sort, count frequency of each element. Done when you use no library sort for the sorting task and handle length 0 and 1.
  6. Matrix programs (medium). Write: matrix addition, multiplication (use the example in the Arrays article), transpose, row and column sums, diagonal sum, spiral print of a 4×4 matrix. Done when it works for non-square matrices where mathematically valid.
  7. Menu-driven calculator (medium). Use a do-while menu with a switch expression, a Scanner and a method per operation; reject division by zero and non-numeric input without crashing. Done when the program survives entering letters at every prompt.
  8. Pass-by-value lab (medium). Write methods that try to swap two ints, two Strings, two array elements, and mutate or reassign a StringBuilder and an int[]. Predict each result on paper, run it, and write one sentence per case explaining what was copied.
  9. Billing with BigDecimal (medium). Read item names, prices and quantities with BufferedReader, compute a subtotal, 18% GST and a total with BigDecimal, round with HALF_UP to two decimals, and print an aligned receipt with printf. Done when 3 × ₹33.33 plus GST matches a hand calculation to the paisa.
  10. Mini project: word and number statistics (harder). Read a text file given as a command-line argument line by line, then print the 5 most frequent words (use a loop and arrays or a Map if you know it), the longest word, and the average word length. Build the final report with a StringBuilder. Done when it handles an empty file and a missing file with a clear message.

Module 2·About 2 weeksMust

Object-oriented programming

30 topics · about 4 h of reading

Object-oriented programming (OOP) is the way almost all Java code is organised. You model a problem as objects — things that hold data together with the code that works on that data — and you describe each kind of object with a class. Spring beans, JPA entities, DTOs, exceptions, collections: everything you touch in a Java project is a class.

This module starts with the basics (classes, objects, constructors, this, static), moves through the four pillars — encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction — and then covers the tools professionals use every day: final, the Object methods (equals, hashCode, toString), composition, nested classes, packages, enums and records. It ends with one worked example that ties everything together.

It is the base for much of what follows: Collections (Module 4) depend on equals and hashCode, modern Java (Module 5) builds on interfaces, records and sealed types, memory (Module 7) explains where objects live, and design principles and patterns (System Design · Module 1) assume you know all of this well.

  • Explain the four pillars with Java code and a real example for each, the way interviewers expect.
  • Write classes with correct constructors, validation, encapsulation and immutability.
  • Predict the output of initialization-order, overloading and overriding puzzles.
  • Choose between an abstract class and an interface, and between inheritance and composition.
  • Implement equals(), hashCode() and toString() correctly.
  • Use enums, records, nested classes and packages the way professional codebases do.

Why OOP: classes, objects, state, behaviour and identity

OOP keeps data and the code that changes it together inside objects, so each object can protect its own rules; a class is the blueprint and an object is one thing built from it.

Before OOP became mainstream, most programs were written in a procedural style: data lives in variables, arrays or simple records, and separate functions read and change that data. This works for small programs. It becomes painful as the program grows, because nothing stops any function from changing any data, and the business rules ("a balance can never go below zero") get copied into many places.

The problem with procedural code

Here is a tiny bank written in a procedural style. The data (holders and balances) sits in arrays, and a function changes it.

public class BankProcedural {
    static String[] holders = {"Ravi", "Asha"};
    static long[] balances = {5_000, 12_000};

    static void withdraw(int index, long amount) {
        balances[index] -= amount;            // no rule is checked here...
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        withdraw(0, 8_000);
        balances[1] = -999;                   // ...and any code can do this
        System.out.println(holders[0] + ": " + balances[0]);
        System.out.println(holders[1] + ": " + balances[1]);
    }
}
Ravi: -3000
Asha: -999

Three problems show up at once:

  • No protection. Any line of code can write balances[1] = -999. The rule "no negative balance" is not enforced anywhere.
  • Scattered rules. If ten functions change balances, each one must remember to check the rule. One forgets, and you have a production bug.
  • Hard to extend. Add a "current account with overdraft" and every function grows another if (type == CURRENT) branch.

The OOP answer: keep data and behaviour together

In OOP you create an Account class. The balance is private, so only the class's own methods can change it, and each method checks the rules once, in one place.

public class Account {
    private final String holder;
    private long balance;                       // hidden: only Account can touch it

    public Account(String holder, long openingBalance) {
        if (openingBalance < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Opening balance cannot be negative");
        }
        this.holder = holder;
        this.balance = openingBalance;
    }

    public void withdraw(long amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        }
        if (amount > balance) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient balance for " + holder);
        }
        balance -= amount;
    }

    public long getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Account ravi = new Account("Ravi", 5_000);
        try {
            ravi.withdraw(8_000);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
        ravi.withdraw(1_500);
        System.out.println("Ravi: " + ravi.getBalance());
        // ravi.balance = -999;   // compile error: balance has private access in Account
    }
}
Insufficient balance for Ravi
Ravi: 3500

The rule now lives in exactly one method, and the compiler itself blocks ravi.balance = -999. When you need a new account type, you add a new class instead of editing every function — that is what inheritance and polymorphism give you.

AspectProceduralObject-oriented
Unit of codeFunctionsClasses (data + methods together)
Data accessUsually open to every functionHidden behind methods (encapsulation)
Business rulesRepeated wherever the data changesWritten once, inside the class that owns the data
Adding a new variantEdit every function (if/switch on a type code)Add a new class (a subclass or a new implementation)
Good fitSmall scripts, simple data pipelinesLarge applications with many entities and rules

Class vs object

A class is a blueprint. It says what data every object of that kind holds and what those objects can do. An object (also called an instance) is one concrete thing built from the blueprint at run time with new. One class, many objects — like one house plan and many houses built from it, each with its own paint colour and its own residents.

ClassObject
What it isA type, a blueprintA value built from the blueprint
When it existsWritten at compile time; loaded once by the JVMCreated at run time, as many times as you like
MemoryClass metadata, loaded onceEach object gets its own memory on the heap
Exampleclass Account { … }new Account("Ravi", 5_000)

State, behaviour and identity

Every object has three things. Interviewers like this definition because it separates "what an object knows", "what it does" and "which one it is".

State
The data the object holds right now — the current values of its fields. Ravi's account: holder "Ravi", balance 3,500.
Behaviour
What the object can do — its methods, such as withdraw() and getBalance(). Behaviour usually reads or changes state.
Identity
What makes this object itself and not another one. Two accounts can have the same holder and the same balance and still be two different objects. In Java, == on two references compares identity.

Keep identity and equality apart in your head: == asks "is this the very same object?", while equals() asks "do these two objects represent the same value?". You decide what "same value" means by overriding equals() — see equals() and hashCode().

The four pillars in one line each

  • Encapsulation — hide the data and expose safe methods that keep it valid.
  • Inheritance — build a new class from an existing one when the new one "is a" kind of the old one.
  • Polymorphism — one method call, different behaviour depending on the actual object.
  • Abstraction — show what an object does and hide how it does it.

Each pillar has its own articles below, and the four pillars summary pulls them together at the end of the module.

In a real Spring Boot project

You write entity classes (Order, Customer), DTO records (OrderResponse), service classes (OrderService) and controllers. Spring creates the service and controller objects for you (they are "beans"); you create entities and DTOs yourself with new, or JPA and Jackson create them for you from database rows and JSON.

Java is not "pure" OOP — and that is fine

Primitives such as int and double are not objects, and static methods belong to no object. Modern Java also mixes in a functional style (lambdas and streams, Module 5) and a data-oriented style (records, sealed types and pattern matching). Good Java uses the right tool for each job.

Mistake: one giant "manager" class

A BankManager class with fifty methods that all work on raw arrays and maps is procedural code wearing a class costume (often called a god class). Model the domain nouns instead — Account, Transaction, Customer — and let each class own its data and its rules.

Interview: "What is OOP and why do we use it?"

  • OOP models software as objects that combine state (fields) and behaviour (methods); a class is the blueprint, an object is an instance.
  • Benefits: encapsulation protects invariants, inheritance and composition give reuse, polymorphism lets you add new types without changing callers, abstraction hides complexity.
  • Give a 20-second example: an Account with a private balance and a withdraw() that checks the rule.
  • Bonus point: mention the trade-off — deep inheritance trees are a design smell; prefer composition (see favor composition).

Classes and objects in code: fields, methods and new

A class declares fields (state), constructors (setup) and methods (behaviour); new creates an object on the heap, runs its constructor and gives you a reference to it.

Anatomy of a class

Here is a realistic class from an e-commerce app. Notice the three main parts: fields, a constructor and methods. The price is stored in whole paise as a long, because double cannot represent money exactly.

public class Product {
    // 1. Fields: the state every Product object carries
    private final String sku;
    private String name;
    private long pricePaise;          // money as whole paise, never double
    private int stock;

    // 2. Constructor: builds a valid object
    public Product(String sku, String name, long pricePaise, int stock) {
        this.sku = sku;
        this.name = name;
        this.pricePaise = pricePaise;
        this.stock = stock;
    }

    // 3. Methods: the behaviour
    public boolean isInStock() {
        return stock > 0;
    }

    public void sell(int quantity) {
        if (quantity > stock) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Only " + stock + " left for " + sku);
        }
        stock -= quantity;
    }

    public String getName() { return name; }
    public int getStock()   { return stock; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Product mouse = new Product("SKU-101", "Wireless Mouse", 49_900, 3);
        Product keyboard = new Product("SKU-102", "Keyboard", 1_29_900, 0);

        mouse.sell(2);
        System.out.println(mouse.getName() + " stock: " + mouse.getStock());
        System.out.println(keyboard.getName() + " in stock? " + keyboard.isInStock());
        try {
            mouse.sell(5);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Wireless Mouse stock: 1
Keyboard in stock? false
Error: Only 1 left for SKU-101

Two objects, mouse and keyboard, came from one class. Each has its own stock: selling a mouse did not touch the keyboard. Underscores in numbers such as 1_29_900 are only for readability; the compiler ignores them.

MemberPurposeExample
Instance fieldState stored separately in each objectprivate int stock;
Static fieldState shared by the whole class (one copy)private static int created;
ConstructorSets up a new object in a valid statepublic Product(…)
Instance methodBehaviour that works on one objectsell(int quantity)
Static methodBehaviour that needs no objectProduct.of(…)
Initializer blockSetup code that runs during construction (rare){ … }, static { … }
Nested typeA class, interface, enum or record declared insidestatic class Builder

Conventions for classes and members

  • Class names are nouns in PascalCase: OrderService, UpiPayment. Method names are verbs in camelCase: placeOrder(), isInStock(). Constants are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: MAX_RETRIES.
  • A file holds at most one public top-level class, and the file must be named after it (Product.java). Otherwise javac reports class Product is public, should be declared in a file named Product.java.
  • Common member order: constants, static fields, instance fields, constructors, public methods, private helpers. Teams enforce it with formatters and Checkstyle.
  • Fields are private by default in professional code; you open access only on purpose (see encapsulation).

Creating an object with new

The line Product mouse = new Product("SKU-101", "Wireless Mouse", 49_900, 3); does three things. Product mouse declares a reference variable of type Product. new Product(…) creates the object. The = stores a reference to the new object in the variable. Since Java 10 you can also write var mouse = new Product(…); — the variable's type is still Product; var only saves typing.

What new does, step by step

  1. Load and initialize the class if this is its first use. Static fields and static blocks run once, here (see initialization order).
  2. Allocate memory on the heap — enough for an object header plus every instance field, including the fields inherited from parent classes.
  3. Set every field to its default value: 0, false, '\u0000' or null.
  4. Run the constructor chain: the parent constructor first (all the way up to Object), then this class's field initializers and instance blocks, then the constructor body.
  5. Return the reference. The assignment stores it in your variable.

The variable does not contain the object. It contains a reference — think of it as the object's address inside the JVM. Local variables live in the method's stack frame and disappear when the method returns. Objects live on the heap and stay there as long as something can still reach them. Module 7 covers the heap, the stack and garbage collection in depth.

The JIT may skip the heap — your mental model stays the same

The JIT compiler uses escape analysis: if an object never leaves a method, the JVM may avoid allocating it on the heap at all. This is an optimisation you cannot see in your program's behaviour, so "objects live on the heap, references point to them" remains the right way to reason about code.

Default values

Fields always start with a default value before any constructor code runs. Local variables do not.

TypeDefault for a fieldLocal variable
byte, short, int, long0No default — must be assigned
float, double0.0No default
char'\u0000' (the NUL character)No default
booleanfalseNo default
Any reference type (String, List, arrays…)nullNo default

Rule: a local variable must be assigned before it is read

Reading an unassigned local variable is a compile error: variable total might not have been initialized. The compiler checks every path through the method (this is called definite assignment). Fields never cause this error because they always have a default — which is exactly why a forgotten field assignment becomes a silent null or 0 bug instead.

References are values: assignment and method calls

Assigning one reference variable to another copies the reference, not the object. Passing an object to a method also copies the reference. The method can change the shared object, but it cannot make your variable point somewhere else.

public class Refs {
    static class Account {
        String holder;
        long balance;
        Account(String holder, long balance) { this.holder = holder; this.balance = balance; }
    }

    static void credit(Account acc, long amount) {
        acc.balance += amount;          // changes the shared object
    }

    static void replace(Account acc) {
        acc = new Account("Someone else", 0);   // changes only the local copy of the reference
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Account a = new Account("Ravi", 1000);
        Account b = a;                  // copies the reference, not the object
        b.balance = 5000;
        System.out.println(a.balance);  // 5000
        System.out.println(a == b);     // true: same object

        credit(a, 500);
        System.out.println(a.balance);  // 5500
        replace(a);
        System.out.println(a.holder);   // Ravi

        Account c = new Account("Ravi", 5500);
        System.out.println(a == c);     // false: different objects, same state
    }
}
5000
true
5500
Ravi
false

Interview: "Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?"

Always pass-by-value. For primitives the value is the number itself; for objects the value is the reference. That is why credit() can change the account (both copies of the reference point to the same object) but replace() cannot change what a points to. A strong answer shows exactly this pair of methods.

null and NullPointerException

A reference can be null, meaning it points to no object. Calling a method or reading a field through null throws NullPointerException (NPE). Since Java 14 the JVM prints helpful NPE messages (on by default since Java 15) that name exactly what was null:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "c.name" is null
	at Npe.main(Npe.java:8)

Variable names such as c.name appear when the class was compiled with debug information (Maven and Gradle do this by default); otherwise you see placeholders like <local1>.

Conventions that prevent most NPEs

  • Validate constructor arguments early: this.name = Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name"); fails fast with a clear message.
  • Return an empty list instead of null from methods that return collections.
  • Use Optional as the return type when "no value" is a normal outcome (Module 5).

When does an object die?

Java has no destructors and no manual free(). When no live reference can reach an object any more, it becomes eligible for garbage collection, and the garbage collector reclaims the memory at a time of its choosing. Setting a local variable to null "to help the GC" is almost never needed; the reference disappears when the method returns. The cases that really matter — objects kept alive by a static collection or a cache — are covered in Module 7.

Mistake: using == to compare objects by value

Wrong: compares identity

Account x = new Account("Ravi", 5500);
Account y = new Account("Ravi", 5500);
if (x == y) {               // false: two different objects
    System.out.println("Same account");
}

Right: compare by value with equals()

// after Account overrides equals() and hashCode()
if (x.equals(y)) {          // true when the fields match
    System.out.println("Same account");
}

Without an overridden equals(), the version inherited from Object also compares identity, so you must override it first (see equals() and hashCode()).

Constructors in depth: default, overloaded, chained and copy

A constructor puts a new object into a valid state; Java adds a no-arg default constructor only when you write none, and constructors reuse each other with this(…) and super(…).

A constructor is a special block of code that runs exactly once for each new object, as part of new. Its job is to make the object valid from its very first moment: required fields set, rules checked. If an object can exist in a half-built state, bugs follow.

A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type — not even void. It can be overloaded, it can have any access modifier, and it can throw exceptions. It is not a method and it is not inherited.

ConstructorMethod
NameExactly the class nameAny name (a camelCase verb)
Return typeNone, not even voidRequired (void if nothing)
How it runsAutomatically, through new, this(…) or super(…)Called explicitly, any number of times
Inherited?NoYes, if accessible
Can be static, final, abstract?No — compile errorYes
Provided automatically?Yes, a default one, if you declare noneNo

The default constructor

If a class declares no constructor at all, the compiler adds a default constructor: it takes no arguments, has the same access as the class (a public class gets a public one; a package-private class gets a package-private one), and its body simply calls super().

The moment you write any constructor yourself, the compiler stops adding the default one. Code that used new Customer() then breaks:

class Customer {
    private String name;
    Customer(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

public class E2 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Customer c = new Customer();   // compile error
    }
}
E2.java:7: error: constructor Customer in class Customer cannot be applied to given types;
        Customer c = new Customer();
                     ^
  required: String
  found:    no arguments
  reason: actual and formal argument lists differ in length

Frameworks that need a no-arg constructor

JPA requires every entity class to have a public or protected no-arg constructor, because Hibernate creates entity objects by reflection and then fills the fields. If you add Order(String id) to an entity, also add protected Order() { }. Jackson, which turns JSON into objects in Spring Boot, needs either a no-arg constructor or a constructor it can bind to — such as a record's canonical constructor or one marked @JsonCreator.

Overloading and chaining with this(…)

A class can have several constructors with different parameter lists — constructor overloading. To avoid copying the validation into each one, let the short constructors delegate to the most complete one using this(…). This is constructor chaining.

public class Ct2 {
    static class Order {
        private final String id;
        private final int quantity;
        private final String note;

        Order(String id) {
            this(id, 1);                          // delegate
        }

        Order(String id, int quantity) {
            this(id, quantity, "");               // delegate
        }

        Order(String id, int quantity, String note) {   // the "main" constructor
            if (id == null || id.isBlank()) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("id is required");
            }
            if (quantity <= 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be > 0");
            }
            this.id = id;
            this.quantity = quantity;
            this.note = note;
            System.out.println("Created " + this);
        }

        @Override public String toString() {
            return "Order[id=" + id + ", quantity=" + quantity + ", note='" + note + "']";
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Order("SW-1001");
        new Order("SW-1002", 3);
        new Order("SW-1003", 2, "Less spicy");
        try {
            new Order("SW-1004", 0);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Created Order[id=SW-1001, quantity=1, note='']
Created Order[id=SW-1002, quantity=3, note='']
Created Order[id=SW-1003, quantity=2, note='Less spicy']
Rejected: quantity must be > 0

Calling the parent with super(…)

Every constructor starts by running a constructor of its parent class. You either write super(…) yourself, or — if you write neither this(…) nor super(…) — the compiler inserts super() with no arguments. If the parent has no no-arg constructor, that hidden call fails:

class Vehicle {
    Vehicle(String regNo) { }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
    Car() { }        // compiler inserts super() here, but Vehicle() does not exist
}
E3.java:5: error: constructor Vehicle in class Vehicle cannot be applied to given types;
    Car() { }
          ^
  required: String
  found:    no arguments
  reason: actual and formal argument lists differ in length

The fix is Car(String regNo) { super(regNo); }. More on parent constructors in inheritance.

Rules for this(…) and super(…)

  • Up to Java 24, this(…) or super(…) must be the very first statement of the constructor. Java 17 says call to super must be first statement in constructor.
  • A constructor can call only one of them — never both.
  • Constructors must not call each other in a loop: javac reports recursive constructor invocation.
  • The arguments you pass to this(…)/super(…) cannot use the object being built. super(makeId()) fails if makeId() is an instance method (cannot reference makeId() before supertype constructor has been called); a static helper is fine.

Java 25: flexible constructor bodies

Java 25 finalised flexible constructor bodies (JEP 513). Statements may now appear before super(…) or this(…) — for example to validate arguments before the expensive parent constructor runs — as long as they do not use the object under construction (no reading fields, no instance method calls). They may assign fields that have no initializer.

class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    private final double rate;

    SavingsAccount(String accountNo, double rate) {
        if (rate < 0 || rate > 0.15) {           // validate BEFORE calling super
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Bad rate: " + rate);
        }
        this.rate = rate;                        // allowed: field has no initializer
        super(accountNo);
    }
}

On Java 17 or 21 this is a compile error. Most projects still target 17 or 21, so write the classic form (call super first, or validate inside a static helper used as an argument) unless your project is on 25.

Copy constructors

A copy constructor takes another object of the same class and builds a new, independent object with the same state. Copy immutable fields (like String) by reference; copy mutable fields (like a List) into a new object, or the two objects will share and change the same list.

import java.util.*;

public class CopyCtor {
    static class Policy {
        private final String holder;
        private final List<String> nominees;

        Policy(String holder, List<String> nominees) {
            this.holder = holder;
            this.nominees = new ArrayList<>(nominees);
        }

        // Copy constructor: a new, independent object with the same state
        Policy(Policy other) {
            this.holder = other.holder;                       // String is immutable: share it
            this.nominees = new ArrayList<>(other.nominees);  // List is mutable: copy it
        }

        void addNominee(String name) { nominees.add(name); }
        List<String> nominees() { return List.copyOf(nominees); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Policy original = new Policy("Meera", List.of("Arjun"));
        Policy copy = new Policy(original);
        copy.addNominee("Kavya");
        System.out.println("original: " + original.nominees());
        System.out.println("copy:     " + copy.nominees());
    }
}
original: [Arjun]
copy:     [Arjun, Kavya]

Notice that Policy(Policy other) reads other.nominees even though the field is private. Access in Java is per class, not per object, so code inside Policy may read the private fields of any Policy. The JDK uses copy constructors everywhere: new ArrayList<>(otherList), new HashMap<>(otherMap). They are preferred over clone() — see copying objects.

Private constructors and static factory methods

A private constructor stops other classes from calling new. You use it for:

  • Utility classes that only have static methods (Math, Collections) — see static.
  • Singletons, where exactly one instance must exist (System Design · Module 2).
  • Static factory methods — static methods that create objects for the caller: List.of(…), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 18), Integer.valueOf(42).

Factories have advantages over constructors: they have names (Money.ofRupees(250) reads better than new Money(25000)), they can return a cached object instead of a new one (Integer.valueOf caches −128 to 127 by default), and they can return a subtype. Their downside is that they are less visible than constructors in the class's API.

Edge cases and surprises

  • A "constructor" with a return type is a method. void FakeCtor() { status = "ACTIVE"; } compiles as an ordinary method named like the class. new FakeCtor() uses the default constructor, the "constructor" never runs, and status stays null. javac does not even warn you.
  • Modifiers: final, static, abstract and synchronized are not allowed on a constructor (modifier final not allowed here).
  • Abstract classes have constructors too. You cannot call them with new, but subclasses call them through super(…).
  • A constructor that throws means new completes abruptly and no reference is assigned — the caller never gets the half-built object.
  • Enums and records follow special rules: enum constructors are always private, and records get a canonical constructor instead of a no-arg one (see enums and records).

Mistake: the parameter shadows the field

Wrong: assigns the parameter to itself

class Customer {
    private String name;
    Customer(String name) {
        name = name;        // field stays null
    }
}

Right: this.name is the field

class Customer {
    private final String name;
    Customer(String name) {
        this.name = name;   // field = parameter
    }
}

Making the field final turns this bug into a compile error, because a final field that is never assigned is reported (variable name might not have been initialized).

Tip: too many constructor parameters? Use a builder

A constructor with seven parameters (several of them optional) is hard to call correctly — new Pizza("L", true, false, true, null, 2, "thin"). This is the telescoping constructor problem. The usual fix is the Builder pattern (a static nested Builder class, see nested classes), or a record plus a few static factories.

Interview: constructor questions

  • Can a constructor be private? Yes — singletons, utility classes, static factories.
  • Can it be final, static or abstract? No. Constructors are not inherited, so final and abstract mean nothing; static makes no sense because a constructor works on a new instance.
  • Can you override a constructor? No (not inherited), but you can overload it.
  • What is constructor chaining? One constructor calling another with this(…) (same class) or super(…) (parent class), first statement, so setup logic is written once.
  • Does a constructor return anything? It has no return type; the new expression produces the reference.

The this keyword: what it is and where you use it

Inside an instance method or constructor, this is a reference to the object being worked on; you use it to separate a field from a parameter, call another constructor, pass the object to someone else, return it for chaining and reach an outer object.

When you write ravi.withdraw(500), the method withdraw runs on one particular object: ravi. Inside the method, the keyword this is a reference to that object. The compiler passes it as a hidden extra argument to every instance method call. Most of the time you do not write it, because Java adds it for you: balance -= amount means this.balance -= amount.

Three facts about this

  • It exists only in instance context: instance methods, constructors, instance initializer blocks and instance field initializers. A static method belongs to the class, not to an object, so it has no this (see static).
  • Its type is the class where the code is written, but at run time it can be an object of a subclass. In a method of Account, this may really be a SavingsAccount. This is what makes polymorphism work.
  • You cannot assign to it: this = other; is a compile error. It is also never null. If you call a method on a null reference, the NullPointerException happens at the call, before the method starts.

Use 1: separate a field from a parameter

When a parameter or local variable has the same name as a field, the parameter shadows (hides) the field. Inside that method, the plain name means the parameter. Write this.name to reach the field.

public class Customer {
    private String name;
    private int age;

    public Customer(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;      // field = parameter
        this.age = age;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;      // same pattern in a setter
    }
}

This is the most common use of this. Using the same name for the parameter and the field is a normal Java style, because the name says exactly what the value is. The risk is forgetting the this. — see the mistake in constructors.

Use 2: call another constructor with this(…)

Inside a constructor, this(…) calls another constructor of the same class. You use it to write the setup and validation once and let the short constructors delegate to the full one. The rules (first statement, no loops, no instance members in the arguments) are in constructors in depth.

Use 3: pass the current object to someone else

Sometimes an object must hand itself to another object — to register as a listener, to add itself to a list, or to ask a helper to work on it. You pass this as the argument.

import java.util.*;

public class PriceDemo {
    static class PriceFeed {
        private final List<PriceAlert> subscribers = new ArrayList<>();
        void subscribe(PriceAlert alert) { subscribers.add(alert); }
        void publish(long paise) {
            for (PriceAlert a : subscribers) a.onPrice(paise);
        }
    }

    static class PriceAlert {
        private final String productId;
        private final long targetPaise;

        PriceAlert(String productId, long targetPaise) {
            this.productId = productId;
            this.targetPaise = targetPaise;
        }

        void watch(PriceFeed feed) {
            feed.subscribe(this);          // "here I am": passes the current object
        }

        void onPrice(long paise) {
            if (paise <= targetPaise) {
                System.out.println("Alert " + productId + ": price dropped to " + paise);
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PriceFeed feed = new PriceFeed();
        new PriceAlert("SKU-101", 45_000).watch(feed);
        feed.publish(49_900);
        feed.publish(44_900);
    }
}
Alert SKU-101: price dropped to 44900

Only the second price is at or below the target of 45,000 paise, so only one alert prints.

Mistake: letting this escape from a constructor

If a constructor passes this to other code before all fields are assigned, that code can see a half-built object. In multithreaded code another thread may even call it at that moment (Module 6).

Wrong: this escapes first

PriceAlert(String productId, long target, PriceFeed feed) {
    feed.subscribe(this);          // a callback now sees productId == null
    this.productId = productId;
    this.targetPaise = target;
}

Right: finish building, then publish

static PriceAlert createAndWatch(String productId, long target, PriceFeed feed) {
    PriceAlert alert = new PriceAlert(productId, target);   // fully built
    feed.subscribe(alert);                                  // then shared
    return alert;
}

Use 4: return this for method chaining

If a method changes the object and then returns this, callers can chain calls on one line. This is called a fluent style. StringBuilder.append() works this way, and builders use it heavily.

import java.util.*;

public class ThisDemo {
    static class Pizza {
        private String size = "M";
        private boolean extraCheese;
        private final List<String> toppings = new ArrayList<>();

        Pizza size(String size) { this.size = size; return this; }
        Pizza extraCheese()     { this.extraCheese = true; return this; }
        Pizza topping(String t) { toppings.add(t); return this; }

        @Override public String toString() {
            return "Pizza[size=" + size + ", extraCheese=" + extraCheese
                    + ", toppings=" + toppings + "]";
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Pizza p = new Pizza().size("L").extraCheese().topping("onion").topping("capsicum");
        System.out.println(p);
    }
}
Pizza[size=L, extraCheese=true, toppings=[onion, capsicum]]

Notice that the methods are named after the property (size(…)), not setSize(…). That is the usual fluent-API naming, and it is different from the JavaBeans naming you will meet in encapsulation. Immutable classes cannot change themselves, so their "chain" methods return a new object instead of this.

Use 5: name the outer object with Outer.this

An inner class (a class declared inside another class, see nested classes) holds a hidden reference to an object of the outer class. If both classes have a field with the same name, Outer.this reaches the outer one.

public class OuterThis {
    private String name = "outer";

    class Inner {
        private String name = "inner";
        void show() {
            System.out.println(name);               // the closest one: inner
            System.out.println(this.name);          // inner
            System.out.println(OuterThis.this.name);// outer
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new OuterThis().new Inner().show();
    }
}
inner
inner
outer

Quick reference

FormMeaningWhere you can use it
thisThe current objectInstance methods, constructors, instance blocks
this.x, this.m()A field or method of the current objectSame; needed only when a local name hides the field
this(…)Call another constructor of the same classFirst statement of a constructor
Outer.thisThe enclosing object of an inner classInside an inner (non-static) class
super.m(), super(…)The parent's version (not this keyword, but its sibling)Subclasses — see inheritance

Rules for this

  • It is allowed only in instance context. In a static method javac says non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context.
  • It cannot be reassigned.
  • this(…) and super(…) must be the first statement of a constructor, and a constructor can use only one of them (Java 25 relaxes the "first" part, see the version note in constructors).

Edge cases

  • Lambdas and anonymous classes differ. Inside a lambda, this means the enclosing object, because a lambda is not a new object. Inside an anonymous class, this is the anonymous object itself, and you write Outer.this for the enclosing one (Module 5).
  • Overridable calls through this. A call like describe() in a constructor really means this.describe(), and it runs the subclass version, even though the subclass is not ready yet (see initialization order).
  • Field initializers may use this, but only fields declared above them are guaranteed to be set at that point.

When to write this

  • Write this. when you must: shadowing, passing the object on, returning it, this(…). Leave it out elsewhere; extra this. everywhere is noise.
  • Some teams require this. on every field access to make fields stand out. Follow your team's style guide and stay consistent.

Interview: "What is this, and can you use it in a static method?"

  • this is a reference to the current object; it is passed implicitly to every instance method and constructor.
  • No, you cannot use it in a static method, because static code runs without any object.
  • Name the uses: disambiguate field vs parameter, this(…) chaining, passing the object, returning it for chaining, Outer.this.
  • Difference to remember: this is a reference to an object; this(…) is a constructor call. They are different things that share a word.

static: shared fields, methods, blocks and utility classes

A static member belongs to the class itself, not to any object: there is one shared copy, you use it without new, and because there is no this a static method cannot touch instance fields.

Normally every object has its own copy of each field. Two Account objects have two balances. Sometimes you need something that exists once for the whole class: a counter of created accounts, a constant, a helper like Math.max(). That is what static is for.

Static fields: one copy for the class

A static field is created once, when the class is first initialized, and every object (and every piece of code) sees the same value. Access it with the class name: Account.totalAccounts.

public class StaticDemo {
    static class Account {
        private static int totalAccounts = 0;   // one copy, shared by all accounts
        private final int id;                   // one copy per account

        Account() {
            id = ++totalAccounts;               // each new account takes the next number
        }

        static int getTotalAccounts() { return totalAccounts; }
        int getId() { return id; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Account a = new Account();
        Account b = new Account();
        System.out.println(a.getId() + " " + b.getId() + " total=" + Account.getTotalAccounts());
    }
}
1 2 total=2

Static fields are good for constants (static final), counters and caches. They are risky for anything that changes, because the one copy is shared by every thread and every user of the program. The line ++totalAccounts above is not safe when two threads create accounts at the same time; Module 6 shows AtomicInteger for that. A static field also lives as long as the class is loaded, which is normally the whole run of the application (Module 7).

Static methods: functions that need no object

A static method is called with the class name and works only on its parameters and on other static members. The JDK is full of them: Math.max(), Integer.parseInt(), Arrays.sort(), List.of(), String.valueOf(). The main method is static because the JVM must start your program before any object exists.

A static method has no this, so it cannot use instance fields or call instance methods directly. The compiler asks the right question: whose field? There may be a hundred Counter objects, and the static method is not running on any of them.

public class Counter {
    private int count = 0;

    static void reset() {
        count = 0;           // whose count?
        this.count = 0;      // there is no this
        increment();         // increment() needs an object too
    }

    void increment() { count++; }
}
Counter.java:5: error: non-static variable count cannot be referenced from a static context
        count = 0;
        ^
Counter.java:6: error: non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context
        this.count = 0;
        ^
Counter.java:7: error: non-static method increment() cannot be referenced from a static context
        increment();
        ^
3 errors

You have three honest fixes. Make the field static if it really is shared state. Make the method an instance method if it works on one object. Or pass an object in: static void reset(Counter c) { c.count = 0; }. A static method can use instance members through an object reference; what it cannot do is use them without one.

Static blocks: one-time setup for the class

A static initializer block is code in static { … } that runs once, when the class is initialized. Use it when a static field needs more than one expression to set up.

import java.util.*;

public class CountryCodes {
    private static final Map<String, String> DIAL_CODES = new HashMap<>();

    static {                                  // runs once, when the class loads
        DIAL_CODES.put("IN", "+91");
        DIAL_CODES.put("US", "+1");
        DIAL_CODES.put("GB", "+44");
    }

    public static String dialCode(String iso) {
        return DIAL_CODES.get(iso);
    }
}
