A class can have several static blocks; they run in the order they appear, mixed with static field initializers. For a small constant map, Map.of("IN", "+91", "US", "+1") is shorter and the result cannot be modified. The exact order of everything is in initialization order.

When a static initializer fails

If a static initializer throws, the class cannot be initialized. The first use gives ExceptionInInitializerError (with the real exception as its cause). Every later use gives NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class …, which hides the original cause and confuses people. Look for the first error in the logs.

public class StaticInitFail {
    static class Config {
        static final int PORT = Integer.parseInt("80x");   // throws while loading Config
        static int port() { return PORT; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try { Config.port(); }
        catch (Throwable t) { System.out.println(t.getClass().getName() + " <- " + t.getCause()); }
        try { Config.port(); }
        catch (Throwable t) { System.out.println(t.getClass().getName() + ": " + t.getMessage()); }
    }
}
java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError <- java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "80x"
java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class StaticInitFail$Config

Static versus instance at a glance

AspectInstance memberStatic member
Belongs toOne objectThe class
CopiesOne per objectOne per class
Created whenEach newThe class is first initialized
Accessed withAn object referenceThe class name
Has this?YesNo
Can use instance members?YesOnly through an object reference
Can use static members?YesYes
OverridingMethods can be overriddenMethods are hidden, never overridden (overriding)

Utility classes

A utility class is a class that only holds static methods, with no state. Math, Arrays, Collections and Objects are examples. Nobody should create an object of such a class, so the convention is: a final class with a private constructor.

public final class RupeeFormat {
    private RupeeFormat() {
        throw new AssertionError("Utility class, do not instantiate");
    }

    // assumes paise >= 0
    public static String ofPaise(long paise) {
        return String.format("Rs. %d.%02d", paise / 100, paise % 100);
    }
}

// RupeeFormat.ofPaise(1_29_900)  returns  "Rs. 1299.00"

The private constructor stops new RupeeFormat() from outside, and the AssertionError stops accidental calls from inside the class. Use static helpers for pure functions (same input, same output, no hidden state). When logic needs state or must be replaced in a test, make it a normal class and let Spring inject it.

Static and inheritance

  • A static field is shared with subclasses: there is still only one copy. A subclass that declares a field with the same name creates a second, separate field (that is hiding, not overriding).
  • A static method is inherited by name, but redeclaring it in a subclass hides it. Which one runs depends on the declared type of the reference, not on the object (overriding rules).
  • Static members cannot be abstract, and an interface may have static methods that are not inherited by the classes that implement it (interfaces).

Edge cases and surprises

  • Calling a static method on a null reference works. Util u = null; u.hello(); prints the result with no NullPointerException, because the compiler uses the declared type Util and ignores the value. Never write code like this; call Util.hello().
  • No static local variables. Unlike C, static int x; inside a method is a compile error. If a value must survive between calls, make it a field.
  • Static fields are not serialized with the object, because they do not belong to it.
  • The main method can be overloaded, but the JVM starts the program only through public static void main(String[] args). Java 25 also allows simpler forms of main, for example without String[] args, mainly to make first programs easier to write (JEP 512); real projects still use the classic form.
  • Constants are inlined. A static final primitive or String with a constant value is copied into the code that uses it (more in final).

Mistake: using static for data that belongs to one user or one request

There is one copy of a static field per JVM. In a web application, one JVM serves all users at the same time, so a static "current user" is shared by everybody. Users see each other's data, and the bug shows up only under load.

Wrong: one value for all users

public class UserContext {
    private static String currentUser;     // shared by every request thread
    public static void set(String user) { currentUser = user; }
    public static String get() { return currentUser; }
}

Right: pass it, or keep it per request

public class OrderService {
    public Order place(String user, Cart cart) {   // pass the user as a parameter
        return new Order(user, cart);
    }
}
// Frameworks keep per-request data in ThreadLocal or request-scoped beans.

Conventions

  • Constants: public static final and UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, for example MAX_RETRIES.
  • Call static members through the class name (Account.getTotalAccounts()), never through an object. IDEs warn about the second form.
  • Keep static mutable state to a minimum. It makes code hard to test and unsafe across threads.
  • Utility class: final + private constructor + only static methods.

In a real Spring Boot project

You write exactly one important static method yourself: public static void main that calls SpringApplication.run(…). Everything else is usually an instance method on a Spring bean. You will still call many static methods from the JDK and libraries (LocalDate.now(), Objects.requireNonNull(), Collectors.toList()) and write a few small static helpers and constants.

Interview: static questions

  • Why is main static? The JVM calls it before any object exists, so it must not need one.
  • Can a static method use instance variables? Not directly — there is no this. It can through an object reference.
  • Can static methods be overridden? No. They are hidden; the declared type of the reference decides which runs.
  • Static block vs instance block? Static: once, at class initialization. Instance: every new, before the constructor body.
  • When does a static block run? When the class is first initialized (first new, static method call, or non-constant static field access).

Initialization order: static blocks, instance blocks and constructors

Static code runs once when the class is first used, parent before child; then for every new, the parent's field initializers, instance blocks and constructor run first, followed by the child's.

Output-prediction questions about "what prints first?" are among the most common Java interview puzzles. They are easy once you know the order and impossible if you guess. This article gives you the order, the reason behind it and the traps.

Two kinds of initialization

Class initialization
Happens once per class, the first time the class is really used. It runs static field initializers and static { } blocks, in the order they are written.
Instance initialization
Happens once per object, during new. It runs instance field initializers, instance blocks { } and the constructor.

An instance initializer block is a plain { … } in the class body. It runs for every object, before the constructor body. Constructor chaining (this(…)) is usually a better way to share code, but you will see instance blocks in puzzles and in anonymous classes, which cannot have constructors.

The order, step by step

Take class Child extends Parent and the statement new Child() executed for the first time:

StepWhat runsHow often
1Parent: static fields and static blocks, in textual orderOnce per class
2Child: static fields and static blocks, in textual orderOnce per class
3Memory for the object is allocated; every field gets its default value (0, false, null)Every new
4The Child constructor starts and first calls super(…) (written or implicit)Every new
5Parent: instance field initializers and instance blocks, in textual orderEvery new
6Parent constructor bodyEvery new
7Child: instance field initializers and instance blocks, in textual orderEvery new
8Child constructor bodyEvery new

The reason for "parent first" is simple: the child may depend on things the parent sets up, so the parent part of the object must be complete before the child part starts. This is also why the super(…) call must come first in a constructor.

A complete example

public class InitOrder {
    static class Parent {
        static { System.out.println("1. Parent static block"); }
        { System.out.println("3. Parent instance block"); }
        Parent() { System.out.println("4. Parent constructor"); }
    }

    static class Child extends Parent {
        static { System.out.println("2. Child static block"); }
        { System.out.println("5. Child instance block"); }
        Child() { System.out.println("6. Child constructor"); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("main starts");
        new Child();
        System.out.println("--- second object ---");
        new Child();
    }
}
main starts
1. Parent static block
2. Child static block
3. Parent instance block
4. Parent constructor
5. Child instance block
6. Child constructor
--- second object ---
3. Parent instance block
4. Parent constructor
5. Child instance block
6. Child constructor

Two things to notice. "main starts" comes first, because the nested classes are not initialized until they are used. And the second object skips the static blocks: they ran once, for the class.

Now a self-check with field initializers. Predict the output before you open the answer.

public class FieldInit {
    static class Part { Part(String n) { System.out.println("Part " + n); } }

    static class Base {
        Part p1 = new Part("Base field");
        Base() { System.out.println("Base()"); }
    }

    static class Sub extends Base {
        Part p2 = new Part("Sub field");
        Sub() { System.out.println("Sub()"); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { new Sub(); }
}
What does new Sub() print? 
Part Base field
Base()
Part Sub field
Sub()

Field initializers run at the start of each class's part of construction (steps 5 and 7), before that class's constructor body, and the parent's part is complete before the child's part begins.

When is a class initialized?

Class initialization is lazy: it happens at the first active use of the class. These count as active use:

  • creating an object with new;
  • calling a static method of the class;
  • reading or writing a static field that is not a compile-time constant;
  • initializing a subclass (the superclass is initialized first);
  • starting the program with the class that has main, or calling Class.forName("…").

These do not trigger initialization: declaring a variable or an array of the type, and reading a constant (a static final primitive or String set from a constant expression), because javac copies the value into the caller. Also, reading a static field through a subclass initializes only the class that declares the field.

public class Trig {
    static class Parent { static int x = 10; static { System.out.println("Parent init"); } }
    static class Child extends Parent { static { System.out.println("Child init"); } }
    static class Consts {
        static final int MAX = 5;                    // constant
        static { System.out.println("Consts init"); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Child.x);                 // x is declared in Parent
        System.out.println(Consts.MAX);              // constant: no initialization
        System.out.println("now touching a non-constant");
        Object o = new Consts();                     // new: initialization happens here
    }
}
Parent init
10
5
now touching a non-constant
Consts init

Textual order and forward references

Field initializers and blocks of the same kind run in the order they appear in the file. If one initializer uses a field that is declared later, the field still has its default value. javac rejects the simplest form of this, but a method call hides it:

public class Fwd {
    static int a = initA();      // runs first
    static int b = 5;            // runs second
    static int initA() { return b + 1; }   // b is still 0 here

    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(a + " " + b); }
}
1 5

If you write static int a = b + 1; directly, javac stops with illegal forward reference. The method call is the loophole: it compiles, and a becomes 1, not 6.

The classic trap: calling an overridable method from a constructor

The parent constructor runs before the child's field initializers. If the parent constructor calls a method that the child overrides, the child's version runs on an object whose child fields are still at their default values.

public class Trap {
    static class Base {
        Base() { describe(); }                      // looks harmless...
        void describe() { System.out.println("Base"); }
    }

    static class Derived extends Base {
        private String name = "Derived";
        private final int size = 10;
        private int count = 5;

        Derived() { super(); }

        @Override void describe() {
            System.out.println("name=" + name + ", size=" + size + ", count=" + count);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) { new Derived(); }
}
name=null, size=10, count=0

The overridden describe() ran in step 4, while name and count were still null and 0 (step 3 defaults). The initializers "Derived" and 5 would run later, in step 7. The field size printed 10 only because private final int size = 10; is a compile-time constant: javac copies the 10 into describe().

Rule: never call an overridable method from a constructor or initializer

A method is overridable if it is not private, static or final. Either call only private or final methods there, or finish construction first and then call a normal method (for example from a static factory). The same advice applies to clone() and deserialization hooks.

Constructors that call this(…)

Instance initializers run as part of the constructor that calls super(…). A constructor that starts with this(…) does not run them again; they run once, in the constructor at the end of the chain.

public class Chain {
    { System.out.println("instance block"); }
    Chain() { this(1); System.out.println("Chain()"); }
    Chain(int x) { System.out.println("Chain(int)"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) { new Chain(); }
}
instance block
Chain(int)
Chain()

Edge cases

  • Exceptions. An exception in an instance block or constructor comes out of new, and you get no object. An exception in a static block becomes ExceptionInInitializerError (see static).
  • Interfaces. Initializing a class does not initialize the interfaces it implements, unless those interfaces declare default methods.
  • Singletons. The JVM runs class initialization under a lock, so private static final Service INSTANCE = new Service(); is created safely once, even with many threads (System Design · Module 2).
  • Enums create all their constants during class initialization, before any static block of the enum runs (enums).

Tip: how to answer an order puzzle

Write the numbers 1 to 8 from the table on paper. First mark which classes are being initialized for the first time (static work), then walk through each new from the top of the hierarchy down. Output puzzles stop being scary when you do it mechanically. Remember the short version: static before instance, parent before child, blocks and field initializers before the constructor body.

Interview: "In what order do static blocks, instance blocks and constructors run?"

  • Static blocks and static fields run once, when the class is first initialized, parent class first.
  • For each object: parent instance initializers, then parent constructor body, then child instance initializers, then child constructor body.
  • Add the trap: an overridden method called from the parent constructor sees default values in the child's fields.
  • Add one edge case: a constant (static final int X = 5) does not trigger class initialization.

Access modifiers: private, package-private, protected and public

Access modifiers decide which code may use a class, field, method or constructor: private means this class only, no modifier means the same package, protected adds subclasses, and public means everyone.

Access modifiers are the tool behind encapsulation. Every member you make visible becomes part of your class's public contract: other code can depend on it, and you cannot change it freely any more. So the rule is to show as little as possible.

The four levels

ModifierSame classSame packageSubclass in another packageEveryone else
private✓✗✗✗
(none) package-private✓✓✗✗
protected✓✓✓ (see below)✗
public✓✓✓✓
  • private — visible only inside the class that declares it (and inside its nested classes). Use it for fields and helper methods. It is the default choice.
  • package-private (also called default access) — you write nothing. Visible to every class in the same package. Use it for things that classes of one package share but the outside world must not see. There is no keyword for it: the word default is used only for interface default methods and switch.
  • protected — visible in the same package and to subclasses in other packages. Use it for deliberate extension points, such as a hook method that subclasses override.
  • public — visible everywhere. Use it only for the API you want other code to rely on.

The four levels across two packages

Access rules are about packages, so an example needs two. Account lives in com.bank; Savings extends it from com.bank.app.

package com.bank;

public class Account {
    private long secret = 1;
    long packageLevel = 2;                 // package-private
    protected long balance = 3;
    public long publicField = 4;

    protected void audit() { System.out.println("audit"); }
    protected Account() { }
    public static Account open() { return new Account(); }
}
package com.bank.app;

import com.bank.Account;

public class Savings extends Account {
    void test(Savings s, Account a) {
        this.balance = 1;                  // ok: inherited protected member
        s.balance = 2;                     // ok: the reference is a Savings
        a.balance = 3;                     // error
        a.audit();                         // error
        long x = secret;                   // error
        long y = packageLevel;             // error
        long z = publicField;              // ok
        Account fresh = new Account();     // error
    }
}
Savings.java:9: error: balance has protected access in Account
Savings.java:10: error: audit() has protected access in Account
Savings.java:11: error: secret has private access in Account
Savings.java:12: error: packageLevel is not public in Account; cannot be accessed from outside package
Savings.java:14: error: Account() has protected access in Account
5 errors

The protected subtlety

Most people think protected means "my subclasses can use it". That is only half the rule. Outside the parent's package, subclass code can use a protected member only on objects of its own type (this, or any reference whose type is the subclass or below). It cannot use it on a plain parent-type reference. In the example, s.balance compiles because s is a Savings, but a.balance does not, because a is an Account and might really be some other subclass, such as a CurrentAccount, that Savings has no business changing.

Two more details follow from the same rule:

  • Inside the same package, protected is as open as package-private plus subclasses. It is wider than package-private, not narrower.
  • A protected constructor cannot be called with new from another package, even from a subclass (last error above). A subclass reaches it through super(…). An anonymous subclass such as new Account() { } is allowed, because it is itself a subclass.

Access rules for classes

A top-level class can only be public or package-private. private and protected do not make sense for it, because there is no enclosing class or subclass context to restrict to.

private class Hidden { }       // error
protected class Prot { }       // error
public class TopLevel { }      // ok
TopLevel.java:1: error: modifier private not allowed here
TopLevel.java:2: error: modifier protected not allowed here

A nested class (declared inside another class) is a member, so it can use all four levels. A public top-level class must be in a file with the same name. A package-private class is invisible outside its package, which makes it a good way to hide helper classes (packages).

Access modifiers in other places

  • Interface members are public by default, so an implementing method must be declared public (interfaces).
  • Overriding may widen access but never narrow it (overriding rules).
  • Enum constructors are always private, and record fields are private and final (enums, records).
  • Access is per class, not per object. Code inside Account may read the private fields of another Account object, which is why equals() and copy constructors can touch other.balance.

Which modifier should I choose?

WhatDefault choiceOpen it up when
FieldsprivateNever, except constants (public static final)
Helper methodsprivateAnother class in the package needs it (package-private) or a test does
Methods that form the APIpublic—
Hook methods for subclassesprotected—
ClassesPackage-privateCode in other packages must use it

Edge cases

  • private is not a security feature. Reflection with setAccessible(true) can read private fields; frameworks such as Hibernate and Jackson do exactly that. Since Java 17 the JDK's own internals are closed to this by default (JEP 403), but your own classes are not.
  • Nested classes and their outer class can see each other's private members. The compiler and JVM treat them as one unit.
  • Sub-packages are unrelated. com.bank and com.bank.app are two different packages; package-private access does not cross between them.
  • Modules (JPMS). If a library uses module-info.java, a public class in a package that the module does not exports is still not reachable from other modules. Most Spring Boot applications do not use modules.

Mistake: public fields

Wrong: anyone can break the rule

public class Account {
    public long balance;       // account.balance = -500; compiles and runs
}

Right: private field, safe methods

public class Account {
    private long balance;
    public void deposit(long amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        balance += amount;
    }
    public long getBalance() { return balance; }
}

Tip: package-private helps testing

A test class in the same package (same folder path under src/test/java) can call package-private methods. So you can keep a helper off the public API and still test it directly. You do not have to make it public only for the test's sake.

In real projects

JPA entities usually have a protected no-argument constructor: Hibernate can use it, but application code in other packages cannot create half-empty objects. Service classes keep their dependencies in private final fields. Most classes in a well-designed package are package-private; only the few that form the package's entry points are public.

Interview: access modifier questions

  • Draw the table. Rows private, default, protected, public; columns class, package, subclass, world.
  • Difference between default and protected? Both allow the same package; protected also allows subclasses in other packages (through a subclass-typed reference).
  • Can a top-level class be private or protected? No — only public or package-private.
  • Can an overriding method have weaker access? No; it can only keep or widen access.
  • Can an object read another object's private field? Yes, if both are of the same class: access is per class.

Encapsulation: private data, safe methods, getters and setters

Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and letting other code change it only through methods that check the rules, so the class alone controls its own state.

Encapsulation is the first of the four pillars. The word comes from "capsule": the data and the code that works on it are packed together, and the outside world sees only a small, safe surface. Why OOP already showed the idea with an Account class; this article gives you the complete set of rules.

Two ideas in one pillar

  • Bundling — the fields and the methods that work on them live together in one class.
  • Information hiding — the fields are private; other code uses public methods only. The class decides what is visible (access modifiers).

Why bother? Four practical benefits:

  • Invariants stay true. An invariant is a rule that must always hold: "a price is positive", "a balance never goes below zero". If only the class can change the data, only the class has to enforce the rule.
  • You can change the inside. Today the price is a long in paise; next year it becomes a BigDecimal. Callers do not break, as long as the public methods stay the same.
  • One place for extra work. Logging, validation, caching and thread safety (synchronized, Module 6) go into the method, not into every caller.
  • A smaller surface. Less public code means less that other developers can misuse or depend on.

Private fields plus methods that guard them

The pattern has two steps: make every field private, then add methods that check the rules before changing anything. Rules that apply to construction go into the constructor, so an invalid object can never exist.

public class ProductDemo {
    static class Product {
        private final String sku;              // never changes: final, no setter
        private String name;
        private long pricePaise;

        Product(String sku, String name, long pricePaise) {
            this.sku = requireText(sku, "sku");
            this.name = requireText(name, "name");
            this.pricePaise = requirePositive(pricePaise, "pricePaise");
        }

        void rename(String newName) { this.name = requireText(newName, "name"); }
        void changePrice(long newPricePaise) {
            this.pricePaise = requirePositive(newPricePaise, "pricePaise");
        }
        String getName()     { return name; }
        long getPricePaise() { return pricePaise; }

        private static String requireText(String value, String field) {
            if (value == null || value.isBlank()) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException(field + " must not be blank");
            }
            return value.strip();
        }

        private static long requirePositive(long value, String field) {
            if (value <= 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException(field + " must be positive, got " + value);
            }
            return value;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Product p = new Product("SKU-1", "  Wireless Mouse ", 49_900);
        p.changePrice(44_900);
        System.out.println(p.getName() + " costs " + p.getPricePaise() + " paise");
        try { p.changePrice(-1); }
        catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
        try { new Product(" ", "Cable", 100); }
        catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("Rejected: " + e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
Wireless Mouse costs 44900 paise
Rejected: pricePaise must be positive, got -1
Rejected: sku must not be blank

Look at the design choices. The checks live in two small private static helpers, so the constructor and the change methods share them. The constructor does not call the public methods rename() or changePrice(), because a subclass could override those, and calling an overridable method from a constructor is a trap (initialization order). And sku has no setter at all: it is final.

Getters and setters, and JavaBeans naming

A getter reads a field and a setter changes it. Java has a naming convention for them, called the JavaBeans convention. Frameworks depend on it: Jackson turns JSON into objects with it, Spring binds configuration properties with it, JPA can read entity state through it, and template engines use it.

FieldGetterSetter
private String namegetName()setName(String name)
private int stockgetStock()setStock(int stock)
private boolean activeisActive()setActive(boolean active)
private String firstNamegetFirstName()setFirstName(String firstName)
  • The property name is the method name without get, is or set, with the first letter in lower case: getFirstName() is the property firstName.
  • A getter has no parameters and returns the value. A setter has one parameter and normally returns void. Both are public.
  • For a primitive boolean, the getter is named isX().
  • A class that has a public no-argument constructor, private fields and getters and setters like this is called a JavaBean. A POJO ("plain old Java object") is looser: any ordinary class that does not depend on a framework.

Records do not follow this convention: a record component name gets an accessor called name(), not getName() (records). Modern Jackson versions know about records.

A setter is not a free pass

Beginners learn "make fields private and add a getter and a setter for each". Followed blindly, this gives you a public field with extra typing: setBalance(-500) breaks the rule just like balance = -500. The goal is not to hide the field; it is to protect the rule.

  • If a value never changes (an id, a creation time), make the field final and write no setter.
  • If a value changes for a business reason, write a method named after that reason: withdraw(), rename(), cancel(), changePrice().
  • If you must have a setter, put the validation in it. A setter that only does this.x = x protects nothing.

Wrong: ask, decide outside, push back

if (order.getStatus() == Status.PLACED) {
    order.setStatus(Status.CANCELLED);   // every caller repeats the rule
}

Right: tell the object what you want

order.cancel();    // Order knows which states may be cancelled
                   // and throws IllegalStateException otherwise

This habit has a name: tell, don't ask. Do not pull data out of an object, make a decision, and push a new value back. Tell the object what to do and let it decide. The business rule then lives in one class.

Do not leak mutable internals

Private fields are not enough if a getter hands out the internal object. A private List returned by a getter is a public list: the caller can add, remove or clear it, and your class never finds out.

import java.util.*;

public class CartDemo {
    static class ShoppingCart {
        private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();

        public void add(String item) { items.add(Objects.requireNonNull(item, "item")); }

        public List<String> leakyItems()    { return items; }                 // BAD
        public List<String> itemsView()     { return Collections.unmodifiableList(items); }
        public List<String> itemsSnapshot() { return List.copyOf(items); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ShoppingCart cart = new ShoppingCart();
        cart.add("Mouse");

        cart.leakyItems().add("Hacked");          // the cart never agreed to this
        System.out.println("after leak: " + cart.itemsSnapshot());

        List<String> view = cart.itemsView();
        List<String> snap = cart.itemsSnapshot();
        cart.add("Keyboard");
        System.out.println("view:     " + view);
        System.out.println("snapshot: " + snap);
        try { view.add("x"); }
        catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("view is read-only"); }
    }
}
after leak: [Mouse, Hacked]
view:     [Mouse, Hacked, Keyboard]
snapshot: [Mouse, Hacked]
view is read-only
What the getter returnsCaller can modify it?Sees later changes?Cost per call
The internal list itselfYes — never do thisYesNone
Collections.unmodifiableList(items) (a view)No (throws UnsupportedOperationException)Yes — it is a window on the live listTiny
List.copyOf(items) (a snapshot)NoNoCopies all elements
new ArrayList<>(items) (a mutable copy)Yes, but it changes only the copyNoCopies all elements

Use a view when callers only read right now. Use a snapshot when they keep the result. The same idea applies to arrays (return prices.clone()), to maps, and to any mutable object, such as java.util.Date. Copying data into the object is just as important; that is covered in immutable classes and defensive copies.

Rule: all fields private, all rules in one place

Declare fields private (constants excepted). Check every rule in the constructor and in the methods that change state, never in the caller. Never return or store a reference to a mutable object you want to protect without copying it.

Conventions

  • Fail fast: reject bad input at the door. Use IllegalArgumentException for a bad value, NullPointerException (through Objects.requireNonNull(x, "x")) for an unexpected null, and IllegalStateException when the object is in the wrong state for the call.
  • Follow the JavaBeans names (getX, isX, setX) for classes that frameworks will read. Avoid names that start with two capital letters, such as getURL(): different tools derive different property names from them.
  • Make fields final by default. Remove final only when the value must change.
  • Money is a long of paise or a BigDecimal, never a double.

Exceptions to "everything private"

  • Constants are public static final.
  • Plain data carriers such as records and DTOs (data transfer objects) have no rules to protect, so hiding gains little; a record's components are its public API.
  • A private nested class that only its outer class can see may have package-private fields (private static class Node { int value; Node next; }) because the class itself is hidden.
  • Runtime errors you will meet: UnsupportedOperationException when you modify a read-only view or List.of(…); NullPointerException from requireNonNull.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Getter and setter for every field (the "anemic" class). It adds ceremony and removes no risk. Think about behaviour first.
  • Returning internal collections or arrays directly, as shown above.
  • Validation only in the controller. Bean Validation on a request object checks the shape of input, but jobs, tests and imports create domain objects too. Keep the core rules in the domain class itself.
  • Calling a public setter from a constructor. A subclass may override it and run before its own fields are ready.

In a real Spring Boot project

JPA entities have private fields, a protected no-argument constructor, getters, and a few behaviour methods such as order.cancel(). Request and response DTOs are usually records. Lombok's @Getter and @Setter generate the boilerplate at compile time; they save typing, but a @Setter on every field brings back the problem of this article. Putting @Data on a JPA entity is widely discouraged, because the generated equals, hashCode and toString can trigger lazy loading and loops.

Interview: "What is encapsulation? Is it just getters and setters?"

  • Encapsulation = bundling data and methods together and hiding the data behind private fields, so that the object controls how its state changes.
  • Getters and setters are only the mechanism. The point is to protect invariants: validate in constructors and setters, expose behaviour (withdraw) rather than raw state, and never leak mutable internals.
  • Give the benefits: invariants, freedom to change internals, one place for logging and thread safety.
  • Be ready for "encapsulation vs abstraction": encapsulation protects state; abstraction hides complexity behind a contract (abstraction).

Immutable classes and defensive copies

An immutable object never changes after it is built; to make a class immutable use a final class, private final fields, no setters, and copy any mutable data that goes in or comes out.

An immutable object is one whose state cannot change after the constructor finishes. The JDK is full of them: String, the wrapper classes (Integer, Long), BigDecimal, LocalDate, Instant, Optional and the collections made by List.of(…). Records are immutable too, with one catch (see records).

Why immutability is worth the effort

  • Thread safety for free. Many threads can read the same object without locks, because nobody can change it (Module 6).
  • Safe to share and to cache. You can pass the object anywhere without copying it. Nobody can alter it behind your back.
  • Safe as a key. A HashMap key whose hash code changes gets lost in the map (equals() and hashCode()). An immutable key can never change its hash.
  • Simple to reason about. An object is either valid or it was never built. There is no "half-updated" state.

The cost is that every "change" creates a new object. For a few objects this is cheap. When you build a big value in many steps (a long string, a large report), use a mutable builder such as StringBuilder and make the final result immutable.

The recipe

  1. Declare the class final (or give it only private constructors), so that no subclass can add mutable state or override a getter.
  2. Make every field private final.
  3. Write no setters and no method that changes a field. To "change" something, return a new object. A method like that is often named withX (a wither).
  4. Copy mutable arguments in the constructor (a defensive copy), so the caller's own reference cannot change your state later.
  5. Never return a mutable field. Return an immutable value, a copy, or a read-only view.
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.*;

public class ImmutableDemo {
    static final class Customer {                          // 1. final class
        private final String name;                         // 2. private final fields
        private final LocalDate dob;                       //    (LocalDate is immutable)
        private final List<String> phones;                 //    (List is not, so we copy it)

        Customer(String name, LocalDate dob, List<String> phones) {
            this.name = Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name");
            this.dob = Objects.requireNonNull(dob, "dob");
            this.phones = List.copyOf(phones);             // 4. defensive copy, immutable
        }

        String getName() { return name; }
        LocalDate getDob() { return dob; }
        List<String> getPhones() { return phones; }        // 5. safe: already immutable

        Customer withName(String newName) {                // 3. "change" = new object
            return new Customer(newName, dob, phones);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> phones = new ArrayList<>(List.of("98100 00001"));
        Customer c = new Customer("Asha", LocalDate.of(1995, 4, 12), phones);

        phones.add("98100 00002");                         // caller changes its own list
        System.out.println(c.getPhones());                 // the customer did not change

        try { c.getPhones().add("x"); }
        catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("cannot modify phones"); }

        Customer c2 = c.withName("Asha K");
        System.out.println(c.getName() + " / " + c2.getName());
    }
}
[98100 00001]
cannot modify phones
Asha / Asha K

Defensive copies: copy in, copy out

A defensive copy is a private copy of a mutable object that you keep so that nobody else can change it. You need one at two points: when the object arrives (constructor or setter argument) and when it leaves (getter return value). The old java.util.Date class is a perfect example of the problem, because it is mutable:

Wrong: stores and returns the caller's Date

final class Event {
    private final Date start;                 // final reference, mutable object
    Event(Date start) { this.start = start; }
    Date getStart()   { return start; }
}

// in main():
Date d = new Date(1_000_000L);
Event e = new Event(d);
d.setTime(0);                                 // caller changes its own object
System.out.println(e.getStart().getTime());   // 0: the Event changed!
e.getStart().setTime(5);                      // a reader changes it via the getter
System.out.println(d.getTime());              // 5

Right: use an immutable type (or copy)

final class Event {
    private final Instant start;              // Instant is immutable
    Event(Instant start) {
        this.start = Objects.requireNonNull(start);
    }
    Instant getStart() { return start; }      // nothing to protect
}
// If you are stuck with Date: copy in and copy out
//   this.start = new Date(start.getTime());
//   return new Date(start.getTime());

The output of the wrong version is 0 and then 5. Modern code uses java.time (Instant, LocalDate, LocalDateTime), which is immutable, so the problem disappears.

Copy first, then validate the copy

When a constructor checks a mutable argument and then stores it, another thread could change the argument between the check and the copy. Copy first, and validate the copy:

final class DiscountSlabs {
    private final List<Integer> thresholdsPaise;

    DiscountSlabs(List<Integer> thresholdsPaise) {
        List<Integer> copy = List.copyOf(thresholdsPaise);  // 1. copy first
        if (copy.isEmpty()) {                               // 2. check the copy,
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("slabs required");   //    not the argument
        }
        this.thresholdsPaise = copy;
    }
}

List.copyOf throws NullPointerException if the list or any element is null, so you get null-checking for free.

Shallow and deep immutability

A final field only means the reference cannot change. An object is deeply immutable only if everything it can reach is immutable too. Ask this question for every field:

Field typeSafe to share?
int, long, boolean, String, BigDecimal, LocalDate, enumsYes: immutable
List.copyOf(…), Map.copyOf(…), List.of(…)Yes, if the elements are immutable too
ArrayList, HashMap, arrays, Date, StringBuilderNo: copy them in and out
Your own classOnly if that class is immutable

A List.copyOf of StringBuilder objects is an immutable list, but each builder inside can still change. That is why the second half of the table says "if the elements are immutable too".

Edge cases

  • Non-final classes break the guarantee. A subclass can add a mutable field or override a getter to return something changing. That is why step 1 matters.
  • String still has a non-final field. It caches its hash code in a private field after the first call. From the outside it is immutable, and this is fine. Immutability is about visible state.
  • Reflection can still change private final fields of ordinary classes (setAccessible(true)). That is abuse, not a design problem you must defend against.
  • Memory model. The Java memory model gives final fields a special guarantee: once the constructor ends, other threads see their correct values even without synchronization, as long as this did not escape during construction (Module 6).
  • Many fields? An immutable class with ten fields is awkward to construct. Use a builder (nested classes) or a record with static factories.

Mistake: thinking final makes the object immutable

Wrong: final reference, mutable list

private final List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();
public List<String> getTags() { return tags; }   // callers can add and remove

Right: immutable inside, immutable outside

private final List<String> tags;
Product(List<String> tags) { this.tags = List.copyOf(tags); }
public List<String> getTags() { return tags; }

In real projects

Value objects such as Money, Email or OrderId, request and response DTOs, domain events, cache values and configuration objects are all good immutable classes. JPA entities are mutable by nature, so keep them out of caches and out of shared state; map them to immutable DTOs at the edges of your service.

Interview: "How do you make a class immutable? Why is String immutable?"

  • List the five steps: final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies in, no mutable internals out.
  • Add the trap: final alone is not enough — a final field can point to a mutable list.
  • Why String is immutable: the string pool can share one object safely; it is used for security-sensitive values (file paths, URLs, class names, credentials); it is thread safe; and its cached hash code makes it a fast HashMap key.
  • Cost: more objects. Mention StringBuilder as the usual escape for heavy changes.

Inheritance: extends, super and the is-a relationship

With extends, a subclass receives the accessible fields and methods of its parent and can add or change behaviour; use it only when the subclass really is a kind of the parent, because it ties the two classes together.

Inheritance lets one class build on another. The existing class is the superclass (also called parent or base class). The new class is the subclass (child or derived class). The subclass inherits the parent's accessible members, so you do not copy code, and an object of the subclass can be used wherever the parent type is expected. That second point is what makes polymorphism possible.

A first example

Every employee has a name and a salary. A manager is an employee who also gets a bonus and can approve leave.

public class Employee {
    private final String name;
    private final long baseSalary;            // rupees per month

    public Employee(String name, long baseSalary) {
        this.name = name;
        this.baseSalary = baseSalary;
    }

    public String getName() { return name; }
    public long monthlyPay() { return baseSalary; }

    @Override public String toString() { return name + " earns " + monthlyPay(); }
}
public class Manager extends Employee {
    private final long bonus;

    public Manager(String name, long baseSalary, long bonus) {
        super(name, baseSalary);               // build the Employee part first
        this.bonus = bonus;
    }

    @Override public long monthlyPay() {
        return super.monthlyPay() + bonus;     // reuse the parent's logic, then add
    }

    public void approveLeave(Employee e) {
        System.out.println(getName() + " approved leave for " + e.getName());
    }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Employee e = new Employee("Asha", 50_000);
        Manager m = new Manager("Ravi", 80_000, 15_000);
        System.out.println(e);
        System.out.println(m);                 // toString() is inherited from Employee
        m.approveLeave(e);

        Employee asEmployee = m;               // a Manager IS-A Employee
        System.out.println(asEmployee.monthlyPay());
    }
}
Asha earns 50000
Ravi earns 95000
Ravi approved leave for Asha
95000

Three things happened. Manager got getName() and toString() without writing them. Manager added a field and a method. And it changed a behaviour by overriding monthlyPay(). The last line shows that a Manager object works through an Employee variable, and still uses its own version of monthlyPay().

What is inherited and what is not

Member of the parentIn the subclass
public and protected fields and methodsInherited and usable by name
Package-private membersInherited only if the subclass is in the same package
private membersNot accessible by name. The data is still inside every object, but only the parent's own methods can touch it
ConstructorsNot inherited. Each class has its own and calls the parent's with super(…)
static membersUsable through the subclass name, but a redeclared static method hides, not overrides
Initializer blocksNot inherited, but the parent's blocks still run when a child object is built

The private rule surprises people. A Manager object does contain the baseSalary field; you can see its effect in monthlyPay(). But code written in Manager cannot name it: return baseSalary; there is a compile error (baseSalary has private access in Employee). The subclass must use the parent's public or protected methods. This keeps the parent in control of its own data.

The three uses of super

FormMeaningExample
super(args)Call a parent constructor. First statement of a constructorsuper(name, baseSalary);
super.method()Call the parent's version of an overridden methodsuper.monthlyPay()
super.fieldReach a parent field hidden by a field of the same name (rare, avoid)super.name

Every constructor runs a parent constructor first. If you write neither this(…) nor super(…), the compiler adds super(). If the parent has no no-argument constructor, you must call a parent constructor yourself. The full story, including the order in which things run, is in constructors and initialization order.

Single inheritance, Object and the diamond problem

A Java class can extend only one class. Every class extends Object, either directly or through its parents, so even Manager has equals() and hashCode() (the Object class). Chains of any length are fine: Object → Employee → Manager → Director.

Why not two parents? Imagine class D extends B, C where B and C both extend A and both override the method work(). Which version does D inherit? This is the diamond problem. If the classes also hold fields, D would get two copies of A's state. Java's designers removed the whole problem by allowing one superclass.

class A { }
class B extends A { }
class C extends A { }
class D extends B, C { }     // javac: error: '{' expected

Java still gives you multiple inheritance of type through interfaces: a class can implement many interfaces. Interfaces carry no instance state, and the rule for conflicting default methods is explicit (interfaces).

KindShapeIn Java?
SingleB extends AYes
MultilevelC extends B, B extends AYes
HierarchicalB extends A and C extends AYes
Multipleone class with two parent classesNot for classes; yes for interfaces
Hybrida mix of the aboveOnly when the multiple part uses interfaces

The is-a test and substitutability

Before you write extends, say the sentence "a Manager is an Employee". If it sounds natural, inheritance may fit. If you would say "has a" (an Order has a list of items), use a field instead — that is composition (composition vs inheritance).

The sentence is not enough. The deeper test is substitutability, known as the Liskov substitution principle: code written for the parent must keep working when it receives any subclass object. A classic failure:

class Rectangle {
    protected int w, h;
    void setWidth(int w)   { this.w = w; }
    void setHeight(int h)  { this.h = h; }
    int area()             { return w * h; }
}

class Square extends Rectangle {          // "a square is a rectangle" in maths...
    @Override void setWidth(int w)  { this.w = w; this.h = w; }
    @Override void setHeight(int h) { this.w = h; this.h = h; }
}

// in main():
Rectangle r = new Square();
r.setWidth(4);
r.setHeight(5);
System.out.println(r.area());             // 25, but a Rectangle user expects 20

A mutable Square breaks the promise that Rectangle makes (width and height change independently). So here the subclass is a bad idea even though the sentence sounded right. The JDK has its own mistakes: Stack extends Vector and Properties extends Hashtable, so both expose methods that break their purpose. The documentation of Stack tells you to prefer Deque.

Keeping the parent in control: protected and final

  • Keep the parent's fields private. Offer protected methods as deliberate extension points (hooks), not protected fields. Fewer details leak to subclasses, and the parent can change its internals.
  • Mark a method final if no subclass should change it. Mark a class final if it is not designed for extension, which is true of most classes (final).
  • A sealed class lets you name exactly which subclasses are allowed (sealed classes).

Benefits

  • Shared code lives in one place
  • A natural type hierarchy for polymorphism
  • Easy to add a new variant by writing a subclass

Costs

  • The subclass depends on the parent's internals (tight coupling)
  • A change in the parent can break every child (fragile base class)
  • Only one parent class; deep trees are hard to read

Edge cases and compiler errors

  • class X extends SomeInterface → no interface expected here. Use implements. The reverse, class Y implements SomeClass, gives interface expected here.
  • class MyString extends String → cannot inherit from final String.
  • class Q extends Q2 and class Q2 extends Q → cyclic inheritance involving Q.
  • Interfaces can extend several interfaces with extends A, B. An interface cannot extend a class.
  • A subclass can add a method with the same name but different parameters. That is overloading, not overriding (overloading).
  • Constructors, static and instance initializers, and private members are never "overridden". Constructors are not inherited at all.

Mistake: extending a class just to reuse its methods

Wrong: an Order is not a list

class Order extends ArrayList<Item> {   // exposes add, remove, clear, sort...
    long total() { /* sum of the items */ }
}

Right: an Order has a list of items

class Order {
    private final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();
    void add(Item item) { items.add(item); }       // only what Order allows
    long total() { /* sum of the items */ }
}

In a real Spring Boot project

You use inheritance in a few predictable places: custom exceptions (class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException), a JPA @MappedSuperclass base entity that carries id and audit fields, framework base classes such as OncePerRequestFilter, and test base classes. For sharing behaviour between your own services, composition (injecting another bean) is the norm.

Interview: inheritance questions

  • What is inherited? Accessible fields and methods. Not constructors, not private members (although a private field still exists inside the object).
  • Why no multiple inheritance of classes? The diamond problem: ambiguous methods and duplicated state. Interfaces give multiple inheritance of type safely.
  • Types of inheritance? Single, multilevel, hierarchical are supported; multiple and hybrid only through interfaces.
  • super vs this? this is the current object; super reaches the parent part of it.
  • Can a subclass access a parent's private field? Not directly; through public or protected methods.
  • Can you extend a final class? No: String, Integer, and records are final.

Method overriding: the rules

A subclass overrides an inherited instance method by declaring one with the same signature; the access may not be narrower, the return type may be a subtype, checked exceptions may not be broader, and @Override makes the compiler check all of it.

Overriding means a subclass provides its own version of an instance method that it inherited. When you call the method on a subclass object, Java runs the subclass version, even if the variable's type is the parent. That is the engine behind polymorphism. You already used it when Manager replaced monthlyPay() in inheritance.

class Account {
    public long monthlyChargePaise() { return 0; }
}

class CurrentAccount extends Account {
    @Override
    public long monthlyChargePaise() { return 15_000; }   // replaces the parent's version
}

// in main():
Account a = new CurrentAccount();
System.out.println(a.monthlyChargePaise());               // 15000

The rules

Overriding is strict. If one rule is broken, the code either fails to compile or quietly does something else. The first column is the rule; the last shows what the compiler tells you when you break it.

RuleDetailIf you break it
Same name and parameter typesThat pair is the signature. A different parameter list makes a new overload, not an overrideWith @Override: method does not override or implement a method from a supertype
Return typeThe same, or a subtype of it for objects (covariant). Primitives and void must match exactlyreturn type long is not compatible with int
AccessThe same or wider: protected may become public, never the other wayattempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public
Checked exceptionsNone, the same, or narrower ones. Unchecked exceptions are always allowedoverridden method does not throw IOException
Not finalA final method cannot be overriddenoverridden method is final
Instance methods onlyStatic methods are hidden, not overridden. Static and instance cannot swap rolesoverridden method is static or overriding method is static
Must be inheritedprivate methods are not inherited. Package-private methods are inherited only inside the same packageNo error: you silently created a new, unrelated method

Rule: remember it as "same, wider, narrower, covariant"

The same signature; wider or equal access; narrower or equal checked exceptions; covariant (same or more specific) return type. The reason is substitutability: code that calls the parent method must still work with any subclass, so a subclass may not promise less (narrower access) or throw more.

Always write @Override

@Override is an annotation that tells the compiler: "I intend to override a method from a parent class or interface. Check it." It has no effect at run time. Its value is that it turns a silent mistake into a compile error. The most famous such mistake is equals:

Wrong: this is an overload, not an override

class Account {
    long id;
    Account(long id) { this.id = id; }

    public boolean equals(Account other) {    // parameter is Account, not Object
        return other != null && id == other.id;
    }
}

Right: @Override catches it for you

class Account {
    long id;
    Account(long id) { this.id = id; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object other) {
        return other instanceof Account a && id == a.id;
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Long.hashCode(id); }
}

With the wrong version, equals seems to work when you call it with an Account variable, and fails everywhere else:

Account a = new Account(1), b = new Account(1);
System.out.println(a.equals(b));              // true: calls equals(Account)
Object o = b;
System.out.println(a.equals(o));              // false: calls Object.equals, a different method
List<Account> list = List.of(a);
System.out.println(list.contains(b));         // false: collections call equals(Object)
true
false
false

Put @Override on every overriding method, including implementations of interface methods. With the annotation, the wrong version above does not compile. It also protects you later: if someone renames the parent method, every override fails to compile instead of silently becoming a dead method.

Covariant return types

An override may return a more specific type than the parent method. Callers who know they hold the subclass get the specific type without a cast.

class Animal {
    Animal reproduce() { return new Animal(); }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    Dog reproduce() { return new Dog(); }      // Dog is a subtype of Animal: allowed
}

// in main():
Dog puppy = new Dog().reproduce();              // no cast needed
Animal other = new Dog().reproduce();           // still fine through the parent type

Behind the scenes, javac adds a hidden bridge method with the parent's return type, so that the JVM can still dispatch the call correctly. You never write it. This is why clone() overrides can declare their own class as the return type.

Exceptions in overriding methods

import java.io.*;

class Importer {
    void load(String file) throws IOException { }
}

class CsvImporter extends Importer {
    @Override void load(String file) throws FileNotFoundException { }   // narrower: OK
}

class CachedImporter extends Importer {
    @Override void load(String file) { }                                // none: OK
}

class BadImporter extends Importer {
    @Override void load(String file) throws Exception { }   // error: broader than IOException
}

The reason is again substitutability. A caller holding an Importer catches only IOException. If a subclass could throw Exception, that caller would be surprised by a checked exception it never prepared for. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its children) are not checked by the compiler, so they are always allowed.

Calling the parent version with super

An override often wants to extend the parent behaviour, not discard it. Call super.method() and add to the result. Two common places: toString() (super.toString() + ", extra=" + extra) and methods that do setup and teardown work in a base class.

Static methods and fields: hidden, not overridden

If a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a static method of its parent, it hides the parent's method. A field with the same name as a parent field hides that field. In both cases, Java picks by the declared type of the reference, not by the object. Only instance methods are chosen by the object.

public class Hiding {
    static class P {
        static String who() { return "P"; }
        String name() { return "P"; }
        String f = "P.f";
    }

    static class C extends P {
        static String who() { return "C"; }                  // hides P.who()
        @Override String name() { return "C"; }              // overrides P.name()
        String f = "C.f";                                    // hides P.f
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        P p = new C();                    // declared type P, real object C
        System.out.println(p.who());      // static: decided by declared type
        System.out.println(p.name());     // instance method: decided by the object
        System.out.println(p.f);          // field: decided by declared type
        System.out.println(((C) p).f);    // after a cast the declared type is C
        System.out.println(C.who());
    }
}
P
C
P.f
C.f
C

Only p.name() printed the subclass value. That single line is polymorphism; the others are not. Do not redeclare a parent's field name in a subclass. If subclasses need different values, expose a method (for example protected String label()) because methods are chosen by the object.

The silent trap: private and package-private methods

A method that is not inherited cannot be overridden. A private method in the parent is invisible to the child, so a method with the same name in the child is a brand-new method. Package-private methods behave the same way when the child is in another package:

package pkg1;

public class Base {
    void hook() { System.out.println("Base hook"); }      // package-private
    public void run() { hook(); }
}
package pkg2;

public class Derived extends pkg1.Base {
    // NOT an override: Base.hook() is invisible in this package
    void hook() { System.out.println("Derived hook"); }
}

// new Derived().run() prints:  Base hook

Nothing warns you about this, except @Override: with the annotation on Derived.hook() the compiler reports method does not override or implement a method from a supertype. Yet another reason to always write it.

Edge cases

  • An override may be final (to stop further overriding). Modifiers such as synchronized are not part of the signature, so they may differ.
  • An abstract class can re-declare an inherited concrete method as abstract, forcing subclasses to implement it again.
  • An abstract method must be overridden by the first concrete subclass, or javac reports … is not abstract and does not override abstract method … (abstract classes).
  • The overriding method may rename parameters and add or drop annotations freely; only the types matter.
  • A call through super.method() is not dynamic: it always runs the parent version.
  • Interface default methods can be overridden too, by a class or by a sub-interface (interfaces).

Mistakes to avoid

  • Leaving out @Override and shipping an overload (the equals(Account) bug above).
  • Breaking the parent's promise. If withdraw() in the parent never throws for a valid amount, a subclass that throws for valid amounts violates substitutability even though it compiles.
  • Calling overridable methods from a constructor (initialization order).
  • Assuming a field behaves like a method. Fields are never overridden.

Tip: design for overriding on purpose

A class that allows overriding must document how (which other methods call this one, what must hold afterwards). If you did not plan for subclasses, mark the class or the key methods final. "Design and document for inheritance, or else prohibit it" is the advice of Effective Java.

Interview: overriding questions

  • What are the rules? Same signature, same or wider access, same or narrower checked exceptions, same or covariant return type, instance methods only, not final.
  • Can we override static or private methods? No. Static methods are hidden; private ones are not inherited.
  • What is a covariant return type? An override that returns a subtype of the parent's return type (since Java 5).
  • Why use @Override? The compiler checks that you really override; it catches typos and wrong parameter types.
  • Can an overriding method throw a broader exception? No for checked exceptions; unchecked exceptions are fine.

Method overloading and how Java picks the method

Overloading means several methods with the same name but different parameter lists; the compiler chooses one at compile time from the declared types of the arguments, trying exact and widening matches first, then boxing, then varargs.

Method overloading lets you reuse one name for related operations on different inputs. The JDK does this constantly: System.out.println has overloads for int, double, char, String, Object and more; Math.max works for int, long, float and double; String.valueOf and StringBuilder.append have a dozen overloads each. The caller writes the same name, and the compiler picks the right version.

public class Calculator {
    public int add(int a, int b)                { return a + b; }
    public double add(double a, double b)       { return a + b; }
    public int add(int a, int b, int c)         { return a + b + c; }
    public String add(String a, String b)       { return a + b; }
}

What counts as a different method

The signature of a method is its name plus the types of its parameters, in order. Two methods in the same class (or in a class and its subclass) may share a name only if their signatures differ.

Rules of overloading

  • The parameter lists must differ in the number, the types or the order of types: f(int, String) and f(String, int) are different methods.
  • These do not make methods different: the return type, the access modifier, the throws clause and the parameter names.
  • Two methods with the same signature and different return types do not compile: method f(int) is already defined in class X.
  • You can overload static methods, instance methods and constructors. A subclass can also add overloads of inherited methods.

Why can the return type not be used? Because the compiler chooses a method from the arguments. A statement like f(); ignores the result, so there would be nothing left to choose with.

How the compiler picks: three phases

When several overloads could accept a call, the compiler works in three phases and stops at the first phase that finds a match:

PhaseWhat is allowedExample conversion
1Exact match, primitive widening, and passing a subtype. No boxing, no varargsbyte → int → long, String → Object
2Phase 1 plus boxing and unboxingint → Integer, double → Double → Object
3Phase 2 plus variable-arity (varargs) methodsf(1, 2) to f(int... x)

Inside one phase, if more than one method applies, the most specific one wins (int is more specific than long; String is more specific than Object). If no single method is most specific, the call is ambiguous and does not compile.

public class OvRes {
    static void f(int x)     { System.out.println("f(int)"); }
    static void f(long x)    { System.out.println("f(long)"); }
    static void f(Integer x) { System.out.println("f(Integer)"); }
    static void f(Object x)  { System.out.println("f(Object)"); }
    static void f(int... x)  { System.out.println("f(int...)"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        byte b = 1;
        f(5);                    // exact match
        f(b);                    // byte widens to int; int is more specific than long
        f(5L);                   // exact match
        f(Integer.valueOf(5));   // exact match
        f(5.0);                  // no widening fits; double boxes to Double, which is an Object
        f("hi");                 // String is an Object
        f();                     // only the varargs method can take zero arguments
        f(1, 2);                 // only the varargs method fits
    }
}
f(int)
f(int)
f(long)
f(Integer)
f(Object)
f(Object)
f(int...)
f(int...)

Two more rules fall out of the phases. Widening beats boxing, because widening is phase 1 and boxing is phase 2. Boxing beats varargs, because varargs is phase 3.

static void g(long x)    { System.out.println("g(long)"); }
static void g(Integer x) { System.out.println("g(Integer)"); }
static void h(Integer x) { System.out.println("h(Integer)"); }
static void h(int... x)  { System.out.println("h(int...)"); }

// in main():
g(5);    // g(long):    int widens to long (phase 1) before boxing is tried
h(5);    // h(Integer): boxing (phase 2) wins over varargs (phase 3)

The declared type decides, not the real object

Overloads are chosen at compile time, so only the declared types of the arguments count. The run-time type of the object is invisible to the compiler.

static void show(Object o) { System.out.println("show(Object)"); }
static void show(String s) { System.out.println("show(String)"); }

// in main():
Object o = "hi";
show(o);                  // show(Object): the declared type of o is Object
show("hi");               // show(String)
show((Object) "hi");      // show(Object): the cast changes the declared type
show(null);               // show(String): null fits both; String is more specific
show(Object)
show(String)
show(Object)
show(String)

This is the key difference from overriding, where the object decides at run time. The first output line surprises many people: the variable holds a String, yet show(Object) runs.

Overloads and null

A null argument fits every reference type, so the compiler picks the most specific overload. If two overloads are equally specific, the call is ambiguous:

static void print(String s) { }
static void print(StringBuilder sb) { }

// print(null);    // error: reference to print is ambiguous
//                 //   both method print(String) and method print(StringBuilder) match
print((String) null);   // fix: cast to the type you mean

The classic trap: List.remove(int) versus remove(Object)

List has two remove methods: remove(int index) and remove(Object o). For a List<Integer>, phase 1 finds an exact match for an int argument, so the index version wins and boxing is never tried.

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30, 1));
nums.remove(1);                        // remove(int index): removes the element at index 1 (20)
System.out.println(nums);              // [10, 30, 1]
nums.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));       // remove(Object): removes the value 1
System.out.println(nums);              // [10, 30]

Edge cases

  • System.out.println('a') prints a, but System.out.println('a' + 1) prints 98: the sum is an int, so the int overload runs.
  • A varargs call with no extra argument prefers the fixed-arity method: log("x") picks log(String) over log(String, Object...).
  • Overloading works across inheritance. In a subclass, eat(Dog) next to an inherited eat(Animal) is an overload, not an override, because the parameter types differ (see the output-prediction puzzles).
  • A generic method and a non-generic method with the same erasure, such as f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>), do not compile as a pair: name clash: … have the same erasure (Module 4).
  • main can be overloaded, but the JVM starts the program only through the classic one.

Conventions for overloading

  • Overload only when the methods do the same thing on different inputs. If the behaviour differs, use different names: DataOutputStream has writeInt and writeLong, not ten write overloads.
  • Avoid overloads with the same number of parameters whose types are related (Object and String, int and Integer). The caller can no longer predict which one runs.
  • Do not overload with different functional interfaces at the same position; lambda arguments become ambiguous (Module 5).
  • To keep the number of constructors small, use chaining with this(…) (constructors) or static factory methods with distinct names.

Interview: overloading questions

  • What is overloading? Same name, different parameter list, resolved at compile time. It is called compile-time or static polymorphism.
  • Can you overload by return type? No; the return type is not part of the signature.
  • Which method runs for f(null)? The most specific overload; ambiguity is a compile error.
  • Order of resolution? Exact or widening, then boxing, then varargs.
  • Overloading vs overriding? The comparison table is in polymorphism.

Polymorphism: compile-time vs runtime, dynamic method dispatch

Polymorphism ("many forms") lets one reference type stand for many real types, so the same call runs different code depending on the actual object: chosen at run time for overriding, at compile time for overloading.

Imagine the checkout page of a shopping app. The customer pays with UPI, a card or cash on delivery. The checkout code should not contain a branch for every payment type. It should say "pay this amount" and let each payment type know how. That is polymorphism, the third pillar of OOP: one interface, many implementations, and the right one runs automatically.

A first example

The type PaymentMethod below is an interface: a type that lists methods without bodies (see interfaces). Everything here works the same with a parent class and overriding.

import java.util.*;

interface PaymentMethod {
    String pay(long amountPaise);
}

class UpiPayment implements PaymentMethod {
    private final String upiId;
    UpiPayment(String upiId) { this.upiId = upiId; }

    @Override public String pay(long amountPaise) {
        return "Paid " + amountPaise + " paise via UPI " + upiId;
    }
    String scanQr() { return "scanning QR"; }              // only UpiPayment has this
}

class CardPayment implements PaymentMethod {
    private final String last4;
    CardPayment(String last4) { this.last4 = last4; }

    @Override public String pay(long amountPaise) {
        return "Paid " + amountPaise + " paise by card ending " + last4;
    }
}

class CashOnDelivery implements PaymentMethod {
    @Override public String pay(long amountPaise) {
        return "Will collect " + amountPaise + " paise at the door";
    }
}

public class Checkout {
    static void checkout(PaymentMethod method, long amountPaise) {   // knows only the interface
        System.out.println(method.pay(amountPaise));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<PaymentMethod> methods = List.of(
                new UpiPayment("asha@upi"), new CardPayment("4242"), new CashOnDelivery());
        for (PaymentMethod m : methods) {
            checkout(m, 49_900);                           // same call, three behaviours
        }
    }
}
Paid 49900 paise via UPI asha@upi
Paid 49900 paise by card ending 4242
Will collect 49900 paise at the door

The method checkout was written once. If the shop adds NetBanking next month, you write one new class, and checkout does not change. New behaviour arrives without editing old, tested code — this is the open/closed idea you will meet again in design principles (System Design · Module 1).

Compile-time and run-time polymorphism

Java has two mechanisms that people call polymorphism. They differ in when the method is chosen.

AspectOverloading (compile-time)Overriding (run-time)
Other namesStatic polymorphism, early bindingDynamic polymorphism, late binding, dynamic method dispatch
WhereSame class, or a class and its subclassParent class and subclass (or interface and implementation)
SignatureMust differMust be the same
Return typeCan be anythingSame or covariant
Access and exceptionsFree to differAccess not narrower; checked exceptions not broader
Chosen byThe compiler, using the declared types of the argumentsThe JVM, using the actual class of the object
Static and private methodsCan be overloadedCannot be overridden
Needs inheritance?NoYes (or an interface)
@OverrideNot usedRecommended always

When an interviewer says "polymorphism" without more words, they usually mean the run-time kind. Details of overloading are in their own article.

Reference type and object type

In PaymentMethod m = new UpiPayment("asha@upi"); there are two types in play:

  • The reference type (also called the declared or compile-time type) is PaymentMethod. It decides which methods you are allowed to call. The compiler checks this.
  • The object type (the actual or run-time type) is UpiPayment. It decides which implementation runs. The JVM decides this while the program runs.

Assigning a subclass object to a parent-type variable is called upcasting. It is always safe and needs no cast. The price is that the variable only offers the parent's methods:

PaymentMethod p = new UpiPayment("ravi@upi");
p.pay(100);        // fine: pay() is in PaymentMethod
p.scanQr();        // compile error: scanQr() exists in UpiPayment, not in PaymentMethod
Checkout2.java:4: error: cannot find symbol
        p.scanQr();
         ^
  symbol:   method scanQr()
  location: variable p of type PaymentMethod

To call scanQr() you would need a downcast; see casting and instanceof. A good design usually avoids the need: put what callers need into the shared type.

How dynamic method dispatch works

Dynamic method dispatch is the run-time lookup that finds the right overriding method. It happens in two steps, one at each time:

In bytecode, a call on a class type is an invokevirtual instruction and a call on an interface type is invokeinterface. Conceptually, each class has a table of its methods (a virtual method table). A subclass starts with a copy of its parent's table and replaces the entries for the methods it overrides. A call looks up the method in the table of the object's real class. The JIT compiler (Module 7) often removes the cost: if a call site has only ever seen one class, it can inline the method directly. So polymorphism is not slow.

What is polymorphic and what is not

Only instance methods that can be overridden are chosen by the object. Everything else is fixed by the compiler. This is also the answer to the interview question "static binding versus dynamic binding": binding means linking a method call to the method body.

ThingChosen byBinding
Overridable instance methodActual class of the objectDynamic (late)
static methodDeclared type of the referenceStatic (early)
private and final methods, constructorsThe class where they are declaredStatic (early)
Field access (p.f)Declared type of the referenceStatic (early)
Which overload to callDeclared types of the argumentsStatic (early)
super.method()The parent classStatic (early)

The proof for fields and static methods is the Hiding example in overriding: p.f gave P.f although the object was a C.

Replace conditionals with polymorphism

Polymorphism removes long if/switch chains on a "type" value. Every new type forces you to find and edit every such chain.

Wrong: branch on a type code

static String pay(String type, long paise) {
