    if (type.equals("UPI"))  { return "UPI " + paise; }
    else if (type.equals("CARD")) { return "Card " + paise; }
    else if (type.equals("COD"))  { return "COD " + paise; }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException(type);   // edit here for every new type
}

Right: let each type know itself

static String pay(PaymentMethod method, long paise) {
    return method.pay(paise);         // new types need no change here
}

Polymorphism is everywhere in Java

  • List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); — you code against List; the object may be an ArrayList or a LinkedList.
  • Comparator, Runnable and Iterator — you pass behaviour; the library calls it.
  • Spring injects a PaymentGateway bean, and your service calls gateway.charge(…) without knowing whether Razorpay or a test fake is behind it.
  • JDBC: your code calls Connection and PreparedStatement; the real classes come from the database driver.

Java also has a third kind, parametric polymorphism: generics let one class or method work for many types (List<T>, Module 4). The run-time and compile-time kinds above are the ones about methods.

Rules to remember

  • The reference type decides what you can call; the object type decides which override runs.
  • Only overridable instance methods are dynamic. Fields, static methods, private methods and overload choice are fixed at compile time.
  • Upcasting is implicit and safe; downcasting needs a cast and can fail at run time.

Edge cases

  • Calling a method on a null reference throws NullPointerException; there is no object to dispatch on.
  • A call to an overridden method from a parent's constructor runs the child's version, before the child's fields are ready (initialization order).
  • Inside a parent's method, calling another overridable method means this.other(), which is dispatched dynamically. This is the basis of the Template Method pattern (abstract classes).
  • Dispatch also works for interface default methods: the most specific implementation of the object's class wins.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Believing the reference type picks the override. It does not: Employee e = new Manager(…); e.monthlyPay() runs the Manager's version.
  • Long instanceof chains in the caller instead of a method in the types (see the Wrong example above).
  • Mixing up overloading and overriding in puzzles. Ask first: is the choice about arguments (compile time) or about the receiver object (run time)?

Interview: "Explain polymorphism with an example"

  • Definition: one type, many forms; the same method call behaves differently depending on the actual object.
  • Two kinds: compile-time (overloading, chosen by the compiler from argument types) and run-time (overriding, chosen by the JVM from the object's class).
  • Example: PaymentMethod with UPI, card and COD; checkout() is written once and works with any of them.
  • How it works: upcasting plus dynamic method dispatch (a virtual method table lookup).
  • What is not polymorphic: fields, static methods, private methods.
  • Benefit: add new types without changing existing code; remove if/else chains.

Upcasting, downcasting, instanceof and ClassCastException

Upcasting (child to parent) is automatic and always safe; downcasting (parent to child) needs an explicit cast and throws ClassCastException at run time if the object is not really that type, so check with instanceof first.

Every object has a real type, fixed when it was created with new. Every variable has a declared type. In Animal a = new Dog(); the object is a Dog and the variable is an Animal (polymorphism). A cast changes the type you use to look at the object. It never changes the object itself.

Upcasting: always safe, always implicit

Treating a subclass object as its parent type is called upcasting (the arrow on a class diagram points up). It needs no cast, because a Dog is an Animal. You pay one price: through the parent variable you can only use the parent's members.

Animal a = new Dog();       // upcast: implicit
a.eat();                    // fine: Animal has eat()
a.bark();                   // compile error: bark() belongs to Dog, and a is declared Animal

Downcasting: explicit and checked twice

To get back the full Dog view, you downcast: Dog d = (Dog) a;. The compiler and the JVM both check it.

  • At compile time the cast must be possible: the two types must be related (one is a subtype of the other, or the target is an interface and the source class is not final). (Integer) "text" fails with incompatible types: String cannot be converted to Integer.
  • At run time the object must really be an instance of the target type. Otherwise the JVM throws ClassCastException.
class Animal { }
class Dog extends Animal {
    void bark() { System.out.println("Woof"); }
    boolean isTrained() { return true; }
}
class Cat extends Animal { }

public class Cast {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal a = new Cat();
        try {
            Dog d = (Dog) a;                       // compiles, fails at run time
        } catch (ClassCastException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }

        Animal b = new Dog();
        if (b instanceof Dog d && d.isTrained()) {   // pattern matching instanceof
            d.bark();
        }
        System.out.println(a instanceof Dog);       // false: a is a Cat
        System.out.println(null instanceof Animal); // false: null is never an instance

        Animal n = null;
        Dog nd = (Dog) n;                           // casting null always works
        System.out.println(nd);

        Object[] objs = new String[2];              // arrays are covariant...
        try {
            objs[0] = Integer.valueOf(1);           // ...so this fails at run time
        } catch (ArrayStoreException e) {
            System.out.println(e);
        }

        Object s = "text";
        if (!(s instanceof String str)) {           // pattern variable in scope after the if
            return;
        }
        System.out.println(str.length());
    }
}
class Cat cannot be cast to class Dog (Cat and Dog are in unnamed module of loader 'app')
Woof
false
false
null
java.lang.ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer
4

The exception message names both classes. The part in brackets says which module and class loader they came from (it looks different for JDK classes). Remember the three lines about null: instanceof is false for it, a cast of it succeeds, and calling a method on it would throw NullPointerException.

The instanceof operator

x instanceof T asks: "is the real object in x an instance of T?" It is true for the class itself, for any subclass, and for any interface the class implements. It is false for null. If the compiler can prove the answer is always no (unrelated classes), it refuses to compile.

The classic way to use it is the guard then cast pair. Since Java 16 you can combine both steps with pattern matching for instanceof: the test also declares a typed variable.

Classic: test, then cast

if (animal instanceof Dog) {
    Dog d = (Dog) animal;      // repeats the type, easy to get wrong
    d.bark();
}

Modern: test and bind in one step

if (animal instanceof Dog d) {
    d.bark();                  // d is already a Dog here
}

The variable d is a pattern variable. It exists only where the compiler knows the test was true: inside the if, on the right side of && (animal instanceof Dog d && d.isTrained()), or after an if (!(animal instanceof Dog d)) return;. Java 21 adds patterns in switch and record patterns; they are covered in Module 5.

instanceof versus getClass()

instanceof accepts subclasses. getClass() gives the exact class. The difference matters when you write equals().

Expression (object is a Dog)Result
obj instanceof Animaltrue (a Dog is an Animal)
obj instanceof Dogtrue
obj.getClass() == Animal.classfalse (exact class is Dog)
obj.getClass() == Dog.classtrue

See equals() and hashCode() for which one to choose.

Edge cases

  • Casting to an interface compiles for any non-final class, because a subclass might implement it. (Runnable) animal compiles and then fails at run time if the object does not implement Runnable.
  • Arrays are covariant. String[] is an Object[], so the compiler lets you store any object in it, and the JVM throws ArrayStoreException for the wrong type (shown above). Generic collections do not have this problem (Module 4).
  • Primitive casts are different. (int) 3.9 converts a number and gives 3; it is not an object cast and does not throw.
  • Generics. A cast to List<String> cannot be checked at run time because of type erasure, so you get an "unchecked" warning instead of an exception, and the failure comes later, in a different place.
  • Boxing in casts. Object o = 1; Long l = (Long) o; throws ClassCastException, because the object is an Integer.

Mistake: casting without checking

Wrong: crashes on the first cat

for (Animal a : animals) {
    ((Dog) a).bark();
}

Right: guard, or better, use polymorphism

for (Animal a : animals) {
    if (a instanceof Dog d) {
        d.bark();
    }
}
// Better: add makeSound() to Animal and call a.makeSound()

When casting is acceptable

  • Inside equals(Object), where the parameter type is fixed to Object.
  • In framework glue and when reading loosely typed data (a Map<String, Object> from JSON).
  • Everywhere else, a downcast is a hint that the design could use polymorphism instead. A chain of instanceof checks on a closed set of types is better as a sealed hierarchy with a switch (sealed classes).

Interview: casting questions

  • Upcasting vs downcasting? Upcasting goes to a parent type, implicit and safe. Downcasting goes to a child type, explicit, and can throw ClassCastException.
  • When does ClassCastException happen? When the real object is not an instance of the target type. The compiler cannot see it, because it only knows the declared type.
  • How do you avoid it? Check with instanceof (or a pattern), or redesign with polymorphism.
  • What does instanceof return for null? Always false.
  • Does a cast change the object? No, only how the compiler sees the reference.

Output-prediction puzzles: overloading, overriding and fields

Almost every "what does this print?" puzzle about methods is solved by one two-step rule: the compiler picks the signature from declared types, then the JVM runs the override found in the real object's class; fields, static and private methods skip the second step.

Interviewers love these puzzles because they test whether you understand the difference between compile time and run time. This article gives you the method first, then six puzzles. Try each one on paper before you open the answer.

The two-step rule

  1. Step 1, compile time. Look at the declared type of the variable you call the method on. Among the methods of that type, pick the best-matching signature, using the declared types of the arguments (overload resolution, overloading).
  2. Step 2, run time. If the chosen method is an overridable instance method, run the version that the real class of the object provides (overriding).
  3. Exceptions to step 2. Fields, static methods and private methods are decided in step 1 only. They use the declared type, never the object.

Puzzle 1: a field and a method with the same name in both classes

class A1 { String name = "A"; String who() { return "A.who"; } }
class B1 extends A1 { String name = "B"; @Override String who() { return "B.who"; } }

// in main():
A1 x = new B1();
System.out.println(x.name + " " + x.who());
What is printed? 
A B.who

x.name is a field, so the declared type A1 decides: "A". x.who() is an overridden instance method, so the real object decides: B.who. A B1 object holds two separate fields called name.

Puzzle 2: the same object, different declared types

static void show(Object o) { System.out.println("show(Object)"); }
static void show(String s) { System.out.println("show(String)"); }

// in main():
Object o = "hi";
show(o);
show("hi");
show((Object) "hi");
show(null);
What is printed? 
show(Object)
show(String)
show(Object)
show(String)

Only step 1 applies: these are overloads, not overrides, so the compiler decides from the declared types. The variable o is declared Object, although it holds a String. A cast changes the declared type. null fits both, and String is the more specific.

Puzzle 3: overloading and overriding together

class Animal {
    void eat(Animal a) { System.out.println("Animal eats Animal"); }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    void eat(Dog d) { System.out.println("Dog eats Dog"); }              // new overload
    @Override void eat(Animal a) { System.out.println("Dog eats Animal"); }
}

// in main():
Animal a = new Dog();
Dog d = new Dog();
a.eat(a);
a.eat(d);
d.eat(a);
d.eat(d);
What is printed? 
Dog eats Animal
Dog eats Animal
Dog eats Animal
Dog eats Dog

Apply the two steps to each call.

  • a.eat(a) — step 1: the declared type Animal has only eat(Animal). Step 2: the real object is a Dog, which overrides it: Dog eats Animal.
  • a.eat(d) — the declared type is still Animal, so eat(Dog) is not even visible. eat(Animal) accepts a Dog. Same result as above.
  • d.eat(a) — the declared type is Dog, which has two methods. The argument is declared Animal, so eat(Dog) does not apply. eat(Animal) runs.
  • d.eat(d) — both methods apply, and eat(Dog) is more specific: Dog eats Dog.

Puzzle 4: a static method called inside an inherited method

class P4 {
    static String id() { return "P"; }
    String run() { return id(); }
}
class C4 extends P4 {
    static String id() { return "C"; }       // hides P4.id()
}

// in main():
System.out.println(new C4().run());
What is printed? 
P

run() is written in P4, where the call id() means P4.id(). Static methods are bound at compile time to the class in which the call is written. The object being a C4 does not matter. If id() were an instance method that C4 overrides, the answer would be C.

Puzzle 5: a private method in the parent

class A5 {
    private void hello() { System.out.println("A.hello"); }
    void call() { hello(); }
}
class B5 extends A5 {
    void hello() { System.out.println("B.hello"); }     // a new method, not an override
}

// in main():
new B5().call();
What is printed? 
A.hello

A private method is not inherited, so B5.hello() cannot override it. Inside A5.call(), the call hello() is bound to A5's own private method. If you remove private from A5.hello() (and keep both classes in one package), B5.hello() becomes an override and the answer changes to B.hello. Adding @Override to the version in B5 would make the original code fail to compile.

Puzzle 6: the parent calls a method the child overrides

class A6 {
    void m() { System.out.println("A.m"); n(); }
    void n() { System.out.println("A.n"); }
}
class B6 extends A6 {
    @Override void n() { System.out.println("B.n"); }
}

// in main():
new B6().m();
What is printed? 
A.m
B.n

m() is inherited and runs from A6, so "A.m" prints. Inside it, n() means this.n(), and this is a B6 object. n() is an overridable instance method, so step 2 picks B6.n(). This is exactly how the Template Method pattern lets a parent class call code that subclasses supply (abstract classes).

More puzzles in other articles

  • Initialization order with static blocks, instance blocks and constructors, and the "overridden method sees null fields" trap: initialization order.
  • Overload resolution with boxing, widening and varargs: overloading.
  • Why a HashSet shows duplicates: equals() and hashCode().

Tip: a checklist for any puzzle

  1. Underline every call and write down the declared type of the receiver and of each argument.
  2. Is the member a field, a static method or a private method? Then you are done: use the declared type.
  3. Otherwise pick the signature from the declared types (most specific wins), then switch to the real object and find the override.
  4. If constructors or blocks are involved, number the steps from initialization order.

Interview: how to talk through such a puzzle

Say the rule out loud before you give the answer: "Overloads are resolved at compile time from the declared types; overrides are resolved at run time from the object; fields and statics follow the declared type." Interviewers care about the reasoning more than the output, and the sentence shows you have one.

Abstraction: hide the how, show the what

Abstraction means showing only what a user of a type needs to know, its contract, and hiding how it works inside; in Java you build it with abstract classes, interfaces and well-chosen public methods.

Abstraction is the fourth pillar. Think of an ATM. You press "withdraw" and enter an amount. You do not know how the cash dispenser works, how the bank checks your balance or what happens when the network is down. The ATM shows you the what (a small set of operations) and hides the how. In code, the same idea lets you change a database, a payment provider or an algorithm without touching the code that uses it.

The idea in code

An order service needs to tell the customer that the order is confirmed. It does not care whether that happens by email, SMS or WhatsApp. So we describe the capability as an interface, and the service depends only on that description.

interface NotificationSender {
    void send(String to, String message);        // the "what": a contract
}

class EmailSender implements NotificationSender {
    @Override public void send(String to, String message) {
        System.out.println("EMAIL to " + to + ": " + message);     // the "how", hidden
    }
}

class SmsSender implements NotificationSender {
    @Override public void send(String to, String message) {
        System.out.println("SMS to " + to + ": " + message);
    }
}

class OrderService {
    private final NotificationSender sender;                     // depends on the contract only
    OrderService(NotificationSender sender) { this.sender = sender; }

    void placeOrder(String customer, String contact) {
        System.out.println("Order saved for " + customer);
        sender.send(contact, "Your order is confirmed");
    }
}

public class Abstraction {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new OrderService(new EmailSender()).placeOrder("Asha", "asha@example.com");
        new OrderService(new SmsSender()).placeOrder("Ravi", "98100 00001");
    }
}
Order saved for Asha
EMAIL to asha@example.com: Your order is confirmed
Order saved for Ravi
SMS to 98100 00001: Your order is confirmed

OrderService never mentions email or SMS. Adding WhatsApp means writing one new class. A test can pass a fake sender that records messages instead of sending them. This is exactly what Spring does when it injects an implementation into your service.

Levels of abstraction

Abstraction is not one feature; it appears at several levels, from small to large:

  • A method. Collections.sort(list) hides the sorting algorithm. You say what you want.
  • A class. ArrayList hides the array that grows. You use add and get, and the private fields and helper methods stay hidden (encapsulation is the tool).
  • A type. An interface or an abstract class describes a contract with no (or partial) implementation. Callers hold the abstract type.
  • A layer. A UserRepository interface hides whether the data is in PostgreSQL, in memory or in a cache.

Ways to get abstraction in Java

ToolWhat it hidesSee
Private members and public methodsThe fields and helper code of a classAccess modifiers
InterfaceThe whole implementation; a pure contractInterfaces
Abstract classPart of the implementation; the rest is shared codeAbstract classes
Package-private classesHelper classes of a packagePackages

Abstraction versus encapsulation

Interviewers ask this pair all the time, and the two ideas do work together, so the difference is easy to blur. A clear way to remember it: encapsulation is about protecting data, and abstraction is about simplifying the view.

QuestionEncapsulationAbstraction
What is the goal?Protect state and keep it validReduce complexity; expose only the essentials
What is hidden?The data and how it is changedThe implementation behind a contract
How in Java?private fields, validating methodsInterfaces, abstract classes, good method names
Works atThe class (implementation level)The type and design level
ExampleAccount keeps balance privatePaymentGateway hides Razorpay or Stripe

One sentence for an interview: "Encapsulation hides how the data is stored and changed; abstraction hides how the work is done."

Program to an interface

  • Declare variables, fields and parameters with the most general type that offers what you need: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();, not ArrayList<String> names.
  • Name methods by what they do, not how: sendReminder(), not sendReminderUsingSmtp().
  • Keep the contract small. Every method you put in an interface is a promise to every implementation.

Abstractions can leak, and can be overdone

  • A leaky abstraction exposes a detail it was meant to hide. If a method returns ArrayList instead of List, every caller now depends on that class. If a repository interface has a method findByPostgresJsonbField(), it is not abstract any more.
  • Abstraction has a cost: more types and more indirection. Creating an interface with exactly one implementation "just in case" often adds noise. A common approach is to start with a class and extract an interface when a second implementation or a test double really appears. In Spring projects, service interfaces are common by habit; judge by the value they bring.

In a real Spring Boot project

You write interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> and never write a class that implements it; Spring Data generates the implementation at start-up. Your OrderService depends on the interface. In tests you replace a payment or email bean with a fake, because the service only knows the contract.

Interview: "What is abstraction? How is it different from encapsulation?"

  • Abstraction = exposing what an object does (its contract) and hiding how. In Java: interfaces and abstract classes, plus small public APIs.
  • Real-life examples: ATM, car steering wheel, List interface.
  • Encapsulation hides data and protects invariants with private fields; abstraction hides complexity behind a contract. They are partners, not synonyms.
  • Add the benefit: implementations can change without changing callers, and tests can use fakes.

Abstract classes and abstract methods

An abstract class is a partly finished class that cannot be instantiated: it shares fields, constructors and ready-made methods with its subclasses and leaves the varying parts as abstract methods that each concrete subclass must implement.

Sometimes a group of classes shares a lot of code, but one step differs for each. You do not want to create an object of the shared "idea" itself: a plain Shape has no area. You want to say "every shape has a name and can describe itself, but each shape computes its own area". An abstract class does exactly that.

Syntax and a first example

Mark the class with abstract. Mark each method that has no body with abstract and end it with a semicolon.

abstract class Shape {
    private final String name;

    Shape(String name) {                   // abstract classes can have constructors
        this.name = name;
    }

    abstract double area();                // abstract method: no body, subclasses must supply it

    String describe() {                    // concrete method: shared code
        return name + " with area " + String.format("%.2f", area());
    }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
    private final double radius;
    Circle(double radius) { super("Circle"); this.radius = radius; }
    @Override double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; }
}

class Rectangle extends Shape {
    private final double w, h;
    Rectangle(double w, double h) { super("Rectangle"); this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    @Override double area() { return w * h; }
}

public class ShapeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2), new Rectangle(3, 4) };
        for (Shape s : shapes) {
            System.out.println(s.describe());          // area() is resolved at run time
        }
        Shape custom = new Shape("Unit square") {      // anonymous subclass
            @Override double area() { return 1; }
        };
        System.out.println(custom.describe());
    }
}
Circle with area 12.57
Rectangle with area 12.00
Unit square with area 1.00

The method describe() is written once in Shape and calls area(). For each object, Java runs that object's own area() (dynamic dispatch). You can declare a variable or an array of type Shape; you just cannot create a plain Shape with new. The last example creates an object of an anonymous subclass (nested classes), which supplies the missing method on the spot.

The rules

Rules for abstract classes and methods

  • An abstract class cannot be instantiated: new Shape() gives Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated.
  • A class that has an abstract method must itself be declared abstract. The reverse is not required: an abstract class may have no abstract methods at all.
  • An abstract method has no body. A body gives abstract methods cannot have a body, and a missing body on a normal method gives missing a method body, or should be declared abstract.
  • The first concrete subclass must implement every inherited abstract method, or it must be abstract too. Otherwise: Circle is not abstract and does not override abstract method area() in Shape.
  • An abstract class can have fields, constructors, static members, initializer blocks and concrete methods of any access level.
  • Illegal combinations: abstract with final (a final class cannot be extended, so it could never be completed), with private (a subclass could not see it) or with static (static methods are not overridden). javac says illegal combination of modifiers: abstract and final and so on.

Abstract classes can have constructors, even though you cannot call them with new. A subclass constructor calls one through super(…), and the abstract class uses it to set up the shared state, as Shape does with name.

The Template Method pattern

The most useful job of an abstract class is the Template Method pattern. The parent fixes the order of the steps in a final method. Some steps are ready-made hooks with defaults, and others are abstract. Subclasses fill in only the varying steps and cannot change the overall flow.

import java.util.*;

abstract class ReportExporter {
    public final String export(List<String> rows) {        // the template: fixed steps
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(header());
        for (String row : rows) {
            sb.append(formatRow(row));
        }
        return sb.append(footer()).toString();
    }

    protected String header() { return ""; }                // hook with a default
    protected String footer() { return ""; }                // hook with a default
    protected abstract String formatRow(String row);        // must be supplied
}

class CsvExporter extends ReportExporter {
    @Override protected String formatRow(String row) { return row + "\n"; }
}

class BulletExporter extends ReportExporter {
    @Override protected String header() { return "Items:\n"; }
    @Override protected String formatRow(String row) { return " - " + row + "\n"; }
    @Override protected String footer() { return "(end)\n"; }
}

public class Exporter {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> rows = List.of("Mouse", "Keyboard");
        System.out.print(new CsvExporter().export(rows));
        System.out.print(new BulletExporter().export(rows));
    }
}
Mouse
Keyboard
Items:
 - Mouse
 - Keyboard
(end)

This pattern is everywhere. HttpServlet decides when to call doGet and doPost; you only fill them in. Spring's JdbcTemplate and test frameworks do the same with callbacks. Making the template method final protects the flow from being broken by a subclass.

Abstract classes in the JDK

  • java.lang.Number is abstract: Integer, Long and Double extend it and supply intValue(), doubleValue() and so on.
  • java.io.InputStream is abstract with one abstract method, read(); every other read method is built on it.
  • AbstractList, AbstractMap and AbstractCollection are skeletons that make writing your own collection easy (see abstract class vs interface).

Edge cases

  • The constructor still runs. Creating a concrete subclass runs the abstract parent's constructor first. If that constructor calls an abstract method, the subclass's version runs before the subclass's fields are set. This is the trap from initialization order.
  • An abstract class may implement an interface and leave some or all interface methods unimplemented. Concrete subclasses must finish the job.
  • An abstract class can have main and static factory methods that return concrete subclasses.
  • Abstract with no abstract methods is a valid way to say "this class is only a base, do not instantiate it".
  • Anonymous subclasses are allowed: new Shape("x") { … } must implement all abstract methods.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Using an abstract class as a pure contract. If it has no state and no shared code, it only uses up the subclass's single inheritance slot. An interface is better (which to use).
  • Forgetting to implement an abstract method in a concrete subclass (compile error), or forgetting to declare a class abstract when it keeps an unimplemented method.
  • Calling an abstract method from the constructor and reading subclass fields in it.
  • Making every method abstract "to be flexible". Share what really is shared.

Interview: abstract class questions

  • Can an abstract class have a constructor? Yes. It runs when a subclass object is built, through super(…).
  • Can it have no abstract methods? Yes, to prevent instantiation.
  • Can an abstract class be final? No: abstract needs subclasses, final forbids them.
  • Can we create an object of an abstract class? Not directly. You can use a reference of that type, or an anonymous subclass.
  • What is the Template Method pattern? A final method in the base class defines the algorithm's steps; subclasses override only the abstract or hook steps.

Interfaces: default, static and private methods

An interface is a pure contract: a list of methods a class promises to provide. A class can implement many interfaces, and since Java 8 an interface can also carry default, static and (Java 9) private methods with bodies.

An interface says what a type can do and nothing about how. A class that implements the interface signs the contract and must provide every abstract method. Interfaces are how Java gets "multiple inheritance of type": one class can implement many interfaces even though it can extend only one class. They are the backbone of abstraction in real projects: List, Map, Comparable, Runnable and every Spring Data repository are interfaces.

Syntax and a first example

interface PaymentMethod {
    int MAX_RETRIES = 3;                          // implicitly public static final

    boolean pay(long amountInPaise);              // implicitly public abstract

    default String receipt(long amountInPaise) {  // default method: has a body
        return "Paid Rs " + amountInPaise / 100.0 + " via " + name();
    }

    String name();

    static PaymentMethod upi(String vpa) {        // static method: called on the interface
        return new Upi(vpa);
    }
}

class Upi implements PaymentMethod {
    private final String vpa;
    Upi(String vpa) { this.vpa = vpa; }

    @Override public boolean pay(long amountInPaise) {   // must be public
        System.out.println("Debiting " + amountInPaise + " paise from " + vpa);
        return true;
    }
    @Override public String name() { return "UPI(" + vpa + ")"; }
}

public class PaymentDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PaymentMethod m = PaymentMethod.upi("asha@bank");   // static call on the interface
        if (m.pay(49900)) {
            System.out.println(m.receipt(49900));           // inherited default method
        }
        System.out.println(PaymentMethod.MAX_RETRIES);
    }
}
Debiting 49900 paise from asha@bank
Paid Rs 499.0 via UPI(asha@bank)
3

What can be inside an interface

MemberImplicit modifiersNotes
Constant fieldpublic static finalMust be initialised. No instance state at all.
Abstract methodpublic abstractThe contract. Implementations must be public.
default methodpublicJava 8. A body that implementers inherit and may override.
static methodpublicJava 8. Called as Iface.m(); not inherited by implementing classes.
private (static) methodprivateJava 9. Shares code between default methods; invisible outside.
Nested typepublic staticRare. A nested class or enum inside an interface.

Why default methods exist

Before Java 8, adding a method to an interface broke every class that implemented it. When the Java team wanted list.stream(), list.forEach(…) and map.getOrDefault(…), they could not touch thousands of implementations, including yours. A default method gave them a body to fall back on. So Collection.stream() and Iterable.forEach() are default methods. This is called interface evolution. Use default methods for the same reason: to add a method to a published interface without breaking implementers, or to give a convenient method built from the abstract ones, as receipt() does above.

Static and private methods

A static method belongs to the interface itself, so it is a natural home for factories and helpers: List.of(…), Comparator.comparing(…), Map.entry(…). It is not inherited: you call PaymentMethod.upi(…), never m.upi(…) or Upi.upi(…). A private method (Java 9) lets two default methods share code without making that helper part of the public contract.

interface AuditLog {
    void write(String line);

    default void info(String msg)  { write(format("INFO", msg)); }
    default void error(String msg) { write(format("ERROR", msg)); }

    private String format(String level, String msg) {   // hidden helper, Java 9+
        return "[" + level + "] " + msg;
    }
}

The diamond conflict with default methods

If a class implements two interfaces that both offer a default method with the same signature, which one should it inherit? Java uses three resolution rules, in this order:

  1. A class always wins. A method declared in the class or inherited from a superclass beats any interface default.
  2. The more specific interface wins. If interface B extends A and both define the default, B's version is used.
  3. Otherwise, you must decide. The compiler reports an error and the class has to override the method. Inside it you can pick one with InterfaceName.super.method().
interface Camera { default String start() { return "camera on"; } }
interface Phone  { default String start() { return "phone on"; } }

// Without the override: "types Camera and Phone are incompatible;
// class CameraPhone inherits unrelated defaults for start()"
class CameraPhone implements Camera, Phone {
    @Override public String start() {
        return Camera.super.start() + " + " + Phone.super.start();   // choose explicitly
    }
}

public class Diamond {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new CameraPhone().start());
    }
}
camera on + phone on

This is why Java allows multiple inheritance of type and behaviour from interfaces but not of state. Interfaces have no instance fields, so the classic "which copy of the field?" part of the diamond problem never appears (inheritance).

Interfaces extending interfaces

An interface can extend one or more interfaces: interface Savings extends Account, Interest { … }. A class that implements Savings must supply everything from all of them. Remember the vocabulary: a class extends a class, a class implements an interface, and an interface extends interfaces.

Functional interfaces

A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (default and static methods do not count, nor do abstract methods that repeat Object methods such as equals). It can be implemented with a lambda: Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("hi");. Add @FunctionalInterface to make the compiler check the rule. Examples: Runnable, Callable, Comparator, Comparable and the java.util.function types such as Function and Predicate. Lambdas and these types get their own module: Module 5.

Marker interfaces

A marker interface has no methods. Implementing it only tags the class, and some other code checks the tag. java.io.Serializable says "this object may be converted to bytes", Cloneable says "Object.clone() may copy me" (clone), and RandomAccess says "indexed access is fast". Today annotations do the same job in most new code (@Entity, @Service), but the JDK keeps its markers.

Rules to remember

  • Interface methods are public. Implementing one with weaker access (void pay() without public) is a compile error: "attempting to assign weaker access privileges".
  • Interface fields are constants. You cannot reassign MAX_RETRIES.
  • You cannot instantiate an interface with new (an anonymous class or a lambda is allowed), and interfaces have no constructors.
  • A default method cannot override equals, hashCode or toString of Object. The compiler rejects it, because a class always inherits those from Object and "the class wins".
  • An interface method cannot be protected or final.
  • A class that does not implement all abstract methods must be declared abstract.

Edge cases

  • Static interface methods are not inherited by implementing classes or sub-interfaces. Only Iface.method() works.
  • Same constant name in two interfaces makes an unqualified use ambiguous: write A.X or B.X.
  • Empty and sealed interfaces. An interface with no methods is legal (a marker). A sealed interface limits who may implement it (sealed classes).
  • Interface constants anti-pattern. Putting only constants in an interface and implementing it "to get the names" is considered bad design. Use a final class or an enum.

Conventions

  • Name interfaces after a capability or a role: Comparable, PaymentMethod, OrderRepository. Do not prefix with I (IPayment is a C# habit).
  • When the implementation is single, name it plainly (JpaOrderRepository), or avoid the Impl suffix if a better name exists.
  • Keep interfaces small and focused. Many small contracts are easier to implement and to fake in tests than one large one.
  • Use default methods sparingly: convenience built from abstract methods, or evolution of an old interface. Do not build a class hierarchy out of them.

Mistake: forgetting public on the implementation

Wrong: weaker access

class Upi implements PaymentMethod {
    boolean pay(long p) { return true; }   // error: weaker access privileges
}

Right

class Upi implements PaymentMethod {
    @Override public boolean pay(long p) { return true; }
}

In a real Spring Boot project

Controllers depend on service interfaces, services on repository interfaces, and Spring picks the implementation to inject. Spring Data repositories are interfaces with no implementing class that you write. Strategy-style code ("pick the right PaymentMethod for this request") is a map of interface implementations. Tests replace real implementations with Mockito mocks of the interface.

Interview: interface questions

  • Why default methods? To add methods to existing interfaces without breaking implementers; this enabled the Streams API on old collections.
  • What if two interfaces have the same default method? The class must override it; it may call A.super.m(). A class method beats any default.
  • Can an interface have a constructor or instance variable? No. Fields are always public static final.
  • Can an interface have a main method? Yes, as a static method; it can be run.
  • What is a functional interface? A marker interface? One abstract method (lambda target) / no methods (a tag).

Abstract class vs interface: which to choose

Use an interface to describe a capability that unrelated classes can share; use an abstract class when closely related classes share state and code. When in doubt, start with an interface, and combine both with a skeleton class if you need shared code.

Since Java 8 the two look more alike, because both can hold method bodies. The real differences are about state, constructors and inheritance count. This table is the one to learn for interviews.

The comparison

FeatureAbstract classInterface
Keywordabstract class, subclass extendsinterface, class implements
How many can a class use?One (single inheritance)Any number
Instance fields (state)Yes, any access levelNo; only public static final constants
ConstructorsYes (called through super(…))No
Method bodiesYes, any kindOnly default, static, private
Method accessAny modifier, including protectedPublic (private helpers since Java 9)
Abstract methodsMust be marked abstractImplicit
Can be final membersYes (final methods)No
Can extend / implementExtends one class, implements many interfacesExtends many interfaces
Lambda targetNoYes, if functional
Models"is-a" with shared implementation"can-do" capability or role

When to use which

Choose an interface when

  • Unrelated classes should share a capability (Comparable, Serializable, Notifier).
  • You want callers to depend on a contract, with many possible or future implementations.
  • A class already has a superclass (frameworks often force it) and still needs the new type.
  • You want lambdas or easy mocks in tests.

Choose an abstract class when

  • Subclasses are closely related and share fields and real code (Shape keeps name).
  • You need a constructor, non-public members or protected helpers.
  • You want a Template Method with final steps (abstract classes).
  • You need to control how the state is initialised for all subclasses.

The best of both: interface plus skeleton class

A common design is to publish an interface and also offer an abstract skeleton implementation that does the boring part. The JDK does this with List and AbstractList, Map and AbstractMap. Users who just need a list-like class extend the skeleton and write two methods. Users who already have a superclass implement the interface directly. Both stay compatible, because callers only see the interface.

import java.util.AbstractList;

interface Greeter { String greet(String name); }

abstract class BaseGreeter implements Greeter {          // skeleton: shared code
    protected abstract String salutation();
    @Override public String greet(String name) { return salutation() + ", " + name + "!"; }
}

class HindiGreeter extends BaseGreeter {
    @Override protected String salutation() { return "Namaste"; }
}

public class SkeletonDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Greeter g = new HindiGreeter();                  // callers see only the interface
        System.out.println(g.greet("Asha"));

        // AbstractList needs only get(int) and size() for a read-only list
        var squares = new AbstractList<Integer>() {
            @Override public Integer get(int i) { return i * i; }
            @Override public int size() { return 5; }
        };
        System.out.println(squares);
    }
}
Namaste, Asha!
[0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

Why not always use default methods in interfaces?

Default methods cannot touch fields, cannot be protected, cannot be final and cannot be a stable base for subclass state. They are for convenience and evolution. If you find yourself wanting state in an interface, you want an abstract class, or better, composition (composition over inheritance).

Overlap and exceptions

  • An abstract class with no state, no constructor logic and only abstract methods is just a worse interface. Convert it.
  • An interface with default methods can offer "mixin" behaviour (Comparator.reversed()), but still no state.
  • Both can have static methods and nested types.
  • If you must keep binary compatibility in a public library, adding an abstract method to either breaks implementers; adding a default method (or a concrete method in the class) does not.

Interview: "Abstract class vs interface?"

  • Lead with the decision rule: state and shared code in a family means abstract class; a capability across unrelated classes means interface.
  • Give three differences: multiple inheritance, instance state and constructors, access modifiers.
  • Mention Java 8 changes: default and static methods narrowed the gap, but interfaces still have no state.
  • Mention the skeleton pattern (List and AbstractList) to show depth.
  • Follow-up: "Why did Java add default methods?" Interface evolution, for stream() and forEach().

The final keyword; final vs finally vs finalize

final means "cannot be changed after this point": a final variable is assigned once, a final method cannot be overridden and a final class cannot be extended; it fixes the reference, not the contents of the object.

The word final appears in four places and means a slightly different "no more changes" in each. Learn the four, and the two look-alike words finally and finalize, which interviewers love to mix into one question.

final variables

A final variable can be assigned exactly once. After that, any assignment is a compile error: cannot assign a value to final variable.

  • Final local variable or parameter. final int tax = 18;. Many teams skip final on locals; it adds noise, though it is useful for a parameter you do not want reassigned.
  • Final instance field. Must be assigned once, either at the declaration, in an instance initializer, or in every constructor. A final field with no initial value is a blank final; the compiler checks that each constructor assigns it exactly once ("variable might not have been initialized").
  • Final static field. Assigned at declaration or in a static block. With a primitive or String constant value, it is a compile-time constant (static final int MAX = 10;), which the compiler copies into the code that uses it. Convention: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.
import java.util.*;

public class FinalDemo {
    static final double GST_RATE = 0.18;           // constant
    private final String orderId;                  // blank final
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();

    FinalDemo(String orderId) {
        this.orderId = orderId;                    // assigned exactly once
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        FinalDemo d = new FinalDemo("OD-1");
        d.items.add("Mouse");                      // OK: the list object is mutable
        d.items.add("Keyboard");
        System.out.println(d.items + " " + d.orderId);
        // d.items = new ArrayList<>();            // error: cannot assign a value to final variable items

        final int[] marks = {40, 50};
        marks[0] = 99;                             // OK: contents of a final array can change
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(marks));
        // marks = new int[3];                     // error
    }
}
[Mouse, Keyboard] OD-1
[99, 50]

final reference is not an immutable object

final locks the variable, not the object it points to. A final List still lets you call add; a final array still lets you change its elements. To get an object that really cannot change, make its class immutable (immutability), or use List.of(…) for an unmodifiable list. This is the most common final interview trap.

Effectively final

A local variable or parameter that is never reassigned after its first assignment is effectively final, even without the keyword. Lambdas and anonymous or local classes may use outer local variables only if they are final or effectively final. The reason: the lambda gets a copy of the value, and the variable may live on a thread's stack that is gone by the time the lambda runs. Allowing changes would give confusing results, so Java forbids them.

int count = 0;
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(count);   // OK only if count is never changed
count++;   // error at the lambda: local variables referenced from a lambda expression
           // must be final or effectively final

// Fix when you need a changing value: use an object or array holder, or AtomicInteger
var counter = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger();
Runnable ok = () -> counter.incrementAndGet();

final methods

A final method cannot be overridden. Use it when the method's behaviour is part of a class's safety or algorithm, such as the Template Method in abstract classes. Object.getClass(), wait() and notify() are final. A private method is effectively final already. Static methods can be marked final too, but it has little meaning, since they are hidden, not overridden.

final classes

A final class cannot be extended: cannot inherit from final String. The JDK uses it for security and immutability: String, Integer and all wrapper classes, LocalDate, Math. Records are implicitly final, and so are enums without constant bodies. For your own classes, making the class final is a good default for value-like types and utility classes, because inheritance is a strong coupling (composition). A middle option is a sealed class, which allows only chosen subclasses (sealed classes). A frequent real-world catch: frameworks that create proxies by subclassing (Spring CGLIB proxies, Hibernate lazy entities) cannot proxy a final class or final method. Spring Boot projects written in Kotlin need the "allopen" plugin for this reason.

final vs finally vs finalize

WordWhat it isPurpose
finalModifier (keyword)Variable assigned once; method not overridable; class not extendable
finallyBlock after tryCleanup code that runs whether or not an exception happened (Module 3)
finalize()Method of ObjectOld hook the garbage collector called before freeing an object. Deprecated for removal since Java 18
 
static int test() {
    try {
        return 1;
    } finally {
        System.out.println("cleanup runs even after return");
    }
}
// test() prints the message, then returns 1.
// finally is skipped only if the JVM stops first (System.exit) or the thread is killed.

finalize() was unpredictable: nobody can say when (or if) it runs, it slowed down the garbage collector, and it could resurrect objects. Do not write it. Close resources with try-with-resources (Module 3) and, for rare native-resource cases, use java.lang.ref.Cleaner. See Module 7 for the garbage collector.

Rules

  • A final field must be definitely assigned by the end of every constructor, once and only once.
  • A final method cannot be overridden; a final class cannot be extended; abstract final is illegal.
  • A lambda or inner class may capture only final or effectively final locals.
  • The same value assigned in a loop to a final local is fine, if declared inside the loop: each iteration is a new variable.

Conventions: where professionals use final

  • On fields, by default. Make fields private final unless they must change. It makes classes simpler and thread-safe by construction.
  • On constants: public static final, upper snake case.
  • On utility and value classes. Not on every local variable, and not on classes meant to be extended.
  • Constructor injection in Spring uses private final fields; it makes the dependency required and unchangeable.

Mistake: thinking final means immutable

Wrong belief

private final List<String> roles;     // "nobody can change roles"
public List<String> getRoles() { return roles; }   // caller can still add and remove

Right: protect the contents too

private final List<String> roles;
public List<String> getRoles() { return List.copyOf(roles); }  // unmodifiable copy

Interview: final questions

  • Final vs finally vs finalize? Keyword / cleanup block / deprecated GC hook. Say what each is in one line.
  • Can a final object's state change? Yes. Only the reference is fixed.
  • Can we override a final method? Extend a final class? No to both.
  • What is a blank final? A final field without an initial value; each constructor must assign it once.
  • What does effectively final mean, and why for lambdas? Never reassigned; lambdas capture copies of local values.
  • Why is String final? Security, caching of hash codes, safe sharing in the string pool, thread safety.

The Object class: toString, getClass and friends

Every class in Java extends java.lang.Object, so every object has toString, equals, hashCode, getClass and a few more methods; override toString in almost every class so that printing and logging show useful data.

If you write class Account { } and do not extend anything, the compiler silently adds extends Object. This is the root of the class tree (inheritance), and it is why a variable of type Object can hold anything, and why List<Object> accepts any element. The methods of Object are the minimum that all objects can do.

The methods of Object

MethodPurposeOverride?
String toString()Text form of the objectYes, nearly always
boolean equals(Object o)Logical equalityFor value types (equals and hashCode)
int hashCode()Number used by hash-based collectionsAlways together with equals
Class<?> getClass()The exact runtime classNo (final)
Object clone()Field-by-field copyRarely (clone and copy)
void finalize()Old GC hookNever; deprecated for removal
wait(), notify(), notifyAll()Thread coordination on the object's monitorNo (final); see Module 6

toString(): the text form

The default toString() returns the class name, an @ and the hash code in hexadecimal, for example Account@1b6d3586. That is useless in a log. Whenever you print an object with println, concatenate it with a string, or the debugger or a logger shows it, Java calls toString() for you.

import java.util.List;

class Plain { }

class Account {
    private final String number;
    private final String holder;
    private long balanceInPaise;

    Account(String number, String holder, long balanceInPaise) {
        this.number = number;
        this.holder = holder;
        this.balanceInPaise = balanceInPaise;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Account{number=" + number + ", holder=" + holder
             + ", balance=" + balanceInPaise / 100.0 + "}";
    }
}

public class ToStringDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Plain());                       // default: Class@hash
        Account a = new Account("SB1001", "Asha", 150000);
        System.out.println(a);                                 // println calls toString()
        System.out.println("Created " + a);                    // so does concatenation
        System.out.println(List.of(a, new Account("SB1002", "Ravi", 5000)));
    }
}
Plain@7a81197d
Account{number=SB1001, holder=Asha, balance=1500.0}
Created Account{number=SB1001, holder=Asha, balance=1500.0}
[Account{number=SB1001, holder=Asha, balance=1500.0}, Account{number=SB1002, holder=Ravi, balance=50.0}]

The hex number after @ changes from run to run, so do not copy it into tests. Collections call toString() on each element, which is why the list prints properly.

A good toString()

  • Include the class name and the fields that identify the object: Account{number=…}. Your IDE generates this; records and Lombok's @ToString do it for you.
  • Never include secrets: passwords, tokens, card numbers, Aadhaar. toString() ends up in logs.
  • Avoid fields that point back to a parent (a bidirectional JPA relationship). Two objects printing each other end in StackOverflowError. Avoid lazy-loaded collections for the same reason (extra queries).
  • Do not use toString() for program logic or parsing. It is for humans.
  • Keep it cheap; it may be called inside a log statement.

getClass(): the exact runtime class

obj.getClass() returns a Class object that describes the real class of obj, never its declared type. It is final. You can ask it for getName(), getSimpleName(), getSuperclass() and, through reflection, its methods and fields (the basis of Spring and Hibernate). A class literal Account.class gives the same kind of object without an instance.

Object o = "text";
System.out.println(o.getClass().getName());          // java.lang.String
System.out.println(o.getClass().getSimpleName());    // String
Number n = Integer.valueOf(5);
System.out.println(n.getClass() == Integer.class);   // true: exact class
System.out.println(n instanceof Number);             // true: any subtype counts
System.out.println(new int[0].getClass().getSimpleName());   // int[]

The difference between getClass() == X.class (exact) and instanceof (any subtype) is the key to writing a correct equals() (see the table in casting and instanceof).

Edge cases

  • String.valueOf(obj) and "" + obj print "null" for a null reference, but obj.toString() throws NullPointerException. Objects.toString(obj) is the null-safe call.
  • On an interface-typed variable you can always call Object's methods, because every interface type is also an Object.
  • An array's toString() is the default ([I@6d06d69c); use Arrays.toString(arr) or Arrays.deepToString.
  • getClass() of a Spring or Hibernate proxy returns the generated proxy class, not your class. This breaks getClass()-based equality on JPA entities.

Interview: Object class questions

  • Which class is the parent of all classes? java.lang.Object, even if you write no extends. An interface type has none, but its objects do.
  • Name the methods of Object. toString, equals, hashCode, getClass, clone, finalize, wait, notify, notifyAll.
  • What does the default toString() print? ClassName@hexHashCode.
  • What does getClass() return, and can you override it? The exact runtime Class; no, it is final.

equals() and hashCode(): the contracts and a correct implementation

Override equals when two objects with the same data should count as equal, follow its five rules, and always override hashCode too so that equal objects return the same number; otherwise HashMap and HashSet silently misbehave.

The default Object.equals() is the same as ==: two references are equal only if they point to the very same object. That is right for a Thread or a database connection, but wrong for a value such as money, a PAN number or an email address. Two Money(100, "INR") objects should be equal. So value classes override equals. The collections framework then relies on that (Module 4; internals in Module 7).

== versus equals()

String a = new String("hi");
String b = new String("hi");
System.out.println(a == b);          // false: two different objects
System.out.println(a.equals(b));     // true: same characters

Integer x = 127, y = 127;
System.out.println(x == y);          // true: small values come from a cache
Integer p = 1000, q = 1000;
System.out.println(p == q);          // false: two objects
System.out.println(p.equals(q));     // true

For objects, == compares identity (the reference), and equals() compares meaning, if the class defines it. For primitives only == exists. Use equals() for objects, always.

The equals contract

The documentation of Object.equals lists five rules for non-null references:

  1. Reflexive: x.equals(x) is true.
  2. Symmetric: x.equals(y) is true exactly when y.equals(x) is.
  3. Transitive: if x.equals(y) and y.equals(z), then x.equals(z).
  4. Consistent: repeated calls give the same answer while the objects are unchanged.
  5. Non-null: x.equals(null) is false (and never throws).

The hashCode contract

  • Called twice on an unchanged object in one run, it returns the same int.
  • If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must be true. This is the rule that matters.
  • Unequal objects may share a hash code (a collision), but fewer collisions mean a faster map.

Rule: override equals and hashCode together

A HashMap first uses hashCode() to pick a bucket, then equals() to find the right key inside it. If equal objects have different hash codes, they land in different buckets and the map never even compares them.

What goes wrong without hashCode

import java.util.*;

class Pan {
    final String number;
    Pan(String number) { this.number = number; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {          // equals overridden...
        return o instanceof Pan p && number.equals(p.number);
    }
    // ...but no hashCode(): the identity hash from Object is used
}

public class Broken {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Set<Pan> set = new HashSet<>();
        set.add(new Pan("ABCDE1234F"));
        set.add(new Pan("ABCDE1234F"));
        System.out.println(set.size());                               // expected 1
        System.out.println(set.contains(new Pan("ABCDE1234F")));      // expected true
    }
}
2
false

Each Pan gets its own identity-based hash code, so the two equal objects usually go to different buckets. "Usually" is the danger: sometimes they land in the same bucket and the bug disappears, which makes it hard to find.

A correct implementation

Use the same fields in both methods. Compare primitives with == (use Double.compare for double), objects with Objects.equals (null-safe), and build the hash with Objects.hash.

import java.util.*;

public final class Customer {
    private final long id;
    private final String email;                  // part of equality
    private String nickname;                     // NOT part of equality

    public Customer(long id, String email, String nickname) {
        this.id = id;
        this.email = email;
        this.nickname = nickname;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;                              // fast path, reflexive
        if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;   // null and type check
        Customer other = (Customer) o;
        return id == other.id && Objects.equals(email, other.email);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(id, email);                          // same fields as equals
    }

    @Override public String toString() { return "Customer{id=" + id + ", email=" + email + "}"; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Customer a = new Customer(1, "asha@example.com", "A");
        Customer b = new Customer(1, "asha@example.com", "Ash");
        Set<Customer> set = new HashSet<>(List.of(a));
        System.out.println(a.equals(b) + " " + (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()));
        System.out.println(set.contains(b));
    }
}
true true
true

The five-step recipe is: same reference, then null and class check, then cast, then compare the significant fields. Java 16+ lets you shorten the check with pattern matching: return o instanceof Customer c && id == c.id && Objects.equals(email, c.email);. A record generates all three methods for you (records).

instanceof or getClass() inside equals?

With getClass() a subclass instance never equals a parent instance, so symmetry and transitivity always hold. With instanceof a ColorPoint and a Point can be "equal" one way and not the other, which breaks symmetry. The safe choices are: use getClass(), or make the class final and use instanceof. Use instanceof with a non-final class only when the parent class defines equality for the whole hierarchy (as AbstractList does for all lists). Know that Hibernate proxies can make the getClass() approach fail for JPA entities, and a common choice there is equality on the id with a constant hashCode; the pitfalls are covered in the Spring Data JPA notes.

Mutable keys

Customer c = new Customer(1, "asha@example.com", "A");
Set<List<String>> sets = new HashSet<>();
List<String> key = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
sets.add(key);
key.add("b");                                  // hash code changes after insertion
System.out.println(sets.contains(key));        // false: wrong bucket now
System.out.println(sets.size());               // 1, the entry is stuck in the old bucket

If a field used in hashCode changes while the object sits in a HashSet or is a HashMap key, the object is lost. Use immutable keys: String, Integer, records, or your own immutable classes (immutability).

Edge cases

  • Float and double fields. Compare with Double.compare(a, b) == 0, not ==, to handle NaN and -0.0. Objects.hash boxes the primitive, which is fine.
  • Arrays in fields. Use Arrays.equals and Arrays.hashCode; Objects.equals on arrays compares references.
  • Constant hashCode. return 42; is legal but turns a map into a linked list or tree. Never do it for performance-sensitive types.
  • Consistency with compareTo. For sorted sets and maps, compareTo should return 0 exactly when equals is true, or TreeSet and HashSet will disagree.
  • Overload instead of override. boolean equals(Customer c) is an overload; collections call equals(Object) and ignore it. @Override catches this at compile time.
  • hashCode() values are not stable between JVM runs for objects with identity hashes; never store them in files or databases.

Mistakes to avoid

Wrong: overload, and compare floats with ==

public boolean equals(Customer c) {        // overload, not override
    return this.id == c.id;                // also NPE on null
}

Right

@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return o instanceof Customer c && id == c.id;
}
@Override public int hashCode() { return Long.hashCode(id); }
  • Different fields in equals and hashCode (the hash uses a field that equals ignores).
  • Using a mutable or generated field (a database id that is null before saving) as the only equality basis.
  • Throwing an exception from equals on null or on a different type.

Tip: let tools write it

Use the IDE generator (it uses Objects.equals and Objects.hash), a record, or Lombok's @EqualsAndHashCode. Then write one test that adds two equal objects to a HashSet and expects size 1. For tests there is also the EqualsVerifier library.

Interview: the favourites

  • What is the contract between equals and hashCode? Equal objects must have equal hash codes. The reverse need not hold.
  • What if you override equals but not hashCode? Hash collections fail to find equal objects. Show the HashSet duplicate example.
  • What if two different objects have the same hash code? A collision. The map falls back to equals() to tell them apart; correctness is kept, only speed suffers.
  • == vs equals? Identity vs logical equality; strings, wrappers and the Integer cache as examples.
  • Can a key change inside a HashMap? Not safely; make keys immutable.
  • See also the full internals in Module 7.

clone(), shallow vs deep copy, and copy constructors

A copy can be shallow (the new object shares the inner objects with the original) or deep (everything is duplicated); Object.clone() is awkward and easy to get wrong, so use a copy constructor, a static factory or an immutable design instead.

Assigning b = a copies only the reference; both variables then point at one object. To get an independent object, you need a real copy. The question is how deep the copy goes.

Shallow versus deep copy

A shallow copy makes a new outer object, but its fields still point to the same inner objects as the original. A deep copy also duplicates the inner objects, recursively. Immutable inner objects (String, Integer, LocalDate) need no duplication.

clone() and the Cloneable interface

Object.clone() is protected and makes a field-by-field (shallow) copy, without calling any constructor. To use it you must: implement the marker interface Cloneable (otherwise CloneNotSupportedException is thrown), override clone() as public and call super.clone(). You may narrow the return type (covariant return, overriding).

import java.util.*;

class Playlist implements Cloneable {
    String name;
    List<String> songs = new ArrayList<>();

    Playlist(String name) { this.name = name; }

    @Override
    public Playlist clone() {
        try {
            Playlist copy = (Playlist) super.clone();      // shallow: songs is shared
            copy.songs = new ArrayList<>(this.songs);      // fix it by hand: deep-ish copy
            return copy;
        } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) {
            throw new AssertionError(e);                   // cannot happen: we are Cloneable
        }
    }
}

public class CloneDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Playlist a = new Playlist("Morning");
        a.songs.add("Kun Faya Kun");
        Playlist b = a.clone();
        b.songs.add("Tum Hi Ho");
        b.name = "Evening";
        System.out.println(a.name + " " + a.songs);
        System.out.println(b.name + " " + b.songs);
    }
}
Morning [Kun Faya Kun]
Evening [Kun Faya Kun, Tum Hi Ho]

If you delete the line that copies songs, adding to b also changes a. And that is only one level; if the songs were mutable objects, you would have to clone them too.

Why clone() is disliked

  • The Cloneable interface has no clone() method; it just flips a switch inside Object.clone(). This is a design mistake that Java keeps for compatibility.
  • It creates objects without running a constructor, so invariants set by constructors are bypassed.
  • It is shallow by default and every mutable field needs manual care.
  • It throws a checked exception you can never really get, and it does not work with final fields that need a new value.
  • Subclasses must also remember to call super.clone() correctly.

One accepted use: array.clone() is a fast, correct shallow copy of an array (int[] copy = arr.clone();). For arrays of mutable objects remember it is shallow.

Better: copy constructor and static factory

A copy constructor takes an object of the same class and builds a new one. It is plain Java: it runs your validation, works with final fields, and makes it obvious what is copied deeply. A static factory such as Playlist.copyOf(other) does the same with a clearer name, like List.copyOf.

import java.util.*;

class Address {
    private String city;
    Address(String city) { this.city = city; }
    Address(Address other) { this.city = other.city; }        // copy constructor
    void setCity(String c) { this.city = c; }
    @Override public String toString() { return city; }
}

class Person {
    private final String name;
    private final Address address;                            // mutable inner object
    private final List<String> phones;

    Person(String name, Address address, List<String> phones) {
        this.name = name;
        this.address = new Address(address);                  // defensive copy in
        this.phones = new ArrayList<>(phones);
    }

    Person(Person other) {                                    // deep copy constructor
        this(other.name, other.address, other.phones);        // reuses the defensive copies
    }

    Address getAddress() { return new Address(address); }    // defensive copy out
    @Override public String toString() { return name + " " + address + " " + phones; }
}

public class Copying {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Address home = new Address("Pune");
        Person asha = new Person("Asha", home, List.of("98100"));
        Person copy = new Person(asha);
        home.setCity("Delhi");                 // does not affect either person
        asha.getAddress().setCity("Goa");      // nor this
        System.out.println(asha);
        System.out.println(copy);
    }
}
Asha Pune [98100]
Asha Pune [98100]

The same defensive-copy habit protects encapsulation (encapsulation). Besides these, other copy routes exist: serialization (slow and fragile), JSON mapping through Jackson (convenient for tests), the new ArrayList<>(other) constructors of collections, List.copyOf (an unmodifiable copy; the elements are not copied), and libraries such as MapStruct for DTO copies. Best of all is to share immutable objects so that no copy is needed (immutability).

Edge cases

  • Collection copy constructors and List.copyOf are shallow: the new list holds the same element objects.
  • Arrays.copyOf and array.clone() are shallow for object arrays; a 2D array needs a loop (or clone per row).
  • A cloned HashMap or ArrayList (they implement clone()) is also a shallow copy.
  • Records cannot be cloned in the usual sense, but they are immutable; copy a record by building a new one, for example new Point(p.x(), 5).
  • Calling clone() on a class that is not Cloneable gives CloneNotSupportedException at run time.

Convention

Prefer: immutable class, then copy constructor or static factory, then clone() only for arrays or when a library demands it. This is the advice of Effective Java and of most style guides.

Interview: copy questions

  • Shallow vs deep copy? Shared inner objects vs fully duplicated ones. Draw the two diagrams.
  • Why is clone() considered broken? Marker interface without the method, bypasses constructors, shallow by default, checked exception.
  • What do you use instead? Copy constructor, static factory, or immutable objects.
  • What does Cloneable do? It only allows Object.clone() to work; without it you get CloneNotSupportedException.

Composition vs inheritance: has-a, is-a and delegation

Inheritance models "is-a" and binds a child tightly to its parent's internals; composition models "has-a" by holding another object and forwarding calls to it, and is usually the safer, more flexible way to reuse code.

Beginners often use extends whenever two classes share code. That couples the child to every detail of the parent: when the parent changes, children can break. The other tool is composition: a class keeps a field that refers to another object and uses it. The classic advice from Effective Java and the Gang of Four book is "favor composition over inheritance".

Association, aggregation and composition

"Has-a" relationships come in three strengths. UML (the common diagram language) names them like this:

Association
One object knows or uses another: a Customer places Orders; a Teacher teaches Students. Both live on their own. Drawn as a plain line or arrow.
Aggregation
A weak "whole-part": a Department has Employees, but an employee exists without the department and may move to another. Hollow diamond.
Composition
A strong "whole-part": a House has Rooms; the rooms are created by and die with the house, and belong to no other. Filled diamond.

In code the difference is about lifetime and ownership. In composition the whole creates the parts and does not hand them out. In aggregation the parts are passed in and may live on.

import java.util.*;

class Room {
    final String name;
    Room(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

class House {                                           // composition
    private final List<Room> rooms = new ArrayList<>();
    House(String... roomNames) {
        for (String n : roomNames) rooms.add(new Room(n));   // House creates and owns the rooms
    }
    int roomCount() { return rooms.size(); }
}

class Employee { final String name; Employee(String n) { name = n; } }

class Department {                                      // aggregation
    private final List<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>();
    void add(Employee e) { staff.add(e); }              // employees come from outside
    int size() { return staff.size(); }
}

public class Relations {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new House("Hall", "Kitchen").roomCount());
        Employee asha = new Employee("Asha");
        Department hr = new Department(), it = new Department();
        hr.add(asha);
        it.add(asha);                                   // the same employee in two departments
        System.out.println(hr.size() + " " + it.size());
    }
}
2
1 1

The fragile base class problem

Inheritance breaks encapsulation: a subclass depends on how the parent works, not only on what it promises. Here is the well-known example. We want a HashSet that counts how many elements were ever added.

import java.util.*;

class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {          // inheritance
    private int added = 0;

    @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); }

    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        added += c.size();
        return super.addAll(c);          // HashSet.addAll calls add() for each element!
    }
    int getAdded() { return added; }
}

public class CountingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CountingSet<String> s = new CountingSet<>();
        s.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
        System.out.println(s.getAdded());     // we expect 3
    }
}
6

The parent's addAll internally calls add for each element, which the subclass has also overridden, so each element is counted twice. If a future JDK changed addAll not to call add, the answer would change again. The child is at the mercy of the parent's private implementation. That is the fragile base class problem. Other costs of inheritance: the child exposes the parent's whole API (a CountingSet also offers remove and clear); the relation is fixed at compile time; and Java allows one parent only.

The fix: composition and delegation

Hold a set as a private field and delegate (forward) the calls to it. You decide which methods to expose, and the wrapped set can be any Set.

import java.util.*;

class CountingSet2<E> {
    private final Set<E> inner;                     // has-a, typed by the interface
    private int added = 0;

    CountingSet2(Set<E> inner) { this.inner = inner; }

    boolean add(E e) { added++; return inner.add(e); }

    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        boolean changed = false;
        for (E e : c) changed |= add(e);              // our own loop: no hidden double count
        return changed;
    }
    int getAdded() { return added; }
    int size() { return inner.size(); }
}

public class CountingDemo2 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CountingSet2<String> s = new CountingSet2<>(new TreeSet<>());   // swap to LinkedHashSet freely
        s.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
        System.out.println(s.getAdded() + " " + s.size());
    }
}
3 3

If you must also be a Set, implement the Set interface and delegate (the "forwarding class" or wrapper pattern; Guava's ForwardingSet exists for this).

A second refactoring: behaviour as a component

Suppose you model vehicles and start with Car extends Engine because a car "uses" an engine. A car is not an engine. Worse, an electric car now inherits petrol-engine methods. Make the engine a component:

Wrong: inheritance for reuse

class Engine { void start() { /* ... */ } }
class Car extends Engine { }          // "a car is an engine"?

Right: composition and an interface

interface Engine { void start(); }
class PetrolEngine implements Engine { public void start() { /* ... */ } }
class ElectricMotor implements Engine { public void start() { /* ... */ } }

class Car {
    private final Engine engine;       // chosen at construction time
    Car(Engine engine) { this.engine = engine; }
    void start() { engine.start(); }   // delegation
}

Now you can build a new Car(new ElectricMotor()) or swap the engine in a test. This is the idea behind the Strategy pattern and behind dependency injection in Spring: an OrderService is composed of a repository and a payment client, it does not extend them (abstraction, Design patterns).

QuestionInheritanceComposition
Relationshipis-ahas-a / uses-a
CouplingTight, to the parent's internalsLoose, to a public interface
When is it fixed?Compile timeCan change at run time (swap the field)
ReuseOne parent onlyAs many components as you like
TestingHard to isolate the parentEasy: pass a fake component

When inheritance is still the right tool

  • There is a true is-a relation that passes the Liskov test: a child can be used wherever the parent is expected, without surprises (a Square that extends a mutable Rectangle fails this).
