  • The parent was designed and documented for extension (AbstractList, abstract classes with Template Methods).
  • Both classes are in the same package or project, so you control both.
  • Otherwise, make classes final or use interfaces plus composition. "Design and document for inheritance, or else prohibit it."

Mistakes to avoid

  • Extending a class only to reuse one method (Stack extends Vector in the JDK is the famous regret: a stack that lets you insert in the middle).
  • Making a domain object extend a utility or framework class, such as class Order extends ArrayList<Item>. Keep a List<Item> field instead.
  • Deep hierarchies of more than two or three levels. They are hard to follow and to change.
  • Aggregation where a part is shared and mutated by many owners without clear ownership.

Interview: composition vs inheritance

  • Give the sentence: "Favor composition over inheritance because inheritance couples the child to the parent's implementation, and composition lets me swap behaviour at run time."
  • Explain the three has-a levels (association, aggregation, composition) with ownership and lifetime.
  • Show the fragile base class with the HashSet.addAll counter.
  • Name patterns that use composition: Strategy, Decorator, Adapter; and Spring DI.
  • Admit the limits: inheritance is fine for real is-a with designed-for-extension parents.

Nested classes: static nested, inner, local and anonymous

A nested class is a class declared inside another class; there are four kinds (static nested, inner, local, anonymous), and the main difference is whether the nested object carries a hidden reference to an outer object.

Normally each class sits in its own file. When a small class exists only to serve one other class, you can declare it inside that class. This keeps related code together, hides helpers from the rest of the program (encapsulation) and gives the helper access to the outer class's private members. The class that holds the others is the outer (enclosing) class.

KindDeclaredHas outer instance?Typical use
Static nestedMember of the class, with staticNoBuilders, helper types, Map.Entry
Inner (member)Member of the class, no staticYesIterators, event handlers tied to one object
LocalInside a method or blockYes, if the method is an instance methodA helper used in one method only
AnonymousAn expression: new Type() { … }Yes, if in an instance contextOne-off implementations; mostly replaced by lambdas

Static nested class

A static nested class behaves like a top-level class that happens to live inside another one, just for grouping. It has no link to an outer object. It can reach the outer class's static members, including private ones. You create it with new Outer.Nested(). It may have any access modifier, so a private static nested class is invisible outside.

public class Pizza {
    private final String size;
    private final boolean cheese;

    private Pizza(Builder b) {                         // can read the builder's private fields
        this.size = b.size;
        this.cheese = b.cheese;
    }

    public static class Builder {                     // static nested class
        private String size = "medium";
        private boolean cheese;

        public Builder size(String s) { this.size = s; return this; }
        public Builder cheese(boolean c) { this.cheese = c; return this; }
        public Pizza build() { return new Pizza(this); }
    }

    @Override public String toString() { return size + " pizza, cheese=" + cheese; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Pizza p = new Pizza.Builder().size("large").cheese(true).build();
        System.out.println(p);
    }
}
large pizza, cheese=true

The JDK uses this style often: Map.Entry, AbstractMap.SimpleEntry, HttpRequest.Builder.

Inner (member) class

An inner class is a non-static member. Each inner object is tied to one outer object and can use all its fields and methods, even private ones, directly. The compiler stores a hidden reference to the outer instance. Inside the inner class, this is the inner object and Outer.this is the outer one.

import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

public class Playlist implements Iterable<String> {
    private final String[] songs = {"Kun Faya Kun", "Tum Hi Ho", "Kesariya"};
    private final String owner = "Asha";

    @Override
    public Iterator<String> iterator() {
        return new SongIterator();                    // created inside an instance method
    }

    private class SongIterator implements Iterator<String> {   // inner class
        private int index = 0;

        @Override public boolean hasNext() { return index < songs.length; }   // outer field

        @Override public String next() {
            if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return songs[index++] + " (" + Playlist.this.owner + ")";       // Outer.this
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String s : new Playlist()) {
            System.out.println(s);
        }
        Playlist p = new Playlist();
        Playlist.SongIterator it = p.new SongIterator();   // outer.new Inner() from outside
        System.out.println(it.next());
    }
}
Kun Faya Kun (Asha)
Tum Hi Ho (Asha)
Kesariya (Asha)
Kun Faya Kun (Asha)

From outside you need an outer object first: outer.new Inner(). Plain new Inner() works only inside an instance method of the outer class. This is how ArrayList implements its iterator.

Inner classes hold on to the outer object

Because an inner object keeps a reference to its outer object, it keeps that outer object alive for the garbage collector. If a long-living inner or anonymous object (a listener, a cache entry) is registered somewhere, it can leak a large outer object. If the inner class does not need the outer instance, make it static. IDEs warn about this, and it is the main reason to prefer static nested classes by default. Also, an inner class cannot declare static members in older Java; since Java 16 it can.

Local classes

A local class is declared in a method body, like a local variable. It is visible only in that block, and it can use the method's parameters and local variables if they are final or effectively final (final). Since Java 16, local records, enums and interfaces are allowed too; they are useful for small data holders inside a stream pipeline.

static void printTotals(double[] prices) {
    final double gst = 0.18;
    class Line {                                       // local class
        final double price;
        Line(double price) { this.price = price; }
        double withTax() { return price * (1 + gst); } // captures the effectively final gst
    }
    for (double p : prices) {
        System.out.printf("%.2f%n", new Line(p).withTax());
    }
}
// printTotals(new double[]{100, 250}) prints 118.00 and 295.00

Anonymous classes and lambdas

An anonymous class declares and instantiates a class in one expression: it extends a class or implements an interface, has no name and exists only here. It is useful for a one-off implementation, with state or several methods.

import java.util.*;

public class AnonDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ravi", "Asha", "Meera"));

        names.sort(new Comparator<String>() {           // anonymous class
            @Override public int compare(String a, String b) {
                return a.length() - b.length();
            }
        });
        System.out.println(names);

        names.sort((a, b) -> a.compareTo(b));              // same idea as a lambda
        System.out.println(names);

        Runnable r = new Runnable() {
            private int runs = 0;                         // own state: a lambda cannot do this
            @Override public void run() { System.out.println("run " + (++runs)); }
        };
        r.run();
        r.run();
    }
}
[Ravi, Asha, Meera]
[Asha, Meera, Ravi]
run 1
run 2

Since Java 8, a lambda replaces an anonymous class when the type is a functional interface (one abstract method). Prefer the lambda; it is shorter (Module 5). The two are not identical:

QuestionAnonymous classLambda
Can implementAny interface, or extend a classOnly a functional interface
Meaning of thisThe anonymous object itselfThe enclosing object
Own fields and extra methodsYesNo
Compiled toA separate class file (Outer$1.class)An invokedynamic call, no class file for it
Shadowing local namesCan declare a variable with the same name as an outer localCannot; same scope as the enclosing method

Access rules in short

  • A nested class can access all members of its outer class, including private ones, and the outer class can access the nested class's private members.
  • A static nested class sees only the outer class's static members directly; for instance members it needs an outer object.
  • Local and anonymous classes can capture only final or effectively final local variables.
  • An anonymous class has no constructor of its own; arguments go to the superclass constructor: new Shape("x") { … }. It cannot be static or abstract.
  • The compiled names are Outer$Nested.class, Outer$1.class and Outer$1Local.class.

Conventions: which kind to choose

  • Start with a static nested class. Use inner only when each instance really needs the outer object.
  • If the nested class is big or used by other classes, move it to its own file.
  • Use a lambda for functional interfaces, an anonymous class only when you need state or a non-functional type, and a local class or local record for a tiny helper inside one method.

Mistake: instantiating an inner class from a static method

Wrong

public static void main(String[] a) {
    Inner i = new Inner();     // error: non-static variable this cannot be referenced
                               // from a static context
}

Right: make it static, or create an outer object

static class Inner { }                    // option 1
// option 2: Outer o = new Outer(); Outer.Inner i = o.new Inner();

Interview: nested class questions

  • Static nested vs inner? Inner holds a reference to an outer instance and can use its instance members; static nested does not.
  • Why can a local or anonymous class use only final variables? It captures a copy of the value; see effectively final.
  • Anonymous class vs lambda? Show the table: this, state, class file, functional-interface limit.
  • Can an inner class be private? Yes; a top-level class cannot (access modifiers).

Packages and imports

A package is a named folder of related classes that prevents name clashes and controls package-private access; you declare it with package, name it with your reversed domain in lowercase, and bring other packages' classes into view with import.

Imagine a project with two classes called Date, one for the database and one for the UI. Without a way to separate them they would clash. A package is a namespace: java.util.Date and java.sql.Date are different classes because their packages differ. Packages also group classes by purpose, and they are the unit for the package-private access level (access modifiers).

Declaring a package and the folder rule

The first statement of a file (before imports and the class) is the package declaration. The folder structure must match it. For a Maven or Gradle project, source files live under src/main/java.

 src/main/java
 └── com
     └── acme
         └── shop
             ├── model
             │   └── Order.java          package com.acme.shop.model;
             ├── service
             │   └── OrderService.java   package com.acme.shop.service;
             └── ShopApp.java            package com.acme.shop;

package com.acme.shop.service;               // must be the first statement

import com.acme.shop.model.Order;            // single-type import
import java.util.List;
import java.util.ArrayList;

public class OrderService {
    private final List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();

    public void place(Order order) {
        orders.add(order);
        System.out.println("Placed " + order.id());
    }
}

The fully qualified name of this class is com.acme.shop.service.OrderService. You can always use it without an import: java.util.List<String> names = new java.util.ArrayList<>();. An import is only a shortcut so that you can write the short name. It does not copy or load anything, and unused imports cost nothing at run time.

To compile and run by hand from the project root:

$ javac -d out src/main/java/com/acme/shop/model/*.java src/main/java/com/acme/shop/service/*.java src/main/java/com/acme/shop/ShopApp.java
$ java -cp out com.acme.shop.ShopApp

The class is run by its fully qualified name; the -d out option creates the matching folders for you. Build tools do this automatically.

Naming conventions

  • All lowercase, no underscores or spaces: com.acme.shop.service.
  • Start with your organisation's domain name reversed: the company acme.com becomes com.acme. Add the project and then layers or features. Open source: org.springframework, com.fasterxml.jackson.
  • If you have no domain, use something unique such as io.github.yourname.
  • Do not start with java. or javax.; those belong to the JDK.
  • Layer-based (controller, service, repository) or feature-based (order, payment) layouts both work. Larger apps tend to prefer feature packages, because a feature's classes can stay package-private and change together.

Imports

FormExampleNotes
Single-typeimport java.util.List;Preferred; the reader sees where each name comes from
On-demand (wildcard)import java.util.*;All classes of that package, not its subpackages
Static singleimport static java.lang.Math.max;Use max(a, b) without Math.
Static wildcardimport static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;Common in tests; avoid in main code
 
import static java.lang.Math.max;
import static java.lang.Math.sqrt;
import java.util.*;                       // List, Map, Set, ... but not java.util.function

public class ImportDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(max(3, 8));              // Math.max, via static import
        System.out.println(sqrt(81));
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();     // no import needed for String: java.lang
        names.add("Asha");
        System.out.println(names);
    }
}
8
9.0
[Asha]

Things you do not need to import: everything in java.lang (String, Math, Integer, System, Object, Exception, Thread…), and classes in the same package. Classes in other packages always need an import or the full name, even if the folders are next to each other.

Name clashes

If two imported packages contain the same simple name, the compiler cannot decide. With two single-type imports of the same name it is an error, with two wildcard imports it is an error only when you use the name ("reference to Date is ambiguous"). Import one and write the other fully qualified:

import java.util.Date;

public class Clash {
    java.util.Date utilDate = new Date();           // from the import
    java.sql.Date sqlDate = new java.sql.Date(0L);  // full name for the other one
}

A single-type import beats a wildcard import, and a class declared in the same package beats a wildcard import. A class in your own file shadows a same-named import (the compiler rejects a conflicting single-type import).

The default package

A file with no package line belongs to the unnamed default package. It is fine for a 20-line experiment. Do not use it in real projects: classes in named packages cannot import classes from the default package, and Spring Boot's component scan will not work properly. Always declare a package.

Packages, access and modules

  • Package-private (no modifier) members are visible to every class in the same package, and nowhere else. Sub-packages are not "inside": com.acme.shop and com.acme.shop.model are separate packages.
  • Package names are a naming scheme; there is no "parent can see child" rule.
  • Java 9 added modules (module-info.java) that group packages and decide which are exported. Most application projects, including typical Spring Boot ones, do not use them; libraries and the JDK itself do.

Version note: module imports in Java 25

Java 25 finalises module import declarations: import module java.base; imports every public class of the packages that module exports. It is meant for scripts and teaching; in team code, explicit single-type imports are still the style.

Rules

  • The package statement comes first; imports come next; then the type declarations. One public top-level class per file, named like the file.
  • A wildcard import does not include subpackages: import java.util.*; does not give you java.util.function.Function.
  • Static imports import members, not classes; a regular import does not make static members available by simple name.
  • Folder structure must match the package for the usual tools; otherwise: class not found errors at run time.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Running java OrderService for a packaged class. You need the full name and a class path: java -cp out com.acme.shop.service.OrderService (the error is Could not find or load main class).
  • Naming a package after a class or using capitals (com.acme.Shop); it confuses readers and file systems.
  • Wildcard imports of two big packages, then an ambiguous List (java.util.List vs java.awt.List).
  • Circular dependencies between packages (model imports service and the reverse). Keep the dependency direction one way.

In a Spring Boot project

The main class sits in the root package (com.acme.shop.ShopApplication), and @SpringBootApplication scans that package and everything below it. A controller placed in a sibling package outside it is silently not found. Your IDE organises imports for you (Ctrl+Alt+O in IntelliJ) and Maven/Gradle compile the folders as packages.

Interview: package questions

  • Why packages? Avoid name clashes, organise code, control access with package-private.
  • Does import java.util.* import subpackages? No.
  • Which package is imported automatically? java.lang.
  • Is importing a lot of classes slower? No; imports are resolved at compile time and leave no run-time cost.
  • What is a static import? It lets you use static members without the class name; use it sparingly.

Enums: type-safe constants with behaviour

An enum is a class with a fixed set of named instances; it replaces int and String constants with a type the compiler checks, and each constant can carry fields, methods and its own behaviour.

Without enums, people wrote static final int PENDING = 0, SHIPPED = 1;. Nothing stops setStatus(42) or mixing an order status with a payment status. An enum (short for enumeration) fixes this: OrderStatus is its own type with exactly the values you list, and the compiler rejects anything else. Use an enum whenever a value comes from a small, known, fixed set: days, order states, roles, payment modes, HTTP methods.

The basics

enum OrderStatus { PLACED, PACKED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }

public class EnumBasics {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderStatus s = OrderStatus.SHIPPED;
        System.out.println(s);                         // SHIPPED (name())
        System.out.println(s.ordinal());               // 2: position in the declaration
        System.out.println(s == OrderStatus.SHIPPED);  // true: == is the right comparison
        System.out.println(s.compareTo(OrderStatus.PLACED));  // 2: ordinal difference

        for (OrderStatus x : OrderStatus.values()) {   // all constants, in order
            System.out.print(x + " ");
        }
        System.out.println();

        OrderStatus y = OrderStatus.valueOf("PACKED"); // from a String; exact, case-sensitive
        System.out.println(y);

        String msg = switch (s) {                      // switch expression, no default needed
            case PLACED, PACKED -> "We are preparing it";
            case SHIPPED        -> "On the way";
            case DELIVERED      -> "Done";
            case CANCELLED      -> "Cancelled";
        };
        System.out.println(msg);
        OrderStatus.valueOf("shipped");                // throws IllegalArgumentException
    }
}
SHIPPED
2
true
2
PLACED PACKED SHIPPED DELIVERED CANCELLED
PACKED
On the way
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: No enum constant OrderStatus.shipped
	at java.base/java.lang.Enum.valueOf(Enum.java:...)

The compiler turns the enum into a class that extends java.lang.Enum. Each constant is a public static final instance, created once when the enum class loads. Because there is exactly one instance of each constant, == is correct and fast (and equals is the same thing). When a switch expression covers every constant, the compiler checks that none is missing, so adding a new constant later makes the build fail where you forgot to handle it. That is a good reason to avoid a default branch there.

Enums with fields, constructors and methods

An enum is a full class. Put data after the constants (note the semicolon), write a constructor and add methods. The constructor is always private (implicitly), because only the enum itself creates its constants.

import java.util.*;

enum PaymentMode {
    UPI("UPI", 0.0),                       // calls the constructor
    CREDIT_CARD("Credit card", 2.0),
    NET_BANKING("Net banking", 1.5),
    COD("Cash on delivery", 0.0);

    private final String label;
    private final double feePercent;

    PaymentMode(String label, double feePercent) {   // implicitly private
        this.label = label;
        this.feePercent = feePercent;
    }

    public String label() { return label; }

    public double fee(double amount) { return amount * feePercent / 100; }

    private static final Map<String, PaymentMode> BY_LABEL = new HashMap<>();
    static {
        for (PaymentMode m : values()) BY_LABEL.put(m.label, m);
    }
    public static Optional<PaymentMode> fromLabel(String label) {   // safe lookup
        return Optional.ofNullable(BY_LABEL.get(label));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (PaymentMode m : values()) {
            System.out.printf("%-12s fee on 1000 = %.1f%n", m.label(), m.fee(1000));
        }
        System.out.println(fromLabel("Net banking").orElseThrow());
        System.out.println(fromLabel("Bitcoin").isPresent());
    }
}
UPI          fee on 1000 = 0.0
Credit card  fee on 1000 = 20.0
Net banking  fee on 1000 = 15.0
Cash on delivery fee on 1000 = 0.0
NET_BANKING
false

Fields of an enum should be final. A mutable enum is shared global state and a bug waiting to happen. The static lookup map is the standard answer to "convert a code or label from the database or a request to an enum without an exception".

Per-constant behaviour

Each constant can have its own body that overrides a method, or supply a missing abstract method. This replaces long if/switch chains (a form of the Strategy pattern, polymorphism).

enum Operation {
    ADD("+") { @Override double apply(double a, double b) { return a + b; } },
    SUBTRACT("-") { @Override double apply(double a, double b) { return a - b; } },
    MULTIPLY("*") { @Override double apply(double a, double b) { return a * b; } };

    private final String symbol;
    Operation(String symbol) { this.symbol = symbol; }

    abstract double apply(double a, double b);        // every constant must implement it

    @Override public String toString() { return symbol; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (Operation op : values()) {
            System.out.println("6 " + op + " 3 = " + op.apply(6, 3));
        }
    }
}
6 + 3 = 9.0
6 - 3 = 3.0
6 * 3 = 18.0

Enums can also implement interfaces (enum Plan implements Billable), which lets them plug into a type hierarchy. They cannot extend a class, because they already extend Enum, and they cannot be extended.

Useful members

MemberWhat it does
values()New array with all constants in declaration order (a copy each call)
valueOf(String)Constant with exactly that name; throws IllegalArgumentException if none, NullPointerException for null
name()The identifier as declared; final, stable
toString()Same as name() by default; override for a friendly text
ordinal()Zero-based position; changes if you reorder
compareTo(E)Compares ordinals, so enums sort in declaration order
getDeclaringClass()The enum type (useful when constants have bodies)

EnumMap and EnumSet

For enum keys, use EnumMap and EnumSet. They store data in a compact array or bit vector indexed by ordinal. They are faster and smaller than HashMap and HashSet, and they iterate in declaration order (more in Module 4).

import java.util.*;

enum Day { MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI, SAT, SUN }

public class EnumCollections {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Day, Integer> orders = new EnumMap<>(Day.class);
        orders.put(Day.WED, 40);
        orders.put(Day.MON, 25);
        System.out.println(orders);                       // ordered by declaration, not insertion

        Set<Day> weekend = EnumSet.of(Day.SAT, Day.SUN);
        Set<Day> weekdays = EnumSet.complementOf(weekend);
        System.out.println(weekdays);
        System.out.println(EnumSet.range(Day.TUE, Day.THU));
    }
}
{MON=25, WED=40}
[MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI]
[TUE, WED, THU]

Enum singleton

A one-constant enum is the simplest safe singleton: the JVM guarantees one instance, it is thread-safe and it survives serialization and reflection attacks. See the Singleton pattern in Design patterns.

enum AppConfig {
    INSTANCE;
    private final String env = System.getenv().getOrDefault("APP_ENV", "dev");
    public String env() { return env; }
}
// usage: AppConfig.INSTANCE.env()

Rules

  • An enum constructor is private; calling new on an enum is a compile error ("enum classes may not be instantiated").
  • Constants come first in the body, separated by commas; a semicolon is needed only if members follow.
  • Enums cannot extend a class or be extended, but can implement interfaces. They are implicitly final unless a constant has a body (then implicitly sealed).
  • In a switch over an enum, case labels use the bare constant name (case SHIPPED), not OrderStatus.SHIPPED in old-style switches.

Edge cases and runtime exceptions

  • valueOf("shipped") throws IllegalArgumentException: No enum constant … (case matters). Catch it or use a lookup map when the input comes from outside.
  • switch on a null enum throws NullPointerException.
  • A static field of the enum cannot be used from its constructor (the constants are built first); use a static block after the constants, as the lookup map above does.
  • Enum constants are serialized by name, so renaming a constant breaks old data.

Mistake: persisting ordinal()

Wrong: stores the position

@Enumerated(EnumType.ORDINAL)      // JPA default! stores 0, 1, 2...
private OrderStatus status;
// Later someone inserts a constant in the middle: every old row now means something else.

Right: store the name

@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)       // stores "SHIPPED"
private OrderStatus status;

Never use ordinal() in your own logic either (no "status + 1"). If you need a number in a database or an API, give the enum a field such as code and a lookup method.

Conventions

  • Enum type names are singular nouns in PascalCase (OrderStatus); constants in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.
  • Use == for comparison. Put behaviour in the enum rather than scattering switch statements across the code base.
  • For a fixed set that has data rather than behaviour and is read from a database, weigh an enum (compile-time safe, needs a deploy to change) against a lookup table (changes at run time).

Interview: enum questions

  • Why enums over constants? Type safety, names in output, can hold data and behaviour, works in switch, EnumMap.
  • Can an enum have a constructor? Be public? Yes; always private, implicitly.
  • Can an enum extend a class or implement an interface? Not extend; implement, yes.
  • How do you get an enum from a String? valueOf, with IllegalArgumentException on failure.
  • How is an enum singleton safe? JVM-guaranteed single instance, serialization-safe, reflection cannot create more.

Records: compact immutable data classes

A record declares an immutable data carrier in one line: the compiler generates the private final fields, the constructor, the accessors, and equals, hashCode and toString; use it for DTOs, value objects and return types, not for JPA entities or mutable state.

A normal data class needs about 30 lines: fields, a constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, toString. Most of it is boilerplate. A record (a standard feature since Java 16) says it in one line, and the intent is clear: "this class is just its data".

record Point(int x, int y) { }                      // that's the whole class

public class RecordBasics {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Point p = new Point(3, 4);
        System.out.println(p.x() + ", " + p.y());   // accessor is x(), not getX()
        System.out.println(p);                      // generated toString
        System.out.println(p.equals(new Point(3, 4)));          // generated equals: by value
        System.out.println(p.hashCode() == new Point(3, 4).hashCode());
        // p.x = 5;       // error: cannot assign a value to final variable x
    }
}
3, 4
Point[x=3, y=4]
true
true

What the compiler generates

  • A private final field for each component (the names in the header).
  • A canonical constructor with all components in order: new Point(3, 4).
  • One public accessor per component, named like the component: x(), y(). There is no getX() and no setters.
  • equals() (all components equal), hashCode() (derived from all components) and toString() in the form Point[x=3, y=4].
  • The record is implicitly final and extends java.lang.Record, so it cannot extend another class. It can implement interfaces.

Compact constructor: validation and normalisation

To check or adjust values, write a compact canonical constructor: the record name with no parameter list. It runs first with the parameters in scope. Assign nothing to the fields yourself; the compiler does it at the end, with whatever the parameters now hold.

import java.util.*;

record Money(long paise, String currency) implements Comparable<Money> {

    static final Money ZERO_INR = new Money(0, "INR");   // static fields are allowed

    Money {                                              // compact constructor
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency");
        if (paise < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("paise must be >= 0: " + paise);
        currency = currency.toUpperCase();               // normalise the parameter
    }

    static Money inr(double rupees) {                    // static factory with a clear name
        return new Money(Math.round(rupees * 100), "INR");
    }

    Money plus(Money other) {                            // custom method
        if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(paise + other.paise, currency);
    }

    @Override public int compareTo(Money o) { return Long.compare(paise, o.paise); }

    @Override public String toString() {                 // you may override generated methods
        return String.format("%s %.2f", currency, paise / 100.0);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(inr(499.5).plus(new Money(250, "inr")));
        try {
            new Money(-1, "INR");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
INR 502.00
paise must be >= 0: -1

Besides the compact form, you can write the full canonical constructor yourself (then you assign the fields with this.x = x), or add extra constructors, which must start with this(…) and so end up in the canonical one. A record may also declare an accessor of its own, for example to return a copy.

Immutability is shallow

The fields of a record are final, but if a component is a mutable object, the object can still change. Copy mutable inputs in the compact constructor and return unmodifiable views.

import java.util.*;

record Team(String name, List<String> members) {
    Team {
        members = List.copyOf(members);          // defensive copy; unmodifiable
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha", "Ravi"));
        Team t = new Team("Core", list);
        list.add("Meera");                       // does not affect the record
        System.out.println(t);
        try {
            t.members().add("X");                // UnsupportedOperationException
        } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
            System.out.println("members are read-only");
        }
    }
}
Team[name=Core, members=[Asha, Ravi]]
members are read-only

Without that line, the caller still holds the list and can change the team's state from outside. This is the same defensive-copy rule as in immutability. For hash-based collections a record with a mutable component also breaks the "mutable keys" rule from equals and hashCode.

Other things records can do

  • Nested and local records. A record declared inside a method is handy for grouping temporary data in a stream pipeline: record Pair(String name, int score) {}.
  • Generics. record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) {}.
  • Interfaces. record Circle(double r) implements Shape (see sealed classes).
  • Record patterns (Java 21). if (o instanceof Point(int x, int y)) { … } takes a record apart in a test or switch (Module 5).
  • Static members are allowed; instance fields other than the components are not.

Records vs Lombok vs a normal class

QuestionRecordLombok @ValueNormal class
BoilerplateNone, built inNone, via annotation processorAll written or IDE-generated
Extra dependencyNoYes (Lombok)No
Getter stylex()getX()Your choice
Mutable fields / settersNoNo (@Data has them)Yes
Can extend a classNoYesYes
Works as a JPA entityNoNo (needs a no-arg constructor)Yes

Rules

  • A record cannot extend a class, cannot be abstract, and cannot declare instance fields beyond its components.
  • In a compact constructor you cannot write this.x = x; assign to the parameter.
  • An explicit canonical constructor cannot be less accessible than the record itself.
  • An overridden accessor must be public and return the component's type.

When not to use a record

  • JPA/Hibernate entities. They need a no-argument constructor, non-final classes (for lazy proxies), mutable fields and an identity that outlives its data. Use a normal class for the entity and a record for the DTO or projection that you return from the API.
  • Mutable state or builder-style construction with many optional parameters (a record with 12 components is hard to read; use a class with a builder).
  • Inheritance hierarchies. Records are final. Model a family with a sealed interface and several records instead.
  • Hiding data. A record is a transparent carrier; its components are its public API. If you need to hide the representation (encapsulation), use a normal class.

In real Spring Boot projects

Records are now the standard way to write request and response DTOs: record CreateOrderRequest(@NotBlank String customerId, @Min(1) int quantity) {} works with Jackson (JSON) and Bean Validation, and with Spring Data projections and @ConfigurationProperties. Also use them for map keys, for returning several values from a method, and for events and messages.

Interview: record questions

  • What is a record, and what does the compiler generate? A final, immutable data class: fields, canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, toString.
  • Are records fully immutable? Only shallowly; copy mutable components.
  • Can a record have a setter, extend a class or implement an interface? No / no / yes.
  • Why not use a record as a JPA entity? No no-arg constructor, final class and fields, no proxies.
  • Record vs Lombok? Language feature with no dependency, but no setters or inheritance.

Sealed classes and interfaces (a teaser)

A sealed class or interface lists exactly which classes may extend or implement it, so the compiler knows every possible subtype and can check that a switch over them is complete.

Normally anyone can extend your public class or implement your public interface. Sometimes you want a closed family: a payment is either UPI, a card or cash on delivery, and nothing else. Enums are closed families of constants; sealed types (final since Java 17) are closed families of types, each of which may carry different data.

sealed interface Payment permits Upi, Card, Cod { }      // the allowed implementations

record Upi(String vpa) implements Payment { }
record Card(String last4, boolean credit) implements Payment { }
record Cod() implements Payment { }

public class SealedDemo {
    static String describe(Payment p) {
        return switch (p) {                                // exhaustive: no default needed
            case Upi u  -> "UPI to " + u.vpa();
            case Card c -> (c.credit() ? "Credit" : "Debit") + " card ending " + c.last4();
            case Cod c  -> "Cash on delivery";
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(describe(new Upi("asha@bank")));
        System.out.println(describe(new Card("4242", true)));
        System.out.println(describe(new Cod()));
    }
}
UPI to asha@bank
Credit card ending 4242
Cash on delivery

If you later add a fourth permitted type, describe stops compiling until you handle it. That is the big gain: the compiler tells you every place a new case matters. It replaces long instanceof chains and the visitor pattern. Pattern-matching switch belongs to Module 5; this article only shows why sealing makes it safe.

The rules

  • Declare with sealed and a permits list. If the permitted classes are in the same file, permits may be omitted.
  • Each permitted subclass must say what happens next: final (no more subclasses), sealed (it restricts its own children) or non-sealed (it opens the hierarchy again).
  • Permitted subclasses must be in the same module, or in the same package when you do not use modules.
  • Records and enums are implicitly final, so they fit perfectly as permitted types.
sealed abstract class Shape permits Circle, Polygon { }
final class Circle extends Shape { }
sealed class Polygon extends Shape permits Triangle, Square { }
final class Triangle extends Polygon { }
non-sealed class Square extends Polygon { }      // anyone may extend Square

When to use sealed types

  • For domain models with a small, known set of variants: results (Success/Failure), payment types, commands, expression trees.
  • When you want exhaustive switch without a default.
  • Not for plugin points where third parties must extend your type. Use a normal interface there.

Interview: one-liner

"A sealed type restricts its direct subtypes with permits; each must be final, sealed or non-sealed. It gives closed hierarchies and compiler-checked exhaustive switches." Compare it with final (no subclasses at all) and with enums (closed, but constants of one type).

The four pillars together: a worked bank example, and SOLID

Encapsulation protects data, abstraction hides complexity behind a contract, inheritance shares code in an is-a family, and polymorphism lets one call behave differently per object; a small bank model shows all four working together.

The four pillars at a glance

PillarIdeaHow Java supports itInterview one-liner
EncapsulationKeep data private and change it only through methods that keep it validprivate fields, public methods, immutability"Bundling data with the code that guards it, and hiding it."
AbstractionExpose what an object does, hide howInterfaces, abstract classes, small public APIs"Showing the essentials, hiding the details."
InheritanceA new class reuses and specialises an existing oneextends, super, protected"Acquiring the properties and behaviour of a parent: an is-a relationship."
PolymorphismOne reference type, many behavioursOverriding and dynamic dispatch (run time); overloading (compile time)"Same call, different behaviour depending on the real object."

Real-world picture: a UPI app. Your account details are not readable by other apps (encapsulation). You tap "Pay" without knowing banks' internal APIs (abstraction). Savings and current accounts share account rules but differ in details (inheritance). Paying through any bank behaves correctly for that bank (polymorphism).

The model

The code

import java.util.*;

interface InterestPolicy {                                // abstraction: a contract
    long interestFor(long balanceInPaise);
}

record Transaction(String type, long amountInPaise, long balanceAfter) { }  // immutable data

abstract class Account {
    private final String number;                          // encapsulation: private state
    private long balance;
    private final List<Transaction> history = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Account(String number) { this.number = number; }

    public final void deposit(long amount) {              // fixed rules: subclasses can't break them
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        post("DEPOSIT", amount);
    }

    public final void withdraw(long amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        if (balance - amount < minimumBalance()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds in " + number);
        }
        post("WITHDRAW", -amount);
    }

    protected abstract long minimumBalance();             // varies per account type
    public void monthEnd() { }                            // hook: default does nothing

    protected final void post(String type, long signedAmount) {
        balance += signedAmount;
        history.add(new Transaction(type, Math.abs(signedAmount), balance));
    }

    public long balance() { return balance; }
    public List<Transaction> history() { return List.copyOf(history); }   // defensive copy

    @Override public String toString() {
        return String.format("%s %s balance=Rs %.2f",
                getClass().getSimpleName(), number, balance / 100.0);
    }
}

class SavingsAccount extends Account {                    // inheritance: is-a Account
    private final InterestPolicy policy;                  // composition: has-a policy

    SavingsAccount(String number, InterestPolicy policy) {
        super(number);
        this.policy = policy;
    }
    @Override protected long minimumBalance() { return 0; }
    @Override public void monthEnd() {
        long interest = policy.interestFor(balance());
        if (interest > 0) post("INTEREST", interest);
    }
}

class CurrentAccount extends Account {
    private final long overdraftLimit;
    CurrentAccount(String number, long overdraftLimit) {
        super(number);
        this.overdraftLimit = overdraftLimit;
    }
    @Override protected long minimumBalance() { return -overdraftLimit; }   // may go negative
}

public class BankDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        InterestPolicy fourPercent = balance -> balance * 4 / 1200;   // lambda: monthly 4% p.a.
        Account s = new SavingsAccount("SB1001", fourPercent);
        Account c = new CurrentAccount("CA2001", 500_000);          // Rs 5,000 overdraft

        s.deposit(1_000_000);                                       // Rs 10,000
        c.deposit(200_000);
        c.withdraw(600_000);                                        // goes to -Rs 4,000: allowed
        try {
            s.withdraw(2_000_000);                                  // not allowed
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }

        List<Account> accounts = List.of(s, c);                     // polymorphism
        accounts.forEach(Account::monthEnd);                        // each type does its own thing
        accounts.forEach(System.out::println);
        System.out.println(s.history());
    }
}
Insufficient funds in SB1001
SavingsAccount SB1001 balance=Rs 10033.33
CurrentAccount CA2001 balance=Rs -4000.00
[Transaction[type=DEPOSIT, amountInPaise=1000000, balanceAfter=1000000], Transaction[type=INTEREST, amountInPaise=3333, balanceAfter=1003333]]

Where each pillar shows up

  • Encapsulation: balance and history are private; the only way to change the balance is through deposit, withdraw or post, which check the rules. history() returns a copy. Money is a long in paise, never a double.
  • Abstraction: InterestPolicy says what is needed, not how; the abstract minimumBalance() names a concept that each account type defines. Callers use Account only.
  • Inheritance: both account types reuse the number, balance, history and all the rules from Account. deposit and withdraw are final, so a subclass cannot weaken them.
  • Polymorphism: accounts.forEach(Account::monthEnd) runs interest for savings and nothing for current, chosen at run time.
  • Composition: interest is a separate strategy object, not a subclass of savings per interest rate (composition). The record Transaction is a simple value type (records).

In production you would add thread safety, BigDecimal or a money type, and persistence, but the structure stays the same. This is also the shape of a Spring service: a class that depends on interfaces and keeps its state private.

SOLID teaser

SOLID is a set of five design guidelines that grow out of the pillars: Single responsibility (a class has one reason to change), Open/closed (open for extension, closed for modification; our new account type needs no change in the loop), Liskov substitution (a subclass must work wherever its parent is expected), Interface segregation (many small interfaces beat one fat one) and Dependency inversion (depend on abstractions such as InterestPolicy, not on concrete classes). The full treatment with examples is in System Design · Module 1.

Mistakes that break the pillars

  • Public fields, or getters that return internal mutable lists (breaks encapsulation).
  • Using extends only to reuse code, or a subclass that cannot do what the parent promises (breaks inheritance and Liskov).
  • Adding instanceof chains instead of overriding methods (misses polymorphism).
  • One interface per class "just because" (abstraction without a reason).
  • Saying "polymorphism is overloading" in an interview. Overloading is the compile-time form; the main idea is runtime polymorphism.

Interview: "Explain the four pillars"

  • Give each pillar in one sentence from the table and a one-line real example.
  • Offer a tie-together example (bank accounts) and point out each pillar in it.
  • Mention that composition and interfaces often serve the goals better than deep inheritance.
  • Expect follow-ups: abstraction vs encapsulation, overloading vs overriding, abstract class vs interface, why Java has no multiple class inheritance.

Interview questions — Object-oriented programming

What are the four pillars of OOP? Give an example of each.

Encapsulation (private fields plus validating methods, e.g. a bank balance), abstraction (an interface such as PaymentGateway hides the provider), inheritance (SavingsAccount extends Account) and polymorphism (account.monthEnd() runs the right version per object). Add that composition and interfaces often replace deep inheritance.

What is the difference between a class and an object?

A class is a blueprint: it defines fields and methods. An object is an instance created from it with new, with its own field values (state), behaviour from the class and an identity. The reference variable lives on the stack, and the object lives on the heap.

Overloading vs overriding?

Overloading: same name, different parameter lists in one class (or its subclasses); chosen at compile time by the declared argument types. Overriding: a subclass gives a new body to an inherited instance method with the same signature; chosen at run time by the object's real class. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads. Static, private and final methods cannot be overridden.

Abstract class vs interface: when do you use which?

An abstract class can hold state, constructors and any-access methods, but a class can extend only one. An interface has only constants, public methods (abstract, default, static, private), no state, and a class can implement many. Use an interface for a capability across unrelated classes and an abstract class for closely related classes sharing fields and code. A skeleton abstract class implementing an interface gives both.

Why does Java not support multiple inheritance of classes? How do interfaces help?

Two parents could both supply the same field or method, so the diamond problem makes it unclear which copy the child inherits. Java allows only one parent class. Interfaces carry no state, so a class may implement many; if two default methods clash, the class must override and pick with A.super.m().

What does this print? 
class A { String n = "A"; String who() { return "A"; } }
class B extends A { String n = "B"; String who() { return "B"; } }
A x = new B();
System.out.println(x.n + x.who());

It prints AB. The field is looked up by the declared type (A), the overridden method by the real object (B). Fields are not polymorphic.

What is the order of initialization when you create an object?

First the class is loaded: parent static blocks and fields, then child static blocks (once). Then for each new: parent instance initializers and fields, parent constructor, then child instance initializers and fields, child constructor. If a parent constructor calls an overridden method, it sees the child's fields still at default values.

What is the contract between equals() and hashCode()? What happens if you break it?

If a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(); the reverse need not hold. equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and false for null. If you override equals only, equal objects get different hash codes, and a HashSet or HashMap stores duplicates or fails to find a key.

Does final make an object immutable?

No. final fixes the reference: you cannot reassign it. The object can still change (final List still allows add). An immutable class needs: final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs. Compare final, finally (cleanup block) and finalize (deprecated GC hook).

Composition or inheritance? Why "favor composition"?

Inheritance couples the child to the parent's implementation (the fragile base class problem, e.g. a HashSet subclass counting addAll twice) and is fixed at compile time with one parent only. Composition holds a component behind an interface and delegates, which is flexible, testable and swappable at run time. Use inheritance for a true is-a with a parent designed for extension.

Static nested class vs inner class?

An inner class belongs to an outer instance and holds a hidden reference to it (usable with Outer.this, created with outer.new Inner()); this can keep the outer object alive. A static nested class has no such reference and is created with new Outer.Nested(). Prefer static nested unless you need the outer instance.

Why use enums instead of int or String constants? What are their pitfalls?

Type safety, readable names, ability to hold fields and per-constant behaviour, exhaustive switch, EnumMap and EnumSet. Pitfalls: valueOf throws IllegalArgumentException on unknown names, ordinal() changes when you reorder (store the name, e.g. EnumType.STRING in JPA), and a new constant must be handled in every switch.

What is a record and when should you not use one?

A record is a concise, final, shallowly immutable data class with generated constructor, accessors (x()), equals, hashCode and toString. Do not use it for JPA entities, for mutable state, or when you need inheritance or hidden representation. Copy mutable components in the compact constructor.

What is the difference between ClassCastException and instanceof? How do you avoid the exception?

instanceof is a test that returns true when the object is an instance of the type (false for null). ClassCastException is what a downcast throws when the test would have been false. Guard with if (a instanceof Dog d), or better, put the behaviour in the parent so no cast is needed.

What is a sealed class and why was it added?

A sealed type lists its permitted direct subtypes with permits, and each must be final, sealed or non-sealed. It models closed hierarchies and lets the compiler check a pattern-matching switch for completeness, without a default branch.

Cheat sheet — Object-oriented programming

  • Class vs object blueprint vs instance; new allocates on the heap, the variable holds a reference.
  • Constructor same name as class, no return type; the default one exists only if you write none; chain with this(...) or super(...) as the first statement.
  • Init order static (parent, child) once; per object: parent fields/blocks, parent constructor, child fields/blocks, child constructor.
  • static belongs to the class; no this, no instance members directly.
  • Access private (class) < package-private < protected (package + subclasses) < public.
  • Encapsulation private fields, validated setters or none, defensive copies; immutable = final class, final fields, no setters.
  • Inheritance extends, one parent; constructors and private members are not inherited; super.m() calls the parent version.
  • Overriding rules same signature, covariant return, access not narrower, no broader checked exceptions; always @Override.
  • Not overridable static (hidden), private, final; fields are hidden, not overridden.
  • Polymorphism overloading = compile time (declared types); overriding = run time (real object).
  • Casting upcast implicit and safe; downcast explicit and may throw ClassCastException; check with instanceof.
  • Abstract class cannot be instantiated; may have state, constructors, concrete and abstract methods; use for the Template Method.
  • Interface constants, abstract/default/static/private methods; no state; implement many; implementations must be public.
  • Default method clash class wins; more specific interface wins; else override and call A.super.m().
  • final variable assigned once; method not overridable; class not extendable; reference, not content.
  • final / finally / finalize keyword / cleanup block / deprecated GC hook.
  • equals + hashCode override together with the same fields; equal objects need equal hashes; use Objects.equals and Objects.hash.
  • toString override it; never include secrets; use Arrays.toString for arrays.
  • Copying shallow shares inner objects; deep duplicates them; prefer copy constructors or immutables over clone().
  • Composition has-a, delegate to a component behind an interface; inheritance only for true is-a.
  • Nested classes static nested (no outer ref), inner (outer ref), local, anonymous; lambdas replace anonymous functional interfaces.
  • Packages reverse-domain lowercase, folders match; java.lang is auto-imported; wildcard excludes subpackages.
  • Enum fixed constants with fields, private constructor, per-constant bodies; compare with ==; store names, not ordinals.
  • Record record P(int x, int y) {}; compact constructor validates; shallow immutable; not for entities.
  • Sealed sealed ... permits; subtypes are final, sealed or non-sealed; enables exhaustive switch.

Practice — Object-oriented programming

  1. Class basics (easy). Write Student with private fields id, name and marks, a constructor that rejects marks outside 0-100, getters, and a good toString. Done when invalid marks throw IllegalArgumentException and printing a list of students shows readable text.
  2. Output prediction: initialization order. Write a parent and a child class, each with a static block, an instance block and a constructor that print a line; add a parent constructor that calls an overridden method reading a child field. Predict the order on paper, then run it. Done when you can explain every line, including why the field is still 0 or null.
  3. Output prediction: overloading vs overriding. Create Animal and Dog with eat(Animal) in both and eat(Dog) in Dog, plus overloads show(Object) and show(String). Call them through Animal and Dog variables with null and cast arguments. Done when you can state the compile-time and run-time step for each call (puzzles).
  4. Library model. Model Book, Member and Loan: a loan links one member and one book with a due date; a member can hold at most 3 loans; Book has an ISBN. Use inheritance or an interface only where it fits (for example Member types with different limits through a LoanPolicy interface). Done when borrowing a 4th book fails with a clear exception and equals/hashCode of Book use the ISBN.
  5. Bank model. Re-create Account, SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount and Transaction from the worked example without looking. Then add a FixedDeposit account that blocks withdrawals until a maturity date, and a second InterestPolicy with tiered rates. Done when the loop over List<Account> needs no change for the new type.
  6. Parking lot. Model ParkingLot, Floor, Slot and vehicles (bike, car, truck) with an enum VehicleType and an enum SlotSize. Decide where inheritance, composition (a lot has floors) and an interface (PricingStrategy) belong, and use a record for Ticket. Done when parking returns a ticket for the nearest fitting free slot, and a full lot reports a clear error.
  7. equals/hashCode test. Write Email as a normal class with a correct equals and hashCode (case-insensitive). First leave out hashCode and show a HashSet holding a duplicate; then fix it and add the same logic as a record with a compact constructor that lowercases the value. Done when both versions keep the set at size 1.
  8. Refactor to composition. Start with class Stack<E> extends ArrayList<E> and show that callers can call add(0, x) and break the stack rule. Rewrite it with a private list field and only push, pop, peek and isEmpty. Done when the public API has just those methods.
  9. Enum and sealed. Create an enum OrderStatus with the legal next states per constant (a method canMoveTo), and a sealed interface PaymentResult with record cases Paid, Failed and Pending. Write a switch over each without a default. Done when removing one case makes the code fail to compile.

Module 3·About 3 daysMust

Exceptions and files

20 topics · about 3 h of reading

Real programs meet problems all the time: a file is missing, a user types "abc" where a number belongs, a payment gateway times out, or a bug passes null where an object was expected. Java reports these problems with exceptions — objects that describe what went wrong and where. Good exception handling is the difference between an app that shows a clear error and keeps serving users, and one that dies with a 300-line stack trace in production.

The second half of the module is about files: reading and writing text, CSV files and huge logs with java.nio.file.Files, plus the classic java.io streams, Java serialization and .properties files. Files and exceptions belong together, because almost every file operation can fail with an IOException.

This module builds on inheritance from Module 2 — exception types form a class hierarchy. Module 4 explains ConcurrentModificationException, Module 5 covers Optional and streams, and the Spring Boot page shows how exceptions become HTTP error responses (Spring Boot · Module 2). After this module you will be able to:

  • Read a stack trace and find the real cause of a failure in seconds.
  • Explain the exception hierarchy and checked vs unchecked exceptions in an interview.
  • Write correct try / catch / finally and try-with-resources code, and predict the output of tricky finally puzzles.
  • Design clean custom exceptions such as InsufficientBalanceException.
  • Read and write text files, CSV files and multi-gigabyte logs with java.nio.file.
  • Know where java.io streams, Java serialization and Properties still fit in modern code.

What an exception is: throwing and stack unwinding

An exception is an object that describes an abnormal event. When it is thrown, Java stops the normal flow and unwinds the call stack, method by method, until a matching catch block handles it — if nothing does, the thread dies and prints a stack trace.

Before exceptions, languages like C reported errors with special return values: -1, null or an error code. That design has two big problems. First, callers forget to check the return value, and the program continues with garbage data. Second, the error checks mix with the business logic, so every line of real work is followed by three lines of "did that fail?".

Java's answer is the exception: an object of a class that extends Throwable. It carries four things:

  • its type — the class name already says a lot (FileNotFoundException, NumberFormatException);
  • a message — a human-readable detail such as "Insufficient wallet balance";
  • a stack trace — the chain of method calls that were active when the exception object was created;
  • an optional cause — another exception that led to this one.

To throw an exception means to hand this object to the JVM and say "I cannot continue normally". To catch it means to say "I know how to deal with this kind of problem". The code that throws and the code that catches can be many method calls apart — that is the whole point.

The call stack

Every time a method is called, the JVM pushes a stack frame onto the current thread's call stack. The frame holds the method's parameters, its local variables and the place to return to. When the method returns, its frame is popped. So at any moment the stack is a record of "who called whom", with the running method on top.

What happens when an exception is thrown

  1. Code creates an exception object, for example new IllegalStateException("Insufficient wallet balance"). The stack trace is recorded at this moment, inside the Throwable constructor — not at the throw statement.
  2. The throw statement hands the object to the JVM. The current block stops immediately; the next line does not run.
  3. The JVM looks for an enclosing try block in the current method that has a catch clause whose type matches. "Matches" means the exception is an instance of the catch type — the same class or a subclass.
  4. If there is no match, the method ends abruptly. Its finally blocks run, its frame is popped, and the exception reappears in the caller, at the line that made the call. This is stack unwinding.
  5. Steps 3 and 4 repeat frame by frame. The first matching catch handles the exception, and execution continues after that whole try statement.
  6. If the exception unwinds past the bottom frame (main for the main thread), it is uncaught. The thread's uncaught-exception handler runs — by default it prints Exception in thread "main" plus the stack trace to System.err — and the thread terminates.

Example: an uncaught exception

A small food-ordering flow: main calls placeOrder, which calls chargeWallet. The wallet has ₹100 and the order costs ₹250.

public class OrderFlow {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("main: start");
        placeOrder(250);
        System.out.println("main: end");                 // never printed
    }

    static void placeOrder(int amount) {
        System.out.println("placeOrder: start");
        chargeWallet(amount);
        System.out.println("placeOrder: confirmed");     // never printed
    }

    static void chargeWallet(int amount) {
        int balance = 100;
        System.out.println("chargeWallet: balance " + balance + ", amount " + amount);
        if (amount > balance) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient wallet balance");
        }
        System.out.println("chargeWallet: charged");     // never printed
    }
}
main: start
placeOrder: start
chargeWallet: balance 100, amount 250
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException: Insufficient wallet balance
    at OrderFlow.chargeWallet(OrderFlow.java:18)
    at OrderFlow.placeOrder(OrderFlow.java:10)
    at OrderFlow.main(OrderFlow.java:4)

The three "never printed" lines did not run. As soon as throw executed, chargeWallet stopped. Then placeOrder stopped at line 10, the line that called it. Then main stopped at line 4. Nobody caught the exception, so the main thread died, the JVM printed the stack trace, and the process ended with exit code 1 instead of 0. A deployment script or CI job sees that non-zero code as a failure.

Example: the same exception, caught

public class OrderFlowCaught {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("main: start");
        try {
            placeOrder(250);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("main: order failed -> " + e.getMessage());
        }
        System.out.println("main: end");
    }

    static void placeOrder(int amount) {
        System.out.println("placeOrder: start");
        chargeWallet(amount);
        System.out.println("placeOrder: confirmed");
    }

    static void chargeWallet(int amount) {
        int balance = 100;
        if (amount > balance) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient wallet balance");
        }
        System.out.println("chargeWallet: charged");
    }
}
main: start
placeOrder: start
main: order failed -> Insufficient wallet balance
main: end

Now main catches the exception, prints a friendly message and carries on. Notice that placeOrder: confirmed is still not printed. Catching an exception does not resume the code after the throw point; execution continues after the try statement that caught it.

Rule: control never returns to the throw point

Java has no "resume". Once an exception is thrown, every statement between the throw and the matching catch is skipped (except finally blocks). If placeOrder had already reserved stock before calling chargeWallet, that reservation is not undone automatically — you must design for it (a finally block, a database transaction, or a compensating action).

Note: uncaught exceptions in other threads

Each thread has its own call stack, so an uncaught exception kills only the thread where it happened. The JVM keeps running while any non-daemon thread is alive. In a web server, the framework catches exceptions from your controllers, so one bad request does not stop the server. With an ExecutorService, an exception from a task started with submit() is stored inside the returned Future and appears only when you call get(), wrapped in an ExecutionException — a classic "silent failure" (see Module 6).

Exceptions vs error codes

AspectReturn codes (C style)Exceptions (Java)
Can be ignored by accidentYes, very easilyNo — an uncaught exception stops the thread
Mixed into business logicYes, a check after every callNo — handling lives in catch blocks
Details carriedA number or nullType, message, stack trace and cause
Passing through layersEvery layer must pass it up by handPropagates automatically until caught
CostVery cheapCreating one is relatively expensive because it captures the stack — use it for exceptional cases, not normal flow

Interview: "What happens when an exception is thrown and nobody catches it?"

  • The JVM searches the current method for a matching catch; if there is none, it runs the method's finally blocks, pops the frame and repeats the search in the caller — this is stack unwinding.
  • If no frame catches it, the thread's uncaught-exception handler prints the stack trace and the thread terminates.
  • For the main thread, when no other non-daemon thread is running, the JVM exits; the java launcher returns exit code 1.
  • Bonus point: the stack trace is captured when the exception object is created, not when it is thrown.

Reading a stack trace

Read a stack trace from the top: the first line gives the exception type and message, the first "at" line shows where it was thrown, the first frame from your own package shows where your code was involved, and the last "Caused by" section usually holds the root cause.

A stack trace is the printed form of an exception: its type, its message and the list of stack frames that were active when it was created. It looks scary because it is long, but it has a fixed structure. Once you know the structure, most bugs take minutes instead of hours to find. Reading stack traces quickly is one of the most valuable debugging skills on a real job.

A chained example

The method below parses a price. Someone typed the letter O instead of the digit zero. The parsing error is caught and wrapped in a new exception that adds context — the original exception becomes the cause.

public class StackTraceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new StackTraceDemo().loadPrice("12O");   // letter O, not zero
    }

    void loadPrice(String raw) {
        try {
            int price = parsePrice(raw);
            System.out.println("Price: " + price);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Bad price in catalog: " + raw, e);
        }
    }

    int parsePrice(String raw) {
        return Integer.parseInt(raw);
    }
}
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Bad price in catalog: 12O
    at StackTraceDemo.loadPrice(StackTraceDemo.java:11)
    at StackTraceDemo.main(StackTraceDemo.java:3)
Caused by: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12O"
    at java.base/java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:67)
    at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:565)
    at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:662)
    at StackTraceDemo.parsePrice(StackTraceDemo.java:16)
    at StackTraceDemo.loadPrice(StackTraceDemo.java:8)
    ... 1 more

The parts of a stack trace

PartExampleWhat it tells you
Thread headerException in thread "main"The exception was not caught and killed this thread
Type and messagejava.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Bad price in catalog: 12OThe fully qualified class name, then getMessage()
Frameat StackTraceDemo.loadPrice(StackTraceDemo.java:11) class.method(file:line). The first frame is where the exception object was created
Module prefixjava.base/java.lang.Integer.parseIntThe class lives in a JDK module (Java 9+). These are JDK frames, not your code
Caused byCaused by: java.lang.NumberFormatExceptionThe wrapped cause, with its own frames. There can be several levels
... n more... 1 moreThe last n frames are the same as the bottom frames of the trace above, so they are not repeated
SuppressedSuppressed: java.io.IOException: close failed An extra exception attached with addSuppressed(), usually by try-with-resources (see try-with-resources)

In the example, ... 1 more stands for the frame main(StackTraceDemo.java:3), which is the bottom frame of both traces. The frame loadPrice appears in both traces but with different line numbers (11 in the outer trace, where the new exception was created, and 8 in the cause, where parsePrice was called), so it is printed twice.

How to read one: four steps

  1. Read the first line. Type plus message is often enough: NumberFormatException: For input string: "12O" already tells you the input was bad.
  2. Jump to the last "Caused by". Outer exceptions are usually wrappers that add context; the deepest cause is the root cause — the thing that really failed.
  3. Find the first frame from your own code in that section. Skip JDK frames (java., jdk., sun.), framework frames (org.springframework., org.hibernate.) and generated proxy frames (names containing $$ or jdk.proxy). Here it is StackTraceDemo.parsePrice(StackTraceDemo.java:16).
  4. Open that line and ask two questions: which value was wrong, and where did that value come from? Then walk down the frames (towards the callers) to trace the value back to its source.

Real project: in Spring Boot the useful part is at the bottom

A database error in a Spring Boot app can produce a 150-line trace. The top says something general; the real reason sits in the last "Caused by". An abridged example:

org.springframework.dao.DataIntegrityViolationException: could not execute statement [...]
    at org.springframework.orm.jpa.vendor.HibernateJpaDialect.convertHibernateAccessException(...)
    ... many framework frames ...
Caused by: org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException: could not execute statement [...]
    ...
Caused by: org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique
constraint "users_email_key"
    ...

Reading only the first line ("could not execute statement") tells you little. The last cause says exactly what happened: a user with this email already exists.

Working with exceptions in code

Method (on Throwable)Returns / does
getMessage()The detail message, or null if none was given
toString()Class name + ": " + message (just the class name when the message is null)
getCause()The wrapped cause, or null
getStackTrace()The frames as a StackTraceElement[] (class, method, file, line)
printStackTrace()Prints the full trace to System.err
getSuppressed()Exceptions attached with addSuppressed()

Wrong: logs only the message — type, trace and cause are lost

try {
    paymentClient.charge(order);
} catch (PaymentException e) {
    log.error("Payment failed: " + e.getMessage());
}

Right: pass the exception as the last argument

try {
    paymentClient.charge(order);
} catch (PaymentException e) {
    // SLF4J prints the full stack trace, including every "Caused by"
    log.error("Payment failed for order {}", order.id(), e);
}

With SLF4J (the logging API Spring Boot uses), a Throwable passed as the last argument, with no {} placeholder left for it, is printed as a full stack trace. Avoid e.printStackTrace() in real applications: it writes to System.err, which bypasses your log format, log levels and log files.

Mistake: wrapping an exception without its cause

throw new IllegalStateException("Could not load config"); inside a catch block throws away the original exception — the stack trace will no longer show why loading failed. Always pass the caught exception as the cause: throw new IllegalStateException("Could not load config", e);.

Note: an exception with no stack trace in production logs

Sometimes a production log shows java.lang.NullPointerException with no frames at all. The HotSpot JIT compiler can replace some built-in exceptions that are thrown very often from the same hot code (such as NullPointerException and ArithmeticException) with a preallocated exception that has no stack trace, to save time. The first occurrences in the log still have full traces, so search earlier lines — or start the JVM with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow to switch the optimization off.

Tip: let the IDE do the clicking

In IntelliJ IDEA, a stack trace printed in the Run window is already clickable. For a trace copied from a log file or a ticket, use the IDE's "Analyze Stack Trace" action: paste the text and every frame becomes a link to the source line.

Interview: "A production API returns 500. How do you find the cause?"

  • Find the error in the logs (by time, request id or trace id) and read the full stack trace, not just the first line.
  • Go to the deepest "Caused by" — the root cause — and the first frame from your own package.
  • Explain the pieces: frames are listed most recent first, ... n more means shared frames were omitted, Suppressed: comes from try-with-resources.
  • Reproduce with the same input in a test, fix, and add the test so it cannot come back.

The exception hierarchy: Throwable, Error and Exception

Everything you can throw extends Throwable. Error means the JVM or the environment is in serious trouble (don't catch it), Exception means a condition your program can respond to, and RuntimeException marks the unchecked exceptions that usually signal bugs or bad input.

Exceptions are ordinary classes, so they form an inheritance tree. The tree matters for two reasons. First, a catch (IOException e) block also catches every subclass of IOException, such as FileNotFoundException. Second, the position of a class in the tree decides whether it is checked (the compiler forces you to handle it) or unchecked (it does not) — see the next article.

The four classes at the top

ClassMeaningChecked?Should you catch it?
ThrowableRoot of everything that can be thrown or caught. Holds the message, cause, stack trace and suppressed exceptionsYes (itself)Only in rare top-level code that must log everything
ErrorA serious problem in the JVM or environment: out of memory, stack overflow, a missing classNoNo — let it crash, then fix the root cause
ExceptionA condition a reasonable program may want to handle: I/O failure, database error, interruptionYesYes, where you can actually do something
RuntimeExceptionUsually a programming bug (null, bad index, bad cast) or an invalid argument or stateNoUsually fix the bug instead; catch at boundaries

Why you should not catch Errors

An Error says the environment is broken, not your business logic. When the heap is full (OutOfMemoryError), even the code inside your catch block may fail to allocate memory. When the stack overflows, the JVM's state is fine but your algorithm is wrong (usually a recursion without a base case). When a class is missing at runtime, the deployment is broken. None of these can be fixed by the method that happens to be running. The right reaction is to let the thread or the process fail, alert someone, and fix the root cause: a memory leak, a too-small -Xmx, infinite recursion, or a missing JAR.

ErrorWhen it happens
OutOfMemoryErrorThe heap is full and garbage collection cannot free enough space ("Java heap space"), or another memory area such as Metaspace runs out. Causes: a memory leak, loading a huge file into memory, a heap size that is too small
StackOverflowErrorThe call stack is too deep — almost always infinite recursion. A real-world classic: two JPA entities whose toString() (or generated JSON) call each other through a bidirectional relationship
NoClassDefFoundErrorA class that existed at compile time cannot be loaded at runtime — a JAR is missing from the runtime classpath, or the class's static initialization failed earlier ("Could not initialize class …")
ExceptionInInitializerErrorA static initializer or a static field initializer threw an exception while the class was being initialized
AssertionErrorAn assert statement failed (assertions must be enabled with -ea). Test frameworks also throw subclasses of it when an assertion fails

Exception to the rule: top-level code may catch Throwable

Framework and infrastructure code at the very top of a thread — a web server's request loop, a scheduler running jobs, a message consumer — often catches Throwable to log the failure and keep the process alive for the next request. Test frameworks catch AssertionError to report failed tests. Business code should never do this.

The common exceptions and when each happens

ExceptionKindWhen it happensTypical trigger
NullPointerExceptionUncheckedUsing a null reference as if it were an object: calling a method, reading a field, unboxing a null Integercustomer.getName() when customer is null
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsExceptionUncheckedArray index below 0 or ≥ lengthseats[seats.length]
IndexOutOfBoundsExceptionUncheckedBad index on a List (and the parent of the array and string versions)list.get(5) on a list of size 3
