ClassCastExceptionUncheckedCasting an object to a type it is not an instance of(Integer) obj when obj holds a String
NumberFormatExceptionUnchecked (a subclass of IllegalArgumentException)Parsing text that is not a valid number — including "", " 42" with a space, and null Integer.parseInt("12a")
IllegalArgumentExceptionUncheckedA method received an argument value it does not acceptThread.sleep(-1), or your own validation
IllegalStateExceptionUncheckedA method was called at the wrong time — the object is not in the right stateiterator.remove() before next(); using a closed Scanner
ArithmeticExceptionUncheckedInteger division by zero, Math.addExact overflow, a non-terminating BigDecimal division total / count with count == 0
ConcurrentModificationExceptionUncheckedA collection was structurally changed while being iterated (see Module 4)Calling list.remove(x) inside a for-each over list
UnsupportedOperationExceptionUncheckedThe object does not support this operationList.of(1, 2).add(3)
NoSuchElementExceptionUncheckedAsking for an element that does not existiterator.next() at the end; Optional.empty().get()
IOExceptionCheckedAn input/output operation failed: file unreadable, disk full, network connection brokenFiles.readString(path)
FileNotFoundExceptionChecked (a subclass of IOException)Classic java.io could not open a file: missing, a directory, or no permissionnew FileInputStream("missing.txt")
SQLExceptionCheckedA JDBC database operation failed: bad SQL, lost connection, constraint violation. Has getSQLState() and getErrorCode()statement.executeQuery(sql)
InterruptedExceptionCheckedA thread waiting in sleep, wait or join was interrupted by another thread (see Module 6)Thread.sleep(1000)

The program below triggers several of these and prints each exception with toString(), so you can see the real messages the JDK produces.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class CommonExceptions {
    static String city;            // a field that is still null

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Runnable> cases = List.of(
            () -> city.length(),
            () -> { int[] seats = new int[3]; seats[3] = 1; },
            () -> new ArrayList<String>().get(0),
            () -> { Object o = "hi"; Integer i = (Integer) o; },
            () -> Integer.parseInt("12a"),
            () -> { int a = 10, b = 0; System.out.println(a / b); },
            () -> List.of(1, 2).add(3),
            () -> new ArrayList<String>().iterator().next()
        );
        for (Runnable r : cases) {
            try {
                r.run();
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                System.out.println(e);       // toString(): class name + message
            }
        }
    }
}
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "CommonExceptions.city" is null
java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3
java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 0 out of bounds for length 0
java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer (...)
java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12a"
java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
java.util.NoSuchElementException

The detailed NullPointerException message ("because … is null") comes from the helpful NullPointerException feature of Java 14+ (see NullPointerException). Also notice that floating-point division by zero does not throw: 10.0 / 0 is Infinity and 0.0 / 0 is NaN. Only integer division throws ArithmeticException.

ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError

This pair is a favourite interview question because the names look alike but they sit on different branches of the tree.

AspectClassNotFoundExceptionNoClassDefFoundError
TypeChecked exceptionError (a LinkageError)
WhenYou load a class by name at runtime and it is not foundA class that was present at compile time cannot be found or initialized at runtime
Thrown byClass.forName("…"), ClassLoader.loadClass("…")The JVM, when your code first uses the class
Typical causeA JDBC driver or plugin JAR missing from the classpathA dependency JAR missing at runtime only, or an earlier failure in the class's static initializer

Rule: only Throwable objects can be thrown

throw "error"; does not compile: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to Throwable. The same applies to catch — the parameter type must be Throwable or a subclass.

Mistake: catch (Throwable t) around business logic

It also catches OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError, so a dying JVM keeps limping along and nobody notices. Catch the specific exceptions you can handle; let errors reach the top-level handler.

Interview: "Explain the exception hierarchy" / "Error vs Exception"

  • Throwable is the root; it has two direct subclasses, Error and Exception.
  • Error = problems a program should not try to handle (OOM, stack overflow, linkage errors). Exception = conditions a program can handle.
  • RuntimeException (under Exception) and Error are unchecked; everything else, including Throwable itself, is checked.
  • Give two or three examples on each branch and say when they happen.

Checked vs unchecked exceptions

The compiler forces you to catch or declare checked exceptions (Exception and its subclasses outside RuntimeException); unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error and their subclasses) can be thrown anywhere without any declaration.

Java is almost alone among popular languages in having checked exceptions. A checked exception is part of a method's contract: Files.readString(Path) declares throws IOException, which says "reading can fail, and you must decide what to do about it". An unchecked exception is not part of the contract the compiler checks: any method may throw a NullPointerException without saying so.

Which is which

  • Unchecked = RuntimeException and its subclasses, plus Error and its subclasses.
  • Checked = every other Throwable: Exception itself, IOException, SQLException, InterruptedException, ClassNotFoundException, your own classes that extend Exception, and even Throwable itself.

The compiler rule: catch or declare

If code inside a method can throw a checked exception, the method must either catch it or declare it in its throws clause. This is called the catch-or-declare rule (also "handle or declare").

import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class Unreported {
    static String readConfig() {
        return Files.readString(Path.of("app.conf"));   // throws IOException
    }
}
Unreported.java:6: error: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown
        return Files.readString(Path.of("app.conf"));
                               ^
1 error

Two ways to fix it — catch it where you can handle it, or declare it and let the caller decide:

// Fix 1: handle it here (for example, fall back to a default)
static String readConfigOrDefault() {
    try {
        return Files.readString(Path.of("app.conf"));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        return "mode=default";
    }
}

// Fix 2: declare it; now every caller must catch or declare it in turn
static String readConfig() throws IOException {
    return Files.readString(Path.of("app.conf"));
}

The second compiler rule: no catching what cannot be thrown

The compiler also rejects a catch block for a checked exception that the try block can never throw — it would be dead code.

static int parse(String s) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(s);       // throws only unchecked exceptions
    } catch (IOException e) {             // compile error
        return -1;
    }
}
NeverThrown.java:7: error: exception IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement

Exception: catch (Exception e) and catch (Throwable t) are always allowed

Even when the try block throws no checked exception, catching Exception or Throwable compiles, because those types also cover unchecked exceptions that any code can throw. Unchecked types like NumberFormatException can always be caught too.

Unchecked exceptions: no rule at all

You may throw IllegalArgumentException from any method without a throws clause, and callers need not catch it. You may list unchecked exceptions in throws, but it changes nothing for the compiler. The professional way to document them is the Javadoc @throws tag:

/**
 * Withdraws money from this account.
 *
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if amount is zero or negative
 * @throws InsufficientBalanceException if the balance is lower than amount
 */
public void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) { ... }

Side by side

AspectCheckedUnchecked
ClassesException and subclasses, except the RuntimeException branchRuntimeException, Error and their subclasses
CompilerMust be caught or declaredNo requirement
Typical meaningA failure outside your control that a caller can react to (file, network, database, interruption)A programming error or invalid input/state
ExamplesIOException, SQLException, InterruptedExceptionNullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, ArithmeticException
Usual handlingRecover, retry, or translate to a higher-level exception Fix the bug; validate input; handle once at a boundary (e.g., an API error handler)

Note: checked exceptions exist only in the compiler

The JVM does not know about checked exceptions. Bytecode may throw any Throwable from anywhere; the catch-or-declare rule is enforced by javac alone. That is why other JVM languages such as Kotlin and Scala have no checked exceptions, and why Lombok's @SneakyThrows can throw a checked exception without declaring it.

The design debate

For checked exceptions

  • The method signature tells you what can go wrong.
  • The compiler stops you from forgetting a failure that really happens in production (a file that is missing, a network that drops).
  • Good for recoverable situations the caller is expected to handle.

Against checked exceptions

  • Boilerplate: catch blocks that do nothing useful, or throws clauses copied up through every layer.
  • They tempt people into swallowing exceptions just to make the code compile.
  • They leak implementation details: a service method should not declare SQLException just because its repository uses JDBC.
  • They do not work with lambdas and streams — Function.apply declares no checked exceptions.
  • Adding a checked exception to a public method breaks every caller.

The modern Java ecosystem leans towards unchecked exceptions. Spring translates JDBC's checked SQLException into its unchecked DataAccessException family, JPA's PersistenceException is unchecked, and most libraries written in the last decade throw unchecked exceptions. Checked exceptions are still the right tool in some places, and the JDK itself uses them heavily for I/O.

Checked exceptions and lambdas

A stream pipeline takes functional interfaces like Function, whose method declares no checked exceptions. So a lambda that calls Files.readString does not compile:

List<String> contents = files.stream()
        .map(p -> Files.readString(p))     // unreported exception IOException
        .toList();

List<String> contents2 = files.stream()
        .map(Files::readString)            // incompatible thrown types IOException
        .toList();

The standard fix is to catch inside the lambda and wrap the checked exception in an unchecked one. The JDK has a ready-made wrapper for I/O, java.io.UncheckedIOException:

List<String> contents = files.stream()
        .map(p -> {
            try {
                return Files.readString(p);
            } catch (IOException e) {
                throw new UncheckedIOException(e);   // keeps the IOException as the cause
            }
        })
        .toList();

If you need this in many places, move the try/catch into a small helper method such as readOrThrow(Path) and use map(Util::readOrThrow).

When to use which

  • Unchecked when the problem is a bug in the caller (null argument, invalid value, wrong order of calls), or when the caller cannot reasonably recover. This is the default in most modern application code, including Spring Boot services.
  • Checked when the failure is expected in normal operation, the caller can really do something about it (retry, choose another file, ask the user), and you want the compiler to make sure they think about it.
  • When in doubt in a Spring Boot app, make business exceptions unchecked and handle them in one central place that maps them to HTTP responses (see best practices).

Convention: throws Exception is for demos only

public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception is legal and handy in quick experiments. In real code, declaring throws Exception hides which failures can actually happen and forces every caller to catch the broadest type. Declare the specific checked types, or wrap them.

Mistake: an empty catch block just to satisfy the compiler

catch (IOException e) { } makes the error disappear — the program continues as if the file had been read. If you cannot handle a checked exception, declare it or wrap it in an unchecked exception with the original as the cause.

Interview: "Checked vs unchecked — and which do you prefer?"

  • Define both by the hierarchy and state the catch-or-declare rule; mention it is a compile-time rule only.
  • Give examples: IOException, SQLException vs NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException.
  • Guideline: checked for recoverable conditions the caller must handle, unchecked for programming errors.
  • Mention the trade-offs (lambdas, boilerplate, leaking details) and that Spring prefers unchecked exceptions, translating SQLException into DataAccessException.

try, catch and finally: rules and flow

Put the code that can fail in try, handle specific failures in catch blocks ordered from most specific to most general, and put cleanup that must always happen in finally.

A try statement marks a region of code whose exceptions you want to deal with. A catch block (also called a handler) says which exception types you handle and how. A finally block holds code that must run whether the try block succeeded or failed — releasing a lock, closing a resource, clearing a thread-local value.

try {
    // code that may throw
} catch (NoSuchFileException e) {          // most specific first
    // handle a missing file
} catch (IOException e) {                  // then more general
    // handle any other I/O problem
} finally {
    // always runs: cleanup
}

Structure rules

  • A try needs at least one catch or a finally (or resource declarations — see try-with-resources). A bare try { } fails with 'try' without 'catch', 'finally' or resource declarations.
  • You may have any number of catch blocks and at most one finally block, which comes last.
  • At most one catch block runs: the first one, from top to bottom, whose type matches the exception (the exception is an instance of that type).
  • Variables declared inside the try block are not visible in catch or finally. If finally needs a variable, declare it before the try.
  • The catch parameter (e) exists only inside its own catch block.

The four possible paths

What happens in tryThenAfter the statement
No exceptionAll catch blocks are skipped; finally runsExecution continues normally
Exception, and a catch matchesThe rest of try is skipped; that catch runs; finally runsExecution continues normally
Exception, no catch matchesThe rest of try is skipped; finally runsThe exception propagates to the caller
A catch block itself throwsfinally runsThe new exception propagates to the caller

Example: all three main paths

public class TryCatchFlow {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Result: " + parseQuantity("3"));
        System.out.println("Result: " + parseQuantity("three"));
        try {
            System.out.println("Result: " + parseQuantity(null));
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("main caught: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
    }

    static int parseQuantity(String input) {
        System.out.println("-- parsing " + input);
        try {
            int quantity = Integer.parseInt(input.trim());   // NPE if input is null
            System.out.println("try: parsed");
            return quantity;
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            System.out.println("catch: not a number, using 1");
            return 1;
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally: runs every time");
        }
    }
}
-- parsing 3
try: parsed
finally: runs every time
Result: 3
-- parsing three
catch: not a number, using 1
finally: runs every time
Result: 1
-- parsing null
finally: runs every time
main caught: NullPointerException

Three things to notice. First, finally runs even though the try and catch blocks execute return — it runs before the method actually returns. Second, with "three" the line try: parsed is skipped, because the exception jumped straight to the catch. Third, with null the exception is a NullPointerException, which the catch block does not match, so finally runs and the exception travels on to main.

Catch order: specific before general

Because the first matching catch wins, a general type placed first would catch everything and the specific block below it could never run. Java treats that unreachable handler as a compile error.

Wrong: general first — does not compile

try {
    Files.readString(Path.of("a.txt"));
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.out.println("I/O problem");
} catch (NoSuchFileException e) {   // error: exception
    System.out.println("missing");  // NoSuchFileException has
}                                   // already been caught

Right: subclass first, superclass last

try {
    Files.readString(Path.of("a.txt"));
} catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
    System.out.println("missing");
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.out.println("I/O problem");
}

The order only matters between types that are related by inheritance. Unrelated types, such as NumberFormatException and IOException, can appear in any order.

Multi-catch (Java 7+)

When two exceptions need the same handling, list them in one catch with | instead of copying the block.

public class MultiOk {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String s : new String[] {"4", "zero", "0"}) {
            try {
                System.out.println("100 / " + s + " = " + 100 / Integer.parseInt(s));
            } catch (NumberFormatException | ArithmeticException e) {
                System.out.println("Cannot divide by '" + s + "': " + e);
            }
        }
    }
}
100 / 4 = 25
Cannot divide by 'zero': java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "zero"
Cannot divide by '0': java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero

Rules of multi-catch

  • The parameter is implicitly final. Assigning to it fails with multi-catch parameter e may not be assigned.
  • The alternatives cannot be subclasses of each other. catch (IOException | NoSuchFileException e) fails with Alternatives in a multi-catch statement cannot be related by subclassing — just catch IOException.
  • Inside the block, you can only use methods of the closest common supertype of the alternatives (here RuntimeException), because e could be either type.

Nested try

A try statement can sit inside a try, catch or finally block. An exception that the inner statement does not catch moves outwards to the outer one.

static int readQuantity(Path file) {
    try {
        String text = Files.readString(file).strip();
        try {
            return Integer.parseInt(text);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {          // inner: bad content
            System.out.println("Not a number in " + file + ": " + text);
            return 0;
        }
    } catch (IOException e) {                        // outer: cannot read the file
        System.out.println("Cannot read " + file + ": " + e);
        return 0;
    }
}
12
Not a number in bad.txt: twelve
0
Cannot read missing.txt: java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException: missing.txt
0

Nested try blocks work, but they are hard to read. Usually it is cleaner to move the inner part into its own method, such as parseOrZero(String text), and call it from a single try statement.

finally: when it runs, and when it does not

The finally block runs when the try block completes normally, when it throws (caught or not), and when try or catch leave early with return, break or continue. That is why it is the place for cleanup. The classic example is releasing a lock:

private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

public void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amount) {
    lock.lock();              // acquire BEFORE the try
    try {
        from.withdraw(amount);
        to.deposit(amount);
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();        // released even if withdraw() throws
    }
}

Lock does not implement AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources cannot help here — this try/finally idiom is still the standard way.

Exceptions: when finally does NOT run

  • System.exit() (or Runtime.halt()) is called inside try or catch. The JVM starts shutting down and the rest of the thread's code, including finally, never runs.
  • The JVM process dies: a native crash, kill -9, a power cut, the container being killed.
  • The try block never finishes: an infinite loop or a thread stuck forever in a deadlock.
  • The code runs in a daemon thread and the JVM exits because all non-daemon threads have finished. Daemon threads are abandoned; their finally blocks do not run.
public class ExitFinally {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            System.out.println("try");
            System.exit(0);
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally");     // never printed
        }
    }
}
try

Shutdown hooks registered with Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(...) do run on System.exit(); finally blocks of the exiting thread do not.

Mistake: an exception thrown from finally hides the original

If the try block throws exception A and the finally block then throws exception B, the caller sees only B — A is lost completely. This happens easily when finally calls close() on a resource that also fails. Use try-with-resources, which keeps the close failure as a suppressed exception instead. A return in finally is even worse: it discards the exception silently (see the puzzles).

Conventions

  • Keep try blocks small: wrap only the statements that can throw what you catch, so it is clear what failed.
  • Catch the most specific type you can handle; let the rest propagate.
  • Use try-with-resources for anything closeable; use finally for other cleanup (locks, resetting state, clearing logging context).
  • Never leave a catch block empty. If ignoring really is correct, write a comment saying why and name the variable ignored (Java 22+ also lets you write catch (IOException _) with an unnamed variable).

Interview: quick-fire questions on try/catch/finally

  • Can we have try without catch? Yes: try-finally, or try-with-resources.
  • Can more than one catch block run? No — only the first matching one.
  • Why must subclasses be caught first? The superclass handler would catch them first, making the subclass handler unreachable — a compile error.
  • Does finally run if try has a return? Yes, before the method returns.
  • When does finally not run? System.exit(), JVM crash/kill, a try block that never ends, daemon threads at JVM exit.

finally and return: output-prediction puzzles

The return value is saved before finally runs, so finally can change a returned object's contents but not a returned primitive or the returned reference; and a return or throw inside finally overrides everything, including a pending exception.

Interviewers love finally puzzles because they test whether you really understand the order of execution. They all become easy once you know how the compiler implements finally.

How javac implements finally

There is no "finally" instruction in bytecode. The compiler copies the finally code into every exit path of the try and catch blocks: the normal exit, each return, and an extra hidden handler that catches any Throwable, runs the finally code, and rethrows. For a return expr; the compiler first evaluates expr and stores the result in a hidden local variable, then runs the finally code, then returns the stored value.

static int puzzle2() {
    int x = 10;
    try {
        return x;
    } finally {
        x = 20;
    }
}
 0: bipush 10
 2: istore_0      // x = 10
 3: iload_0
 4: istore_1      // hidden slot 1 = x   (the return value is saved here)
 5: bipush 20
 7: istore_0      // finally code: x = 20
 8: iload_1
 9: ireturn       // return the SAVED value: 10
10: astore_2      // hidden catch-any handler: save the exception
11: bipush 20
13: istore_0      // finally code copied again
14: aload_2
15: athrow        // rethrow the saved exception

With that picture in mind, each puzzle below is mechanical: evaluate the return expression, save it, run finally, then return the saved value — unless finally itself returns or throws. Try each one before opening the answer.

Puzzle 1: return inside try

static int puzzle1() {
    try {
        System.out.println("try");
        return 1;
    } finally {
        System.out.println("finally");
    }
}
// main: System.out.println("P1 -> " + puzzle1());
What does it print? 
try
finally
P1 -> 1

finally runs before the method returns, so "finally" is printed before main receives the value 1 and prints it.

Puzzle 2: changing a primitive in finally

static int puzzle2() {
    int x = 10;
    try {
        return x;
    } finally {
        x = 20;
    }
}
Does it return 10 or 20?

10. The value of x was copied into the hidden slot when return x ran. Changing x afterwards does not change the copy (see the bytecode above).

Puzzle 3: changing an object in finally

static StringBuilder puzzle3() {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Hello");
    try {
        return sb;
    } finally {
        sb.append(" World");
        sb = null;
    }
}
// main: System.out.println("P3 -> " + puzzle3());
Does it print "Hello", "Hello World" or "null"? 
P3 -> Hello World

The saved return value is a copy of the reference, which still points to the same StringBuilder object. append changes that object, so the caller sees "Hello World". sb = null changes only the local variable, not the saved copy, so the method does not return null. Same rule as Java's pass-by-value for references.

Puzzle 4: return in both try and finally

static int puzzle4() {
    try {
        return 1;
    } finally {
        return 2;
    }
}
What is returned?

2. The try block saves 1 and runs finally, but finally executes its own return 2, which completes the method. The saved 1 is thrown away. Compiling with javac -Xlint:finally warns: finally clause cannot complete normally.

Puzzle 5: an exception and a return in finally

static int puzzle5() {
    try {
        throw new IllegalStateException("boom");
    } finally {
        return 42;
    }
}
// main: System.out.println("P5 -> " + puzzle5());
Does main see the exception? 
P5 -> 42

No. The hidden catch-any handler saves the exception and runs the finally code — but that code returns, so the athrow that would rethrow the exception is never reached. The exception is silently swallowed: no log, no stack trace. This is the main reason for the rule "never return from finally".

Puzzle 6: three exceptions

static void puzzle6() {
    try {
        throw new IllegalStateException("from try");
    } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("from catch");
    } finally {
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException("from finally");
    }
}
// main: try { puzzle6(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("P6 -> " + e); }
Which exception reaches main? 
P6 -> java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: from finally

The try exception is caught. The catch block throws a new exception, so finally runs before it can leave. finally throws a third exception, which replaces the pending one. Only the last one escapes; the other two are lost (not even attached as suppressed).

Puzzle 7: finally inside a loop

static void puzzle7() {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
        try {
            if (i == 2) continue;
            if (i == 3) break;
            System.out.println("body " + i);
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally " + i);
        }
    }
    System.out.println("after loop");
}
What does it print? 
body 1
finally 1
finally 2
finally 3
after loop

continue and break leave the try block, so finally runs on each exit: for i = 2 before continuing, for i = 3 before breaking out of the loop.

Puzzle 8: return from catch

static String puzzle8() {
    try {
        Integer.parseInt("x");
        return "try";
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return "catch";
    } finally {
        System.out.println("finally runs first");
    }
}
// main: System.out.println("P8 -> " + puzzle8());
What does it print? 
finally runs first
P8 -> catch

The exception skips return "try". The catch block saves "catch" as the return value, finally prints its line, and then the saved value is returned.

Puzzle 9: side effects on a field

static int counter = 0;

static int puzzle9() {
    try {
        return ++counter;
    } finally {
        counter += 10;
    }
}
// main: System.out.println("P9 -> " + puzzle9() + ", counter = " + counter);
What are the returned value and the final counter? 
P9 -> 1, counter = 11

++counter makes counter 1 and saves 1 as the return value. finally then adds 10 to the field, so the field is 11, but the saved return value is still 1. String concatenation evaluates left to right, so puzzle9() runs before counter is read.

Rule: never return, throw, break or continue out of a finally block

Any of these makes the finally block "complete abruptly", which discards the pending return value or exception. Code reviewers and static analysis tools flag it; javac -Xlint:finally warns about it. Keep finally blocks short and limited to cleanup. If cleanup can itself throw, catch that inside finally (and log it), or use try-with-resources.

Interview: how to answer any finally puzzle

  1. Find which block exits first and how: normal end, return, or an exception.
  2. For a return, evaluate the expression now and remember the value (a primitive value or a reference).
  3. Run finally. If it returns or throws, that wins and the remembered value or exception is lost.
  4. Otherwise, return the remembered value or rethrow the remembered exception. Mention that objects can be mutated through the remembered reference.

try-with-resources and AutoCloseable

try-with-resources closes every resource declared in its header automatically, in reverse order, even when an exception is thrown, and keeps failures from close() as suppressed exceptions instead of losing the original one.

A resource is an object that holds something outside the JVM's memory that must be given back: an open file handle, a database connection, a network socket. The garbage collector does not close these for you in any predictable way. Forget to close them and you get a resource leak: after a few thousand requests the operating system refuses to open more files ("Too many open files"), or the database connection pool runs dry and every request starts timing out.

The problem with the old way

Before Java 7, correct cleanup looked like this:

BufferedReader reader = null;
try {
    reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("orders.csv"));
    return reader.readLine();
} finally {
    if (reader != null) {
        try {
            reader.close();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            // ignore? log? -- and the original exception may already be lost
        }
    }
}

It is long, easy to get wrong, and it has a hidden bug: if the body throws and then close() also throws, the close exception replaces the original one. You can see the original error vanish:

public class OldStyleLost {
    static class FlakyConnection implements AutoCloseable {
        @Override
        public void close() {
            throw new IllegalStateException("close failed");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            FlakyConnection c = new FlakyConnection();
            try {
                throw new RuntimeException("query failed");    // the real problem
            } finally {
                c.close();                                     // throws, replacing it
            }
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught: " + e.getMessage());
            System.out.println("Suppressed count: " + e.getSuppressed().length);
        }
    }
}
Caught: close failed
Suppressed count: 0

The log would say "close failed" and nobody would ever learn that the query failed.

The syntax

Declare the resources in parentheses after try. When the block ends — normally or with an exception — Java calls close() on each one.

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;

public class ErrorCounter {
    static long countErrors(Path log) throws IOException {
        try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(log)) {
            long count = 0;
            String line;
            while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
                if (line.contains("ERROR")) {
                    count++;
                }
            }
            return count;
        }   // reader.close() runs here, even if readLine() throws
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path log = Path.of("app.log");
        Files.write(log, List.of(
                "10:00:01 INFO  Order 101 placed",
                "10:00:02 ERROR Payment gateway timeout",
                "10:00:05 INFO  Order 102 placed",
                "10:00:09 ERROR Inventory service down"));
        System.out.println("Errors: " + countErrors(log));
    }
}
Errors: 2

The resource variable is implicitly final, and its scope is the try block. A try-with-resources statement may still have catch and finally blocks.

AutoCloseable vs Closeable

A resource must implement java.lang.AutoCloseable. Its older cousin java.io.Closeable was retrofitted to extend it, so every Closeable works too.

AspectAutoCloseableCloseable
Package, sincejava.lang, Java 7java.io, Java 5
Methodvoid close() throws Exceptionvoid close() throws IOException
Repeated close()Not required to be idempotent (but strongly encouraged)Must be idempotent: closing an already closed stream has no effect
RelationshipThe parent interfaceCloseable extends AutoCloseable
Typical implementationsJDBC Connection, Statement, ResultSet; Stream; ExecutorService (Java 19+); HttpClient (Java 21+)InputStream, OutputStream, Reader, Writer, Scanner, FileChannel

When you implement close() yourself, narrow the signature: an override may throw fewer exceptions, so public void close() with no throws clause spares your callers a pointless catch block.

Multiple resources and closing order

Separate resources with semicolons. They are opened left to right and closed in reverse order — the last opened is closed first, which is right because later resources often depend on earlier ones (a statement depends on its connection).

public class TwrOrder {
    static class Resource implements AutoCloseable {
        private final String name;

        Resource(String name) {
            this.name = name;
            System.out.println("open " + name);
        }

        @Override
        public void close() {
            System.out.println("close " + name);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Resource a = new Resource("A");
             Resource b = new Resource("B")) {
            System.out.println("body");
            throw new IllegalStateException("body failed");
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("catch: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            System.out.println("finally");
        }
    }
}
open A
open B
body
close B
close A
catch: body failed
finally

Rule: resources are closed before catch and finally run

The order is: open resources → body → close resources (reverse order) → matching catch → finally. So inside catch and finally the resources are already closed — you cannot use them there.

If opening a resource fails, the ones already opened are still closed, and the failed one is not (it was never assigned):

open A
close A
catch: cannot open B

Suppressed exceptions

When the body throws exception A and close() then throws exception B, try-with-resources keeps A as the main exception and attaches B to it with A.addSuppressed(B). Nothing is lost. You can read the attached exceptions with getSuppressed(), and the stack trace prints them under Suppressed:.

public class SuppressedDemo {
    static class FlakyConnection implements AutoCloseable {
        @Override
        public void close() {
            throw new IllegalStateException("close failed");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (FlakyConnection c = new FlakyConnection()) {
            throw new RuntimeException("query failed");
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught: " + e.getMessage());
            for (Throwable s : e.getSuppressed()) {
                System.out.println("Suppressed: " + s.getMessage());
            }
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
    }
}
Caught: query failed
Suppressed: close failed
java.lang.RuntimeException: query failed
    at SuppressedDemo.main(SuppressedDemo.java:11)
    Suppressed: java.lang.IllegalStateException: close failed
        at SuppressedDemo$FlakyConnection.close(SuppressedDemo.java:5)
        at SuppressedDemo.main(SuppressedDemo.java:10)

Compare with the old-style output above: the real problem ("query failed") is now the main exception. If only close() throws (the body succeeded), that close exception is simply thrown as the main exception.

Java 9: using an existing variable as a resource

Since Java 9 you can put an existing variable in the header, as long as it is final or effectively final (never reassigned). This is handy when the resource is a parameter.

static void copyLines(BufferedReader reader, BufferedWriter writer) throws IOException {
    try (reader; writer) {             // both closed at the end, writer first
        String line;
        while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
            writer.write(line);
            writer.newLine();
        }
    }
}

If the variable is reassigned anywhere, compilation fails with variable reader used as a try-with-resources resource neither final nor effectively final.

Edge cases

  • A null resource is allowed. If the resource expression is null, the body runs and close() is simply skipped — no NullPointerException.
  • Only declared resources are closed. In try (var r = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(f))) only the outer reader is a resource; closing it closes the inner one too, because wrapper streams close what they wrap.
  • Not every cleanup is AutoCloseable. Lock is not; keep using try/finally with unlock().

What the compiler generates

The Java Language Specification defines try-with-resources as a translation into ordinary try/catch/finally. Simplified, for one resource:

final Resource r = open();
Throwable primary = null;
try {
    // body
} catch (Throwable t) {
    primary = t;
    throw t;
} finally {
    if (r != null) {
        if (primary != null) {
            try {
                r.close();
            } catch (Throwable closeFailure) {
                primary.addSuppressed(closeFailure);   // keep the original exception
            }
        } else {
            r.close();
        }
    }
}

Wrong: returning a resource that the try already closed

static Stream<String> lines(Path p) throws IOException {
    try (Stream<String> s = Files.lines(p)) {
        return s;          // closed on the way out
    }
}
// caller: lines(p).forEach(...) throws
// IllegalStateException: stream has already
// been operated upon or closed

Right: finish the work inside the try

static List<String> errorLines(Path p) throws IOException {
    try (Stream<String> s = Files.lines(p)) {
        return s.filter(l -> l.contains("ERROR"))
                .toList();   // fully read before close
    }
}

The same trap with a BufferedReader fails with java.io.IOException: Stream closed at the caller. If a method must hand an open resource to its caller, do not close it there — document that the caller owns it and must close it.

Real project: where you still write it by hand

  • Plain JDBC code: Connection, PreparedStatement and ResultSet in one header.
  • Files.lines, Files.list and Files.walk streams — they hold open file handles.
  • Spring Data repository methods that return Stream<T>: the stream keeps a database cursor open and must be closed (and used inside a transaction).
  • In typical Spring code you rarely close connections yourself — JdbcTemplate and JPA do it — but you still close the files, streams and clients you open.

Interview: "What is try-with-resources and what are suppressed exceptions?"

  • Java 7 feature: resources declared in the header are closed automatically in reverse order; the resource type must implement AutoCloseable.
  • If the body and close() both throw, the body's exception propagates and the close failure is attached as suppressed (getSuppressed()), unlike try/finally where the original was lost.
  • Resources are closed before catch/finally run. Java 9 allows effectively final variables in the header.
  • Closeable vs AutoCloseable: IOException vs Exception, and the idempotency requirement.

throw vs throws

throw is a statement that raises one exception object right now; throws is a clause in a method signature that tells callers which checked exceptions the method may let escape.

The two keywords differ by one letter, and beginners mix them up all the time. Keep them apart with one idea: throw does something while the program runs, but throws only describes something — for the compiler and for the people who call your method.

throw: raising an exception

A throw statement takes one exception object and starts the unwinding process from What an exception is: the current method stops at once, and Java looks for a matching catch block in the callers. Usually you create the object on the same line: throw new IllegalArgumentException("message"). The expression after throw can also be a variable that holds an exception, for example one you caught a moment ago.

throws: declaring what can escape

A throws clause sits in a method or constructor declaration, after the parameter list. It lists the checked exception types that the method does not handle itself, so they may come out of it. The compiler uses the list at every call site: the caller must catch those types or declare them in its own throws clause (the catch-or-declare rule from Checked vs unchecked exceptions).

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class ThrowsDemo {

    // Unchecked exceptions need no throws clause
    static int parsePort(String text) {
        int port = Integer.parseInt(text.trim());
        if (port < 1 || port > 65535) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Port must be 1-65535 but was " + port);
        }
        return port;
    }

    // IOException is checked: the method must declare it
    static int readPort(Path file) throws IOException {
        String text = Files.readString(file);
        return parsePort(text);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path dir = Files.createTempDirectory("ports-");
        Path good = Files.writeString(dir.resolve("good.txt"), "8080");
        Path bad = Files.writeString(dir.resolve("bad.txt"), "70000");
        Path missing = dir.resolve("missing.txt");

        for (Path file : new Path[] {good, bad, missing}) {
            String name = file.getFileName().toString();
            try {
                System.out.println(name + " -> port " + readPort(file));
            } catch (IOException e) {
                System.out.println(name + " -> cannot read (" + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ")");
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
                System.out.println(name + " -> invalid: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}
good.txt -> port 8080
bad.txt -> invalid: Port must be 1-65535 but was 70000
missing.txt -> cannot read (NoSuchFileException)

Read the example in two layers. parsePort contains a throw statement, but it needs no throws clause because IllegalArgumentException is unchecked. readPort contains no throw statement at all, yet it has a throws clause: the exception comes from inside Files.readString, and readPort chooses to pass it on instead of handling it. So throws is about what can come out of a method, no matter who threw it. main declares throws IOException as well, because createTempDirectory and writeString throw it outside the try block.

Side by side

Aspectthrowthrows
What it isA statementA clause in a method or constructor declaration
WhereInside a body: method, constructor, lambda, initializer, switch arm After the parameter list: void save() throws IOException
Followed byOne exception object (new X(...) or a variable)One or more exception class names, separated by commas
When it actsAt run time: it really raises the exceptionAt compile time: it is only a declaration the compiler checks
Required forNothing — you throw when something is wrongChecked exceptions that the method lets escape (unchecked ones are optional)

Catch it, declare it or wrap it?

Every time a checked exception can reach your code you have three choices. The flowchart gives the usual order of thinking.

Catch only when you can do something useful. Declare when the caller is the right place to decide — for a file-reading method, the caller knows whether a missing file is fatal or just means "use the defaults". Wrap (next article) when the exception type would leak an implementation detail upwards.

Rules for the throw statement

  • The expression must be a Throwable. throw "error"; does not compile.
  • A throw ends the normal flow, so a statement right after it is unreachable and fails with error: unreachable statement.
  • If you throw a checked exception, the method must catch it or declare it. Throwing new IOException("x") in a method without a throws clause gives unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown.
  • throw is a statement, not an expression, so you cannot use it in the middle of a ternary a ? b : throw ....

Edge cases of throw and throws

  • throw in a switch expression. An arrow arm may be a throw statement. This is the clean way to reject unknown values: 
    String label = switch (status) {
    case "PAID" -> "Paid";
    case "PENDING" -> "Pending";
    default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown status: " + status);
};
  • throw null compiles, because null can be assigned to any reference type. At run time it throws a NullPointerException instead (message: Cannot throw exception because "null" is null).
  • A throws clause may name unchecked exceptions (throws IllegalStateException) and checked types the body never throws. The compiler accepts both. This is useful on interface and abstract methods, where implementations may need to throw something the interface method itself does not.
  • The opposite is an error: a catch for a checked exception that the try block cannot throw is a compile error (see the second compiler rule in Checked vs unchecked).
  • Constructors can have a throws clause too. Throwing from a constructor means the object is never created.

The stack trace shows where the exception was created

The trace is recorded when the exception object is constructed (inside the Throwable constructor), not when throw runs. Most of the time both happen on the same line, so you never notice. They differ when you build an exception in one place and throw it in another:

public class ThrowLocation {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        RuntimeException saved = new IllegalStateException("created early");
        try {
            throwIt(saved);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            System.out.println("trace starts at: " + e.getStackTrace()[0]);
            System.out.println("same object: " + (e == saved));
        }
    }

    static void throwIt(RuntimeException e) {
        throw e;
    }
}
trace starts at: ThrowLocation.main(ThrowLocation.java:3)
same object: true

The trace points at line 3, where the object was created, not at line 12, where it was thrown. Never keep an exception in a constant to throw it again later: every throw would show the same stale trace and mislead whoever reads the log. Always write throw new ... at the place where the problem is detected.

Common mistakes

Mistake: creating an exception and forgetting to throw it

new IllegalStateException("never thrown"); compiles, runs and does nothing: the object is created and immediately thrown away, and execution continues as if nothing was wrong. The method prints "finished normally" even though you meant to fail. Write throw new IllegalStateException(...). Most IDEs flag the unused result.

Mistake: writing throw where throws belongs

void save() throw IOException { ... } fails with '{' or ';' expected — the parser does not expect the keyword throw in a declaration. The reverse (throws new IOException() in a body) is a syntax error as well. Declarations take throws plus a class name; bodies take throw plus an object.

Wrong: throws Exception hides what can fail

public Order load(long id) throws Exception {
    // callers must now catch the broadest type
    // and cannot tell what can really go wrong
}

Right: declare the specific type

/**
 * @throws IOException if the order file cannot be read
 */
public Order load(long id) throws IOException {
    // callers see exactly what they must handle
}

Conventions

  • Declare the narrowest checked types in throws; never throws Exception in application code (it is fine in main of a quick demo).
  • Document every exception a caller might care about, checked or not, with Javadoc @throws.
  • Throw as early as you can detect the problem (validate arguments at the top of the method), and always create the exception at the throw site.
  • Prefer a standard exception when it says exactly what happened (IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException), and a custom one when callers need to react to it differently (see custom exceptions).

Interview: "What is the difference between throw and throws?"

  • throw is a statement that raises one exception object at run time; throws is a clause in a method signature that declares the checked exceptions it may pass to its caller — checked at compile time.
  • You can throw only one exception at a time but list many in throws.
  • Follow-ups: Can a method have throws without throw? Yes — it may just pass on what a called method throws. Can you throw a checked exception without throws? Only if you catch it in the same method.
  • Bonus point: the stack trace is captured when the exception is created, not when it is thrown.

Rethrowing, wrapping and exception chaining

When you cannot fully handle an exception, rethrow it unchanged or wrap it in a more suitable exception that keeps the original as its cause — the chain of causes is what you read as "Caused by" in a log.

A catch block does not have to be the end of the story. Often the right move is to do a little work and pass the failure on. There are three reasons to do that:

  • Undo or clean up first — release a reserved seat, roll back a half-finished change — and then let the caller know that the operation failed.
  • Translate the exception to the level of abstraction of the caller. An OrderService should not make its callers deal with SQLException: that tells them how the data is stored, which is none of their business.
  • Add context that the low-level exception cannot know: which order, which file, which user.

Plain rethrow: throw e

Throwing the caught exception again keeps the very same object, so the original type, message and stack trace stay intact. Use it when you only need to react to the failure.

void checkout(Order order) throws PaymentException {
    inventory.reserve(order);
    try {
        payments.charge(order);
    } catch (PaymentException e) {
        inventory.release(order);   // undo the partial work
        throw e;                    // the caller still sees the original failure
    }
}

Precise rethrow (Java 7)

Suppose you catch Exception to run some cleanup, and then rethrow it. Before Java 7 the method then had to declare throws Exception. Since Java 7 the compiler is smarter: if the catch parameter is never reassigned (effectively final), it knows the rethrown exception can only be what the try block can throw.

import java.io.IOException;

public class PreciseRethrow {

    static void risky(boolean io) throws IOException {
        if (io) {
            throw new IOException("disk problem");
        }
    }

    // Java 7+: only IOException can arrive in the catch block,
    // so the method may declare just "throws IOException"
    static void process() throws IOException {
        try {
            risky(true);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.println("cleaning up after: " + e.getMessage());
            throw e;           // precise rethrow
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            process();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("main got " + e);
        }
    }
}
cleaning up after: disk problem
main got java.io.IOException: disk problem

If you assign something else to e before the throw e, the precise analysis is switched off and the compiler asks for throws Exception again. Unchecked exceptions never need declaring, so they pass through any rethrow.

Wrapping with a cause: exception chaining

To wrap an exception, create a new one and pass the original as its cause. The result is an exception chain: the outer exception says what the operation could not do, and the cause says why. Most exception classes offer these constructors:

ConstructorMessageCause
X()nullnone
X(String message)your textnone
X(String message, Throwable cause)your textthe original
X(Throwable cause)cause.toString(), such as java.io.IOException: disk fullthe original

Prefer the (message, cause) form: your message adds the context, and the cause keeps the detail.

import java.sql.SQLException;

public class ChainDemo {

    static class OrderRepository {
        void save(int orderId) throws SQLException {
            // pretend the database rejected the insert
            throw new SQLException("duplicate key value violates unique constraint \"orders_pkey\"",
                    "23505");
        }
    }

    static class OrderService {
        private final OrderRepository repository = new OrderRepository();

        void placeOrder(int orderId) {
            try {
                repository.save(orderId);
            } catch (SQLException e) {
                // translate: the service layer should not leak SQLException
                throw new IllegalStateException("Could not save order " + orderId, e);
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            new OrderService().placeOrder(101);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            // walk the chain from the outermost exception to the root cause
            for (Throwable t = e; t != null; t = t.getCause()) {
                System.out.println(t.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + t.getMessage());
            }
            e.printStackTrace(System.out);
        }
    }
}
IllegalStateException: Could not save order 101
SQLException: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_pkey"
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Could not save order 101
    at ChainDemo$OrderService.placeOrder(ChainDemo.java:21)
    at ChainDemo.main(ChainDemo.java:28)
Caused by: java.sql.SQLException: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_pkey"
    at ChainDemo$OrderRepository.save(ChainDemo.java:8)
    at ChainDemo$OrderService.placeOrder(ChainDemo.java:18)
    ... 1 more

The loop in main uses getCause(), which returns the wrapped exception or null at the end of the chain. The last exception it prints is the root cause. The stack trace prints the whole chain for you: the top part is the new IllegalStateException with its own frames, and the Caused by: part holds the original SQLException, including the line in save where it was created. If you had not passed e as the cause, that second part would be gone and nobody could tell what the database complained about. The diagram shows the usual journey of such an exception through a layered application.

initCause: for exceptions without a cause constructor

Some old exception classes have no constructor that accepts a cause — NumberFormatException and IndexOutOfBoundsException are examples. For those, initCause(Throwable) sets it after creation. It works at most once, and not at all if a constructor already set the cause (even when that cause was null).

import java.io.IOException;

public class InitCauseDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // NumberFormatException has no constructor that takes a cause
        NumberFormatException nfe = new NumberFormatException("Bad quantity in row 7");
        nfe.initCause(new IOException("stream closed"));
        System.out.println("cause = " + nfe.getCause());

        try {
            nfe.initCause(new IOException("again"));        // second call
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("second initCause -> " + e.getMessage());
        }

        Exception e2 = new Exception("with cause", new IOException("x"));
        try {
            e2.initCause(new IOException("y"));             // constructor already set it
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("after constructor -> " + e.getMessage());
        }

        Exception e3 = new Exception(new IOException("disk full"));
        System.out.println("message when only a cause is given: " + e3.getMessage());
    }
}
cause = java.io.IOException: stream closed
second initCause -> Can't overwrite cause with java.io.IOException: again
after constructor -> Can't overwrite cause with java.io.IOException: y
message when only a cause is given: java.io.IOException: disk full

Wrapping a checked exception in an unchecked one

When a method cannot declare a checked exception — because it overrides a method without a throws clause, because it is a lambda, or because you do not want the type to leak — wrap it in an unchecked exception. For I/O the JDK provides java.io.UncheckedIOException; its constructors accept only an IOException as the cause. For other checked exceptions use IllegalStateException or one of your own runtime exceptions.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class WrapIo {

    static String loadConfig(String file) {
        try {
            return Files.readString(Path.of(file));
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException("Cannot load config " + file, e);
        }
    }

    static void startApp() {
        String config = loadConfig("missing.properties");
        System.out.println(config);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        startApp();
    }
}
Exception in thread "main" java.io.UncheckedIOException: Cannot load config missing.properties
    at WrapIo.loadConfig(WrapIo.java:12)
    at WrapIo.startApp(WrapIo.java:17)
    at WrapIo.main(WrapIo.java:22)
Caused by: java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException: missing.properties
    at java.base/sun.nio.fs.WindowsException.translateToIOException(...)
    ... JDK-internal frames omitted ...
    at java.base/java.nio.file.Files.readString(...)
    at WrapIo.loadConfig(WrapIo.java:10)
    ... 2 more

The program crashes, as it should — the config file is missing — but the trace says everything: Cannot load config missing.properties (your context), caused by NoSuchFileException (the real reason), and the line numbers lead straight to the code. The frame names inside sun.nio.fs depend on the operating system (Linux shows UnixException); the rest is the same everywhere.

Let your own exceptions pass through

A very common mistake is a catch-all wrapper that also swallows exceptions your callers need to recognise. If the controller layer wants to answer "insufficient balance" with a clear message, a generic wrapper in the service layer ruins it.

Wrong: wraps everything, even domain exceptions

public void transfer(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount) {
    try {
        ledger.move(from, to, amount);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        throw new RuntimeException("Transfer failed", e);
    }   // InsufficientBalanceException is now hidden inside a RuntimeException
}

Right: translate only the technical exception

public void transfer(String from, String to, BigDecimal amount) {
    try {
        ledger.move(from, to, amount);
    } catch (SQLException e) {
        throw new TransferFailedException("Transfer " + from + " -> " + to + " failed", e);
    }   // InsufficientBalanceException is unchecked and flows through untouched
}

Mistake: wrapping again and again without adding anything

If every layer catches an exception and wraps it with the same message, the log shows a ladder of six "Caused by" sections that all say "Operation failed". Wrap only when you change the abstraction (SQL to domain) or add useful information (an id, a file name). Otherwise let the exception travel up unchanged.

Conventions

  • Always keep the cause: new X("context", e), never new X(e.getMessage()).
  • Write the message for the new level (what you were trying to do and with which data); let the cause carry the technical detail.
  • Translate at layer boundaries: repository to service to controller. Inside one layer, let exceptions flow.
  • Do not log and rethrow at every layer. Log once, where the exception is finally handled (see best practices).
  • To find the root cause in code, loop on getCause(). Libraries such as Spring (NestedExceptionUtils.getRootCause) and Apache Commons Lang (ExceptionUtils.getRootCause) already provide helpers.

Interview: "What is exception chaining?" / "throw e vs throw new X(e)"

  • Chaining means attaching the original exception as the cause of a new one, via the (message, cause) constructor or initCause. getCause() reads it, and the stack trace prints it as "Caused by".
  • throw e rethrows the same object — same type, same trace. throw new X(msg, e) creates a new exception (new type, new message, new trace) and keeps the old one inside.
  • Why wrap: translate low-level exceptions to the caller's level, add context, turn a checked exception into an unchecked one — without losing the root cause.
  • Precise rethrow (Java 7): rethrowing a caught Exception that is effectively final lets the method declare only the checked types the try block can really throw.

Writing custom exceptions

A custom exception is a small class that extends Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked), has a specific name ending in Exception, and carries the data a caller needs to react.

The JDK exceptions describe technical problems. Your application has its own failures: an account has too little money, an order does not exist, a coupon has expired. You could report these with IllegalStateException("insufficient balance"), but then a caller can only tell them apart by reading the message text, which is fragile. A custom exception gives the failure a name, lets callers catch it separately, and can carry data such as the account id and the missing amount.

Create one only when a standard exception does not fit

If IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException or NoSuchElementException says exactly what went wrong, use it. Create a custom type when callers will handle that failure differently from others (show a specific message, retry, map it to an HTTP status) or when the failure carries data.

The smallest custom exception

public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {

    public OrderNotFoundException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

That is all it takes: extend a base class and pass the message to super. Use it with throw new OrderNotFoundException("Order 1042 not found"). The base class decides whether the compiler checks it, see below.

Constructors to provide

The JDK's own exceptions follow a pattern, and callers expect the same from yours. Provide the constructors that make sense:

ConstructorProvide it when
X(String message)Almost always — the basic case
X(String message, Throwable cause)The exception wraps another one (see chaining). Always provide it for wrapper exceptions
X(Throwable cause)Optional; handy for pure wrappers
X()Rarely: an exception without a message is hard to understand in a log
Custom, such as X(String accountId, BigDecimal balance, ...)The exception carries data: build the message from the data inside the constructor, so every throw site gets the same good message

Adding fields: InsufficientBalanceException

This is the roadmap example. The exception stores what a caller needs to react: which account, how much it has, how much was asked. A user interface can then say "You are short by ₹500" without parsing a message.

import java.math.BigDecimal;

public class InsufficientBalanceException extends RuntimeException {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    private final String accountId;
    private final BigDecimal balance;
    private final BigDecimal requested;

    public InsufficientBalanceException(String accountId, BigDecimal balance, BigDecimal requested) {
        super("Account " + accountId + " has " + balance + " but " + requested + " was requested");
        this.accountId = accountId;
        this.balance = balance;
        this.requested = requested;
    }

    public String getAccountId() {
        return accountId;
    }

    public BigDecimal getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }

    public BigDecimal getRequested() {
        return requested;
    }

    public BigDecimal getShortfall() {
        return requested.subtract(balance);
    }
}
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Objects;

public class Account {
    private final String id;
    private BigDecimal balance;

    public Account(String id, BigDecimal openingBalance) {
        this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id must not be null");
        if (openingBalance.signum() < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Opening balance cannot be negative: " + openingBalance);
        }
        this.balance = openingBalance;
    }

    public void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) {
        if (amount.signum() <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive: " + amount);
        }
        if (amount.compareTo(balance) > 0) {
            throw new InsufficientBalanceException(id, balance, amount);
        }
        balance = balance.subtract(amount);
    }

    public String getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public BigDecimal getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}
import java.math.BigDecimal;

public class BankApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Account account = new Account("ACC-1001", new BigDecimal("5000.00"));
        String[] requests = {"1500.00", "4000.00", "-10"};

        for (String text : requests) {
            BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(text);
            try {
                account.withdraw(amount);
                System.out.println("Withdrew " + amount + ", balance now " + account.getBalance());
            } catch (InsufficientBalanceException e) {
                System.out.println("Declined: short by " + e.getShortfall());
                System.out.println("  detail: " + e.getMessage());
            } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
                System.out.println("Invalid request: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}
Withdrew 1500.00, balance now 3500.00
Declined: short by 500.00
  detail: Account ACC-1001 has 3500.00 but 4000.00 was requested
Invalid request: Amount must be positive: -10

Notice the two different failures. A negative amount is a bug in the caller, so the standard IllegalArgumentException fits. Too little money is a business situation that the caller must handle, so it gets its own type, and main reacts to it differently from the other one. Also notice that the money values are BigDecimal, never double.

Checked or unchecked?

The choice is a single word after extends, but it changes how every caller works. Compare the two versions of the same exception:

public class InsufficientBalanceException extends Exception {        // checked
    // ... same fields and constructor ...
}

public void withdraw(BigDecimal amount) throws InsufficientBalanceException {
    // ...
}

// every caller must now catch it or declare it
try {
    account.withdraw(amount);
} catch (InsufficientBalanceException e) {
    // ...
}
Extend Exception (checked)Extend RuntimeException (unchecked)
CompilerForces callers to catch or declareNo forcing
SignaturesEvery method on the way up needs throwsUnchanged
Lambdas and streamsAwkward: cannot be thrown from a FunctionWorks everywhere
Spring @TransactionalDoes not roll back by defaultRolls back by default
Good forLibraries where callers must decide, expected and recoverable failuresApplication code, business rules, most Spring Boot services

Modern application code leans towards unchecked for business exceptions: the failure travels up to one central handler that turns it into a response, and no signature is polluted. Choose checked when you write a library or API where ignoring the failure would be a real bug and the caller can recover (retry, pick another option). When unsure, go unchecked.

Real project: why the transaction rule matters

In Spring, a method annotated with @Transactional rolls back the database changes when a RuntimeException or Error leaves it, but commits when a checked exception leaves it, unless you add rollbackFor. A checked InsufficientBalanceException thrown after the debit would silently commit half a transfer. This is one of the main reasons Spring projects use unchecked business exceptions.

A base exception and error codes

In a real application, give all exceptions of one area a common parent, and add a machine-readable error code. The API layer can then catch the parent once, and clients get a stable code instead of a message that may change.

public enum ErrorCode {
    INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE,
    ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND,
    ACCOUNT_FROZEN
}
public abstract class BankException extends RuntimeException {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    private final ErrorCode code;

    protected BankException(ErrorCode code, String message) {
        super(message);
        this.code = code;
    }

    protected BankException(ErrorCode code, String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
        this.code = code;
    }

    public ErrorCode getCode() {
        return code;
    }
}
public class AccountNotFoundException extends BankException {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    public AccountNotFoundException(String accountId) {
        super(ErrorCode.ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND, "No account with id " + accountId);
    }
}

InsufficientBalanceException would now extend BankException and pass ErrorCode.INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE to super. A single catch block at the edge of the application handles all of them:

try {
    transferService.transfer(from, to, amount);
} catch (BankException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getCode() + " -> " + e.getMessage());
}
ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND -> No account with id ACC-9
INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE -> Account ACC-1 has 10 but 25 was requested

The Spring Boot article in this module shows how the same code becomes a JSON error response.

Naming, packages and structure

  • End the name with Exception (OrderNotFoundException). Never Error — that suggests a JVM Error.
  • Be specific. MyException, CustomException and AppException say nothing. Name the failure, not the layer.
  • Keep the hierarchy shallow: one base class per area at most. Deep trees of exception classes are hard to maintain.
  • Put them near the code that throws them (the same package as the domain class, or an exception sub-package) and make them public when callers use them.

Rules for custom exception classes

  • An exception class cannot be generic: class Failure<T> extends Exception fails with a generic class may not extend java.lang.Throwable. The runtime cannot tell Failure<String> from Failure<Integer> in a catch block (type erasure, Module 4).
  • A record cannot be an exception, because records cannot extend another class.
  • Throwable implements Serializable, so declare private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;. Without it, javac -Xlint:serial warns: serializable class X has no definition of serialVersionUID. Keep fields serializable or mark them transient.

Edge case: exceptions without a stack trace

Creating an exception is relatively expensive, because the JVM walks the stack to fill in the trace. The protected constructor super(message, cause, false, false) turns off suppression and the writable stack trace. A few high-volume frameworks use this for exceptions that work as control signals. For normal business exceptions do not do this — the trace is what you read in the log when something goes wrong.

Mistakes with custom exceptions

  • Everything extends Exception. Every caller up the chain gets a throws clause, and people start writing throws Exception or empty catch blocks.
  • Dropping the cause in wrapper exceptions — give wrappers the (message, cause) constructor and use it.
  • Sensitive data in the message. Messages end up in logs and sometimes in API responses. Never put passwords, tokens, OTPs or full card numbers in them.
  • Heavy fields: storing a whole entity or a request object inside the exception keeps it alive and may not be serializable. Store ids and amounts.
  • Business logic inside the exception class. It should only describe the failure.

Interview: "How do you create a custom exception?"

  • Extend Exception for a checked exception or RuntimeException for an unchecked one; end the name with Exception; call super(message) or super(message, cause); add serialVersionUID.
  • Add fields (an id, an error code) so callers can react without parsing messages.
  • Explain checked vs unchecked and your default: unchecked for business rules in Spring apps (including the @Transactional rollback rule), checked for recoverable failures in libraries.
  • Mention a small hierarchy with a base class and error codes, and handling it centrally.

Overriding methods and exceptions

An overriding method may throw fewer or narrower checked exceptions than the method it overrides, but never new or broader ones; unchecked exceptions are always allowed.

When a subclass overrides a method, the compiler checks the throws clause too, not only the name and parameters. The reason is simple. Code that calls a method through the parent type has already decided how to handle the parent's checked exceptions. If a child could suddenly throw a new checked exception, that code would break at run time without any warning. This is the Liskov substitution principle: wherever the parent type is used, a child must be usable without surprises (see System Design · Module 1).

The rule

For every checked exception that the overriding method declares, the overridden method must declare the same type or a superclass of it. The child's list can be shorter or empty, never wider. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error and their subclasses) are not part of this check.

Parent declaresChild declaresAllowed?
throws IOExceptionthrows IOExceptionYes — the same
throws IOExceptionthrows FileNotFoundExceptionYes — narrower (a subclass)
throws IOExceptionnothingYes — fewer
throws IOExceptionthrows IllegalStateExceptionYes — unchecked is always allowed
throws IOExceptionthrows ExceptionNo — broader
throws IOExceptionthrows SQLExceptionNo — an unrelated checked type
throws IOExceptionthrows IOException, InterruptedExceptionNo — InterruptedException is new
nothingthrows IOExceptionNo — the parent promises no checked exceptions
nothingthrows RuntimeExceptionYes — unchecked

Allowed overrides

import java.io.FileNotFoundException;
import java.io.IOException;

class Reader1 {
    void load() throws IOException {
        System.out.println("Reader1.load");
    }
}

class FileReader1 extends Reader1 {
    @Override
    void load() throws FileNotFoundException {     // narrower: allowed
        System.out.println("FileReader1.load");
    }
}

class CachedReader extends Reader1 {
    @Override
    void load() {                                  // none at all: allowed
        System.out.println("CachedReader.load");
    }
}

class StrictReader extends Reader1 {
    @Override
    void load() throws IllegalStateException {     // unchecked: always allowed
        System.out.println("StrictReader.load");
    }
}

public class Ok1 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Reader1 viaParent = new CachedReader();
        viaParent.load();                          // compiler uses Reader1's throws list

        CachedReader viaChild = new CachedReader();
        viaChild.load();                           // no try/catch needed here
    }
}
CachedReader.load
CachedReader.load

Not allowed: the compiler errors

import java.io.IOException;

class Parent {
    void load() throws IOException {
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void load() throws Exception {      // broader than IOException
    }
}
Bad1.java:10: error: load() in Child cannot override load() in Parent
    void load() throws Exception {      // broader than IOException
         ^
  overridden method does not throw Exception
1 error

The message is the same for an unrelated type such as SQLException and for any checked exception added to a method whose parent declares none. When a class implements an interface method, the wording changes only slightly. For example, public void run() throws Exception inside a class that implements Runnable gives run() in Task cannot implement run() in Runnable and the same last line. That is also why you cannot call Thread.sleep() in a Runnable lambda without a try/catch: Runnable.run() declares nothing. Callable.call(), in contrast, declares throws Exception, so a Callable lambda may throw any checked exception.

The reference type decides what the caller must handle

The compiler checks a call against the declared type of the variable, not the object behind it. So the same object can need a try/catch through one variable and none through another:

class Reader2 {
    void load() throws IOException { }
}

class CachedReader2 extends Reader2 {
    @Override
    void load() { }                   // declares nothing
}

// in main (which has no throws clause):
Reader2 viaParent = new CachedReader2();
viaParent.load();     // error: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared
