Here Reader2.load() declares IOException, so the call through Reader2 must handle it, even though CachedReader2.load() throws nothing. With a variable of type CachedReader2 the same call compiles without any handling. This is why coding against interfaces (List, not ArrayList) means living with the interface's exception contract.

Constructors, static methods and overloading

  • Constructors are not overridden, but there is a related rule. If a superclass constructor declares a checked exception, every subclass constructor must declare it too — it cannot be caught, because super(...) must be the first statement. A subclass that relies on the implicit default constructor fails with unreported exception IOException in default constructor; write an explicit constructor with a throws clause.
  • Static methods are hidden, not overridden, but the compiler applies the same throws rule to them.
  • Overloaded methods (same name, different parameters) are different methods, so they may declare any exceptions. The rule is only for overriding and implementing.
  • Generic throws: a method can declare a type variable, as Optional.orElseThrow(Supplier<? extends X>) does with throws X. The caller decides the type, which keeps the checked-exception rules intact.

Rule: an override may only make the exception contract narrower

Same type, a subclass, nothing at all, or any unchecked exception. If you need to throw a broader checked exception from an override, catch it and wrap it in an unchecked exception (see rethrowing and chaining), or change the parent method's signature — which breaks all of its callers.

Design tip: implement close() without a throws clause

AutoCloseable.close() declares throws Exception. Your own class may override it as public void close() with no throws clause (or with something narrower), as the earlier try-with-resources article showed. Callers that use your class by its own type are then spared a useless catch block.

Interview: "Rules for overriding with exceptions"

  • The overriding method can throw the same checked exceptions, subclasses of them, or none. It cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions.
  • It can throw any unchecked exception, whatever the parent declares.
  • Give the reason: the caller compiled against the parent's contract (Liskov substitution).
  • Typical trick questions: Parent throws IOException; can the child throw FileNotFoundException? Yes. Can it throw Exception? No. Parent declares nothing; can the child throw ArithmeticException? Yes, it is unchecked.

Exception handling best practices

Handle an exception only where you can do something useful, keep the cause and the context, log it once, and never swallow it silently.

Knowing the syntax of try and catch is the easy part. What separates clean exception handling from the kind that wakes a team up at 3 a.m. is a set of habits. This article lists them in the order you will meet them in a real code review. Each one has a reason, and most have a wrong-and-right pair.

1. Never swallow an exception

An empty catch block makes the problem disappear while the program carries on in a broken state. The payment failed, but the code continues as if it had succeeded; the bug shows up three screens later and nobody can say why.

Wrong: the failure vanishes

try {
    inventory.reserve(orderId);
} catch (Exception e) {
    // TODO handle later
}

Right: decide something, or let it travel

try {
    inventory.reserve(orderId);
} catch (OutOfStockException e) {
    return OrderResult.rejected("Item is out of stock");   // a real decision
}
// every other failure propagates to the central handler

Printing is not handling either. e.printStackTrace() writes to System.err, outside your log format, level and files, and the code still continues as if all was well. If ignoring an exception is truly correct (best-effort cleanup, for example), say so in a comment and name the variable ignored.

2. Catch specific exceptions, not Exception or Throwable

catch (Exception e) also catches every RuntimeException: the NullPointerException or ClassCastException that is a bug you want to see, not hide. It catches InterruptedException, which you must not swallow (see item 10). catch (Throwable t) adds OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError. Name the exceptions you really know how to handle.

try {
    BigDecimal rate = rateClient.fetch(currency);
    return amount.multiply(rate);
} catch (RateServiceUnavailableException e) {      // I know how to handle this one:
    return amount.multiply(lastKnownRate(currency));   // fall back to the cached rate
}   // a NullPointerException here is a bug: let it surface

Exception: boundaries may catch everything

The outermost layer of a thread — a web request handler, a scheduled job, a message listener, a thread-pool task — must not die from one bad request. There, and only there, catch Exception (or even Throwable) to log it and move on to the next unit of work. In Spring Boot this is the @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) method of your global handler.

3. Log or rethrow — not both

If every layer logs the exception and then rethrows it, one failure produces three or four log entries with the same stack trace. Searching the logs becomes a maze, and it looks as if three separate things failed.

Wrong: every layer logs and rethrows

// repository
catch (SQLException e) {
    log.error("DB error", e);
    throw new DataAccessFailureException("DB error", e);
}
// service
catch (DataAccessFailureException e) {
    log.error("Could not place order", e);
    throw new OrderFailedException("Could not place order", e);
}
// controller
catch (OrderFailedException e) {
    log.error("Request failed", e);
    return ResponseEntity.status(500).build();
}

Right: wrap with context, log once at the top

// repository: translate and keep the cause, no logging
catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new DataAccessFailureException("Could not save order " + id, e);
}
// service: no try/catch at all, the exception just flows
// controller advice: the one place that logs
log.error("Request failed", ex);

Rule of thumb: a catch block does one of three things — handle the exception completely, rethrow or wrap it, or log it because it is the final stop. Never two of them at once.

4. Log the exception itself, at the right level

Pass the exception object as the last argument to the logger so that the stack trace and all "Caused by" sections are printed — see the wrong-and-right pair in Reading a stack trace. Use ERROR for unexpected failures that need attention. An expected business outcome, such as "insufficient balance", is not an error of the system; log it at INFO or WARN, or not at all. Logging is covered in Module 8.

5. Write messages with context

The message is the first thing a person reads at 3 a.m. It should answer: what were we trying to do, with which values, and what was expected?

Poor messageUseful message
"Error""Could not save order 1042 for customer 77"
"Invalid input""Quantity must be between 1 and 10 but was 25"
"File not found""Config file not found: /etc/shop/app.properties"
"Null value""couponCode must not be null"

Never put secrets in a message: passwords, tokens, OTPs, full card numbers. Messages travel into logs, monitoring tools and sometimes API responses.

6. Fail fast: validate at the door

Check arguments at the top of a method and in constructors, so that a bad value is rejected where it enters instead of causing a confusing failure far away. An object should never exist in an invalid state.

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Objects;

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {
    public Money {                       // compact constructor: runs before the fields are set
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount must not be null");
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency must not be null");
        if (amount.signum() < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must not be negative: " + amount);
        }
    }
}

Note: assert is not validation

The assert statement is for internal invariants ("this can never be negative here"). It is switched off by default and only active with java -ea, so it must never validate arguments of public methods or user input. Use exceptions for that.

7. Use standard exceptions when they fit

Callers already understand the JDK's exceptions. Throw a standard one when it describes the situation exactly:

ExceptionThrow it whenExample
IllegalArgumentExceptionAn argument has a value the method cannot acceptage < 0, an unknown country code
IllegalStateExceptionThe object is in the wrong state for this callwithdrawing from a closed account; starting a job twice
NullPointerExceptionA required argument is null — via Objects.requireNonNulla constructor receiving a null name
UnsupportedOperationExceptionAn optional operation is not supported by this classadd on an immutable list
IndexOutOfBoundsExceptionAn index is outside the valid range Objects.checkIndex(i, size)
NoSuchElementExceptionThere is no (more) element to return iterator.next() at the end of the data

Do not throw RuntimeException, Exception or Throwable directly: they say nothing and cannot be caught selectively. Do not throw Error types such as OutOfMemoryError yourself either.

8. Do not use exceptions for normal control flow

An exception means "something unexpected happened". Using it as a normal way to leave a loop or to report an everyday outcome is slow (building the stack trace costs time), hard to read, and hides real bugs because the same catch block also swallows genuine errors.

Wrong: exceptions as flow

// finding the end of an array by crashing into it
try {
    int i = 0;
    while (true) {
        total += prices[i++];
    }
} catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
    // done
}

// "not found" is an everyday outcome, not an exception
try {
    return repository.getByEmail(email);
} catch (UserNotFoundException e) {
    return null;
}

Right: ordinary control flow

for (int price : prices) {
    total += price;
}

// the return type says "may be absent"
Optional<User> user = repository.findByEmail(email);

Catching a NumberFormatException to reject a bad input at the edge of the program is fine. Doing it millions of times in a loop just to test "is this a number?" is not — validate first, or write a small helper that returns an OptionalInt.

9. Clean up reliably

Close files, connections and streams with try-with-resources; release locks and reset shared state in finally. Never return or throw from a finally block (see the puzzles).

10. Respect InterruptedException

When another thread interrupts a thread that is sleeping or waiting, Java throws InterruptedException and clears the thread's interrupted flag. That flag is how executors and frameworks ask your code to stop. If you swallow the exception, the request is lost and the thread keeps running. Either let the exception propagate, or restore the flag:

try {
    Thread.sleep(500);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();       // restore the flag
    throw new IllegalStateException("Interrupted while waiting for the payment gateway", e);
}

Threads are covered in Module 6.

11. Throw early, catch late — at the right boundary

Detect problems as early as you can (item 6). But catch them as late as possible: at the level that has enough knowledge to decide — retry, show a message, return an error response. Deep inside a utility method nobody knows what the user should see. Real applications use a few fixed boundaries:

  • the web layer — one global handler turns exceptions into HTTP responses (see the Spring Boot article),
  • a job or message listener — catch, log, then continue with the next message,
  • a thread-pool task — an exception inside submit() is stored in the Future and lost if nobody calls get(), so catch and log inside the task,
  • a safety net for everything else, so that no thread dies without a trace:
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, ex) ->
        log.error("Uncaught exception in thread {}", thread.getName(), ex));

12. Document what can be thrown

Describe the exceptions callers should expect with Javadoc @throws, including unchecked ones such as IllegalArgumentException. The method signature shows only the checked ones.

13. Prefer empty results and Optional to null

Do not return null to signal "nothing" or "failure". Return an empty collection or an Optional, and throw an exception for real errors. See NullPointerException, requireNonNull and Optional.

The checklist

DoDo not
Catch the specific type you can handleCatch Exception or Throwable in business code
Wrap with context and keep the causeThrow a new exception without the cause
Log once, at the boundary, with the stack traceLog and rethrow at every layer
Validate arguments earlyLet bad values travel deep into the code
Use standard exceptions where they fitThrow RuntimeException or Exception directly
Return Optional or empty collectionsUse exceptions for everyday outcomes or return null
Use try-with-resourcesReturn or throw inside finally
Restore the interrupt flagSwallow InterruptedException

Real project: what a clean setup looks like

Input is validated at the edge of the API. Services throw unchecked domain exceptions with clear messages. Repositories translate technical exceptions (SQL, HTTP clients) and keep the cause. One @RestControllerAdvice maps each exception type to an HTTP status and a JSON error body, and logs unexpected ones once, with a request id, so a support engineer can find the single log entry for a failed request in seconds.

Interview: "How do you handle exceptions in a real project?"

  • Validate early and throw specific exceptions with good messages; use standard exceptions where they fit, custom ones for business failures.
  • Never swallow; catch only what you can handle; wrap with the cause when changing layers.
  • Handle centrally at the boundary (for example @RestControllerAdvice) and log once with the stack trace; do not leak internals to clients.
  • Use try-with-resources for cleanup, restore the interrupt flag, and keep exceptions out of normal control flow.

NullPointerException, requireNonNull and Optional

Most NullPointerExceptions come from a null that should have been rejected earlier: validate inputs with Objects.requireNonNull, return Optional or an empty collection instead of null, and read the helpful NPE message to find the exact null.

null means "no object". Calling a method on it has no meaning, so the JVM throws a NullPointerException (NPE). It is the most common exception in Java programs. The inventor of null references, Tony Hoare, called it his "billion-dollar mistake", and Java still has it, so you need to know where nulls come from and how to keep them out of your code.

Where NullPointerExceptions come from

  • Calling an instance method on null: email.trim().
  • Reading or writing a field of null: customer.address.city.
  • Using null as an array: scores[0] or scores.length.
  • Unboxing a null wrapper: int qty = map.get(key) when the key is missing.
  • A for-each loop over a null collection or array.
  • throw null, synchronized (null), and a switch on a null string or enum (unless it has a case null).
  • Library methods that reject null on purpose, such as List.of(...) and Optional.of(null) (table below).

The helpful NullPointerException message

Before Java 14 the message was empty and you had to guess which part of a.b().c.d() was null. Java 14 added helpful NullPointerExceptions (JEP 358); since Java 15 they are on by default. The JVM now describes the failed action and the null expression. The text is built only when something asks for the message, so it costs nothing until then.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

public class NpeMessages {

    static class Address {
        String city;
    }

    static class Customer {
        String name;
        Address address;

        String getName() {
            return name;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Customer customer = new Customer();
        String email = null;
        int[] scores = null;
        Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();
        List<String> tags = null;

        List<Runnable> cases = List.of(
                () -> email.trim(),
                () -> customer.getName().length(),
                () -> System.out.println(customer.address.city),
                () -> System.out.println(scores[0]),
                () -> { int qty = stock.get("P-100"); },
                () -> { for (String t : tags) { System.out.println(t); } }
        );
        for (Runnable r : cases) {
            try {
                r.run();
            } catch (NullPointerException e) {
                System.out.println(e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}
Cannot invoke "String.trim()" because "email" is null
Cannot invoke "String.length()" because the return value of "NpeMessages$Customer.getName()" is null
Cannot read field "city" because "customer.address" is null
Cannot load from int array because "scores" is null
Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because the return value of "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null
Cannot invoke "java.util.List.iterator()" because "tags" is null

Each message has two halves. The first half says what the code tried (Cannot invoke "String.trim()", Cannot read field "city", Cannot load from int array). The because half names the null expression: a variable, a field path, or the return value of a method. The fifth line shows the classic hidden unboxing: you wrote int qty = stock.get(...) and the JVM calls Integer.intValue() on the null that get returned. The last line shows that a for-each loop calls iterator().

Edge case: local variable names need javac -g

The class file contains local variable names only when it was compiled with -g. Without it you see placeholders such as "<local4>" instead of "email". Maven, Gradle and IntelliJ compile with -g by default, so in normal projects you see the real names. Field names, method names and class names are always shown.

Fail fast with Objects.requireNonNull

The best NPE is the one thrown where the null enters, with a clear message, not 200 lines later where it is finally used. java.util.Objects has helpers for this and for null-safe code in general:

MethodWhat it does
requireNonNull(obj)Returns obj, or throws an NPE with no message
requireNonNull(obj, "message")The same, with your message — the usual form
requireNonNull(obj, supplier)The message is built only when needed
requireNonNullElse(obj, other)Returns obj, or other when obj is null
requireNonNullElseGet(obj, supplier)Same, but computes the default lazily
isNull(obj) / nonNull(obj)Predicates for method references, as in filter(Objects::nonNull)
toString(obj, "default")Text of obj, or the default when null
equals(a, b)Null-safe equality; two nulls are equal
 
import java.util.Objects;

public class Customer {
    private final String name;
    private final String email;

    public Customer(String name, String email) {
        this.name = Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name must not be null");
        this.email = Objects.requireNonNull(email, "email must not be null");
    }
}

// new Customer("Asha", null) throws immediately:
// java.lang.NullPointerException: email must not be null
//     at Customer.<init>(Customer.java:9)

By convention a null argument is reported with NullPointerException, not IllegalArgumentException, and requireNonNull does exactly that. The message shows which argument was wrong, and the stack trace points at the constructor, not at the code that eventually used the value.

Return empty collections and Optional, not null

A method that returns null forces every caller to remember a check. Two simple rules remove most of the problem:

  • Collections and arrays: return an empty one (List.of(), Collections.emptyList(), new String[0]), never null. Callers can then loop without a check.
  • A single value that may be absent: return Optional<T>. The type tells the caller that "no result" is possible, and the compiler makes them deal with it.
public Optional<Customer> findByEmail(String email) {
    // ... returns Optional.empty() when nobody has this email
}

// no null checks, no NPE
String city = findByEmail("asha@example.com")
        .map(Customer::getAddress)
        .map(Address::getCity)
        .orElse("unknown");

Use Optional as a return type. Do not use it for fields, method parameters or inside collections, and never call get() without checking. The full API, including orElse vs orElseGet and orElseThrow, is in Module 5.

Defensive habits that work

  • Put the known value first: "PAID".equals(status) never throws when status is null, but status.equals("PAID") does.
  • Use Objects.equals(a, b) when both sides may be null.
  • Use defaults for lookups: map.getOrDefault(key, 0) instead of unboxing a possible null.
  • Print safely: String.valueOf(obj) and string concatenation turn a null into the text "null" instead of throwing.
  • Initialize fields (private final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();) so they are never null.
  • Check where the null comes from — a missing map key, a database NULL, a JSON field that was absent — instead of adding != null everywhere.

Which classes accept null?

The surprising rows are the sorted, concurrent and immutable collections: they reject nulls that ArrayList and HashMap accept. See Module 4 for the collections themselves.

ClassNull element or keyNull value
ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSetAllowed —
HashMap, LinkedHashMapOne null key allowedAllowed
TreeMap, TreeSetNPETreeMap allows null values
ArrayDeque, PriorityQueueNPE—
Hashtable, ConcurrentHashMapNPENPE
List.of, Set.of, Map.of, List.copyOf NPE — even for contains(null) and get(null)NPE
Arrays.asList, Collections.unmodifiableList, Stream.toList()Allowed—

Mistakes with null

  • Catching NullPointerException to deal with a null. An NPE is a bug signal. Find out why the value is null and fix that, or check it explicitly.
  • Returning null from a method that returns a collection. Return an empty one.
  • Hidden unboxing: int stock = stockByItem.get(itemId); throws when the item is unknown. Use getOrDefault(itemId, 0).
  • Optional.of(value) with a possibly-null value throws immediately. Use Optional.ofNullable(value).
  • Passing null as a "not given" marker in a long parameter list. Use an overload, a builder, or Optional in the return of a getter instead.

Tip: let tools catch nulls before the JVM does

IntelliJ's inspections warn about possible NullPointerExceptions while you type. Null annotations (such as the JSpecify @Nullable) document intent and are checked by IDEs and static analysers like SpotBugs or NullAway. Kotlin builds the idea into the language. None of this changes the bytecode — it only finds mistakes earlier.

Interview: "How do you avoid NullPointerException?"

  • Do not create nulls: initialize fields, return empty collections, return Optional for "may be absent".
  • Reject them early: Objects.requireNonNull in constructors and public methods.
  • Write null-safe code: "literal".equals(x), Objects.equals, getOrDefault, Optional.map(...).orElse(...).
  • When it happens anyway, read the helpful NPE message (Java 14+, default since 15): it names the exact null expression.

From exception to HTTP response in Spring Boot

In a Spring Boot API, services throw domain exceptions and one @RestControllerAdvice class turns each type into an HTTP status and a JSON error body — no try/catch in controllers.

This is a first look; the Spring Boot page covers it fully in Spring Boot · Module 2. It belongs here because it is where everything in this module pays off: custom exceptions, unchecked exceptions, wrapping, and "handle at the boundary".

The idea

A web request passes through a controller, a service and a repository. Any of them can fail. If each controller method had its own try/catch, the code would be full of repeated error handling and every endpoint would answer errors a little differently. Spring lets you write the error handling once, in a class outside the controllers.

The code

The service throws a domain exception. The controller has no error handling at all.

public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    public OrderNotFoundException(long id) {
        super("Order " + id + " not found");
    }
}
@Service
public class OrderService {
    // ... repository injected by the constructor ...

    public OrderDto findOrder(long id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
                .map(OrderDto::from)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id));
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrderController {
    // ... service injected by the constructor ...

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderDto getOrder(@PathVariable long id) {
        return orderService.findOrder(id);     // no try/catch: failures flow to the advice
    }
}

The error body is a tiny record, and the handler class is the one place that maps exceptions to responses:

public record ApiError(String code, String message) { }
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(GlobalExceptionHandler.class);

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleNotFound(OrderNotFoundException ex) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                .body(new ApiError("ORDER_NOT_FOUND", ex.getMessage()));
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(InsufficientBalanceException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleInsufficientBalance(InsufficientBalanceException ex) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
                .body(new ApiError("INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE", ex.getMessage()));
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)          // the safety net: everything unexpected
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleUnexpected(Exception ex) {
        log.error("Unexpected error", ex);       // logged once, with the stack trace
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
                .body(new ApiError("INTERNAL_ERROR", "Something went wrong. Please try again later."));
    }
}
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{"code":"ORDER_NOT_FOUND","message":"Order 42 not found"}

Spring picks the most specific @ExceptionHandler for the exception that arrives, so the Exception.class handler only receives what no other handler wants. The unexpected case deliberately does not send ex.getMessage() to the client: it might contain SQL, file paths or other internals. The details go to the log; the client gets a generic message.

What happens without a handler

Spring MVC translates its own exceptions by default: a wrong HTTP method gives 405, an unsupported content type 415, an unreadable JSON body 400. Any other exception that nobody handles ends as 500 Internal Server Error through Boot's /error endpoint. The default JSON body has fields such as timestamp, status, error and path; Boot leaves out the exception message and the stack trace unless you switch them on with the server.error.include-* properties — do not do that in production.

Choosing the status code

SituationTypical exceptionStatus
Invalid or unreadable inputMethodArgumentNotValidException, HttpMessageNotReadableException400 Bad Request
Not logged in, bad tokenAuthenticationException (Spring Security) 401 Unauthorized
Logged in but not allowedAccessDeniedException (Spring Security) 403 Forbidden
Resource does not existYour OrderNotFoundException404 Not Found
Duplicate value or conflict with current stateDataIntegrityViolationException, your InsufficientBalanceException409 Conflict
A bug or anything unexpectedAny other Exception500 Internal Server Error
A service you call is downA wrapped client exception502, 503 or 504

Spring Security's 401 and 403 are produced in its filter chain, before MVC, so they are configured separately (Spring Boot · Module 4). Teams differ on edge cases: some map "insufficient balance" to 422 or 400. What matters is to choose a rule and apply it consistently.

Lighter alternatives

  • @ResponseStatus on the exception class — the status is fixed for that type, without any handler method: 
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException { /* ... */ }
  • ResponseStatusException — thrown directly, no custom class: throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Order 42 not found"). It is quick, but it ties service code to HTTP; domain exceptions plus an advice keep layers clean.
  • ProblemDetail — Spring Framework 6 and later can return the standard "problem details" JSON format (type, title, status, detail, instance) with content type application/problem+json, defined by RFC 9457 (which replaced RFC 7807). A handler method can return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage()) instead of a custom error class.

Boot 3.x and 4.x

The annotations on this page (@RestControllerAdvice, @ExceptionHandler, @ResponseStatus) work the same in Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x. Boot 4 is built on Spring Framework 7. Boot 3 and 4 use the jakarta.* packages for validation and servlet classes, not javax.*.

Rules for error responses

  • Never send stack traces, SQL text or internal class names to a client.
  • Use one error body shape for the whole API (for example code plus message, or ProblemDetail).
  • Log unexpected exceptions once, with the stack trace and a request or trace id.
  • Unchecked exceptions let @Transactional roll back by default; a checked exception commits unless you configure rollbackFor (see custom exceptions).

Interview: "How do you handle exceptions in a Spring Boot REST API?"

  • Throw domain exceptions (unchecked) from services; no try/catch in controllers.
  • One @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods maps each exception to a status and a consistent JSON body; a last Exception.class handler returns 500 with a generic message and logs the details.
  • Mention @ResponseStatus, ResponseStatusException and ProblemDetail as alternatives, and that validation errors become 400.
  • Add: never leak internals; log once; unchecked exceptions and transaction rollback.

Paths: Path, Path.of and the working directory

A Path is an immutable object that names a location in the file system; build one with Path.of("data", "orders.csv"), combine paths with resolve, and remember that a relative path is looked up from the working directory of the running JVM.

Almost every program touches files: configuration, uploads, reports, logs. Java 7 added a modern file API in the package java.nio.file (called NIO.2), and it is what you should use in new code. It has three main parts:

  • Path — an object that describes where a file or folder is. It does not touch the disk.
  • Files — a class of static methods that do things: read, write, copy, move, delete, list. The next articles cover it.
  • Paths — an older helper with one method, Paths.get(...). Since Java 11 you can write Path.of(...) instead; both give the same result.

The older java.io.File class still exists; File vs Path compares the two.

Creating a Path

Path a = Path.of("data", "2026", "orders.csv");        // pieces: separators added for you
Path b = Path.of("data/2026/orders.csv");              // one string works too
Path c = Paths.get("data", "orders.csv");              // older style, same result
Path d = new java.io.File("data/orders.csv").toPath(); // from a legacy File
Path e = Path.of("/var/app/uploads");                  // absolute on Linux and macOS
Path f = Path.of("C:\\Users\\priya\\shop");            // absolute on Windows (escape the \)

Pass the pieces as separate arguments and let Java insert the right separator (/ on Linux and macOS, \ on Windows). Never build paths with string concatenation and a hard-coded separator. A Path is only a name: the file does not have to exist, and creating a Path never fails because of a missing file. Like String, a Path is immutable: every method that "changes" it returns a new Path.

Absolute, relative and the working directory

An absolute path starts at the root of the file system (/var/app, or C:\app on Windows) and means the same thing wherever the program runs. A relative path (data/orders.csv) has no root. Java resolves it against the working directory: the folder in which the JVM was started, stored in the system property user.dir.

The working directory depends on how you start the program, which is the root of many "works on my machine" problems. IntelliJ uses the project or module folder by default, Maven and Gradle tests use the module folder, a Docker container uses its WORKDIR, and a service started by systemd uses whatever the unit file says. When a file is "not found", print where Java really looks:

Path orders = Path.of("data", "orders.csv");
System.out.println(orders.toAbsolutePath());        // /home/priya/shop/data/orders.csv
System.out.println(System.getProperty("user.dir")); // /home/priya/shop
System.out.println(Path.of("").toAbsolutePath());   // the working directory itself

For anything that must not depend on the working directory — uploads, data, logs of a server — use an absolute base directory taken from configuration (an environment variable or application.properties), and build paths below it with resolve.

Taking a path apart

import java.nio.file.Path;

public class PathDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path p = Path.of("data", "2026", "orders.csv");
        System.out.println("path         : " + p);
        System.out.println("getFileName  : " + p.getFileName());
        System.out.println("getParent    : " + p.getParent());
        System.out.println("getRoot      : " + p.getRoot());
        System.out.println("getNameCount : " + p.getNameCount());
        System.out.println("getName(0)   : " + p.getName(0));
        System.out.println("subpath(1, 3): " + p.subpath(1, 3));
        System.out.println("isAbsolute   : " + p.isAbsolute());
        System.out.println("startsWith(\"data\")    : " + p.startsWith("data"));
        System.out.println("endsWith(\"orders.csv\"): " + p.endsWith("orders.csv"));
        System.out.println("endsWith(\"csv\")       : " + p.endsWith("csv"));
    }
}
path         : data/2026/orders.csv
getFileName  : orders.csv
getParent    : data/2026
getRoot      : null
getNameCount : 3
getName(0)   : data
subpath(1, 3): 2026/orders.csv
isAbsolute   : false
startsWith("data")    : true
endsWith("orders.csv"): true
endsWith("csv")       : false

Two details. startsWith and endsWith compare whole name elements, not characters, so endsWith("csv") is false: the last element is orders.csv, not csv. And getParent() and getRoot() can return null (a single name has no parent; a relative path has no root), so check before you chain calls.

MethodReturns
getFileName()The last element: the file or folder name
getParent()The path without its last element, or null
getRoot()/ or C:\, or null for a relative path
getNameCount(), getName(i)Number of elements, and one element
subpath(from, to)A relative path made of some elements
isAbsolute(), toAbsolutePath()Whether it starts at a root; the absolute form
toString(), toUri(), toFile()Text, file: URI, legacy File

Combining paths: resolve, relativize, normalize

Path base = Path.of("uploads");
Path file = base.resolve("avatars/asha.png");
System.out.println(file);                                  // uploads/avatars/asha.png
System.out.println(file.resolveSibling("asha-small.png")); // uploads/avatars/asha-small.png
System.out.println(base.relativize(file));                 // avatars/asha.png

Path messy = Path.of("reports/./2026/../2025/summary.txt");
System.out.println(messy.normalize());                     // reports/2025/summary.txt

System.out.println(base.resolve("/etc/passwd"));           // /etc/passwd
  • resolve(other) appends other to this path. It is the right way to build "folder + file name". If other is absolute, it wins and is returned unchanged (the last line).
  • resolveSibling(name) replaces the last element: "the file next to this one".
  • relativize(other) is the opposite of resolve: the path that leads from this one to other. Both paths must be of the same kind (both relative or both absolute), or you get IllegalArgumentException: 'other' is different type of Path.
  • normalize() removes . and folds name/... It works on the text only; it does not look at the disk, so it cannot know about symbolic links.

Never trust a user-supplied file name

If a web application builds a path from a name the user sends, a name such as ../../etc/passwd climbs out of the upload folder. This attack is called path traversal and it is a classic security hole. The defence is to normalize and then check that the result is still inside the base folder.

Wrong: uses the name as it comes

Path target = uploadDir.resolve(userFileName);
Files.copy(in, target);          // userFileName = "../../etc/passwd" escapes uploadDir

Right: normalize, then check

static Path safeResolve(Path base, String userFileName) {
    Path target = base.resolve(userFileName).normalize();
    if (!target.startsWith(base)) {              // compares whole name elements
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Illegal file name: " + userFileName);
    }
    return target;
}
// base = /var/app/uploads (absolute and normalized)
// safeResolve(base, "avatars/asha.png")  -> /var/app/uploads/avatars/asha.png
// safeResolve(base, "../../etc/passwd")  -> IllegalArgumentException

Even better, do not use the client's name at all: store the file under a generated name (a UUID) and keep the original name in the database.

Comparing paths and finding the real file

  • equals compares the text of the paths: Path.of("a/../b").equals(Path.of("b")) is false, but it is true after normalize().
  • Files.isSameFile(p1, p2) asks the file system whether both paths lead to the same file, following symbolic links. For two different paths, both files must exist.
  • toRealPath() returns the real, absolute, normalized path with symbolic links resolved. Unlike toAbsolutePath(), it touches the disk and throws NoSuchFileException when the file does not exist.

Edge cases and exceptions

  • InvalidPathException (unchecked) is thrown by Path.of for a string the operating system cannot accept as a path, such as a NUL character anywhere, or <, ? or | in a name on Windows.
  • Path.of("") is the empty path; operations treat it as the current directory.
  • Whether names are case-sensitive depends on the operating system and file system: Orders.csv and orders.csv are the same file on Windows and usually different files on Linux. Be exact with names so that code behaves the same everywhere.
  • A Path is Iterable<Path> over its name elements and Comparable, so you can sort paths (the order is lexicographic by name).

Conventions

  • Use Path (not String) as the parameter and field type for files, so callers cannot pass nonsense.
  • Build paths with resolve from a configured base directory; never concatenate strings.
  • Use forward slashes in string literals if you must write one; Java accepts them on Windows too. A single backslash in a Java string literal is an escape character ("C:\data" does not compile).

Interview: "Path vs File, relative vs absolute"

  • Path (Java 7, java.nio.file) describes a location and is used together with Files; File is the old class from Java 1.0 with weaker error reporting.
  • A relative path is resolved against the working directory (user.dir), which differs between IDE, Maven, Docker and servers — a common source of "file not found".
  • resolve, relativize and normalize are text operations; toRealPath and isSameFile use the real file system.
  • Mention path traversal and how to prevent it.

Reading and writing text files with Files

For small files use Files.readString, writeString and readAllLines; for big files stream with Files.lines or a buffered reader; always know your charset (UTF-8) and say with StandardOpenOption whether you create, overwrite or append.

The Files class turns most file work into one line. Before NIO.2 (Java 7) the same job needed a reader, a loop and a try/finally. Every method below throws the checked IOException, so they sit inside a method that declares throws IOException or inside a try block.

The methods you will use

MethodPurposeMemory
Files.readString(path)Whole file as one String (Java 11) Whole file
Files.readAllLines(path)Whole file as a List<String> Whole file
Files.readAllBytes(path)Whole file as byte[] (binary data) Whole file
Files.lines(path)A lazy Stream<String> of lines — must be closed One line at a time
Files.newBufferedReader(path)A BufferedReader for a manual loop One line at a time
Files.writeString(path, text, options...)Write a String (Java 11) Text in memory
Files.write(path, lines, options...)Write an Iterable of lines, or a byte[] Lines in memory
Files.newBufferedWriter(path, options...)A BufferedWriter for many small writes Small buffer

Example: a to-do file and a log file

import java.io.BufferedWriter;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class FilesReadWrite {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path dir = Files.createTempDirectory("notes-");
        Path todo = dir.resolve("todo.txt");

        // 1. write a String: creates the file, or overwrites it
        Files.writeString(todo, "Buy milk\nCall the bank\n");

        // 2. read it all back
        System.out.print(Files.readString(todo));

        // 3. append lines (the file already exists, so CREATE is not needed)
        Files.write(todo, List.of("Pay electricity bill", "Book train ticket"),
                StandardOpenOption.APPEND);

        // 4. read as a list of lines
        List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(todo);
        System.out.println(lines.size() + " lines: " + lines);

        // 5. a log file: create it if missing, otherwise append
        Path log = dir.resolve("app.log");
        for (String msg : List.of("INFO  Order 1042 placed", "ERROR Payment timeout",
                "INFO  Order 1043 placed")) {
            try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(log, StandardCharsets.UTF_8,
                    StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.APPEND)) {
                writer.write(msg);
                writer.newLine();
            }
        }

        // 6. stream a file lazily and close it
        try (Stream<String> stream = Files.lines(log)) {
            stream.filter(l -> l.startsWith("ERROR")).forEach(System.out::println);
        }
    }
}
Buy milk
Call the bank
4 lines: [Buy milk, Call the bank, Pay electricity bill, Book train ticket]
ERROR Payment timeout

Step 5 opens and closes the log file on every message just to keep the example short. In a real program, open the writer once before the loop and close it after.

StandardOpenOption: create, overwrite or append

The write and writeString methods and the buffered-writer methods take a list of options. If you give none, the default is CREATE, TRUNCATE_EXISTING and WRITE: create the file if missing, and erase the old content if it exists. Once you give any option, only the ones you list apply.

OptionMeaning
CREATECreate the file if it does not exist (no error if it does)
CREATE_NEWCreate it; fail with FileAlreadyExistsException if it already exists. The check and the creation are one atomic step
TRUNCATE_EXISTINGEmpty an existing file before writing
APPENDWrite at the end of the file. The file must exist unless you also give CREATE
WRITE, READOpen for writing or reading (usually implied)
DELETE_ON_CLOSEDelete the file when the stream is closed (temporary files)
 
Files.writeString(p, text);                                   // create or overwrite
Files.writeString(p, text, CREATE, APPEND);                   // create or append (logs)
Files.writeString(p, text, CREATE_NEW);                       // only if it does not exist yet
Files.writeString(p, text, APPEND);                           // append; fails if the file is missing
// (with: import static java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption.*;)

Running the failure cases from the example program prints:

APPEND on a missing file -> NoSuchFileException
CREATE_NEW on an existing file -> FileAlreadyExistsException
missing parent directory -> NoSuchFileException

The last line is the third common one: Files never creates missing parent folders. Call Files.createDirectories(path.getParent()) first (see the next article). Two details about line endings: write(path, lines) ends each line with the platform's separator (\r\n on Windows), while writeString writes exactly the text you give it, so add "\n" yourself.

Charsets: always UTF-8

A text file is bytes; a charset (character encoding) says how bytes map to characters. UTF-8 is the standard for new files: it covers every language, and ₹ or é survive a round trip. The Files methods without a charset parameter always use UTF-8. Many other APIs use the default charset of the machine instead.

APICharset when you do not pass one
Files.readString, readAllLines, lines, writeString, newBufferedReader/WriterUTF-8, always
new FileReader(f), new FileWriter(f), new Scanner(file), new String(bytes), text.getBytes()The default charset: depended on the operating system before Java 18; UTF-8 from Java 18 on (JEP 400)

Because you may meet Java 8, 11 or 17 projects, and files from other tools, pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly whenever the API accepts a charset.

Real-life trap: a CSV from Excel is not valid UTF-8

Windows tools often save "CSV" as windows-1252 (a single-byte encoding, close to ISO-8859-1). A name like café then contains the byte 0xE9, which is not valid UTF-8, and Files.readString throws java.nio.charset.MalformedInputException (Input length = ...). Files.lines throws an UncheckedIOException whose cause is the same exception. Fix it by reading with the charset the file really has:

List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(path, Charset.forName("windows-1252"));
// [name, café]

The other classic is the BOM (byte order mark): Excel's "CSV UTF-8" starts the file with the three bytes EF BB BF. Java does not remove them, so the first header becomes "\uFEFFid" and header.equals("id") is false although it prints like id:

String header = lines.get(0);
if (header.startsWith("\uFEFF")) {      // strip the byte order mark
    header = header.substring(1);
}

Large files: do not load them whole

readString, readAllLines and readAllBytes put the entire file into memory — fine for a config file, an OutOfMemoryError for a 3 GB log. For big files use Files.lines or Files.newBufferedReader and process one line at a time. The CSV article after next builds on this.

Files.lines returns a lazy stream: the file is read as you consume the stream, and the stream holds an open file handle. Close it with try-with-resources, as in step 6 above. If you forget, the handle can stay open for a long time: on Windows you cannot delete the file, and on a busy server you eventually hit "Too many open files". If reading fails halfway, the stream throws UncheckedIOException instead of IOException, because stream lambdas cannot throw checked exceptions.

Common mistakes

Wrong: every call overwrites the file

for (String line : report) {
    Files.writeString(file, line + "\n");   // default option = TRUNCATE_EXISTING
}
// the file now contains only the LAST line

Right: append, or open the file once

try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(file)) {
    for (String line : report) {
        writer.write(line);
        writer.newLine();
    }
}

More mistakes

  • Forgetting to close Files.lines, Files.list or Files.walk — use try-with-resources.
  • readAllLines on a huge file — stream it instead.
  • Relying on the default charset — pass UTF-8 or the file's real charset.
  • APPEND without CREATE on a file that may not exist yet.
  • A single backslash in a Windows path string — write "C:\\data\\a.txt" or use Path.of("C:", "data", "a.txt").
  • Swallowing the IOException with an empty catch. Report which file failed: the exception message already contains the path.

Interview: "How do you read a file in Java?"

  • Small text file: Files.readString or readAllLines. Large file: Files.lines (close it!) or newBufferedReader in a loop — constant memory.
  • Always state the charset; know that Files methods default to UTF-8 while FileReader depended on the platform before Java 18.
  • Writing: writeString / write with StandardOpenOption (CREATE, APPEND, TRUNCATE_EXISTING, CREATE_NEW); the default truncates.
  • Handle IOException (checked), and use try-with-resources for readers, writers and streams.

Files and directories: create, copy, move, delete, list, walk

Files has one-liners to check, create, copy, move, delete, list and walk files and folders; handle the specific failures (already exists, not empty, missing) and close every Stream that holds a directory open.

Reading and writing content is half of file work. The other half is managing the files themselves: does it exist, create a folder, move a processed file to an archive, clean up a temp folder. All of these are static methods of Files, and all of them throw IOException subclasses that tell you exactly what went wrong.

Checking: exists, size, type

MethodAnswers
Files.exists(p)Does something exist at this path? false also when the answer cannot be determined (no permission)
Files.notExists(p)Is it certain that nothing exists there? Not the same as !exists(p) in the "cannot tell" case
Files.isRegularFile(p), isDirectory(p)A normal file? A folder?
Files.isReadable(p), isWritable(p)Does the JVM have access?
Files.size(p)Size in bytes; NoSuchFileException if missing. Do not use it for folders
Files.getLastModifiedTime(p)A FileTime (.toInstant() converts it)
Files.readAttributes(p, BasicFileAttributes.class)Size, times and type in one call

Do not check first, then act

if (!Files.exists(p)) Files.createFile(p); has a gap: another thread or process can create the file between the two lines. Prefer the operation that does the check atomically and handle the exception: Files.createFile(p) throws FileAlreadyExistsException, and writeString(..., CREATE_NEW) does the same. This "check-then-act" race is called time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU).

Creating

  • Files.createFile(p) — an empty file; fails if it exists.
  • Files.createDirectory(p) — one folder; the parent must exist; fails if it exists.
  • Files.createDirectories(p) — the folder and every missing parent, like mkdir -p. It does nothing if the folder already exists. It fails with FileAlreadyExistsException only if the path exists and is a file. This is the method you want before writing into a new folder.
  • Files.createTempFile("report-", ".csv") and createTempDirectory("work-") — a uniquely named file or folder in the system's temp location (/tmp on Linux).

Copy, move and delete

  • Files.copy(source, target, options...) fails with FileAlreadyExistsException when the target exists, unless you pass StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING. File attributes such as times and permissions are only copied if you add COPY_ATTRIBUTES. Copying a folder creates only an empty folder; its contents are not copied. There are also copy(InputStream, Path) and copy(Path, OutputStream), which are handy for saving an upload or sending a file.
  • Files.move(source, target, options...) moves or renames. Moving inside one folder is a rename. Options: REPLACE_EXISTING and ATOMIC_MOVE (all or nothing, cannot leave a half-moved file).
  • Files.delete(p) throws NoSuchFileException if the path is missing and DirectoryNotEmptyException for a folder with content. Files.deleteIfExists(p) returns false instead of throwing for a missing path (but still throws for a non-empty folder).
Path temp = Files.createTempFile(target.getParent(), "settings-", ".tmp");
Files.writeString(temp, newContent);
Files.move(temp, target, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE);   // readers see the old or the new file, never half

With ATOMIC_MOVE all other options are ignored, and whether an existing target is replaced is up to the file system (on Linux and macOS it is). The temp file must be in the same folder (the same file store) as the target.

Listing and walking

MethodGives you
Files.list(dir)A Stream<Path> of the entries of one folder, not recursive (files and sub-folders)
Files.walk(start) / walk(start, maxDepth)All entries below start, depth-first, including start itself
Files.find(start, depth, matcher)Like walk, filtered by a (path, attributes) predicate
Files.newDirectoryStream(dir, "*.csv")An Iterable of one folder's entries that match a glob pattern
Files.walkFileTree(start, visitor)Full control with a FileVisitor: skip folders, act before and after each folder

Three rules apply to all of them. The order is not guaranteed, so call sorted() when the result must be predictable. The streams from list, walk and find keep the directory open, so close them with try-with-resources. And problems that occur while iterating (a folder you may not read) surface as UncheckedIOException. walk does not follow symbolic links unless you pass FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS.

Example: process an inbox and archive the files

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.UncheckedIOException;
import java.nio.file.DirectoryNotEmptyException;
import java.nio.file.FileAlreadyExistsException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class FilesManage {

    static void tree(Path root) throws IOException {
        try (Stream<Path> walk = Files.walk(root)) {
            walk.sorted().skip(1).forEach(p ->
                    System.out.println("  " + root.relativize(p) + (Files.isDirectory(p) ? "/" : "")));
        }
    }

    static void deleteTree(Path root) throws IOException {
        try (Stream<Path> walk = Files.walk(root)) {
            walk.sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).forEach(p -> {   // children before parents
                try {
                    Files.delete(p);
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
                }
            });
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path root = Files.createTempDirectory("inbox-demo-");
        Path inbox = Files.createDirectories(root.resolve("inbox"));
        Path archive = root.resolve("archive");
        Files.createDirectories(archive.resolve("2026").resolve("10"));   // creates every missing level

        Files.writeString(inbox.resolve("order-1.csv"), "id,total\n1,250\n");
        Files.writeString(inbox.resolve("order-2.csv"), "id,total\n2,990\n");
        Files.writeString(inbox.resolve("notes.txt"), "ignore me");
        System.out.println("After setup:");
        tree(root);

        // list ONE level, only CSV files, sorted
        System.out.println("CSV files in inbox:");
        try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(inbox)) {
            files.filter(p -> p.getFileName().toString().endsWith(".csv"))
                 .sorted()
                 .forEach(p -> System.out.println("  " + p.getFileName() + " (" + sizeOf(p) + " bytes)"));
        }

        // copy keeps the original; a second copy fails unless REPLACE_EXISTING is given
        Path backup = root.resolve("backup-order-1.csv");
        Files.copy(inbox.resolve("order-1.csv"), backup);
        try {
            Files.copy(inbox.resolve("order-1.csv"), backup);
        } catch (FileAlreadyExistsException e) {
            System.out.println("second copy -> FileAlreadyExistsException");
        }
        Files.copy(inbox.resolve("order-1.csv"), backup, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);

        // move processed files into the archive folder
        try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(inbox)) {
            for (Path p : files.filter(f -> f.toString().endsWith(".csv")).toList()) {
                Files.move(p, archive.resolve("2026").resolve("10").resolve(p.getFileName()));
            }
        }
        System.out.println("After moving:");
        tree(root);

        // delete variants
        try {
            Files.delete(inbox);
        } catch (DirectoryNotEmptyException e) {
            System.out.println("delete(inbox) -> DirectoryNotEmptyException (notes.txt is still inside)");
        }
        try {
            Files.delete(root.resolve("nothing.txt"));
        } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
            System.out.println("delete(missing) -> NoSuchFileException");
        }
        System.out.println("deleteIfExists(missing) -> " + Files.deleteIfExists(root.resolve("nothing.txt")));

        deleteTree(root);
        System.out.println("root still exists after deleteTree? " + Files.exists(root));
    }

    static long sizeOf(Path p) {
        try {
            return Files.size(p);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
        }
    }
}
After setup:
  archive/
  archive/2026/
  archive/2026/10/
  inbox/
  inbox/notes.txt
  inbox/order-1.csv
  inbox/order-2.csv
CSV files in inbox:
  order-1.csv (15 bytes)
  order-2.csv (15 bytes)
second copy -> FileAlreadyExistsException
After moving:
  archive/
  archive/2026/
  archive/2026/10/
  archive/2026/10/order-1.csv
  archive/2026/10/order-2.csv
  backup-order-1.csv
  inbox/
  inbox/notes.txt
delete(inbox) -> DirectoryNotEmptyException (notes.txt is still inside)
delete(missing) -> NoSuchFileException
deleteIfExists(missing) -> false
root still exists after deleteTree? false

Three things are worth studying in this program. deleteTree deletes a whole folder tree. A folder must be empty before it can be deleted, so children must go first. A path always sorts after its own parent, so sorting in reverse order puts every child before its parent. The helper sizeOf exists because lambdas cannot throw IOException (see wrapping). And the move loop first collects the list with toList(), so the directory stream is not being read while files leave the folder.

The same cleanup with a FileVisitor needs no lambda wrapping, because the visitor methods may throw IOException:

Files.walkFileTree(root, new SimpleFileVisitor<>() {
    @Override
    public FileVisitResult visitFile(Path file, BasicFileAttributes attrs) throws IOException {
        Files.delete(file);                    // every file first
        return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE;
    }

    @Override
    public FileVisitResult postVisitDirectory(Path dir, IOException exc) throws IOException {
        Files.delete(dir);                     // then the now-empty folder
        return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE;
    }
});

Spring users also have FileSystemUtils.deleteRecursively(Path) for this.

The IOException family for files

The file exceptions live in java.nio.file. Most extend FileSystemException (itself an IOException), whose getFile() and getReason() methods describe the failure. Catch the specific one when you can react differently:

ExceptionTypical cause
NoSuchFileExceptionReading, deleting or appending to a path that does not exist, or writing into a missing folder
FileAlreadyExistsExceptioncreateFile, createDirectory, copy or move onto an existing path (without a replace option); CREATE_NEW
DirectoryNotEmptyExceptionDeleting a folder that still has content
NotDirectoryExceptionFiles.list or newDirectoryStream on something that is not a folder
AccessDeniedExceptionNo permission to read, write or list. (On Windows, deleting a file that is still open elsewhere, even by your own unclosed stream, gives a plain FileSystemException: "being used by another process")
MalformedInputExceptionThe bytes are not valid in the charset you read with (a CharacterCodingException)
UncheckedIOExceptionAn IOException that happened inside a stream pipeline

Real project: handling uploaded files

  • At startup call Files.createDirectories(uploadDir), so the folder always exists.
  • Save with a generated name (UUID.randomUUID() + ".png"), never the client's name: Files.copy(file.getInputStream(), target); see path traversal in Paths.
  • Keep uploads outside the application folder, because a container filesystem is thrown away with the container; mount a volume or use object storage (S3).
  • Use createTempFile for intermediate files and delete them in finally.

Mistakes

  • Using the old File.delete() or mkdir(), which only return false when they fail and say nothing about why.
  • Assuming Files.copy copies a folder's contents. It copies the folder entry only.
  • Forgetting that Files.walk includes the start folder itself (use skip(1), or filter it out) — especially in a recursive delete.
  • Not closing Files.list / walk streams.
  • Expecting a stable order from list or walk; the result differs between operating systems.

Interview: "How do you delete a directory with files in Java?"

  • Files.delete throws DirectoryNotEmptyException for a non-empty folder, so you delete the contents first.
  • Either walk the tree and delete in reverse order (Files.walk(root).sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())), or use Files.walkFileTree with a visitor that deletes files in visitFile and folders in postVisitDirectory.
  • Close the walk stream, and wrap IOException in UncheckedIOException inside a lambda.

Classic java.io: streams, readers and writers

The old java.io package moves data as streams: byte streams (InputStream/OutputStream) for any data, character streams (Reader/Writer) for text, and small wrapper classes that you stack on top of each other to add buffering and conversion.

Why you still need to know it

New code should prefer java.nio.file.Files (see reading and writing with Files). But java.io is everywhere: servlet request bodies, socket streams, System.in, ZipInputStream, JDBC Blob and Clob, multipart uploads in Spring (MultipartFile.getInputStream()) and a huge amount of older code. Interviews also like the "byte stream vs character stream" and "decorator" questions. Even the NIO helper Files.newBufferedReader hands you a java.io.BufferedReader.

A stream is a sequence of data that you read or write one piece after another, without jumping around. You do not hold the whole content in memory; you process it piece by piece. That is why streams work for a 5 GB log file as well as for a 5-byte one.

Byte streams vs character streams

A byte stream moves raw bytes (values 0 to 255). Use it for anything that is not text: images, PDFs, ZIP files, encrypted data, network packets. The base classes are the abstract InputStream and OutputStream.

A character stream moves characters. It converts between bytes and characters using a charset (a character encoding such as UTF-8). Use it for text files, CSV, JSON and logs. The base classes are the abstract Reader and Writer.

PointByte streamsCharacter streams
Base classesInputStream, OutputStreamReader, Writer
Unitbyte (read() returns an int 0–255, or -1 at the end)char (read() returns an int, or -1 at the end)
File classesFileInputStream, FileOutputStreamFileReader, FileWriter
Buffered wrapperBufferedInputStream, BufferedOutputStreamBufferedReader, BufferedWriter
Use forBinary data, copying any fileText, line-by-line processing
EncodingNone; you get bytesNeeds a charset

The bridge classes connect the two worlds: InputStreamReader wraps an InputStream and decodes bytes into characters with a charset you give; OutputStreamWriter does the reverse. This is how you read text from a socket or from System.in.

Copying a file with byte streams

Reading one byte at a time is slow because every call may go to the operating system. Read into a byte array (a buffer) instead. read(byte[]) returns how many bytes it actually filled, or -1 at the end of the stream; always use that count when you write.

import java.io.*;

public class CopyBytes {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        try (InputStream in = new FileInputStream("photo.jpg");
             OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("photo-copy.jpg")) {

            byte[] buffer = new byte[8192];     // 8 KB at a time
            int count;
            long total = 0;
            while ((count = in.read(buffer)) != -1) {
                out.write(buffer, 0, count);    // write only 'count' bytes
                total += count;
            }
            System.out.println("Copied " + total + " bytes");
        }   // both streams closed here, out first, then in
    }
}
Copied 248113 bytes

Since Java 9 you can also write in.transferTo(out), which does the loop for you. And Files.copy(Path, Path) is simpler still. The loop above is what they do inside.

Reading and writing text

FileReader and FileWriter read and write characters. Wrap them in BufferedReader and BufferedWriter: the buffer cuts the number of disk calls, and BufferedReader adds readLine(), which returns one line without the line break, or null at the end.

import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class TextIo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        // Write three lines (UTF-8 chosen explicitly)
        try (BufferedWriter w = new BufferedWriter(
                new OutputStreamWriter(new FileOutputStream("orders.txt"),
                                       StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
            w.write("1001,Asha,499.50");
            w.newLine();                    // correct line separator for this OS
            w.write("1002,Ravi,1200.00");
            w.newLine();
            w.write("1003,Meera,89.99");
        }

        // Read them back
        try (BufferedReader r = new BufferedReader(
                new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream("orders.txt"),
                                      StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
            String line;
            int n = 0;
            while ((line = r.readLine()) != null) {
                n++;
                System.out.println(n + ": " + line);
            }
        }
    }
}
1: 1001,Asha,499.50
2: 1002,Ravi,1200.00
3: 1003,Meera,89.99

In newer code you can shorten the setup: new FileReader("orders.txt", StandardCharsets.UTF_8) (constructor with charset since Java 11) or Files.newBufferedReader(path), which defaults to UTF-8.

Default charset changed in Java 18

Before Java 18, new FileReader("x.txt") used the operating system's default charset (often Windows-1252 on Windows, UTF-8 on Linux), so the same program could read the same file differently on two machines. Since Java 18 the default is UTF-8 almost everywhere (JEP 400). Even so, name the charset in your code. It costs one argument and removes a whole class of bugs.

The decorator idea

Notice how the example builds objects by wrapping: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(...))). This is the decorator pattern: each class implements the same interface (Reader) and holds another object of that interface. It forwards the calls and adds behaviour. You choose the features you need and stack them, instead of having one giant class like BufferedCompressedEncryptedFileReader. More about the pattern in System Design · Module 2.

The decorators you will meet most: BufferedInputStream/OutputStream (buffering), DataInputStream/DataOutputStream (read and write primitives like int and double in binary form), ObjectOutputStream (see serialization), GZIPOutputStream (compression), PrintWriter and PrintStream (println, printf; System.out is a PrintStream).

When you close the outermost wrapper, close() passes down and closes the inner ones too. With try-with-resources, declaring only the outermost object is enough, but declaring each one is the safer habit (if a middle constructor throws, the earlier resource is still closed).

File vs Path

java.io.File is the old way to represent a file or directory path. java.nio.file.Path (Java 7) is the modern one. A File is just a path name in an object, even if nothing exists on disk.

PointFile (java.io)Path (java.nio.file)
IntroducedJava 1.0Java 7
OperationsMethods on the object: exists(), delete(), mkdir()Static helpers in Files; Path only describes the location
Failure reportingReturns false with no reason (for example delete())Throws a specific IOException subclass
Symbolic links, attributes, permissionsWeak supportFull support
Walking trees, watching foldersAwkward (listFiles())Files.walk, WatchService
Conversionfile.toPath()path.toFile()

Use Path in new code. Convert with toPath() / toFile() at the border where a library still wants a File.

System.in and Scanner

System.in is an InputStream for the keyboard. Scanner parses tokens from it (nextInt(), nextLine()); it is fine for small programs and coding-practice sites. For fast input in DSA problems people use new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)) because it is much faster than Scanner.

Rules

  • Always close streams: use try-with-resources. A leaked stream keeps a file handle open (on Windows it can lock the file).
  • Use byte streams for binary data and character streams for text. Never read a PDF or an image through a Reader; the decoding corrupts it.
  • When reading into a buffer, use the count returned by read. The buffer is often only partly filled.
  • Do not mix Scanner and BufferedReader on the same System.in; each buffers input and will "steal" data from the other.

Conventions

  • Wrap with a buffer whenever you read or write many small pieces.
  • Name the charset explicitly (StandardCharsets.UTF_8).
  • Prefer Files methods for whole-file or line-by-line work; use streams directly when the data comes from a network, a request body, a ZIP or a database.
  • Use transferTo or Files.copy instead of writing your own copy loop.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • FileNotFoundException — the FileInputStream / FileReader constructor cannot open the file: it does not exist, is a directory or you have no permission. FileOutputStream creates the file if it does not exist, but fails when the folder is missing.
  • new FileOutputStream("a.txt") and new FileWriter("a.txt") truncate the file. Pass true as the second argument to append.
  • IOException from close() in try-with-resources is added to the suppressed list if the body already threw.
  • BufferedWriter keeps data in memory. If the program ends without close() or flush(), the last part is lost.
  • read() on a closed stream throws IOException ("Stream closed").

Mistake: reading text with a stream and a cast

Wrong: breaks non-ASCII text

int b;
while ((b = in.read()) != -1) {
    sb.append((char) b);   // each byte treated as a char
}

Right: decode with a charset

try (var r = new BufferedReader(
        new InputStreamReader(in, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
    r.lines().forEach(sb::append);
}

In UTF-8, a character like "₹" takes three bytes. Casting each byte to a char gives three wrong characters.

Interview: "Byte stream vs character stream", "Why BufferedReader?", "File vs Path"

  • Byte streams move raw bytes; character streams decode bytes to chars with a charset.
  • Buffering reduces expensive system calls and adds readLine().
  • Decorator pattern: wrappers share an interface and add behaviour; closing the outer one closes the inner.
  • Path/Files is the modern API with better errors and attributes.

Serialization: Serializable, transient and serialVersionUID

Java serialization turns an object graph into a byte stream and back using ObjectOutputStream and ObjectInputStream; it is fragile and has serious security risks, so use JSON for new work and treat serialization as legacy knowledge you must still understand.

What it is

Serialization converts an object (and everything it references) into a sequence of bytes that you can store in a file, send over a network or keep in a cache. Deserialization does the reverse and rebuilds an equivalent object. Java has built-in support: a class opts in by implementing the marker interface java.io.Serializable. A marker interface has no methods; it just tells the JVM "this class may be serialized".

import java.io.Serializable;

public class Customer implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    private final String name;
    private final String email;
    private transient String sessionToken;   // not saved
    private static int totalCustomers;       // belongs to the class, not saved

    public Customer(String name, String email, String sessionToken) {
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
        this.sessionToken = sessionToken;
        totalCustomers++;
    }

    @Override public String toString() {
        return "Customer[" + name + ", " + email + ", token=" + sessionToken + "]";
    }
}
import java.io.*;

public class SerializeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Customer c = new Customer("Asha", "asha@mail.in", "abc123");

        try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(
                new FileOutputStream("customer.bin"))) {
            out.writeObject(c);                       // serialize
        }

        try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(
                new FileInputStream("customer.bin"))) {
            Customer copy = (Customer) in.readObject();   // deserialize
            System.out.println(copy);
            System.out.println(copy == c);                // a new object
        }
    }
}
Customer[Asha, asha@mail.in, token=null]
false

The token came back as null, because it is transient. The copy is a different object with the same data. Note that deserialization creates the object without calling the constructor of the serializable class.

Rules that decide what is saved

  • Every field must be serializable (a primitive, a String, or an object whose class is Serializable), or be marked transient. Otherwise writeObject throws NotSerializableException. Collections like ArrayList and HashMap are serializable, but only if their contents are.
  • transient fields are skipped. After deserialization they hold the default value (null, 0, false). Use it for passwords, tokens, caches, threads and anything derived or sensitive.
  • static fields are not part of an object's state and are not serialized.
  • The whole object graph is saved: if Order refers to Customer, both are written. Shared references stay shared, and cycles are handled.
  • If a parent class is not serializable, its fields are not saved, and on deserialization the parent's no-argument constructor runs to initialise them. If the parent has none, you get an InvalidClassException.
  • Subclasses of a serializable class are serializable automatically.

serialVersionUID

Every serializable class has a version number, serialVersionUID, a long. It is written into the byte stream. When you deserialize, Java compares the number in the stream with the number of the class currently loaded. If they differ, it throws InvalidClassException ("local class incompatible"). This protects you from loading old data into a class whose shape has changed.

If you do not declare the field, the compiler computes one from the class details (name, fields, methods). Then any small change, even adding a method, gives a new number and breaks old data. So you declare it yourself:

private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

Rules of thumb: keep the same number when your change is compatible (adding a field is compatible: the old data gives the new field its default value); change the number when the change is incompatible (removing a field, changing a field's type, changing the class hierarchy) and you want old data to be rejected. IDEs can generate the field for you.

Customising: readObject, writeObject, Externalizable

A class can define private methods writeObject(ObjectOutputStream) and readObject(ObjectInputStream) to add steps, for example to encrypt a field or to rebuild a transient cache after loading. Call defaultWriteObject() / defaultReadObject() inside to handle the normal fields. Externalizable goes further: you write all the state yourself and need a public no-argument constructor. In practice you will almost never write these.

private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in)
        throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
    in.defaultReadObject();        // restore normal fields
    this.sessionToken = null;      // or recompute a cache here
    if (email == null) {           // validate: the stream may be hostile
        throw new InvalidObjectException("email is required");
    }
}

Records and enums

Enums serialize by name, so the constants stay singletons. A record can implement Serializable; on deserialization Java calls the record's canonical constructor, so the validation in your constructor runs again. That makes records a safer choice than ordinary classes if you must serialize.

Why JSON is preferred today

PointJava serializationJSON (Jackson)
ReadableNo, binaryYes, plain text
Other languagesJava onlyEvery language and browser
VersioningFragile: serialVersionUID, class shapeTolerant: ignore unknown fields, optional fields
SecuritySerious risk with untrusted dataMuch smaller risk (still validate input)
Constructor and validationConstructor skippedNormal constructors or builders
Size and speedLarger, slower than good binary formatsText overhead; binary options exist (Protobuf, Avro)

Spring Boot uses Jackson for REST bodies; it turns objects into JSON with ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString(obj) and back with readValue(json, Customer.class). For a bank-style "save to a file" task you would also use JSON or CSV. Java serialization still shows up in legacy code, in HttpSession replication between servers, and in some caches (Redis with JdkSerializationRedisSerializer, which is why many teams switch Redis to a JSON serializer).

The security risk

Deserialization runs code chosen by whoever produced the bytes. When your program calls readObject() on data from an untrusted source, an attacker can craft a stream that makes Java build objects from classes already on your classpath (a "gadget chain"), so that a harmless-looking readObject or hashCode call ends up running a system command. This has caused many real remote-code-execution vulnerabilities in widely used Java libraries and servers. The danger exists even if the class you cast to is safe, because the objects are created before the cast.

Rule: never deserialize untrusted data with ObjectInputStream

If you must read Java-serialized data, restrict it with a serialization filter (ObjectInputFilter, Java 9+; for example set with ObjectInputStream.setObjectInputFilter or the JVM-wide jdk.serialFilter property) that allows only the classes you expect. Better: do not accept Java serialization at all.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NotSerializableException — a field (or an element inside a collection) is not Serializable. The message names the class.
  • InvalidClassException — serialVersionUID mismatch, or a non-serializable parent without a no-arg constructor.
