  • ClassNotFoundException — the class is not on the classpath of the reader; it is a checked exception of readObject.
  • StreamCorruptedException — the file is not a serialization stream, or is damaged.
  • Singletons break: deserializing creates a second instance unless you add readResolve() (or use an enum).
  • Writing the same object twice to one stream writes a back-reference the second time, so changes made between two writeObject calls are not saved (use reset()).

Mistake: forgetting that the parent class matters

You make Manager implements Serializable but its parent Employee does not. The Employee fields (name, salary) silently come back as defaults, because they were never written. Make the parent serializable too.

Interview: "What is serialVersionUID?", "What does transient do?", "Why is serialization risky?"

  • Serializable is a marker interface; the object graph is written; the constructor is not called.
  • transient and static fields are skipped.
  • serialVersionUID is a version check; mismatch gives InvalidClassException; declare it yourself.
  • Risks: gadget chains and remote code execution on untrusted input; use filters or, better, JSON.

Properties files and the Properties class

A .properties file stores simple key=value settings; java.util.Properties loads it into a map-like object so your program can read configuration without hard-coding it.

What and why

Settings such as the database URL, a timeout or a feature flag should not live inside your code. A properties file is the simplest configuration format in Java: one key=value pair per line. You change the file, not the code, and no recompile is needed. Spring Boot's application.properties is exactly this format (see Spring Boot · Module 1), and resource bundles for translations (messages_hi.properties) use it too.

# Database settings
db.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
db.user=shop_app
# Values may contain spaces; leading spaces are removed
app.name = Order Service
app.retries=3
# Line continuation with a backslash
app.welcome=Welcome to \
            the shop
feature.newCheckout=true

File format rules

  • Lines starting with # or ! are comments.
  • The key ends at the first =, : or whitespace. Spaces around the separator are ignored.
  • A trailing \ continues the value on the next line.
  • Everything is a string. app.retries=3 gives you the text "3"; you convert it with Integer.parseInt.
  • Special characters (\n, \t, \\) use backslash escapes; non-ASCII characters can be written as ₹. If you read the file with a UTF-8 Reader, you can type them directly.
  • Quotes are not special: name="Asha" stores the quote characters.

The Properties class

Properties extends Hashtable<Object,Object> (an old design choice), but you should only use its String methods.

MethodPurpose
load(Reader) / load(InputStream)Read the pairs from a file or stream. Prefer Reader with UTF-8
getProperty(key)Value, or null if the key is missing
getProperty(key, default)Value, or the default if the key is missing
setProperty(key, value)Add or change a pair in memory
stringPropertyNames()All keys as a Set<String>
store(Writer, comments)Write the pairs to a file, with a header comment
 
import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.Properties;

public class ConfigDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Properties props = new Properties();

        try (Reader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(
                Path.of("app.properties"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            props.load(reader);
        }

        String url = props.getProperty("db.url");
        int retries = Integer.parseInt(props.getProperty("app.retries", "1"));
        boolean newCheckout =
                Boolean.parseBoolean(props.getProperty("feature.newCheckout"));
        String timeout = props.getProperty("db.timeout", "30");   // missing: default

        System.out.println("url        = " + url);
        System.out.println("retries    = " + retries);
        System.out.println("checkout   = " + newCheckout);
        System.out.println("timeout    = " + timeout);
        System.out.println("welcome    = " + props.getProperty("app.welcome"));

        // Change and save
        props.setProperty("app.retries", "5");
        try (Writer writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(
                Path.of("app-new.properties"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            props.store(writer, "Updated settings");
        }
    }
}
url        = jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
retries    = 3
checkout   = true
timeout    = 30
welcome    = Welcome to the shop

The saved file starts with the comment line, then a timestamp comment, then the pairs. The order of the pairs is not guaranteed because the class is hash-based.

Reading from the classpath

A file in src/main/resources is packaged inside the JAR, so you cannot open it with a file path in production. Load it from the classpath instead:

try (InputStream in = ConfigDemo.class.getResourceAsStream("/app.properties")) {
    if (in == null) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("app.properties not found on classpath");
    }
    props.load(new InputStreamReader(in, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
}

The leading / means "from the root of the classpath". getResourceAsStream returns null (not an exception) when the resource is missing, so check it.

Layering: defaults, files and environment

Real applications combine several sources: defaults in code, a file in the JAR, an override file on the server, and environment variables or system properties (-Dapp.retries=5, read with System.getProperty; environment variables with System.getenv). new Properties(defaults) accepts another Properties object as fallback. Spring Boot does this layering for you with a clear order of precedence, and @Value or @ConfigurationProperties bind the values to typed fields.

Rules

  • Never commit secrets (passwords, API keys) in a properties file in Git. Read them from environment variables or a secrets manager.
  • Convert strings to the right type yourself, and fail with a clear message when a required key is missing.
  • Use getProperty, not get: get comes from Hashtable and returns an Object, and it does not use the defaults.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NumberFormatException — the value is not a number (app.retries=three).
  • NullPointerException — you call Integer.parseInt(props.getProperty("missing")); use a default or check for null.
  • IllegalArgumentException — load finds a malformed \uXXXX escape.
  • load(InputStream) assumes ISO-8859-1. That garbles UTF-8 text; use the Reader version.
  • A key written twice: the last value wins, with no warning.
  • Trailing spaces at the end of a value are kept, a classic cause of "true " not parsing as expected with some libraries.

Real projects

You will rarely call Properties.load yourself in a Spring Boot app. You write application.properties (or YAML) and let the framework read it. You will meet Properties directly in plain-Java tools, JDBC driver settings (DriverManager.getConnection(url, props)), Kafka client configuration and test utilities.

Interview: "How do you externalise configuration in Java?"

  • Key=value file loaded with Properties.load; all values are strings.
  • Classpath resources via getResourceAsStream; overrides through system properties and environment variables.
  • In Spring Boot: application.properties/YAML, profiles, @Value and @ConfigurationProperties.
  • Keep secrets out of Git.

Interview questions — Exceptions and files

What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?

Checked exceptions are subclasses of Exception that are not RuntimeException (for example IOException, SQLException). The compiler forces you to catch them or declare them with throws. Unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException and its subclasses (and Error); the compiler does not check them. Use checked exceptions for failures the caller can reasonably recover from, and unchecked for programming errors and for failures the caller cannot fix. Modern frameworks such as Spring prefer unchecked exceptions.

Draw the exception hierarchy. Why should you not catch Error?

Throwable has two children: Error and Exception. RuntimeException is a subclass of Exception. Errors such as OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError signal that the JVM itself is in trouble. Your code usually cannot repair that, and trying to continue can leave the application in a corrupt state. Let the error propagate, log it at the top level, and let the process or container restart.

Does finally always run? What does this code print? 
static int test() {
    try {
        return 1;
    } finally {
        System.out.println("finally");
    }
}

It prints finally and then returns 1. The return value is computed first, then finally runs, then the method returns. finally does not run if the JVM exits (System.exit(), a crash, power loss), if the thread is killed, or if the code loops forever before reaching it. If finally itself has a return, it overrides the earlier return and swallows any exception, so never write one.

What is the difference between throw and throws?

throw is a statement that throws one exception object at run time: throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount <= 0"). throws is part of a method signature and lists the checked exceptions the method may pass to its caller: void read() throws IOException. throw is used inside the body; throws is used in the declaration and can list several types.

Why must catch blocks go from specific to general?

Java checks catch blocks from top to bottom and uses the first one that matches. If you put catch (Exception e) before catch (IOException e), the second block can never run, and the compiler reports an error ("exception IOException has already been caught"). In a multi-catch (A | B) the two types must not be related by inheritance, for the same reason.

What is try-with-resources and what are suppressed exceptions?

It declares resources that implement AutoCloseable in the parentheses of try. Java closes them automatically in reverse order of declaration, whether the body succeeds or throws. If the body throws exception A and then close() throws exception B, A is thrown and B is attached to it as a suppressed exception, readable with a.getSuppressed(). In a hand-written finally, B would replace A and the real cause would be lost.

Can an overriding method throw a broader exception than the method it overrides?

No, not for checked exceptions. The overriding method may throw the same checked exception, a narrower one, or none. It may throw any unchecked exception. The reason: code that uses the parent type only prepared for the exceptions in the parent's throws clause. If the child method could throw something broader, that caller would be surprised. A constructor and a method that is overridden follow the same rule.

How do you create a custom exception? Checked or unchecked?

Extend Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked), name it ...Exception, and provide constructors for a message and for a message plus cause. Add fields when callers need data, such as an error code or the missing amount. Choose checked when the caller can and should recover (for example InsufficientBalanceException in a payment flow where the UI offers "add money"); choose unchecked for business-rule violations that a global handler converts to an HTTP response, which is the common choice in Spring applications.

What is exception chaining and why wrap exceptions?

Chaining means passing the original exception as the cause of a new one: throw new OrderException("Cannot place order " + id, e). The stack trace then shows "Caused by: ...", so nothing is lost. Wrapping lets a service layer hide low-level details (SQLException) behind its own exception type, and converts a checked exception into an unchecked one when the caller cannot handle it. Always pass the cause; throwing a new exception without it destroys the evidence.

Why is catching Exception or swallowing an exception bad?

A broad catch (Exception e) also catches bugs (NullPointerException, ClassCastException) and interruptions that you did not plan for. An empty catch block hides the failure completely, so the program continues in a wrong state and you debug it weeks later with no log. Catch the specific type you can handle. Either handle it or rethrow it. Do not both log and rethrow at every layer, because one failure then appears ten times in the logs.

How do you avoid NullPointerException?

Validate inputs early (Objects.requireNonNull(x, "x must not be null")), return empty collections instead of null, return Optional from methods that may have no result, use constant-first comparison ("PAID".equals(status)), and avoid long chains of calls on possibly-null values. Since Java 14 the NPE message names the null expression, such as Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "name" is null, which makes debugging faster.

How does Spring Boot turn exceptions into HTTP responses?

An exception that escapes a controller is passed to exception resolvers. You normally write a class annotated with @RestControllerAdvice containing @ExceptionHandler methods, each mapping an exception type to a status code and a JSON error body. Without one, Spring Boot returns a default error response with status 500 for unhandled exceptions. You can also annotate an exception with @ResponseStatus. See Spring Boot · Module 2.

Files.readAllLines vs Files.lines vs BufferedReader: which for a large file?

readAllLines loads every line into a List, so memory use grows with the file size. It is fine for small files. Files.lines returns a lazy Stream<String> that reads as you consume it; it must be closed, so use try-with-resources. Files.newBufferedReader with readLine() is the same lazy idea in a classic loop. For a multi-gigabyte log, use lines or the reader, not readAllLines or readString.

Byte streams vs character streams? What does BufferedReader add?

Byte streams (InputStream, OutputStream) move raw bytes and suit binary data. Character streams (Reader, Writer) decode bytes to characters with a charset and suit text. BufferedReader wraps another reader, reads big blocks into memory so there are fewer system calls, and adds readLine(). It is an example of the decorator pattern.

What does transient mean, and what is serialVersionUID for?

A transient field is skipped during Java serialization; after loading it has its default value. serialVersionUID is a version number stored in the stream. On deserialization Java compares it with the class's number and throws InvalidClassException if they differ. You declare it explicitly, otherwise the compiler generates one from the class structure and a small edit breaks old data.

Why is Java serialization considered dangerous?

Deserializing a stream creates objects and calls code in classes on your classpath before your code can check anything. An attacker who controls the bytes can chain existing classes ("gadgets") to run commands on your server. So never deserialize untrusted input. Use a serialization filter if you must, and prefer JSON or another data-only format for storage and APIs.

Cheat sheet — Exceptions and files

  • Hierarchy Throwable → Error (do not catch) / Exception → RuntimeException (unchecked).
  • Checked Exception minus RuntimeException: catch or declare. Examples: IOException, SQLException, InterruptedException.
  • Unchecked RuntimeException: NPE, IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, ArithmeticException, ClassCastException.
  • Catch order most specific first; a parent before its child is a compile error.
  • Multi-catch catch (A | B e); types must be unrelated; e is effectively final.
  • finally runs on return and on exceptions; not after System.exit(), a crash or an endless loop. Never return in it.
  • try-with-resources AutoCloseable resources closed in reverse order; extra close errors go to getSuppressed().
  • throw statement that throws one object. throws signature clause listing checked types.
  • Chaining new MyException("msg", cause) keeps "Caused by:" in the trace.
  • Overriding may throw the same, narrower or no checked exceptions, never broader.
  • Custom exception name ends with Exception; constructors (msg) and (msg, cause); add an error code field if useful.
  • Do not swallow, catch Throwable, log and rethrow in every layer, or use exceptions for normal flow.
  • Fail fast validate arguments first; Objects.requireNonNull(x, "msg").
  • Stack trace read top frame first (where it was thrown), then down to your code, then each "Caused by:" from the bottom.
  • Files (small) Files.readString, readAllLines, writeString, write; name UTF-8.
  • Files (large) Files.lines (close it!), newBufferedReader, newBufferedWriter.
  • Options StandardOpenOption.APPEND and CREATE to add to a file; default write truncates.
  • Directories createDirectories, list (one level), walk (tree), copy, move, deleteIfExists.
  • io bytes: InputStream/OutputStream; text: Reader/Writer; wrap with Buffered* (decorator).
  • File vs Path File is legacy; Path + Files is modern; convert with toPath().
  • Serialization Serializable marker; transient and static skipped; declare serialVersionUID; constructor not called.
  • Serialization risk never read untrusted data with ObjectInputStream; use JSON.
  • Properties load(Reader), getProperty(key, default), store; all values are strings.
  • Classpath file Class.getResourceAsStream("/name") returns null if missing.

Practice — Exceptions and files

  1. Predict the output. Without running it, write what this prints, then check. Done when you can explain each line, including why the value 3 is returned. 
    static int f() {
    int x = 1;
    try {
        x = 2;
        throw new RuntimeException("boom");
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        x = 3;
        return x;
    } finally {
        x = 4;
        System.out.println("finally x=" + x);
    }
}
public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println(f()); }
  2. Break and fix catch order. Write a method that parses a number from a string and reads a file. Put catch (Exception e) above catch (IOException e), read the compiler message, then fix it. Done when it compiles with the specific catch first and a multi-catch for two unrelated types.
  3. Read a stack trace. Write three methods a() calls b() calls c(), where c() parses "abc" as an int and b() wraps the error in your own exception with the cause. Print the trace. Done when you can point to the top frame, the line in your code and the "Caused by" line.
  4. try-with-resources and suppressed exceptions. Create a class Res implements AutoCloseable whose close() throws. Use two of them in one try block and throw from the body. Done when you print the closing order and the contents of getSuppressed().
  5. CSV to objects. Create orders.csv with lines such as 1001,Asha,499.50. Use Files.lines in try-with-resources to turn each line into a record Order(int id, String customer, double amount), skipping and reporting bad lines (wrong column count, bad number). Done when good rows are printed with a total and bad rows are listed with line numbers.
  6. Bank model with InsufficientBalanceException. Build the model below. Done when withdrawing too much throws your exception with the missing amount, the exception has a cause-capable constructor, and a test shows the balance unchanged after the failure. 
    public class InsufficientBalanceException extends Exception {
    private final long shortfallInPaise;

    public InsufficientBalanceException(String message, long shortfallInPaise) {
        super(message);
        this.shortfallInPaise = shortfallInPaise;
    }
    public long getShortfallInPaise() { return shortfallInPaise; }
}
    public class Account {
    private final String id;
    private long balanceInPaise;

    public Account(String id, long balanceInPaise) {
        this.id = id;
        this.balanceInPaise = balanceInPaise;
    }

    public void withdraw(long amount) throws InsufficientBalanceException {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive: " + amount);
        }
        if (amount > balanceInPaise) {
            throw new InsufficientBalanceException(
                "Account " + id + " has " + balanceInPaise + " but needs " + amount,
                amount - balanceInPaise);
        }
        balanceInPaise -= amount;      // change state only after all checks pass
    }

    public String getId() { return id; }
    public long getBalanceInPaise() { return balanceInPaise; }
}
  7. Save and load the bank model. Write the accounts to accounts.csv (id,balanceInPaise) with Files.write and read them back into a Map<String, Account>. Done when a program that saves two accounts, restarts and loads them shows the same balances, and a missing or corrupt file gives a clear message instead of a stack trace. 
    import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;

public class AccountStore {
    public static void save(Path file, Collection<Account> accounts) throws IOException {
        List<String> lines = accounts.stream()
                .map(a -> a.getId() + "," + a.getBalanceInPaise())
                .toList();
        Files.write(file, lines);              // UTF-8, creates or truncates
    }

    public static Map<String, Account> load(Path file) throws IOException {
        Map<String, Account> result = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        if (Files.notExists(file)) {
            return result;                     // first run: nothing saved yet
        }
        int lineNo = 0;
        for (String line : Files.readAllLines(file)) {
            lineNo++;
            String[] p = line.split(",");
            if (p.length != 2) {
                throw new IOException("Bad line " + lineNo + ": " + line);
            }
            try {
                result.put(p[0], new Account(p[0], Long.parseLong(p[1].trim())));
            } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
                throw new IOException("Bad balance on line " + lineNo, e);
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}
  8. Stretch: properties and serialization. Store the data folder name in bank.properties and load it with Properties (with a default). Then make Account implement Serializable with a serialVersionUID, write one with ObjectOutputStream, change a field type, and observe the InvalidClassException or default values. Done when you can explain why you would use JSON for this in a real project.
4

Module 4·About 1.5 weeksMust

Collections and generics

14 topics · about 2 h of reading

Almost every Java program keeps groups of things: the items in a Flipkart cart, the employees of a department, the orders waiting to be packed, a map from user id to profile. The Collections Framework (package java.util) is Java's ready-made toolbox for this. It gives you lists, sets, maps, queues and the algorithms (sorting, searching, shuffling) that work on them. Generics are the feature that lets these containers be type-safe: List<String> holds only strings, and the compiler checks it.

This is the most-asked module in Java interviews. "How does HashMap work internally?", "ArrayList vs LinkedList", "Comparable vs Comparator" and "what is ConcurrentModificationException?" appear in nearly every round. It builds on equals and hashCode from Module 2, and it leads straight into streams (Module 5) and thread-safe collections (Module 6). Spring Data, JPA and REST controllers return and accept collections all day.

After this module you will be able to:

  • draw the Collections hierarchy and pick the right interface and implementation for a job;
  • explain ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeSet, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue with their time complexity;
  • explain step by step how HashMap stores and finds an entry — hashing, buckets, collisions, resizing and treeification;
  • iterate safely, remove while iterating, and explain ConcurrentModificationException;
  • sort objects with Comparable and Comparator, and avoid the classic comparator bugs;
  • use the Collections utility class and know exactly which lists are mutable, immutable, views or copies;
  • write generic classes and methods, use bounded types and wildcards (PECS), and explain type erasure and its limits.

The Collections Framework: hierarchy and choosing a type

The framework is a small set of interfaces (List, Set, Queue, Deque, Map) with several implementations each; you code against the interface and pick the implementation for the performance and ordering you need.

An array has a fixed size, no helper methods and no built-in "add" or "remove". A collection is an object that holds a group of other objects and grows and shrinks as needed. The Java Collections Framework (JCF) is the set of interfaces, implementation classes and algorithms in java.util that standardise this. Because every list has the same methods, you can swap an ArrayList for a LinkedList by changing one word.

The hierarchy

Iterable
The top interface. Anything that implements it can be used in an enhanced for loop. It has one key method, iterator().
Collection
A group of elements. Common methods: add, remove, contains, size, isEmpty, clear, addAll, removeAll, retainAll, stream, toArray.
List
An ordered sequence with positions (index 0, 1, 2…). Allows duplicates. Use it when order and position matter.
Set
No duplicates. "Duplicate" is decided by equals() (and hashCode() for hash sets). Use it for unique ids, tags, visited nodes.
Queue / Deque
A queue holds elements to be processed, normally first in, first out (FIFO). A deque (double-ended queue, said "deck") allows add and remove at both ends, so it also works as a stack.
Map
Key → value pairs with unique keys. It is not a Collection, because its elements are pairs, not single values. Views such as keySet(), values() and entrySet() give you collections.

Sequenced collections (Java 21)

Before Java 21, getting "the last element" was different for every type: list.get(list.size() - 1), deque.getLast(), sortedSet.last(), and for a LinkedHashSet you had to iterate everything. Java 21 added three interfaces for collections that have a defined encounter order: SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap. They add getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst(), addLast(), removeFirst(), removeLast() and reversed() (a reverse-order view). Maps get firstEntry(), lastEntry(), pollFirstEntry(), putFirst(), putLast() and reversed().

import java.util.*;

public class Sequenced {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> steps = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Cart", "Address", "Payment"));
        System.out.println(steps.getFirst() + " / " + steps.getLast());   // Java 21
        System.out.println(steps.reversed());                             // a view

        LinkedHashSet<String> seen = new LinkedHashSet<>(List.of("A", "B", "C"));
        seen.addFirst("Z");                       // moves/adds at the front
        System.out.println(seen);

        LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> stock = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        stock.put("pen", 10);
        stock.put("book", 4);
        System.out.println(stock.firstEntry() + " " + stock.lastEntry());
    }
}
Cart / Payment
[Payment, Address, Cart]
[Z, A, B, C]
pen=10 book=4

List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap, SortedSet and SortedMap all became sequenced. HashSet and HashMap did not, because they have no defined order.

Interface vs implementation — program to the interface

An interface (List) says what you can do. An implementation (ArrayList, LinkedList) decides how it is done and how fast. Declare variables, fields, parameters and return types with the interface; use the implementation name only after new.

Wrong: locked to one implementation

ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

public ArrayList<String> findAll() { ... }

Right: depends on the behaviour only

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

public List<String> findAll() { ... }

Now you can change to new LinkedList<>() or return List.of(...) without touching callers. Use the concrete type only when you need a method the interface lacks, such as ArrayList.ensureCapacity or TreeMap's NavigableMap methods (then declare it as NavigableMap).

Master comparison of the main implementations

ClassOrderDuplicates and nullsThread-safeTime: get / add / remove / contains
ArrayListInsertion, by indexDuplicates yes; nulls yesNoO(1) / O(1) amortized at end / O(n) / O(n)
LinkedListInsertion, by indexDuplicates yes; nulls yesNoO(n) / O(1) at ends / O(1) at ends, O(n) by value / O(n)
HashSetNoneNo duplicates; one nullNo– / O(1) / O(1) / O(1)
LinkedHashSetInsertionNo duplicates; one nullNo– / O(1) / O(1) / O(1)
TreeSetSortedNo duplicates; no null (natural order)No– / O(log n) / O(log n) / O(log n)
HashMapNoneUnique keys; one null key; null values yesNoO(1) / O(1) / O(1) / O(1) on key
LinkedHashMapInsertion or accessAs HashMapNoO(1) for all four
TreeMapSorted by keyNo null key; null values yesNoO(log n) for all four
ArrayDequeFIFO or LIFO at the endsDuplicates yes; no nullsNo– / O(1) at ends / O(1) at ends / O(n)
PriorityQueueMin-heap by priorityDuplicates yes; no nullsNopeek O(1) / offer O(log n) / poll O(log n) / O(n)

Hash-based costs are average case and assume a good hashCode(). The thread-safe alternatives — ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentLinkedQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue — live in java.util.concurrent and are covered in Module 6. The legacy Vector, Stack and Hashtable are synchronized but avoided (see Queues and deques).

Three names that look alike

  • Collection (singular) is the interface.
  • Collections (plural) is a utility class full of static methods such as sort and unmodifiableList (see The Collections utility class).
  • Arrays is another utility class, for arrays: Arrays.sort, Arrays.asList, Arrays.toString.

Collections hold objects, not primitives

You cannot write List<int>. Use the wrapper class List<Integer>. Java converts automatically (autoboxing on the way in, unboxing on the way out). This costs memory — an Integer object is about 16 bytes versus 4 for an int — so for millions of numbers, prefer int[] or IntStream. Unboxing a null throws NullPointerException, and comparing two Integer objects with == works only for small cached values (−128 to 127); always use equals.

Rule: elements of hash-based and sorted collections must behave well

Elements of a HashSet and keys of a HashMap must have consistent equals() and hashCode(). Elements of a TreeSet and keys of a TreeMap must be Comparable or you must pass a Comparator. Otherwise you get missing elements or ClassCastException.

Conventions

  • Declare with the interface: List, Set, Map, Deque. Plural or descriptive names: orders, emailsByUser.
  • Default choices: ArrayList for lists, HashMap for maps, HashSet for sets, ArrayDeque for stacks and queues. Change only when you have a reason.
  • Return an empty collection, never null, from a method that finds nothing.

Edge cases and exceptions

  • NullPointerException — adding null to List.of, ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue, TreeSet or ConcurrentHashMap.
  • UnsupportedOperationException — modifying an immutable collection.
  • ConcurrentModificationException — structurally changing a collection while iterating it.
  • NoSuchElementException — getFirst(), element(), iterator().next() on an empty or finished collection.
  • ClassCastException — putting non-comparable objects into a sorted collection.

Interview: "Explain the Collections hierarchy"

  • Iterable → Collection → List, Set, Queue (→ Deque); Map is separate and does not extend Collection.
  • List = ordered with duplicates; Set = unique; Queue/Deque = processing order; Map = key to value.
  • Mention Java 21 sequenced collections: getFirst, getLast, reversed.
  • "Program to the interface" and why: swap implementations without changing callers.

List: ArrayList vs LinkedList

ArrayList is a resizable array with fast random access and is the right default; LinkedList is a doubly linked list that is almost never faster in practice.

A List is an ordered collection that allows duplicates and lets you read or change an element by its index. The two classic implementations store data very differently, and that difference is the whole interview question.

ArrayList internals

ArrayList keeps its elements in a plain Object[] called elementData and a counter called size. The capacity is the length of the array; the size is how many slots are in use.

  1. new ArrayList<>() starts with an empty shared array — no memory is allocated yet.
  2. The first add allocates an array of default capacity 10.
  3. add(e) writes to elementData[size] and does size++.
  4. When the array is full, ArrayList allocates a new array about 1.5 times bigger (newCapacity = old + old/2: 10 → 15 → 22 → 33 → 49) and copies the old elements across with Arrays.copyOf.
  5. add(index, e) and remove(index) shift every later element one place with System.arraycopy.

Growing by a fixed fraction instead of a fixed amount makes add amortized O(1): an occasional expensive copy is spread over many cheap adds, so the average cost per add stays constant. A single add that triggers a resize is O(n), but that happens rarely.

  • new ArrayList<>(1000) allocates 1,000 slots at once. Do this when you know the final size, to avoid repeated resizing.
  • ensureCapacity(n) grows the array up front before a big batch of adds.
  • trimToSize() shrinks the array to exactly size. remove and clear never shrink the array on their own, so a list that was once huge keeps its memory until you trim it or drop it.
  • ArrayList implements the marker interface RandomAccess, which tells algorithms that get(i) is cheap.

LinkedList internals

LinkedList is a doubly linked list: each element lives in its own Node object holding the item, a link to the next node and a link to the previous node. The list keeps references to the first and last node. It implements both List and Deque.

Adding or removing at either end only changes a couple of links: O(1). But get(i) must walk from the nearer end, one node at a time: O(n). Inserting in the middle is O(1) only if you are already standing at that node (for example with a ListIterator); finding the position first is O(n).

Which one wins in practice?

OperationArrayListLinkedList
get(i) / set(i, x)O(1)O(n)
add(e) at the endO(1) amortizedO(1)
add(0, e) at the frontO(n) (shifts everything)O(1)
add(i, e) / remove(i) in the middleO(n) — fast arraycopyO(n) to find + O(1) to link
contains(x) / indexOf(x)O(n)O(n)
Memory per elementOne reference (4–8 bytes)A node object, roughly 24 bytes or more
CPU cache behaviourExcellent — contiguous memoryPoor — nodes scattered on the heap

On paper LinkedList wins at the front and the middle. In real programs ArrayList still wins almost every time: array copying is done by fast native code and the CPU cache loves contiguous memory, while a linked list must chase a pointer to every node and allocate an object for every add. Even for a queue, ArrayDeque beats LinkedList. The advice from the author of the framework is simple: use ArrayList unless a measurement tells you otherwise.

The List API you use every day

MethodWhat it does
add(e), add(i, e), addAll(c)Append, insert at index, append many
get(i), set(i, e)Read or replace at an index (set returns the old value)
remove(int i), remove(Object o)Remove by position, or the first element equal to o
indexOf(o), lastIndexOf(o), contains(o)Search using equals; -1 when absent
removeIf(pred), replaceAll(op)Bulk remove or transform with a lambda
sort(cmp)Sort in place; null means natural order
subList(from, to)A view of a range (from inclusive, to exclusive)
toArray(new String[0])Copy into a typed array
getFirst(), getLast(), reversed()Java 21 sequenced methods
 
import java.util.*;

public class ListBasics {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> cart = new ArrayList<>();
        cart.add("Phone");
        cart.add("Charger");
        cart.add(1, "Cover");               // insert at index 1
        cart.add("Charger");                // duplicates are fine
        System.out.println(cart);

        System.out.println(cart.get(2));
        System.out.println(cart.indexOf("Charger") + " " + cart.lastIndexOf("Charger"));
        cart.set(0, "Phone Pro");
        cart.remove("Charger");             // removes the FIRST match only
        cart.removeIf(item -> item.startsWith("Cover"));
        System.out.println(cart);

        String[] array = cart.toArray(new String[0]);
        System.out.println(array.length + " " + Arrays.toString(array));

        try {
            cart.get(5);
        } catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
            System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
[Phone, Cover, Charger, Charger]
Charger
2 3
2 [Phone Pro, Charger]
Index 5 out of bounds for length 2

Trap: remove(int) vs remove(Object) on List<Integer>

List has two overloads: remove(int index) and remove(Object o). With a List<Integer>, a plain int argument picks the index version, because no boxing is needed for an exact match.

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30, 1));

nums.remove(1);                     // int  → removes the element at INDEX 1
System.out.println(nums);

nums.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));    // Object → removes the VALUE 1
System.out.println(nums);
[10, 30, 1]
[10, 30]

subList is a view, not a copy

subList(from, to) returns a window onto the same data. Changes to the sublist write through to the original list, and vice versa. This is useful for clearing a range in one line, and dangerous if you forget it.

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6));
List<Integer> middle = list.subList(1, 4);   // elements at index 1, 2, 3
System.out.println(middle);

middle.set(0, 99);                           // writes through to the original
System.out.println(list);

middle.clear();                              // removes the range from the original
System.out.println(list);

list.add(7);                                 // structural change to the PARENT
try {
    System.out.println(middle.size());       // the view is now invalid
} catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
    System.out.println("CME: view is stale");
}

List<Integer> copy = new ArrayList<>(list.subList(0, 2));   // a real, independent copy
[2, 3, 4]
[1, 99, 3, 4, 5, 6]
[1, 5, 6]
CME: view is stale

LinkedList as a Deque

Because LinkedList is also a Deque, it has addFirst, removeLast, push, pop, peek and friends. It works, but ArrayDeque is faster and lighter for these jobs, with one exception: LinkedList allows null elements and ArrayDeque does not (see Queues and deques).

Rule: indexes must be in range, and lists use equals()

Valid indexes are 0 to size() - 1. add(i, e) also accepts i == size(). Searching methods (contains, indexOf, remove(Object)) compare with equals(), so your element class needs a correct equals.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • IndexOutOfBoundsException (message like Index 5 out of bounds for length 2) — get, set, remove or add(i, e) with a bad index. On an array the exception is ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
  • ConcurrentModificationException — changing the list while a for-each loop or an old subList is using it (see Iteration).
  • new ArrayList<>(-1) throws IllegalArgumentException; new ArrayList<>(0) is fine.
  • An empty list's getFirst() (Java 21) throws NoSuchElementException.
  • Removing from the middle of a huge ArrayList in a loop is O(n²). Use removeIf or build a new list.

Mistake: removing inside a for-each loop

for (String s : list) { if (...) list.remove(s); } usually throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use list.removeIf(...) or an Iterator.

Tips

  • Copy a list: new ArrayList<>(other). Make a read-only copy: List.copyOf(other).
  • Need to insert or remove at the front a lot? Use ArrayDeque, not LinkedList.
  • Pre-size with new ArrayList<>(expectedSize) when loading many rows from a database.

Real projects

Spring Data repositories return List<Entity> (an ArrayList underneath), and REST controllers return lists that Jackson turns into JSON arrays. In the whole of a typical codebase you will see ArrayList hundreds of times and LinkedList almost never.

Interview: "ArrayList vs LinkedList"

  • ArrayList: dynamic array, O(1) random access, amortized O(1) add at the end, O(n) insert/remove in the middle, default capacity 10, grows about 1.5×.
  • LinkedList: doubly linked nodes, O(n) access by index, O(1) at the ends, also a Deque, more memory per element.
  • Strong answer: "ArrayList in almost all cases, because of cache locality and cheap copying; LinkedList's O(1) insert is only real when you already hold the node."
  • Follow-ups: what is amortized O(1)? What does subList return? What does list.remove(1) do on a List<Integer>?

How HashMap works inside

HashMap turns each key into a bucket index with hashCode(), stores the entry in that bucket, and uses equals() to find the exact key inside the bucket; it doubles its table when 75% full and turns long buckets into red-black trees.

A HashMap<K, V> stores key → value pairs and finds a value by its key in O(1) on average — whether the map has ten entries or ten million. This is the most asked Java interview topic, so we will build it up step by step. The idea: do not search; calculate where the entry must be.

The data structure: a table of buckets

Inside a HashMap there is an array called table. Each slot of the array is a bucket. A bucket is either empty (null) or holds a chain of Node objects. Each Node stores four things: the hash of the key, the key, the value, and a next link to the next node in the same bucket.

The table is created lazily — new HashMap<>() allocates nothing; the first put creates a table of the default capacity 16. Capacity is always a power of two.

Step 1 to 3: from key to bucket index

  1. hashCode() — call key.hashCode(), which returns an int. (A null key gets hash 0.)
  2. Spread — HashMap mixes the high bits into the low bits: h ^ (h >>> 16). This is the method hash(key) inside HashMap.
  3. Index — index = (n - 1) & hash, where n is the table length.

Why the spread? The index uses only the low bits of the hash (for n = 16, only the lowest 4 bits). Many real hash codes differ mainly in their upper bits, so without mixing they would pile into the same buckets. h ^ (h >>> 16) XORs the upper 16 bits into the lower 16 — cheap, and it makes every bit of the hash count a little.

Why (n - 1) & hash and not hash % n? When n is a power of two, n - 1 is a mask of all ones (for 16: 0b1111), and hash & mask equals hash % n for non-negative numbers — but it is a single fast CPU instruction, and it also works for negative hashes (% can return a negative number). It also makes resizing simple, as you will see below. Because of this trick the capacity must be a power of two; new HashMap<>(20) is rounded up to 32.

public class IndexDemo {
    static int spread(int h) {
        return h ^ (h >>> 16);               // same formula as HashMap.hash()
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int n = 16;                              // table length
        for (int key : new int[] {1, 17, 33, 65553}) {
            int h = spread(Integer.hashCode(key));   // Integer.hashCode(k) is k itself
            System.out.println(key + " -> hash " + h + " -> index " + (h & (n - 1)));
        }
        System.out.println("Aa".hashCode() + " " + "BB".hashCode());
    }
}
1 -> hash 1 -> index 1
17 -> hash 17 -> index 1
33 -> hash 33 -> index 1
65553 -> hash 65552 -> index 0
2112 2112

Look at the first three lines: 1, 17 and 33 land in the same bucket — they differ only in bits above the lowest four. The key 65553 (binary 1 0000 0000 0001 0001) would have gone to bucket 1 without the spread; the XOR with its upper half moved it to bucket 0. The last line shows two different strings with the same hash code, 2112 — a hash collision in the strict sense.

put(key, value) step by step

How two keys are judged equal inside a bucket: first hash == otherHash (a cheap int comparison that rejects most non-matches), then key == otherKey (same reference), then key.equals(otherKey). This is why hashCode picks the bucket and equals picks the exact entry. Inserting a key that already exists replaces the value, keeps the old key object, and returns the old value (or null if there was none).

get(key) step by step

  1. Compute the hash and the bucket index, exactly as in put.
  2. If the bucket is empty, return null.
  3. If the first node matches (hash equal and key same or equals), return its value.
  4. Otherwise walk the rest of the chain (or search the tree) with the same comparison. Return the value on a match, null if you reach the end.

With a good hash function and a low load factor, chains are 0 to 2 nodes long, so get does a constant amount of work. That is the O(1).

Capacity, load factor, threshold and resizing

Capacity
The length of the table. Default 16, always a power of two.
Load factor
How full the table may get before it grows. Default 0.75 — a balance between wasted space (low factor) and long chains (high factor).
Threshold
capacity × load factor. With the defaults it is 16 × 0.75 = 12. When the number of entries goes above the threshold (the 13th put), the map resizes.
Resize (rehash)
Create a new table of double the capacity and move every node into it. Capacity 16 → 32 → 64 → 128; thresholds 12 → 24 → 48 → 96.

Resizing is O(n), but it is rare, so put is still O(1) amortized. The index depends on the table length, so entries must move. Because the new length is exactly double, the new index of a node is either its old index or old index + old capacity. The extra bit that decides is hash & oldCapacity: if it is 0 the node stays, if it is 1 the node moves up by oldCapacity. Java 8 uses this to split each bucket into a "low" and a "high" chain without recomputing indexes, and it keeps the relative order of the nodes (the old Java 7 code reversed chains, which could create infinite loops in racy multi-threaded code).

Tip: size the map when you know the data

To hold 1,000 entries without any resize, the table needs a threshold above 1,000, so capacity 2,048 (1,000 / 0.75 = 1,334, rounded up to a power of two). new HashMap<>(1000) is not enough: it rounds to 1,024, threshold 768. Use new HashMap<>((int) (1000 / 0.75f) + 1), or since Java 19 the clearer HashMap.newHashMap(1000). This matters only for big maps in hot code.

Collisions: chains, then trees

A collision happens when two different keys land in the same bucket. It cannot be avoided: there are about 4 billion possible hash codes, far more keys than buckets, and the table is much smaller than that. HashMap handles it by separate chaining: nodes in one bucket are linked in a list, and a lookup walks the list using equals.

If many keys share a bucket (a poor hashCode, or an attacker choosing keys on purpose), the chain becomes long and lookup degrades to O(n). Java 8 added a defence:

ConstantValueMeaning
TREEIFY_THRESHOLD8When a chain reaches 8 nodes and another is added (the bucket would hold 9), it is considered for conversion to a tree
MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY64The table must have at least 64 buckets; if smaller, the map resizes instead, hoping to spread the keys
UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD6A tree bin that shrinks to 6 nodes or fewer (after removals or a resize split) turns back into a chain

A tree bin is a red-black tree (a self-balancing binary search tree). Nodes are ordered first by hash; if two hashes are equal, by compareTo when the key class implements Comparable of its own type, and otherwise by a tie-breaking identity hash. Lookup in a tree bin is O(log n) instead of O(n). So the worst case of get in Java 8+ is O(log n) when keys are Comparable, and the common case is O(1). The gap between 8 (treeify) and 6 (untreeify) prevents a bucket from flipping back and forth when entries are added and removed around one number.

Null key and null values

HashMap allows one null key (its hash is 0, so it lives in bucket 0) and any number of null values. Because get(k) returns null both for "absent" and for "present with a null value", use containsKey(k) to tell them apart. Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap reject null keys and values with a NullPointerException.

Why equals() and hashCode() must agree

The lookup first jumps to a bucket using hashCode(), then confirms with equals(). The contract between them: if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). The reverse is not required (collisions are allowed). If you override equals but not hashCode, two "equal" objects get different identity-based hash codes, so they usually point to different buckets and the map never compares them. See equals() and hashCode() in Module 2.

import java.util.*;

public class MissingHashCode {
    static class Pt {                       // overrides equals only
        final int x, y;
        Pt(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            return o instanceof Pt p && p.x == x && p.y == y;
        }
    }

    record Pos(int x, int y) {}             // a record gets equals AND hashCode

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Pt, String> bad = new HashMap<>();
        bad.put(new Pt(1, 2), "home");
        System.out.println(bad.get(new Pt(1, 2)));      // equal object, different hash

        Map<Pos, String> good = new HashMap<>();
        good.put(new Pos(1, 2), "home");
        System.out.println(good.get(new Pos(1, 2)));
    }
}
null
home

(The first line is null in practice; in the rare run where the two identity hashes land in the same bucket it would still be null because the stored hash values differ.) Records, Lombok's @EqualsAndHashCode and your IDE's generator all produce a matching pair.

Pitfall: mutable keys

If a field used in hashCode changes after the key is in the map, the node stays in the old bucket with the old stored hash, but a lookup now computes a new hash and looks in the wrong place. The entry is still counted in size(), yet get cannot find it. It is lost until the key is changed back.

import java.util.*;

public class MutableKey {
    static class Key {
        int id;
        Key(int id) { this.id = id; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            return o instanceof Key k && k.id == id;
        }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(id); }   // 31 + id
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Key, String> map = new HashMap<>();
        Key k = new Key(1);
        map.put(k, "order-1");

        k.id = 2;                                   // mutate a field used in hashCode
        System.out.println("size = " + map.size());
        System.out.println("get = " + map.get(k));
        System.out.println("containsKey = " + map.containsKey(k));

        k.id = 1;                                   // restore it
        System.out.println("get after restore = " + map.get(k));
    }
}
size = 1
get = null
containsKey = false
get after restore = order-1

The fix is to use immutable keys: String, Integer, Long, enums, UUID, records with immutable fields. That is why String is such a popular key. A good key class has final fields and a stable hashCode.

Iteration order is not defined

HashMap iterates bucket by bucket, from index 0 up, and each chain in order. That order depends on the hash codes, the table size and the insert history, and it can change after a resize or between Java versions. Small Integer keys often come out sorted by accident (the hash is the number, the index is the number), which fools beginners. Never rely on it: if you need an order, use LinkedHashMap (insertion order) or TreeMap (sorted), see Map implementations.

HashMap is not thread-safe

Two threads calling put on the same HashMap can overwrite each other's entries, lose updates, corrupt the structure during a resize, or throw ConcurrentModificationException in readers. The result is not "slightly wrong" but undefined. If several threads share a map, choose one of these:

FeatureHashMapHashtableConcurrentHashMapCollections.synchronizedMap
Thread-safeNoYesYesYes
LockingNoneOne lock on the whole map for every methodNo lock for reads; writes lock only one bucket (compare-and-swap into empty buckets)One lock on the whole map
Null key / valuesOne null key; null valuesNeither allowedNeither allowedAs the wrapped map
IteratorsFail-fastFail-fast (Enumeration is not)Weakly consistent, never throw CMEFail-fast; you must lock manually while iterating
Atomic compound opsNoNoYes: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, mergeNo
Use todaySingle threadLegacy — avoidThe default for shared mapsRarely

Details of how ConcurrentHashMap achieves this are in Module 6.

Complexity summary

OperationAverageWorst (Java 8+)
put, get, remove, containsKeyO(1)O(log n) with tree bins and Comparable keys; O(n) if keys are not comparable and all collide
containsValueO(n)O(n) — scans every entry
Iterate all entriesO(capacity + n)A huge, mostly empty table makes iteration slow
ResizeO(n), rare—

Rules for map keys

  • Override equals and hashCode together, using the same fields.
  • Do not change fields used by hashCode while the object is a key.
  • Do not rely on iteration order. Do not share a plain HashMap between threads.

Edge cases and exceptions

  • Constructor arguments: negative capacity or a load factor ≤ 0 throws IllegalArgumentException. A very high load factor saves memory but lengthens chains; a low one wastes memory.
  • Maximum capacity is 230 (about 1.07 billion buckets). Past that the table stops growing and chains lengthen.
  • ConcurrentModificationException — adding or removing an entry while iterating keySet(), values() or entrySet(). Changing the value of an existing key does not count as a structural change.
  • A key with a constant hashCode() (like return 1;) is legal but makes the map behave like a list or tree: correct, but slow.
  • Keys that are float/double wrappers: Double.NaN equals itself in Double.equals, and 0.0 and -0.0 are different keys.

Mistake: a key class without hashCode, or with a mutable key

"I put the object in the map and now get returns null." Nine times out of ten the key class lacks hashCode, or a key field was changed after insertion. Use records or immutable keys.

Real projects

HashMap is used for lookups by id (Map<Long, Customer>), grouping (Collectors.groupingBy returns a HashMap), counting, and in-memory caches. Hibernate's first-level cache, Spring's bean registry and Jackson's field maps are all hash maps. For a cache shared across requests use ConcurrentHashMap (or a library such as Caffeine), never a plain HashMap.

Interview: "How does HashMap work internally?" — the model answer

  • An array of buckets (Node[] table), default capacity 16, load factor 0.75, threshold 12.
  • put: hashCode() → spread with h ^ (h >>> 16) → index (n - 1) & hash. Empty bucket: store the node. Otherwise compare hash then equals along the chain; replace the value on a match, else append.
  • get: same index, then walk the bucket comparing hash and equals.
  • Collisions use a linked list; at 8+ nodes (table ≥ 64) the bucket becomes a red-black tree, back to a list at 6.
  • When size exceeds the threshold the table doubles and nodes are redistributed (old index or old index + old capacity).
  • Allows one null key; not thread-safe; iteration order undefined; keys must have a consistent equals/hashCode and should be immutable.
  • Likely follow-ups: HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap; why capacity is a power of two; what happens with a bad hashCode; how to make it thread-safe.

Map: the API, HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap

A Map stores unique keys with one value each; HashMap is the fast default, LinkedHashMap remembers order, TreeMap keeps keys sorted, and the Java 8 methods merge, computeIfAbsent and getOrDefault replace most if-else code.

A Map<K, V> maps a key to a value. Keys are unique (decided by equals, or by the comparator in a TreeMap); values can repeat. Putting a key that already exists replaces its value. Think of a phone book, a Redis cache, or "order id → order". The three everyday implementations differ only in order and speed:

PointHashMapLinkedHashMapTreeMap
Iteration orderUndefinedInsertion order (or access order)Sorted by key
Speed of get / put / removeO(1) averageO(1) averageO(log n)
Null keyOne allowedOne allowedNot allowed (with natural order)
Built onTable of bucketsHashMap + doubly linked list of entriesRed-black tree
Keys needequals + hashCodeequals + hashCodeComparable or a Comparator
Extra methods—removeEldestEntry, Java 21 sequenced methodsNavigableMap: floorKey, headMap, …

The Map methods you must know

MethodWhat it does
put(k, v)Insert or replace; returns the old value or null
get(k)Value or null — also null if the stored value is null
getOrDefault(k, d)Value, or d if the key is absent
containsKey(k) / containsValue(v)Key check (fast) / value check (scans everything)
putIfAbsent(k, v)Put only if the key is absent (or maps to null); returns the existing value
computeIfAbsent(k, fn)If absent, compute the value from the key and store it; returns the value
computeIfPresent(k, fn)If present, replace with fn(k, oldValue); returning null removes the entry
compute(k, fn)Always run fn(k, oldValueOrNull) and store the result
merge(k, v, fn)If absent store v; else store fn(old, v). The counting idiom
remove(k), remove(k, v)Remove by key; remove only if the value matches too
replaceAll(fn), forEach((k, v) -> …)Transform all values; loop over all pairs
keySet(), values(), entrySet()Live views of the keys, values and pairs
Map.entry(k, v)An immutable key-value pair (no nulls)
 
import java.util.*;

public class MapMethods {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Integer> stock = new TreeMap<>();   // TreeMap: stable printing

        stock.put("pen", 10);
        System.out.println(stock.putIfAbsent("pen", 99));    // 10, value unchanged
        System.out.println(stock.putIfAbsent("book", 5));    // null, inserted
        System.out.println(stock);
        System.out.println(stock.getOrDefault("bag", 0));    // 0, "bag" is NOT added

        stock.merge("pen", 5, Integer::sum);                 // 10 + 5
        stock.computeIfAbsent("cap", k -> 3);                // absent → 3
        stock.computeIfPresent("book", (k, v) -> v - 1);     // 5 → 4
        stock.compute("pen", (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);   // 15 → 16
        System.out.println(stock);

        stock.remove("cap");
        stock.replaceAll((k, v) -> v * 2);
        System.out.println(stock);

        for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : stock.entrySet()) {   // best way to loop
            System.out.println(e.getKey() + " = " + e.getValue());
        }
        stock.forEach((k, v) -> System.out.println(k + " -> " + v));
    }
}
10
null
{book=5, pen=10}
0
{book=4, cap=3, pen=16}
{book=8, pen=32}
book = 8
pen = 32
book -> 8
pen -> 32

Loop over entrySet() when you need both key and value. Looping over keySet() and calling get(key) inside does a second lookup for every key.

Word frequency — the classic example

Counting is the most common map task. There are three styles; the second is the idiom to learn.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class WordCount {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String text = "to be or not to be that is the question";
        String[] words = text.split(" ");

        // 1. Classic: getOrDefault
        Map<String, Integer> counts1 = new TreeMap<>();
        for (String w : words) {
            counts1.put(w, counts1.getOrDefault(w, 0) + 1);
        }

        // 2. merge: shortest and safe — "if absent put 1, else add 1"
        Map<String, Integer> counts2 = new TreeMap<>();
        for (String w : words) {
            counts2.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);
        }

        // 3. Streams
        Map<String, Long> counts3 = Arrays.stream(words)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w, TreeMap::new,
                        Collectors.counting()));

        System.out.println(counts1);
        System.out.println(counts2.equals(counts1));
        System.out.println(counts3);
    }
}
{be=2, is=1, not=1, or=1, question=1, that=1, the=1, to=2}
true
{be=2, is=1, not=1, or=1, question=1, that=1, the=1, to=2}

Grouping with computeIfAbsent

To build a "multi-map" (one key → a list of values), computeIfAbsent creates the list the first time and returns it, so you can add in the same line:

record Employee(String name, String city) {}

List<Employee> staff = List.of(new Employee("Ravi", "Mumbai"),
        new Employee("Asha", "Pune"), new Employee("Meera", "Mumbai"));

Map<String, List<String>> byCity = new TreeMap<>();
for (Employee e : staff) {
    byCity.computeIfAbsent(e.city(), city -> new ArrayList<>()).add(e.name());
}
System.out.println(byCity);          // {Mumbai=[Ravi, Meera], Pune=[Asha]}

Sorting a map by value

A map has no order to sort, so you stream its entries, sort them, and collect into an order-preserving map such as LinkedHashMap.

Map<String, Integer> marks = Map.of("Asha", 82, "Ravi", 91, "Meera", 75);

List<Map.Entry<String, Integer>> ranked = marks.entrySet().stream()
        .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Integer>comparingByValue().reversed())
        .toList();
System.out.println(ranked);          // [Ravi=91, Asha=82, Meera=75]

Immutable maps

Map.of(k1, v1, k2, v2, …) (up to 10 pairs), Map.ofEntries(Map.entry(…), …) and Map.copyOf(map) create immutable maps. They reject null keys and values, throw IllegalArgumentException for duplicate keys, and their iteration order is deliberately unspecified and can differ from one JVM run to the next. Never write a test that depends on it.

LinkedHashMap: order, and an LRU cache

LinkedHashMap is a HashMap in which every entry also sits in a doubly linked list. Lookups are as fast as HashMap, and iteration follows the list. The list order is insertion order by default (re-inserting an existing key does not move it). With the constructor new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) the order becomes access order: every get or put of a key moves that entry to the end, so the first entry is always the least recently used.

The method protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) is called after each insert. If you return true, the eldest (first) entry is removed. Together these give an LRU cache (least recently used: when full, throw away the entry unused for the longest time) in a dozen lines:

import java.util.*;

public class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;

    public LruCache(int capacity) {
        super(16, 0.75f, true);              // true = access order
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
        return size() > capacity;              // evict when over capacity
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LruCache<String, Integer> cache = new LruCache<>(3);
        cache.put("a", 1);
        cache.put("b", 2);
        cache.put("c", 3);
        cache.get("a");                      // "a" becomes most recently used
        cache.put("d", 4);                   // size 4 > 3 → evict eldest, which is "b"
        System.out.println(cache);
    }
}
{c=3, a=1, d=4}

Remember two things. In access-order mode even get changes the structure, so calling get inside a loop over the same map throws ConcurrentModificationException. And the class is not thread-safe; wrap it with Collections.synchronizedMap or use a cache library for shared use. "Design an LRU cache" is a popular interview question; the other answer is your own hash map plus a doubly linked list (see the DSA notes).

Rule: keys are unique and a Map is not a Collection

A second put with an equal key replaces the value. Map does not extend Collection, so you cannot use it in a for-each loop directly or call stream() on it; use entrySet(), keySet() or values().

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NullPointerException — unboxing a missing value: int n = map.get("x"); where the key is absent. Use getOrDefault.
  • NullPointerException — null key in TreeMap / Map.of / ConcurrentHashMap.
  • UnsupportedOperationException — put on Map.of(…), Map.copyOf or Collections.unmodifiableMap.
  • ConcurrentModificationException — map.put or map.remove inside a loop over its own views. Use entrySet().removeIf(…) or map.values().removeIf(…).
  • computeIfAbsent with a function that modifies the same map throws ConcurrentModificationException in HashMap (this is why recursive memoisation with it is risky).
  • putIfAbsent and computeIfAbsent treat a key mapped to null as absent.

Conventions

  • Name maps by what they hold: customerById, ordersByStatus (valueByKey reads naturally: customerById.get(id)).
  • Use merge for counting and summing, computeIfAbsent for grouping.
  • Use an EnumMap when keys are enum constants: it is a compact array internally and iterates in enum order. WeakHashMap and IdentityHashMap exist for special cases.

Mistake: check-then-act on a shared map

if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v); is two steps. With a ConcurrentHashMap and several threads, another thread can insert between them. Use the single atomic call putIfAbsent or computeIfAbsent.

Interview: "HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap"

  • HashMap: no order, O(1), one null key. LinkedHashMap: insertion (or access) order, O(1), slightly more memory. TreeMap: sorted keys, O(log n), no null key, has NavigableMap methods.
  • "Build an LRU cache" → LinkedHashMap with access order and removeEldestEntry.
  • "Count word frequency" → map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum).

TreeMap and NavigableMap: sorted keys and range queries

TreeMap keeps its keys sorted in a red-black tree, so every operation costs O(log n) but you gain first/last, floor/ceiling and range views that a HashMap cannot do.

A TreeMap stores entries in a red-black tree: a self-balancing binary search tree in which the left child is smaller and the right child is larger. The tree rebalances itself on insert and delete, so its height stays about log₂(n). Searching 1,000,000 keys takes about 20 comparisons. Keys are sorted by their natural order (Comparable) or by a Comparator you pass to the constructor.

The NavigableMap methods

TreeMap implements NavigableMap (which extends SortedMap). These methods answer questions like "what is the nearest key to this value?" in O(log n).

MethodReturns
firstKey(), lastKey()Smallest and largest key (NoSuchElementException if empty)
firstEntry(), lastEntry()Same, as entries (null if empty)
floorKey(k)Greatest key ≤ k, or null
ceilingKey(k)Smallest key ≥ k, or null
lowerKey(k) / higherKey(k)Greatest key < k / smallest key > k (strict)
headMap(to), headMap(to, inclusive)View of keys below to (exclusive by default)
tailMap(from), tailMap(from, inclusive)View of keys from from upward (inclusive by default)
subMap(from, to)View of from (inclusive) up to to (exclusive)
descendingMap(), descendingKeySet()Reverse-order views
pollFirstEntry(), pollLastEntry()Remove and return the smallest / largest entry
 
import java.util.*;

public class TreeMapDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TreeMap<Integer, String> t = new TreeMap<>();
        for (int k : new int[] {30, 10, 50, 20, 40}) {
            t.put(k, "v" + k);                       // inserted in any order
        }
        System.out.println(t);                       // always sorted by key
        System.out.println(t.firstKey() + " " + t.lastKey());
        System.out.println(t.floorKey(25) + " " + t.ceilingKey(25));
        System.out.println(t.lowerKey(30) + " " + t.higherKey(30));
        System.out.println(t.floorKey(5));           // nothing at or below 5
        System.out.println(t.headMap(30));           // keys < 30
        System.out.println(t.headMap(30, true));     // keys <= 30
        System.out.println(t.tailMap(30));           // keys >= 30
        System.out.println(t.subMap(20, 40));        // 20 <= key < 40
        System.out.println(t.descendingMap());
        System.out.println(t.pollFirstEntry() + " -> " + t.firstKey());
    }
}
{10=v10, 20=v20, 30=v30, 40=v40, 50=v50}
10 50
20 30
20 40
null
{10=v10, 20=v20}
{10=v10, 20=v20, 30=v30}
{30=v30, 40=v40, 50=v50}
{20=v20, 30=v30}
{50=v50, 40=v40, 30=v30, 20=v20, 10=v10}
10=v10 -> 20

headMap, tailMap and subMap return views of the original map, like subList: changes write through. Putting a key outside a view's range into the view throws IllegalArgumentException.

A realistic use: slab lookup

Discounts by cart value ("₹500 and above: 5%", "₹1,000 and above: 10%") are a perfect fit for floorEntry: find the greatest slab start that is not above the amount.

TreeMap<Integer, Integer> slabs = new TreeMap<>();
slabs.put(0, 0);          // cart value from → discount percent
slabs.put(500, 5);
slabs.put(1000, 10);
slabs.put(5000, 15);

int[] carts = {120, 500, 1200, 9999};
for (int cart : carts) {
    System.out.println("Cart ₹" + cart + " → " + slabs.floorEntry(cart).getValue() + "%");
}
Cart ₹120 → 0%
Cart ₹500 → 5%
Cart ₹1200 → 10%
Cart ₹9999 → 15%

Other uses: time-series data keyed by timestamp (find the reading just before a time), leaderboards, interval and calendar problems, and "find the closest value" in interviews.

Custom ordering

TreeMap<String, Integer> byLength =
        new TreeMap<>(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
                .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
byLength.put("UPI", 1);
byLength.put("NEFT", 2);
byLength.put("IMPS", 3);
byLength.put("RTGS", 4);
System.out.println(byLength);       // {UPI=1, IMPS=3, NEFT=2, RTGS=4}

TreeMap<String, Integer> ci = new TreeMap<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
ci.put("Mumbai", 1);
ci.put("MUMBAI", 2);                // "equal" according to the comparator → replaces
System.out.println(ci);             // {Mumbai=2}

Rule: a TreeMap decides key equality with compareTo, not equals

If compare(a, b) == 0 the keys are the same key, whatever equals says. That is why the second put above replaced the first. Make your ordering consistent with equals (compare equal exactly when equals is true), or the map will behave differently from a HashMap holding the same data.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • ClassCastException — keys that are not Comparable and no comparator given. It is thrown on the very first put.
  • NullPointerException — a null key with natural ordering (null values are fine).
  • firstKey() on an empty map throws NoSuchElementException; firstEntry() returns null.
  • Not thread-safe. The concurrent sorted map is ConcurrentSkipListMap.
  • Iteration over a TreeMap is O(n) in sorted order; there is no capacity or load factor to tune.

Tip: sort once with TreeMap, or build a HashMap and sort at the end?

If you only need sorted output once, collect into a HashMap and then copy: new TreeMap<>(map). If you keep inserting and also query by range or nearest key, use a TreeMap all along.

Why the tree stays balanced

A plain binary search tree can degrade into a linked list if you insert sorted keys (1, 2, 3, 4…), and then every search costs O(n). A red-black tree prevents that with colour rules: the root is black, a red node never has a red child, and every path from the root to an empty spot has the same number of black nodes. After each put or remove the tree fixes itself with colour flips and rotations (small local re-arrangements). These rules guarantee that the longest path is at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most about 2·log₂(n+1). You never see this work; you only get O(log n) for get, put, remove, containsKey, floorKey and the other navigation methods.

TreeMap vs HashMap vs LinkedHashMap

PointHashMapLinkedHashMapTreeMap
Key orderNone guaranteedInsertion (or access) orderSorted by key
get / putO(1) averageO(1) averageO(log n)
Equality of keyshashCode + equalshashCode + equalscompareTo / comparator
null keyOne allowedOne allowedNot with natural ordering
Range and nearest-key queriesNoNoYes
MemoryTable + nodesMore (extra links)One node per entry, no table

See HashMap internals for the hash-based side and the other Map classes for LinkedHashMap. Choose TreeMap only when you need the sort or the navigation methods; otherwise HashMap is faster.

Entries, views and live changes

The entries returned by firstEntry(), floorEntry(k), pollFirstEntry() and the like are snapshots. Calling setValue on them throws UnsupportedOperationException; change the map with put instead. The entries you get while iterating entrySet() are the real ones and setValue works there.

TreeMap<Integer, String> t = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(10, "a", 20, "b", 30, "c", 40, "d"));
NavigableMap<Integer, String> mid = t.subMap(15, true, 35, true);   // 20 and 30
System.out.println(mid);                  // {20=b, 30=c}

t.put(25, "x");                           // change the original map...
System.out.println(mid);                  // {20=b, 25=x, 30=c}  ...the view sees it

mid.remove(20);                           // change the view...
System.out.println(t);                    // {10=a, 25=x, 30=c, 40=d}  ...the map changes

try {
    mid.put(99, "out");                   // outside 15..35
} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
    System.out.println("key out of range");
}
{20=b, 30=c}
{20=b, 25=x, 30=c}
{10=a, 25=x, 30=c, 40=d}
key out of range

The four-argument subMap(from, fromInclusive, to, toInclusive) lets you choose either end. The same idea exists for sets: TreeSet is built on a TreeMap and offers floor, ceiling, headSet, tailSet and subSet (see Sets).

Another realistic use: the reading just before a time

Sensor readings, price history or audit entries keyed by a timestamp. "What was the price at 10:07?" is the entry with the greatest key not after 10:07.

TreeMap<LocalTime, Integer> price = new TreeMap<>();
price.put(LocalTime.of(9, 15), 2400);
price.put(LocalTime.of(10, 0), 2450);
price.put(LocalTime.of(11, 30), 2390);

var at = LocalTime.of(10, 7);
System.out.println("At 10:07 → " + price.floorEntry(at).getValue());        // 2450
System.out.println("Next change → " + price.higherKey(at));                  // 11:30
System.out.println("Before open → " + price.floorEntry(LocalTime.of(9, 0))); // null

Always check for null from floorEntry, ceilingEntry, lowerEntry and higherEntry: there may be no such key.

Mistake: BigDecimal keys and other "equal but not equals" keys

new BigDecimal("1.0") and new BigDecimal("1.00") are not equals, but compareTo returns 0. A HashMap keeps two entries; a TreeMap keeps one and overwrites the value. Neither is wrong, but you must know which one you have. The reverse also happens: a comparator that looks at only one field (say, the name) treats two different employees with the same name as one key, and the second silently replaces the first.

Wrong: changing a key's sort field after insertion

TreeMap<Employee, String> m = new TreeMap<>(
        Comparator.comparing(Employee::getSalary));
m.put(emp, "Pune");
emp.setSalary(900_000);        // the tree is now in the wrong order
m.get(emp);                    // may return null

Right: remove, change, re-insert

String city = m.remove(emp);
emp.setSalary(900_000);
m.put(emp, city);
// better: use an immutable key such as an id or a record

More edge cases

  • ConcurrentModificationException — you change the map (not through the iterator) while iterating it. Remove with iterator.remove() or entrySet().removeIf(...).
  • headMap(k) returns keys below k; tailMap(k) includes k. This asymmetry is a frequent off-by-one, so pass the inclusive flag explicitly.
  • Do not use size() on a sub-map in a hot loop: counting a view walks the entries, so it is O(n) rather than O(1).

Conventions

  • Declare the variable as NavigableMap<K, V> when you use navigation methods, or as Map when you only need sorted iteration.
  • Pass a comparator built with Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...) and include a unique field (like an id) at the end so that different objects never compare as equal by accident.
  • Use immutable keys: String, numbers, LocalDate, records.

Interview: "When would you use TreeMap?"

  • When keys must stay sorted or you need range/nearest queries: floorKey, ceilingKey, headMap, tailMap.
  • Cost: O(log n) per operation, no null key, keys need an ordering consistent with equals.
  • Internals: red-black tree (a balanced BST); height stays O(log n).

Set: HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet

A Set holds no duplicates; HashSet is a HashMap in disguise and is the fast default, LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order, and TreeSet keeps elements sorted.

A Set<E> is a collection with no duplicate elements and no index. Use it for "have I seen this before?", unique tags, unique ids, and to remove duplicates. The main method is add(e), which returns true if the element was new and false if an equal element was already there.

import java.util.*;

public class SetBasics {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Set<String> emails = new HashSet<>();
        System.out.println(emails.add("a@x.in"));      // true  — new
        System.out.println(emails.add("a@x.in"));      // false — duplicate ignored
        System.out.println(emails.size());             // 1
        System.out.println(emails.contains("a@x.in")); // true, O(1)

        List<Integer> withDupes = List.of(3, 1, 3, 2, 1);
        System.out.println(new LinkedHashSet<>(withDupes));   // dedupe, keep order
    }
}
true
false
1
true
[3, 1, 2]

HashSet — a HashMap inside

HashSet is implemented with a HashMap. Your element is stored as the key, and every key points to the same dummy object (a private static constant named PRESENT). So add(e) is map.put(e, PRESENT) == null, and everything you learned in How HashMap works inside applies: buckets, load factor, collisions, resizing. Elements need correct equals and hashCode; do not mutate them while they are in the set; the iteration order is undefined; one null is allowed.

LinkedHashSet

A HashSet that also threads its elements on a linked list (it uses LinkedHashMap inside). It iterates in insertion order, costs a little more memory, and is still O(1). Re-adding an existing element does not change its position. Since Java 21 it is a SequencedSet with getFirst, getLast and reversed. The most common use: remove duplicates but keep the original order.

TreeSet — sorted

TreeSet uses a TreeMap inside, so it is a red-black tree: elements stay sorted, and add, remove and contains are O(log n). It implements NavigableSet, which gives first(), last(), floor(e), ceiling(e), lower(e), higher(e), headSet, tailSet, subSet, descendingSet(), pollFirst() and pollLast(). These work exactly like the TreeMap methods in the previous article.

TreeSet<Integer> marks = new TreeSet<>(List.of(72, 91, 55, 88, 91));
System.out.println(marks);                    // sorted, duplicate 91 dropped
System.out.println(marks.first() + " " + marks.last());
System.out.println(marks.floor(80) + " " + marks.ceiling(80));
System.out.println(marks.headSet(72));        // below 72
System.out.println(marks.tailSet(88));        // 88 and above
System.out.println(marks.descendingSet());
[55, 72, 88, 91]
55 91
72 88
[55]
[88, 91]
[91, 88, 72, 55]

Comparator must be consistent with equals
