A TreeSet never calls equals; two elements are "the same" when compareTo (or the comparator) returns 0. For well-behaved classes both agree. BigDecimal is the famous exception: new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00")) is false (the scales differ) while compareTo returns 0.

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.*;

Set<BigDecimal> hash = new HashSet<>();
Set<BigDecimal> tree = new TreeSet<>();
for (String s : new String[] {"1.0", "1.00"}) {
    hash.add(new BigDecimal(s));
    tree.add(new BigDecimal(s));
}
System.out.println("HashSet size = " + hash.size());
System.out.println("TreeSet size = " + tree.size());
HashSet size = 2
TreeSet size = 1

For your own classes: if you sort by a single field (say salary) and put employees into a TreeSet, two different employees with the same salary will be treated as duplicates and one silently disappears. Always add a tie-breaker (thenComparing(Employee::id)).

Set operations

The bulk methods give you the maths operations. They modify the set you call them on, so copy first.

OperationCode
Union (A ∪ B)result.addAll(b)
Intersection (A ∩ B)result.retainAll(b)
Difference (A − B)result.removeAll(b)
Subset (B ⊆ A)a.containsAll(b)
 
Set<Integer> a = new TreeSet<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4));
Set<Integer> b = new TreeSet<>(List.of(3, 4, 5, 6));

Set<Integer> union = new TreeSet<>(a);
union.addAll(b);
Set<Integer> common = new TreeSet<>(a);
common.retainAll(b);
Set<Integer> onlyA = new TreeSet<>(a);
onlyA.removeAll(b);
Set<Integer> either = new TreeSet<>(union);       // symmetric difference
either.removeAll(common);

System.out.println(union + " " + common);
System.out.println(onlyA + " " + either);
System.out.println(a.containsAll(common));
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] [3, 4]
[1, 2] [1, 2, 5, 6]
true

Run time of removeAll depends on the argument: with a List argument it can be O(n·m), so pass a set.

Immutable sets and EnumSet

Set.of(a, b, c) and Set.copyOf(c) are immutable, reject null (even in contains(null), which throws), throw IllegalArgumentException on duplicate elements in Set.of, and have an unspecified iteration order. EnumSet is a very fast, compact set for enum values (internally a bit mask).

Rule: uniqueness comes from equals/hashCode (hash sets) or compare (tree sets)

A HashSet of objects whose class has no hashCode override accepts "duplicates". A TreeSet of objects that are not Comparable throws ClassCastException on the first add.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • TreeSet.add(null) throws NullPointerException; HashSet and LinkedHashSet allow one null.
  • Mutating an element after adding it (changing a field used by hashCode or the ordering) breaks contains and remove, as with map keys.
  • A set has no get(i). To read one element, iterate, or use a sorted/sequenced set method such as first().
  • NoSuchElementException — TreeSet.first() on an empty set; pollFirst() returns null instead.

Mistake: expecting a HashSet to keep the order you added

A HashSet of strings prints in an order that looks random. If the order matters, use LinkedHashSet; if the sort matters, use TreeSet.

Real projects

Sets hold roles and authorities (Set<String> roles in a user), visited ids in graph searches, permission checks, and many-to-many JPA associations (Set<Course> avoids duplicate rows and the "multiple bag fetch" problem). Always give JPA entities a sensible equals/hashCode before putting them in a Set.

Interview: "How does HashSet work?" and "HashSet vs TreeSet"

  • HashSet is backed by a HashMap: the element is the key, the value is a constant dummy object. add returns false for duplicates. O(1) average.
  • LinkedHashSet adds insertion order. TreeSet adds sorted order with O(log n) and NavigableSet methods.
  • Duplicate detection: hashCode + equals for hash sets; compareTo / comparator for TreeSet — and they should agree.

Queue and Deque: ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue and legacy classes

Use ArrayDeque for every stack and plain queue, PriorityQueue when you always need the smallest (or largest) element next, and avoid Stack, Vector and Hashtable.

A queue holds elements waiting to be processed — print jobs, Swiggy orders, tasks. A Queue normally works first in, first out (FIFO). A stack works last in, first out (LIFO): think of the browser's back button. A Deque (double-ended queue) can add and remove at both ends, so one class serves as a queue and as a stack.

The Queue methods: two versions of each

Every queue operation exists twice: one version throws an exception on failure, the other returns a special value.

OperationThrows an exceptionReturns null / false
Insert at the tailadd(e)offer(e)
Remove the headremove()poll()
Look at the head (no removal)element()peek()

remove() and element() throw NoSuchElementException on an empty queue; poll() and peek() return null. add throws IllegalStateException("Queue full") when a bounded queue has no room; offer returns false. Prefer offer/poll/peek in normal code.

The Deque interface repeats the set for both ends: addFirst/offerFirst, addLast/offerLast, removeFirst/pollFirst, removeLast/pollLast, getFirst/peekFirst, getLast/peekLast. For stack use it adds three names: push(e) = addFirst, pop() = removeFirst, and peek() = peekFirst.

ArrayDeque

ArrayDeque is a resizable circular array with a head and a tail index. Adding or removing at either end is O(1) amortized and needs no object allocation per element. It is faster than LinkedList as a queue and faster than Stack as a stack. It does not allow null elements (because poll() uses null to mean "empty") and is not thread-safe.

import java.util.*;

public class QueueAndStack {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // As a QUEUE (FIFO): offer at the tail, poll from the head
        Queue<String> orders = new ArrayDeque<>();
        orders.offer("order-1");
        orders.offer("order-2");
        orders.offer("order-3");
        System.out.println(orders.peek());     // order-1 (not removed)
        System.out.println(orders.poll());     // order-1 (removed)
        System.out.println(orders);

        // As a STACK (LIFO): push and pop at the head
        Deque<String> history = new ArrayDeque<>();
        history.push("home");
        history.push("search");
        history.push("product");
        System.out.println(history);           // top of the stack is on the left
        System.out.println(history.pop());     // product
        System.out.println(history.peek());    // search

        Queue<String> empty = new ArrayDeque<>();
        System.out.println(empty.poll());      // null
        try {
            empty.remove();
        } catch (NoSuchElementException e) {
            System.out.println("remove() on empty queue throws");
        }
    }
}
order-1
order-1
[order-2, order-3]
[product, search, home]
product
search
null
remove() on empty queue throws

A classic stack use case — checking balanced brackets:

static boolean isBalanced(String s) {
    Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
        switch (c) {
            case '(', '[', '{' -> stack.push(c);
            case ')' -> { if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.pop() != '(') return false; }
            case ']' -> { if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.pop() != '[') return false; }
            case '}' -> { if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.pop() != '{') return false; }
            default -> { }
        }
    }
    return stack.isEmpty();
}

System.out.println(isBalanced("{[()]}"));   // true
System.out.println(isBalanced("{[(])}"));   // false

PriorityQueue — always the smallest next

A PriorityQueue is a queue ordered by priority, not by arrival. poll() always returns the smallest element according to natural order or a Comparator. Inside it is a binary min-heap stored in an array: a complete binary tree in which every parent is ≤ its children, so the smallest element is always at index 0. For index i, the parent is at (i - 1) / 2 and the children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

  • offer and poll: O(log n) (the height of the tree). peek: O(1).
  • contains and remove(Object): O(n) — a heap is not searchable.
  • Default initial capacity 11; it grows automatically. No null elements. Not thread-safe (use PriorityBlockingQueue).
  • Elements must be Comparable, or you pass a Comparator; otherwise ClassCastException.
  • Iteration and toString() are not sorted. They show the array order. Only poll() gives sorted order.
  • Elements with equal priority come out in no guaranteed order (it is not a stable queue).
import java.util.*;

public class PriorityQueueDemo {
    record Task(String name, int priority) {}      // 1 = most urgent

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();
        for (int n : new int[] {5, 1, 4, 2, 3}) {
            minHeap.offer(n);
        }
        System.out.println(minHeap);               // heap array, NOT sorted
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        while (!minHeap.isEmpty()) {
            sb.append(minHeap.poll()).append(' ');
        }
        System.out.println(sb);

        // Max-heap: reverse the order
        PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
        maxHeap.addAll(List.of(5, 1, 4, 2, 3));
        System.out.println(maxHeap.poll() + " " + maxHeap.poll());

        // Objects with a comparator
        PriorityQueue<Task> tasks =
                new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority));
        tasks.offer(new Task("Pay bill", 2));
        tasks.offer(new Task("Send newsletter", 5));
        tasks.offer(new Task("Fix prod bug", 1));
        while (!tasks.isEmpty()) {
            System.out.println(tasks.poll());
        }

        // Top-3 largest numbers with a min-heap of size 3
        int[] data = {7, 2, 9, 4, 11, 5};
        PriorityQueue<Integer> top = new PriorityQueue<>();
        for (int x : data) {
            top.offer(x);
            if (top.size() > 3) {
                top.poll();                         // drop the smallest of the four
            }
        }
        List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!top.isEmpty()) {
            result.add(top.poll());
        }
        System.out.println("Top 3: " + result);
    }
}
[1, 2, 4, 5, 3]
1 2 3 4 5
5 4
Task[name=Fix prod bug, priority=1]
Task[name=Pay bill, priority=2]
Task[name=Send newsletter, priority=5]
Top 3: [7, 9, 11]

The top-K trick is a favourite in interviews: a min-heap of size K keeps the K largest items in O(n log K) time and O(K) memory, without sorting everything.

Legacy classes and why to avoid them

Legacy classProblemUse instead
VectorEvery method is synchronized: slow, and still not safe for compound actions like check-then-addArrayList (or CopyOnWriteArrayList if shared)
StackExtends Vector (so it is synchronized and exposes get(i), add(i, e), breaking the stack idea)ArrayDeque through the Deque interface
HashtableOne lock for the whole map; no null keys or valuesHashMap, or ConcurrentHashMap when shared
EnumerationOld iteration interfaceIterator

One visible difference: Stack iterates from bottom to top, while an ArrayDeque used with push iterates top to bottom. For thread-safe queues (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue, ConcurrentLinkedQueue) see Module 6; they power producer-consumer designs.

Rule: choose by the operations you need

FIFO queue or LIFO stack → ArrayDeque. Always the smallest or largest next → PriorityQueue. Need null elements or List methods too → LinkedList (rare).

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NullPointerException — offer(null) or push(null) on ArrayDeque or PriorityQueue.
  • NoSuchElementException — remove(), element(), pop(), getFirst() on an empty queue or deque.
  • ClassCastException — a PriorityQueue of objects that are not Comparable and no comparator. It fails on the first offer.
  • ArrayDeque.push adds at the front; if you want stack order but then add at the end, you get a mix. Pick one set of method names and stick to it.

Mistake: printing or looping a PriorityQueue to see the order

The output [1, 2, 4, 5, 3] for the values 1 to 5 surprises many people. Sorted order exists only when you poll() repeatedly. If you need a sorted snapshot, copy to a list and sort it.

Mistake: a subtraction comparator in a PriorityQueue

(a, b) -> a - b overflows for large ints and silently breaks the heap order. Use Integer.compare(a, b) or Comparator.comparingInt (details in Comparable vs Comparator).

Interview: "Stack vs ArrayDeque", "How does PriorityQueue work?"

  • Do not use Stack: it is a synchronized Vector subclass. Deque<Integer> s = new ArrayDeque<>() with push/pop/peek is the standard.
  • PriorityQueue: binary min-heap in an array; offer/poll O(log n), peek O(1); max-heap with Comparator.reverseOrder(); iteration is not sorted.
  • Queue method pairs: add/offer, remove/poll, element/peek — exception vs special value.
  • Use cases: BFS (queue), DFS and undo (stack), Dijkstra, top-K, task scheduling (priority queue).

Iteration: Iterator, ListIterator and ConcurrentModificationException

An Iterator walks a collection one element at a time and is the only safe way to remove elements during a loop; changing a collection behind a running loop's back throws ConcurrentModificationException.

To visit every element of a collection you have four tools: an index loop (lists only), the enhanced for loop, an explicit Iterator, and forEach with a lambda. Behind the second, third and fourth sits the same idea: the Iterator.

Iterator

An Iterator<E> is a cursor that moves through a collection. Every Collection has an iterator() method (it comes from Iterable).

MethodMeaning
boolean hasNext()Is there another element?
E next()Return the next element and move forward; NoSuchElementException if none is left
void remove()Remove the element last returned by next(); IllegalStateException if next() was not called first, or if you call it twice in a row
void forEachRemaining(action)Apply a lambda to all remaining elements

The enhanced for loop is syntax sugar. The compiler rewrites it into an iterator loop, which is exactly why the same exceptions appear:

for (String name : names) {
    System.out.println(name);
}

// is compiled to roughly:
for (Iterator<String> it = names.iterator(); it.hasNext(); ) {
    String name = it.next();
    System.out.println(name);
}

Any class that implements Iterable<T> can be used in a for-each loop. You only write iterator():

import java.util.Iterator;

public class Range implements Iterable<Integer> {
    private final int from, to;                 // from inclusive, to exclusive

    public Range(int from, int to) {
        this.from = from;
        this.to = to;
    }

    @Override
    public Iterator<Integer> iterator() {
        return new Iterator<>() {
            private int next = from;
            @Override public boolean hasNext() { return next < to; }
            @Override public Integer next() { return next++; }
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int n : new Range(1, 5)) {
            System.out.print(n + " ");
        }
    }
}
1 2 3 4

An array cannot be used as an Iterable directly, but it works in for-each because the compiler treats arrays specially.

ListIterator — both directions, with set and add

list.listIterator() returns a ListIterator, available only for lists. It can move backwards (hasPrevious, previous), report positions (nextIndex, previousIndex), and change the list while walking: set(e) replaces the last returned element and add(e) inserts at the cursor. list.listIterator(list.size()) starts at the end.

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));

ListIterator<String> it = list.listIterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    String s = it.next();
    if (s.equals("b")) {
        it.set("B");           // replace the element just returned
        it.add("b2");          // insert after it
    }
}
System.out.println(list);

ListIterator<String> back = list.listIterator(list.size());
while (back.hasPrevious()) {
    System.out.print(back.previous() + " ");     // walk backwards
}
[a, B, b2, c]
c b2 B a

Fail-fast iterators and ConcurrentModificationException

Collections such as ArrayList, HashMap and HashSet keep a counter named modCount that goes up on every structural modification (add, remove, clear — anything that changes the size; set(i, e) and changing a map value do not count). When an iterator is created it remembers the counter. On every next() it compares the two values. If they differ, someone changed the collection behind the iterator's back, and it throws ConcurrentModificationException (CME) immediately — it fails fast instead of returning garbage later.

  1. iterator() stores expectedModCount = modCount.
  2. Your loop body calls list.remove(…), so modCount increases.
  3. The next call to it.next() sees modCount != expectedModCount and throws.
  4. it.remove() removes and then updates expectedModCount, so it never triggers the exception.
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha", "Ravi", "Meera", "Kiran"));
try {
    for (String n : names) {
        if (n.equals("Ravi")) {
            names.remove(n);               // structural change inside the loop
        }
    }
} catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) {
    System.out.println("CME thrown");
}

// A surprise: remove the SECOND-TO-LAST element and nothing is thrown
List<String> three = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha", "Ravi", "Meera"));
for (String n : three) {
    System.out.println("visiting " + n);
    if (n.equals("Ravi")) {
        three.remove(n);
    }
}
System.out.println(three);
CME thrown
visiting Asha
visiting Ravi
[Asha, Meera]

In the second loop, after removing "Ravi" the size drops to 2 and the cursor is also 2, so hasNext() says "finished" and the check in next() never runs — "Meera" is silently skipped. This is why fail-fast is only best effort: it helps find bugs, but you must never write code that depends on the exception being thrown.

The right ways to remove while iterating

List<String> base = List.of("Asha", "Ravi", "Meera", "Kiran");

// 1. Iterator.remove() — works for every Collection
List<String> a = new ArrayList<>(base);
Iterator<String> it = a.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().startsWith("R")) {
        it.remove();
    }
}

// 2. removeIf(predicate) — the shortest and best (Java 8+)
List<String> b = new ArrayList<>(base);
b.removeIf(n -> n.startsWith("R"));

// 3. Build a new list with a stream
List<String> c = base.stream().filter(n -> !n.startsWith("R")).toList();

// 4. Map: remove through a view
Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(Map.of("pen", 0, "book", 4));
stock.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue() == 0);

System.out.println(a + " " + b + " " + c + " " + stock);
[Asha, Meera, Kiran] [Asha, Meera, Kiran] [Asha, Meera, Kiran] {book=4}

A fifth way for lists only: loop by index from the end to the start, removing as you go (removing from the end never shifts the indexes you have not visited). It works but removeIf is cleaner.

Fail-safe and weakly consistent iterators

The collections in java.util.concurrent never throw CME. They work in two styles (the name "fail-safe" is common in interviews, but the Javadoc does not use it):

  • CopyOnWriteArrayList — every write copies the whole array, and an iterator walks a snapshot taken at the time the iterator was created. It never sees later changes. Good for lists that are read a lot and written rarely, such as listener lists. Its iterator does not support remove().
  • ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue — weakly consistent iterators. They work on the live structure, may or may not show changes made after creation, and never throw CME.
PointFail-fast (ArrayList, HashMap)Snapshot / weakly consistent (concurrent classes)
Change during iterationThrows CME (best effort)No exception
Sees changes made after creationNot applicable — it throwsSnapshot: never. Weak: maybe
iterator.remove()SupportedSnapshot: not supported. Concurrent map: supported
CostNoneCopy cost on every write (CopyOnWriteArrayList)

CME is not only about threads. The example above fails with a single thread. With several threads, a plain ArrayList needs real synchronisation or a concurrent collection (Module 6).

Rule: never structurally modify a collection while iterating it, except through the iterator

Use Iterator.remove() (or ListIterator.add/set/remove), removeIf, or build a new collection. Calling list.add/list.remove/map.put/map.remove inside a for-each over the same collection is a bug even when it happens to run.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • ConcurrentModificationException — structural change during iteration, including from subList views whose parent changed, and a get inside a loop over an access-order LinkedHashMap.
  • NoSuchElementException — next() after hasNext() returned false.
  • IllegalStateException — remove() before the first next(), or twice after one next().
  • UnsupportedOperationException — remove() on the iterator of an immutable collection.
  • Changing the value of an existing map entry (entry.setValue, or map.put for an existing key) during iteration is allowed; adding or removing keys is not.

Mistake: counting on the CME

Do not write try { for … remove } catch (CME) as flow control. The "second-to-last" case shows the exception is not guaranteed. Fix the loop instead.

Tip: which loop to use

  • Just reading: for-each. Need the index or going backwards: index loop or ListIterator.
  • Removing: removeIf. Transforming into another collection: streams (Module 5).
  • Map: loop over entrySet() or use map.forEach((k, v) -> …).

Interview: "What is ConcurrentModificationException? How do you avoid it?"

  • Thrown by fail-fast iterators when the collection's modCount changes during iteration, by anything other than the iterator itself.
  • Avoid with Iterator.remove(), removeIf, a new filtered list, or a concurrent collection (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap).
  • Fail-fast is best effort, not a guarantee (the second-to-last example); the for-each loop is an iterator in disguise.
  • Fail-fast vs fail-safe: concurrent collections give snapshot or weakly consistent iterators.

Comparable vs Comparator: sorting objects

Comparable defines the one natural order inside the class itself; Comparator defines any number of orders outside it, and the comparing/thenComparing helpers make sorting by several fields a one-liner.

Sorting needs a rule for "which of these two comes first". Java gives you two ways to supply the rule.

Comparable — the natural order

A class implements Comparable<T> and its single method int compareTo(T other). The result is negative if this comes before other, zero if they are equal in order, and positive if this comes after. String, all number wrappers, LocalDate, BigDecimal and enums already implement it, so Collections.sort(listOfStrings) just works. Sorted collections (TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue) and Arrays.sort(Object[]) use it when you give no comparator.

The compareTo contract:

  • Antisymmetry — sign(x.compareTo(y)) == -sign(y.compareTo(x)).
  • Transitivity — if x > y and y > z, then x > z.
  • Consistency — if x.compareTo(y) == 0, then x and y sort the same against every other element.
  • Recommended: consistent with equals — x.compareTo(y) == 0 exactly when x.equals(y). If not, say so in the Javadoc; BigDecimal is the known exception.
  • x.compareTo(null) must throw NullPointerException.

Comparator — any order you like, outside the class

A Comparator<T> has one abstract method, int compare(T a, T b), with the same negative/zero/positive meaning. Because it is a functional interface, you write it as a lambda. You pass it to list.sort(cmp), Collections.sort(list, cmp), Arrays.sort(array, cmp), stream.sorted(cmp), or the constructors of TreeSet, TreeMap and PriorityQueue. Use it when the class has no natural order, you cannot change the class, or you need several orders.

The Comparator helper methods

MethodPurpose
Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor)Compare by a key taken from each object (the key must be Comparable)
comparing(keyExtractor, keyComparator)Same, with a custom comparator for the key
comparingInt / comparingLong / comparingDoublePrimitive keys, no boxing
thenComparing(…), thenComparingInt(…)Tie-breaker when the first comparison says equal
reversed()The opposite order
Comparator.naturalOrder() / reverseOrder()The natural order, or its reverse
Comparator.nullsFirst(cmp) / nullsLast(cmp)Wrap a comparator so null elements are allowed

Sorting a list of employees

import java.util.*;

public class SortingDemo {
    record Employee(int id, String name, String dept, double salary)
            implements Comparable<Employee> {

        @Override
        public int compareTo(Employee other) {           // natural order: by id
            return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id);
        }
    }

    static String names(List<Employee> list) {
        return list.stream().map(Employee::name).toList().toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> staff = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
                new Employee(3, "Ravi", "IT", 90000),
                new Employee(1, "Asha", "HR", 65000),
                new Employee(2, "Meera", "IT", 90000),
                new Employee(4, "Kiran", "HR", 72000)));

        Collections.sort(staff);                            // uses compareTo
        System.out.println("By id:          " + names(staff));

        staff.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::name));
        System.out.println("By name:        " + names(staff));

        staff.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::salary).reversed()
                .thenComparing(Employee::name));
        System.out.println("Salary desc, name: " + names(staff));

        staff.sort(Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
                .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())
                .thenComparing(Employee::name));
        System.out.println("Dept, salary desc: " + names(staff));

        List<String> withNull = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("Ravi", null, "Asha"));
        withNull.sort(Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
        System.out.println(withNull);
        withNull.sort(Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
        System.out.println(withNull);
    }
}
By id:          [Asha, Meera, Ravi, Kiran]
By name:        [Asha, Kiran, Meera, Ravi]
Salary desc, name: [Meera, Ravi, Kiran, Asha]
Dept, salary desc: [Kiran, Asha, Meera, Ravi]
[null, Asha, Ravi]
[Asha, Ravi, null]

Read the chain like a sentence: "order by department, then by salary descending, then by name". Each thenComparing is used only when all earlier comparators returned zero.

Comparable vs Comparator

PointComparable<T>Comparator<T>
Packagejava.langjava.util
MethodcompareTo(T other) — one argumentcompare(T a, T b) — two arguments
Where it livesInside the class being sortedIn a separate class, lambda or static constant
Number of ordersOne (the natural order)As many as you want
Change the class?Yes — the class must implement itNo — works with classes you cannot edit
Used automatically byCollections.sort(list), TreeMap, TreeSetOnly when you pass it in

The subtraction bug

A very common comparator is (a, b) -> a - b. It is wrong for large values because integer subtraction can overflow and flip the sign.

Comparator<Integer> bad = (a, b) -> a - b;
System.out.println(bad.compare(Integer.MAX_VALUE, -1));          // MAX − (−1) overflows
System.out.println(Integer.compare(Integer.MAX_VALUE, -1));      // correct

Comparator<Double> alsoBad = (a, b) -> (int) (a - b);
System.out.println(alsoBad.compare(1.2, 1.0));                   // (int) 0.2 = 0 → "equal"
-2147483648
1
0

The first comparator claims MAX_VALUE is smaller than −1. Always use Integer.compare, Double.compare, Long.compare or Comparator.comparingInt(…).

Other details worth knowing

  • Stability. List.sort, Collections.sort and Arrays.sort(Object[], cmp) use TimSort, which is stable: elements that compare equal keep their original relative order. That is why sorting by salary and then by dept is not the same as one chained sort — chaining is the safe way. Arrays.sort(int[]) uses dual-pivot quicksort; stability does not matter for primitives.
  • Lambda type inference with reversed(). Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary).reversed() compiles, but Comparator.comparing(e -> e.salary()).reversed() does not: with a lambda the compiler cannot infer the type of e through the chained call. Use a method reference, write (Employee e) -> …, or use comparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder()).
  • Records can share one comparator. Keep a static final Comparator<Employee> and call it from compareTo so the rule is written once.
  • Comparison is a total order. A comparator that is inconsistent (says A < B, B < C, C < A) can make TimSort throw IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!.

Rule: compare must be antisymmetric, transitive and null-safe by design

Handle ties with thenComparing. If you sort by one field and put objects in a TreeSet or use them as TreeMap keys, objects that tie are treated as duplicates. Include a unique field such as the id as the last tie-breaker.

Conventions

  • Implement Comparable only when the order is obvious and unique (ids, dates, versions, money). Otherwise write Comparators.
  • Keep reusable comparators as named static final constants: BY_SALARY_DESC.
  • Prefer comparingInt/comparingDouble for primitive fields and Integer.compare over subtraction.
  • Keep compareTo consistent with equals and document it when it is not.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • ClassCastException: class X cannot be cast to class java.lang.Comparable — sorting or adding to a TreeSet objects of a class that does not implement Comparable with no comparator supplied.
  • NullPointerException — a null element or a null key (for example a null name in comparing(Employee::name)). Wrap the key comparator with nullsFirst or nullsLast.
  • String.compareTo is case-sensitive: uppercase letters sort before lowercase. Use String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER or a Collator for language-aware sorting.
  • Double.compare treats NaN as greater than everything and -0.0 as less than 0.0, unlike the < operator.

Mistake: a comparator that cannot handle ties or overflow

Returning only -1 or 1 (never 0) for equal items, or using subtraction, breaks the contract. Delegate to Integer.compare or the Comparator factory methods.

Real projects

Most sorting in a Spring Boot app is done by the database (ORDER BY, Spring Data Sort). Java comparators are used for in-memory lists, stream pipelines (sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::createdAt).reversed())) and priority queues in schedulers.

Interview: "Comparable vs Comparator"

  • Comparable: one natural order, compareTo(T), inside the class, java.lang. Comparator: many orders, compare(T, T), outside the class, java.util.
  • Show chaining: Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept).thenComparing(Employee::salary).reversed() — and mention nullsFirst.
  • Mention the subtraction overflow bug and stable sorting (TimSort).
  • "What does a TreeSet do with two objects whose comparator returns 0?" Keeps only one — consistency with equals.

The Collections utility class and immutable collections

Collections and Arrays hold ready-made static algorithms, and Java gives you five different "read-only-ish" list factories whose differences — view or copy, nulls, fixed size or immutable — are a favourite source of bugs and interview questions.

java.util.Collections (plural, a class of static methods) is the toolbox for the collection types. Remember: Collection is the interface, Collections is the helper class.

The methods you will use

MethodWhat it does
sort(list), sort(list, cmp)Sort a list in place (stable TimSort, O(n log n))
reverse(list), shuffle(list), swap(list, i, j), rotate(list, d)Reorder in place; shuffle accepts a seeded Random
max(c), min(c) (and with a comparator)Largest or smallest element; NoSuchElementException on empty
frequency(c, o)How many elements equal o
nCopies(n, o)An immutable list of n copies of one object
binarySearch(list, key)Index of the key in a sorted list; −(insertion point) − 1 if absent
unmodifiableList/Set/Map(c)Read-only view of another collection
synchronizedList/Set/Map(c)Thread-safe wrapper with one lock on every method
emptyList(), emptySet(), emptyMap(), singletonList(x)Immutable shared empty or single-element collections
addAll(c, a, b, c…), disjoint(c1, c2), fill, reverseOrder()Add several; true if no common element; overwrite all; reverse comparator
 
import java.util.*;

public class CollectionsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 3, 8, 1));

        Collections.sort(nums);
        System.out.println(nums);
        Collections.reverse(nums);
        System.out.println(nums);
        Collections.swap(nums, 0, 3);
        System.out.println(nums);
        System.out.println(Collections.max(nums) + " " + Collections.min(nums));

        List<Integer> marks = List.of(1, 3, 3, 2);
        System.out.println(Collections.frequency(marks, 3));
        System.out.println(Collections.nCopies(3, "ab"));

        List<Integer> sorted = List.of(1, 3, 5, 8);        // binarySearch needs sorted input
        System.out.println(Collections.binarySearch(sorted, 5));
        System.out.println(Collections.binarySearch(sorted, 4));   // −(2) − 1

        List<Integer> r = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
        Collections.rotate(r, 2);
        System.out.println(r);

        Collections.shuffle(nums);                              // different every run
        Collections.shuffle(nums, new Random(42));              // repeatable with a seed
    }
}
[1, 3, 5, 8]
[8, 5, 3, 1]
[1, 5, 3, 8]
8 1
2
[ab, ab, ab]
2
-3
[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]

Collections.sort needs a mutable list. On List.of(…) it throws UnsupportedOperationException because it writes into the list. The Arrays class is the same idea for arrays: Arrays.sort, Arrays.fill, Arrays.copyOf, Arrays.copyOfRange, Arrays.equals, Arrays.toString, Arrays.deepToString, Arrays.binarySearch and Arrays.asList.

Immutable, unmodifiable, fixed-size, view, copy — the table

Six ways to get a list look alike but behave very differently:

Methodadd / removeset(i, e)NullsView or copy
Arrays.asList(array)Throws (fixed size)AllowedAllowedView of the array: writes go both ways
List.of(a, b, …) (Java 9)ThrowsThrowsNPE, even in contains(null)Independent immutable list
Collections.unmodifiableList(list)ThrowsThrowsAllowedRead-only view; sees changes made to the original
List.copyOf(collection) (Java 10)ThrowsThrowsNPEImmutable copy (may return the same instance if already immutable)
stream.toList() (Java 16)ThrowsThrowsAllowedNew unmodifiable list
new ArrayList<>(collection)AllowedAllowedAllowedMutable copy
 
String[] arr = {"a", "b", "c"};
List<String> fixed = Arrays.asList(arr);
fixed.set(0, "A");                          // allowed, writes through to the array
System.out.println(arr[0]);
try {
    fixed.add("d");                         // fixed size
} catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) {
    System.out.println("asList: cannot add");
}

List<String> src = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(src);
List<String> snap = List.copyOf(src);
src.add("z");
System.out.println(view);                   // the view shows the change
System.out.println(snap);                   // the copy does not

try {
    List.of("a", null);
} catch (NullPointerException e) {
    System.out.println("List.of: NPE for null");
}

int[] prim = {1, 2, 3};
System.out.println(Arrays.asList(prim).size());   // a List with ONE element: the array
A
asList: cannot add
[x, y, z]
[x, y]
List.of: NPE for null
1

The last line is a classic trap: Arrays.asList(int[]) does not box the numbers, because a generic method cannot take a primitive array as T…; it makes a List<int[]> with a single element. Use an Integer[], List.of(1, 2, 3) or Arrays.stream(prim).boxed().toList().

All immutable collections are only shallowly immutable: if the elements are mutable objects (say StringBuilder or your own class with setters), their fields can still change. Set.of and Map.of follow the same rules as List.of (no nulls, immutable, iteration order unspecified).

Synchronized wrappers

Collections.synchronizedList(list) returns a wrapper where every method is guarded by one lock. Single calls are safe, but a loop over it is not: you must hold the lock yourself.

List<String> safe = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
// ... other threads add to it ...
synchronized (safe) {                  // required while iterating
    for (String s : safe) {
        System.out.println(s);
    }
}

In new code prefer CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap and the other classes from Module 6.

Rule: know whether you hold a view or a copy

A view (unmodifiableList, subList, Arrays.asList, keySet) shares data with its source. A copy (List.copyOf, new ArrayList<>(…), stream.toList()) does not. If you return a collection from a getter, return a copy or an unmodifiable view, never your internal list.

Conventions

  • Constants and small fixed data: List.of(…), Set.of(…), Map.of(…).
  • Defensive copy in constructors and getters: this.items = List.copyOf(items);.
  • Return List.of() or Collections.emptyList(), not null, for "no results".
  • Need a mutable list from a factory: wrap it — new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3)).

Exceptions and edge cases

  • UnsupportedOperationException — any mutating call on List.of, List.copyOf, unmodifiableList, stream.toList(), Collections.emptyList(), nCopies, or add/remove on Arrays.asList.
  • NullPointerException — List.of / Set.of / Map.of with null; also list.contains(null) on them.
  • IllegalArgumentException — duplicate elements in Set.of or duplicate keys in Map.of.
  • Collections.unmodifiableList(list) does not protect you if someone else still holds the original and changes it.
  • binarySearch on an unsorted list returns a meaningless result without any error.

Mistake: sorting or modifying a List.of

List<String> names = List.of("b", "a"); Collections.sort(names); throws UnsupportedOperationException. Copy first: new ArrayList<>(names), or use names.stream().sorted().toList().

Interview: "Arrays.asList vs List.of vs Collections.unmodifiableList"

  • Arrays.asList: fixed size, set allowed, backed by the array. List.of: truly immutable, no nulls. unmodifiableList: read-only view, still changes when the source changes. List.copyOf: immutable snapshot.
  • "How do you make a class immutable if it has a list field?" Copy in the constructor with List.copyOf and return an unmodifiable list from the getter.
  • Collections vs Collection vs Arrays; Arrays.asList(int[]) pitfall.

Choosing the right collection

Ask three questions — key-value or single values, duplicates allowed, and what order or access pattern — and the answer is almost always ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet or ArrayDeque.

Picking a collection is a design decision, not a habit. The wrong one still compiles, but it can make a loop O(n²) or lose entries silently. Use the flowchart, then check the table of everyday scenarios.

Everyday scenarios

NeedUseWhy
Rows returned by a query, a cart's itemsArrayListOrder, index access, cheap iteration
Look up a customer by idHashMap<Long, Customer>O(1) lookup
"Have I seen this id already?"HashSetO(1) contains, no duplicates
Remove duplicates but keep orderLinkedHashSetUnique and insertion-ordered
Unique values in sorted orderTreeSetSorted, with range methods
Count words, group by cityHashMap + merge / computeIfAbsentCounting and grouping idioms
LRU cache, "recently viewed"LinkedHashMap (access order)Built-in eviction hook
Price slabs, nearest timestampTreeMapfloorKey / ceilingKey
Task queue, BFSArrayDequeFast FIFO, no node objects
Undo history, DFS, bracket matchingArrayDeque as a stackFast LIFO
Scheduler, top-K, DijkstraPriorityQueueO(log n) smallest-next
Keys are enum constantsEnumMap / EnumSetCompact and fast
Shared between threadsConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, blocking queuesSafe without manual locks

Rules of thumb

  • Default to ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet, ArrayDeque. Change only for a clear reason: order, sorting, thread safety or a measured bottleneck.
  • Repeated list.contains(x) on a big list is a red flag. It is O(n) each time; keep a HashSet next to it, or switch to one.
  • Sorted data needed once? Sort an ArrayList. Sorted data with constant inserts and queries? TreeMap/TreeSet.
  • Need both order and fast lookup? LinkedHashMap, or a list plus a map.
  • Collections of millions of primitive numbers: consider int[] — boxing makes List<Integer> about four times larger.
  • Expose the interface in public signatures (List, Map) and keep the concrete class inside.

Mistake: a List used as a lookup table

Searching a List<Customer> for an id inside a loop over orders is O(n × m). Build a Map<Long, Customer> once (Collectors.toMap) and look up in O(1).

Cost of the main operations

When two choices both "work", the cost of the operation you repeat most decides. Know this table; interviews ask for it often. (Details are in the neighbouring articles: lists, HashMap, TreeMap, sets, queues and deques.)

ClassGet / containsAddRemove
ArrayListget(i) O(1); contains O(n)End: amortised O(1); middle O(n)By index: O(n) shifting
LinkedListget(i) O(n); contains O(n)Ends O(1); middle O(n) to find the spotEnds O(1)
HashMap / HashSetO(1) averageO(1) averageO(1) average
TreeMap / TreeSetO(log n)O(log n)O(log n)
ArrayDequePeek at an end O(1); contains O(n)Either end O(1)Either end O(1)
PriorityQueuepeek O(1); contains O(n)O(log n)poll O(log n)

"Average" for hash classes assumes a decent hashCode. A bad one pushes many keys into one bucket, and the cost drifts toward O(n) (O(log n) once Java turns a long bucket into a tree).

Null, order and thread-safety at a glance

ClassNullsOrderThread-safe?
ArrayListAllowedInsertionNo
HashMap, HashSetOne null key; null valuesNoneNo
LinkedHashMapSame as HashMapInsertion or accessNo
TreeMap, TreeSetNo null key (natural order)SortedNo
ArrayDeque, PriorityQueueNo nullsDeque order / priorityNo
ConcurrentHashMapNo null key or valueNoneYes
List.of, Set.of, Map.ofNo nullsFixed (set and map order varies)Immutable, so safe to share

Three worked decisions

1. Duplicate emails in an uploaded file. You need to know if you have seen a value already, and the order of first appearance for the report. Answer: a LinkedHashSet, or a HashSet for the check plus an ArrayList for the order.

List<String> emails = List.of("a@x.in", "b@x.in", "a@x.in", "c@x.in", "b@x.in");
Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
Set<String> duplicates = new LinkedHashSet<>();
for (String e : emails) {
    if (!seen.add(e)) {              // add returns false when already present
        duplicates.add(e);
    }
}
System.out.println(duplicates);      // [a@x.in, b@x.in]

2. Orders per customer. Key-value with a list per key: Map<Long, List<Order>>, built with computeIfAbsent(id, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(order) or Collectors.groupingBy. If the report must list customers in id order, use a TreeMap instead of a HashMap.

3. "Next ticket to serve" with priorities (VIP first). You always want the smallest or largest element next, not a full sort. That is a PriorityQueue with a comparator. A sorted list re-sorted after every insert would cost O(n log n) per ticket.

Wrong: LinkedList "because inserts are O(1)"

List<Integer> list = new LinkedList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) list.add(i);
long sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) {
    sum += list.get(i);          // each get walks the chain: O(n)
}

Right: ArrayList, or iterate with for-each

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) list.add(i);
long sum = 0;
for (int x : list) {
    sum += x;                    // O(1) per step
}

In practice ArrayList beats LinkedList in nearly every real workload, because its elements sit next to each other in memory and the CPU cache likes that. Reach for ArrayDeque when you want queue behaviour at both ends.

Runtime exceptions that point at a wrong choice

  • UnsupportedOperationException — you called add or remove on List.of(...), Collections.unmodifiableList or the fixed-size list from Arrays.asList.
  • NullPointerException — a null put into List.of, ConcurrentHashMap, ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue or a TreeMap key.
  • ConcurrentModificationException — a plain collection changed during iteration or shared across threads without protection. Switch to a concurrent class or fix the loop.
  • ClassCastException — elements put into a TreeSet or PriorityQueue that are not Comparable and no comparator was given.

Conventions

  • Return List.copyOf(list) or an unmodifiable view from a method that exposes internal state, so callers cannot damage it.
  • Size big collections when you know the size: new ArrayList<>(n). For a HashMap of n entries, HashMap.newHashMap(n) (Java 19+) picks a table size that avoids resizing.
  • If the key type is an enum, always prefer EnumMap; if the set has a few fixed flags, EnumSet.
  • Choose by the operation you repeat most, then measure only if it is truly the bottleneck.

In real projects

A Spring service typically holds a Map<Long, Customer> cache (often ConcurrentHashMap), returns List<OrderDto> from repositories, and uses a Set<String> for allowed roles. Anything heavier, such as caching with expiry or distributed queues, moves to a library (Caffeine, Redis) rather than a hand-made collection.

Interview: "Which collection would you use for…?"

  • Answer with the question you ask yourself: key-value? duplicates? order? thread-safety? Then name the class and its complexity.
  • Typical prompts: unique sorted names (TreeSet), first non-repeating character (LinkedHashMap), top-K (min-heap PriorityQueue), LRU cache (LinkedHashMap), undo stack (ArrayDeque).

Generics: generic classes, interfaces and methods

Generics let a class or method work with a type that you name later (List<String>), so the compiler checks the types for you and you never write a cast.

Before Java 5 (2004) a list held plain Objects. You could add anything, and you had to cast every value you read. A wrong cast failed only at runtime. Generics move that check to compile time: you write a type parameter in angle brackets, and the compiler makes sure only that type goes in and comes out.

Wrong (raw type): fails at runtime

List names = new ArrayList();
names.add("Asha");
names.add(42);                       // accepted
String s = (String) names.get(1);    // ClassCastException

Right (generic): fails at compile time

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Asha");
names.add(42);   // error: incompatible types
String s = names.get(0);             // no cast

Generics give you three things: type safety (bugs caught by the compiler), no casts (cleaner code), and reuse (one Box class works for every type, instead of StringBox, IntBox, …).

A generic class

Put the type parameter after the class name. Inside the class, T is used like any other type.

public class Box<T> {
    private T value;

    public Box(T value) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    public T get() {
        return value;
    }

    public void set(T value) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Box<String> name = new Box<>("Asha");
        Box<Integer> age = new Box<>(30);
        String s = name.get();                 // no cast needed
        int a = age.get() + 1;                 // auto-unboxing
        System.out.println(s + " " + a);
        // name.set(5);                        // compile error: int cannot be converted to String
    }
}
Asha 31

A class can have more than one parameter. Records can be generic too:

public record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) {
    public Pair<B, A> swap() {
        return new Pair<>(second, first);
    }
}

Pair<String, Integer> p = new Pair<>("Asha", 30);
System.out.println(p + " -> " + p.swap());
Pair[first=Asha, second=30] -> Pair[first=30, second=Asha]

A generic interface

Generic interfaces describe a contract for any type. This Repository shape is exactly what Spring Data's CrudRepository<T, ID> looks like:

import java.util.*;

interface Repository<T, ID> {
    void save(T entity);
    Optional<T> findById(ID id);
    List<T> findAll();
}

record Customer(Long id, String name) {}

class InMemoryCustomerRepository implements Repository<Customer, Long> {
    private final Map<Long, Customer> store = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    @Override public void save(Customer c) { store.put(c.id(), c); }
    @Override public Optional<Customer> findById(Long id) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(id));
    }
    @Override public List<Customer> findAll() { return new ArrayList<>(store.values()); }
}

When you implement a generic interface you either fill in the types (Repository<Customer, Long>) or stay generic (class Cache<T> implements Repository<T, Long>).

A generic method

A generic method declares its own type parameter list before the return type. The method can live in a normal class, and the type parameter is valid only inside that method. Static methods cannot use the class's type parameter, so they must declare their own.

import java.util.*;

public class GenericMethods {
    // <T> before the return type declares the type parameter
    static <T> T firstOrDefault(List<T> list, T fallback) {
        return list.isEmpty() ? fallback : list.get(0);
    }

    static <T> void swap(T[] array, int i, int j) {
        T temp = array[i];
        array[i] = array[j];
        array[j] = temp;
    }

    static <K, V> Map<V, K> invert(Map<K, V> map) {
        Map<V, K> result = new HashMap<>();
        map.forEach((k, v) -> result.put(v, k));
        return result;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(firstOrDefault(List.of("UPI", "NEFT"), "none"));
        System.out.println(firstOrDefault(new ArrayList<Integer>(), -1));

        String[] cities = {"Pune", "Delhi", "Chennai"};
        swap(cities, 0, 2);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(cities));

        System.out.println(invert(Map.of("A", 1)));
        System.out.println(Collections.<String>emptyList());   // explicit type witness
    }
}
UPI
-1
[Chennai, Delhi, Pune]
{1=A}
[]

Type inference. You almost never write the type argument at the call: the compiler infers T from the arguments (firstOrDefault(List.of("UPI"), "none") gives T = String) and, if needed, from the target (the variable you assign the result to). You write it explicitly — Collections.<String>emptyList(), called a type witness — only when inference fails, which is rare in modern Java. Generic methods can also appear in constructors (<T> MyClass(T x)) and in non-generic classes.

Type parameter names

By convention a type parameter is a single capital letter:

LetterMeansExample
TType (the general one)Box<T>, Optional<T>
EElement of a collectionList<E>, Set<E>
K, VKey and valueMap<K, V>
RResult / return typeFunction<T, R>
NNumber<N extends Number>
U, SSecond and third typesBiFunction<T, U, R>
IDIdentifier type (a longer name is fine when clearer)Repository<T, ID>

The diamond operator and raw types

The diamond <> (Java 7) tells the compiler to infer the type arguments on the right side: Map<String, List<Order>> m = new HashMap<>();. Since Java 9 it also works with anonymous classes. With var you must put the type on the right: var list = new ArrayList<String>(); — writing var list = new ArrayList<>(); infers ArrayList<Object>.

A raw type is a generic class used without type arguments (List list). It exists only so that pre-Java-5 code still compiles. The compiler cannot check anything on a raw type, and it prints a warning such as Note: Foo.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations. Never use raw types in new code. When you must call old code, confine the cast and add @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") on the smallest possible scope, with a comment explaining why it is safe.

Generics are invariant

Although Integer is a Number, a List<Integer> is not a List<Number>. If it were, this would be legal and break type safety:

List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>();
List<Number> nums = ints;       // compile error — suppose it were allowed...
nums.add(3.14);                 // ...then a Double would land in a List<Integer>
int x = ints.get(0);            // ...and this would blow up

Arrays took the opposite choice: Integer[] is a Number[] (arrays are covariant), so the same mistake compiles and fails at runtime with ArrayStoreException. Wildcards (next article) give you safe flexibility when you need it.

Rules

  • Type arguments must be reference types: List<Integer>, never List<int>.
  • The type parameter of a class cannot be used in static members; a static generic method declares its own.
  • A generic method declares its parameters before the return type: public static <T> T pick(…).
  • List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number> (invariance), but ArrayList<Integer> is a subtype of List<Integer>.

Conventions

  • Use the standard letters (T, E, K, V, R). Use a longer descriptive name only when several parameters would be confusing.
  • Always use the diamond on the right: new ArrayList<>().
  • Do not write a generic class just because you can. If every use is String, write a normal class.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • ClassCastException at a place that has no cast in your source — the sign of a raw type or unchecked cast polluting a generic collection (see Type erasure).
  • ArrayStoreException — storing a wrong type into a covariant array (Object[] o = new String[1]; o[0] = 1;).
  • NullPointerException — auto-unboxing a null from Box<Integer> into an int.
  • You can specify nested generics: Map<String, List<Order>>; before Java 7 you had to write a space between the closing brackets.

Mistake: using the raw type "to keep it simple"

List list = new ArrayList(); turns off every compile-time check on that variable and throws away the reason generics exist. If you do not care about the element type, write List<?>; if you need Object, write List<Object>.

Real projects

You use generics every day without writing them: ResponseEntity<List<UserDto>>, JpaRepository<User, Long>, Optional<Order>, CompletableFuture<String>. You write your own generic code for shared building blocks: an ApiResponse<T> wrapper, a PageResult<T>, a base service or mapper Mapper<S, T>, a generic cache.

Interview: "Why generics? What is a generic method?"

  • Compile-time type safety, no explicit casts, code reuse.
  • Generic method: declares <T> before the return type; inference picks T from the arguments.
  • Invariance: List<Integer> is not a List<Number>; arrays are covariant and fail at runtime.
  • Raw types exist only for backward compatibility; they bypass checks.

Bounded types and wildcards: extends, super and PECS

Use "T extends X" to limit what a type parameter can be, use "? extends T" for collections you only read from, and "? super T" for collections you only write to — Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

Bounded type parameters

A bare T can be any type, so you can only call Object methods on it. A bound restricts T and in return lets you call the bound's methods. The keyword is extends for both classes and interfaces.

import java.util.*;

public class Bounds {
    // T must be a Number (Integer, Double, BigDecimal, ...)
    static <T extends Number> double sum(List<T> items) {
        double total = 0;
        for (T item : items) {
            total += item.doubleValue();         // allowed because T is a Number
        }
        return total;
    }

    // T must be comparable with itself
    static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items) {
        T best = items.get(0);
        for (T item : items) {
            if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) {
                best = item;
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    // multiple bounds: ONE class (first) and any number of interfaces, joined by &
    static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> T largest(T a, T b) {
        return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(sum(List.of(1, 2, 3)));
        System.out.println(sum(List.of(1.5, 2.5)));
        System.out.println(max(List.of("pune", "delhi", "mumbai")));
        System.out.println(largest(7, 12));
        // sum(List.of("a", "b"));    // compile error: String is not a Number
    }
}
6.0
4.0
pune
12

Rules for bounds: the class bound must come first (<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>), you can have at most one class, and the same bound syntax is used for interfaces (extends, never implements). A type parameter may refer to itself, as in T extends Comparable<T>; this is called a recursive bound and means "T can compare itself to other Ts". The JDK's own signature is slightly more flexible: <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, which also accepts a class that inherited its compareTo from a parent (a java.sql.Timestamp compares as a Date).

Why wildcards exist

Because List<Integer> is not a List<Number>, this method is too narrow:

static double total(List<Number> nums) { ... }

total(List.of(1, 2, 3));        // compile error: List<Integer> is not List<Number>

The wildcard ? means "some unknown type". Combined with bounds it expresses a whole family of types.

FormMeansCan read asCan write
List<?>List of some unknown typeObjectOnly null
List<? extends Number>List of Number or any subtype (upper bound)NumberOnly null
List<? super Integer>List of Integer or any supertype (lower bound)ObjectInteger (and subtypes)
List<Number>Exactly List<Number>NumberNumber and subtypes

? extends T — read-only "producers"

List<? extends Number> accepts a List<Integer>, a List<Double> or a List<Number>. You can safely read every element as a Number. You cannot add: the real list might be a List<Integer>, and the compiler cannot prove that your Double fits.

static double total(List<? extends Number> nums) {
    double sum = 0;
    for (Number n : nums) {                    // reading is fine
        sum += n.doubleValue();
    }
    // nums.add(1);                            // compile error: cannot add to ? extends
    return sum;
}

System.out.println(total(List.of(1, 2, 3)));        // List<Integer>
System.out.println(total(List.of(1.5, 2.5)));       // List<Double>

? super T — write-only "consumers"

List<? super Integer> accepts a List<Integer>, a List<Number> or a List<Object>. You can safely add an Integer, because every one of those lists can hold it. When you read, you only get Object, since the list might hold anything above Integer.

static void fillWithSquares(List<? super Integer> sink, int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
        sink.add(i * i);                       // writing an Integer is fine
    }
    // Integer first = sink.get(0);            // compile error: only Object comes out
}

List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object> objects = new ArrayList<>();
fillWithSquares(numbers, 3);
fillWithSquares(objects, 2);
System.out.println(numbers + " " + objects);
[1, 4, 9] [1, 4]

PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super

The memory rule from Effective Java: if a parameter produces values you read, use ? extends T. If it consumes values you write, use ? super T. If it does both, use an exact type (no wildcard). A copy method shows both sides: the source produces, the destination consumes.

import java.util.*;

public class Pecs {
    static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) {
        for (T item : src) {                   // read from the producer
            dest.add(item);                    // write to the consumer
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> ints = List.of(1, 2, 3);
        List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
        copy(numbers, ints);                   // T = Integer
        System.out.println(numbers);

        List<Object> objects = new ArrayList<>();
        copy(objects, List.of("a", "b"));      // T = String
        System.out.println(objects);
    }
}
[1, 2, 3]
[a, b]

The JDK follows PECS everywhere, which is why signatures look scary but make sense:

MethodWhy the wildcard
Collection.addAll(Collection<? extends E> c)The argument produces Es you read
Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)Exactly the example above
List.sort(Comparator<? super E> c)A Comparator<Object> or Comparator<Number> can order Integers; the comparator consumes elements
Stream.map(Function<? super T, ? extends R> f)The function consumes Ts and produces Rs
Collectors.toMap(Function<? super T, ? extends K>, …)Same idea

The unbounded wildcard List<?>

Use ? when the code does not care about the element type and only uses Object methods or size().

static void printAll(Collection<?> items) {
    for (Object o : items) {
        System.out.println(o);
    }
}

printAll(List.of(1, 2));
printAll(Set.of("x"));
List<?> unknown = new ArrayList<String>();
// unknown.add("a");      // compile error — only null may be added

List<?> is not the same as List<Object>. A List<Object> accepts adds but only matches lists of exactly Object; a List<?> accepts any list but you cannot add to it.

Wildcard capture: a helper method

Sometimes you need to modify a List<?> and the compiler refuses, because it does not know the element type. The trick is a private generic helper: calling it makes the compiler "capture" the unknown type as a name.

static void swapFirstAndLast(List<?> list) {
    swapHelper(list);                          // the unknown type is captured as T
}

private static <T> void swapHelper(List<T> list) {
    T first = list.get(0);
    list.set(0, list.get(list.size() - 1));
    list.set(list.size() - 1, first);
}

Choosing between the three

  • Method only reads elements: List<? extends T>.
  • Method only adds elements: List<? super T>.
  • Method both reads and adds, or returns elements of the same type it was given: use a type parameter <T> … List<T>.
  • Does not care about the type: List<?>.
  • Do not use wildcards in return types — they force callers to deal with them. Return List<Integer>, not List<? extends Number>.

Rule: you cannot add to a "? extends" collection or read specific types from "? super"

With List<? extends Number> the only value you may add is null. With List<? super Integer> everything you read is typed as Object. Wildcards cannot be used when creating an object: new ArrayList<?>() is an error (use new ArrayList<Object>() or new ArrayList<>()).

Conventions

  • Apply PECS to method parameters, which gives callers flexibility; keep return types exact.
  • Prefer a wildcard over a type parameter when the type appears only once in the signature: double total(List<? extends Number> list) is clearer than <T extends Number> double total(List<T> list).
  • Use Comparable<? super T> and Comparator<? super T> in your own generic utilities, as the JDK does.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • The compile errors people see: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to CAP#1 (adding to ? extends) and incompatible types: CAP#1 cannot be converted to Integer (reading specific types from ? super). "CAP#1" is the compiler's name for the captured unknown type.
  • You can still call remove(Object), contains(Object), clear() and size() on a List<? extends X>; they do not take E.
  • ? extends does not apply to primitive arrays or primitives; use the wrapper type.

Mistake: using List<Number> as a parameter and being surprised

A method that takes List<Number> rejects List<Integer> and List<Double>. If it only reads, change it to List<? extends Number>.

Interview: "Explain ? extends vs ? super — what is PECS?"

  • ? extends T = some subtype of T: safe to read as T, not safe to write. ? super T = some supertype of T: safe to write T, reads give Object.
  • PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Give the copy(dest, src) example and say which side is which.
  • Why List<Integer> is not a List<Number> (invariance) and how wildcards fix it safely.
  • Name JDK examples: Collections.copy, List.sort(Comparator<? super E>), Stream.map.

Type erasure and the limits of generics

The compiler checks generic types and then erases them, so at runtime a List<String> is just a List — which is why you cannot do new T(), new T[], instanceof List<String> or use primitive type arguments.

Generics were added in Java 5 without changing the JVM, so old code and new code could work together. To make that possible, the compiler uses type erasure: after it has checked your generic code, it removes the type arguments and generates ordinary bytecode.

  1. Each type parameter is replaced by its bound, or by Object when there is no bound (T becomes Object; T extends Number becomes Number).
  2. The compiler inserts casts where a value of the generic type is used (String s = list.get(0) becomes (String) list.get(0)).
  3. For overridden generic methods it adds bridge methods to keep polymorphism working. For example, a class implementing Comparable<Employee> gets a synthetic compareTo(Object) that calls your compareTo(Employee).
// You write:
class Box<T> {
    private T value;
    T get() { return value; }
}
Box<String> b = new Box<>();
String s = b.get();

// After erasure it is roughly:
class Box {
    private Object value;
    Object get() { return value; }
}
Box b = new Box();
String s = (String) b.get();      // cast inserted by the compiler

Because the information is gone at runtime, ArrayList<String> and ArrayList<Integer> are the same class:

List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(strings.getClass() == ints.getClass());
System.out.println(strings.getClass().getName());
true
java.util.ArrayList

What you cannot do — and what to do instead

Not allowedWhyWorkaround
new T()The JVM does not know what T isPass a Supplier<T> (Foo::new) or a Class<T>
new T[10]Arrays need their exact element type at runtimeUse List<T>, or (T[]) new Object[10] with a suppressed warning, or Array.newInstance(clazz, n)
List<int>Type arguments must be reference typesList<Integer>; primitive streams for big data
obj instanceof List<String><String> does not exist at runtimeobj instanceof List<?>, then check elements
static T field;Statics belong to the class, not to one parameterisationMake the member non-static, or a static generic method
void f(List<String>) and void f(List<Integer>) togetherBoth erase to f(List) — a "name clash: same erasure"Rename one method
class MyEx<T> extends Exception; catch (T e)The JVM cannot choose a catch block by generic typeUse a normal exception class
T.class, t instanceof TNo runtime typePass Class<T> as a parameter
 
import java.lang.reflect.Array;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public class ErasureWorkarounds<T> {
    private final Supplier<T> factory;
    private T[] items;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public ErasureWorkarounds(Supplier<T> factory, Class<T> type, int size) {
        this.factory = factory;
        this.items = (T[]) Array.newInstance(type, size);   // real T[] at runtime
    }

    public T create() {
        return factory.get();            // instead of new T()
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ErasureWorkarounds<StringBuilder> w =
                new ErasureWorkarounds<>(StringBuilder::new, StringBuilder.class, 3);
        System.out.println(w.create().append("ok"));
        System.out.println(w.items.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}
ok
StringBuilder[]

Heap pollution: a ClassCastException far from the cause

Raw types and unchecked casts can put the wrong type into a generic collection. The compiler warned you ("unchecked"), but the JVM sees nothing wrong at the add. The failure appears later, at an innocent-looking line that reads the element. This is called heap pollution.

List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
List raw = strings;                  // raw alias: unchecked warning
raw.add(42);                         // compiles; erasure means no runtime check
System.out.println(strings.size());  // 1
String s = strings.get(0);           // ClassCastException here, at the READ
1
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCastException:
    class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String

@SafeVarargs is a related annotation. A varargs parameter of generic type (T...) is secretly a T[], which can cause pollution; if your static, final or private method only reads the array, mark it @SafeVarargs to silence the warning (the JDK does this for List.of, Arrays.asList).

Arrays vs generics

PointArraysGenerics
SubtypingCovariant: Integer[] is an Object[]Invariant: List<Integer> is not a List<Object>
Type known at runtimeYes (reified)No (erased)
Wrong type storedArrayStoreException at runtimeCompile error
Primitive elementsYes (int[])No

Mixing the two gives warnings and surprises, so the practical advice is: prefer List<T> over T[] in generic code.

Getting generic types at runtime (when you must)

The type argument of a class declaration is kept in the class file. Libraries use this: Jackson's new TypeReference<List<User>>() {} creates an anonymous subclass so that getGenericSuperclass() can read List<User>. Spring's ParameterizedTypeReference works the same way. You need this when deserialising JSON into List<User>, because List.class alone loses the element type.

Rule: generics exist only at compile time

Do not write code that depends on a generic argument at runtime (instanceof, .class, overloads that differ only by type argument). Pass a Class<T>, a Supplier<T> or a type-reference token when you need the type.

Conventions

  • Treat every "unchecked" warning as a bug until proven otherwise. Keep @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") on the smallest scope (one local variable or one method) and explain why in a comment.
  • Compile with -Xlint:unchecked to see the details.
  • Never expose raw types in public APIs.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • ClassCastException at a read of a generic value — heap pollution through a raw type.
  • ArrayStoreException — storing into a covariant array, including (T[]) new Object[n] being returned to code that expects a String[].
  • Reifiable types (known at runtime): primitives, non-generic classes, raw types, List<?> and arrays of those. instanceof and array creation work only with them.
  • Overloading by erasure: void print(Object) and <T> void print(T) in the same class clash.

Mistake: casting to T and thinking it checks anything

(T) obj compiles to no check at all (the cast erases to Object or the bound). The error shows up later, in the caller. Validate with a real Class<T>: type.cast(obj) throws ClassCastException immediately.

Interview: "What is type erasure? What are its consequences?"

  • The compiler checks generics, then replaces type parameters by their bounds (or Object), inserts casts and generates bridge methods. Done for backward compatibility with pre-Java-5 code.
  • Consequences: no new T(), no new T[], no primitives as type arguments, no instanceof List<String>, no static fields of type T, no overloads that differ only in type arguments, no generic exceptions.
  • Heap pollution with raw types shows up as a ClassCastException far from the bug.
  • Contrast with C++ templates and C# generics, which keep the type at runtime.

Interview questions — Collections and generics

What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList? Which do you use and why?

ArrayList is backed by a resizable array: get(i) is O(1), adding at the end is amortized O(1), inserting or removing in the middle is O(n) because elements shift. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: access by index is O(n), adding or removing at the ends is O(1), and each element costs a node object. I use ArrayList almost always: contiguous memory is cache-friendly and array copying is fast, so LinkedList rarely wins even where Big-O says it should. For a queue or stack I use ArrayDeque.

How does HashMap work internally?

It has an array of buckets (default 16). For put(k, v) it computes hashCode(), spreads it with h ^ (h >>> 16), and finds the bucket as (n - 1) & hash. An empty bucket gets a new node. Otherwise it walks the chain comparing the hash and then equals; a match replaces the value, no match appends a node. get follows the same path. When the size exceeds capacity × 0.75 the table doubles and entries are redistributed. A bucket with 8 or more nodes becomes a red-black tree if the table has at least 64 buckets (otherwise the table resizes instead), and turns back into a list at 6 nodes. Average cost is O(1); worst case O(log n) in Java 8+.

What is the contract between equals() and hashCode()? What happens if you break it?

If a.equals(b) is true then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Unequal objects may share a hash code (a collision), but equal objects must not differ. If you override equals only, two equal objects hash to different buckets, so HashMap.get and HashSet.contains fail to find an entry you "just" added. The same happens if a field used in hashCode is mutated after the object becomes a key: the entry stays in the old bucket and is effectively lost. Use immutable keys or records.

Compare HashMap, Hashtable, ConcurrentHashMap and Collections.synchronizedMap.

HashMap is not thread-safe and allows one null key and null values. Hashtable is a legacy class that locks the whole map on every method and allows no nulls. Collections.synchronizedMap wraps any map with one lock, and you must still lock manually to iterate. ConcurrentHashMap allows no nulls, lets reads proceed without locking, locks only a bucket for writes, has weakly consistent iterators, and offers atomic putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent and merge. Use HashMap in single-threaded code and ConcurrentHashMap when threads share a map.

How does HashSet avoid duplicates? Why is HashSet.add O(1)?

A HashSet wraps a HashMap; your element is the key and the value is a shared dummy object. add(e) calls map.put(e, PRESENT) and returns true only if the key was new. Duplicates are detected by hashCode and equals, so it is O(1) on average like HashMap. A TreeSet detects duplicates with compareTo instead and costs O(log n).

What is a fail-fast iterator? When do you get ConcurrentModificationException, and how do you avoid it?

Fail-fast iterators of ArrayList, HashMap and similar classes compare the collection's modCount with the value they saved at creation, and throw ConcurrentModificationException if the collection was structurally changed by anything other than the iterator itself. A for-each loop that calls list.remove(x) is the typical case, and it needs only one thread. Fix it with Iterator.remove(), removeIf, a filtered copy, or a concurrent collection such as CopyOnWriteArrayList. The check is best effort, not a guarantee.

Comparable vs Comparator: when do you use each?

Comparable (compareTo(T), in java.lang) gives a class one natural order and is used automatically by Collections.sort, TreeSet and TreeMap. Comparator (compare(T, T), in java.util) is an external rule, so you can have many orders and sort classes you cannot edit. Build them with Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept).thenComparing(Employee::salary).reversed(). Never write a - b; it can overflow. Use Integer.compare.

What is the difference between Arrays.asList, List.of and Collections.unmodifiableList?

Arrays.asList(array) is a fixed-size list backed by the array: set works and writes through, add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. List.of is fully immutable and rejects null. Collections.unmodifiableList(list) is a read-only view: it cannot be modified itself, but it shows changes made to the original list. List.copyOf makes an immutable copy. All of them are shallow: mutable elements can still change.

What does this print? 
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(3));
list.remove(0);
System.out.println(list);

[2, 4, 5]. remove(Integer.valueOf(3)) calls remove(Object) and removes the value 3, giving [1, 2, 4, 5]. remove(0) uses the int overload and removes the element at index 0, which is 1. With a plain list.remove(3) on the original list you would have removed the element at index 3 (the value 4) instead.

How does PriorityQueue work? How do you get a max-heap? Is iteration sorted?

It is a binary min-heap stored in an array. offer adds at the end and sifts up, poll removes the root and sifts down: both O(log n); peek is O(1); contains and remove(Object) are O(n). Pass Comparator.reverseOrder() (or any comparator) for a max-heap. Iteration and toString() show the heap array, which is not sorted; only repeated poll() returns sorted order. It rejects null and is not thread-safe.

Why should you not use Stack, Vector and Hashtable?

They are Java 1.0 classes with every method synchronized, which costs performance and still does not make compound actions safe. Stack extends Vector, so it exposes index methods that break the stack idea. Use ArrayList, ArrayDeque (via Deque) and HashMap, or the java.util.concurrent classes when threads share the data.

What is type erasure? What can you not do because of it?

The compiler checks generic types, then removes them: a type parameter becomes its bound or Object, casts are inserted, and bridge methods are generated. At runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class. So you cannot write new T(), new T[n], List<int>, obj instanceof List<String>, a static field of type T, two overloads that differ only by type argument, or a generic exception class. Workarounds: pass a Supplier<T> or Class<T>, or use List<T> instead of T[].

Explain ? extends and ? super. What is PECS?

List<? extends Number> may be a list of any Number subtype: you can read elements as Number but cannot add (except null). List<? super Integer> may be a list of Integer or any supertype: you can add Integers but reads give only Object. PECS = Producer Extends, Consumer Super. In copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) the source produces and the destination consumes. This also explains why List<Integer> is not a List<Number> (invariance): wildcards add the safe flexibility.

Scenario: remove duplicates from a list but keep the first-seen order; then count how often each word appears.

For de-duplication: List<String> unique = new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)); — the set removes duplicates, and being linked, keeps insertion order. For counting: Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>(); for (String w : list) counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);. With streams, list.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w, Collectors.counting())). Both approaches are O(n); the naive if (!result.contains(x)) on a list would be O(n²).

How would you build an LRU cache in Java?

Extend LinkedHashMap with the constructor super(16, 0.75f, true) for access order, and override removeEldestEntry to return size() > capacity. Every get or put moves the entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used and is evicted automatically. All operations are O(1). It is not thread-safe, so wrap it with Collections.synchronizedMap or use a library such as Caffeine. The manual version is a HashMap from key to node plus a doubly linked list.

Cheat sheet — Collections and generics

  • Hierarchy Iterable → Collection → List / Set / Queue → Deque; Map is separate. Java 21 adds SequencedCollection with getFirst, getLast, reversed.
  • Program to the interface List<String> x = new ArrayList<>();
