  • Defaults ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet, ArrayDeque.
  • ArrayList array-backed; default capacity 10 (lazy); grows ×1.5; get O(1); add end amortized O(1); insert/remove middle O(n); trimToSize, ensureCapacity.
  • LinkedList doubly linked, also a Deque; get(i) O(n); ends O(1); more memory; rarely the right choice.
  • HashMap index hash = h ^ (h >>> 16); index = (n - 1) & hash; capacity is always a power of two.
  • HashMap numbers default capacity 16; load factor 0.75; threshold 12; resize doubles; treeify at 8+ nodes if table ≥ 64; untreeify at 6.
  • HashMap rules one null key; not thread-safe; order undefined; keys immutable with matching equals/hashCode; O(1) average.
  • Thread-safe maps ConcurrentHashMap (no nulls, atomic merge/computeIfAbsent) over Hashtable and synchronizedMap.
  • Map idioms getOrDefault, putIfAbsent, merge(k, 1, Integer::sum), computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ArrayList<>()).add(v), loop with entrySet().
  • LinkedHashMap insertion order; (16, 0.75f, true) = access order; override removeEldestEntry for an LRU cache.
  • TreeMap / TreeSet red-black tree, sorted, O(log n), no null key; floorKey, ceilingKey, lowerKey, higherKey, headMap, tailMap, subMap; equality by compareTo.
  • Set HashSet is backed by a HashMap; add returns false for duplicates; union addAll, intersection retainAll, difference removeAll.
  • Queue pairs add/offer, remove/poll, element/peek = throws vs returns null/false.
  • ArrayDeque stack: push/pop/peek; queue: offer/poll; no nulls; replaces Stack.
  • PriorityQueue binary min-heap; offer/poll O(log n); peek O(1); iteration not sorted; max-heap with Comparator.reverseOrder().
  • Fail-fast structural change during iteration → ConcurrentModificationException; remove with iterator.remove() or removeIf.
  • remove trap List<Integer>: remove(1) = by index, remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) = by value.
  • Sorting Comparable.compareTo (natural, inside class); Comparator.comparing(..).thenComparing(..).reversed(); never a - b; sort is stable.
  • Read-only lists Arrays.asList fixed size and write-through; List.of immutable, no nulls; unmodifiableList is a view; List.copyOf is a copy.
  • Views subList, keySet, headMap, unmodifiableX, Arrays.asList share data with their source.
  • Generics compile-time type safety; invariant (List<Integer> is not List<Number>); letters T, E, K, V, R; diamond <>.
  • Bounds <T extends Comparable<T>>; multiple: <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> (class first).
  • PECS Producer Extends, Consumer Super: copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src).
  • Erasure limits no new T(), new T[], List<int>, instanceof List<String>, static T fields; raw types and unchecked casts cause heap pollution.

Practice — Collections and generics

  1. Word frequency (easy). Read a paragraph into words (lower-case, strip punctuation), count them with merge, and print the top 3 words with counts. Break ties alphabetically. Done when the output is the same on every run and you can say why a HashMap alone could not guarantee that order.
  2. Set operations (easy). Given two lists of student ids, print the ids in both lists, only in the first, and in exactly one (symmetric difference), all sorted. Then remove duplicates from a list while keeping the first-seen order. Done when you use retainAll, removeAll, TreeSet and LinkedHashSet and copy before each bulk call.
  3. Sorting employees (easy–medium). Create an Employee record (id, name, dept, salary, and a nullable manager name). Give it a natural order by id with Comparable, then sort by dept, salary descending, name; and by manager name with nulls last. Done when no comparator uses subtraction and a TreeSet of employees sorted by salary does not drop employees with equal salary.
  4. Break and fix a loop (medium). Write a loop that removes all even numbers from a list with list.remove inside a for-each and make it throw ConcurrentModificationException. Then fix it three ways: Iterator.remove(), removeIf, and a stream. Also reproduce the "second-to-last element" case that does not throw. Done when you can explain modCount in two sentences.
  5. LRU cache (medium). Build LruCache<K, V> on LinkedHashMap with capacity 3 and test eviction after a get. Stretch goal: rebuild it with your own HashMap plus a doubly linked list so get and put stay O(1). Done when the printed order matches a hand-traced sequence of 10 operations.
  6. Generic utilities (medium). Write <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> c), <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src), a generic Pair<A, B> with swap(), and static double sum(List<? extends Number> list). Done when each compiles with the "wrong" call commented out and you can explain the compiler error for it.
  7. Build MyArrayList<T> (roadmap exercise, medium). Implement a growable list from scratch, backed by an Object[]: 
    public class MyArrayList<T> implements Iterable<T> {
    private Object[] data = new Object[10];
    private int size;

    public void add(T item) { /* grow when full: new length = old + old / 2 */ }
    public void add(int index, T item) { /* shift right with System.arraycopy */ }
    public T get(int index) { /* check range, cast with @SuppressWarnings */ return null; }
    public T set(int index, T item) { return null; }
    public T remove(int index) { /* shift left, null the last slot */ return null; }
    public int size() { return size; }
    public boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
    public Iterator<T> iterator() { return null; }   // hasNext/next, bonus: fail-fast
}
    Done when 1,000 adds work, a bad index throws IndexOutOfBoundsException with a clear message, removed slots are set to null (no memory leak), and a for-each loop over it works. Bonus: add trimToSize() and a modCount check.
  8. Build MyHashMap<K, V> (roadmap exercise, hard). Use an array of buckets, each a singly linked chain of nodes: 
    public class MyHashMap<K, V> {
    private static class Node<K, V> {
        final int hash; final K key; V value; Node<K, V> next;
        Node(int hash, K key, V value, Node<K, V> next) { /* assign */ }
    }

    private Node<K, V>[] table;            // create with (Node<K, V>[]) new Node[16]
    private int size;

    public V put(K key, V value) { return null; }   // replace value or add; resize at 0.75
    public V get(K key) { return null; }
    public V remove(K key) { return null; }
    public boolean containsKey(K key) { return false; }
    public int size() { return size; }
}
    Use hash = h ^ (h >>> 16) with 0 for a null key, index (n - 1) & hash, compare keys with Objects.equals, and double the table when size exceeds capacity * 0.75, moving every node. Done when it passes a test with a key class whose hashCode always returns 1 (everything collides), with the null key, with 100,000 random puts and removes that match a real HashMap, and you can explain why the table length must be a power of two.
  9. Top-K frequent words (stretch). Return the K most frequent words of a text using a HashMap for counts and a size-K min-heap PriorityQueue. Done when the time complexity is O(n log K) and you can justify why a min-heap, not a max-heap, keeps the K largest.

Module 5·About 1 weekMust

Modern and functional Java

22 topics · about 3 h of reading

Java 8 (2014) was the biggest change in the language's history. It added lambdas, method references and the Stream API, so you can pass behaviour around as a value and describe what you want instead of writing every loop by hand. It also added Optional and the java.time API. Every release since then has added more: var, text blocks, switch expressions, records, pattern matching, sealed classes, sequenced collections and unnamed variables.

This is not optional syntax sugar. Spring Boot code, code reviews and interviews all assume you can read and write it fluently — "find the second highest salary using streams" is one of the most asked Java interview questions. This module builds on OOP (Module 2) and collections (Module 4). The functional interfaces you learn here come back in CompletableFuture (Module 6) and all over Spring.

After this module you will be able to:

  • write lambdas and method references, and explain target typing and the "effectively final" rule;
  • pick the right interface from java.util.function and compose small functions into bigger ones;
  • build stream pipelines that filter, map, sort, group and reduce — and solve the common stream interview questions;
  • use Optional the way it was designed and avoid NullPointerException;
  • handle dates, times, time zones and durations correctly with java.time;
  • use var, text blocks, switch expressions, pattern matching, record patterns, sealed classes and sequenced collections, and say which Java version brought each one.

Functional programming ideas in one page

Functional style means treating behaviour as a value you can pass around, preferring pure functions and immutable data, and describing what result you want instead of how to loop for it.

Java is an object-oriented language, and it stays one. Since Java 8, though, it has borrowed a few ideas from functional programming (FP) — a style where programs are built mainly from functions that take values and return new values. You do not need to learn Haskell. You need five ideas, because lambdas, streams and Optional are all built on them.

The five ideas

Behaviour as data
A piece of code can be stored in a variable, passed to a method and returned from a method, just like a number or a string. In "sort these orders by price", the "by price" part is behaviour that you hand to sort(). A method that accepts or returns behaviour is called a higher-order function; filter, map and Comparator.comparing are examples.
Pure functions
A pure function returns a result that depends only on its arguments and does nothing else. It does not change fields, modify its arguments, print, write to a database or read the clock. Call it twice with the same input and you always get the same output.
Side effects
A side effect is anything a function does besides returning a value: printing, saving a row, changing a shared list, sending an SMS. Real programs need side effects. The goal is to keep them few, obvious and at the edges of the program.
Immutability
An immutable object cannot change after it is created. String, Integer, records with immutable fields, List.of(...) and every java.time type are immutable. To "change" one, you create a new one.
Declarative style
Imperative code says how: create a list, loop, check, add, sort. Declarative code says what: "names of active customers in Mumbai, in upper case, sorted". Streams are Java's declarative tool.

Imperative vs declarative — the same task twice

import java.util.*;

public class FunctionalIdeas {
    record Customer(String name, String city, boolean active) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Customer> customers = List.of(
                new Customer("Ravi", "Mumbai", true),
                new Customer("Asha", "Pune", true),
                new Customer("Kiran", "Mumbai", false),
                new Customer("Meera", "Mumbai", true));

        // Imperative: say HOW, step by step, with a mutable result list
        List<String> result1 = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Customer c : customers) {
            if (c.active() && c.city().equals("Mumbai")) {
                result1.add(c.name().toUpperCase());
            }
        }
        Collections.sort(result1);

        // Declarative: say WHAT you want; each step is a small function
        List<String> result2 = customers.stream()
                .filter(Customer::active)
                .filter(c -> c.city().equals("Mumbai"))
                .map(c -> c.name().toUpperCase())
                .sorted()
                .toList();

        System.out.println(result1);
        System.out.println(result2);
    }
}
[MEERA, RAVI]
[MEERA, RAVI]

Both are correct. The second one reads like the requirement, has no temporary list to manage and no index to get wrong. Each step (filter, map) receives a small function — behaviour as data.

Behaviour as data in a real setting

Suppose each payment mode has its own fee rule. Instead of a long if-else chain, store the rules as values in a map:

Map<String, Function<Long, Long>> feeRules = Map.of(
        "UPI", amount -> 0L,                               // no fee
        "CARD", amount -> amount * 2 / 100,                // 2%
        "WALLET", amount -> Math.min(amount / 100, 50L));  // 1%, at most ₹50

System.out.println(feeRules.get("UPI").apply(1500L));      // 0
System.out.println(feeRules.get("CARD").apply(1500L));     // 30
System.out.println(feeRules.get("WALLET").apply(10000L));  // 50

Adding a new payment mode is now one new map entry, not a new branch in five places. This is the strategy pattern without writing a class per strategy.

Pure vs impure

public class GstCalculator {
    private int gstPercent = 18;   // anyone with a reference can change this
    private int callCount = 0;

    // Impure: reads mutable state, changes state and does I/O
    public long withGstImpure(long amount) {
        callCount++;                                   // side effect
        System.out.println("Calculating GST...");      // side effect
        return amount + amount * gstPercent / 100;     // depends on a field
    }

    // Pure: the result depends only on the arguments; nothing else happens
    public static long withGst(long amount, int gstPercent) {
        return amount + amount * gstPercent / 100;     // withGst(1000, 18) is always 1180
    }
}

Why prefer the pure version where you can:

  • Easy to test — no setup, no mocks: give an input, check the output.
  • Safe with threads — nothing shared is modified, so there is nothing to race on (see Module 6).
  • Easy to reason about — you can replace a call with its result in your head. This property is called referential transparency.
  • Cacheable — same input, same output, so a result can be stored and reused.

Imperative vs declarative at a glance

AspectImperative (loops)Declarative (streams, lambdas)
FocusHow to do it, step by stepWhat result you want
StateCounters, temporary lists, flagsValues flow through steps; little mutable state
ReadingYou trace the loop to find the intentReads close to the requirement
Parallel workManual threads and locksPossible with parallelStream() if functions are pure
DebuggingSimple step-throughDeeper stack traces; use small named methods

Rule: functions you pass to streams must not modify the stream's source

The Stream API requires the functions you give it to be non-interfering (they never modify the source collection) and, in most cases, stateless (the result does not depend on state that changes while the pipeline runs). Break this and you get wrong results or a ConcurrentModificationException. Details in Streams vs loops.

Edge cases: what "immutable" really means in Java

  • final makes the reference constant, not the object. final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); still allows names.add("x").
  • Collections.unmodifiableList(list) returns a read-only view. If someone changes the original list, the view shows the change.
  • List.of and List.copyOf are unmodifiable, but only shallowly: if the elements are mutable objects, those objects can still change.
  • Java is not a pure functional language. Lambdas can still change state, and there is no tail-call optimisation, so deep recursion still ends in StackOverflowError.

Mistake: leaking an internal mutable list

A getter that returns its private list lets any caller change your object's state behind your back.

Wrong: the caller can add to or clear the cart

public class Cart {
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();

    public List<String> getItems() {
        return items;
    }
}

Right: return an unmodifiable snapshot

public class Cart {
    private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();

    public List<String> getItems() {
        return List.copyOf(items);
    }
}

Real projects: functional core, imperative shell

In a Spring Boot service, keep calculations — pricing, discount rules, validation, entity-to-DTO mapping — as pure methods that take values and return values. Keep the side effects (repository calls, Kafka publishing, HTTP calls, logging) in the outer service and controller layer. The pure core is unit-tested in milliseconds without starting Spring; the shell is thin. Records with a compact constructor that calls List.copyOf(...) are a common way to make value objects truly immutable.

Interview: "Is Java a functional language? What is a pure function?"

  • Java is object-oriented with functional features since Java 8: lambdas, functional interfaces, method references, streams and Optional.
  • A function in Java is still an object — an instance of a functional interface — but you can pass it around like a value.
  • A pure function: same input → same output, no side effects. Benefits: easy testing, thread safety, caching, readable code.
  • Immutability removes a whole class of bugs (shared mutable state) and makes objects safe to share between threads.
  • Mention a trade-off: debugging long pipelines is harder, and not every loop should become a stream.

Lambda expressions: syntax, target typing and captured variables

A lambda is a short anonymous function — parameters, an arrow and a body — that the compiler turns into an object of the functional interface the surrounding code expects.

Before Java 8, passing behaviour meant writing an anonymous inner class: a class with no name, declared and instantiated in one expression. Sorting names by length looked like this:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Priya", "Om", "Lakshmi"));

// Before Java 8: anonymous inner class — five lines of ceremony
Collections.sort(names, new Comparator<String>() {
    @Override
    public int compare(String a, String b) {
        return Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length());
    }
});

// Java 8+: a lambda keeps only the idea
names.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length()));

// Even shorter: a ready-made comparator plus a method reference
names.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));

System.out.println(names);   // [Om, Priya, Lakshmi]

A lambda expression is that idea written as (parameters) -> body. It has no name, no class declaration and no @Override. It can only be used where Java expects a functional interface — an interface with exactly one abstract method (next article). The lambda is the implementation of that one method.

Syntax variants

FormExampleNotes
No parameters() -> "Namaste"Empty parentheses are required
One parametern -> n * nParentheses are optional only for one untyped parameter
Several parameters(a, b) -> a + bParentheses required
Explicit types(Integer a, Integer b) -> a + bType all parameters or none
var parameters (Java 11)(var a, var b) -> a + bUseful when you want to put an annotation on a parameter
Expression bodyn -> n * nNo braces, no return; the value of the expression is returned
Block bodymsg -> { log(msg); }Statements in braces; write return if a value is returned
 
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;

public class LambdaSyntax {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Supplier<String> greeting = () -> "Namaste";
        UnaryOperator<Integer> square = n -> n * n;
        BinaryOperator<Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b;
        BinaryOperator<Integer> addTyped = (Integer a, Integer b) -> a + b;
        BinaryOperator<Integer> addVar = (var a, var b) -> a + b;

        Consumer<String> printer = msg -> {          // block body, no return value
            String line = "[LOG] " + msg;
            System.out.println(line);
        };

        Function<Integer, String> grade = marks -> {  // block body with return
            if (marks >= 60) {
                return "First class";
            }
            return "Keep going";
        };

        System.out.println(greeting.get());
        System.out.println(square.apply(7));
        System.out.println(add.apply(2, 3) + " " + addTyped.apply(2, 3) + " "
                + addVar.apply(2, 3));
        printer.accept("Order placed");
        System.out.println(grade.apply(72));
    }
}
Namaste
49
5 5 5
[LOG] Order placed
First class

Target typing: a lambda takes its type from the context

A lambda has no type of its own. The compiler looks at where it appears — the target type — and checks that the lambda fits the single abstract method of that interface. Target typing works in assignments, method arguments, return statements and casts. The same lambda text can therefore become different types:

Predicate<String> isEmptyP = s -> s.isEmpty();         // boolean test(String)
Function<String, Boolean> isEmptyF = s -> s.isEmpty();  // Boolean apply(String)

System.out.println(isEmptyP.test("") + " " + isEmptyF.apply("UPI"));   // true false

Object o = () -> System.out.println("hi");                // compile error
Object ok = (Runnable) () -> System.out.println("hi");    // fine: the cast is the target
error: incompatible types: Object is not a functional interface

Because the parameter types come from the target, you rarely write them. In names.sort((a, b) -> ...), the compiler knows sort takes a Comparator<String>, so a and b are String.

What the compiler and JVM do with a lambda

  1. javac moves the lambda body into a private method of your class, with a generated name such as lambda$run$0.
  2. Where the lambda is created, javac emits an invokedynamic instruction instead of new SomeClass().
  3. The first time that instruction runs, the JVM (through LambdaMetafactory) generates a small class at runtime that implements the interface and calls the private method.
  4. After that, creating the lambda is cheap. A lambda that captures nothing is usually created once and reused — an implementation detail, so never compare lambdas with ==.
$ javac ThisDemo.java
$ ls *.class
ThisDemo$1.class  ThisDemo.class
$ javap -p ThisDemo
Compiled from "ThisDemo.java"
public class ThisDemo {
  public ThisDemo();
  public java.lang.String toString();
  void run();
  public static void main(java.lang.String[]);
  private void lambda$run$0();
}

ThisDemo$1.class is the anonymous class from the demo below. The lambda has no class file — only the private method lambda$run$0.

Capturing variables: the "effectively final" rule

A lambda can use local variables of the method it is written in. This is called capturing. The rule: a captured local variable must be final or effectively final — never assigned again after its first assignment, so adding final would not cause an error.

String city = "Pune";                         // effectively final
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Delivering in " + city);
r.run();                                      // Delivering in Pune

int count = 0;
orders.forEach(o -> count++);                 // compile error
error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final

Even a reassignment after the lambda (city = "Delhi"; on a later line) makes city not effectively final, and the lambda line fails to compile.

Why Java has this rule:

  1. A local variable lives in the method's stack frame, which disappears when the method returns. A lambda can live longer — it can be stored in a field or run later on another thread. So the lambda receives a copy of the value when it is created.
  2. If you could change the variable later, the copy and the original would disagree. Forbidding reassignment guarantees they are always equal, so "copy" and "same variable" behave identically.
  3. Local variables are private to one thread by design. If lambdas running on other threads could write to them, every local would become a possible data race.

What you can do:

  • Read and modify fields (instance and static). The lambda captures this — a reference — and reaches the field through the object on the heap. It compiles, but it is still a side effect, and it is unsafe in parallel streams.
  • Modify the object a final variable points to: audit.add(s) inside a lambda is fine when audit itself is never reassigned. Effectively final is about the variable, not the object.
  • Use a holder such as AtomicInteger when you truly need a counter — but first ask whether a stream operation (count(), sum()) gives the answer directly.

this in a lambda vs in an anonymous class

A lambda does not create a new scope. Inside it, this means the enclosing object, exactly as on the line before the lambda. Inside an anonymous class, this means the anonymous object itself.

public class ThisDemo {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "ThisDemo object";
    }

    void run() {
        Runnable lambda = () -> System.out.println("lambda    -> this = " + this);

        Runnable anonymous = new Runnable() {
            @Override
            public void run() {
                System.out.println("anonymous -> this = " + this);
            }

            @Override
            public String toString() {
                return "anonymous Runnable object";
            }
        };

        lambda.run();
        anonymous.run();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new ThisDemo().run();
    }
}
lambda    -> this = ThisDemo object
anonymous -> this = anonymous Runnable object

The same "no new scope" idea explains another rule: a lambda parameter cannot reuse the name of a local variable from the enclosing method. With String name = "Ravi"; in scope, name -> name.length() fails with variable name is already defined in method main(String[]). An anonymous class may shadow it.

Lambda vs anonymous class

PointLambdaAnonymous class
Can implementOnly a functional interfaceAny interface (any number of methods) or a class
this meansThe enclosing objectThe anonymous object
New scopeNo — cannot redeclare enclosing localsYes — can shadow enclosing names
Own fields/stateNoYes
Compiled toPrivate method + invokedynamicA separate Outer$1.class file
Captured localsFinal or effectively finalFinal or effectively final (since Java 8)

Checked exceptions inside lambdas

The interfaces in java.util.function do not declare any checked exceptions. So a lambda passed to map cannot let an IOException escape:

List<String> texts = paths.stream()
        .map(p -> Files.readString(p))      // readString throws IOException
        .toList();
error: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown

The clean fix is a small named method that converts the checked exception into an unchecked one. UncheckedIOException exists exactly for this.

static String readFile(Path path) {
    try {
        return Files.readString(path);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException(e);   // keeps the original as the cause
    }
}

List<String> texts = paths.stream()
        .map(FileReport::readFile)            // method reference keeps the pipeline clean
        .toList();

Rules the compiler enforces

  • A lambda needs a functional interface as its target type.
  • Captured local variables must be final or effectively final.
  • Give types to all parameters or to none: (Integer a, b) -> a + b fails with cannot mix implicitly-typed and explicitly-typed parameters. Mixing var with explicit types fails too.
  • A lambda parameter or local cannot reuse a name already in scope in the enclosing method.
  • A block body that returns a value must return on every path.

Conventions

  • Keep a lambda to one expression or a few lines. If it grows, move the logic to a named private method and pass a method reference.
  • Prefer an expression body over { return ...; }, and leave out parameter types unless they make the code clearer.
  • Use meaningful parameter names in business code (order -> order.total()); single letters are fine in tiny lambdas like (a, b) -> a + b.
  • Do not use lambdas for side effects inside stream pipelines; return values instead.

Edge cases

  • return inside a lambda leaves only the lambda. In list.forEach(s -> { if (s.isEmpty()) return; print(s); }) it skips one element, like continue.
  • You cannot break out of forEach. Use a normal loop, or a short-circuiting stream operation such as anyMatch or takeWhile.
  • s -> audit.add(s) fits a Consumer<String> even though add returns boolean: when the body is a method call, the result may be discarded.
  • An exception thrown inside a lambda appears when the functional method runs — possibly much later, or on another thread. Stack traces show frames like lambda$main$0.

Mistake: counting with a local variable inside forEach

Wrong: does not compile (and is not functional style)

int emptyCount = 0;
items.forEach(s -> {
    if (s.isEmpty()) {
        emptyCount++;   // captured local is modified
    }
});

Right: let the stream compute the value

long emptyCount = items.stream()
        .filter(String::isEmpty)
        .count();

Interview: "Why must captured variables be effectively final?" and "Lambda vs anonymous class?"

  • The lambda gets a copy of a local's value, because locals live on the stack and the lambda may outlive the method or run on another thread. Forbidding reassignment keeps the copy and the original identical and avoids data races on locals.
  • Fields are not copied — they are reached through the captured this reference — so they can be modified (but should not be, in streams).
  • Lambda vs anonymous class: lambdas implement only functional interfaces, have no state, share the enclosing scope (this is the outer object), and compile to a private method plus invokedynamic instead of a separate class file.
  • Target typing: a lambda's type is decided by the context; the same lambda can be a Predicate or a Function.

Functional interfaces and the java.util.function package

A functional interface has exactly one abstract method; java.util.function gives you 43 ready-made ones, and Predicate, Function, Consumer and Supplier are the four you use every day.

A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method — often called a SAM (single abstract method) type. Any lambda or method reference whose parameters and return type fit that method can be used as an instance of the interface. Interfaces you already know, such as Runnable (void run()), Callable<V> (V call()) and Comparator<T> (int compare(T, T)), are functional interfaces.

What counts as "one abstract method"

  • Default methods and static methods do not count. A functional interface can have many of them — Function has andThen, compose and identity.
  • Abstract methods that match public methods of Object (equals, hashCode, toString) do not count, because every implementing class already has them. That is why Comparator, which declares boolean equals(Object), is still functional.
  • An interface that inherits one abstract method and declares no new one is also functional.

The @FunctionalInterface annotation

@FunctionalInterface is optional. Any interface with one abstract method works with lambdas. The annotation does two things: it documents your intent, and it makes the compiler fail if someone later adds a second abstract method.

@FunctionalInterface
interface PaymentGateway {
    void pay(long amount);
    void refund(long amount);   // second abstract method
}
error: Unexpected @FunctionalInterface annotation
  PaymentGateway is not a functional interface
    multiple non-overriding abstract methods found in interface PaymentGateway

The core four

InterfaceMethodShapeTypical use
Predicate<T>boolean test(T t)T → booleanfilter, validation rules, removeIf
Function<T, R>R apply(T t)T → Rmap, converting entity → DTO
Consumer<T>void accept(T t)T → nothingforEach, ifPresent, logging
Supplier<T>T get()nothing → TorElseGet, lazy values, factories

Memory trick: a Predicate answers yes/no, a Function transforms, a Consumer eats a value and returns nothing, a Supplier produces a value from nothing.

The rest of the family

InterfaceMethodShapeWhere you meet it
BiFunction<T, U, R>R apply(T, U)(T, U) → RMap.replaceAll, Map.compute
BiConsumer<T, U>void accept(T, U)(T, U) → nothingMap.forEach((k, v) -> ...)
BiPredicate<T, U>boolean test(T, U)(T, U) → booleanTwo-argument checks, Files.find
UnaryOperator<T>T apply(T)T → TList.replaceAll, Stream.iterate
BinaryOperator<T>T apply(T, T)(T, T) → Treduce, the merge function of toMap

UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T, T>, and BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T, T, T>. They are just shorter names for "same type in, same type out".

Primitive specializations — avoiding boxing

Generics work only with objects, so a Function<Integer, Integer> boxes every int into an Integer object and unboxes it again. In a loop over millions of numbers this creates garbage and costs time. Primitive specializations work on int, long and double directly. Their names follow a pattern:

Name patternMeaningExamples (method)
IntXxxTakes an intIntPredicate (test), IntConsumer (accept), IntFunction<R> (apply)
ToIntXxxReturns an intToIntFunction<T> (applyAsInt), ToIntBiFunction<T, U>
IntToLongXxxTakes int, returns longIntToLongFunction, IntToDoubleFunction
IntUnaryOperator, IntBinaryOperatorint in, int outapplyAsInt(int), applyAsInt(int, int)
IntSupplier, BooleanSupplierProduces a primitivegetAsInt(), getAsBoolean()
ObjIntConsumer<T>Takes an object and an intaccept(T, int)

The same set exists for Long and Double (LongPredicate, ToDoubleFunction, DoubleUnaryOperator, …). Together with the generic ones, the package has 43 interfaces. Primitive streams (IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream) use these, which is why mapToInt(Employee::salary) takes a ToIntFunction.

Which interface do I need?

You want to…Use
Check a conditionPredicate<T> / IntPredicate
Convert A into BFunction<A, B>
Convert A into another AUnaryOperator<A>
Combine two A values into one ABinaryOperator<A>
Do something with a value, return nothingConsumer<T>
Produce a value later, on demandSupplier<T>
Work with two inputsBiFunction, BiConsumer, BiPredicate
Work with int/long/double without boxingIntPredicate, ToIntFunction, IntUnaryOperator, …
Run code with no input and no resultRunnable (in java.lang)

Composing functions

Many functional interfaces have default methods that build a new function out of existing ones. This is composition: small, tested pieces snapped together.

InterfaceMethodResult
Predicatep.and(q), p.or(q), p.negate()Logical AND / OR / NOT (AND and OR short-circuit)
PredicatePredicate.not(p) (Java 11)Negation that works with method references
Functionf.andThen(g)Run f first, then g on its result
Functionf.compose(g)Run g first, then f
FunctionFunction.identity()A function that returns its input unchanged
Consumerc1.andThen(c2)Give the value to c1, then to c2
BiFunctionbf.andThen(f)Apply f to the result
BinaryOperatorBinaryOperator.minBy(cmp), maxBy(cmp)Pick the smaller / larger of two values
 
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Compose {
    record User(String name, int age, String email) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // andThen vs compose: the order is the whole difference
        Function<Integer, Integer> times2 = x -> x * 2;
        Function<Integer, Integer> plus3 = x -> x + 3;
        System.out.println(times2.andThen(plus3).apply(5));   // (5 * 2) + 3
        System.out.println(times2.compose(plus3).apply(5));   // (5 + 3) * 2

        Function<String, String> clean = ((Function<String, String>) String::trim)
                .andThen(String::toLowerCase);
        System.out.println("[" + clean.apply("  Ravi@Example.COM ") + "]");

        // Predicate composition: build rules from small pieces
        Predicate<User> isAdult = u -> u.age() >= 18;
        Predicate<User> hasEmail = u -> u.email() != null && !u.email().isBlank();
        Predicate<User> canRegister = isAdult.and(hasEmail);

        List<User> users = List.of(
                new User("Asha", 25, "asha@mail.in"),
                new User("Rohan", 16, "rohan@mail.in"),
                new User("Kiran", 30, " "));
        System.out.println(users.stream().filter(canRegister).map(User::name).toList());
        System.out.println(users.stream().filter(canRegister.negate())
                .map(User::name).toList());
        System.out.println(users.stream().filter(isAdult.or(hasEmail))
                .map(User::name).toList());

        List<String> words = List.of("java", " ", "", "spring");
        System.out.println(words.stream()
                .filter(Predicate.not(String::isBlank)).toList());

        // identity(): "the element itself" as the map value
        Map<String, User> byName = users.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(User::name, Function.identity()));
        System.out.println(byName.get("Asha"));

        Consumer<String> log = s -> System.out.println("LOG: " + s);
        Consumer<String> audit = s -> System.out.println("AUDIT: " + s);
        log.andThen(audit).accept("payment 499");

        BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> multiply = (a, b) -> a * b;
        System.out.println(multiply.andThen(r -> "Result = " + r).apply(6, 7));

        BinaryOperator<String> longer =
                BinaryOperator.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));
        System.out.println(longer.apply("UPI", "NEFT"));

        // Primitive specializations: no Integer objects created
        IntPredicate even = n -> n % 2 == 0;
        ToIntFunction<String> length = String::length;
        IntBinaryOperator max = Math::max;
        System.out.println(even.test(10) + " " + length.applyAsInt("Swiggy") + " "
                + max.applyAsInt(3, 9));
    }
}
13
16
[ravi@example.com]
[Asha]
[Rohan, Kiran]
[Asha, Rohan, Kiran]
[java, spring]
User[name=Asha, age=25, email=asha@mail.in]
LOG: payment 499
AUDIT: payment 499
Result = 42

Note the cast in the clean line: a method reference on its own has no type, so you cannot call .andThen on String::trim directly. Assign it to a typed variable first (Function<String, String> trim = String::trim;) or cast it, as shown.

Writing your own functional interface

Use the standard interfaces first. Write your own when you need a domain name that makes code clearer, more than two parameters, or a method that throws a checked exception. You can add default and static methods to make it composable:

@FunctionalInterface
public interface DiscountPolicy {
    long apply(long amount);                       // the single abstract method

    default DiscountPolicy then(DiscountPolicy next) {
        return amount -> next.apply(this.apply(amount));
    }

    static DiscountPolicy percent(int pct) {
        return amount -> amount - amount * pct / 100;
    }

    static DiscountPolicy flat(long off) {
        return amount -> Math.max(0, amount - off);
    }
}

// Usage
DiscountPolicy festive = DiscountPolicy.percent(10).then(DiscountPolicy.flat(100));
System.out.println(festive.apply(2000));                  // 2000 → 1800 → 1700
System.out.println(DiscountPolicy.flat(500).apply(300));  // never below 0 → 0
1700
0

Rule: exactly one abstract method

A lambda can target an interface only if it has exactly one abstract method after ignoring default methods, static methods and public Object methods. Abstract classes never work as lambda targets, even with one abstract method.

Conventions

  • Prefer the standard interfaces in method signatures; everyone knows what a Predicate<Order> is.
  • Put @FunctionalInterface on every interface you write to be used with lambdas.
  • Use primitive specializations (IntPredicate, ToLongFunction) in hot code paths and with primitive streams.
  • Name predicates as questions or adjectives (isAdult, hasEmail) so compositions read like sentences: isAdult.and(hasEmail).

Edge cases

  • Unboxing null throws NullPointerException: a Function<Integer, Integer> written as x -> x * 2 fails if it receives null.
  • p.and(q) short-circuits: q is not evaluated when p is false. Order cheap or null-guarding checks first.
  • Supplier has no composition methods; Runnable and Callable have none either.
  • Function<T, Boolean> and Predicate<T> are different types; you cannot pass one where the other is expected, even if the lambda text is the same.

Mistake: mixing up andThen and compose

f.andThen(g) reads left to right: f, then g. f.compose(g) runs g first — like maths notation f(g(x)). When in doubt, use andThen; it matches reading order and most people never need compose.

Interview: "What is a functional interface? Is @FunctionalInterface required?"

  • An interface with exactly one abstract method; default, static and Object-method declarations do not count.
  • The annotation is optional; it documents intent and makes the compiler reject a second abstract method.
  • Name the core four with their methods: Predicate.test, Function.apply, Consumer.accept, Supplier.get.
  • UnaryOperator/BinaryOperator are Function/BiFunction with all types the same.
  • Primitive specializations exist to avoid boxing cost and null-unboxing errors.
  • Older interfaces such as Runnable, Callable and Comparator are functional too, which is why lambdas work with threads and sorting.

Method references: the four kinds

A method reference such as String::toUpperCase is a shorter way to write a lambda that does nothing except call one existing method; there are four kinds — static, bound instance, unbound instance and constructor.

Many lambdas only forward their arguments to a method that already exists: s -> s.toUpperCase(), x -> System.out.println(x), () -> new ArrayList<>(). A method reference names that method directly with the :: operator. It compiles to the same thing as the lambda, but it is shorter and says what is being called instead of how the arguments are passed.

The four kinds

KindSyntaxExampleSame as the lambda
1. Static methodClassName::staticMethodInteger::parseInts -> Integer.parseInt(s)
2. Bound instance method (a specific object)object::methodSystem.out::printlnx -> System.out.println(x)
3. Unbound instance method (any object of a type)ClassName::methodString::toUpperCases -> s.toUpperCase()
4. ConstructorClassName::newArrayList::new() -> new ArrayList<>()

Bound vs unbound — the one that confuses people

In a bound reference, the object is fixed when you write the reference: System.out::println always prints to that one PrintStream. All lambda parameters become method arguments.

In an unbound reference, you name a type, not an object. The first lambda parameter becomes the object the method is called on, and the remaining parameters become arguments:

  • String::toUpperCase as a Function<String, String> → s -> s.toUpperCase()
  • String::compareToIgnoreCase as a Comparator<String> → (a, b) -> a.compareToIgnoreCase(b)
  • String::startsWith as a BiFunction<String, String, Boolean> → (s, p) -> s.startsWith(p)

All four in one program

import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class MethodRefs {
    record Employee(String name, String dept) {
        Employee(String name) {            // second constructor
            this(name, "UNASSIGNED");
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Static method
        Function<String, Integer> parse = Integer::parseInt;
        System.out.println(parse.apply("42") + 1);

        // 2. Bound instance method: the receiver (System.out) is fixed
        Consumer<String> printer = System.out::println;
        printer.accept("bound to System.out");

        // 3. Unbound instance method: the first argument is the receiver
        Function<String, String> upper = String::toUpperCase;
        System.out.println(upper.apply("upi"));

        List<String> cities = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pune", "Agra", "delhi", "Bhopal"));
        // same as (a, b) -> a.compareToIgnoreCase(b)
        cities.sort(String::compareToIgnoreCase);
        System.out.println(cities);

        // 4. Constructor: the target type picks the constructor
        Supplier<List<String>> listMaker = ArrayList::new;             // no-arg
        Function<String, Employee> newEmp = Employee::new;             // (String)
        BiFunction<String, String, Employee> newEmp2 = Employee::new;  // (String, String)
        IntFunction<int[]> newArray = int[]::new;                      // new int[n]
        System.out.println(listMaker.get().size() + " " + newEmp.apply("Ravi") + " "
                + newEmp2.apply("Asha", "HR") + " " + newArray.apply(3).length);

        // Typical stream usage
        String[] arr = Stream.of("a", "b").toArray(String[]::new);
        List<Employee> emps = Stream.of("Kiran", "Meera").map(Employee::new).toList();
        TreeSet<String> set = Stream.of("b", "a", "b")
                .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));
        List<String> noNulls = Stream.of("x", null, "y")
                .filter(Objects::nonNull)
                .toList();

        System.out.println(arr.length + " " + emps + " " + set + " " + noNulls);
    }
}
43
bound to System.out
UPI
[Agra, Bhopal, delhi, pune]
0 Employee[name=Ravi, dept=UNASSIGNED] Employee[name=Asha, dept=HR] 3
2 [Employee[name=Kiran, dept=UNASSIGNED], Employee[name=Meera, dept=UNASSIGNED]] [a, b] [x, y]

How the compiler matches a method reference

  1. It looks at the target functional interface and its one method — for Function<String, Integer> that is Integer apply(String).
  2. For ClassName::name it searches for a static method name(String) and for an instance method name() called on the first parameter.
  3. Overloads are resolved by the parameter types, exactly like a normal call. System.out::println works for Consumer<String> and Consumer<Integer> because the right println overload is picked each time.
  4. If both a static and an instance method fit, the reference is ambiguous and does not compile.
Function<Integer, String> f = Integer::toString;   // toString(int) or toString()?
error: incompatible types: invalid method reference
    reference to toString is ambiguous
      both method toString(int) in Integer and method toString() in Integer match

Fix it with a lambda that says what you mean: i -> Integer.toString(i), or use String::valueOf.

this:: and super::

Inside an instance method you can reference your own methods with this::validate and the parent's version with super::describe. orders.forEach(this::process) is a common pattern in Spring services: the loop body lives in a named, testable method.

Edge case: a bound receiver is evaluated immediately

For object::method, Java evaluates object when the reference is created, not when it runs. Two visible effects:

  • If object is null, you get a NullPointerException at creation time. The equivalent lambda () -> object.method() fails only when it is called.
  • The variable does not need to be effectively final, because only its current value is captured. After String s = "abc"; Supplier<Integer> len = s::length; s = "abcdef";, len.get() returns 3.
Order order = null;
Runnable lambda = () -> order.confirm();   // created fine
Runnable ref = order::confirm;             // NullPointerException right here
lambda.run();                              // the lambda throws only now

Rule: the referenced method must fit the functional method

The number and types of parameters must match (for an unbound reference, counting the receiver as the first parameter), and the return type must be compatible. A method returning a value may be used where void is expected (the value is discarded), but not the other way round.

Conventions: when to use a method reference

  • Use one when the lambda only forwards its parameters: prefer map(Employee::name) over map(e -> e.name()).
  • Keep the lambda when it does more than one call or passes extra values: map(e -> e.salary() * 12) has no method-reference form.
  • For chains of getters, split them: .map(User::address).map(Address::city) reads better than one long lambda.
  • Do not force it. If Foo::bar hides which argument goes where, the lambda is clearer.

Mistake: calling a default method directly on a method reference

String::trim.andThen(...) does not compile ("method reference not expected here"), and var f = String::trim; fails with "method reference needs an explicit target-type". A method reference has no type until it is assigned or passed. Assign it to a typed variable first: Function<String, String> trim = String::trim;.

Interview: "What are the types of method references?"

  • Four kinds: static (Integer::parseInt), bound instance (System.out::println), unbound instance (String::length), constructor (ArrayList::new, int[]::new).
  • Give the lambda equivalent of each — interviewers often ask for it.
  • Unbound: the first parameter becomes the receiver, which is why String::compareToIgnoreCase works as a Comparator<String>.
  • The target type decides which overload or constructor is used.
  • Bonus point: a bound receiver is evaluated when the reference is created (null check happens then).

What a stream is: pipeline, laziness and sources

A stream is a one-time pipeline over a source of elements: a chain of lazy intermediate operations followed by one terminal operation, which triggers all the work and produces the result.

A stream (java.util.stream.Stream<T>) is a sequence of elements that you process with a chain of operations. It is not a data structure: it stores nothing. It pulls elements from a source — a collection, an array, a file, a generator — and pushes them through the operations one by one. It never modifies the source; a filter on a stream of a list leaves the list untouched.

Stream vs collection

PointCollection (List, Set)Stream
PurposeStores and manages elementsDescribes a computation over elements
StorageHolds all elements in memoryHolds nothing; elements flow through
When work happensImmediately (eager)Only when a terminal operation runs (lazy)
ReuseIterate as often as you likeSingle use — consumed by the terminal operation
SizeFiniteCan be infinite (Stream.iterate, generate)
IterationExternal (you write the loop)Internal (the stream runs the loop for you)

The pipeline: source → intermediate → terminal

Source
Where elements come from: list.stream(), Arrays.stream(arr), Files.lines(path).
Intermediate operation
Returns a new Stream and does no work yet: filter, map, sorted, distinct, limit. You can chain any number of them.
Terminal operation
Produces a result or a side effect and ends the stream: collect, toList, forEach, count, reduce, findFirst. A pipeline has exactly one, at the end.

Laziness and short-circuiting — see it with peek

Lazy means intermediate operations only record what to do. The work starts when the terminal operation asks for elements. The stream then processes elements one at a time, through the whole chain ("vertically"), not one operation at a time over the whole list. Some operations are short-circuiting: they can finish without looking at every element (findFirst, anyMatch, limit). peek(action) lets you watch elements pass by.

List<String> names = List.of("Asha", "Bharat", "Chirag", "Deepa", "Esha");

Stream<String> pipeline = names.stream()
        .peek(n -> System.out.println("source: " + n))
        .filter(n -> n.length() > 4)
        .peek(n -> System.out.println("  passed filter: " + n))
        .map(String::toUpperCase);

System.out.println("Pipeline built, nothing processed yet");
Optional<String> first = pipeline.findFirst();       // terminal: work starts here
System.out.println("Result: " + first.get());
Pipeline built, nothing processed yet
source: Asha
source: Bharat
  passed filter: Bharat
Result: BHARAT

Three things to notice. Nothing printed before findFirst(). "Asha" failed the filter and went no further. And after "Bharat" produced a result, the stream stopped — "Chirag", "Deepa" and "Esha" were never read. With a million names, that saves a million checks.

Stateful operations break the one-at-a-time flow

Most intermediate operations are stateless: each element is handled on its own (filter, map). Stateful operations need to remember other elements. sorted() cannot emit the smallest element until it has seen all of them; distinct() must remember what it has already seen.

Stream.of("c", "a", "b")
        .peek(s -> System.out.println("before sorted: " + s))
        .sorted()
        .forEach(s -> System.out.println("after sorted:  " + s));
before sorted: c
before sorted: a
before sorted: b
after sorted:  a
after sorted:  b
after sorted:  c

This is why sorted() on an infinite stream never finishes, and why it uses memory proportional to the number of elements.

A stream can be used only once

Stream<String> once = names.stream();
System.out.println(once.count());   // 5
once.count();                       // throws
5
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed

A terminal operation consumes the stream. If you need the data twice, keep the source (the list) and call stream() again, or use a Supplier<Stream<T>>. Calling two intermediate operations on the same stream object (branching) fails the same way.

Where streams come from

SourceCodeNotes
Any collectionlist.stream(), set.stream()The most common source
A mapmap.entrySet().stream()Map itself has no stream(); use keySet(), values() or entrySet()
Fixed valuesStream.of("a", "b")Stream.ofNullable(x) (Java 9): empty if x is null
ArraysArrays.stream(arr), Arrays.stream(arr, from, to)An int[] gives an IntStream
Number rangesIntStream.range(0, 5), IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5)range excludes the end (0–4); rangeClosed includes it (1–5)
IterationStream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2)Infinite — add limit. Java 9 form with a condition: Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n * 3)
GeneratorStream.generate(UUID::randomUUID)Infinite; each element from a Supplier
File linesFiles.lines(path)Reads lazily; must be closed (try-with-resources)
Texttext.lines() (Java 11), text.chars()chars() gives an IntStream of char codes
OthersStream.empty(), Stream.concat(a, b), Pattern.splitAsStreamconcat joins two streams
 
System.out.println(IntStream.range(0, 5).boxed().toList());
System.out.println(IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).sum());
System.out.println(Stream.iterate(1, n -> n * 2).limit(6).toList());
System.out.println(Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 100, n -> n * 3).toList());
System.out.println(Stream.generate(() -> "hi").limit(3).toList());

int[] marks = {72, 85, 64};
System.out.println(Arrays.stream(marks).max().getAsInt());
System.out.println("hello".chars().filter(ch -> ch == 'l').count());

Map<String, Integer> stock = new TreeMap<>(Map.of("pen", 12, "book", 4, "bag", 0));
System.out.println(stock.entrySet().stream()
        .filter(e -> e.getValue() == 0)
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
        .toList());

// I/O-backed streams hold an open file: always close them
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(Path.of("orders.csv"))) {
    long failed = lines.filter(l -> l.endsWith(",FAILED")).count();
    System.out.println("Failed orders: " + failed);
}
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
15
[1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
[1, 3, 9, 27, 81]
[hi, hi, hi]
85
2
[bag]
Failed orders: 2

Kinds of streams and encounter order

There are four stream types: Stream<T> for objects, and IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream for primitives (with extras like sum() and average()). A stream from a List, an array or a range has an encounter order, and operations keep it. A stream from a HashSet has no defined order, so findFirst() on it can return any element.

Rules

  • Exactly one terminal operation per stream; after it, the stream is closed.
  • Without a terminal operation, nothing runs — not even peek or map.
  • Do not modify the source while the stream runs (no list.add inside the pipeline).
  • Close streams backed by I/O (Files.lines, Files.list, Files.walk) with try-with-resources. Streams over collections do not need closing.

Conventions

  • Put each operation on its own line, aligned under .stream(). Diffs and stack traces become readable.
  • Return collections from methods, not streams, unless the caller clearly needs lazy processing. A returned stream can be consumed only once.
  • Use peek only for debugging; never for logic.

Edge cases

  • Stream.of(intArray) gives a stream with one element — the array itself (Stream<int[]>). Stream.of(new int[]{1, 2, 3}).count() is 1. Use Arrays.stream(intArray) or IntStream.of(1, 2, 3).
  • An infinite stream without limit, takeWhile or a short-circuiting terminal never ends; with sorted() or collect it eventually throws OutOfMemoryError.
  • Files.lines throws UncheckedIOException during processing if a line cannot be decoded (for example, wrong charset); the file-not-found IOException is thrown when you open it.

Mistake: keeping a stream to use it twice

Wrong: IllegalStateException on the second use

Stream<Order> paid = orders.stream()
        .filter(Order::isPaid);
long count = paid.count();
List<Order> list = paid.toList();   // throws

Right: collect once, then reuse the list

List<Order> paid = orders.stream()
        .filter(Order::isPaid)
        .toList();
long count = paid.size();

Interview: "What is a stream? Intermediate vs terminal? What is lazy evaluation?"

  • A stream is a pipeline over a source; it stores nothing and does not change the source.
  • Intermediate operations return a stream and are lazy; terminal operations produce a result and trigger processing.
  • Elements flow one at a time through the whole chain; short-circuiting operations stop early. Show the peek demo if you can.
  • Stateful operations (sorted, distinct) must see many or all elements.
  • Streams are single-use: reuse throws IllegalStateException.

Intermediate operations: filter, map, flatMap, sorted and friends

Intermediate operations turn one stream into another, lazily: filter keeps elements, map transforms them, flatMap flattens nested data, sorted and distinct reorder or deduplicate, and limit, skip, takeWhile and dropWhile cut the stream.

The intermediate operations table

OperationWhat it doesKindExample
filter(Predicate)Keeps elements that matchStatelessfilter(o -> o.amount() > 800)
map(Function)Transforms each element (one in, one out)Statelessmap(Order::id)
flatMap(Function)Each element → a stream; all streams joined into oneStatelessflatMap(o -> o.items().stream())
mapToInt / mapToLong / mapToDoubleConverts to a primitive streamStatelessmapToInt(Employee::salary)
boxed(), mapToObj(...)Primitive stream → object streamStatelessIntStream.range(0, 3).boxed()
distinct()Removes duplicates using equals/hashCodeStatefulmap(Order::customer).distinct()
sorted(), sorted(Comparator)Natural order, or the given orderStatefulsorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::name))
peek(Consumer)Looks at each element as it passes (debugging)Statelesspeek(e -> log.debug("{}", e))
limit(n)Keeps the first n elementsShort-circuitinglimit(3)
skip(n)Drops the first n elementsStatefulskip(10)
takeWhile(Predicate) (9)Takes elements while the test is true; stops at the first falseShort-circuitingtakeWhile(n -> n < 5)
dropWhile(Predicate) (9)Drops elements while true; keeps everything afterStateless after the first falsedropWhile(n -> n < 5)

filter and map — the workhorses

record Order(String id, String customer, int amount, List<String> items) {}

List<Order> orders = List.of(
        new Order("O1", "Ravi", 1200, List.of("Phone case", "Charger")),
        new Order("O2", "Asha", 350, List.of("Notebook")),
        new Order("O3", "Ravi", 899, List.of("Earphones", "Charger")),
        new Order("O4", "Meera", 2500, List.of("Shoes")));

List<String> bigOrderIds = orders.stream()
        .filter(o -> o.amount() > 800)     // keep orders above ₹800
        .map(Order::id)                    // Order → String
        .toList();
System.out.println(bigOrderIds);           // [O1, O3, O4]

System.out.println(orders.stream().map(Order::customer).distinct().toList());
// [Ravi, Asha, Meera]

map vs flatMap

map is one-to-one: each element becomes exactly one new element. When each element holds a collection, map gives you a stream of collections. flatMap is one-to-many: the function returns a stream for each element, and flatMap joins ("flattens") all of them into a single stream.

List<List<String>> nested = orders.stream()
        .map(Order::items)                         // Stream<List<String>>
        .toList();
System.out.println(nested);

List<String> allItems = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.items().stream())          // Stream<String>
        .toList();
System.out.println(allItems);

List<String> uniqueItems = orders.stream()
        .flatMap(o -> o.items().stream())
        .distinct()
        .sorted()
        .toList();
System.out.println(uniqueItems);

List<String> lines = List.of("upi is fast", "cards are common");
System.out.println(lines.stream()
        .flatMap(line -> Arrays.stream(line.split(" ")))   // sentences → words
        .toList());
[[Phone case, Charger], [Notebook], [Earphones, Charger], [Shoes]]
[Phone case, Charger, Notebook, Earphones, Charger, Shoes]
[Charger, Earphones, Notebook, Phone case, Shoes]
[upi, is, fast, cards, are, common]

sorted with Comparator

sorted() uses the natural order (elements must implement Comparable, like String and Integer). For anything else, pass a Comparator, usually built with the helper methods from Module 4:

HelperMeaning
Comparator.comparing(Employee::name)Order by a key that is Comparable
Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary)Order by an int key without boxing
.thenComparing(Employee::name)Tie-breaker when the first key is equal
.reversed()Reverse the whole comparator built so far
Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())Reverse only this key
Comparator.nullsFirst(...), nullsLast(...)Decide where null values go instead of throwing
 
record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary, int age) {}

List<Employee> emps = List.of(
        new Employee("Ravi", "IT", 90000, 31),
        new Employee("Asha", "HR", 60000, 28),
        new Employee("Kiran", "IT", 90000, 26),
        new Employee("Meera", "IT", 120000, 35),
        new Employee("John", "HR", 75000, 40));

// Salary high → low, then name A → Z for equal salaries
System.out.println(emps.stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary).reversed()
                .thenComparing(Employee::name))
        .map(e -> e.name() + ":" + e.salary())
        .toList());

// Department A → Z, and inside each department salary high → low
System.out.println(emps.stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
                .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder()))
        .map(e -> e.dept() + "/" + e.name())
        .toList());
[Meera:120000, Kiran:90000, Ravi:90000, John:75000, Asha:60000]
[HR/John, HR/Asha, IT/Meera, IT/Ravi, IT/Kiran]

In the second result, Ravi and Kiran both earn 90,000, and they stay in their original order. For ordered streams, sorted is stable: equal elements keep their encounter order.

limit and skip — pagination

int page = 1, size = 2;                   // page index starts at 0
System.out.println(emps.stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::name))   // Asha, John, Kiran, Meera, Ravi
        .skip((long) page * size)
        .limit(size)
        .map(Employee::name)
        .toList());                       // [Kiran, Meera]

Good for in-memory lists. For database data, paginate in SQL (LIMIT/OFFSET or Spring Data's Pageable) instead of loading everything and skipping in Java.

takeWhile and dropWhile vs filter

List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 3, 10, 4, 5);
System.out.println(nums.stream().takeWhile(n -> n < 5).toList());   // [1, 2, 3]
System.out.println(nums.stream().filter(n -> n < 5).toList());      // [1, 2, 3, 4]
System.out.println(nums.stream().dropWhile(n -> n < 5).toList());   // [10, 4, 5]

takeWhile stops at the first element that fails — 4 is never reached. filter checks every element. Use takeWhile on data that is already sorted or ordered by the condition (log lines by time, prices ascending), where stopping early is both correct and faster.

Primitive streams: mapToInt, boxed, mapToObj

int total = emps.stream().mapToInt(Employee::salary).sum();                 // 435000
double avg = emps.stream()
        .mapToDouble(Employee::salary)
        .average()
        .getAsDouble();                                                      // 87000.0

List<Integer> squares = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5)
        .map(n -> n * n)       // IntStream → IntStream
        .boxed()               // IntStream → Stream<Integer>
        .toList();             // [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

List<String> seats = IntStream.range(0, 3)
        .mapToObj(i -> "Seat-" + i)
        .toList();             // [Seat-0, Seat-1, Seat-2]

Object streams have no sum(); convert with mapToInt first. Primitive streams cannot be collected with Collectors directly; convert back with boxed() or mapToObj.

Version note: mapMulti (Java 16)

mapMulti((element, sink) -> ...) is an alternative to flatMap: instead of returning a stream, you push zero or more results into sink. It avoids creating many small streams. orders.stream().<String>mapMulti((o, sink) -> o.items().forEach(sink)) gives the same 6 items as the flatMap example. flatMap remains the common, readable choice.

Rules

  • The function given to map must return a value. map(s -> System.out.println(s)) does not compile, because println returns void.
  • The function given to flatMap must return a Stream, not a List — write o.items().stream().
  • sorted() without a comparator requires Comparable elements.

Edge cases and runtime exceptions

  • sorted() on elements that are not Comparable compiles, but throws ClassCastException (… cannot be cast to class java.lang.Comparable) when the terminal operation runs.
  • distinct() relies on equals and hashCode. Records have them; a plain class without them is compared by identity, so "duplicates" stay.
  • If the function in flatMap returns null, that element contributes nothing (it is treated as an empty stream).
  • takeWhile/dropWhile on an unordered source (a HashSet) give unpredictable results.
  • Sorting with null keys throws NullPointerException; wrap the key comparator with Comparator.nullsLast(...).

Mistake: a lambda key extractor before reversed()

Comparator.comparing(e -> e.name()).reversed() fails with "cannot find symbol: method name(), location: variable e of type Object". With .reversed() chained on, the compiler cannot use the target type to infer e, so it falls back to Object. Use a method reference (Employee::name) or type the parameter: (Employee e) -> e.name().

Wrong: does not compile

emps.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(e -> e.name()).reversed())
    .toList();

Right: method reference gives the type

emps.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::name).reversed())
    .toList();

Tip: filter early, map late

Put filter before expensive map calls and before sorted. Sorting 100 filtered elements is far cheaper than sorting 100,000 and filtering afterwards. The result is the same; the work is not.

Interview: "Difference between map and flatMap?" and "What is a stateful operation?"

  • map: one input → one output. flatMap: one input → a stream of outputs, all joined into one stream. Example: orders → items.
  • Stateful operations (sorted, distinct, skip, limit) need information about other elements; stateless ones (filter, map) handle each element alone.
  • takeWhile stops at the first failure; filter checks every element.
  • reversed() reverses the whole comparator chain; use Comparator.reverseOrder() as a second argument to reverse one key.

Terminal operations: collect, reduce, count, match and find

A terminal operation starts the pipeline and closes the stream: it returns a result (a collection, a number, an Optional, a boolean) or acts on every element, and the short-circuiting ones — findFirst, anyMatch and a few others — can stop before the end.

Intermediate operations only describe work. The terminal operation is the one that makes the stream run, and it decides what you get back: a list, a number, a yes/no answer, or nothing at all. A pipeline has exactly one, at the end. When it finishes, the stream is used up (see What a stream is).

Terminal operations at a glance

OperationReturnsShort-circuits?Typical use
forEach(Consumer), forEachOrdered(Consumer)voidNoAn action per element: print, log, send
collect(Collector)Whatever the collector buildsNoList, Set, Map, String, statistics
toList() (Java 16)Unmodifiable List<T>NoThe everyday "give me a list"
toArray(), toArray(String[]::new)Object[] or T[]NoWhen an API needs an array
reduce(...)Optional<T> or one valueNoCombine all elements into one value
count()longNoHow many elements
min(Comparator), max(Comparator)Optional<T>NoSmallest or largest element
anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatchbooleanYesYes/no questions about the data
findFirst(), findAny()Optional<T>YesOne element that passed the pipeline
sum(), average(), min(), max(), summaryStatistics()A number, an OptionalInt / OptionalDouble, or a statistics objectNoOnly on IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream

The sample data for this article and the next three

Eight employees. Two earn exactly 90,000 and two names start with A and K — that is on purpose, because ties and repeated letters are where stream code goes wrong.

record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary, int age) {}

List<Employee> emps = List.of(
        new Employee("Ravi",   "IT",      90000, 31),
        new Employee("Asha",   "HR",      60000, 28),
        new Employee("Kiran",  "IT",      90000, 26),
        new Employee("Meera",  "IT",     120000, 35),
        new Employee("John",   "HR",      75000, 40),
        new Employee("Kavya",  "Finance", 82000, 29),
        new Employee("Sanjay", "Finance", 95000, 45),
        new Employee("Anita",  "IT",      70000, 24));

forEach and forEachOrdered

forEach runs an action for each element and returns nothing. On a normal (sequential) stream it follows the encounter order. On a parallel stream it does not: elements can be handled in any order, by different threads. forEachOrdered keeps the encounter order even in parallel, but loses part of the speed-up.

emps.stream()
        .filter(e -> e.dept().equals("HR"))
        .forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.name() + " works in HR"));
Asha works in HR
John works in HR

Use forEach only for actions that leave the pipeline — printing, logging, sending an e-mail. Do not use it to build a result; that is the job of collect and toList(). If you already have a collection, list.forEach(...) works without .stream(), and map.forEach((key, value) -> ...) works on a map. Inside the lambda, return only leaves the lambda — it behaves like continue. You cannot break out of a forEach.

Getting a list: toList() vs Collectors.toList()

Pointstream.toList() (Java 16)collect(Collectors.toList())Collectors.toUnmodifiableList() (Java 10)
Can you add or remove?No — UnsupportedOperationExceptionYes in practice (an ArrayList), but the Javadoc promises nothingNo
Allows null elements?YesYesNo — NullPointerException
Best forRead-only results — most codeOld code; or when you modify the list afterwardsRead-only, and you want null rejected early
 
List<String> readOnly = emps.stream().map(Employee::name).toList();
// readOnly.add("Zoya");   // throws UnsupportedOperationException

// Need to modify the result? Say so explicitly. It guarantees an ArrayList.
List<String> editable = emps.stream()
        .map(Employee::name)
        .collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new));
editable.add("Zoya");
System.out.println(editable.size());

Object[] objects = emps.stream().map(Employee::name).toArray();
String[] names = emps.stream().map(Employee::name).toArray(String[]::new);
int[] salaries = emps.stream().mapToInt(Employee::salary).toArray();
System.out.println(names.length + " " + salaries[0]);
9
8 90000

toArray() without arguments gives an Object[], which is rarely what you want. Pass an array constructor reference (String[]::new) to get a typed array.

reduce: many values into one

reduce repeatedly combines two values into one. "Sum of a list" is the classic case: start at 0, add the first element, add the second, and so on. It has three forms:

FormReturnsUse it when
reduce(BinaryOperator<T> op)Optional<T>There is no natural starting value and the stream may be empty
reduce(T identity, BinaryOperator<T> op)TInput and result have the same type; the identity is the answer for an empty stream
reduce(U identity, BiFunction<U, T, U> accumulator, BinaryOperator<U> combiner)UThe result type differs from the element type; the combiner merges partial results of a parallel run

The identity is a value that changes nothing when combined with any element: 0 for addition, 1 for multiplication, "" for string concatenation. Form 1 has no identity, so it cannot answer for an empty stream — it returns an empty Optional instead.

List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4);

int sum = nums.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);                       // form 2
Optional<Integer> product = nums.stream().reduce((a, b) -> a * b);    // form 1
int totalLetters = List.of("java", "is", "fun").stream()               // form 3
        .reduce(0, (acc, word) -> acc + word.length(), Integer::sum);
System.out.println(sum + " " + product + " " + totalLetters);

// What happens step by step
int total = nums.stream().reduce(0, (acc, n) -> {
    System.out.println(acc + " + " + n);
    return acc + n;
});
System.out.println("total = " + total);
10 Optional[24] 9
0 + 1
1 + 2
3 + 3
6 + 4
total = 10

In the three-argument form the accumulator folds one element into the running result (a number plus a word's length). The combiner is only used when the stream runs in parallel: each thread reduces its own chunk, and the combiner joins the chunk results. Even if you never go parallel, supply a correct one.

Rule: a reduce function must be associative, stateless and consistent with the identity

  • Associative: (a op b) op c must equal a op (b op c). Addition, multiplication, max and string concatenation qualify. Subtraction and division do not, so reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b) gives wrong answers in parallel.
  • Identity: op(identity, x) must equal x. Using 10 as the "starting value" of a sum is not an identity (see the next mistake).
  • Stateless: the function must not read or change outside variables.

Mistake: a starting value that is not an identity

nums.stream().reduce(10, Integer::sum) returns 20 on a sequential stream. On a parallel stream every chunk starts from 10. If the list splits into four one-element chunks, you get (10+1) + (10+2) + (10+3) + (10+4) = 50. Add the offset after the reduce: 10 + nums.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum).

reduce vs collect

reduce builds one immutable value (a number, a maximum). collect uses a mutable container (a list, a map, a StringBuilder) that it fills in place. Building a container with reduce means creating a new one at every step — slow, and unsafe in parallel.

Wrong: string building with reduce

String s = emps.stream()
        .limit(2)
        .map(Employee::name)
        .reduce("", (a, b) -> a + ", " + b);
// ", Ravi, Asha"  (leading comma, and O(n²) copying)

Right: collect with joining

String s = emps.stream()
        .limit(2)
        .map(Employee::name)
        .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
// "Ravi, Asha"

count, min and max

count() returns a long. min and max take a Comparator and return an Optional, because an empty stream has no smallest element.

long itCount = emps.stream().filter(e -> e.dept().equals("IT")).count();
String top = emps.stream()
        .max(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::salary))
        .map(Employee::name).orElse("nobody");
String youngest = emps.stream()
        .min(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::age))
        .map(Employee::name).orElse("nobody");

boolean anyAbove1Lakh = emps.stream().anyMatch(e -> e.salary() > 100000);
boolean allAdults = emps.stream().allMatch(e -> e.age() >= 18);
boolean noneInSales = emps.stream().noneMatch(e -> e.dept().equals("Sales"));
String firstHr = emps.stream()
        .filter(e -> e.dept().equals("HR"))
        .findFirst().map(Employee::name).orElse("nobody");

System.out.println(itCount + " " + top + " " + youngest);
System.out.println(anyAbove1Lakh + " " + allAdults + " " + noneInSales + " " + firstHr);
4 Meera Anita
true true true Asha

anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch — and the empty stream

OperationTrue whenOn an empty streamStops at
anyMatch(p)At least one element matchesfalseThe first match
allMatch(p)Every element matchestrueThe first non-match
noneMatch(p)No element matchestrueThe first match

On an empty stream, allMatch and noneMatch return true because nothing breaks the rule — logicians call this vacuous truth. It surprises people when a filter removes everything: orders.stream().filter(Order::isPaid).allMatch(Order::hasInvoice) is true even when there are no paid orders.

findFirst vs findAny

Both return an Optional with one element of the stream. findFirst() returns the first element in encounter order. findAny() may return any element: on a sequential stream it almost always returns the first, but on a parallel stream it is free to return whichever thread finishes first — and that is faster. Use findAny() when any match will do and the stream is parallel; otherwise use findFirst().

Terminal operations on primitive streams

int[] marks = {72, 85, 64, 91};
IntSummaryStatistics st = Arrays.stream(marks).summaryStatistics();
System.out.println(st);
System.out.println(Arrays.stream(marks).average().orElse(0));
System.out.println(IntStream.empty().sum());
System.out.println(IntStream.empty().max());
System.out.println(IntStream.empty().average());
IntSummaryStatistics{count=4, sum=312, min=64, average=78.000000, max=91}
78.0
0
OptionalInt.empty
OptionalDouble.empty

sum() of an empty stream is 0. max(), min() and average() return OptionalInt or OptionalDouble, because there is no sensible answer for no data. Read them with getAsInt(), orElse(...) or orElseThrow().

Edge cases

  • count() may skip your pipeline. Since Java 9, if the count can be worked out from the source alone (a List with no filter in between), the stream does not run — so peek and map never execute. A filter makes the size unknown, and then the pipeline runs. Do not put side effects in a stream that ends in count().
  • IntStream.sum() overflows silently. IntStream.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1).sum() is -2147483648. Use mapToLong or asLongStream() when totals can be large: IntStream.of(Integer.MAX_VALUE, 1).asLongStream().sum() is 2147483648.
  • findFirst() and findAny() throw NullPointerException if the element they would return is null, because an Optional cannot hold null.
  • Optional.get() on an empty result throws NoSuchElementException: No value present.
  • A second terminal operation on the same stream throws IllegalStateException.
List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 3);
long a = nums.stream().peek(n -> System.out.println("peek " + n)).count();
System.out.println("count = " + a);
long b = nums.stream().filter(n -> n > 1)
        .peek(n -> System.out.println("peek " + n)).count();
System.out.println("count = " + b);
count = 3
peek 2
peek 3
count = 2

Mistakes: forEach to build a result, and get() without a check

Wrong: side effect on an outside list

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
emps.stream().forEach(e -> names.add(e.name()));
// breaks (lost updates) on a parallel stream

Right: let the stream build it

List<String> names = emps.stream()
        .map(Employee::name)
        .toList();

Wrong: NoSuchElementException

String n = emps.stream()
        .filter(e -> e.dept().equals("Sales"))
