Look at the third and fourth lines. withZoneSameInstant keeps the moment and changes the clock reading (18:30 in Kolkata is 09:00 in New York). withZoneSameLocal keeps the clock reading and therefore changes the moment — a different moment, 9.5 hours later. You almost always want withZoneSameInstant.

Daylight saving: gaps and overlaps

When clocks jump forward, some local times never exist (a gap). When they fall back, some happen twice (an overlap). ZonedDateTime handles both, and LocalDateTime cannot.

ZoneId ny = ZoneId.of("America/New_York");

// 8 March 2026: clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00, so 02:30 does not exist
System.out.println(ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 8, 2, 30, 0, 0, ny));

// 1 November 2026: 01:30 happens twice; the earlier one is the default
ZonedDateTime overlap = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 11, 1, 1, 30, 0, 0, ny);
System.out.println(overlap + " | " + overlap.withLaterOffsetAtOverlap());

// "One day later" vs "24 hours later" across the 8 March change
ZonedDateTime before = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 7, 12, 0, 0, 0, ny);
System.out.println(before.plus(Period.ofDays(1)) + " | " + before.plus(Duration.ofHours(24)));
2026-03-08T03:30-04:00[America/New_York]
2026-11-01T01:30-04:00[America/New_York] | 2026-11-01T01:30-05:00[America/New_York]
2026-03-08T12:00-04:00[America/New_York] | 2026-03-08T13:00-04:00[America/New_York]

The gap time moved forward to 03:30. Period.ofDays(1) keeps the same clock time (12:00 the next day), while Duration.ofHours(24) adds exact time (13:00, because that day had only 23 hours). Choose the one that matches the business rule: "same time tomorrow" or "24 hours from now".

Formatting and parsing with DateTimeFormatter

DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe, so create it once, as a static final constant — the opposite of SimpleDateFormat. format turns a date-time into text; parse turns text into a date-time. The ready-made ISO constants (ISO_LOCAL_DATE, ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME, ...) match each type's default toString(), and the pattern letters give you everything else:

PatternMeaningExample
yyyy or uuuuYear (uuuu is safer in strict mode)2026
MM, MMM, MMMMMonth: number, short name, full name10, Oct, October
dd, dDay of month, with or without a leading zero05, 5
EEE, EEEEDay of the week, short or fullWed, Wednesday
HH, hh with aHour 0–23, or hour 1–12 with AM/PM18, 06 PM
mm, ss, SSSMinutes, seconds, milliseconds30, 05, 000
XXXOffset from UTC (Z for zero)+05:30
z, VVZone name, zone idIST, Asia/Kolkata
'T'Literal text inside single quotesT
 
LocalDateTime dt = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 10, 21, 18, 30, 5);
ZonedDateTime zdt = dt.atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));

System.out.println(dt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd MMM yyyy", Locale.ENGLISH)));
System.out.println(dt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE, d MMMM uuuu", Locale.ENGLISH)));
System.out.println(dt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MM-yyyy hh:mm a", Locale.ENGLISH)));
System.out.println(dt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm:ss")));
System.out.println(zdt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ssXXX")));
System.out.println(zdt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm z VV", Locale.ENGLISH)));
System.out.println(zdt.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME));
21 Oct 2026
Wednesday, 21 October 2026
21-10-2026 06:30 PM
21/10/2026 18:30:05
2026-10-21T18:30:05+05:30
18:30 IST Asia/Kolkata
2026-10-21T18:30:05+05:30

Always pass a Locale when the pattern prints words (month or day names, AM/PM). Without one, Java uses the JVM's default locale, and the same code prints different text on different machines.

DateTimeFormatter dmy = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy");
System.out.println(LocalDate.parse("21/10/2026", dmy));
System.out.println(LocalDateTime.parse("2026-10-21T18:30"));     // ISO needs no formatter

LocalDate.parse("2026-13-45");
LocalDate.parse("21-10-2026");
LocalDate.parse("21-10-2026", dmy);
2026-10-21
2026-10-21T18:30
Exception in thread "main" java.time.format.DateTimeParseException:
    Text '2026-13-45' could not be parsed: Invalid value for MonthOfYear (valid values 1 - 12): 13
    Text '21-10-2026' could not be parsed at index 0
    Text '21-10-2026' could not be parsed at index 2

Each of the last three lines is a separate exception (shown together to save space). The index tells you where parsing stopped. For user input, catch DateTimeParseException and return a clear error, for example an HTTP 400 with "date must be dd/MM/yyyy".

Edge case: lenient (SMART) parsing silently repairs impossible dates

By default a formatter uses the SMART resolver. LocalDate.parse("31/04/2026", dmy) does not fail — April has 30 days, so you get 2026-04-30. For input validation, switch to strict mode, which needs uuuu for the year:

DateTimeFormatter strict = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/uuuu")
        .withResolverStyle(ResolverStyle.STRICT);
System.out.println(LocalDate.parse("30/04/2026", strict));
LocalDate.parse("31/04/2026", strict);
2026-04-30
Exception in thread "main" java.time.format.DateTimeParseException:
    Text '31/04/2026' could not be parsed: Invalid date 'APRIL 31'

With yyyy instead of uuuu, strict mode fails even for valid dates, because year-of-era needs an era. Use uuuu with STRICT.

Mistakes in patterns: YYYY, mm and shared formatters

  • YYYY is the week-based year, not the calendar year. LocalDate.of(2025, 12, 29) formatted with YYYY-MM-dd and Locale.US gives 2026-12-29, because that week belongs to 2026. It looks fine for 360 days a year and fails around New Year. Use yyyy (or uuuu).
  • mm is minutes, MM is months. dd/mm/yyyy on a LocalDateTime prints the minutes where the month should be, without any error.
  • Using SimpleDateFormat as a shared static field. It is not thread-safe. Replace it with a static final DateTimeFormatter.

Storing and exchanging timestamps: use UTC

The rule used by most backend teams: store and pass around moments in UTC (Instant), and convert to a user's zone only at the edge, when you display them. UTC has no daylight saving, so every value is unambiguous, sorting and comparing just work, and moving the server to another region cannot change your data. Bugs of the "works on my laptop" kind usually come from code that relies on the default zone: the laptop runs in IST, the cloud server in UTC. Set the zone explicitly (-Duser.timezone=UTC for the JVM, and with Hibernate spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.time_zone=UTC) and never call a method that silently uses the default.

You need to storeJava typePostgreSQLMySQL
A date: birthday, holiday, due dateLocalDatedateDATE
A time of day: opening timeLocalTimetimeTIME
A moment that happened: created at, paid atInstant (or OffsetDateTime in UTC)timestamptz (timestamp with time zone)TIMESTAMP, or DATETIME holding UTC
A future appointment in a user's zoneLocalDateTime plus a zone id column (or ZonedDateTime)timestamp plus a text column for the zoneDATETIME plus a text column for the zone
Showing a time to a userConvert Instant to ZonedDateTime in their zone, then format——

Why the zone id for future appointments? Governments change daylight-saving rules. "10:00 on 5 November in Kolkata" must stay 10:00 local, so you keep the local time and the zone, and compute the instant when you need it. A moment that has already happened never changes, so UTC is enough.

Database details

  • PostgreSQL timestamptz stores UTC internally and shows values in the session's time zone. Plain timestamp stores no zone information at all.
  • MySQL TIMESTAMP is stored as UTC and converted using the session time zone, with a range that ends in 2038. DATETIME stores exactly what you give it, with no conversion and no zone.
  • With Spring Data JPA and a current Hibernate, entity fields of type LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Instant, OffsetDateTime and ZonedDateTime all work. Prefer Instant for audit columns such as createdAt.
  • Spring MVC parses LocalDate request parameters in ISO format by default; use @DateTimeFormat(pattern = "dd-MM-yyyy") on the parameter for another format.

Converting legacy Date, Calendar and java.sql types

Old libraries and JDBC drivers still hand you java.util.Date, Calendar and java.sql types. Convert at the boundary, go through Instant, and keep java.time inside your code.

FromToCode
java.util.DateInstantdate.toInstant()
Instantjava.util.DateDate.from(instant)
DateLocalDateTimedate.toInstant().atZone(zone).toLocalDateTime()
java.sql.DateLocalDatesqlDate.toLocalDate() and java.sql.Date.valueOf(localDate)
java.sql.TimestampLocalDateTimets.toLocalDateTime() and Timestamp.valueOf(localDateTime)
CalendarInstantcalendar.toInstant()
 
java.util.Date legacy = new java.util.Date(0L);
Instant instant = legacy.toInstant();
System.out.println(instant);
System.out.println(Instant.ofEpochMilli(legacy.getTime())
        .atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata")).toLocalDateTime());

java.sql.Date sqlDate = java.sql.Date.valueOf(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 21));
java.sql.Timestamp ts = java.sql.Timestamp.valueOf(LocalDateTime.of(2026, 10, 21, 18, 30));
System.out.println(sqlDate.toLocalDate() + " " + ts.toLocalDateTime());
1970-01-01T00:00:00Z
1970-01-01T05:30
2026-10-21 2026-10-21T18:30

Edge cases

  • A zone is needed to turn an Instant into a date. new GregorianCalendar(2026, 9, 21) is midnight in the JVM's zone. On a machine in India, calendar.toInstant().atZone(ZoneId.of("UTC")).toLocalDate() gives 2026-10-20, because midnight in Kolkata is 18:30 UTC the day before. Use the zone the value was created in, usually ZoneId.systemDefault().
  • Do not use three-letter zone ids. ZoneId.of("IST") throws ZoneRulesException: Unknown time-zone ID: IST (IST could mean India, Israel or Ireland). Use region ids: Asia/Kolkata.
  • Instant, OffsetDateTime and ZonedDateTime that denote the same moment are not all equals: two ZonedDateTime values with different zones are unequal even if they are the same instant. Compare with toInstant().equals(...), or isEqual.

Conventions

  • Store moments as Instant / timestamptz in UTC; convert to a ZoneId only for display.
  • Exchange text in ISO-8601 (2026-10-21T13:00:00Z); let the front end format it for the user's locale.
  • Always give formatters an explicit Locale and keep them as static final constants.
  • Use region ids (Asia/Kolkata), never abbreviations (IST).
  • Do not use Date, Calendar or SimpleDateFormat in new code.

Interview: "How do you handle time zones in a backend? What do you store in the database?"

  • Store UTC (Instant, timestamptz); convert to the user's ZoneId at the edge; use ISO-8601 in APIs.
  • ZoneId (region with rules) vs ZoneOffset (fixed). withZoneSameInstant vs withZoneSameLocal.
  • Never depend on the server's default zone; set it explicitly and inject a Clock.
  • Parsing: DateTimeParseException; strict resolver for validation. Formatting: yyyy not YYYY; MM vs mm.
  • DateTimeFormatter is thread-safe; SimpleDateFormat is not.
  • Legacy: Date.toInstant() and Date.from(instant).

var and text blocks

var (Java 10) lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable from its initializer, and text blocks (Java 15) let you write multi-line strings between triple quotes without escape noise.

var: local variable type inference

var tells the compiler: "work out the type from the right-hand side". The variable is still statically typed; the type is fixed at compile time and you cannot later put a different type into it. It is not dynamic typing like JavaScript.

import java.util.*;

public class VarDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var name = "Asha";                       // String
        var count = 3;                           // int
        var prices = new ArrayList<Double>();   // ArrayList<Double>
        var byCity = new HashMap<String, List<String>>();

        prices.add(499.5);
        byCity.computeIfAbsent("Pune", k -> new ArrayList<>()).add("Asha");

        for (var p : prices) {                   // double -> Double
            System.out.println(p);
        }
        // count = "three";   // compile error: int cannot hold a String
        System.out.println(name + " " + count + " " + byCity);
    }
}
499.5
Asha 3 {Pune=[Asha]}

Where var is allowed and where it is not

PlaceAllowed?Why
Local variable with initializerYesThe type comes from the initializer
Enhanced for variable, classic for indexYesfor (var e : list)
try-with-resources variableYestry (var in = Files.newBufferedReader(p))
Lambda parameters (Java 11)YesMainly to add annotations: (@NonNull var s) -> s.length()
Fields, method parameters, return typesNoThese are part of an API; the type must be written
var x; with no initializerNoNothing to infer from
var x = null;Nonull has no type
var a = {1, 2};NoArray initializer needs a target type
var f = () -> 1;NoA lambda needs a target functional interface

Readability guidance

var removes repetition when the type is obvious: var users = new ArrayList<User>() is better than ArrayList<User> users = new ArrayList<User>(). It hurts when the reader cannot see the type. Compare:

Wrong: the type is a mystery

var result = service.process(request);
var data = repo.load(id);
var x = compute() / 3;      // int? long? double?

Right: obvious from the right side

var users = new ArrayList<User>();
var path = Path.of("orders.csv");
Invoice result = service.process(request);

Good habits: use meaningful variable names (the name now carries more meaning), keep methods short so the declaration is near the use, and write the explicit type when the right-hand side is a method call whose return type is not obvious. Two traps: var list = new ArrayList<>() infers ArrayList<Object> because the diamond has no target type; and var n = 10 is an int, so use 10L if you want a long. Also, var is not a keyword but a "reserved type name": you can still have a variable called var, but you cannot name a class var.

Text blocks

Before Java 15, a JSON or SQL string in code was a mess of \", \n and +. A text block starts with """ followed by a line break and ends with """.

public class TextBlockDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String json = """
                {
                  "orderId": 1001,
                  "customer": "Asha",
                  "items": ["pen", "notebook"]
                }
                """;
        System.out.print(json);

        String sql = """
                SELECT id, name
                FROM employees
                WHERE department = 'IT'
                ORDER BY name
                """;
        System.out.println(sql.lines().count() + " lines of SQL");
    }
}
{
  "orderId": 1001,
  "customer": "Asha",
  "items": ["pen", "notebook"]
}
4 lines of SQL

The SQL text block has four lines (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY). The closing """ on its own line adds a final line break to the string but no extra line for lines().

Indentation rules

  1. Java finds the least-indented line among all content lines and the line with the closing """, and removes that much leading white space from every line. This is called incidental white space.
  2. So the closing delimiter controls the indent. If you put """ on its own line at the left edge, nothing more is removed; if you put it at the end of the last content line, there is no final line break.
  3. Trailing spaces on each line are removed.
  4. Line breaks inside are normalized to \n, whatever the source file uses.

Escapes: \, \s and quotes

  • A backslash at the end of a line joins it with the next line (no line break is inserted). Good for long single-line text in your source.
  • \s is a single space and is not trimmed, so use it to keep trailing space.
  • Normal escapes (\n, \t, \", \\) work. A single " needs no escape. To write three quotes in a row, escape one: \""".
String msg = """
        Dear %s, your order %d has shipped. \
        It will arrive by %s.
        """.formatted("Asha", 1001, "Friday");
System.out.print(msg);
Dear Asha, your order 1001 has shipped. It will arrive by Friday.

String.formatted(...) (Java 15) is the same as String.format(this, ...), and it chains nicely after a text block. Related String methods you will use with them: stripIndent(), translateEscapes() and lines().

Rules

  • The opening """ must be followed by a line break; content on the same line is a compile error.
  • A text block is still a normal String: same type, immutable, works with equals.
  • var needs an initializer that tells the type; use it only for local variables.

Mistake: building SQL from user input in a text block

A text block makes SQL easier to read, but concatenating user values into it is still SQL injection. Use PreparedStatement parameters or named parameters in Spring.

Interview: "Is var dynamic typing?"

  • No. It is compile-time inference; the type is fixed.
  • Only for locals, loop variables and lambda parameters; not fields or method signatures.
  • Use it when the type is clear from the right side; avoid it when it hides the type.

Switch expressions, arrow labels and yield

Since Java 14 a switch can be an expression that produces a value, uses arrow labels with no fall-through, groups labels with commas, and must cover every possible input.

The old switch and its problems

The classic switch statement uses case X: with break. Forget one break and execution falls through into the next case, a famous source of bugs. You also needed a temporary variable to get a value out of it.

int days;
switch (month) {
    case "FEB":
        days = 28;
        break;
    case "APR": case "JUN": case "SEP": case "NOV":
        days = 30;
        break;
    default:
        days = 31;      // forgetting a break above would silently change results
}

The new switch expression

public class SwitchDemo {
    enum Day { MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI, SAT, SUN }

    static String typeOf(Day d) {
        return switch (d) {                    // switch is an expression: it has a value
            case SAT, SUN -> "Weekend";        // several labels in one case
            case MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI -> "Weekday";
        };                                     // no default needed: all enum values covered
    }

    static int days(String month, boolean leap) {
        return switch (month) {
            case "FEB" -> leap ? 29 : 28;
            case "APR", "JUN", "SEP", "NOV" -> 30;
            default -> 31;                     // required for String: values are unbounded
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(typeOf(Day.SUN));
        System.out.println(days("FEB", true));
        System.out.println(days("JAN", false));
    }
}
Weekend
29
31

Differences you must remember:

  • Arrow labels (->) do not fall through. Only the code to the right runs. No break is needed.
  • The right side of an arrow is an expression, a block { ... }, or a throw statement.
  • A switch expression must be exhaustive: every possible value needs a result. For an enum you can list all constants; for int, String and other open types you need default.
  • You can use the arrow form as a statement too (no value needed, and then exhaustiveness is not required for old-style types).

Blocks and yield

When a case needs several statements, use a block and give the value with yield.

static double shippingCost(String zone, double weightKg) {
    return switch (zone) {
        case "LOCAL" -> 40;
        case "METRO" -> {
            double base = 60;
            double extra = Math.max(0, weightKg - 1) * 20;
            yield base + extra;                      // value of this case
        }
        case "REMOTE" -> {
            if (weightKg > 20) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Too heavy for remote delivery");
            }
            yield 150 + weightKg * 30;
        }
        default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown zone: " + zone);
    };
}

yield works in the old colon style as well, for people who prefer it:

int code = switch (status) {
    case "OK":
        yield 200;
    case "NOT_FOUND":
        yield 404;
    default:
        yield 500;
};

Do not mix arrows and colons in one switch; that is a compile error.

Comparing old and new

PointOld statement (case X:)New (case X ->)
Fall-throughYes, unless breakNo
Produces a valueNoYes (as an expression)
Multiple values per casecase A: case B:case A, B ->
Exhaustiveness checkNoYes for expressions and for pattern switches
Variable scopeOne scope for all casesEach case has its own scope

What can you switch on?

int, char, short, byte (and their wrappers), String, enums, and, since Java 21, any reference type with patterns (see pattern matching). Not long, float, double or boolean.

Rules

  • A switch expression must produce a value on every path: either cover all cases or add default.
  • Inside a switch expression you cannot break, continue or return out of it. Use yield for a value or throw.
  • String case labels must be compile-time constants and unique; duplicate labels do not compile.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NullPointerException — switching on a null String or enum (unless you use a pattern switch with case null).
  • MatchException (Java 21) — an exhaustive switch with no default meets an enum constant or subtype that was added after the switch was compiled (only possible when jars are compiled separately).
  • Omitting default on an enum is a feature: when you add a new constant, the compiler flags every switch expression that does not handle it.

Convention

Prefer arrow switch for new code. Skip default for enums and sealed types so the compiler checks exhaustiveness for you. Keep each case short; move long logic into a method and call it.

Result type, scope and statements

All arms of a switch expression must produce values that fit one type. If the arms give int and double, the result is double, just like a conditional ?:. If you assign the switch to a variable, every arm must be compatible with that variable. Each arm also has its own scope, so two cases can declare a local with the same name without clashing, which was a trap in the old form.

An arrow case can also be a plain statement when the switch is a statement. Then the right side is an expression statement, a block or a throw:

enum Event { PLACED, PACKED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }

static void notifyCustomer(Event e, String orderId) {
    switch (e) {                                       // a statement, arrow form
        case PLACED, PACKED -> System.out.println("Order " + orderId + " is being prepared");
        case SHIPPED -> System.out.println("Order " + orderId + " is on the way");
        case DELIVERED -> {
            System.out.println("Order " + orderId + " delivered");
            System.out.println("Please rate your experience");
        }
        case CANCELLED -> throw new IllegalStateException("No message for cancelled orders");
    }
}

As a rule: if you want a value, use an expression and make the compiler check coverage; if you only want a side effect, the statement form is fine.

HTTP status to message: a realistic example

static String describe(int status) {
    return switch (status / 100) {                    // group by the first digit
        case 2 -> status == 204 ? "No content" : "Success";
        case 3 -> "Redirect";
        case 4 -> switch (status) {                   // a switch inside a switch
            case 400 -> "Bad request";
            case 401, 403 -> "Not allowed";
            case 404 -> "Not found";
            default -> "Client error";
        };
        case 5 -> "Server error";
        default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Not an HTTP status: " + status);
    };
}

// describe(204) → No content    describe(403) → Not allowed    describe(503) → Server error

Old-style fall-through still has a place

A colon switch statement can fall through on purpose, for example to run steps from some point onward. The arrow form cannot do this; there you list the labels instead. Prefer the arrow form unless you truly want the cascade, and mark deliberate fall-through with a comment.

switch (stage) {
    case "ORDER":   validate();       // falls through
    case "PAYMENT": charge();         // falls through
    case "SHIP":    dispatch();       // ORDER runs all three; SHIP runs only this one
}

Wrong: leaving the expression with return or break

String label = switch (code) {
    case 1 -> "one";
    case 2 -> { return "two"; }   // compile error
    default -> { break; }          // compile error
};

Right: yield the value

String label = switch (code) {
    case 1 -> "one";
    case 2 -> { yield "two"; }
    default -> "many";
};

Common mistakes

  • Mixing -> and : in the same switch is a compile error.
  • Forgetting default on a String or int switch expression. The compiler reports that the switch expression does not cover all possible input values.
  • Adding default to an enum switch "to be safe". It hides the compile error that would tell you a new constant is unhandled. Leave it out unless unknown values are truly possible.
  • Using a non-constant as a label. case limit -> compiles only if limit is a final variable with a constant value.
  • Writing a method called yield and calling it unqualified. yield is a restricted identifier now; call Thread.yield() with the class name.

More edge cases

  • Switching on an enum in a separate module or jar: if a new constant is added later and the switch is not recompiled, an exhaustive switch expression without default throws MatchException (older versions threw IncompatibleClassChangeError).
  • A throw arm has no value, so it fits any result type. It is the usual way to reject unknown input in a default arm.
  • Since Java 21 you may also write the enum constant with its type name (case Day.SAT). Both forms work.
  • A switch statement over a String compares with equals internally (through the hash code first), so it is case-sensitive: "fri" does not match "FRI". Normalise with toUpperCase() first.

In real projects

Switch expressions are common for mapping an enum to a label, a fee, a Spring HttpStatus or an error code; for choosing a strategy by a request type; and for turning a database status string into a domain enum. When the same switch appears in many places, that is a hint to move the behaviour into the enum itself (an abstract method per constant) or into a sealed hierarchy with pattern matching.

Interview: "What is new in switch since Java 14?"

  • Switch as an expression with a value; arrow labels; comma-separated labels; no fall-through.
  • yield returns a value from a block; exhaustiveness is enforced.
  • Java 21 adds pattern matching, guards (when) and case null.

Pattern matching: instanceof, record patterns and switch

Pattern matching lets you test a value's type and pull it apart in one step: instanceof binds a typed variable (Java 16), record patterns deconstruct records, and switch can choose by type with guards and null handling (Java 21).

Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16)

The old code tests the type and then casts, repeating the type name three times:

if (obj instanceof String) {
    String s = (String) obj;
    System.out.println(s.length());
}

With a type pattern you declare the variable in the test. If the test is true, the variable is already cast:

if (obj instanceof String s) {
    System.out.println(s.length());
}
// combined with a condition (s is in scope on the right of &&)
if (obj instanceof String s && s.length() > 5) {
    System.out.println(s.toUpperCase());
}

The binding variable s exists only where the compiler can prove the test was true. That is the "scope of a pattern variable":

if (!(obj instanceof String s)) {
    return;                    // leave early when it is NOT a String
}
System.out.println(s.length());   // s is in scope here: we only get here if it matched

// if (obj instanceof String s || s.isEmpty())   // compile error: s not definite in ||

A typical use is a clean equals method: return o instanceof Point p && x == p.x && y == p.y;. Note that instanceof is false for null, so no extra null check is needed.

Record patterns (Java 21)

A record (see Module 2) is a transparent holder of data, so Java can take it apart in a pattern. The pattern Point(int x, int y) checks the type and extracts the components.

record Point(int x, int y) { }
record Line(Point from, Point to) { }

static String describe(Object o) {
    if (o instanceof Point(int x, int y)) {
        return "Point at " + x + "," + y;
    }
    if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2))) {   // nested
        return "Line from " + x1 + "," + y1 + " to " + x2 + "," + y2;
    }
    return "Unknown";
}

Nested patterns remove chains of getter calls. Inside a record pattern you can use var to infer a component's type.

Pattern matching for switch (Java 21)

A switch can now have type patterns as labels. This replaces long if / else if (x instanceof ...) chains. Consider payments:

public class SwitchPatterns {
    sealed interface Payment permits Upi, Card, Cash { }
    record Upi(String vpa) implements Payment { }
    record Card(String last4, boolean credit) implements Payment { }
    record Cash(int amount) implements Payment { }

    static String fee(Payment p) {
        return switch (p) {
            case Upi u -> "No fee for " + u.vpa();
            case Card(String last4, boolean credit) when credit -> "2% fee on card " + last4;
            case Card c -> "Flat Rs 5 on debit card " + c.last4();
            case Cash(int amount) when amount > 50_000 -> "Cash limit exceeded";
            case Cash c -> "No fee";
        };
    }

    static String show(Object o) {
        return switch (o) {
            case null -> "null value";
            case Integer i when i > 100 -> "big int " + i;
            case Integer i -> "int " + i;
            case String s -> "text of length " + s.length();
            case int[] arr -> "int array of " + arr.length;
            default -> "something else: " + o;
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(fee(new Upi("asha@upi")));
        System.out.println(fee(new Card("4242", true)));
        System.out.println(fee(new Cash(60_000)));
        System.out.println(show(500));
        System.out.println(show(7));
        System.out.println(show(null));
    }
}
No fee for asha@upi
2% fee on card 4242
Cash limit exceeded
big int 500
int 7
null value

Guards, order and dominance

  • A guard is when condition after the pattern. The case matches only if the pattern matches and the condition is true.
  • Labels are tested top to bottom. A label that can never match because an earlier one covers it is a compile error: this is dominance. case Integer i placed before case Integer i when i > 100 does not compile. Put guarded and more specific cases first.
  • A switch with patterns must be exhaustive. Over a sealed type (see sealed classes) it is exhaustive when all permitted subtypes are covered; otherwise add default.

Handling null

The old rule stays: a switch throws NullPointerException for a null selector. To handle null, add case null (as above), or case null, default -> to treat null like the default. This is opt-in, so old code does not change behaviour.

Rules

  • A pattern variable is in scope only where the match is certain; you cannot use it in an || branch or after a failed test.
  • Pattern switches must be exhaustive and must not have dominated labels.
  • when guards can use pattern variables but should be simple, side-effect-free conditions.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NullPointerException — a pattern switch with no case null receives null.
  • MatchException — thrown if an exhaustive switch (or a record pattern whose accessor throws) finds no match at run time, for example after a sealed hierarchy was extended without recompiling the switch.
  • An instanceof pattern that the compiler knows always matches (for example String s instanceof String t) is allowed in modern Java, but gives no benefit.
  • Generic types: obj instanceof List<String> l is an error unless the check is safe; use List<?>.

Versions

Pattern matching for instanceof: final in Java 16. Pattern matching for switch and record patterns: final in Java 21 (both were previews in Java 17 to 20). Java 25 has primitive types in patterns still as a preview feature; do not rely on it.

Real projects

Pattern switches over sealed types model domain results cleanly: Success / Failure results from a payment gateway, AST nodes in a parser, event types in an event-sourced system. They replace the visitor pattern in many places.

Interview: "What is pattern matching for instanceof / switch?"

  • Test and cast in one step with a scoped binding variable.
  • Record patterns deconstruct records, also nested.
  • Switch by type with when guards, case null, dominance rules and exhaustiveness.

Sealed classes and interfaces

A sealed class or interface lists exactly which classes may extend it, so the compiler knows every subtype and can check switch statements for completeness.

The problem

Normally any class can extend your class, and any class can implement your interface. With final nobody can extend; with a public class everybody can. Often you want something in between: "a Shape is a Circle, a Rectangle or a Triangle and nothing else". Before Java 17 you could only fake this with package-private constructors. A sealed type states the closed list of subtypes in the language itself.

Syntax

public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle { }

public record Circle(double radius) implements Shape { }
public record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape { }
public final class Triangle implements Shape {
    final double base, height;
    public Triangle(double base, double height) { this.base = base; this.height = height; }
}

Each permitted subclass must choose exactly one modifier:

ModifierMeaning
finalNo more subclasses. Records and enums are implicitly final
sealedContinues the closed hierarchy with its own permits list
non-sealedOpens that branch again: anyone may extend it
 
public abstract sealed class Account permits Savings, Current, Loan { }
public final class Savings extends Account { }
public non-sealed class Current extends Account { }   // others may extend Current
public sealed class Loan extends Account permits HomeLoan, CarLoan { }
public final class HomeLoan extends Loan { }
public final class CarLoan extends Loan { }

If the subclasses are in the same source file as the sealed type, you can leave out permits and the compiler infers the list. Otherwise they must be in the same package (or the same named module) as the sealed class.

The big benefit: exhaustive switch

static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
        case Rectangle r -> r.width() * r.height();
        case Triangle t -> 0.5 * t.base * t.height;
        // no default: the compiler knows these three are all the Shape subtypes
    };
}

Now somebody adds Pentagon to the permits list. Every switch that does not handle it fails to compile, so you find all the places that need updating. With an ordinary interface you would get a silent bug at run time. If you add a default, you lose this safety: avoid default when the type is sealed.

Sealed vs enum vs abstract class

ToolClosed set of...Each case can carry its own data?
enumInstances (singletons)Same fields for all constants
sealed hierarchyTypesYes, each type has its own fields (often records)
open abstract classNothing: anyone can extendYes, but no completeness checks

Sealed result types

A very common modern pattern is a sealed type for "one of several outcomes", which models success and failure without exceptions for expected cases:

sealed interface PaymentResult {
    record Success(String txnId) implements PaymentResult { }
    record Declined(String reason) implements PaymentResult { }
    record GatewayDown(int retryAfterSeconds) implements PaymentResult { }
}

static String message(PaymentResult r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case PaymentResult.Success s -> "Paid, ref " + s.txnId();
        case PaymentResult.Declined d -> "Declined: " + d.reason();
        case PaymentResult.GatewayDown g -> "Try again in " + g.retryAfterSeconds() + "s";
    };
}
Declined: low balance

Rules

  • Every permitted subclass must directly extend or implement the sealed type, and must be final, sealed or non-sealed.
  • Permitted subclasses must be accessible: same package, or same module, or same file.
  • A sealed class cannot be anonymous or a lambda target (a sealed interface is not a functional interface target).

Exceptions and edge cases

  • IncompatibleClassChangeError / MatchException — a class is loaded that is not in the permitted list, or a switch meets an unknown subtype at run time. This happens when jars are compiled separately.
  • Reflection: Class.isSealed() and getPermittedSubclasses() read the list at run time.
  • Sealed does not mean immutable; the subclasses can have mutable fields.

Versions

Sealed classes were a preview in Java 15 and 16 and became final in Java 17 (LTS). Exhaustive pattern switches over them are final in Java 21.

Sealed vs final vs package-private

TechniqueWho can extendCompiler knows the full list?
Normal public classAnyoneNo
final classNobodyNot applicable
Package-private constructor (old trick)Only classes in the same packageNo: the compiler does not use it for switches
sealed ... permitsOnly the listed classesYes, so exhaustive switches work

The difference with the old trick is important: sealing is part of the type, so the compiler can use it, and the JVM enforces it at run time too. The sealed type can still be public and used everywhere; only extending it is restricted.

A recursive hierarchy: a small expression tree

Sealed types shine for data that is "one of these shapes", especially recursive data such as expressions, JSON values or UI events. With records and Java 21 record patterns the evaluator reads like the definition:

sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { }
record Num(int value) implements Expr { }
record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }
record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }

public class ExprDemo {
    static int eval(Expr e) {
        return switch (e) {
            case Num n -> n.value();
            case Add(Expr l, Expr r) -> eval(l) + eval(r);      // record pattern
            case Mul(Expr l, Expr r) -> eval(l) * eval(r);
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Expr e = new Add(new Num(2), new Mul(new Num(3), new Num(4)));   // 2 + 3 * 4
        System.out.println(eval(e));
        System.out.println(e);
    }
}
14
Add[left=Num[value=2], right=Mul[left=Num[value=3], right=Num[value=4]]]

Add a new case such as Sub to permits and eval stops compiling until you handle it. That is the whole point: the compiler is your checklist. See pattern matching for the pattern syntax and switch expressions for exhaustiveness.

Reading the hierarchy at run time

System.out.println(Shape.class.isSealed());
for (Class<?> c : Shape.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
    System.out.println(c.getSimpleName());
}
true
Circle
Rectangle
Triangle

Wrong: a permitted subclass without a modifier

sealed interface Vehicle permits Car, Bike { }
class Car implements Vehicle { }     // compile error: must be final, sealed or non-sealed
record Bike() implements Vehicle { }

Right: choose the modifier on purpose

sealed interface Vehicle permits Car, Bike { }
final class Car implements Vehicle { }
record Bike() implements Vehicle { }    // records are implicitly final

Common mistakes

  • Adding default to a switch over a sealed type. It compiles, but then a new subtype is handled by the fallback silently and you lose the compile-time check.
  • Using non-sealed without thinking. It reopens that branch to every class, so exhaustive switches still work (the non-sealed class itself is a case) but you no longer know all the real subtypes.
  • Sealing a type that other teams need to extend. Sealing is a design decision: a library that wants plug-in subclasses should stay open.
  • Forgetting that a sealed interface lists direct subtypes only. A class that extends a permitted non-sealed class is allowed, but it is not in the permits list.

More edge cases

  • Compile errors you will meet: "class is not allowed to extend sealed class" (the class is not in permits), and "sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected". Both are caught at compile time.
  • A final class cannot also be sealed; local classes and anonymous classes cannot be sealed or extend a sealed class.
  • A sealed class needs at least one permitted subclass. An enum can implement a sealed interface; its constants count as one permitted type.
  • With permits omitted, the subclasses must be in the same source file. Subclasses spread over several files need an explicit permits.
  • Sealed types and serialization libraries: JSON libraries such as Jackson do not guess which subtype to build from JSON. You still declare the type information yourself (for example with @JsonTypeInfo and @JsonSubTypes).

Conventions

  • Prefer a sealed interface with records for data variants; use a sealed abstract class only when the variants share state or code.
  • Nest the variants inside the sealed interface when they belong together (as in PaymentResult); then permits can be left out.
  • Keep the hierarchy shallow. Two levels cover almost all domain models.
  • Do not add default to switches over sealed types.

In real projects

Typical uses: API or service results (Success / Failure / Retry), domain events (OrderPlaced, OrderShipped), parser and rule-engine syntax trees, state machines, and commands in a message handler. Adding a case then forces every handler to be reviewed. Remember that adding a subtype to a published library is a breaking change for callers who switch exhaustively on it.

Interview: "What is a sealed class and why use it?"

  • It restricts which classes can extend it (permits); subclasses are final, sealed or non-sealed.
  • Gives you closed hierarchies for domain modelling and exhaustive switches without default.
  • Works well with records.

Sequenced collections and unnamed variables

Java 21 adds getFirst, getLast and reversed to every collection that has a defined order, and Java 22 lets you write _ for variables you do not use.

The problem with "first" and "last"

Before Java 21, getting the first and last element looked different for every collection: list.get(0) and list.get(list.size() - 1) for a list; deque.getFirst() for a deque; sortedSet.first() for a SortedSet; linkedHashSet.iterator().next() for a LinkedHashSet, and no easy way at all for the last one. Reversing was just as inconsistent.

New interfaces

Three new interfaces describe collections with an encounter order (a defined first, second, ... last): SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap. List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, SortedSet/TreeSet, LinkedHashMap and SortedMap/TreeMap now implement them. HashSet and HashMap do not, because they have no order.

MethodDoes
getFirst(), getLast()Return the first/last element; throw NoSuchElementException if empty
addFirst(e), addLast(e)Insert at an end (not supported on unmodifiable lists)
removeFirst(), removeLast()Remove and return an end element
reversed()A view in reverse order (changes show through to the original)
firstEntry(), lastEntry(), pollFirstEntry(), putFirst, putLast, reversed()The map versions on SequencedMap
 
import java.util.*;

public class SequencedDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> steps = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Cart", "Address", "Payment"));
        System.out.println(steps.getFirst());          // Cart  (was steps.get(0))
        System.out.println(steps.getLast());           // Payment
        steps.addFirst("Login");
        System.out.println(steps.reversed());

        LinkedHashSet<String> seen = new LinkedHashSet<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
        System.out.println(seen.getLast());            // c  (impossible before 21)

        LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> stock = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        stock.put("pen", 10);
        stock.put("book", 4);
        System.out.println(stock.firstEntry());
        System.out.println(stock.reversed());
    }
}
Cart
Payment
[Payment, Address, Cart, Login]
c
pen=10
{book=4, pen=10}

Edge cases

  • NoSuchElementException — getFirst() or getLast() on an empty collection. Compare with list.get(0), which throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.
  • UnsupportedOperationException — addFirst on List.of(...), or on a TreeSet (its position is decided by the sort order).
  • A custom List implementation compiled against old versions gets default implementations of the new methods, so it keeps working.
  • The name clash risk: if your own interface already had getFirst() with a different return type, upgrading to 21 could break compilation. Rare, but it is a known migration note.

Unnamed variables and patterns: _ (Java 22)

Sometimes the language forces you to declare a variable that you never use. Java 22 allows the underscore _ as the name, which says clearly "I ignore this" and stops IDE warnings. (Using _ as an identifier was an error from Java 9 to 21.)

// 1. Unused catch parameter
try {
    Integer.parseInt(input);
} catch (NumberFormatException _) {
    System.out.println("Not a number");
}

// 2. Unused loop variable: just counting
int total = 0;
for (var _ : orders) {
    total++;
}

// 3. Unused lambda parameter
map.computeIfAbsent(city, _ -> new ArrayList<>()).add(name);

// 4. Unused part of a record pattern
if (shape instanceof Rectangle(var w, _)) {   // only width matters
    System.out.println("width " + w);
}

// 5. try-with-resources you only need to open
try (var _ = lock.acquire()) { /* ... */ }

// 6. In a switch pattern: ignore the binding
case Card _ -> "card payment";

Rules: _ cannot be read, and you can declare it many times in one scope (each is a separate unused variable). It cannot be used for fields or method parameters. A single _ as a pattern alone (an unnamed pattern) matches anything inside a record pattern.

Versions

Sequenced collections: final in Java 21. Unnamed variables and patterns: preview in Java 21, final in Java 22. If you are on Java 17, neither is available.

Interview: "What did Java 21 add to collections?"

  • SequencedCollection/Set/Map give uniform getFirst, getLast, addFirst, removeLast and reversed().
  • reversed() returns a view, not a copy.
  • Hash-based collections are not sequenced.

From Java 8 to Java 25: the LTS timeline

Java ships a new version every six months, but only the long-term support (LTS) releases 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25 are used for years in production; knowing the headline features of each lets you read old code and use new features safely.

Release model

Since Java 9, a feature release arrives every March and September. Most releases get support for only six months. An LTS (long-term support) release gets patches for years from vendors such as Oracle, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto and Microsoft. Companies upgrade from LTS to LTS. Today (late 2026) Java 25 is the newest LTS; Java 21 and 17 are both common; Java 8 and 11 remain in older systems. Spring Boot 3.x needs Java 17 or newer, and Spring Boot 4.x also has Java 17 as its baseline.

What each LTS brought

VersionReleasedHeadline features (including the non-LTS releases before it)
Java 8March 2014Lambdas, functional interfaces, method references, Stream API, Optional, java.time, default and static methods in interfaces
Java 9Sept 2017Module system (JPMS), List.of/Set.of/Map.of, private interface methods, JShell
Java 11Sept 2018var (10), standard HttpClient, new String methods (isBlank, strip, lines, repeat), Files.readString/writeString, var in lambda parameters, running a single source file with java File.java
Java 12 to 162019–2021Switch expressions (14), helpful NPE messages (14), text blocks (15), records (16), pattern matching for instanceof (16), Stream.toList() (16)
Java 17Sept 2021Sealed classes (final), the above features all standard, strong encapsulation of JDK internals, new pseudo-random number generator API
Java 18 to 202022–2023UTF-8 default charset (18), simple web server jwebserver (18), previews of virtual threads and pattern matching for switch
Java 21Sept 2023Virtual threads (final), pattern matching for switch and record patterns (final), sequenced collections, generational ZGC
Java 22 to 242024–2025Unnamed variables _ (22), Stream Gatherers (24), no more pinning of virtual threads by synchronized (24)
Java 25Sept 2025Scoped values, compact source files with instance main methods, module import declarations, flexible constructor bodies (all final in 25)

Items marked with a version in parentheses arrived in that non-LTS release but are normally first used in production once the next LTS ships. Structured concurrency, primitive patterns and a few other APIs were still previews in Java 25; do not use preview features in production code (they need --enable-preview).

What the move between LTS versions means for you

  • 8 to 11: mainly runtime and library changes. Old Java EE modules (JAXB, JAX-WS) and some internal APIs (sun.misc.*) were removed or locked, so old apps need dependency updates.
  • 11 to 17: the biggest language upgrade: records, text blocks, switch expressions, sealed classes, pattern matching for instanceof. Reflection into JDK internals is blocked by default.
  • 17 to 21: virtual threads, pattern matching for switch, record patterns, sequenced collections.
  • 21 to 25: mostly incremental. Fewer pinning problems for virtual threads, scoped values, simpler first programs, and performance improvements.

A feature at a glance

// Java 8
Map<String, List<Employee>> byDept = new HashMap<>();
for (Employee e : employees) {
    if (!byDept.containsKey(e.getDept())) {
        byDept.put(e.getDept(), new ArrayList<Employee>());
    }
    byDept.get(e.getDept()).add(e);
}

// Modern (Java 17+)
var byDept = employees.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept));
record Employee(String name, String dept, double salary) { }

Practical guidance

  • New projects: start on Java 21 or 25, depending on what your cloud platform and libraries support.
  • Check your framework's baseline before using a feature (Spring Boot 3 and 4 require 17+; Java 21 is needed for virtual threads).
  • Set maven.compiler.release (or the Gradle toolchain) so the compiler rejects APIs newer than your target.

Interview: "Which Java version are you using and what is new?"

  • Name the LTS you used and 3 or 4 features you actually used: records, text blocks, switch expressions, var, streams.
  • Know the order: lambdas and streams (8), var (10), switch expressions (14), records (16), sealed classes (17), virtual threads and pattern switch (21).

Interview questions — Modern and functional Java

What is a functional interface? Name the four core ones.

A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, so a lambda or method reference can implement it. It may have default and static methods, and @FunctionalInterface makes the compiler check the rule. The core four in java.util.function: Predicate<T> (T → boolean), Function<T,R> (T → R), Consumer<T> (T → void) and Supplier<T> (() → T).

Why must variables used in a lambda be effectively final?

A lambda may run later or on another thread. Local variables live on the stack of the method, and the lambda gets a copy of their value. If the original could change, the copy would be out of date, and sharing a changing local between threads would be unsafe. So the compiler requires that captured locals are never reassigned. Fields and array elements are not copied, so you can change them, but then thread safety is your job.

What are the four kinds of method reference?

Static method: Integer::parseInt is s -> Integer.parseInt(s). Bound instance: System.out::println uses one specific object. Unbound instance: String::length is s -> s.length(), the first argument is the receiver. Constructor: ArrayList::new is () -> new ArrayList<>().

What is a stream? Is it a data structure?

No. A stream is a pipeline that describes computations over a source (collection, array, file). It does not store elements. It is lazy: intermediate operations such as filter and map do nothing until a terminal operation such as collect or count starts the work. A stream can be consumed only once; reusing it throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed.

map vs flatMap?

map turns each element into exactly one new element. flatMap turns each element into a stream of zero or more elements and flattens all of them into one stream. Example: a list of orders, each with a list of items: orders.stream().flatMap(o -> o.items().stream()) gives one stream of items. With map you would get a stream of lists.

What does this print, and why? 
Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc", "dddd")
      .filter(s -> { System.out.println("filter " + s); return s.length() > 1; })
      .map(s -> { System.out.println("map " + s); return s.toUpperCase(); })
      .findFirst();

It prints filter a, filter bb, map bb. Elements flow one at a time through the whole pipeline (not stage by stage), and findFirst is short-circuiting, so after "bb" reaches the end nothing else is processed.

toList() vs Collectors.toList()? What happens with duplicate keys in toMap?

Stream.toList() (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list and allows nulls; Collectors.toList() returns an ArrayList (no promise about the type) that you can modify. Collectors.toMap(keyFn, valueFn) throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key ... when two elements give the same key. Pass a merge function as a third argument, such as (a, b) -> a, or use groupingBy if you expect many values per key.

When should you NOT use parallel streams?

For small data, for cheap operations, for ordered or stateful operations, for sources that split badly (LinkedList, Stream.iterate), when tasks do blocking I/O, or when lambdas have side effects or touch shared mutable state. Parallel streams use the common ForkJoinPool shared by the whole JVM. Measure first; it is often slower.

orElse vs orElseGet?

orElse(x) evaluates its argument always, even when the Optional has a value. orElseGet(supplier) calls the supplier only when the Optional is empty. If the fallback is costly (a database call or a new object with side effects), use orElseGet. For a constant, orElse is fine.

Where should you use Optional and where not?

Use it as a return type for methods that may have no result (findById). Do not use it for fields, method parameters, collection elements or in JPA entities. Never return null from a method that returns Optional, and do not call get() without checking; prefer orElseThrow, map and ifPresent.

Why is java.util.Date bad, and what replaced it?

Date is mutable (so not thread-safe), its months are zero-based, years start from 1900 in the deprecated getters, and it mixes date and time with no time zone clarity. SimpleDateFormat is also not thread-safe. The java.time package (Java 8) is immutable, thread-safe and clear: LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Instant, ZonedDateTime, Duration, Period and DateTimeFormatter.

What are records, and how do they differ from a normal class with Lombok's @Data?

A record is a final class for immutable data. The compiler generates the constructor, accessors (name(), not getName()), equals, hashCode and toString. All fields are final; records cannot extend other classes but can implement interfaces. They are a language feature with no library needed, they suit DTOs and pattern matching, and they cannot be JPA entities. Lombok's @Data makes mutable classes with setters.

What is new in switch, and what is pattern matching for switch?

Switch expressions (Java 14) return a value, use -> with no fall-through, allow multiple labels per case and need to be exhaustive; yield gives the value from a block. Java 21 added patterns: case Circle c ->, record patterns, when guards and case null. Over a sealed type, no default is needed and the compiler checks that all subtypes are handled.

What is a sealed class and why would you use it?

A sealed class or interface names its allowed direct subtypes with permits. Each subtype must be final, sealed or non-sealed. It models a closed set of alternatives, such as payment results, and combined with a pattern switch it gives compile-time exhaustiveness: add a new subtype and every switch that misses it fails to compile.

What is the difference between LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime and Instant? What do you store in the database?

LocalDateTime is a date and time on a wall clock with no zone, so it does not identify a moment. ZonedDateTime adds a zone such as Asia/Kolkata. Instant is a point on the UTC timeline. Store timestamps in UTC (an Instant or OffsetDateTime in a timestamptz column) and convert to the user's zone only for display. Use LocalDate for dates without time, such as a birthday.

Cheat sheet — Modern and functional Java

  • Lambda (a, b) -> a + b; implements a functional interface; captured locals must be effectively final.
  • Core interfaces Predicate<T> test, Function<T,R> apply, Consumer<T> accept, Supplier<T> get; plus BiFunction, UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator.
  • Composing and, or, negate; andThen, compose; Function.identity().
  • Method refs Class::static, obj::method, Class::instance, Class::new.
  • Pipeline source → intermediate (lazy) → terminal (starts work). One use only.
  • Intermediate filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted, peek, limit, skip, takeWhile, mapToInt, boxed.
  • Terminal forEach, collect, toList(), reduce, count, min/max, anyMatch/allMatch/noneMatch, findFirst, toArray.
  • Primitive streams IntStream.range(0, n), sum(), average() (OptionalDouble), no boxing.
  • Collectors toList, toSet, toMap (duplicate key = IllegalStateException), joining, groupingBy, partitioningBy, counting, summingInt, averagingDouble, mapping.
  • groupingBy groupingBy(classifier, downstream); map type via groupingBy(f, TreeMap::new, downstream).
  • Avoid side effects inside lambdas, reusing a stream, parallel streams on small or I/O work.
  • Optional create with of, ofNullable, empty; read with orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow; transform with map, flatMap, filter.
  • Optional rules return type only; not for fields or parameters; never get() unchecked; never return null for it.
  • java.time LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Instant; immutable, so plusDays returns a new object.
  • Spans Duration (time-based), Period (date-based), ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(a, b).
  • Formatting DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd-MM-yyyy"); bad input gives DateTimeParseException. Store in UTC.
  • var locals only, needs an initializer, not null, not for fields/parameters; still static typing.
  • Text block """ + newline; closing delimiter sets the indent; \ joins lines; \s keeps a space; formatted().
  • Switch expression case A, B -> value; no fall-through; yield in blocks; must be exhaustive.
  • Pattern instanceof if (o instanceof String s && s.isEmpty()); binding in scope only where matched.
  • Pattern switch (21) type patterns, record patterns, when guards, case null; specific cases before general.
  • Records immutable data carriers; accessors x(); canonical constructor can validate.
  • Sealed sealed ... permits; subclasses final / sealed / non-sealed; exhaustive switch without default.
  • Sequenced (21) getFirst, getLast, addFirst, reversed() (a view) on lists, deques, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap.
  • Unnamed (22) _ for unused catch, loop, lambda and pattern variables.
  • LTS 8 lambdas/streams, 11 var/HttpClient, 17 records/sealed/text blocks, 21 virtual threads/pattern switch, 25 current LTS.

Practice — Modern and functional Java

  1. Rewrite loops as streams. Take five loops you wrote earlier (sum of even numbers, names in upper case, count of strings longer than 5, first item over 1000, join names with commas). Rewrite each with a stream. Done when the results are identical and you can say, for each, whether the loop or the stream is easier to read.
  2. The streams drill. From a list of employees find the average salary per department, the top 3 earners and the names grouped by first letter. Done when your output matches the sample below and you can explain each collector. 
    import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class EmployeeDrill {
    record Employee(String name, String dept, double salary) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee> emps = List.of(
                new Employee("Asha", "IT", 90_000),
                new Employee("Arjun", "HR", 55_000),
                new Employee("Meera", "IT", 120_000),
                new Employee("Ravi", "Sales", 70_000),
                new Employee("Rohit", "IT", 80_000),
                new Employee("Mohan", "HR", 65_000));

        // 1. average salary per department
        Map<String, Double> avg = emps.stream().collect(
                Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::dept,
                        TreeMap::new, Collectors.averagingDouble(Employee::salary)));
        System.out.println(avg);

        // 2. top 3 earners
        List<String> top3 = emps.stream()
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::salary).reversed())
                .limit(3)
                .map(Employee::name)
                .toList();
        System.out.println(top3);

        // 3. names grouped by first letter
        Map<Character, List<String>> byLetter = emps.stream().collect(
                Collectors.groupingBy(e -> e.name().charAt(0),
                        TreeMap::new,
                        Collectors.mapping(Employee::name, Collectors.toList())));
        System.out.println(byLetter);
    }
}
    {HR=60000.0, IT=96666.66666666667, Sales=70000.0}
[Meera, Asha, Rohit]
{A=[Asha, Arjun], M=[Meera, Mohan], R=[Ravi, Rohit]}
  3. Ten stream exercises. Use the same employee list (add two more with duplicate salaries and one with a duplicate name) and solve each in a single pipeline. Done when you have a tested method for every item and you can explain its time cost.
    1. Names of employees earning more than 75,000, sorted alphabetically.
    2. The second-highest salary (use distinct, sorted, skip).
    3. Total salary per department as a Map<String, Double>.
    4. The highest-paid employee in each department (groupingBy with maxBy).
    5. Duplicate names in the list.
    6. A frequency map of the characters in a sentence.
    7. Flatten a List<List<Integer>> into one sorted list without duplicates.
    8. Sort employees by department, then by salary descending (thenComparing).
    9. Partition employees into "salary at least 80,000" and the rest; print the counts.
    10. Join all names into "[Asha, Meera, ...]" using Collectors.joining with prefix and suffix.
  4. Optional and dates. Write Optional<Employee> findByName(String) and use map, orElseGet and orElseThrow on it without calling get(). Then compute the number of days between today and a hard-coded joining date, the date 90 days from now, and format a LocalDate as dd-MMM-yyyy. Done when invalid input produces a DateTimeParseException that you handle with a clear message.
  5. Modernise a class hierarchy. Take an old Shape abstract class with instanceof and casts. Convert it to a sealed interface with records, write area as a pattern switch without default, and add a guard case for a very large circle. Done when adding a new record makes the switch fail to compile until you handle it.

Module 6·Basics now · depth in months 9–10Must

Multithreading and concurrency

16 topics · about 2 h of reading

A thread is an independent path of execution inside your program. Multithreading lets one Java process do several things at once: a web server handles hundreds of requests together, a Swiggy-style backend calls the restaurant, payment and delivery services in parallel, and a background job sends emails while the user keeps browsing. Almost every Spring Boot application is multithreaded whether you write a single Thread or not — Tomcat runs each request on a pool thread, and your singleton beans are shared by all of them.

Concurrency is also where the hardest bugs live: wrong totals that appear once in a thousand runs, a service that hangs forever, a memory leak that only shows after a week. This module teaches the model (memory visibility, atomicity, locks), the tools (executors, CompletableFuture, concurrent collections, synchronizers) and the modern answer for I/O-heavy code (virtual threads, Java 21). It builds on collections (Module 4), lambdas (Module 5) and connects to the JVM memory model in Module 7. For the operating-system view of processes and threads, see CS Fundamentals · Module 1.

After this module you will be able to:

  • create, start, join and interrupt threads correctly, and explain start() vs run() and the six thread states;
  • explain atomicity, visibility and ordering, and why count++ is not thread-safe;
  • fix a race condition with synchronized, AtomicInteger or a lock, and know when volatile is enough;
  • run work on thread pools, use Future and chain async calls with CompletableFuture;
  • pick the right concurrent collection, latch, barrier or semaphore;
  • recognise, prevent and diagnose a deadlock;
  • use ThreadLocal safely and decide when virtual threads are the right tool;
  • choose a thread-safety strategy for any shared data.

Why concurrency: processes, threads, concurrency vs parallelism

A process is a running program with its own memory; a thread is a lightweight path of execution inside a process that shares that memory, which lets a program use all CPU cores and keep working while it waits for I/O.

Your laptop has several CPU cores, and each core runs one instruction stream at a time. A program with one thread uses at most one core. Worse, most real programs spend their time waiting: for a database reply, an HTTP response, a disk read. While one thread waits, the core sits idle. Multithreading fixes both problems.

Why use threads

  • Use all cores — split a CPU-heavy job (image resizing, report calculation) across cores to finish sooner.
  • Hide waiting — while thread A waits for the payment gateway, thread B serves another customer. This is the main reason servers use threads.
  • Stay responsive — a UI or a main loop hands slow work to a background thread so it does not freeze.
  • Model independent tasks naturally — one thread per request is easy to read and debug.

Process vs thread

A process is a program that the operating system is running: it owns its own virtual address space (memory), open files and security context. Running java MyApp starts one process, which contains one JVM. A thread lives inside a process. All threads of a process share the same heap (all your objects) but each thread has its own call stack and program counter.

PointProcessThread
MemorySeparate address space per processShares the heap with other threads; own stack
Creation costHeavy (new memory map, resources)Lighter, but a platform thread still reserves about 1 MB of stack by default on 64-bit systems
CommunicationNeeds IPC: pipes, sockets, files, shared memoryJust read and write shared objects (which is also the danger)
IsolationA crash in one process leaves others aliveAn uncaught OutOfMemoryError or a shared-data bug can hurt the whole JVM
Context switchExpensiveCheaper, still not free

This picture explains the whole module. Local variables (primitives and references on a stack) are private to a thread, so they are automatically safe. Objects on the heap and static fields are shared, and every bug in this module is about two threads touching the same shared object at the wrong time.

Concurrency vs parallelism

These words are often confused. Concurrency means several tasks are in progress during the same period — their execution is interleaved, even on a single core. Parallelism means several tasks are literally running at the same instant on different cores. Concurrency is about structuring a program to deal with many things; parallelism is about doing many things at once to go faster.

PointConcurrencyParallelism
IdeaMany tasks in progress, taking turnsMany tasks running at the same instant
Needs multiple coresNoYes
Main goalResponsiveness, handling many requestsThroughput on CPU-heavy work
ExampleA server juggling 500 requests on 8 coresSumming a huge array in 8 chunks on 8 cores

CPU-bound vs I/O-bound work

This distinction decides almost every design choice later (pool size, virtual threads). CPU-bound work keeps the core busy computing: sorting, encryption, image processing. More threads than cores will not make it faster. I/O-bound work mostly waits: database queries, REST calls, file and network reads. You can run many more threads than cores because most of them are sleeping at any moment.

A first look: two threads, one program

public class FirstThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
        System.out.println("Cores available: " + cores);

        Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(
                "Hello from " + Thread.currentThread().getName()));
        t.start();
        t.join();   // wait for t to finish
        System.out.println("Hello from " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}
Cores available: 8
Hello from Thread-0
Hello from main

Rule: threads share the heap, not the stack

Local variables and method parameters are thread-confined and need no protection. Anything reachable from two threads — a field, a static, a collection, an object passed to a task — needs a thread-safety plan (see thread-safety strategies).

Edge cases and limits

  • More threads is not always faster. For CPU-bound work, threads beyond the core count only add context-switch cost. Every thread also uses memory for its stack, so a few thousand platform threads can cause OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread.
  • Not every task can be split. Amdahl's law says the part that must run in sequence limits the speed-up: if 20% of a job is sequential, even infinite cores give at most 5× speed-up.
  • The JVM itself runs extra threads (garbage collector, JIT compiler), so "one thread" programs are rarely truly single-threaded.

Interview: "Process vs thread? Concurrency vs parallelism?"

  • Process: own memory, heavy, isolated, talks via IPC. Thread: shares the process heap, own stack, light, talks through shared objects.
  • Concurrency is dealing with many tasks by interleaving; parallelism is running them simultaneously on multiple cores. You can have one without the other.
  • Threads help in two ways: use more cores for CPU work, and overlap waiting for I/O work.
  • Shared heap is the benefit and the danger — it is the root of race conditions.

Creating and controlling threads: Thread, Runnable, join, sleep, daemon, interrupt

You describe the work as a Runnable, hand it to a Thread, and call start(); join() waits for it, sleep() pauses it, and interrupt() politely asks it to stop.

There are three classic ways to give a thread its work. All end in the same place: the thread runs a run() method.

Three ways to create a thread

public class CreateThreads {

    // 1. Extend Thread (works, but ties the task to the thread type)
    static class Worker extends Thread {
        @Override
        public void run() {
            System.out.println("Extending Thread: " + getName());
        }
    }

    // 2. Implement Runnable (the task is a separate object; reusable with pools)
    static class EmailTask implements Runnable {
        @Override
        public void run() {
            System.out.println("Runnable class: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread t1 = new Worker();
        Thread t2 = new Thread(new EmailTask(), "email-sender");
        // 3. Lambda (Runnable is a functional interface) - the usual choice today
        Thread t3 = new Thread(
                () -> System.out.println("Lambda: " + Thread.currentThread().getName()),
                "report-builder");

        t1.start();
        t2.start();
        t3.start();
        t1.join();
        t2.join();
        t3.join();
        System.out.println("All done");
    }
}
Extending Thread: Thread-0
Runnable class: email-sender
Lambda: report-builder
All done

Prefer Runnable (or a lambda) over extending Thread. Java has single inheritance, so extending Thread uses up your one superclass. A Runnable is just a task: it can later be handed to an executor, run by a virtual thread, or tested directly. Extending Thread mixes "what to do" with "how to run it".

start() vs run() — the classic question

start() asks the JVM to create a new thread of execution, which then calls run(). Calling run() yourself is just a normal method call on the current thread — no new thread exists.

Thread t = new Thread(() ->
        System.out.println("Running in: " + Thread.currentThread().getName()), "worker");

t.run();     // plain method call, runs in main
t.start();   // new thread "worker" runs the body
t.join();
t.start();   // IllegalThreadStateException: a thread can be started only once
Running in: main
Running in: worker
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalThreadStateException

The Thread API you use

MethodWhat it does
start()Starts a new thread that runs run(); legal once per object
join() / join(ms)Current thread waits until the target thread ends (or the time passes)
Thread.sleep(ms)Pauses the current thread; does not release any locks it holds
Thread.currentThread()The thread that is running this code
getName() / setName()Thread name; default names are Thread-0, Thread-1, …
getId() / threadId()Unique id (threadId() is the current API since Java 19)
setDaemon(true) / isDaemon()Mark as daemon; must be set before start()
setPriority(n)A hint from 1 to 10 for the scheduler (default 5)
interrupt(), isInterrupted(), Thread.interrupted()Cooperative cancellation (see below)
Thread.yield()Hint that the current thread is willing to give up the core; rarely useful
isAlive(), getState()Is it running or not; current lifecycle state

Always give threads meaningful names (new Thread(task, "order-sync")). Thread names appear in logs and thread dumps, and "Thread-37" tells you nothing at 2 a.m.

Daemon threads

The JVM exits when all non-daemon (user) threads have finished. A daemon thread is a background helper that does not keep the JVM alive: when the last user thread ends, daemon threads are stopped abruptly, with no finally blocks guaranteed to run. Garbage collection and many timers are daemon threads. Use daemons for housekeeping that can safely vanish (cache cleaners, heartbeats), never for work that must finish, such as writing a file or a payment record. A new thread inherits the daemon status of the thread that created it.

Thread ticker = new Thread(() -> {
    while (true) {
        System.out.println("tick");
        try { Thread.sleep(300); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; }
    }
});
ticker.setDaemon(true);   // set BEFORE start()
ticker.start();
Thread.sleep(700);
System.out.println("main ends - JVM exits even though ticker loops forever");
tick
tick
tick
main ends - JVM exits even though ticker loops forever

Priorities — and why not to rely on them

setPriority(Thread.MAX_PRIORITY) (10) or MIN_PRIORITY (1) is only a hint. How it maps to the operating system differs between Linux, Windows and macOS, and some systems ignore it. Never use priorities for correctness. If task A must run before task B, use join(), a latch or a CompletableFuture chain.

Interruption done right

Java has no safe way to force-kill a thread (Thread.stop() was deprecated for removal and is disabled in modern Java). Instead Java uses cooperative cancellation: you call t.interrupt(), which sets the thread's interrupt flag. The thread must notice and stop on its own.

  • If the thread is blocked in sleep, wait, join or a blocking queue call, it wakes up and throws InterruptedException. Throwing it clears the flag.
  • If the thread is busy computing, nothing happens until it checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() itself.
  • isInterrupted() reads the flag; the static Thread.interrupted() reads and clears it.
public class InterruptDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
            int processed = 0;
            while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {   // check the flag
                try {
                    Thread.sleep(100);                           // simulate work
                    processed++;
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    // sleep() cleared the flag. Restore it, then stop.
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                }
            }
            System.out.println("Stopping cleanly after " + processed + " items");
        }, "batch-worker");

        worker.start();
        Thread.sleep(350);
        worker.interrupt();   // ask politely
        worker.join();
    }
}
Stopping cleanly after 3 items

Wrong: swallows the interrupt

try {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    // ignored: flag is lost, caller never
    // learns that a stop was requested
}

Right: restore the flag (or rethrow)

try {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    return;   // stop what you were doing
}

Rule: never swallow InterruptedException

Either declare it (throws InterruptedException) and let the caller handle it, or catch it, call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to restore the flag, and stop the work. A swallowed interrupt makes a pool or application impossible to shut down cleanly.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • IllegalThreadStateException — calling start() twice, or setDaemon() after start().
  • An exception thrown in run() kills only that thread; main never sees it. The default handler prints the stack trace to System.err. Install your own with t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, ex) -> log.error(th.getName(), ex)). Tasks in executors behave differently (see Callable and Future).
  • join() on a thread that was never started returns at once.
  • sleep(ms) never releases locks; Object.wait() does.
  • Thread.sleep(ms) is not an exact timer — it sleeps at least roughly that long.

Mistake: calling run() and expecting parallel work

Code review classic: new Thread(task).run(); works, prints the right output and is completely sequential. Always start().

Real projects

You rarely write new Thread(...) in production. Raw threads are for demos, tests and rare background loops; business code uses executors (next articles), Spring's @Async, or virtual threads. But you must understand the primitives, because pools, frameworks and thread dumps are built from them.

Interview: "start() vs run()", "Runnable vs Thread", "How do you stop a thread?"

  • start() creates a new thread that calls run(); run() alone is a plain call. start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException.
  • Prefer Runnable: separates task from thread, allows another superclass, works with executors.
  • Stop a thread with interruption: set a flag with interrupt(), check isInterrupted(), handle InterruptedException by restoring the flag and exiting. Never Thread.stop().
