  • Daemon threads do not stop the JVM from exiting and may be killed mid-work.

Thread lifecycle and states

A Java thread is always in one of six states — NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING or TERMINATED — and specific method calls move it between them.

The enum Thread.State defines exactly six states, and thread.getState() returns the current one. This is a snapshot for monitoring; do not build logic on it because it can change right after you read it.

StateMeaningHow a thread gets there
NEWObject created, not startednew Thread(...)
RUNNABLERunning on a core or ready and waiting for one (Java does not separate these)start(); also while blocked in some native I/O calls
BLOCKEDWaiting to enter a synchronized block because another thread holds the monitorEntering a locked synchronized block
WAITINGWaiting indefinitely for another thread's actionObject.wait(), t.join(), LockSupport.park() (used by locks and queues)
TIMED_WAITINGWaiting with a time limitsleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms), tryLock(time), poll(time)
TERMINATEDFinishedrun() returned or threw

Watching the states

public class StatesDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Object lock = new Object();
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
            synchronized (lock) {                 // main holds the lock first
                try { Thread.sleep(300); } catch (InterruptedException e) { }
            }
        });
        System.out.println("1. " + t.getState());       // NEW

        synchronized (lock) {
            t.start();
            Thread.sleep(100);
            System.out.println("2. " + t.getState());   // BLOCKED: needs lock
        }                                                // main releases the lock

        Thread.sleep(100);
        System.out.println("3. " + t.getState());       // TIMED_WAITING in sleep

        t.join();
        System.out.println("4. " + t.getState());       // TERMINATED
    }
}
1. NEW
2. BLOCKED
3. TIMED_WAITING
4. TERMINATED

BLOCKED vs WAITING — the confusing pair

BLOCKED means "I want a synchronized lock and someone else has it." WAITING means "I gave up on running until another thread signals me." A thread that calls wait() goes to WAITING; after notify() it moves to BLOCKED (it must re-acquire the monitor) and then to RUNNABLE. Threads waiting on a ReentrantLock show as WAITING, not BLOCKED, because those locks use park(). In a thread dump, many threads BLOCKED on the same monitor means a hot lock; many threads WAITING in a pool means idle workers.

Rule: a thread ends once and cannot restart

After TERMINATED you cannot call start() again. Create a new Thread, or better, submit tasks to a pool that reuses threads.

Edge cases

  • A thread reading from a socket or file is RUNNABLE in Java terms even though it is really waiting inside the operating system.
  • Thread.sleep(0) and yield() keep the thread RUNNABLE.
  • interrupt() on a WAITING or TIMED_WAITING thread wakes it with InterruptedException. On a BLOCKED thread it only sets the flag; the thread keeps waiting for the lock.

start() vs run(), and what start() really does

Calling t.start() asks the JVM to create a new operating-system thread (for a platform thread), which then calls run(). Calling t.run() directly is just an ordinary method call: it runs in the caller's thread, no new thread exists, and the state stays NEW. This is a classic interview trap and a classic bug.

Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("in " + Thread.currentThread().getName()));
t.run();                        // prints "in main"      (no new thread)
t.start();                      // prints "in Thread-0"  (a real new thread)
t.join();
t.start();                      // IllegalThreadStateException: it already ran

Calling start() a second time throws IllegalThreadStateException whatever the state (even if the thread is still running). The only legal move out of NEW is one start().

What each blocking call does to locks and state

CallState while waitingReleases the monitor?Ends when
Thread.sleep(ms)TIMED_WAITINGNoTime passes or interrupt
obj.wait()WAITINGYesnotify, notifyAll, interrupt
obj.wait(ms)TIMED_WAITINGYesSame, or time passes
t.join()WAITINGNot terminates or interrupt
LockSupport.park()WAITINGNot applicableunpark or interrupt
Thread.yield()RUNNABLENoImmediately; only a hint to the scheduler
Entering synchronizedBLOCKED if lockedNot applicableMonitor becomes free

wait(), notify() and notifyAll() must be called while holding the object's monitor. Otherwise they throw IllegalMonitorStateException. See locks and waiting for the full producer-consumer pattern.

Seeing WAITING

public class WaitingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Object lock = new Object();
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
            synchronized (lock) {
                try { lock.wait(); }                    // releases the lock and waits
                catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("woken by interrupt"); }
            }
        });
        t.start();
        Thread.sleep(100);
        System.out.println("A. " + t.getState());       // WAITING
        t.interrupt();                                  // wake it without notify
        t.join();
        System.out.println("B. " + t.getState());       // TERMINATED
    }
}
A. WAITING
woken by interrupt
B. TERMINATED

Thread dumps: reading states in production

When an application hangs or is slow, take a thread dump with jstack <pid> or jcmd <pid> Thread.print (or press Ctrl+Break on Windows). Each thread prints its name, its state and its stack. The state line looks like this:

java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping)

How to read it: many threads BLOCKED on the same lock address means lock contention; threads WAITING (parking) inside a ThreadPoolExecutor are idle workers waiting for tasks; a thread RUNNABLE at 100% CPU in the same method across dumps points to a busy loop. Two threads BLOCKED on each other's locks form a deadlock, and the JVM prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" at the end of the dump.

Common mistakes

  • Calling run() instead of start() and wondering why there is no parallelism.
  • Calling start() twice, or trying to restart a finished thread.
  • Using getState() or isAlive() to decide what to do next. The answer is stale the moment you get it; coordinate with join(), a latch or a Future instead.
  • Treating sleep() as a way to wait for another thread to finish. Use join(); sleeping gives only a guess about timing.

More edge cases and exceptions

  • IllegalThreadStateException — start() on a thread that was started before.
  • IllegalMonitorStateException — wait/notify without owning the monitor.
  • InterruptedException — thrown inside sleep, wait or join when the thread is interrupted. The interrupt flag is cleared when this exception is thrown, so catch blocks that swallow it should restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().
  • A thread can be TERMINATED because run() threw an uncaught exception. The thread dies, the stack trace goes to the thread's uncaught-exception handler (stderr by default), and other threads carry on.
  • Daemon threads (setDaemon(true), before start()) do not keep the JVM alive. When the last non-daemon thread ends, the JVM exits even if daemon threads are still RUNNABLE.
  • Thread pools reuse threads, so a worker moves between RUNNABLE and WAITING many times and reaches TERMINATED only when the pool shuts down. See executors.

In real projects

You rarely call getState() in business code. You read states in thread dumps, in monitoring tools (VisualVM, Java Flight Recorder, APM dashboards), and in post-mortems of hung services. Name your threads (new Thread(task, "invoice-sync") or a thread factory) so the dump is readable; the default names Thread-0, Thread-1 tell you nothing. Related: creating threads and synchronized.

Interview: "Explain the thread lifecycle"

  • Name all six states and draw NEW → RUNNABLE → (BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING) → RUNNABLE → TERMINATED.
  • Give the trigger for each: start(), monitor contention, wait()/join(), sleep(), end of run().
  • Say that Java has no separate "running" state; RUNNABLE covers running and ready.
  • Mention that sleep() keeps locks and wait() releases them.

The Java Memory Model: atomicity, visibility, ordering and happens-before

Threads can disagree about what memory contains, so correct concurrent code must guarantee atomicity (no half-finished updates), visibility (writes are seen by others) and ordering (steps are not reordered unsafely) — and the happens-before rules tell you when that is guaranteed.

It is easy to imagine memory as one board that all threads read and write instantly. Real hardware is different. Each core has fast private caches and registers, and the CPU and the JIT compiler are free to reorder instructions for speed as long as a single thread cannot tell the difference. With several threads, you can tell. The Java Memory Model (JMM) is the specification of what values a read may see when threads share data. It gives you three properties to think about.

Atomicity
An operation is atomic if it happens completely or not at all, with no other thread able to see it half-done. Reads and writes of references and of most primitives are atomic. Reads and writes of long and double are guaranteed atomic only if the variable is volatile, although current 64-bit JVMs do it atomically anyway. Compound actions such as count++ are not atomic.
Visibility
When thread A writes a value, when does thread B see it? Without a guarantee, B may keep reading a stale value from its cache or register, possibly forever.
Ordering
The compiler and CPU may reorder independent statements. Another thread can observe writes in a different order from the one in your source code.

Why count++ is not atomic

One line of Java becomes three steps: read the value, add one, write it back. This is a read-modify-write sequence. Two threads can interleave between the steps and one update is lost.

Visibility problem in real code

public class VisibilityBug {
    static boolean ready = false;      // not volatile

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread reader = new Thread(() -> {
            while (!ready) { }          // may spin forever: never re-reads memory
            System.out.println("Reader saw ready = true");
        });
        reader.start();
        Thread.sleep(500);
        ready = true;                   // writer thread sets the flag
        System.out.println("Main set ready = true");
    }
}
Main set ready = true
(the program never ends: the reader keeps spinning on a stale value)

The JIT compiler may hoist the read of ready out of the loop, because nothing in this thread changes it. Making ready volatile fixes it (see volatile and atomics).

Happens-before in simple words

The JMM defines a relation called happens-before. If action A happens-before action B, then everything A did (all writes) is guaranteed to be visible to B and ordered before it. If there is no happens-before relation between a write and a read of the same variable, the read may see old or new data — this is called a data race. You do not need to memorise the full specification; know these rules:

RuleMeaning in plain words
Program orderWithin one thread, each statement happens-before the next one (as that thread sees it)
Monitor lockAn unlock of a monitor happens-before every later lock of the same monitor. So everything written inside synchronized is visible to the next thread that enters it
volatileA write to a volatile variable happens-before every later read of that variable
Thread startEverything before t.start() happens-before the first action in t
Thread joinEverything in t happens-before another thread returns from t.join()
TransitivityIf A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C
Concurrent utilitiesSubmitting a task to an executor, a Future.get(), putting an element into a concurrent collection before another thread takes it, CountDownLatch.countDown() before await() returns — all create happens-before edges

Practical meaning: any time you use a lock, a volatile field, an atomic class, a concurrent collection or an executor correctly, the visibility and ordering problems are handled for you. Problems appear only when threads share plain fields with no such link.

Safe publication

Publishing an object means making it reachable by other threads. Safe publication means the publication creates a happens-before edge, so other threads see a fully constructed object. Safe ways: store it in a volatile or final field, store it in a field accessed under a lock, put it in a concurrent collection, or pass it to a task submitted to an executor. A reference stored in a plain field can show another thread a half-built object.

Rule: shared mutable data needs a happens-before edge

For every variable that one thread writes and another reads, ensure a lock, a volatile, an atomic, a concurrent collection or a thread-join/executor hand-off links the two. Otherwise your program has a data race, and its behaviour is not defined by "what the code looks like".

Edge cases

  • final fields get a special guarantee: once the constructor finishes normally, any thread that sees the object sees the correct values of its final fields, even if the object was published unsafely — provided this did not escape during construction. This is one reason immutable objects are thread-safe.
  • Escaping this: starting a thread or registering a listener inside a constructor lets another thread see the object before it is fully built.
  • Data races are timing-dependent. A test may pass a thousand times and fail in production on a machine with more cores, because the bug depended on the hardware and the JIT.

Interview: "What is the Java Memory Model? What is happens-before?"

  • The JMM specifies when one thread's writes are visible to another and what reorderings are allowed.
  • Three concerns: atomicity, visibility, ordering. Locks give all three; volatile gives visibility and ordering but not atomicity of compound actions; atomics give atomic single-variable updates.
  • Happens-before: if A happens-before B, A's effects are visible to B. Sources: unlock → lock, volatile write → read, start, join, executor hand-off.
  • count++ is read–modify–write, so concurrent increments can be lost.

Race conditions and synchronized

A race condition happens when the result depends on how threads interleave; synchronized makes a block of code a critical section that only one thread at a time can enter, using the lock (monitor) of one chosen object.

A race condition is a bug where the outcome depends on the timing of threads. The most common form is check-then-act or read-modify-write on shared data without protection. The code that touches the shared data and must not be interleaved is called a critical section.

The roadmap exercise: two threads, one counter

Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter 1,000,000 times. The expected total is 2,000,000.

public class RaceCondition {
    static int counter = 0;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Runnable task = () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
                counter++;                 // read, add, write: NOT atomic
            }
        };
        Thread t1 = new Thread(task, "t1");
        Thread t2 = new Thread(task, "t2");
        t1.start();
        t2.start();
        t1.join();
        t2.join();
        System.out.println("Expected 2000000, got " + counter);
    }
}
Expected 2000000, got 1316742

Updates are lost whenever both threads read the same old value (the picture in the memory model article). The wrong answer is silent: no exception, no warning.

Fix 1: synchronized

public class SyncCounter {
    private int count = 0;

    public synchronized void increment() {   // lock = this
        count++;
    }

    public synchronized int get() {
        return count;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        SyncCounter c = new SyncCounter();
        Runnable task = () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
                c.increment();
            }
        };
        Thread t1 = new Thread(task);
        Thread t2 = new Thread(task);
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("Expected 2000000, got " + c.get());
    }
}
Expected 2000000, got 2000000

Fix 2: AtomicInteger

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class AtomicCounter {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
        Runnable task = () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
                counter.incrementAndGet();   // one atomic operation, no lock
            }
        };
        Thread t1 = new Thread(task);
        Thread t2 = new Thread(task);
        t1.start(); t2.start();
        t1.join();  t2.join();
        System.out.println("Expected 2000000, got " + counter.get());
    }
}
Expected 2000000, got 2000000

Both are correct. AtomicInteger is simpler and faster for a single counter (details in the next article). synchronized is the general tool when several variables must change together.

How synchronized works: the monitor

Every Java object has a hidden intrinsic lock, also called its monitor. synchronized acquires that lock on entry and releases it on exit — even if an exception is thrown. While one thread holds the lock, any other thread that wants the same lock goes to the BLOCKED state and waits. Entering also gives a happens-before edge: the next thread to take the lock sees everything the previous holder wrote. So synchronized gives you both mutual exclusion (atomicity of the block) and visibility.

Synchronized methods vs blocks: which object is locked

FormLock used
public synchronized void m()this (the instance)
public static synchronized void m()The Class object, e.g. Bank.class
synchronized (this) { … }this
synchronized (lockObj) { … }The object you name, often a private final field
synchronized (Bank.class) { … }The class object

Two threads exclude each other only if they use the same lock object. A static synchronized method and an instance synchronized method use different locks (the class and the instance) and do not block each other. Two different instances of the same class have two different locks.

public class Account {
    private final Object lock = new Object();   // private: nobody else can lock on it
    private long balance;
    private int transactions;

    public void deposit(long amount) {
        validate(amount);                 // slow, thread-safe work outside the lock
        synchronized (lock) {             // keep the critical section small
            balance += amount;
            transactions++;               // both fields change together
        }
    }

    public long getBalance() {
        synchronized (lock) {             // reads need the same lock for visibility
            return balance;
        }
    }

    private void validate(long amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
    }
}

Reentrancy

Intrinsic locks are reentrant: a thread that already holds a lock can enter another synchronized block on the same lock without blocking itself. The JVM keeps a hold count. Without this, a synchronized method calling another synchronized method of the same object would deadlock on itself.

class Printer {
    synchronized void printAll() {
        printOne();                       // same lock, same thread: allowed
    }
    synchronized void printOne() {
        System.out.println("printing by " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}

Keep critical sections small

While a thread is inside a lock, all others wait. Do only the shared-data work inside, and do slow things (network calls, file I/O, heavy computation, sleep) outside. Never call unknown code — a callback or overridable method — while holding a lock; it may take other locks and cause a deadlock.

Synchronized vs no synchronization at all

Wrong: check-then-act without a lock

if (!cache.containsKey(id)) {
    cache.put(id, load(id));   // two threads
}                              // may both load

Right: one atomic operation

cache.computeIfAbsent(id, this::load);
// cache is a ConcurrentHashMap

Rules for synchronized

  • Protect every access (read and write) to a shared variable with the same lock. A synchronized setter with an unsynchronized getter is still a bug.
  • Synchronize compound actions as a unit (check-then-act, read-modify-write, "update two fields together").
  • Constructors cannot be synchronized; the keyword is a compile error there.
  • synchronized cannot be put on fields or on a method in an interface.

Conventions

  • Prefer a private final lock object over synchronized(this) or a synchronized method: outside code can lock this and interfere with you.
  • Never lock on a String literal, a boxed Integer or a pooled/shared object: unrelated code may lock the same instance. Never lock on a value that changes (a non-final field).
  • Document which lock guards which field (Java Concurrency in Practice style: // guarded by lock).
  • Keep lock order consistent when taking more than one lock (see deadlock).

Edge cases

  • synchronized (null) throws NullPointerException.
  • If a synchronized block throws, the lock is still released.
  • Synchronization does not stop a thread from being interrupted or from being BLOCKED forever — there is no timeout. Use ReentrantLock.tryLock when you need one.
  • Locks are per object, so synchronized on a method protects instance data only per instance. For a shared static field you need a static lock.
  • Locking is not fair: the thread that waited longest is not guaranteed to get the lock next.

Mistake: locking on a different object each time

synchronized (new Object()) { … } locks a brand-new object that no other thread ever sees, so it protects nothing. Likewise synchronized (counter) where counter is an Integer that gets re-boxed on every counter++ locks a different object each time.

Real projects

Spring singletons (@Service, @Controller) are shared by all request threads. Avoid mutable instance fields in them; if you need one (a counter, a cache), make it a concurrent type or an atomic, rather than adding synchronized to every method. Heavy use of synchronized on hot paths causes lock contention: many threads in BLOCKED, low CPU, high latency.

Interview: "What does synchronized do? Which lock does a static synchronized method use?"

  • Mutual exclusion plus visibility, via the object's monitor. Release on exit even on exceptions.
  • Instance method → this; static method → the Class object; block → the object in parentheses.
  • Reentrant: the same thread can re-enter locks it holds.
  • Keep blocks small; do not lock on public or shared objects; same lock for every access.
  • Alternatives: atomics for one variable, concurrent collections, ReentrantLock for timeouts and fairness.

volatile and the atomic classes

volatile guarantees that every thread sees the latest write to a variable but does not make count++ atomic; atomic classes such as AtomicInteger make single-variable updates atomic without locks by using compare-and-set (CAS).

volatile: visibility and ordering, not atomicity

Marking a field volatile tells the JVM that reads and writes go to main memory in a way every thread can see. A write to a volatile variable happens-before every later read of it, and the compiler may not reorder surrounding code across it unsafely. It is a light-weight tool, but a narrow one.

Use case 1: a stop flag
public class StopFlag {
    private static volatile boolean running = true;   // fixes the visibility bug

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
            long loops = 0;
            while (running) {
                loops++;
            }
            System.out.println("Worker stopped after looping");
        });
        worker.start();
        Thread.sleep(300);
        running = false;       // visible to the worker immediately
        worker.join();
    }
}
Worker stopped after looping

This works because one thread writes and the others only read. For stopping a thread, interrupt() is usually better (see interruption), since it also wakes a sleeping thread.

Why volatile does not fix count++
static volatile int counter = 0;
// two threads each run: for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) counter++;
// Result: still less than 2,000,000
Expected 2000000, got 1543180

Each thread sees fresh values, but read–add–write is still three steps, and another thread can slip in between them. volatile fixes visibility only.

Use case 2: safe publication of an immutable snapshot

Swap a whole immutable object by writing one volatile reference. Readers always see either the old or the new complete object (a config reload is a typical case).

public class ConfigHolder {
    record Config(String region, int timeoutMs) { }

    private volatile Config current = new Config("ap-south-1", 3000);

    public Config get() { return current; }                  // lock-free read
    public void reload(Config fresh) { current = fresh; }    // one atomic reference write
}
Use case 3: double-checked locking needs volatile

A lazy singleton avoids locking on every call by checking twice. Without volatile, another thread can see a non-null reference to an object whose constructor has not finished, because the reference write may be reordered before the field writes.

public class Singleton {
    private static volatile Singleton instance;      // volatile is required

    private Singleton() { }

    public static Singleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {                      // first check: no lock
            synchronized (Singleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) {              // second check: under the lock
                    instance = new Singleton();
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

Simpler alternatives: an enum singleton, or the initialization-on-demand holder idiom (a private static nested class that holds the instance, loaded lazily by the class loader). Prefer those, or let Spring manage the singleton.

Pointvolatilesynchronized
VisibilityYesYes
Atomic compound actionsNoYes
Blocks other threadsNoYes
Applies toFields onlyMethods and blocks
Can be null / sleep insideNot applicableHolds lock while inside

Atomic classes and CAS

The package java.util.concurrent.atomic has AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, AtomicReference<V>, array versions, and more. They are built on a CPU instruction called compare-and-swap (CAS): "set the value to new only if it is currently expected; tell me whether it worked." Code that uses CAS is lock-free: no thread is ever blocked; a thread whose CAS fails just retries.

MethodWhat it does
get() / set(v)Volatile read / write
incrementAndGet(), getAndIncrement()Atomic ++x / x++
addAndGet(n), getAndAdd(n)Atomic add
compareAndSet(expected, new)Sets only if the value equals expected; returns true/false
updateAndGet(fn), getAndUpdate(fn)Atomic update with a function (must be side-effect free; may run more than once)
accumulateAndGet(x, fn)Atomic combine with x
getAndSet(v)Atomic swap; returns old value
 
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

public class AtomicDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AtomicInteger stock = new AtomicInteger(5);

        // Reserve one item safely: never goes below zero
        boolean reserved = false;
        while (true) {
            int current = stock.get();
            if (current == 0) break;                                  // sold out
            if (stock.compareAndSet(current, current - 1)) {          // CAS
                reserved = true;
                break;
            }
            // CAS failed: another thread changed stock; loop and try again
        }
        System.out.println("reserved=" + reserved + ", left=" + stock.get());

        AtomicLong visits = new AtomicLong();
        System.out.println(visits.incrementAndGet() + " " + visits.addAndGet(10));

        AtomicInteger maxSeen = new AtomicInteger(3);
        maxSeen.accumulateAndGet(9, Math::max);       // atomic "max so far"
        System.out.println(maxSeen.get());

        AtomicReference<String> status = new AtomicReference<>("PENDING");
        System.out.println(status.compareAndSet("PENDING", "PAID") + " "
                + status.compareAndSet("PENDING", "FAILED") + " " + status.get());
    }
}
reserved=true, left=4
1 11
9
true false PAID

LongAdder for high contention

With many threads hammering one AtomicLong, most CAS attempts fail and retry, wasting CPU. LongAdder (and LongAccumulator, DoubleAdder) spreads updates across several internal cells and adds them up when you read. It is much faster for write-heavy counters such as metrics and request counts. The trade-off: sum() is not an exact snapshot while updates are in flight, and you cannot do compare-and-set on it.

LongAdder hits = new LongAdder();
hits.increment();      // many threads, low contention cost
hits.add(5);
System.out.println(hits.sum());   // 6

The ABA problem (brief)

CAS only checks "is the value still equal to what I read?" If another thread changed A → B → A in between, CAS succeeds although things changed. For plain counters this is harmless. For linked structures it can corrupt data; AtomicStampedReference adds a version stamp to detect it.

Rule: atomic operations compose only within one variable

Two separate atomic calls are not atomic together. if (a.get() < 10) a.incrementAndGet(); has a gap between the check and the update. Use compareAndSet in a loop, updateAndGet, or a lock. Likewise, two atomics that must stay consistent with each other need a lock around both.

Edge cases

  • volatile on an array or object reference makes the reference volatile, not the elements or fields it points to.
  • AtomicReference.compareAndSet compares with == (reference identity), not equals(). For boxed numbers or strings that are not the same instance, CAS may fail unexpectedly.
  • The function passed to updateAndGet may be called several times under contention. Keep it pure.
  • A volatile long or double read/write is atomic; a plain one technically is not (in practice 64-bit JVMs do it).

Mistake: using volatile for a counter or a check-then-act

Reviewers see private volatile int count; count++; far too often. Use AtomicInteger or LongAdder.

Conventions

  • Reach for the highest-level tool first: concurrent collection, then atomic, then lock. Plain volatile is for flags and snapshot references.
  • Metrics counters: LongAdder (or Micrometer, which Spring Boot uses). Sequence numbers or IDs where you need the exact next value: AtomicLong.

Interview: "volatile vs synchronized vs AtomicInteger"

  • volatile: visibility + ordering for a single variable; no atomicity of read-modify-write; never blocks.
  • synchronized: mutual exclusion + visibility for any block; blocks other threads.
  • AtomicInteger: atomic read-modify-write on one value via CAS; lock-free; retries on contention.
  • Why does double-checked locking need volatile? Without it, publication can be reordered and a thread may see a half-constructed object.
  • High contention counters: LongAdder.

wait/notify, BlockingQueue and explicit locks

wait() and notify() let threads hand signals to each other inside synchronized code but are low-level and error-prone, so modern code uses BlockingQueue for producer-consumer and ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock and Condition when synchronized is not flexible enough.

wait, notify, notifyAll (legacy, but asked in interviews)

Sometimes a thread must pause until a condition becomes true — a queue gets an item, a payment is confirmed. The old way uses three methods of Object:

  • wait() — release the monitor and sleep until another thread notifies (state WAITING).
  • notify() — wake one waiting thread of this monitor.
  • notifyAll() — wake all waiting threads (safer default).

Rules: you must hold the object's lock (be inside synchronized on that same object) when you call them, otherwise you get IllegalMonitorStateException. Always call wait() inside a while loop that re-checks the condition, because of spurious wake-ups (the thread may wake without any notify) and because another thread may have consumed the item first.

import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.Queue;

public class SimpleBuffer {
    private final Queue<Integer> queue = new LinkedList<>();
    private final int capacity = 2;

    public synchronized void put(int item) throws InterruptedException {
        while (queue.size() == capacity) {   // while, never if
            wait();                          // releases the lock while waiting
        }
        queue.add(item);
        notifyAll();                         // wake consumers waiting for items
    }

    public synchronized int take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (queue.isEmpty()) {
            wait();
        }
        int item = queue.remove();
        notifyAll();                         // wake producers waiting for space
        return item;
    }
}

This works, but note how easy it is to get wrong: wrong lock, if instead of while, missed notification, notify waking the wrong kind of thread. That is why you rarely write it by hand.

BlockingQueue: the modern producer–consumer

A BlockingQueue is a thread-safe queue where put() waits if the queue is full and take() waits if it is empty. All the wait/notify logic is inside. A producer adds work; a consumer processes it. This decouples the two speeds and gives you back-pressure (a full bounded queue slows producers down).

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ProducerConsumer {
    private static final int POISON = -1;   // signal "no more work"

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(3);   // bounded

        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int orderId = 1; orderId <= 5; orderId++) {
                    queue.put(orderId);              // waits if the queue is full
                    System.out.println("Produced order " + orderId);
                }
                queue.put(POISON);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }, "producer");

        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                while (true) {
                    int orderId = queue.take();      // waits if the queue is empty
                    if (orderId == POISON) break;
                    System.out.println("  Processed order " + orderId);
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }, "consumer");

        producer.start();
        consumer.start();
        producer.join();
        consumer.join();
    }
}
Produced order 1
Produced order 2
  Processed order 1
Produced order 3
  Processed order 2
Produced order 4
  Processed order 3
Produced order 5
  Processed order 4
  Processed order 5
OperationThrowsReturns special valueBlocksTimes out
Insertadd(e)offer(e)put(e)offer(e, time, unit)
Removeremove()poll()take()poll(time, unit)

The poison-pill value (a special item meaning "stop") is a common way to shut consumers down. Implementations are covered in concurrent collections.

ReentrantLock

java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock is an explicit lock object with the same reentrant mutual exclusion as synchronized, plus features synchronized lacks: try to lock without waiting, lock with a timeout, interruptible waiting, optional fairness, and multiple conditions. The price: you must unlock manually, always in finally.

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public class Wallet {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();   // fair=false by default
    private long balance;

    public void deposit(long amount) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            balance += amount;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();                  // runs even if an exception is thrown
        }
    }

    public boolean tryDeposit(long amount) throws InterruptedException {
        if (lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {   // give up after 200 ms
            try {
                balance += amount;
                return true;
            } finally {
                lock.unlock();
            }
        }
        return false;                       // could not get the lock in time
    }
}
FeaturesynchronizedReentrantLock
ReleaseAutomatic at block endManual: unlock() in finally
Try without waiting / timeoutNotryLock(), tryLock(time, unit)
Interruptible while waitingNolockInterruptibly()
Fairness optionNonew ReentrantLock(true) (FIFO, slower)
Multiple wait conditionsOne per monitorMany Condition objects
Simplicity, fewer bugsBetterEasy to forget unlock

Use synchronized by default; reach for ReentrantLock only for the extra features. A fair lock gives the lock to the longest-waiting thread; this prevents starvation but lowers throughput. Calling unlock() when you do not hold the lock throws IllegalMonitorStateException.

ReadWriteLock

Many reads, few writes? ReentrantReadWriteLock lets any number of readers hold the read lock at once, but a writer needs the write lock exclusively.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;

public class PriceCache {
    private final ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    private final Map<String, Long> prices = new HashMap<>();

    public Long get(String sku) {
        rw.readLock().lock();                 // many readers at the same time
        try { return prices.get(sku); }
        finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
    }

    public void put(String sku, long price) {
        rw.writeLock().lock();                // exclusive
        try { prices.put(sku, price); }
        finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }
}

A thread holding the read lock cannot upgrade to the write lock (it would deadlock); it can downgrade (take the read lock before releasing the write lock). For most cases a ConcurrentHashMap is simpler. Java 8 also added StampedLock with optimistic reads — an advanced tool; know it exists.

Condition

A Condition (from lock.newCondition()) is the wait/notify of explicit locks, but a lock can have several, e.g. notFull and notEmpty. Methods: await(), signal(), signalAll(). The same rules apply: hold the lock, and wait in a while loop.

class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Object[] items = new Object[10];
    private int putIdx, takeIdx, count;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    void put(T x) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == items.length) notFull.await();   // wait for space
            items[putIdx] = x;
            putIdx = (putIdx + 1) % items.length;
            count++;
            notEmpty.signal();                               // wake one consumer
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
    // take() is the mirror image: await notEmpty, then signal notFull
}

Rules

  • wait/notify require holding the monitor, or IllegalMonitorStateException.
  • Always wait()/await() in a while loop that re-checks the condition.
  • lock.lock() goes before the try; unlock() goes in finally.
  • Lock and unlock the same number of times (locks are reentrant with a hold count).

Mistake: lock() inside try, or no finally

If lock() is inside the try and fails, finally calls unlock() on a lock you do not hold. If you skip finally, one exception leaves the lock held forever and every other thread hangs.

Edge cases

  • notify() before any thread is waiting is lost — notifications are not remembered. That is why you check the condition in a loop first.
  • notify() can wake the wrong type of thread (a producer waking a producer) and leave the system stuck; notifyAll() avoids this.
  • BlockingQueue does not allow null elements (NullPointerException).
  • Starvation: with an unfair lock, a thread can wait very long under heavy contention.

Interview: "wait vs sleep", "How do you implement producer–consumer?"

  • wait() belongs to Object, needs the monitor, releases it, wakes on notify. sleep() belongs to Thread, holds locks, wakes on time.
  • Producer–consumer: best answer is BlockingQueue (put/take); second answer is wait/notify with a while loop.
  • Why a while loop? Spurious wake-ups and stolen conditions.
  • ReentrantLock vs synchronized: tryLock, timeout, fairness, multiple conditions; must unlock in finally.

Executors and thread pools

A thread pool keeps a fixed set of reusable worker threads that take tasks from a queue, so you submit tasks instead of creating threads; ThreadPoolExecutor is the engine behind every factory method in Executors.

Why thread pools

Creating a platform thread is expensive (stack memory, operating-system work), and an unlimited number of threads can crash the JVM. A thread pool starts a limited number of worker threads once and reuses them. You submit tasks (Runnable or Callable) and the pool decides which worker runs each. Benefits: lower creation cost, a hard limit on resource use, a queue to absorb bursts, and one place to shut everything down. The Executor interface (one method, execute(Runnable)) separates what to run from how to run it; ExecutorService adds lifecycle and result handling.

Factory methods in Executors

FactoryBehaviourWatch out
newFixedThreadPool(n)Exactly n workers; extra tasks wait in an unbounded queueQueue can grow without limit and exhaust memory
newCachedThreadPool()Creates workers as needed, reuses idle ones, removes ones idle for 60 secondsMaximum size is effectively unlimited; a burst can create thousands of threads
newSingleThreadExecutor()One worker; tasks run one after another in submission orderUnbounded queue too
newScheduledThreadPool(n)Run a task after a delay or repeatedlyA task that throws stops its own repetition
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()A new virtual thread for every task (Java 21)Not a pool; do not limit work by pool size, use a semaphore
 
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class PoolBasics {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Java 19+: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable; close() waits for tasks to finish
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) {
            for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
                int orderId = i;
                pool.execute(() -> System.out.println(
                        "Order " + orderId + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()));
            }
        }   // close(): stops accepting new tasks, waits for the running ones
        System.out.println("All orders done");
    }
}
Order 1 on pool-1-thread-1
Order 2 on pool-1-thread-2
Order 3 on pool-1-thread-3
Order 4 on pool-1-thread-1
Order 5 on pool-1-thread-2
All orders done

Five tasks, three threads: threads are reused. Before Java 19 you wrote pool.shutdown() plus awaitTermination yourself (see below).

ThreadPoolExecutor: the real parameters

Every factory above builds a ThreadPoolExecutor. In production code you often create it directly to control all the knobs:

import java.util.concurrent.*;

ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        4,                                   // corePoolSize: threads kept alive
        8,                                   // maximumPoolSize: upper limit
        60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,                // keepAliveTime for threads above core
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),       // bounded work queue
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("invoice-", 1).factory(),   // names: invoice-1, ...
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());          // rejection policy

Order of events when you submit a task:

  1. If fewer than corePoolSize workers are running, start a new worker for this task (even if others are idle).
  2. Otherwise try to put the task in the work queue.
  3. If the queue is full and fewer than maximumPoolSize workers exist, start an extra worker.
  4. If the queue is full and the pool is at maximum, the task is rejected: the rejection policy decides what happens.

Note the surprise: extra threads above the core size are created only when the queue is full. With an unbounded queue (the default for fixed and single pools) step 3 never happens, so maximumPoolSize is ignored and the pool never grows beyond core.

Rejection policyEffect
AbortPolicy (default)Throws RejectedExecutionException
CallerRunsPolicyThe submitting thread runs the task itself; this slows the producer down (natural back-pressure)
DiscardPolicySilently drops the new task
DiscardOldestPolicyDrops the oldest queued task and retries the new one

The same task is also rejected after you call shutdown().

Why unbounded queues are risky

A fixed pool of 10 threads with an unbounded queue never rejects anything. If tasks arrive faster than 10 threads can process them, the queue grows until the JVM dies with OutOfMemoryError, and users wait minutes for responses long before that. A bounded queue plus a rejection policy turns overload into a visible, controllable event: return HTTP 429/503, slow the caller, or drop low-value work. Likewise newCachedThreadPool bounds nothing on the thread side. Many style guides therefore say: build ThreadPoolExecutor yourself with a bounded queue.

execute vs submit

Pointexecute(Runnable)submit(...)
Defined inExecutorExecutorService
AcceptsRunnable onlyRunnable or Callable
ReturnsvoidA Future
Exception in the taskGoes to the thread's uncaught-exception handler (printed)Captured inside the Future; silent unless you call get()

Shutting down properly

Non-daemon pool threads keep the JVM alive, so a program that forgets to shut down its pool never exits.

  • shutdown() — stop accepting new tasks; already queued and running tasks finish. Returns at once.
  • shutdownNow() — stop accepting tasks, try to stop running ones by interrupting them, and return the list of tasks that never started.
  • awaitTermination(time, unit) — block until all tasks finish or the time passes; returns true if the pool terminated.
pool.shutdown();                                    // no new tasks
try {
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
        pool.shutdownNow();                         // interrupt stragglers
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            System.err.println("Pool did not terminate");
        }
    }
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    pool.shutdownNow();
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
}

Since Java 19, ExecutorService.close() does this "shutdown, then wait" for you, which is why try-with-resources works. If the waiting thread is interrupted, close() calls shutdownNow().

Scheduled tasks

ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1);

scheduler.schedule(() -> System.out.println("Run once after 1s"), 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

// scheduleAtFixedRate: every 5 s measured from start to start
// scheduleWithFixedDelay: 5 s pause AFTER each run finishes
scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(
        () -> System.out.println("Sync inventory"), 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
// ... later: scheduler.shutdown();

If a repeating task throws an exception, later runs are cancelled silently. Wrap the body in try/catch and log. In Spring you use @Scheduled, which sits on the same idea.

How many threads? Sizing pools

Work typeRule of thumbWhy
CPU-boundAbout the number of cores (availableProcessors()) or cores + 1Threads are always busy; extra threads only add context switching
I/O-bound (blocking)cores × (1 + wait time / compute time)Threads mostly wait, so more can be productive; measure and tune. Or use virtual threads
MixedSeparate pools for CPU and I/O workA slow I/O task must not starve CPU tasks

Example: 8 cores, each task computes 10 ms and waits 90 ms for the database. Compute-to-wait ratio is 9, so about 8 × (1 + 9) = 80 threads could keep the cores busy. Treat this as a starting point; the database connection pool size is usually the real limit.

Rules

  • Always shut down pools you create (try-with-resources, or shutdown in a lifecycle hook). Pools managed by Spring are closed with the application context.
  • Never block a pool thread waiting for another task in the same pool — with all workers waiting, no one runs the tasks they wait for (pool-induced deadlock).
  • Do not create a new pool per request; create one and reuse it.

Conventions

  • Name your threads with a ThreadFactory, so logs and thread dumps are readable (invoice-1, not pool-3-thread-7).
  • Use a bounded queue and an explicit rejection policy for production pools; monitor queue size and active count.
  • Catch and log exceptions inside tasks, so failures are not lost.
  • In Spring Boot, configure a TaskExecutor (e.g. ThreadPoolTaskExecutor) bean rather than building raw pools.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • RejectedExecutionException — pool shut down, or queue and max threads full (with AbortPolicy).
  • IllegalArgumentException — e.g. corePoolSize > maximumPoolSize or a non-positive pool size.
  • Core threads are not removed when idle unless allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true).
  • shutdownNow() only interrupts; a task that ignores interrupts keeps running.
  • Thread-local data of a pool thread survives between tasks (see ThreadLocal).

Mistake: using Executors.newFixedThreadPool for unbounded traffic

"It never throws" is the problem, not the benefit. Under overload it hides the failure until memory runs out. Size the queue.

Interview: "Explain ThreadPoolExecutor parameters and what happens when a task is submitted"

  • Core size, max size, keep-alive, work queue, thread factory, rejection handler.
  • Order: core threads first, then the queue, then extra threads up to max, then rejection.
  • Unbounded queue means max size is never used and memory can run out.
  • execute vs submit; shutdown vs shutdownNow.
  • Sizing: CPU-bound ≈ cores; I/O-bound larger, or virtual threads.

Callable, Future and invokeAll

Callable is a task that returns a value and may throw a checked exception; submitting it to an executor gives you a Future, a handle you use to wait for the result, set a timeout or cancel.

Runnable.run() returns nothing and cannot throw checked exceptions. When a task must give back a result, such as a price lookup, use Callable<V>.

PointRunnableCallable<V>
Methodvoid run()V call() throws Exception
Returns a resultNoYes
Checked exceptionsCannot throwCan throw
Packagejava.lang (Java 1.0)java.util.concurrent (Java 5)
Can be given to new ThreadYesNo (use an executor or FutureTask)

Future

A Future<V> represents a result that may not exist yet.

MethodPurpose
get()Block until done; return the value or throw
get(time, unit)Same, but throws TimeoutException if too slow
isDone()true when finished, failed or cancelled; does not block
cancel(mayInterrupt)Try to cancel; with true the running thread is interrupted
isCancelled()Was it cancelled before completion?
resultNow(), exceptionNow(), state()Added in Java 19: read the result of a finished future without blocking or checked exceptions
 
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class FutureDemo {
    static int fetchPrice(String sku) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(500);                  // pretend this is a remote call
        return sku.length() * 100;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
            Future<Integer> f1 = pool.submit(() -> fetchPrice("PHONE"));
            Future<Integer> f2 = pool.submit(() -> fetchPrice("CASE"));

            System.out.println("Submitted; main is free to do other work");
            System.out.println("Phone: " + f1.get());   // blocks until ready
            System.out.println("Case : " + f2.get());

            Future<Integer> slow = pool.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(5000); return 1; });
            try {
                slow.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            } catch (TimeoutException e) {
                System.out.println("Too slow, cancelling");
                slow.cancel(true);          // interrupts the sleeping task
            }
            System.out.println("cancelled=" + slow.isCancelled());
        }
    }
}
Submitted; main is free to do other work
Phone: 500
Case : 400
Too slow, cancelling
cancelled=true

Both prices were fetched in parallel, so the total wait was about 500 ms, not 1,000 ms. A lambda that returns a value becomes a Callable; one that returns nothing becomes a Runnable. If the compiler cannot tell (a lambda that just calls a method returning a value), cast or use a block with return.

Exceptions in tasks: ExecutionException

An exception thrown inside a submitted task is caught by the executor and stored in the Future. It reappears when you call get(), wrapped in ExecutionException; the real cause is e.getCause().

Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("gateway down"); });
try {
    f.get();
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    System.out.println("Task failed: " + e.getCause());   // the original exception
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
}
Task failed: java.lang.IllegalStateException: gateway down

invokeAll and invokeAny

  • invokeAll(tasks) runs a collection of Callables and waits for all to finish; it returns a list of Futures in the same order as the tasks.
  • invokeAny(tasks) returns the result of one task that completed successfully (usually the fastest) and cancels the rest. Use it for "ask three mirrors, use the first answer".
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class InvokeAllDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<Callable<String>> calls = List.of(
                () -> "inventory ok",
                () -> "payment ok",
                () -> "address ok");

        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) {
            for (Future<String> f : pool.invokeAll(calls)) {   // waits for all
                System.out.println(f.get());
            }
            System.out.println("First finisher: " + pool.invokeAny(calls));
        }
    }
}
inventory ok
payment ok
address ok
First finisher: inventory ok

Rules

  • Future.get() blocks the calling thread. Use the timeout version when the caller must stay responsive.
  • Always handle InterruptedException (restore the flag) and ExecutionException (look at the cause).
  • Cancelling a task with cancel(true) only works if the task responds to interruption.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • ExecutionException — the task threw. TimeoutException — get(time) ran out of time (the task keeps running unless cancelled). CancellationException — get() on a cancelled future (unchecked). InterruptedException — the waiting thread was interrupted.
  • A submitted Runnable that throws is silent unless somebody calls get() — a common source of "my background job never runs and nothing is logged".
  • Future cannot be chained or combined and cannot be completed by hand. That is why CompletableFuture exists.

Mistake: calling get() right after submit in a loop

Submitting a task and immediately calling get() makes the work sequential. First submit all tasks, collect the futures, then call get() on each (as in the example above), or use invokeAll.

The submit and execute overloads

An ExecutorService gives you several ways to hand over work, and the difference matters for results and errors.

CallReturnsIf the task throws
execute(Runnable)NothingException goes to the thread's uncaught-exception handler (printed on stderr)
submit(Runnable)Future<?>; get() gives nullStored in the Future; silent until get()
submit(Runnable, T result)Future<T> with the fixed result you passedStored in the Future
submit(Callable<V>)Future<V>Stored; get() throws ExecutionException
invokeAll(tasks)List<Future<V>>, all finishedStored per task
invokeAny(tasks)One value VFailures are ignored while another task can still succeed

The executor itself and its thread lifecycle are explained in Executors and thread pools; here we focus on the results.

How a Future works inside: FutureTask

When you submit a Callable, the executor wraps it in a FutureTask. A FutureTask is both a Runnable (the pool thread runs it) and a Future (you wait on it). It stores the outcome — a value or an exception — and wakes everyone blocked in get() when the task completes. You can use it without a pool too, which is the way to give a Callable to a plain Thread:

FutureTask<String> task = new FutureTask<>(() -> "report ready");
new Thread(task, "report-thread").start();
System.out.println(task.get());          // report ready  (blocks until done)
System.out.println(task.isDone());       // true

The life of a Future

A Future ends in exactly one of three ways, and since Java 19 you can ask which with future.state(), which returns Future.State: RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED.

  • Completed normally: get() returns the value.
  • Failed: get() throws ExecutionException with the original exception as the cause.
  • Cancelled: get() throws CancellationException. isDone() is also true after a cancel.

cancel(false) only stops a task that has not started yet; a running task finishes normally. cancel(true) also interrupts the running thread, but the task must check for interruption (blocking calls like sleep do; a tight CPU loop does not unless it tests Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()). cancel returns false if the task had already finished.

invokeAll with a failing task and a time limit

List<Callable<String>> calls = List.of(
        () -> "stock: 12",
        () -> { throw new IllegalStateException("price service down"); },
        () -> { Thread.sleep(3000); return "reviews: 4.5"; });

try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) {
    List<Future<String>> results = pool.invokeAll(calls, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    for (Future<String> f : results) {
        try {
            System.out.println("OK    " + f.get());
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            System.out.println("FAIL  " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            System.out.println("LATE  cancelled after the time limit");
        }
    }
}
OK    stock: 12
FAIL  price service down
LATE  cancelled after the time limit

The timed invokeAll cancels every task that is not finished when the time is up. The returned futures are all in a done state, so get() never blocks here. Plain invokeAll never throws because a task failed; each failure waits in its own Future. invokeAny throws ExecutionException only if every task fails.

Java 21: one cheap thread per task

Because Callable tasks are mostly blocking calls (HTTP, database), they suit virtual threads. Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() gives a new virtual thread per submitted task, so you can run thousands of blocking Callables with the same submit/get code and no pool-size tuning.

Wrong: sequential, because get() is called inside the loop

List<Integer> prices = new ArrayList<>();
for (String sku : skus) {
    prices.add(pool.submit(() -> fetchPrice(sku)).get());   // waits every time
}

Right: submit all first, then collect

List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
for (String sku : skus) {
    futures.add(pool.submit(() -> fetchPrice(sku)));
}
List<Integer> prices = new ArrayList<>();
for (Future<Integer> f : futures) {
    prices.add(f.get());
}

More mistakes

  • Catching Exception around get() and printing e.getMessage(). For an ExecutionException that message is just the wrapper's text; log e.getCause().
  • Using submit for fire-and-forget work and never calling get(). Errors vanish. Use execute with a handler, or log inside the task.
  • Swallowing InterruptedException around get() with an empty catch. Restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt().
  • Forgetting to shut the executor down (or to use try-with-resources on Java 19+), which keeps the JVM alive.

Conventions

  • Always call the timed get(timeout, unit) on calls that leave your process, and decide what a timeout means (default value, retry or error).
  • Keep tasks independent and side-effect free where you can; then invokeAll is easy to reason about.
  • Prefer CompletableFuture for pipelines (call A, then B, then combine); use plain Future for "run these N things and collect the answers".

In real projects

A typical use is a product page that needs price, stock and reviews from three internal services. Submit three Callables, wait with a 500 ms limit each, and show the page with a default for any part that failed. The same shape is used for fan-out searches, batch file parsing and report generation. Note that Spring's @Async methods return CompletableFuture, which implements Future too.

Interview: "Runnable vs Callable", "What is a Future? What does get() throw?"

  • Callable returns a value and may throw checked exceptions; Runnable does neither.
  • Future is a handle to an async result: get, get(timeout), cancel, isDone.
  • get() throws ExecutionException (wrap of the real error), InterruptedException, and TimeoutException in the timed version.
  • Limits of Future: blocking, no chaining, no callbacks — solved by CompletableFuture.

CompletableFuture: async pipelines

CompletableFuture lets you start async work, chain steps on its result without blocking, combine several futures, and handle errors in the same pipeline.

A plain Future makes you wait. CompletableFuture<T> (Java 8) implements Future and also CompletionStage: you attach callbacks that run when the result arrives, like a stream pipeline for asynchronous values. It can also be completed by hand with complete(value) or completeExceptionally(ex).

Starting a task

MethodUse
supplyAsync(Supplier)Run async and produce a value
runAsync(Runnable)Run async, no value (CompletableFuture<Void>)
completedFuture(value)An already-finished future (useful in tests)
new CompletableFuture<>()An empty future you complete yourself

Transforming and chaining

MethodTakesMeaning (like in streams / Optional)
thenApply(fn)T → Umap: transform the result
thenAccept(consumer)T → voidUse the result, return CompletableFuture<Void>
thenRun(runnable)nothingRun something after, ignore the result
thenCompose(fn)T → CompletableFuture<U>flatMap: the next step is itself async
thenCombine(other, bifn)(T, U) → VWait for two independent futures, then merge

thenApply vs thenCompose: if your function returns a plain value, use thenApply. If it returns another CompletableFuture (it calls another async service), use thenCompose; thenApply would give you a nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>. It is the same difference as map vs flatMap in streams.

import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class ChainDemo {
    static CompletableFuture<String> findUserId(String email) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "U-" + email.length());
    }
    static CompletableFuture<Integer> loadCartTotal(String userId) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 1499);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CompletableFuture<String> message =
                findUserId("asha@mail.in")                    // step 1: async
                .thenCompose(ChainDemo::loadCartTotal)        // step 2: async, needs step 1
                .thenApply(total -> total * 118 / 100)        // step 3: plain function (GST)
                .thenApply(total -> "Pay Rs " + total);       // step 4: format

        System.out.println(message.join());
    }
}
Pay Rs 1768

Combining many futures

  • thenCombine — two futures into one value.
  • CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2, f3) — returns CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all are done; read each result with join() afterwards.
  • CompletableFuture.anyOf(f1, f2) — completes when the first one completes; returns CompletableFuture<Object>.

Realistic example: three services in parallel

A product page needs price, stock and reviews from three services, each taking about 300 ms. Sequential calls cost about 900 ms; in parallel about 300 ms.

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class ProductPage {
    record Page(String price, String stock, String reviews) { }

    static String slow(String what, String value) {
        try { Thread.sleep(300); } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            throw new IllegalStateException("interrupted calling " + what);
        }
        return value;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)) {   // our own pool
            long start = System.currentTimeMillis();

            var price   = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> slow("price", "Rs 999"), io);
            var stock   = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> slow("stock", "In stock"), io);
            var reviews = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> slow("reviews", "4.3 stars"), io)
                    .orTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)                    // Java 9+
                    .exceptionally(ex -> "reviews unavailable");       // fallback

            Page page = CompletableFuture.allOf(price, stock, reviews)
                    .thenApply(v -> new Page(price.join(), stock.join(), reviews.join()))
                    .join();

            System.out.println(page);
            System.out.println("took ~" + (System.currentTimeMillis() - start) / 100 * 100
                    + " ms");
        }
    }
}
Page[price=Rs 999, stock=In stock, reviews=4.3 stars]
took ~300 ms

Error handling

MethodRuns whenCan change the result?
exceptionally(ex → value)Only on failureYes: supplies a fallback value
handle((value, ex) → result)Always (success or failure)Yes: you produce the new result
whenComplete((value, ex) → void)AlwaysNo: for logging; the original result or failure passes through
 
CompletableFuture<Integer> risky = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    if (true) throw new IllegalStateException("bank timeout");
    return 100;
});

System.out.println(risky.exceptionally(ex -> -1).join());
System.out.println(risky.handle((v, ex) -> ex == null ? "ok " + v
        : "failed: " + ex.getClass().getSimpleName() + " / "
          + ex.getCause().getMessage()).join());
risky.whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("logged, ex=" + (ex != null)));
risky.join();   // still throws
-1
failed: CompletionException / bank timeout
logged, ex=true
Exception in thread "main" java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: bank timeout

Note the wrapping: inside handle on a later stage, the exception arrives wrapped in CompletionException with your exception as its cause. Check getCause().

join() vs get()

Pointjoin()get()
Checked exceptionsNone: throws unchecked CompletionExceptionThrows checked InterruptedException and ExecutionException
Timeout versionNo (use orTimeout / completeOnTimeout)Yes, get(time, unit)
Use in lambdasConvenient (no checked exceptions)Awkward

Async variants and which thread runs what

Every step has an Async twin (thenApplyAsync). The plain version may run on the thread that completed the previous stage, or on the caller if it was already complete. The Async version always submits to an executor. Without an executor argument, supplyAsync and the Async methods use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() — a shared pool sized to about the number of cores minus one, whose threads are daemon threads.

Mistake: blocking I/O on the common pool

If you run slow blocking calls (database, HTTP) in supplyAsync(...) with no executor, they occupy the few common-pool threads. Parallel streams and other code share that pool and will slow down or stall. Pass your own executor, as in the example: supplyAsync(task, ioExecutor). Also, because those threads are daemons, a main method that does not wait can end before the work does.

Rules

  • Do not call join()/get() in the middle of a pipeline; chain with thenApply/thenCompose and block only once at the edge (or never, in a reactive/async controller).
  • An exception in any stage skips the following thenApply stages and flows to the first exceptionally/handle.
  • Use thenCompose when the function returns a CompletableFuture.

Edge cases

  • Cancelling a CompletableFuture does not interrupt the running thread; it only completes the future exceptionally. Plan for cooperative stop yourself.
  • An exception that nobody observes (no join, no handle) disappears silently.
  • allOf with zero arguments is already complete; one failing future makes the combined future fail, but the others keep running.
  • orTimeout/completeOnTimeout exist since Java 9 and complete the future only; they do not stop the underlying work.

Real projects

Spring's @Async methods can return CompletableFuture<T>; aggregator or "backend for frontend" services use allOf to fan out to several microservices. With virtual threads (Java 21), many teams go back to plain blocking code in parallel tasks because it is easier to read — but CompletableFuture is still everywhere in existing code and libraries.

Interview: "thenApply vs thenCompose", "How do you run three calls in parallel?", "Where does supplyAsync run?"

  • thenApply = map (function returns a value); thenCompose = flatMap (function returns a future); thenCombine merges two independent futures.
  • Parallel calls: start each with supplyAsync, then allOf(...).thenApply(...) and read with join().
  • Default executor is the common ForkJoinPool; for blocking I/O supply your own executor.
  • Errors: exceptionally (fallback), handle (both paths), whenComplete (side effect). join() throws CompletionException.

Concurrent collections: ConcurrentHashMap and friends

The java.util.concurrent collections are built for many threads: ConcurrentHashMap gives fast thread-safe reads and atomic updates like merge and compute, CopyOnWriteArrayList suits read-heavy lists, and the BlockingQueue family passes work between threads.

Why ordinary collections break

HashMap and ArrayList are not thread-safe. Two threads calling put at the same time can lose entries, corrupt the internal structure, or (in old Java versions) even loop forever during a resize. Iterating while another thread modifies the collection throws ConcurrentModificationException. The old fix, Collections.synchronizedMap, makes every call take one lock, which is safe but slow under load. The concurrent collections solve this with smarter designs.

ConcurrentHashMap

ConcurrentHashMap is the default thread-safe map. It does not allow null keys or values: in a concurrent map, get(k) == null must unambiguously mean "absent", and a stored null would make that unclear (NullPointerException if you try).

How it is thread-safe (Java 8 and later)
  • The table is an array of bins (buckets), like HashMap.
  • Putting into an empty bin uses a lock-free CAS (compare-and-set: "set this slot to the new node only if it is still empty").
  • Putting into a bin that already has nodes takes a synchronized lock on that bin's first node only. Threads working on different bins never block each other. (Java 7 used a fixed number of segments; Java 8 replaced them with this per-bin locking.)
  • get takes no lock: node values and next-pointers are volatile, so reads see recent writes.
  • Long collision chains turn into trees, as in HashMap (when a bin has at least 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 slots).
  • The size is kept in counter cells (like LongAdder) so many threads can update it without fighting over one variable. size() is therefore an estimate while updates are running; mappingCount() returns a long.
  • Iterators are weakly consistent: they never throw ConcurrentModificationException, and they may or may not show changes made after the iterator was created.

Atomic compound operations

Each single call (get, put) is atomic, but two calls together are not. This is the classic check-then-act race:

Wrong: not atomic, two threads can both see null

Integer old = map.get(word);
if (old == null) {
    map.put(word, 1);
} else {
    map.put(word, old + 1);    // lost updates
}

Right: one atomic call

map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);
MethodAtomic action
putIfAbsent(k, v)Put only if the key is missing; returns the previous value or null
computeIfAbsent(k, fn)If missing, compute the value with fn and store it (the multi-value map idiom)
computeIfPresent(k, fn)Recompute only if present
compute(k, fn)Recompute whether present or not; returning null removes the entry
merge(k, v, fn)If missing store v; otherwise store fn(old, v)
replace(k, old, new)Compare-and-replace
 
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class HitCounter {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Map<String, Integer> safe = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        Map<String, Integer> unsafe = new HashMap<>();

        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
            for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) {
                pool.execute(() -> {
                    for (int i = 0; i < 50_000; i++) {
                        safe.merge("/home", 1, Integer::sum);        // atomic
                        unsafe.merge("/home", 1, Integer::sum);      // data race!
                    }
                });
            }
        }
        System.out.println("ConcurrentHashMap: " + safe.get("/home"));
        System.out.println("HashMap          : " + unsafe.get("/home"));
    }
}
ConcurrentHashMap: 200000
HashMap          : 143871

The HashMap result changes on every run and is usually below 200,000 (it can even throw an exception, or hang in some versions). The ConcurrentHashMap result is always exact.

Rule: keep the function passed to compute and merge short

The function runs while a bin is locked. It must be quick, must not block, and must not modify the same map (that can deadlock or throw IllegalStateException: Recursive update).

synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap

PointCollections.synchronizedMapConcurrentHashMap
LockingOne lock for the whole mapCAS plus per-bin locks; reads lock-free
ConcurrencyOne thread at a timeMany threads at once
Null keys/valuesAllowed (if the wrapped map allows)Not allowed
IterationMust lock the map yourself; otherwise ConcurrentModificationExceptionWeakly consistent; safe without locking
Atomic compound opsNeed external synchronizedmerge, compute, putIfAbsent built in
Use whenRarely; low traffic, need null or sorted wrappingThe default choice

Also avoid the legacy Hashtable (a single lock on every method). For a sorted concurrent map use ConcurrentSkipListMap (and ConcurrentSkipListSet). For a concurrent set backed by a hash map: ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().

CopyOnWriteArrayList

Every write (add, set, remove) makes a fresh copy of the internal array. Readers use the old array, with no locks, and an iterator works on a snapshot: it never throws ConcurrentModificationException and never sees later changes.

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;

public class Listeners {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("email", "sms"));

        for (String l : listeners) {           // iterating a snapshot
            System.out.println("notify " + l);
            if (l.equals("email")) {
                listeners.add("push");         // fine: no exception
            }
        }
        System.out.println(listeners);
    }
}
notify email
notify sms
[email, sms, push]

Good for: lists that are read very often and changed rarely, such as event listeners or a list of feature flags. Bad for: large lists with frequent writes, since each write copies everything (O(n)). With an ordinary ArrayList the same loop would throw ConcurrentModificationException. A set version exists: CopyOnWriteArraySet.

BlockingQueue implementations

A BlockingQueue makes put wait when full and take wait when empty, so producers and consumers need no wait/notify. It extends Queue with timed versions (offer(e, time, unit), poll(time, unit)).

ClassCapacityNotes
ArrayBlockingQueueFixed at creationFIFO, one lock; optional fairness. Predictable memory
LinkedBlockingQueueOptional bound; default Integer.MAX_VALUEFIFO, two locks (put and take) for higher throughput. Unbounded by default, so give it a limit
PriorityBlockingQueueUnboundedOrdered by Comparable or a Comparator, not FIFO; put never blocks
SynchronousQueueZeroEach put waits for a take; a direct hand-off (used by newCachedThreadPool)
DelayQueueUnboundedElements become available after a delay (scheduling, expiry)

For the non-blocking world: ConcurrentLinkedQueue and ConcurrentLinkedDeque are unbounded, lock-free (CAS-based) queues. poll() returns null when empty; there is no waiting. Use them when you never want to block. Note that their size() walks the whole queue, so it is O(n).

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NullPointerException — ConcurrentHashMap.put(k, null) or a null key; also null elements in blocking queues.
  • IllegalStateException: Queue full — add() on a full bounded queue (offer returns false, put blocks).
  • UnsupportedOperationException — remove() on an iterator of CopyOnWriteArrayList, which works on a snapshot.
  • Thread-safe collections do not make your compound logic safe: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) is still a race. Use putIfAbsent.
  • Values stored in the map are not protected: a ConcurrentHashMap<String, List<String>> with an ArrayList value still needs the inner list to be thread-safe.

Real projects

In-memory caches (computeIfAbsent to load once per key), counters and rate-limit buckets per user, registries of active sessions or WebSocket connections, and work queues between an HTTP thread and background workers. Careful: computeIfAbsent with a slow loader holds the bin lock; for real caching use Caffeine.

Interview: "How does ConcurrentHashMap work? synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap?"

  • Java 8+: CAS for empty bins, synchronized on the first node of a bin otherwise; lock-free reads; no nulls; weakly consistent iterators.
  • Atomic merge, compute, putIfAbsent prevent check-then-act races.
  • synchronizedMap uses one global lock and needs manual locking for iteration and compound actions.
  • Copy-on-write is for read-mostly lists; blocking queues for producer-consumer.

Synchronizers: CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier and Semaphore

Synchronizers coordinate threads without you writing wait/notify: a CountDownLatch waits for a number of events once, a CyclicBarrier makes a group of threads wait for each other repeatedly, and a Semaphore limits how many threads use a resource at once.

CountDownLatch: wait until N things are done

A latch starts with a count. Worker threads call countDown() when they finish; another thread calls await() and blocks until the count reaches zero.
