It is one-shot: once at zero it stays open and cannot be reset. Typical use: wait for services to start, or start many threads at the same instant (a "starting gun" with count 1).

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class StartupCheck {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(3);

        for (String svc : new String[] {"database", "cache", "queue"}) {
            Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
                try {
                    Thread.sleep(200);                 // pretend to start up
                    System.out.println(svc + " started");
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                } finally {
                    ready.countDown();                 // always count down
                }
            });
        }

        ready.await();                                 // main waits here
        System.out.println("All services up, accepting traffic");
    }
}
cache started
database started
queue started
All services up, accepting traffic

Put countDown() in a finally. If a worker fails and never counts down, await() waits forever; the overload await(timeout, unit) returns false on timeout and is safer.

CyclicBarrier: wait for each other, again and again

A barrier is created for N parties. Each thread calls await(); the first N-1 block, and when the Nth arrives they all continue together. Then the barrier resets and can be used again, which makes it suit phased algorithms ("everyone finish step 1 before anyone starts step 2"). An optional barrier action runs once per round, in the last thread to arrive.

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class BarrierDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3,
                () -> System.out.println("-- all three finished this round --"));

        for (int w = 1; w <= 3; w++) {
            int id = w;
            Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
                try {
                    for (int round = 1; round <= 2; round++) {
                        System.out.println("worker " + id + " done round " + round);
                        barrier.await();               // wait for the others
                    }
                } catch (InterruptedException | BrokenBarrierException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                }
            });
        }
    }
}
worker 2 done round 1
worker 1 done round 1
worker 3 done round 1
-- all three finished this round --
worker 3 done round 2
worker 1 done round 2
worker 2 done round 2
-- all three finished this round --

Semaphore: limit concurrent access

A semaphore holds a number of permits. acquire() takes one (blocking when none are left); release() gives one back. With N permits at most N threads are inside the protected section. With 1 permit it works like a lock (but without an owner, so any thread can release). Use cases: limit calls to a rate-limited partner API, cap the number of open DB-heavy jobs, or limit concurrency when using virtual threads.

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class RateLimit {
    static final Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(3);       // max 3 calls at once
    static final AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger();

    static void callPartnerApi(int id) throws InterruptedException {
        permits.acquire();
        try {
            int now = inside.incrementAndGet();
            System.out.println("request " + id + " running, concurrent=" + now);
            Thread.sleep(300);                                // the slow call
        } finally {
            inside.decrementAndGet();
            permits.release();                                // always release
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) {
            for (int i = 1; i <= 8; i++) {
                int id = i;
                pool.execute(() -> {
                    try { callPartnerApi(id); }
                    catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
                });
            }
        }
    }
}
request 1 running, concurrent=1
request 2 running, concurrent=2
request 3 running, concurrent=3
request 4 running, concurrent=3
request 5 running, concurrent=3
request 6 running, concurrent=3
request 7 running, concurrent=3
request 8 running, concurrent=2

Eight threads exist but never more than three are in the section at once. Other useful methods: tryAcquire() (do not wait; return false), tryAcquire(time, unit), availablePermits() and the fair constructor new Semaphore(3, true) (longest waiter first).

Which one?

PointCountDownLatchCyclicBarrierSemaphore
PurposeWait for N eventsN threads meet at a pointLimit concurrent users of a resource
ReusableNoYesYes
Who waitsThe waiters; the counters do not waitAll parties waitThreads without a permit
Counting down byAny thread, any number of timesEach party once per roundAcquire and release

Beyond these: Phaser (a flexible multi-phase barrier) and Exchanger (two threads swap objects) exist but are rare.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • BrokenBarrierException — another party timed out, was interrupted or the barrier was reset; every waiting thread gets the exception.
  • TimeoutException — timed CyclicBarrier.await ran out of time.
  • IllegalArgumentException — negative count for a latch, or fewer than 1 party for a barrier.
  • A permit leak: acquire() without a release() in finally slowly drains the semaphore until everything blocks.
  • Calling release() more often than acquire() increases the permits beyond the initial value; a Semaphore does not check the owner.

Mistake: latch count that never reaches zero

If three workers must count down but one throws before reaching countDown(), the waiting thread hangs forever. Count down in finally, and prefer await(timeout, unit) in production.

How they work, and why not wait/notify

All three keep a small counter of "permits" or "arrivals" and park threads that must wait. CountDownLatch and Semaphore are built on AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS), the same queue-and-park machinery behind ReentrantLock; CyclicBarrier uses a ReentrantLock and a condition. You get correct blocking, fairness options, timeouts and interruption for free. Writing the same with wait() and notifyAll() is possible (see locks and waiting) but easy to get wrong: lost wake-ups, missing loops, wrong lock. Use the ready-made class whenever one fits.

Method reference

ClassKey methodsNotes
CountDownLatch(n)countDown(), await(), await(t, unit), getCount()Extra countDown() calls at zero do nothing
CyclicBarrier(n, action)await(), await(t, unit), getParties(), getNumberWaiting(), reset(), isBroken()await() returns the arrival index (n-1 for the first, 0 for the last)
Semaphore(permits, fair)acquire(), acquire(n), tryAcquire(), release(), availablePermits()No owner: any thread may release

Two latches in one test harness

Two latches together are a standard pattern for measuring or testing concurrent code: a start gate (count 1) so that all workers begin together, and a done gate (count N) so that the caller knows when all have finished.

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class StartGate {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        int workers = 4;
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(workers);
        AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();

        for (int i = 0; i < workers; i++) {
            Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> {
                try {
                    start.await();                       // all workers wait here
                    for (int j = 0; j < 1000; j++) counter.incrementAndGet();
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                } finally {
                    done.countDown();
                }
            });
        }
        start.countDown();                               // fire the starting gun
        done.await();                                    // wait for everybody
        System.out.println("Total = " + counter.get());
    }
}
Total = 4000

Semaphore as a mutex, and the permit-leak trap

With one permit a semaphore allows a single thread at a time, but unlike synchronized or ReentrantLock it is not reentrant (a thread that acquires twice blocks itself) and has no owner. That can be useful (acquire in one thread, release in another, as in a hand-off) and dangerous. Placing acquire() inside the try block creates a subtle bug:

Wrong: release runs even when acquire never succeeded

try {
    permits.acquire();            // interrupted here → no permit taken
    doWork();
} finally {
    permits.release();            // still releases: permits grow past the limit
}

Right: acquire before the try

permits.acquire();
try {
    doWork();
} finally {
    permits.release();
}

For "do not wait if the resource is busy" use tryAcquire(): it returns false at once, and you can return a "429 Too Many Requests" or skip the job.

Deadlock with a barrier and a small thread pool

A CyclicBarrier(4) needs four threads waiting at the same time. If you run the four parties on a fixed pool of only two threads, the first two block at the barrier and the other two tasks never start. Nothing fails; the program just hangs. Make the pool at least as large as the number of parties, or use plain threads. The same trap exists for a latch when the task that must count down is queued behind tasks that are blocked in await().

Phaser and Exchanger in one paragraph

Phaser is a barrier whose number of parties can change while it runs (register, arriveAndDeregister) and that has numbered phases. It suits tasks that join and leave a multi-step process. Exchanger lets exactly two threads swap objects at a meeting point, for example a producer handing a full buffer to a consumer and taking back an empty one. Both are rare in application code; know the names and the idea.

Rules

  • A latch cannot be reset. For a repeating event use CyclicBarrier or a new latch each round.
  • Release a semaphore in finally, and acquire before the try.
  • The number of parties in a barrier must match the number of threads that will call await() each round.
  • Do not hold a lock (synchronized) while waiting on a synchronizer unless you are sure the others can still make progress; it is a common way to build a deadlock.

Conventions

  • Use the timed await or tryAcquire forms in production and log what happened on timeout.
  • Restore the interrupt flag when you catch InterruptedException.
  • For ordinary "run these tasks and wait for all", prefer invokeAll or CompletableFuture.allOf (see Callable and Future); use a latch when the events come from different places.
  • Use a semaphore to cap concurrency; use a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue to cap threads. They solve different problems.

In real projects

Latches appear in integration tests (wait until the Kafka consumer has processed the message) and in startup code. Semaphores guard connections to a partner API with a "10 calls at a time" contract, and bound the number of concurrent downloads in a virtual-thread application, where thread count no longer limits you. Barriers are the least common: parallel simulations and phased batch processing.

Interview: "CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier", "What is a Semaphore?"

  • Latch: one-shot, waiting for events; barrier: reusable meeting point for the same threads.
  • Semaphore: counted permits; limit concurrent access; acquire / release in finally.
  • Give a real example for each: startup gate, phased computation, API rate limit.

Deadlock, livelock and starvation

A deadlock happens when threads wait for each other's locks forever; you prevent it by always taking locks in the same order, using timeouts, or holding fewer locks, and you find it with a thread dump.

What a deadlock is

Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Neither can continue, and nothing will release the locks, so the program hangs (while using no CPU). The classic business example is a bank transfer: transferring from account X to Y locks X then Y, while a simultaneous transfer from Y to X locks Y then X.

A minimal deadlock program

public class DeadlockDemo {
    static final Object lockA = new Object();
    static final Object lockB = new Object();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
            synchronized (lockA) {
                System.out.println("T1 holds A");
                pause();                                   // let T2 grab B
                synchronized (lockB) {
                    System.out.println("T1 holds A and B");
                }
            }
        }, "T1");

        Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
            synchronized (lockB) {
                System.out.println("T2 holds B");
                pause();
                synchronized (lockA) {
                    System.out.println("T2 holds B and A");
                }
            }
        }, "T2");

        t1.start();
        t2.start();
    }

    static void pause() {
        try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { }
    }
}
T1 holds A
T2 holds B

Neither "holds A and B" line is ever printed. The sleep makes the problem happen every time; in real code the timing is rare, which is why deadlocks pass testing and appear in production under load.

The four Coffman conditions

A deadlock needs all four of these at once. Remove any one and it cannot happen.

Mutual exclusion
A resource can be held by only one thread at a time (a lock).
Hold and wait
A thread keeps what it has while waiting for more.
No preemption
A lock cannot be taken away from its holder; only the holder releases it.
Circular wait
A cycle exists: A waits for B, B waits for ... waits for A.

Prevention

  1. Lock ordering (breaks circular wait): every thread takes locks in the same global order. For transfers, lock the account with the smaller id first.
  2. tryLock with timeout (breaks hold and wait / no preemption): use ReentrantLock.tryLock(time, unit); if you cannot get the second lock, release the first, wait a random short time and retry.
  3. Fewer locks, smaller critical sections: one lock for related data, no calls to unknown code ("alien methods", listeners, callbacks) while holding a lock.
  4. Prefer higher-level tools: concurrent collections, atomics and immutable objects need no locks at all.
public class Transfer {
    static class Account {
        final long id;
        long balance;
        Account(long id, long balance) { this.id = id; this.balance = balance; }
    }

    static void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) {
        // Always lock the account with the lower id first: same order for every thread
        Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to;
        Account second = from.id < to.id ? to : from;

        synchronized (first) {
            synchronized (second) {
                if (from.balance < amount) {
                    throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient balance");
                }
                from.balance -= amount;
                to.balance += amount;
            }
        }
    }
}

Now transfer(x, y, 100) and transfer(y, x, 50) both lock the same account first, so a cycle is impossible. And a version with tryLock:

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

boolean transferWithTimeout(ReentrantLock a, ReentrantLock b) throws InterruptedException {
    if (a.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
        try {
            if (b.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                try {
                    // ... move the money ...
                    return true;
                } finally {
                    b.unlock();
                }
            }
        } finally {
            a.unlock();
        }
    }
    return false;       // caller retries later or reports failure
}

Detecting a deadlock with a thread dump

A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread's state and stack. Find your process id with jps (or the task manager), then:

$ jps
12840 DeadlockDemo
$ jstack 12840
$ jcmd 12840 Thread.print      # same result

On Linux you can also send Ctrl+\ (SIGQUIT) to a program started in the terminal. In IntelliJ, use the "Get Thread Dump" camera button while debugging. The JVM analyses the lock graph and prints a section like this (shortened):

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"T1":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x... (object 0x..., a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "T2"
"T2":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x... (object 0x..., a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "T1"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
"T1":
        at DeadlockDemo.lambda$main$0(DeadlockDemo.java:13)
        - waiting to lock <0x...> (a java.lang.Object)
        - locked <0x...> (a java.lang.Object)

Read the stack lines to see which code line each thread is stuck on. Your own code can also check: ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() returns the ids of deadlocked threads (or null). Monitoring tools use this. Thread dumps help for other hangs too: a thread state BLOCKED or WAITING everywhere points to a lock or pool problem.

Livelock and starvation

  • Livelock: threads are not blocked; they keep reacting to each other and make no progress, like two people in a corridor who both step aside in the same direction again and again. CPU is busy but nothing is done. A typical cause is a retry loop where both threads back off and retry at the same time. Fix: add a random delay (jitter) or a clear priority rule.
  • Starvation: a thread never gets the resource because others keep winning. Examples: low-priority threads that never get CPU time, an unfair lock where one thread always loses, or one long task that fills a small thread pool. Fix: fair locks (new ReentrantLock(true), with some throughput cost), separate pools, shorter critical sections.
ProblemThreads are...CPU useTypical fix
DeadlockBlocked forever, in a cycleNoneLock ordering, timeouts
LivelockRunning but uselessHighRandom back-off
StarvationWaiting too long, others progressNormalFairness, bounded work

Rules

  • If you need more than one lock, define and document the order in which they are taken.
  • Never call code you do not control (callbacks, overridable methods, other services) while holding a lock.
  • Always release locks in finally.

Edge cases

  • Deadlocks are not only about synchronized. They also happen with database row locks (two transactions updating the same two rows in opposite order; the database aborts one with a deadlock error), with a thread pool whose tasks wait for other tasks of the same pool, and with join() cycles.
  • synchronized blocks cannot be interrupted while waiting for the lock; ReentrantLock.lockInterruptibly() can.
  • A deadlock with synchronized leaves the JVM running; only restarting (or killing a thread through a different design) recovers.

Interview: "What is a deadlock? How do you prevent and detect it?"

  • Define it with a two-lock example and name the four Coffman conditions.
  • Prevent: consistent lock order, tryLock with timeout, fewer and smaller locks.
  • Detect: jstack/jcmd Thread.print, IntelliJ dump, ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads().
  • Differentiate livelock (busy but no progress) and starvation (never gets a turn).

ThreadLocal: per-thread data and its leaks

A ThreadLocal gives every thread its own private copy of a variable, which is handy for per-request context, but in thread pools the copy outlives the task, so you must remove it or you leak data between requests.

What it is

Normally a field is shared by all threads. A ThreadLocal<T> is a variable where each thread that calls get() or set() sees its own value, stored inside the Thread object itself. No locks are needed because the data is never shared; this is called thread confinement.

public class ThreadLocalDemo {
    // each thread starts with its own value from the supplier
    private static final ThreadLocal<Integer> counter = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> 0);

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Runnable task = () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
                counter.set(counter.get() + 1);
            }
            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " counter=" + counter.get());
        };
        Thread a = new Thread(task, "worker-A");
        Thread b = new Thread(task, "worker-B");
        a.start(); b.start();
        a.join(); b.join();
        System.out.println("main counter=" + counter.get());
    }
}
worker-A counter=3
worker-B counter=3
main counter=0

Each thread counted to 3 on its own copy, and main still has 0. No race condition is possible because nothing is shared.

MethodPurpose
ThreadLocal.withInitial(supplier)Create with a per-thread default value
get()Value for the current thread (initial value if unset)
set(value)Set the current thread's value
remove()Delete the current thread's value; the next get() gives the initial value again

Common uses

  • Per-request context in a web server that uses one thread per request: the current user, a request id for logging (SLF4J's MDC is a ThreadLocal map), the tenant id. Spring's SecurityContextHolder, RequestContextHolder and transaction synchronization work this way, so deep service code can find "the current user" without passing it through every method.
  • Non-thread-safe helper objects that are costly to create, such as the old SimpleDateFormat or a MessageDigest. Each thread gets its own copy. (For dates, simply use the immutable DateTimeFormatter instead.)
  • Per-thread random generators or buffers to avoid contention (the JDK's ThreadLocalRandom is built on this idea).

The leak in thread pools

Threads in a pool are reused. A ThreadLocal value stays attached to the thread until it is removed or the thread dies. So when task 1 sets a value and finishes without cleaning up, task 2 running on the same thread sees task 1's data. That is a bug and a security problem (user B served with user A's identity).

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class LeakDemo {
    static final ThreadLocal<String> currentUser = new ThreadLocal<>();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()) {   // 1 thread reused
            pool.submit(() -> currentUser.set("asha")).get();               // request 1 forgets remove()
            pool.submit(() -> System.out.println(
                    "request 2 sees user = " + currentUser.get())).get();
        }
    }
}
request 2 sees user = asha

Request 2 never set a user, yet it sees "asha". The cure is always to clean up in finally:

static void handleRequest(String user, Runnable work) {
    currentUser.set(user);
    try {
        work.run();
    } finally {
        currentUser.remove();      // always, even when work throws
    }
}

A second form of leak is memory. The values are strongly referenced from the thread, and a pool thread lives as long as the application. A large object (a big buffer, a user session graph) left in a ThreadLocal stays in memory. In application servers where the web app can be redeployed, a ThreadLocal holding an object of the app's classes can keep the whole old class loader alive ("ClassLoader leak", the cause of OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace after several redeploys). Frameworks like Spring clean their own ThreadLocals; the leaks usually come from your own code.

Related: InheritableThreadLocal, virtual threads and scoped values

  • InheritableThreadLocal copies the parent thread's value to a new child thread at creation. It does not help with pools, because the pool threads were created earlier; frameworks use task decorators to copy context into tasks.
  • Virtual threads support ThreadLocal, but because you may create millions of virtual threads, per-thread caches become expensive. Do not put heavy objects in them.
  • Scoped values (ScopedValue) are a modern, safer alternative: immutable data bound for the duration of a block of code and automatically gone afterwards. They were a preview API in Java 21 to 24 and became a final feature in Java 25.

Rules

  • Declare ThreadLocal as private static final.
  • Call remove() in finally whenever a thread might be reused (pools, servlet containers).
  • Store small, preferably immutable values; never large caches.

Exceptions and edge cases

  • NullPointerException — get() returns null when no initial value was set, and unboxing it (int x = tl.get()) fails.
  • ThreadLocal values do not follow work onto another thread: CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, @Async and parallel streams run on different threads, so the "current user" is missing there unless you pass it explicitly.
  • A ThreadLocal is hidden global state: it makes code harder to test and to reason about. Prefer plain method parameters when the call chain is short.

Interview: "What is ThreadLocal? What problems can it cause?"

  • Per-thread variable; no locking needed; uses: request context, MDC, non-thread-safe helpers.
  • In pools, values survive between tasks: stale or leaked data and memory leaks; fix with remove() in finally.
  • Does not propagate to async tasks; scoped values (final in Java 25) are the modern alternative.

Virtual threads (Java 21)

Virtual threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM that let you write simple blocking code and still handle hundreds of thousands of concurrent tasks, because a virtual thread that waits on I/O frees its carrier platform thread.

The problem they solve

The classic server model is thread-per-request: one thread handles one request from start to finish. It is easy to write and debug. The trouble: a platform thread maps one-to-one to an operating-system thread and costs memory (typically about 1 MB of stack is reserved) and scheduling time, so a machine can hold only a few thousand. Most of the time a request thread is not computing; it waits for the database or another service. A server with 200 threads and 200 ms of waiting per request tops out at about 1,000 requests per second, while the CPU is almost idle.

Developers escaped this with asynchronous, callback-based code (CompletableFuture, reactive libraries), which is efficient but harder to read, debug and profile. Virtual threads (Project Loom, final in Java 21) keep the simple style and remove the thread limit.

Platform vs virtual threads

PointPlatform threadVirtual thread
Managed byOperating systemJVM
Mapping1 Java thread = 1 OS threadMany virtual threads share a few OS threads
Stack memoryLarge, reserved up frontSmall, stored on the heap, grows as needed
Cost to createHigh: pool themVery low: create one per task
Practical limitThousandsMillions
Blocking I/OBlocks the OS threadUnmounts; the OS thread does other work
Daemon / priorityConfigurableAlways daemon; priority fixed
Best forCPU-heavy work, long-lived workersMany tasks that mostly wait on I/O

How they work

The JVM runs virtual threads on a small pool of platform threads called carrier threads (a ForkJoinPool with, by default, as many carriers as CPU cores). When a virtual thread runs, it is mounted on a carrier. When it hits a blocking operation that the JDK has made virtual-thread-aware (socket I/O, Thread.sleep, locks and queues from java.util.concurrent), the JVM saves its stack to the heap and unmounts it. The carrier is now free to run another virtual thread. When the I/O completes, the virtual thread is scheduled again, possibly on a different carrier.

Creating virtual threads

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

public class VirtualDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // 1. Builder API
        Thread t1 = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-1").start(
                () -> System.out.println("virtual? " + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()));
        t1.join();

        // 2. Shortcut
        Thread t2 = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> System.out.println("hello from t2"));
        t2.join();

        // 3. Executor: a NEW virtual thread for every task (not a pool)
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        try (ExecutorService exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            IntStream.range(0, 10_000).forEach(i -> exec.submit(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1));      // 10,000 tasks each waiting 1 s
                return i;
            }));
        }   // close() waits for all tasks
        System.out.println("10,000 tasks took ~"
                + (System.currentTimeMillis() - start) / 1000.0 + " s");
    }
}
virtual? true
hello from t2
10,000 tasks took ~1.4 s

Ten thousand tasks that each wait one second finish in about one second in total, on a handful of carrier threads. With a fixed pool of 200 platform threads the same job would need about 50 seconds. The code is plain blocking code.

When they help and when they do not

  • Help: high-concurrency servers whose requests mostly wait: REST APIs calling databases and other services, batch jobs that fetch thousands of URLs, message consumers doing I/O.
  • Do not help: CPU-bound work (image processing, encryption, big computations). Throughput is limited by the number of cores no matter how many threads you have. Use a pool sized to the cores.
  • They improve throughput under load, not the speed of one request.

Rules and good habits

  1. Do not pool virtual threads. They are cheap; pooling defeats the purpose. Create one per task.
  2. Limit concurrency with a Semaphore, not with pool size, when a downstream resource has limits (for example a database that allows 20 connections, or a partner API).
  3. Keep using ReentrantLock or synchronized for short critical sections, but avoid long blocking I/O inside them.
  4. Avoid heavy ThreadLocal data (see ThreadLocal); a million threads times a big cache is a lot of memory.
  5. Do not tune with thread priorities or rely on thread-count assumptions.

Pinning

A virtual thread is pinned when it cannot unmount while blocked: it stays stuck to its carrier thread and blocks it. Before Java 24 this happened when the thread blocked inside a synchronized block or method, and it still happens when blocked inside native code or a foreign function call. A few pinned threads are harmless; many pinned threads can starve the small carrier pool. Java 24 (JEP 491) removed the synchronized case, so in Java 24 and later (including 25) blocking inside synchronized no longer pins the carrier in most cases. On Java 21 you can switch to ReentrantLock in hot code that blocks, and use the JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned to find pinning.

Spring Boot

With Spring Boot 3.2 and later (so also 4.x) on Java 21+, one property switches request handling to virtual threads:

spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true

Embedded Tomcat or Jetty then runs each request on a virtual thread, and Boot's task execution and scheduling beans also use virtual threads. Your controllers and JDBC code stay unchanged. Details are in Spring Boot · Module 6. Remember that the database connection pool (HikariCP, default 10 connections) remains the next bottleneck: ten thousand virtual threads will still wait for ten connections.

Versions and structured concurrency

Virtual threads were a preview in Java 19 and 20 and are final in Java 21. Structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope), which treats a group of subtasks as one unit of work with clean cancellation, was still a preview API in Java 25, so treat it as "coming" and do not use it in production code yet. Observability: thread dumps from jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json file include virtual threads; the classic jstack output does not list them all.

Edge cases

  • IllegalArgumentException — setting a priority on a virtual thread other than normal is ignored; setting it to be non-daemon with setDaemon(false) throws.
  • Code that assumes Thread.currentThread().getName() is unique or non-empty: virtual threads have an empty name unless you set one.
  • Unlimited creation can overwhelm the thing behind them (database, other APIs). Protect it with a semaphore or a bulkhead.

Mistake: using virtual threads for CPU-bound loops

A million virtual threads each crunching numbers will queue on the few carriers and give no speed-up. Pick a fixed pool of about availableProcessors() threads (or a parallel stream) for computation.

Interview: "What are virtual threads and when would you use them?"

  • JVM-managed lightweight threads, mounted on carrier threads, unmounted on blocking I/O; final in Java 21.
  • Thread-per-request code scales to very many concurrent waits; not helpful for CPU-bound tasks.
  • Do not pool them; limit with a semaphore; know pinning (fixed for synchronized in Java 24).
  • Spring Boot: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true.

Thread-safety strategies: a decision summary

Make code thread-safe in this order of preference: share nothing, share only immutable data, use concurrent collections and atomics, and only then use locks.

What thread-safe means

A class is thread-safe if it behaves correctly when used by many threads at once, with no extra synchronization by the callers. The dangerous situation always has three ingredients: shared data, mutable data and unsynchronized access. Remove any one and the problem disappears. That gives the five strategies below.

The strategies

  1. Do not share (confinement). Keep data in local variables (each thread has its own stack), in method parameters, or in a ThreadLocal. Hand an object to exactly one thread at a time (for example through a BlockingQueue). Local variables are always safe.
  2. Do not mutate (immutability). Immutable objects can be shared freely: String, Integer, LocalDate, records with immutable components, List.of(...). To change, create a new object. Make fields private final, no setters, copy mutable inputs, and do not leak this from constructors.
  3. Use thread-safe building blocks. ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, BlockingQueue, and atomic classes (AtomicInteger, LongAdder, AtomicReference) give atomic operations without you writing locks.
  4. Synchronize access. synchronized or ReentrantLock around every access to the shared state (reads too), using the same lock; keep the critical section small; use volatile only for a simple flag or safe publication.
  5. Use higher-level coordination. Executors, CompletableFuture, latches, semaphores and virtual threads so that tasks communicate by passing results instead of sharing variables.

Decision table

SituationChooseWhy
Data is only needed inside one methodLocal variablesConfined to the thread's stack
Configuration or reference data, read often, never changedImmutable object / record, safely published (final field or volatile reference)No synchronization needed
One counter or flag updated by many threadsAtomicInteger, LongAdder (very high contention), volatile boolean for a stop flagLock-free; atomic single operation
Shared map with counts or cachesConcurrentHashMap with merge / computeIfAbsentAtomic compound operations
List read constantly, changed rarelyCopyOnWriteArrayListLock-free reads and snapshot iteration
Hand work from producers to consumersBlockingQueueBuilt-in waiting and back-pressure
Several fields must change together (balance and history)synchronized / ReentrantLock on one lockInvariants that span variables need one lock
Read-heavy shared object, occasional writesReadWriteLock or StampedLock (after measuring)Many readers at once
Per-request user or trace idThreadLocal with remove() (or ScopedValue in Java 25)Confinement; clean up in pools
Many blocking I/O tasksVirtual threads plus a semaphore for limitsSimple code, high concurrency

Real-world application: Spring beans

Spring creates singleton beans (controllers, services, repositories) by default, and one instance serves all request threads. So a service must be stateless: no mutable instance fields that hold per-request data. This code is a classic bug:

Wrong: shared mutable state in a singleton

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private Order currentOrder;          // shared by all requests!
    public void process(Order o) {
        this.currentOrder = o;
        validate();
        save(currentOrder);              // may save another user's order
    }
}

Right: pass data through parameters

@Service
public class OrderService {
    public void process(Order o) {
        validate(o);
        save(o);                         // o is local to this call
    }
}

Other thread-safety hot spots in Spring apps: caches held in plain HashMap fields, SimpleDateFormat as a field, counters as int fields, lazy initialization of fields, and mutable static variables. Each has a fix from the table above.

Checking your class

  • List all shared mutable fields. For each, name the one thing that protects it: a lock, an atomic, a concurrent type or immutability.
  • Look for check-then-act (if (!map.containsKey), if (x == null) x = ...) and read-modify-write (count++) sequences. They need to be one atomic step.
  • Do not expose internal mutable collections; return copies or unmodifiable views.
  • Document thread-safety in the class comment (immutable, thread-safe, not thread-safe, guarded by lock X).

Rules

  • Every access to shared mutable data, reads and writes, needs the same protection.
  • Thread-safe parts do not make a thread-safe whole: two atomic operations in a row are not atomic together.
  • Prefer the simplest tool that works: immutability before atomics, atomics before locks.

Conventions

  • Make classes immutable by default; use records for data.
  • Prefer java.util.concurrent over hand-written wait/notify.
  • Test concurrency with many threads and many repetitions, and use tools such as thread dumps and, in bigger projects, stress-testing libraries. A passing single-thread test proves nothing.

Interview: "How do you make a class thread-safe?"

  • Say the three ingredients (shared, mutable, unsynchronized) and the five ways to remove one: confinement, immutability, concurrent collections/atomics, locks, higher-level coordination.
  • Give the Spring example: singleton services must be stateless.
  • Mention check-then-act and read-modify-write as the typical bugs.

Interview questions — Multithreading and concurrency

Process vs thread? What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?

A process is a running program with its own memory space; a thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and threads of one process share its heap but each has its own stack. Threads are cheaper to create and communicate through shared memory, which also makes them risky. Concurrency means managing many tasks that overlap in time (possibly on one core, by switching); parallelism means actually running tasks at the same instant on several cores.

start() vs run()? Can you start a thread twice?

start() asks the JVM to create a new thread, which then calls run(). Calling run() directly just executes the method in the current thread like any normal call, so no concurrency happens. Calling start() a second time throws IllegalThreadStateException, because a thread that has been started (even if finished) cannot be restarted.

Name the thread states and what moves a thread between them.

NEW (created, not started), RUNNABLE (running or ready to run), BLOCKED (waiting to enter a synchronized block), WAITING (wait(), join(), LockSupport.park() with no timeout), TIMED_WAITING (sleep, wait(ms), join(ms)) and TERMINATED (finished). start() moves NEW to RUNNABLE; lock contention gives BLOCKED; notify, a timeout or an interrupt brings a thread back.

Why is count++ not thread-safe?

It is three steps: read the value, add one, write it back. Two threads can both read 5, both compute 6 and both write 6, so one increment is lost. This is a read-modify-write race. Fix with synchronized, AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() (uses CAS) or LongAdder for heavy contention. volatile does not help because it gives visibility but not atomicity.

synchronized vs volatile?

synchronized gives mutual exclusion (one thread in the block at a time, on the same lock) plus visibility: changes made before leaving the block are seen by the next thread that enters. volatile gives only visibility and ordering for one variable: a write is seen by later reads in other threads. Use volatile for simple flags (volatile boolean running) and safe publication; use synchronized or atomics when the action is a compound one like increment.

Which object does a synchronized method lock?

An instance method locks this; a static synchronized method locks the Class object (MyClass.class). A synchronized block locks the object you name. Threads using different locks do not block each other, so instance and static synchronized methods do not exclude one another. The lock is reentrant: a thread that already holds it can enter another synchronized block on the same object.

Explain ThreadPoolExecutor and what happens when the queue is full.

Parameters: core size, maximum size, keep-alive time, work queue, thread factory and rejection handler. A new task starts a core thread if fewer than core are running; otherwise it goes into the queue; if the queue is full a thread up to the maximum is created; if that is also full the rejection policy runs (default AbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException). With an unbounded queue the maximum is never used and memory can run out.

Runnable vs Callable; execute vs submit; what does Future.get() throw?

Callable returns a value and may throw checked exceptions. execute takes a Runnable and returns nothing, and an uncaught exception goes to the thread's handler. submit returns a Future and captures any exception inside it. get() throws ExecutionException (the real error is the cause), InterruptedException, and TimeoutException in the timed version, or CancellationException if cancelled.

thenApply vs thenCompose in CompletableFuture. How do you run three calls in parallel?

thenApply maps the result with a normal function (like map); thenCompose is for a function that itself returns a CompletableFuture (like flatMap), avoiding a nested future. For three parallel calls, start each with supplyAsync(..., executor), combine with CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c), then read each with join(). Use your own executor for blocking calls, because the default common pool is small.

How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety? How does it differ from synchronizedMap?

In Java 8 and later it uses CAS to insert into an empty bin and a synchronized lock on the first node of a bin otherwise, so threads that touch different bins run in parallel; reads take no lock. It forbids null keys and values and has weakly consistent iterators. Methods such as merge and computeIfAbsent are atomic. Collections.synchronizedMap guards every method with one lock, and iteration needs manual locking.

What is a deadlock? Give an example and how to prevent it.

Thread 1 holds lock A and waits for B; thread 2 holds B and waits for A; both wait forever. It needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait (the four Coffman conditions). Prevent by taking locks in a fixed global order, using tryLock with a timeout, holding fewer locks and not calling foreign code under a lock. Detect with jstack or jcmd <pid> Thread.print, which prints "Found one Java-level deadlock".

CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Semaphore?

A latch lets threads wait until a count of events reaches zero and cannot be reset. A barrier makes a fixed group of threads wait for each other at a point and then resets for the next round. A semaphore holds permits and limits how many threads can use a resource at once, for example 3 concurrent calls to a partner API.

What is ThreadLocal and what goes wrong with thread pools?

It stores a separate value for each thread, used for request context such as the logged-in user or a trace id. Pool threads are reused, so a value set by one task stays visible to the next task on that thread unless you call remove(). That leaks data between requests and keeps objects alive. Always remove in finally. Values also do not carry over to tasks run on other threads.

What are virtual threads and how do they differ from platform threads?

Virtual threads (final in Java 21) are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM onto a few carrier platform threads. When they block on I/O they unmount, so the carrier serves other virtual threads. Creating a million of them is feasible, so you use one per task and do not pool them. They help with blocking, I/O-heavy work and do nothing for CPU-bound work. Pinning (blocked inside native code, or inside synchronized before Java 24) is the known limitation. Spring Boot enables them with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true.

How do you stop a thread properly?

Java has no safe forced stop (Thread.stop() was removed from use). You ask the thread to stop cooperatively: call interrupt(), and the task checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() or handles InterruptedException from blocking calls. When you catch InterruptedException and cannot rethrow it, restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). A volatile boolean flag also works for loops that do not block.

Cheat sheet — Multithreading and concurrency

  • Process vs thread process = own memory; threads share the heap, each has its own stack.
  • Create new Thread(runnable).start(), a lambda, or an executor. start() runs in a new thread; run() is a plain call.
  • States NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.
  • Interrupt cooperative; on InterruptedException rethrow or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt().
  • Race condition count++ is read, add, write; lost updates without protection.
  • Memory model atomicity, visibility, ordering; happens-before links a write to later reads (lock release/acquire, volatile, start/join).
  • synchronized mutual exclusion plus visibility; instance method locks this, static locks the Class; reentrant; keep it small.
  • volatile visibility only, no atomicity; good for flags and double-checked locking.
  • Atomics AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(), compareAndSet (CAS); LongAdder under heavy contention.
  • Locks ReentrantLock: lock() then unlock() in finally; tryLock(time); fairness optional.
  • wait/notify legacy; hold the lock, loop on the condition; prefer BlockingQueue.
  • ThreadPoolExecutor core, max, keep-alive, queue, factory, rejection; order: core, queue, max, reject.
  • Pools newFixedThreadPool, newCachedThreadPool, newSingleThreadExecutor, newScheduledThreadPool; prefer bounded queues.
  • Shutdown shutdown() + awaitTermination; shutdownNow() interrupts; Java 19+ try-with-resources.
  • Sizing CPU-bound about cores; I/O-bound more, or virtual threads.
  • Callable/Future submit returns a Future; get throws ExecutionException; get(timeout) may throw TimeoutException.
  • CompletableFuture supplyAsync, thenApply (map), thenCompose (flatMap), thenCombine, allOf, exceptionally, handle; own executor for blocking I/O.
  • ConcurrentHashMap no nulls; atomic merge/compute/putIfAbsent; lock-free reads; weakly consistent iterators.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList snapshot iteration, writes copy the array; for read-heavy lists.
  • BlockingQueue put/take block; ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded), LinkedBlockingQueue (set a bound), PriorityBlockingQueue, SynchronousQueue.
  • Synchronizers CountDownLatch one-shot; CyclicBarrier reusable; Semaphore permits (release in finally).
  • Deadlock four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Fix: lock order, tryLock, fewer locks. Detect: jstack / jcmd Thread.print.
  • ThreadLocal per-thread value; remove() in finally with pools; scoped values are final in Java 25.
  • Virtual threads Java 21; one per task, never pooled; limit with a Semaphore; not for CPU-bound work; pinning fixed for synchronized in Java 24; Spring: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true.
  • Thread safety order do not share, do not mutate, use concurrent classes and atomics, then lock. Spring singleton beans must be stateless.

Practice — Multithreading and concurrency

  1. Start vs run. Print Thread.currentThread().getName() from a task, first by calling run() and then start(). Done when you can explain why the two names differ and what happens if you call start() twice.
  2. The counter race, fixed two ways. Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter 1,000,000 times. First show the wrong result, then fix it with synchronized, then with AtomicInteger. Done when the broken version prints less than 2,000,000 on most runs and both fixed versions always print exactly 2,000,000. 
    import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class CounterRace {
    static int unsafeCount = 0;
    static int syncCount = 0;
    static final AtomicInteger atomicCount = new AtomicInteger();
    static final Object lock = new Object();

    static void runTwoThreads(Runnable task) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread a = new Thread(task);
        Thread b = new Thread(task);
        a.start(); b.start();
        a.join(); b.join();                       // wait for both to finish
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        final int N = 1_000_000;

        runTwoThreads(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) unsafeCount++; });

        runTwoThreads(() -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
                synchronized (lock) { syncCount++; }
            }
        });

        runTwoThreads(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) atomicCount.incrementAndGet(); });

        System.out.println("unsafe      : " + unsafeCount);
        System.out.println("synchronized: " + syncCount);
        System.out.println("atomic      : " + atomicCount.get());
    }
}
    unsafe      : 1374920
synchronized: 2000000
atomic      : 2000000
    Then time each version with System.nanoTime() and note which one is faster on your machine, and why a single lock of this size is cheap here.
  3. Visibility with volatile. Write a worker with a boolean running = true flag looped on by a thread, and stop it from main after one second. Run it with and without volatile (it may hang without). Done when you can explain visibility and why volatile does not fix count++.
  4. Thread pool and Future. Create a fixed pool of 4 threads, submit 10 Callables that each sleep 200 ms and return their square, collect the results through Future.get(), and shut down the pool. Done when the total time is about 600 ms (three rounds) and one task that throws shows up as an ExecutionException.
  5. Parallel calls with CompletableFuture. Simulate three services (price, stock, reviews) that each sleep 300 ms. Combine them with allOf into one result, add a timeout and a fallback for reviews. Done when the whole page takes about 300 ms and the fallback appears if you raise the review delay to 2 s.
  6. Concurrent word count. Split a text into four parts, count words in four threads into one ConcurrentHashMap with merge, then repeat with a plain HashMap and compare totals. Done when the concurrent map always matches the single-threaded count.
  7. Producer-consumer. Use an ArrayBlockingQueue of size 5 with one producer and two consumers; the producer ends with "poison pill" values. Done when all items are consumed exactly once and the program exits cleanly.
  8. Make it deadlock, then fix it. Reproduce the two-lock deadlock, take a thread dump with jstack, find the "Found one Java-level deadlock" section, and then fix it with lock ordering. Done when the fixed version finishes 1,000 opposite transfers without hanging.
  9. Virtual threads. Run 10,000 tasks that sleep one second using newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor and compare the time with a fixed pool of 200 threads. Add a Semaphore(100) to cap concurrency. Done when you can explain the difference in time and why you would still keep a limit.

Module 7·Interview level · about 3 daysInterview

JVM and memory

6 topics · about 58 min of reading

You can write Java for years without thinking about the JVM — until the day an app dies with OutOfMemoryError, a request freezes for two seconds during a GC pause, or a HashMap "loses" an object. This module explains what the JVM does with your code: where variables and objects live, how memory is reclaimed, how classes are loaded, and why equals and hashCode must agree. It is an interview module first (these questions appear in nearly every Java interview) and a production-debugging module second.

It builds on Module 1 (references, pass-by-value, strings) and Module 2 (objects and classes). It pairs with Module 4 (how HashMap uses hashCode) and Module 6 (each thread has its own stack).

After this module you will be able to:

  • draw the JVM architecture and say what the heap, the stacks, Metaspace and the execution engine do;
  • trace a small program and say exactly where each variable, object, static field and string lives;
  • explain generational garbage collection, GC roots and the main collectors (G1, ZGC and others), and choose between them;
  • recognise the common memory leaks and find them with a heap dump;
  • use the important JVM flags and tools (-Xmx, jcmd, jstack, JFR);
  • explain class loading, parent delegation and the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError;
  • write correct equals and hashCode and show what breaks in a HashSet when you do not.

JVM architecture: class loader, memory areas and execution engine

The JVM has three main parts — a class loader subsystem that brings classes in, runtime data areas (heap, stacks, Metaspace) that hold data, and an execution engine (interpreter, JIT compiler, garbage collector) that runs the code.

The JVM is a program (written mostly in C++) that provides a complete environment for bytecode: memory, threads, security checks and an instruction executor. The Java language specification only defines what the JVM must do; vendors implement it. The most common implementation is HotSpot (used in Oracle JDK, OpenJDK, Temurin, Corretto and others), and everything here describes HotSpot.

1. Class loader subsystem

Finds .class files (in folders, JARs, modules, or from the network), loads them into memory when first needed, checks them and prepares them for use. Details are in Class loading.

2. Runtime data areas

Heap
One area shared by all threads. Every object and every array created with new lives here, as do the String pool and the static fields of classes (HotSpot keeps them inside each class's Class object). The garbage collector manages it. Size is set with -Xms (initial) and -Xmx (maximum).
Metaspace (method area)
Stores class metadata: the structure of each class, method bytecode, the runtime constant pool. Before Java 8 this was the fixed-size PermGen inside the heap; since Java 8 it is Metaspace in native (OS) memory and grows on demand. It can still run out (OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace), typically when an app keeps generating or reloading classes. Limit it with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
JVM stack (one per thread)
A stack of frames. Each method call pushes a frame holding its local variables, an operand stack and a reference to the constant pool; returning pops it. Size per thread is set with -Xss.
PC register (one per thread)
Holds the address of the bytecode instruction that the thread is executing right now.
Native method stack (one per thread)
Used when the thread runs native (non-Java) code via JNI. In HotSpot it is part of the same thread stack.

Note which areas are shared (heap, Metaspace — so they need care with threads) and which are per thread (stack, PC register). This is why local variables are naturally thread-safe and objects on the heap are not.

3. Execution engine

  • Interpreter. Reads bytecode one instruction at a time and executes it. Starts instantly but is slow.
  • JIT compiler. Compiles frequently run bytecode into native machine code at runtime (see below).
  • Garbage collector. Finds objects that nothing can reach and frees their memory (Garbage collection).

4. JNI

The Java Native Interface lets Java call code written in C or C++ and lets native code call Java. The JDK itself uses it for file, network and OS operations. You rarely write JNI yourself, but native memory (outside the heap) is one reason a Java process can use more memory than -Xmx.

JIT compilation: C1, C2 and tiered compilation

The JVM counts how often each method is called and each loop runs. Methods that cross a threshold are hot and get compiled to machine code by the JIT (just-in-time) compiler. HotSpot has two JIT compilers:

  • C1 (client compiler) compiles quickly with light optimisation.
  • C2 (server compiler) compiles slowly but applies heavy optimisation, using profile data collected while the code ran.

Tiered compilation (the default) combines both: code starts in the interpreter, moves to C1 when warm, and to C2 when very hot. The result is a fast start-up and a high peak speed. Typical C2 optimisations are inlining (copying a small method's body into its caller), removing dead code, and unrolling loops. If an assumption turns out wrong (for example a new subclass is loaded), the JVM deoptimises: it throws away the compiled code and falls back to the interpreter.

Consequences you can see: the first requests to a freshly started service are slower (warm-up); micro-benchmarks written with a simple System.nanoTime() loop are misleading (use JMH); and short-lived command-line tools never reach peak speed. -XX:+PrintCompilation prints what gets compiled.

Escape analysis

When C2 compiles a method, escape analysis checks whether an object created inside it ever "escapes" — is stored in a field, returned or passed somewhere the JIT cannot see. If it does not escape, the JIT can skip the heap allocation and keep the object's fields in CPU registers (scalar replacement), or remove locks on it (lock elision). So a short-lived new Point(x, y) in a hot loop may cost nothing. Objects are not literally moved to the stack; they simply disappear. Do not write ugly code to "save allocations"; write clear code first and measure.

Where the memory of a Java process goes

AreaLives inControlled byOut-of-memory message
HeapJVM-managed memory-Xms, -XmxJava heap space
MetaspaceNative memory-XX:MaxMetaspaceSizeMetaspace
Thread stacksNative memory-Xss, number of threadsStackOverflowError, or unable to create native thread
JIT code cache, GC structures, direct buffersNative memoryVarious -XX flagsRarely hit

So the real memory used by a Java process (the RSS you see in top or Task Manager) is always larger than -Xmx. In containers, leave headroom (see the flags article).

Rule: heap and Metaspace are shared; stack and registers are per thread

Anything on the heap can be reached by several threads and needs synchronisation or immutability. Local variables on a thread's stack are private to it.

Edge cases

  • "PermGen" appears in old tutorials and interview questions. It was removed in Java 8 (replaced by Metaspace); -XX:PermSize flags are ignored by modern JVMs.
  • The JVM spec describes a "method area"; HotSpot implements it as Metaspace. The String pool and static fields moved into the heap in Java 7 and 8.
  • Other JVMs exist (Eclipse OpenJ9, GraalVM) with different internals; the model above still holds.

Interview: "Explain the JVM architecture"

  • Three parts: class loader subsystem, runtime data areas, execution engine (plus JNI and native libraries).
  • Data areas: heap and Metaspace shared; stack, PC register and native stack per thread.
  • Execution engine: interpreter for fast start, JIT (C1 then C2, tiered) for hot code, garbage collector for memory.
  • Add the details that show depth: Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8; string pool is on the heap; escape analysis can remove allocations.

Stack vs heap: where variables and objects live

Local variables and method-call frames live on a thread's stack; objects, arrays and the String pool live on the shared heap; a local reference variable sits on the stack and points to its object on the heap.

The two main memory areas

PointStackHeap
HoldsFrames: local variables, parameters, operand stack, return addressObjects, arrays, boxed values, String pool
OwnerOne per thread (private)One per JVM (shared by all threads)
LifetimeUntil the method returnsUntil the object is unreachable and garbage collected
CleanupAutomatic: frame is poppedGarbage collector
SpeedVery fast (just move a pointer)Slower to allocate and manage
SizeSmall (typically 512 KB to 1 MB per thread, set by -Xss)Large (by default a quarter of physical memory, set by -Xmx)
When fullStackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Thread safetyNaturally safe (private)Needs care

A worked example

Follow this small program from main into compute:

public class Shop {
    static int orders = 0;                       // static field

    static class Product {
        String name;                             // instance fields live inside the object
        double price;
        Product(String name, double price) { this.name = name; this.price = price; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int qty = 3;                             // primitive local
        String label = "Pen";                    // reference to a pooled literal
        Product p = new Product("Pen", 12.5);    // reference local + object on heap
        int total = compute(p, qty);             // call: new frame
        orders++;
        System.out.println(total);
    }

    static int compute(Product item, int q) {
        double sum = item.price * q;             // 37.5
        return (int) sum;
    }
}

Read the picture like this:

  • qty, q and sum are primitives: the number itself is stored in the frame.
  • p, item and label are references: the stack holds only the reference. p and item hold copies of the same reference, so they point to one Product — this is exactly pass-by-value.
  • The Product object is on the heap. Its fields are inside the object: the primitive price by value, and name as a reference to the pooled "Pen".
  • When compute returns, its frame is popped and sum, q, item disappear. The Product survives because p still points to it.
  • When main ends, p goes away; the Product becomes unreachable and the GC can free it later.

Where does each thing live?

ItemLocation
Local primitive (int qty)Stack frame (the value)
Local reference (Product p)Stack frame (the reference); the object is on the heap
Object created with newHeap
Instance field (primitive or reference)Inside its object, on the heap
Array (even int[])Heap; the variable holding it is a reference
Static fieldWith the class: in HotSpot, in the Class object on the heap (conceptually the "method area")
String literalString pool (part of the heap since Java 7)
new String("x"), strings built at runtimeNormal heap
Boxed IntegerHeap (small values come from the cache)
Lambda captured valuesInside the lambda object on the heap
Class definitions, method bytecodeMetaspace

Stack frames in more detail

Each frame has: an array of local variables (parameters first, with this as slot 0 in instance methods); an operand stack, a small work area where bytecode instructions push operands and pop results; and a link to the constant pool of the class. For a + b the bytecode is: load a onto the operand stack, load b, add (pops two, pushes the result), store into a local. You can see this with javap -c. A thread's stack is a chain of frames; the stack trace printed with an exception is a readout of that chain.

StackOverflowError

Each thread's stack has a fixed maximum size. Infinite or very deep recursion keeps pushing frames until it is full:

public class StackDemo {
    static int depth = 0;

    static void recurse() {
        depth++;
        recurse();                      // no base case
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            recurse();
        } catch (StackOverflowError e) {
            System.out.println("Overflow after about " + depth + " calls");
        }
    }
}
Overflow after about 10000-20000 calls

(The exact depth depends on frame size, JVM and -Xss; typical values are in the thousands to tens of thousands.) StackOverflowError is an Error, not an Exception. Fixes: add or correct the base case, convert recursion to a loop, or (rarely) increase -Xss. Common real-world causes: mutual recursion between toString() methods of two objects that reference each other, bidirectional JPA entities serialised to JSON, and a getter that calls itself.

OutOfMemoryError

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class HeapDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<byte[]> hog = new ArrayList<>();
        while (true) {
            hog.add(new byte[1024 * 1024]);      // keep 1 MB blocks reachable forever
        }
    }
}
$ java -Xmx64m HeapDemo.java
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space

Requested array size exceeds VM limitArray too largeBug in size calculation
PointStackOverflowErrorOutOfMemoryError
AreaThread stackHeap, Metaspace or native memory

AffectsOne threadWhole JVM (other threads may fail next)
