Rule: a reference is never the object

A variable of a class type holds a reference (or null). Assigning, passing and returning copies the reference, not the object. Two references to one object see each other's changes.

Edge cases

  • "Primitives live on the stack" is only true for local primitives. A primitive field of an object lives inside that object on the heap, and the elements of an int[] are on the heap.
  • Escape analysis can remove an allocation altogether (JVM architecture). The model above is what the language guarantees, not what the JIT physically does.
  • Catching OutOfMemoryError is almost never a good idea: the JVM may be in an inconsistent state. Let it crash and restart (-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError) after saving a heap dump.
  • Virtual threads (Java 21) have small stacks stored on the heap that grow and shrink; the stack-versus-heap picture changes slightly there (Module 6).

Common mistakes

  • Believing that objects can be created on the stack in Java as in C++ (Product p(...)). In Java, new always means heap (as far as the language is concerned).
  • Saying "the object is passed by reference". The reference is copied.
  • Treating StackOverflowError as a memory-size problem when it is a recursion bug.

Interview: "Stack vs heap" and "StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError"

  • Stack: per thread, frames with locals, fast, freed on return. Heap: shared, objects, managed by GC.
  • Walk through Product p = new Product(...): reference p on the stack, object on the heap.
  • Static fields with the class data; string literals in the pool in the heap; Metaspace holds class metadata.
  • SOE = too deep call chain (fix recursion). OOM = too much live data (fix leak, size, or algorithm). Name two OOM messages.

Garbage collection: generations, roots, collectors and references

The garbage collector frees objects that can no longer be reached from a GC root; the heap is split into young and old generations because most objects die young, and modern collectors (G1, ZGC) do most of their work concurrently to keep pauses short.

In Java you create objects with new and never free them. The garbage collector (GC) does it. An object is garbage when no live part of the program can reach it any more. This removes whole classes of bugs (use-after-free, double free) but introduces GC pauses and tuning.

Reachability and GC roots

Java does not use reference counting (which fails on cycles). The GC starts from a set of GC roots and follows references; everything it can reach is live, everything else is garbage. The roots include:

  • local variables and parameters in every thread's stack frames;
  • static fields of loaded classes;
  • active threads and JNI references;
  • other internal JVM references (such as class loaders and monitor locks).

The basic algorithm is mark and sweep: mark every reachable object, then reclaim the rest. Most collectors also compact or copy the survivors so free memory is one contiguous block (no fragmentation).

The generational hypothesis

Studies of real programs show that most objects die young (a request object, a temporary string, an iterator) and a few live very long (caches, connection pools, Spring beans). So the heap is divided into generations and the young one is collected often and cheaply:

  1. New objects are allocated in Eden (allocation is just a pointer bump, very fast).
  2. When Eden is full, a minor GC runs. It copies the live objects from Eden and the current survivor space into the other survivor space and frees Eden completely. Cost depends on the number of live objects, not on the garbage, so it is quick.
  3. Each survivor object has an age, increased at every minor GC it survives. When the age passes a threshold (at most 15 by default, and the JVM adapts it), the object is promoted to the old generation. Very large objects may be placed in the old generation directly.
  4. When the old generation fills up, an old-generation collection (a major GC) is needed. A full GC collects the entire heap, including young and old generations and Metaspace, and is the slowest, with the longest pauses.

Stop-the-world pauses

Some GC steps need the application threads to stop so that the object graph does not change while the GC walks it. This is a stop-the-world (STW) pause. Users see it as a request that suddenly takes 800 ms. The aim of modern collectors is to keep pauses short by doing most work concurrently with your threads. Throughput (how much CPU goes to your code) and latency (pause length) pull in opposite directions; different collectors choose different balances.

The collectors

CollectorFlagCharacterUse it for
Serial-XX:+UseSerialGCSingle GC thread, simple, STWTiny heaps, single-CPU containers, small tools
Parallel-XX:+UseParallelGCMany GC threads, maximum throughput, longer pausesBatch jobs where total time matters more than pauses
G1 (Garbage-First)-XX:+UseG1GCHeap split into regions; collects the regions with most garbage first; pause-time goal (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, default 200 ms)Default since Java 9 on typical server machines; a good general choice
ZGC-XX:+UseZGCAlmost fully concurrent; very short pauses, works on very large heaps; generational in modern JDKsLatency-sensitive services, big heaps
Shenandoah-XX:+UseShenandoahGCConcurrent compaction, low pausesLow-latency services; available in many OpenJDK builds, but not in every vendor's JDK
  • The JVM picks Serial instead of G1 automatically on a very small machine or container (roughly fewer than two CPUs or about 1.8 GB of memory).
  • CMS (Concurrent Mark Sweep), common in old tutorials, was removed in Java 14.
  • Do not tune GC blindly. Start with the default (G1), set -Xmx sensibly, measure with GC logs, and change collector or flags only with data. Print GC activity with -Xlog:gc (Java 9+).
[0.512s][info][gc] GC(3) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 56M->12M(128M) 4.215ms
[7.904s][info][gc] GC(9) Pause Full (System.gc()) 90M->11M(128M) 31.820ms

Read it as: a young pause took 4 ms and the heap dropped from 56 MB to 12 MB (of 128 MB committed). A pause marked System.gc() shows that someone called the method explicitly.

System.gc(), finalize() and Cleaner

  • System.gc() is only a hint; the JVM may ignore it, and when it runs it often causes a full GC pause. Do not call it in application code. (Some libraries do; -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns it off.)
  • finalize() was meant to clean up before an object is collected. It is unpredictable (no guarantee when or whether it runs), slow, and can resurrect objects. It has been deprecated for removal since Java 18. Never write it.
  • For resources (files, sockets, DB connections) use try-with-resources with AutoCloseable, so they are closed at a known point. For a safety net around native resources, use java.lang.ref.Cleaner:
import java.lang.ref.Cleaner;

public class NativeBuffer implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();

    // The cleanup action must NOT refer to the NativeBuffer, or it can never be collected
    private static class State implements Runnable {
        public void run() { System.out.println("native memory freed"); }
    }

    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;

    public NativeBuffer() {
        this.cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, new State());
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        cleanable.clean();               // runs the action once, now
    }
}

Reference types

A normal variable is a strong reference: while it exists, the object is kept. java.lang.ref offers weaker references that the GC may clear:

TypeCollected whenTypical use
Strong (Object o = new Object())Never while reachableEverything normal
SoftReferenceThe JVM is short of memory (before OutOfMemoryError)Memory-sensitive caches
WeakReferenceAt the next GC, if only weakly reachableWeakHashMap, canonical-object maps, listeners
PhantomReferenceAfter the object is finalised; get() always returns nullPost-mortem cleanup (Cleaner is built on it)
 
import java.lang.ref.WeakReference;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.WeakHashMap;

public class WeakDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Object big = new Object();
        WeakReference<Object> weak = new WeakReference<>(big);
        System.out.println(weak.get() != null);      // true: big still strongly held

        big = null;                                  // drop the only strong reference
        System.gc();                                 // a hint, but works in practice here
        Thread.sleep(100);
        System.out.println(weak.get());              // null (normally)

        Map<Object, String> cache = new WeakHashMap<>();
        Object key = new Object();
        cache.put(key, "metadata");
        key = null;                                  // no strong reference to the key remains
        System.gc();
        Thread.sleep(100);
        System.out.println(cache.size());            // 0 (normally): the entry vanished
    }
}
true
null
0

A WeakHashMap removes an entry when its key is no longer strongly reachable. If the value refers to the key strongly, the entry never disappears — a common mistake.

Helping the GC (and not hurting it)

  • Keep objects' scopes small. Local variables disappear when the method returns; you do not need to write x = null (except for a long-lived field that you want to release, or an element removed from your own array-based structure).
  • Do not hold on to data you no longer need: clear caches, unregister listeners, cap collection sizes.
  • Avoid creating huge numbers of short-lived objects in hot loops (boxing, string concatenation) — they are cheap, but not free.
  • Stream large results and process in batches instead of loading millions of rows into a list.

Rule: reachability, not scope, decides what is collected

An object is collectable when no GC root can reach it, even if it was never explicitly dereferenced or if it points to other garbage. A static field holding a collection keeps everything in it alive for the life of the class.

Edge cases

  • Objects in a cycle (A points to B, B to A) are still collected if nothing reaches the cycle.
  • "Humongous" objects (very large arrays) are allocated specially in G1 and can cause extra GC work if you create many.
  • A thread that is still running keeps its Runnable, and everything that Runnable references, alive.
  • GC can run at any time between any two bytecode instructions; never rely on it for program correctness or timing.

Common mistakes

  • Calling System.gc() "to free memory". It rarely helps and often hurts.
  • Relying on finalize() to close files or connections.
  • Increasing -Xmx to hide a leak: the app just dies later, with a bigger heap dump.
  • Setting a huge young generation or many GC flags copied from a blog without measuring.

Interview: "How does garbage collection work? Which collectors do you know?"

  • Objects not reachable from GC roots are garbage; mark and sweep/copy/compact; generational because most objects die young.
  • Eden + two survivors + old; minor GC copies live objects, age increments, promotion to old; full GC is the expensive one; stop-the-world pauses.
  • Collectors: Serial, Parallel (throughput), G1 (default, balanced, regions), ZGC and Shenandoah (low latency). CMS was removed.
  • System.gc() is a hint; finalize() is deprecated for removal — use try-with-resources and Cleaner.
  • Soft, weak and phantom references; WeakHashMap.
  • Follow-up: "Can you force GC?" No. "Can a Java program leak memory?" Yes — see the next article.

Memory leaks, JVM flags and diagnostic tools

A Java memory leak means objects that are no longer needed are still reachable; find them with a heap dump, size the JVM with -Xmx and friends, and inspect running processes with jcmd, jstack, jmap, JFR and VisualVM.

What is a memory leak in a garbage-collected language?

The GC cannot free an object that is still reachable, even if your program will never use it again. A leak in Java is therefore "unintentional reachability": something keeps a reference to dead data. Memory use climbs over hours or days, GC runs more and more often, and finally you see OutOfMemoryError. The symptom on a graph is a saw-tooth whose baseline (heap after each full GC) keeps rising.

Common causes

Static collections
A static Map or List that is only ever added to lives as long as the class. Typical: a hand-made cache or a registry.
Caches without eviction
A HashMap used as a cache that grows with every new key (user IDs, request URLs). Use a bounded cache with expiry (Caffeine, Spring's cache abstraction) instead.
Listeners and callbacks never removed
Registering an object as an observer or event listener makes the publisher hold it. If you never call remove, the listener — and everything it references — stays.
ThreadLocal in thread pools
Pool threads live forever, so a value stored in a ThreadLocal and not remove()d lives forever too. In app servers it can also pin the whole web application's class loader.
Unclosed resources
Streams, Connections, ResultSets, HTTP clients and Scanners that are not closed leak native memory and OS handles (and sometimes heap). Use try-with-resources.
Wrong equals/hashCode or mutable keys
Entries put into a HashMap/HashSet that can never be found again can never be removed (next articles).
Inner-class references
A non-static inner class or an anonymous class silently holds a reference to its outer instance. A long-lived callback created in a short-lived object keeps the outer object alive.
Unbounded queues and sessions
A queue whose producers are faster than consumers, or HTTP sessions that never expire.

Wrong: unbounded static cache

public class PriceService {
    private static final Map<String, Price> CACHE = new HashMap<>();

    public Price get(String productId) {
        return CACHE.computeIfAbsent(productId, this::loadFromDb);
        // grows forever; also not thread-safe
    }
}

Right: bounded and expiring (Caffeine)

public class PriceService {
    private final Cache<String, Price> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(10_000)
            .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
            .build();

    public Price get(String productId) {
        return cache.get(productId, this::loadFromDb);
    }
}
private static final ThreadLocal<UserContext> CONTEXT = new ThreadLocal<>();

void handle(Request req) {
    CONTEXT.set(new UserContext(req.user()));
    try {
        process(req);
    } finally {
        CONTEXT.remove();          // always clean up on pooled threads
    }
}

Finding a leak

  1. Confirm the pattern. Turn on GC logging (-Xlog:gc) or watch a monitoring dashboard. A rising post-GC heap and more frequent full GCs mean a leak (or simply a too-small heap).
  2. Capture a heap dump while memory is high. Automatically on failure with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps, or on demand with jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof. Take two dumps some time apart to compare.
  3. Analyse it in Eclipse MAT (Memory Analyzer), VisualVM or IntelliJ's profiler. In MAT, run the Leak Suspects report and the Dominator Tree: it shows which objects keep the largest amount of memory alive.
  4. Follow the path to GC roots from the suspicious object ("Path to GC Roots, exclude weak references") to see which static field, thread or collection holds it.
  5. Fix and verify: bound or clear the structure, then watch the post-GC baseline stay flat.

A quick view without a full dump: jmap -histo <pid> (or jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram) prints how many instances of each class exist. A class whose count only grows is your suspect.

Heap dumps contain all data in memory — passwords, tokens, personal data. Treat them as secrets: do not email them or upload them to public tools.

$ java -Xms512m -Xmx512m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
       -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
       -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log -jar app.jar
  • Setting -Xms equal to -Xmx avoids heap resizing pauses and makes memory use predictable.
  • Containers. Since Java 10 (and 8u191) the JVM reads the container's memory and CPU limits. Total process memory is more than the heap (Metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers), so do not set -Xmx to 100% of the container limit; -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 is a common starting point. A container killed with exit code 137 without a Java OutOfMemoryError usually means the Linux OOM killer ended the process because total memory exceeded the limit.
  • Flags starting with -X are standard-ish and stable; -XX: flags are HotSpot-specific and can change between versions. Check the documentation for your JDK version before adding flags.

In production, Spring Boot Actuator exposes heap and GC metrics over HTTP (Spring Boot · Module 6). To catch a deadlock, take a thread dump with jstack; it reports "Found one Java-level deadlock" and names the threads and locks involved.

Rule: always run production JVMs with a heap-dump-on-OOM flag and a GC log

You usually get one chance to see why a service died. Without -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError the evidence is gone after the restart.

Common mistakes

  • Treating every OutOfMemoryError as "the heap is too small". Check the message: Metaspace, native threads and heap are different problems.
  • Setting -Xmx equal to the container limit and getting the process killed by the OS.
  • Adding a dozen old -XX flags from an article written for Java 8.
  • Profiling only in the IDE with tiny data: leaks and GC behaviour show up under production-like load.

Interview: "How do you find and fix a memory leak in production?"

  • Symptoms: rising heap after full GC, frequent GCs, eventually OOM.
  • Capture a heap dump (jcmd GC.heap_dump or dump on OOM), open it in Eclipse MAT, read the leak suspects and the dominator tree, follow the path to GC roots.
  • Typical culprits: static collections, unbounded caches, listeners, ThreadLocals, unclosed resources.
  • Fix by bounding or clearing, then confirm with monitoring. Mention JFR and jmap -histo as lighter tools.

Class loading: loaders, delegation and initialization

The JVM loads a class the first time it is needed, in three steps — loading, linking (verify, prepare, resolve) and initialization — using a chain of class loaders that always ask their parent first.

Java does not load all classes at start-up. A class is brought into memory lazily, the first time the program needs it. Each class is loaded by a class loader, and the pair (class name, loader) identifies the class: the same .class file loaded by two loaders gives two different classes in the JVM.

The three phases

  1. Loading. A class loader finds the bytes of the class (from a folder, a JAR, a module or the network) and creates its runtime representation in Metaspace, plus a java.lang.Class object on the heap.
  2. Linking, in three sub-steps:
    • Verification — the bytecode verifier checks the class file is well-formed and safe.
    • Preparation — memory for static fields is allocated and set to default values (0, false, null), not yet to your assigned values.
    • Resolution — symbolic references in the constant pool (names of other classes, methods, fields) are replaced by direct references. HotSpot often does this lazily.
  3. Initialization. The JVM runs the class's static initializers: static field assignments and static { } blocks, in the order they appear in the source. The superclass is initialized first. This happens at most once per class and is thread-safe.

The class loader hierarchy

LoaderLoadsNotes
BootstrapCore JDK classes (java.base: java.lang.*, java.util.*, …)Built into the JVM, written in native code; getClassLoader() returns null for these classes
PlatformThe other JDK platform modules (SQL, XML, logging, …)Named "platform"; replaced the "extension" loader of Java 8
Application (system)Your classes and libraries from the classpath/module pathNamed "app"; the default loader of your code
Custom loadersWhatever you write them forApp servers (Tomcat gives each web app its own), plugin systems, hot reload, OSGi
 
public class LoaderDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(String.class.getClassLoader());          // null: bootstrap
        ClassLoader app = LoaderDemo.class.getClassLoader();
        System.out.println(app.getName());                          // app
        System.out.println(app.getParent().getName());              // platform
        System.out.println(app.getParent().getParent());            // null: bootstrap
    }
}
null
app
platform
null

Parent delegation

When a loader is asked for a class, it does not look itself first. It delegates to its parent, and the parent to its own parent, up to bootstrap. Only if no parent can load the class does the child try.

Why this design?

  • Security. You cannot replace a core class: if someone puts a fake java.lang.String on the classpath, the bootstrap loader finds the real one first and the fake is never used.
  • No duplicates. A class is loaded once by the loader that "owns" it, so everyone sees the same Object and String.
  • Consistency for shared types. (Web containers deliberately bend the rule so each webapp can have its own library versions.)

When is a class initialized?

Initialization runs on the first active use:

  • creating an instance with new;
  • calling a static method;
  • reading or writing a static field that is not a compile-time constant;
  • Class.forName("pkg.Name") (reflection) — this initializes the class;
  • initializing a subclass (the superclass is initialized first);
  • running the class that contains main.

These do not initialize it: reading a static final primitive or String constant (the compiler copies its value into the caller), using Config.class, and declaring an array Config[].

class Config {
    static final int MAX = 10;                 // compile-time constant
    static int counter = 0;
    static { System.out.println("Config initialized"); }
}

class Parent {
    static { System.out.println("Parent static block"); }
    Parent() { System.out.println("Parent constructor"); }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    static { System.out.println("Child static block"); }
    Child() { System.out.println("Child constructor"); }
}

public class InitDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("start");
        int x = Config.MAX;                    // constant: Config NOT initialized
        System.out.println(x);
        Config.counter++;                      // real static access: initialization runs
        new Child();                           // Parent static, Child static, then constructors
        new Child();                           // static blocks do not run again
    }
}
start
10
Config initialized
Parent static block
Child static block
Parent constructor
Child constructor
Parent constructor
Child constructor

If a static initializer throws an exception, the class fails with ExceptionInInitializerError, and every later use of that class throws NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class …. Static initialization order across classes can be tricky: avoid heavy logic and circular dependencies in static blocks.

ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError

PointClassNotFoundExceptionNoClassDefFoundError
KindChecked ExceptionError (a LinkageError)
Thrown whenCode explicitly loads a class by name and it is not found: Class.forName("com.x.Driver"), ClassLoader.loadClass, reflection, or a bad class name in configA class that was present at compile time is missing at runtime, or its static initialization failed earlier
Typical causeJAR missing from the classpath; typo in a class-name string (driver, plugin)Dependency not packaged, version mismatch, scope provided but not supplied by the server, earlier ExceptionInInitializerError
Handle it?Yes: you must catch it (checked)No; fix the packaging or the root cause

Related errors: NoSuchMethodError or NoSuchFieldError (the class exists but a different version of it, without that method, was loaded — a typical "dependency version conflict" symptom, see Maven) and UnsupportedClassVersionError (class compiled for a newer Java than the running JVM). Read the first error in the log: a NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X is only the echo of an earlier failure.

Why you should care

  • Start-up time: lazy loading and class verification are part of why a big Spring Boot app takes seconds to start.
  • Metaspace leaks: redeploying web apps repeatedly creates new class loaders; if anything (a ThreadLocal, a driver, a static) still references an old loader, all its classes stay in Metaspace.
  • JDBC drivers: older code used Class.forName("org.postgresql.Driver") to load and register the driver. Since JDBC 4 (Java 6) drivers on the classpath register themselves automatically, so this line is no longer needed.

Rule: loaders delegate to the parent first

A class with the same name on the classpath cannot override a core JDK class. Order inside the classpath matters for duplicates: the first JAR that contains the class wins.

Edge cases

  • A compile-time constant is inlined, so changing Config.MAX without recompiling the callers leaves them with the old value.
  • static final objects (static final List<String> X = new ArrayList<>()) are not constants and do trigger initialization.
  • With the module system (Java 9+), a class can be on the path but not readable from another module (IllegalAccessError, "module does not export").
  • Instance initializer blocks and constructors run on every new; static blocks run once per class per loader.

Interview: "Explain class loading" and "ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError"

  • Loading, linking (verify, prepare, resolve), initialization. Lazy: first active use.
  • Bootstrap, platform, application loaders; parent delegation for security and uniqueness.
  • Initialization triggers: new, static method or non-constant static field, Class.forName, subclass.
  • CNFE: checked exception from an explicit by-name load. NCDFE: error from implicit linking when a class that existed at compile time is missing or failed to initialize.
  • Output order for parent/child static blocks and constructors is a classic puzzle: statics (parent, child) first, then constructors (parent, child).

== vs equals, and why hashCode must agree with equals

== compares primitives by value and objects by reference; equals compares by meaning when a class overrides it, and whenever you override equals you must override hashCode so that equal objects land in the same hash bucket.

Module 2 introduced the basics (equals and hashCode in OOP). Here we go deeper: what each comparison really does, the formal contracts, how to write both methods correctly, and exactly what breaks when they disagree.

== versus equals for each kind of value

Type== doesequals does
Primitives (int, char, …)Compares the valuesNot available (no methods)
Wrappers (Integer, …)Compares references; true for cached −128…127 only by luckCompares the value and the type: Integer.valueOf(1).equals(1L) is false
StringSame object? (pool trap)Compares characters
Your class (no override)Same object?Inherited from Object: same as ==
Your class (with override)Same object?Whatever you define (usually field values)
ArraysSame array object?Same as ==; use Arrays.equals
enumCorrect and null-safe: only one instance per constantSame as ==
BigDecimalSame object?Same value and scale (2.0 ≠ 2.00)
recordSame object?Generated: all components equal
 
int a = 5; long b = 5L; double c = 5.0;
System.out.println(a == b);                          // true: compared as long
System.out.println(a == c);                          // true: compared as double
System.out.println(Integer.valueOf(1).equals(1L));   // false: Long is not Integer
System.out.println(new int[]{1}.equals(new int[]{1}));        // false: identity
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.equals(new int[]{1}, new int[]{1}));   // true
Object x = new Object(), y = new Object();
System.out.println((x == y) + " " + x.equals(y));    // false false: default equals is ==

The equals contract

The Object.equals documentation requires, for non-null references:

  • Reflexive: x.equals(x) is true.
  • Symmetric: if x.equals(y) is true then y.equals(x) is true.
  • Transitive: if x.equals(y) and y.equals(z) then x.equals(z).
  • Consistent: repeated calls give the same answer while the objects are not modified.
  • Non-null: x.equals(null) is false (and never throws).

The usual way to break symmetry is comparing with a different kind of object. A class that "helpfully" lets itself equal a plain String: ci.equals("abc") is true, but "abc".equals(ci) is false. Transitivity breaks with subclasses that add a field: Point(1,2) equals ColorPoint(1,2,RED) if the check ignores colour, and equals ColorPoint(1,2,BLUE) too, yet the two colour points are not equal.

The hashCode contract

  • Consistent: during one run, if the fields used in equals do not change, hashCode() returns the same int every time. (It may differ between runs.)
  • Equal objects ⇒ equal hash codes: if x.equals(y), then x.hashCode() == y.hashCode(). This is the rule that gets broken.
  • Unequal objects may have the same hash code (a collision), but a good function spreads values evenly because collisions make hash tables slower.

The inverse is false: the same hash code does not imply equal objects. "Aa".hashCode() and "BB".hashCode() are both 2112. The default Object.hashCode() is derived from object identity (often loosely based on a memory address or a random number); it is why two "equal" objects have different hashes unless you override.

How a hash collection uses both methods

  1. hashCode() is called on the key; the result selects a bucket (array slot).
  2. Inside that bucket, entries are compared with equals() to find the exact key (see Module 4 for HashMap internals).
  3. If equals says two keys are equal but their hash codes differ, the lookup goes to a different bucket and never calls equals — the entry is "lost".

Demo: what breaks when you override only equals

import java.util.*;

public class BrokenKey {
    static class BadPoint {
        final int x, y;
        BadPoint(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }

        @Override
        public boolean equals(Object o) {                // overridden...
            if (this == o) return true;
            if (!(o instanceof BadPoint other)) return false;
            return x == other.x && y == other.y;
        }
        // ...but hashCode() is NOT overridden: Object's identity hash is used
    }

    static class GoodPoint {
        final int x, y;
        GoodPoint(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }

        @Override
        public boolean equals(Object o) {
            if (this == o) return true;
            if (!(o instanceof GoodPoint other)) return false;
            return x == other.x && y == other.y;
        }

        @Override
        public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new BadPoint(1, 2).equals(new BadPoint(1, 2)));   // true

        Set<BadPoint> bad = new HashSet<>();
        bad.add(new BadPoint(1, 2));
        bad.add(new BadPoint(1, 2));
        System.out.println(bad.size());                                       // 2 (!)
        System.out.println(bad.contains(new BadPoint(1, 2)));                 // false (!)

        Set<GoodPoint> good = new HashSet<>();
        good.add(new GoodPoint(1, 2));
        good.add(new GoodPoint(1, 2));
        System.out.println(good.size());                                      // 1
        System.out.println(good.contains(new GoodPoint(1, 2)));               // true

        Map<GoodPoint, String> names = new HashMap<>();
        names.put(new GoodPoint(0, 0), "origin");
        System.out.println(names.get(new GoodPoint(0, 0)));                   // origin
    }
}
true
2
false
1
true
origin

The two BadPoint objects are "equal", yet the set holds both and cannot find a copy. (Very rarely the identity hashes collide by chance, which makes this bug appear and disappear — the worst kind of bug.)

Writing equals and hashCode correctly

import java.util.Objects;

public final class Customer {
    private final String email;       // identity of a customer
    private final String name;

    public Customer(String email, String name) {
        this.email = email;
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;                          // 1. same reference: fast path
        if (!(o instanceof Customer other)) return false;    // 2. null or wrong type
        return Objects.equals(email, other.email)            // 3. compare significant fields
                && Objects.equals(name, other.name);         //    null-safe
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(email, name);                    // same fields as equals
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Customer[" + email + ", " + name + "]";
    }
}
  • Use the same fields in both methods. A field used in equals but not in hashCode is fine for correctness (equal objects still hash equally); a field in hashCode but not in equals breaks the contract.
  • Objects.equals(a, b) is null-safe equality. Objects.hash(a, b, c) builds a hash from values using the formula result = 31 * result + hash(element) starting at 1, so Objects.hash(1, 2) is 994. It boxes primitives into an array; for hot code compute it by hand with Integer.hashCode, Double.hashCode, and so on.
  • Compare float/double fields with Double.compare(a, b) == 0, not ==, to treat NaN correctly. Compare arrays with Arrays.equals and hash them with Arrays.hashCode.
  • You can generate both methods in IntelliJ (Alt+Insert → equals() and hashCode()), with Lombok (@EqualsAndHashCode, or @Data), or with a record.

instanceof versus getClass()

ApproachBehaviourUse when
o instanceof CustomerTrue for subclasses too; keeps symmetry as long as the class is final or subclasses do not change equalityFinal classes, value objects, records; also when equality is defined by an interface
o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()Only exactly the same class is equal; safe against symmetry problems with subclasses that add stateNon-final classes with subclasses that add significant fields

Pick one deliberately. getClass() breaks with runtime proxies (a Hibernate lazy proxy is a generated subclass of your entity, so getClass() differs from the real class), which is one reason many JPA codebases use instanceof (or compare only the id) in entity equality.

Mutable keys

If a field used by hashCode changes while the object is inside a HashSet or is a HashMap key, the stored position no longer matches the new hash. The entry is still there but unreachable:

class Key {
    int id;
    Key(int id) { this.id = id; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Key k && k.id == id; }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Integer.hashCode(id); }
}

Set<Key> set = new HashSet<>();
Key k = new Key(1);
set.add(k);
k.id = 2;                                   // mutated after insertion
System.out.println(set.contains(k));        // false: looks in the bucket for hash(2)
System.out.println(set.size());             // 1:     but the entry is still stored (a leak)

Use immutable keys (String, Integer, records of immutable fields, enums). That is also why String is a perfect key.

Records and enums

record Money(long paise, String currency) {}

Money m1 = new Money(49900, "INR");
Money m2 = new Money(49900, "INR");
System.out.println(m1.equals(m2));                    // true: generated, component-wise
System.out.println(m1.hashCode() == m2.hashCode());   // true: generated, consistent
System.out.println(m1);                               // Money[paise=49900, currency=INR]
System.out.println(m1 == m2);                         // false

A record gets equals, hashCode and toString generated from its components. The exact hash formula is unspecified, but it is consistent with equals. Caution: an array component is compared by identity (record Bag(int[] items)), so two records with equal-content arrays are not equal. Enums inherit identity-based equals/hashCode (final in Enum), which is correct since each constant is a singleton.

Related: Comparable and equals

Sorted collections (TreeSet, TreeMap) use compareTo/compare, not equals, to decide whether two elements are the same. It is strongly recommended that compareTo(x) == 0 agrees with equals(x). BigDecimal violates this: 2.0 and 2.00 are different for equals (a HashSet holds both) but equal for compareTo (a TreeSet holds one).

Rule: override equals and hashCode together, using the same fields

Equal objects must return the same hash code, or HashMap, HashSet, Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap will not find them. If you only need identity, override neither.

Conventions

  • Annotate with @Override; a signature like equals(Customer c) (overload, not override) is silent and never used by collections.
  • Prefer immutable value classes or records; make fields final.
  • Use Objects.equals and Objects.hash unless profiling says otherwise.
  • For JPA entities, base equality on a business key or the id with care for unsaved (null id) objects; do not include lazy collections in equals/hashCode (they trigger database loads).
  • Never use == on strings or wrappers; use Objects.equals(a, b) when either may be null.

Edge cases

  • hashCode() may be any int, including negative; the collection maps it to an index internally.
  • A constant hashCode() (return 1;) is legal but turns a hash table into a list (O(n) lookups); modern HashMap converts long buckets into balanced trees if keys are Comparable, but do not rely on it.
  • Calling an overridable method or accessing lazy state inside equals can cause recursion or extra queries.
  • Cyclic references (A has B, B has A) in equals/hashCode/toString produce StackOverflowError.

Common mistakes

  • Overriding only one of the two.
  • Writing equals(MyClass other) instead of equals(Object other).
  • Using a mutable object (or an object whose hash depends on mutable fields) as a map key.
  • Throwing ClassCastException by casting without checking instanceof/getClass.
  • Comparing Integer values with == (cache trap).

Interview: "What is the contract between equals and hashCode? What if you override only equals?"

  • If a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(); hash codes must be stable while the object is unchanged; unequal objects may collide.
  • Only equals overridden: equal objects get different identity hashes, land in different buckets; HashSet allows duplicates and contains/get fail.
  • The five properties of equals: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, non-null.
  • How to write them: same fields, Objects.equals, Objects.hash, instanceof or getClass() with the trade-off.
  • Records generate both; keys should be immutable; Integer cache trap for ==.

Interview questions — JVM and memory

Explain the JVM architecture.

Three main parts. The class loader subsystem loads, links and initializes classes. The runtime data areas: heap and Metaspace shared by all threads, and per thread a JVM stack of frames, a PC register and a native method stack. The execution engine: interpreter, JIT compiler (C1 and C2, tiered) and garbage collector. JNI connects Java to native code.

What is stored in the stack and what in the heap?

The stack (one per thread) holds frames with local primitives, local references, parameters and the operand stack; frames disappear when the method returns. The heap (shared) holds all objects and arrays, including instance fields, boxed values and the String pool. A local variable Product p = new Product() keeps the reference on the stack and the object on the heap. Static fields live with the class data, and class metadata lives in Metaspace.

What is the difference between StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError?

StackOverflowError means one thread's stack is full, nearly always from runaway recursion; fix the base case or use a loop. OutOfMemoryError means the JVM cannot allocate more memory in the heap (Java heap space), Metaspace, or for a new native thread. It usually comes from a leak, too much data loaded at once, or a heap that is too small. Both are Errors, not exceptions you normally catch.

How does garbage collection decide what to remove?

The GC traces from GC roots (local variables on thread stacks, static fields, active threads, JNI references) and marks everything reachable. Unreachable objects are garbage, even when they reference each other in a cycle. Memory is reclaimed by sweeping, copying or compacting. Java does not use reference counting.

What are the young and old generations, and what is a minor vs a full GC?

Most objects die young, so the heap is split into a young generation (Eden plus two survivor spaces) and an old generation. New objects go to Eden. A minor GC copies the live objects of Eden and one survivor into the other survivor; each survival raises an object's age, and old-enough objects are promoted to the old generation. When the old generation fills, a major GC runs; a full GC collects the whole heap and causes the longest stop-the-world pause.

Which garbage collectors do you know and when would you use each?

Serial for tiny heaps and single-CPU containers; Parallel for throughput-oriented batch work; G1, the default since Java 9, for balanced pause times and throughput using heap regions and a pause goal; ZGC and Shenandoah for low-latency services and large heaps with mostly concurrent work. CMS was removed in Java 14. Start with the default, measure with GC logs, and change only for evidence.

Can you force garbage collection? What about finalize()?

No. System.gc() is only a request that the JVM may ignore, and calling it often triggers an expensive full GC. finalize() has no timing guarantee, is slow, and is deprecated for removal since Java 18. Release resources with try-with-resources (AutoCloseable), and use Cleaner as a safety net for native resources.

Can a Java program have memory leaks? Give examples and say how you would find one.

Yes, when unneeded objects stay reachable: static collections that only grow, caches without eviction, listeners never unregistered, ThreadLocal values in pooled threads, unclosed resources, and mutable keys in hash maps. To find one, watch the heap after GC, take heap dumps (jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump or -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError), open them in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM, and follow the path to GC roots from the largest retained objects.

What do strong, soft, weak and phantom references mean?

A strong reference is a normal variable and prevents collection. A SoftReference object is cleared only when memory is short, so it suits caches. A WeakReference is cleared at the next GC if no strong reference remains, as used by WeakHashMap. A PhantomReference is enqueued after the object is finalised and is used for cleanup actions; Cleaner builds on it.

Describe class loading and the parent delegation model.

A class is loaded lazily: loading (read bytes, create the class in Metaspace), linking (verify, prepare statics with defaults, resolve references) and initialization (run static initializers once). The loaders are bootstrap (core JDK), platform and application. A loader first delegates to its parent and only loads the class itself if the parent cannot. This prevents applications from replacing core classes like java.lang.String and avoids duplicate loading.

What is the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?

ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception thrown when code loads a class by name (Class.forName, loadClass) and it is not on the classpath. NoClassDefFoundError is an Error thrown when a class that was available at compile time is missing at runtime, or when its static initialization already failed. Typical fixes: add the dependency to the package, fix scopes, or find the earlier ExceptionInInitializerError.

What is the difference between == and equals()?

For primitives, == compares values. For objects, == compares references (are they the same object?), while equals() compares by meaning if the class overrides it; the default Object.equals is identical to ==. String, wrappers, BigDecimal and records override it. Use equals for content and == only for primitives, enums and identity checks.

Why must hashCode() be overridden when you override equals()?

The contract says equal objects must have equal hash codes. Hash collections use the hash code to choose a bucket before they call equals. If two equal objects hash differently, they go to different buckets, so a HashSet can hold "duplicates" and contains or HashMap.get cannot find an equal key. Use the same fields in both methods, via Objects.equals and Objects.hash, or a record.

What are the properties of a correct equals(), and instanceof vs getClass()?

Reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and false for null. instanceof accepts subclasses and works well for final classes and records; getClass() requires exactly the same class and avoids symmetry problems when subclasses add significant state, but fails with runtime proxies such as Hibernate lazy proxies. Choose one on purpose and document it.

What are C1, C2 and escape analysis?

C1 and C2 are HotSpot's JIT compilers: C1 compiles quickly with light optimisation, C2 compiles hot code with deep optimisation (tiered compilation uses both). Escape analysis lets C2 prove that an object never leaves a method, so it can avoid heap allocation (scalar replacement) or remove locks (lock elision). It explains JVM warm-up and why micro-benchmarks need JMH.

Cheat sheet — JVM and memory

  • JVM parts class loader subsystem, runtime data areas, execution engine, JNI.
  • Per thread JVM stack (frames), PC register, native method stack.
  • Shared heap (objects, arrays, String pool, statics) and Metaspace (class metadata, native memory).
  • Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8; limit with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.
  • Stack frame local variables, operand stack, constant pool link; popped on return.
  • Reference vs object reference on stack (or in a field), object on heap; assignment copies the reference.
  • StackOverflowError too deep recursion; fix base case or loop; -Xss sets stack size.
  • OutOfMemoryError heap space, Metaspace, GC overhead limit, unable to create native thread.
  • GC roots stack locals, statics, active threads, JNI refs.
  • Generations Eden + S0/S1 (young), tenured (old); minor GC is cheap, full GC is expensive.
  • Generational hypothesis most objects die young.
  • Collectors Serial, Parallel (throughput), G1 (default), ZGC, Shenandoah (low pause); CMS removed in 14.
  • System.gc() only a hint; finalize() deprecated for removal; use try-with-resources and Cleaner.
  • References strong, SoftReference (cache), WeakReference (WeakHashMap), PhantomReference.
  • Leak causes static collections, no-eviction caches, listeners, ThreadLocal in pools, unclosed resources, mutable keys.
  • Find leaks -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, jcmd GC.heap_dump, Eclipse MAT, jmap -histo.
  • Flags -Xms -Xmx -Xss -XX:MaxRAMPercentage -Xlog:gc.
  • Tools jps, jcmd, jstack (deadlocks), jmap, jstat, JFR, VisualVM.
  • JIT interpreter → C1 → C2 (tiered); warm-up; escape analysis can remove allocations.
  • Class loading loading → linking (verify, prepare, resolve) → initialization.
  • Loaders bootstrap → platform → application; parent first.
  • Initialization triggers new, static method, non-constant static field, Class.forName, subclass.
  • CNFE vs NCDFE checked exception from by-name load vs error for a missing or failed class at runtime.
  • equals contract reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, null → false.
  • hashCode contract equal objects ⇒ equal hash codes; stable while fields do not change.
  • Write both same fields, Objects.equals, Objects.hash; records do it for you; keys should be immutable.

Practice — JVM and memory

  1. Draw it (easy). For the Shop example in the stack-vs-heap article, change compute to also take a String and an int[]. Redraw the stack and heap at the deepest point. Done when each primitive, reference, object and array is in the right place.
  2. Recursion crash (easy). Write a recursive method without a base case, catch StackOverflowError, print the depth, then rerun with -Xss512k and -Xss4m. Done when you can explain the three depths you saw.
  3. Make an OutOfMemoryError (easy). Run the heap demo with -Xmx64m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and find the .hprof file. Done when you have the dump file and the error message.
  4. Watch the GC (medium). Run a loop that creates many short-lived objects with -Xlog:gc and with -XX:+UseSerialGC, -XX:+UseParallelGC and -XX:+UseG1GC. Compare the number and length of pauses. Done when you can describe the difference in one paragraph.
  5. Plant and find a leak (medium). Write a service class with a static HashMap cache that grows on every call. Run it under load with -Xmx128m, watch it with jstat -gc or VisualVM, take a dump with jcmd, open it in Eclipse MAT, and find the map. Then fix it with a bounded cache. Done when the post-GC heap stays flat.
  6. Weak vs strong (medium). Reproduce the WeakReference, SoftReference and WeakHashMap demos. Then make the WeakHashMap value strongly refer to its key and observe that the entry never disappears. Done when you can explain why.
  7. Class loading experiments (medium). Print the class loader of String, java.sql.Connection and your own class. Create classes with static blocks and predict the output order for new Child(), for reading a static final int constant, and for Class.forName. Done when all predictions match.
  8. Break and fix a HashMap key (medium). Write the BadPoint class, show that a HashSet contains duplicates, then fix it with equals and hashCode. Add a mutable-key demo and a record version. Done when all four variants print what the article predicts.
  9. Contract test (harder). Write a small test helper assertEqualsContract(a, b, c) that checks reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and null properties plus the hash code rule for three objects. Run it against a correct class, a class with only equals, and a subclass that adds a field with instanceof. Done when it catches both broken cases.
  10. Diagnose a crash (harder). Take any Spring Boot or plain Java app, start it with -Xmx64m, flood it with requests (a loop or a load tool), and write a short diagnosis: the error message, the area (heap, Metaspace, threads), the evidence from a heap dump or jstack, and the fix. Done when your note could be handed to a teammate.
8

Module 8·About 3 daysMust

Tools every Java developer uses

8 topics · about 1 h of reading

Knowing the language is half the job. The other half is the toolbox that every Java developer opens every day: a debugger to see what the program is really doing, a build tool (Maven or Gradle) to compile, test and package it, JUnit to prove it works, JDBC to talk to a database, and a logging library to know what happened in production. Spring Boot hides much of this behind starters and annotations, but when something breaks, you need to understand what is underneath.

This module connects to the rest of the notes: JDBC is what Spring Data JPA is built on (Spring Boot · Module 3), JUnit is the base of Spring testing (Spring Boot · Module 5), and the SQL you write here is covered in SQL · Module 1. It ends with the first portfolio project of the roadmap.

After this module you will be able to:

  • debug in IntelliJ with line, conditional and exception breakpoints, stepping, watches and expression evaluation, and attach to a remote JVM;
  • read and write a pom.xml, explain scopes, transitive dependencies and the build lifecycle, and run the common Maven commands; read a basic Gradle build;
  • write JUnit 5 tests with lifecycle methods, assertions, exceptions and parameterised data;
  • write a JDBC DAO with PreparedStatement, try-with-resources and transactions, and show how SQL injection works and how to stop it;
  • log properly with SLF4J: levels, parameterised messages, exceptions, and what never to log;
  • write Javadoc and follow a consistent code style.

Debugging in IntelliJ: breakpoints, stepping, watches and remote debug

A debugger pauses your program at a breakpoint so you can step line by line, inspect variables, evaluate expressions and even change values — far faster and more reliable than adding System.out.println everywhere.

Printing values to find a bug means edit, compile, run, read, repeat, and you only see what you thought to print. A debugger lets you stop the running program, look at everything, and move forward one step at a time. The ideas are the same in Eclipse, VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA; the keys below are IntelliJ's default keymap on Windows.

Starting a debug session

  1. Click in the gutter (the grey strip left of the line numbers) next to a line, or press Ctrl+F8. A red dot appears: a line breakpoint.
  2. Start the program with Debug (the bug icon, or Shift+F9) instead of Run. For a test, click the green arrow beside the test method and choose Debug.
  3. When execution reaches the line, the program suspends before running it, and the Debug window shows frames, variables and watches.
  4. Step, inspect, then press F9 (Resume) to run to the next breakpoint or the end.

A bug to practise on

import java.util.List;

public class Cart {
    record Item(String name, int price, int qty) {}

    static int total(List<Item> items) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < items.size() - 1; i++) {      // bug: skips the last item
            Item item = items.get(i);
            sum += item.price() * item.qty();
        }
        return sum;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Item> items = List.of(
                new Item("Pen", 10, 5),
                new Item("Book", 120, 2),
                new Item("Bag", 800, 1));
        System.out.println("Total: " + total(items));      // expected 1090
    }
}
Total: 290

Set a breakpoint on sum += ..., debug, and press F9 repeatedly. The Variables panel shows i = 0, then 1, and then the loop ends without ever seeing i = 2. Add the watch items.size() and the off-by-one is obvious: the loop stops at size() - 1. This "stop and look" approach finds in a minute what takes ten minutes with prints.

Kinds of breakpoints

TypeHow to set itUse it when
LineClick in the gutterYou know roughly where the problem is
ConditionalRight-click the red dot, type a condition such as i == 500 or order.getId() == 1042Bug appears only for one item in a loop or for one request
Logging (no suspend)In the same dialog untick Suspend and tick Evaluate and logYou want a print without editing code or stopping
ExceptionRun → View Breakpoints (Ctrl+Shift+F8) → + → Java Exception Breakpoints, e.g. NullPointerExceptionStops where the exception is thrown, even if you do not know the line
MethodClick the gutter at a method declaration (diamond icon)Stop on any call of a method or interface implementation (slow; use sparingly)
Field watchpointClick the gutter at a field declarationFind who changes a field

Breakpoint options also include Pass count (stop on the 100th hit), Enable only after another breakpoint, and choosing whether to suspend All threads or only the Thread that hit it (use Thread in servers so other requests keep running). Mute Breakpoints disables them all temporarily without deleting.

Stepping

ActionKeyWhat it does
Step OverF8Run the current line completely, including any method calls on it, and stop at the next line
Step IntoF7Go inside the method called on the current line (skips JDK/library code by default)
Smart Step IntoShift+F7Choose which of several calls on the line to enter
Force Step IntoAlt+Shift+F7Enter even library code
Step OutShift+F8Finish the current method and stop in its caller
Run to CursorAlt+F9Continue until execution reaches the line where your cursor is
ResumeF9Continue to the next breakpoint
Drop FrameDebug toolbarThrow away the current frame and re-run the method from its start (side effects already done are not undone)
StopCtrl+F2End the session

Typical rhythm: step over most lines; step into only your own method that you suspect; step out when you realise the bug is not in this method.

Looking at data

  • Frames panel. The call stack of the paused thread (the same chain as a stack trace). Click an older frame to see its local variables and the line that made the call: invaluable for "how did we get here?"
  • Variables panel. All locals, parameters and this. Expand objects to see fields. Hover over a variable in the editor for a quick look. IntelliJ also shows values inline, in grey, next to your code.
  • Watches. Click + in the Watches area and enter any expression (items.size(), order.total() > 1000). It is re-evaluated at every stop.
  • Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8). A mini-console: type any Java, including method calls, and see the result. Example: items.stream().mapToInt(Item::price).sum(). Beware of methods with side effects (they really run).
  • Set Value (F2 on a variable). Change a variable at runtime — set i back to 0, or force a null to a real object — to test a fix without restarting.
  • Mark Object. Give an object a label (F11) so you can recognise the same instance across stops.
  • Debugging streams. On a line with a stream pipeline, click Trace Current Stream Chain in the debug toolbar. It shows the elements before and after every step (filter, map, …), which solves most "why is my stream empty?" questions.

Hot reload

If you edit a method body while paused, IntelliJ can reload the changed class (Build → Recompile, then confirm the reload prompt) so you can continue with the new code. It works for changes inside method bodies only; adding or removing methods or fields needs a restart.

Remote debugging

A remote debug attaches your IDE to a JVM running somewhere else (another process, a Docker container, a test server). The JVM must be started with the JDWP (Java Debug Wire Protocol) agent:

$ java -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=*:5005 -jar app.jar
Listening for transport dt_socket at address: 5005
  • server=y — the JVM waits for a debugger to connect; suspend=n — start running at once (use suspend=y to pause until a debugger attaches, handy to debug start-up code).
  • address=*:5005 — listen on all network interfaces, port 5005. A bare address=5005 listens only on localhost in recent JDKs.
  • In IntelliJ: Run → Edit Configurations → + → Remote JVM Debug, enter the host and port 5005, click Debug. Breakpoints now work in the remote process. The source code must match the deployed code.
  • With Maven and Spring Boot you can pass the same flag as a JVM argument; in Docker, publish port 5005 (-p 5005:5005).

Rule: never leave the debug port open in production

Anyone who can reach a JDWP port can run arbitrary code inside your JVM. Use remote debugging only on local or protected test environments, and never expose port 5005 to the internet.

IntelliJ shortcuts worth learning (Windows)

KeysAction
Shift+F10 / Shift+F9Run / Debug the selected configuration
Ctrl+Shift+F10Run the class or test at the cursor
Shift ShiftSearch everywhere (classes, files, actions, settings)
Ctrl+N / Ctrl+Shift+NGo to class / file
Ctrl+B / Ctrl+Alt+BGo to declaration / implementations
Alt+F7Find usages
Alt+EnterShow quick fixes and intentions
Alt+InsertGenerate constructor, getters, equals/hashCode, toString
Shift+F6Rename (safe refactoring)
Ctrl+Alt+V / Ctrl+Alt+MExtract variable / method
Ctrl+Alt+L / Ctrl+Alt+OReformat code / optimise imports
Ctrl+D / Ctrl+YDuplicate line / delete line
Ctrl+Shift+TJump between a class and its test, or create one

Tips

  • Put the breakpoint before the problem, not on it; you can always step forward but not back (except with Drop Frame).
  • For a loop that fails on iteration 5,000, use a conditional breakpoint or pass count rather than pressing F9 5,000 times.
  • If breakpoints show a crossed-out grey dot, the line has no executable code, the class is not loaded yet, or the source differs from the compiled class: rebuild.
  • Read the stack trace of an exception first: the line number of your own code at the top of the "at com.shop…" frames is the best place for the first breakpoint.

Edge cases

  • Pausing at a breakpoint in a web app suspends that thread; HTTP clients may time out while you think. Increase timeouts in debug runs.
  • Evaluating an expression that calls code with side effects (saving to a database, sending an email) executes it for real.
  • Optimised or generated code (Lombok, proxies, lambdas) may show unexpected frames; IntelliJ hides many of them by default.
  • A debugger changes timing, so race conditions can disappear while debugging (a "Heisenbug"). Use logs for concurrency problems.

Interview: "How do you debug a problem in a Java application?"

  • Reproduce, read the stack trace, set a breakpoint before the suspected line, step through, and inspect variables and the call stack.
  • Name the tools: conditional and exception breakpoints, watches, evaluate expression, step over/into/out, run to cursor, stream trace, remote debug with JDWP.
  • For production: logs, thread dumps (jstack), heap dumps, JFR — not a remote debugger on a live server.

Maven: pom.xml, dependencies, lifecycle and commands

Maven builds a Java project from one pom.xml: it downloads dependencies, compiles, tests, packages and installs, following a fixed lifecycle and a standard folder layout.

A build tool automates the repeatable work: downloading libraries, compiling, running tests, creating a JAR and publishing it. Without one, you would copy JAR files by hand and call javac yourself. Maven (Apache) is the most widely used in Java companies and the default in many Spring Boot tutorials. Its idea is convention over configuration: if you follow the standard layout, you need very little configuration.

Coordinates

Every artifact has unique coordinates (GAV):

groupId
The organisation or project group, usually a reversed domain: com.shop, org.postgresql.
artifactId
The name of the module: order-service, postgresql. It becomes the JAR file name.
version
For example 1.0.0 (a release) or 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT (a work in progress).
packaging
jar (default), war or pom (for parent projects).

Standard directory layout

order-service/
├── pom.xml
├── mvnw, mvnw.cmd, .mvn/        (Maven wrapper)
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/shop/        production code
│   │   └── resources/            application.properties, logback.xml, SQL files
│   └── test/
│       ├── java/com/shop/        test code (JUnit)
│       └── resources/            test-only resources
└── target/                       build output (never commit this)

A complete annotated pom.xml

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
                             https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <!-- Coordinates of THIS project -->
    <groupId>com.shop</groupId>
    <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>
    <name>Order Service</name>

    <!-- Values reused below, and settings read by plugins -->
    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
        <junit.version>5.10.2</junit.version>
    </properties>

    <!-- Central place to fix versions (a BOM); dependencies below omit the version -->
    <dependencyManagement>
        <dependencies>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.junit</groupId>
                <artifactId>junit-bom</artifactId>
                <version>${junit.version}</version>
                <type>pom</type>
                <scope>import</scope>
            </dependency>
        </dependencies>
    </dependencyManagement>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>                                  <!-- logging implementation + SLF4J -->
            <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
            <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
            <version>1.5.6</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>                                  <!-- JDBC driver: needed only at run time -->
            <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
            <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
            <version>42.7.3</version>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>                                  <!-- tests only; version from the BOM -->
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>                                  <!-- compiles src/main/java -->
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.13.0</version>
            </plugin>
            <plugin>                                  <!-- runs *Test classes in the test phase -->
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.2.5</version>
            </plugin>
            <plugin>                                  <!-- builds the JAR and its manifest -->
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-jar-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.4.1</version>
                <configuration>
                    <archive>
                        <manifest>
                            <mainClass>com.shop.App</mainClass>
                        </manifest>
                    </archive>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

The versions shown are real releases, but use the current ones for your project (Maven Central search or your IDE's dependency completion shows them). Spring Boot projects normally inherit from spring-boot-starter-parent, which already manages hundreds of versions in a BOM, so most dependencies there have no <version> line.

Dependency scopes

ScopeCompile classpathTest classpathRuntime / packagedExample
compile (default)YesYesYesJackson, Guava
providedYesYesNo (the server provides it)Servlet API on Tomcat, Lombok
runtimeNoYesYesJDBC driver
testNoYesNoJUnit, Mockito

Two more exist: system (a local file; avoid) and import (only inside dependencyManagement, for BOMs).

Transitive dependencies and conflicts

When you add library A and A needs B, Maven downloads B too. That is a transitive dependency. Show the whole tree with:

$ mvn dependency:tree
[INFO] com.shop:order-service:jar:1.0.0-SNAPSHOT
[INFO] +- ch.qos.logback:logback-classic:jar:1.5.6:compile
[INFO] |  +- ch.qos.logback:logback-core:jar:1.5.6:compile
[INFO] |  \- org.slf4j:slf4j-api:jar:2.0.13:compile
[INFO] +- org.postgresql:postgresql:jar:42.7.3:runtime
[INFO] \- org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:jar:5.10.2:test

Trouble starts when two libraries need different versions of the same artifact (a version conflict). Maven keeps only one, chosen by two rules: the nearest to your project in the tree wins, and if the distance is equal the first declared wins. The loser may lack a method the other library needs, causing NoSuchMethodError or NoClassDefFoundError at runtime. How to fix it:

  • Find it with mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose (shows omitted duplicates) and search for the artifact.
  • Pin one version in dependencyManagement (this overrides what transitive paths ask for).
  • Remove an unwanted transitive dependency with an <exclusions> block inside the dependency.
  • In Spring Boot, prefer the version managed by the Boot BOM and override only deliberately.
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>legacy-client</artifactId>
    <version>2.3.0</version>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>commons-logging</groupId>
            <artifactId>commons-logging</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

The build lifecycle

A lifecycle is an ordered list of phases. When you run a phase, Maven runs every phase before it, in order. The default lifecycle's main phases:

PhaseWhat happensPlugin goal bound by default (jar projects)
validateChecks the project is correct and all information is available—
compileCompiles src/main/java into target/classescompiler:compile
testCompiles and runs unit tests (does not need the JAR)compiler:testCompile, surefire:test
packageCreates the JAR/WAR in target/jar:jar
verifyRuns checks on the package, such as integration testsfailsafe if configured
installCopies the artifact to your local repository ~/.m2 so other local projects can use itinstall:install
deployUploads to a remote repository (Nexus, Artifactory, GitHub Packages)deploy:deploy

There are two other lifecycles: clean (mvn clean deletes the target folder) and site (documentation). A plugin is the code that does the work, and a goal is one task of a plugin, written plugin:goal (for example dependency:tree). Phases are just slots; goals are bound to phases. Key plugins: compiler (javac), surefire (unit tests; picks classes named *Test, Test*, *Tests), failsafe (integration tests named *IT, run in integration-test/verify), jar, and for Spring Boot the spring-boot-maven-plugin that creates an executable "fat" JAR.

Common commands

CommandMeaning
mvn cleanDelete target/
mvn compileCompile main code
mvn testCompile and run unit tests
mvn packageBuild the JAR (runs tests first)
mvn clean installClean build, run tests, install into ~/.m2 — the everyday full build
mvn test -Dtest=OrderServiceTestRun one test class (or -Dtest=OrderServiceTest#shouldCreateOrder for one method)
mvn package -DskipTestsCompile tests but do not run them
mvn package -Dmaven.test.skip=trueDo not even compile tests
mvn dependency:treePrint the dependency tree
mvn help:effective-pomShow the final POM after inheritance and defaults
mvn -U clean installForce-update snapshots and releases that failed to download
mvn -o ...Offline mode, use only the local repository
mvn versions:display-dependency-updatesList newer versions of your dependencies
mvn -q ...Quiet output
 
$ mvn clean install
[INFO] --- clean:3.2.0:clean (default-clean) @ order-service ---
[INFO] --- compiler:3.13.0:compile (default-compile) @ order-service ---
[INFO] --- surefire:3.2.5:test (default-test) @ order-service ---
[INFO] --- jar:3.4.1:jar (default-jar) @ order-service ---
[INFO] --- install:3.1.1:install (default-install) @ order-service ---
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

The local repository, SNAPSHOT vs release, and the wrapper

  • Local repository: ~/.m2/repository (on Windows C:\Users\you\.m2\repository). Downloaded dependencies are cached there; ~/.m2/settings.xml holds mirrors, proxy and repository credentials. The default remote is Maven Central.
  • Release (1.2.0) is immutable: once published, the same version always contains the same bytes. -SNAPSHOT (1.3.0-SNAPSHOT) means "work in progress"; Maven re-checks remote repositories for newer snapshot builds (daily by default). Never depend on a SNAPSHOT in a release.
  • Maven Wrapper: the files mvnw, mvnw.cmd and .mvn/ download and use a fixed Maven version, so every developer and the CI server build with the same one. Run ./mvnw clean install (Linux/macOS) or mvnw.cmd clean install (Windows). Spring Initializr adds it automatically; mvn wrapper:wrapper adds it to an existing project. Commit it to Git.

Multi-module projects (a glimpse)

Large systems split into modules (for example common, order-service, payment-service) under a parent POM with <packaging>pom</packaging> and a <modules> list. Children inherit the parent's properties, dependencyManagement and plugin settings. Build a single module and what it needs with mvn -pl order-service -am install.

Rules

  • The packaged artifact is target/<artifactId>-<version>.jar.
  • Running a phase runs all earlier phases; mvn install therefore runs the tests.
  • Do not commit target/ (add it to .gitignore); do commit pom.xml and the wrapper files.
  • Test dependencies must have <scope>test</scope>, or they end up in the shipped application.

Conventions

  • Define versions once in <properties> or dependencyManagement; never hard-code the same version in several places.
  • Set Java with maven.compiler.release (not only source/target), so the code is checked against that version's API.
  • Pin plugin versions for reproducible builds.
  • Keep dependencies minimal; remove unused ones. Every dependency is code you must keep updated and secure.

Common mistakes

  • Abusing -DskipTests. Skipping tests to "make the build pass" hides real failures and ships bugs. Use it only for a quick local packaging when you have just run the tests, never in the CI pipeline for release builds.
  • Wrong scope: a JDBC driver at test scope (the app fails at runtime with "No suitable driver"), or Lombok at compile in a WAR.
  • Putting JARs in the project folder instead of using dependencies.
  • IDE shows red code after editing pom.xml: reload the Maven project (the small "m" button or Ctrl+Shift+O in the Maven window).
  • A corrupt download in ~/.m2 (.lastUpdated files): delete the artifact's folder or run mvn -U.

Errors you will meet

  • Could not resolve dependencies — wrong coordinates, no network/proxy, or a private repository without credentials.
  • invalid target release: 21 or release version 21 not supported — Maven is running on an older JDK than the release you set. Check mvn -version and JAVA_HOME.
  • No tests were executed or tests silently not found — the class name does not match the Surefire pattern, or the JUnit version is wrong for the Surefire plugin.
  • Could not find or load main class — the manifest has no mainClass; plain jar packaging also does not include dependencies, which is why Spring Boot uses its own plugin.

Interview: "What is Maven? Explain the lifecycle and dependency scopes."

  • Build and dependency-management tool driven by pom.xml; coordinates groupId, artifactId, version; standard layout; central repository and ~/.m2 cache.
  • Lifecycle phases in order: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy; running one runs the earlier ones; plugin goals do the work.
  • Scopes: compile, provided, runtime, test. Transitive dependencies, nearest-wins conflict resolution, dependencyManagement and BOMs, exclusions.
  • install vs deploy: local repository vs remote repository. SNAPSHOT vs release.
  • Why the wrapper: same Maven version for everyone.

Gradle basics and Maven vs Gradle

Gradle is the other major JVM build tool: build files are code (Kotlin or Groovy), dependencies are declared by configuration such as implementation and testImplementation, and everything you run is a task.

Gradle is used by Android projects and by many Java and Kotlin teams. Spring Initializr offers both Maven and Gradle, so you should be able to read a Gradle build even if your team uses Maven. Instead of XML, Gradle uses a script, written in the Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts, the current default) or the Groovy DSL (build.gradle).

plugins {
    java                                   // adds compileJava, test, jar, build ...
    application                            // adds the run task
}

group = "com.shop"
version = "1.0.0"

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion.set(JavaLanguageVersion.of(21))   // build with Java 21
    }
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()                         // same Maven Central, same artifacts
}

dependencies {
    implementation("ch.qos.logback:logback-classic:1.5.6")   // compile + runtime
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql:42.7.3")          // runtime only
    testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:5.10.2"))
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")    // tests only
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}

application {
    mainClass.set("com.shop.App")
}

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()                     // run JUnit 5 tests
}

Dependency configurations

GradleMaven scope (roughly)Meaning
implementationcompileNeeded to compile and run; not exposed to consumers of your library
api (java-library plugin)compilePart of your library's public API, visible to consumers
compileOnlyprovidedNeeded to compile only (Lombok, servlet API)
runtimeOnlyruntimeNeeded at run time only (JDBC driver)
testImplementationtestFor compiling and running tests
annotationProcessor—Annotation processors such as Lombok or MapStruct

Tasks and the wrapper

Gradle's unit of work is a task. Plugins add tasks; tasks depend on one another, forming a graph, and Gradle runs only what is needed (and skips tasks whose inputs did not change: UP-TO-DATE). Always use the Gradle Wrapper (gradlew / gradlew.bat plus gradle/wrapper/), which fetches the right Gradle version, just like mvnw.

$ ./gradlew build              # compile, test, assemble the JAR (output in build/libs)
$ ./gradlew test               # run tests only
$ ./gradlew clean build        # delete build/ first
$ ./gradlew run                # run the application plugin's main class
$ ./gradlew tasks              # list available tasks
$ ./gradlew dependencies       # print the dependency tree
$ ./gradlew build -x test      # build but exclude the test task

On Windows use gradlew.bat (or .\gradlew in PowerShell). Gradle puts its output under build/ (Maven uses target/) and caches downloads in ~/.gradle. A project also has settings.gradle.kts that names the project and lists modules.

Maven vs Gradle

PointMavenGradle
Build filepom.xml (XML, declarative)build.gradle(.kts) (script, programmable)
Learning curveEasy: fixed lifecycle, uniform projectsSteeper: flexible, so builds differ more
SpeedGood; rebuilds more than neededFaster on repeated builds (incremental builds, build cache, daemon)
CustomisingVia plugins and configurationWrite logic directly in the script
Output foldertarget/build/
Common inEnterprise Java, many Spring Boot servicesAndroid, Kotlin, large multi-module builds
Wrappermvnwgradlew

Neither is "better". Learn Maven deeply first (it dominates interviews and Indian service-company projects), and be able to read Gradle. Both resolve the same artifacts from Maven Central.

Common mistakes

  • Using a globally installed gradle instead of the wrapper, so teammates and CI use other versions.
  • Forgetting useJUnitPlatform(): Gradle then finds no JUnit 5 tests.
  • Using implementation where a JDBC driver should be runtimeOnly, or api everywhere, which leaks dependencies.

Interview: "Maven vs Gradle?"

  • Both manage dependencies and builds from Maven Central. Maven: XML, fixed lifecycle, convention. Gradle: script-based, task graph, incremental builds and caching, more flexible.
  • Map the vocabulary: scope test ↔ testImplementation, provided ↔ compileOnly, runtime ↔ runtimeOnly, phase ↔ task.
  • Say which you use and why; show you can read the other.

JUnit 5: writing and running unit tests
