A unit test is a small method that calls your code with known input and asserts the expected result; JUnit 5 finds methods marked @Test, runs them in isolation and reports which ones fail.

A unit test checks one small piece of behaviour (usually one method or class) automatically and quickly, without a database or network. Tests catch bugs when you write the code, and — more importantly — when someone changes it six months later. JUnit 5 is the standard Java test framework (the Spring Boot test starter includes it). It consists of the Platform (runs tests), Jupiter (the API and engine you write against: org.junit.jupiter.api) and Vintage (runs old JUnit 4 tests). Spring-specific testing (@SpringBootTest, mocks, MockMvc) is covered in Spring Boot · Module 5.

Setup

Add the dependency with test scope (as in the pom.xml above): org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter, which brings the API, the engine and parameterised tests. Use a recent Surefire plugin (2.22 or newer) so Maven can run JUnit 5. Test classes go in src/test/java, in the same package as the class under test.

A first test

package com.shop;

public class PriceCalculator {
    /** Price in paise after a percentage discount (0-100). */
    public long finalPrice(long amount, int discountPercent) {
        if (amount < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must not be negative");
        }
        if (discountPercent < 0 || discountPercent > 100) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("discount must be between 0 and 100");
        }
        return amount - amount * discountPercent / 100;
    }
}
package com.shop;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.BeforeEach;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.DisplayName;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class PriceCalculatorTest {

    private PriceCalculator calculator;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        calculator = new PriceCalculator();       // fresh object for every test
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("10% discount on 1000 gives 900")
    void shouldApplyDiscount() {
        // Arrange
        long amount = 1000;
        // Act
        long result = calculator.finalPrice(amount, 10);
        // Assert
        assertEquals(900, result);
    }

    @Test
    void shouldReturnSameAmountWhenNoDiscount() {
        assertEquals(1000, calculator.finalPrice(1000, 0));
    }

    @Test
    void shouldRejectNegativeAmount() {
        IllegalArgumentException ex = assertThrows(
                IllegalArgumentException.class,
                () -> calculator.finalPrice(-1, 10));
        assertEquals("amount must not be negative", ex.getMessage());
    }
}

Test classes and methods need not be public in JUnit 5 (package-private is fine), but must not be private or static. JUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method, so fields set in one test never leak into another.

Run tests from IntelliJ by clicking the green arrow beside the class or method, or with Ctrl+Shift+F10 at the cursor. From Maven:

$ mvn test
[INFO] Running com.shop.PriceCalculatorTest
[ERROR] PriceCalculatorTest.shouldApplyDiscount:25 expected: <900> but was: <1000>
[ERROR] Tests run: 3, Failures: 1, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD FAILURE

A failure means an assertion was false. An error means an unexpected exception was thrown. Surefire writes reports to target/surefire-reports.

Annotations

AnnotationPurpose
@TestMarks a test method
@BeforeEach / @AfterEachRun before / after every test method (create objects, clean up)
@BeforeAll / @AfterAllRun once before / after all tests in the class; the method must be static (unless the lifecycle is per-class)
@DisplayName("…")Readable name shown in reports
@Disabled("reason")Skip a test or class (always give a reason)
@NestedGroup related tests in an inner class
@ParameterizedTestRun the same test with several inputs
@RepeatedTest(n), @TimeoutRepeat; fail if it takes too long
@Tag("slow")Label tests so you can include or exclude groups

JUnit 4 (org.junit.Test, @Before, @After, @RunWith) still exists in old projects; the names above are the JUnit 5 versions. Do not mix the two packages in one class.

Assertions

All are static methods of org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions. Put the expected value first, actual second, so failure messages read correctly.

AssertionChecks
assertEquals(expected, actual)Equal by equals (or numerically for primitives); overloads with a delta for doubles: assertEquals(0.3, x, 1e-9)
assertNotEqualsNot equal
assertTrue(cond), assertFalse(cond)A boolean condition
assertNull, assertNotNullNull checks
assertSame, assertNotSameSame object (==)
assertArrayEqualsArrays element by element
assertIterableEqualsCollections element by element, in order
assertThrows(Type.class, executable)The code throws that exception type (returns it for more checks)
assertDoesNotThrowThe code throws nothing
assertAll(a1, a2, …)Runs all assertions and reports all failures, not only the first
assertTimeout(duration, executable)Finishes within the time
fail("message")Fail explicitly
 
@Test
void shouldCheckSeveralThingsAtOnce() {
    Customer c = new Customer("asha@mail.in", "Asha");
    assertAll("customer",
            () -> assertEquals("asha@mail.in", c.email()),
            () -> assertEquals("Asha", c.name()),
            () -> assertNotNull(c.toString()));
}

@Test
void shouldCompareDoubleWithTolerance() {
    assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2, 1e-9);        // not assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2)
}

Libraries such as AssertJ (assertThat(list).hasSize(3).contains("a")) make assertions more readable; many Spring projects use it together with JUnit.

Parameterised tests

Instead of copying a test five times with different numbers, feed one test method a table of inputs.

import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;

class PriceCalculatorParamTest {
    private final PriceCalculator calculator = new PriceCalculator();

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} paise with {1}% off is {2}")
    @CsvSource({
            "1000, 10, 900",
            "1000, 0, 1000",
            "1000, 100, 0",
            "999, 50, 500"          // 999 * 50 / 100 = 499 (integer division), 999 - 499
    })
    void shouldCalculateFinalPrice(long amount, int percent, long expected) {
        assertEquals(expected, calculator.finalPrice(amount, percent));
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(ints = {-1, 101, 1000})
    void shouldRejectInvalidDiscount(int percent) {
        assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
                () -> calculator.finalPrice(100, percent));
    }
}

Other sources: @MethodSource("method") (a static method returning a stream of arguments — for objects), @EnumSource, @NullAndEmptySource, @CsvFileSource. Each row appears as a separate test in the report.

Arrange-Act-Assert and naming

  1. Arrange — create the object under test and its input.
  2. Act — call the one method you are testing.
  3. Assert — check the result or the state.

Keep the three parts visible (a blank line between them). A test checks one behaviour. Name tests after the behaviour: shouldRejectNegativeAmount, givenExpiredCoupon_whenApply_thenThrows, returnsEmptyListForUnknownCustomer — or use @DisplayName with a full sentence. A test name should tell you what broke without opening the file.

What makes a good unit test (FIRST)

  • Fast — milliseconds. Slow tests do not get run.
  • Isolated — no dependence on test order, shared state, the clock, or external systems. Replace collaborators with fakes or mocks (Mockito, see Module 5 of Spring Boot).
  • Repeatable — same result on every machine, every run (no randomness without a seed, no real dates).
  • Self-validating — pass or fail by itself; no reading of console output.
  • Timely — written with (or before) the code.

Test the edges: zero, one, many, null, empty string, boundary values (0, 100, 101), and error paths — not only the happy path. Aim for meaningful coverage of business logic rather than a 100% number.

Rules

  • Test methods are void, take no arguments (except in parameterised tests), and are not private or static.
  • Tests must not depend on execution order; JUnit does not guarantee one.
  • Surefire only picks classes named *Test, Test*, *Tests or *TestCase by default.
  • @BeforeAll/@AfterAll must be static in the default lifecycle.

Common mistakes

  • Swapping expected and actual, which makes failure messages misleading.
  • Tests with no assertion (they pass but prove nothing).
  • Catching the exception manually in a try/catch and forgetting fail(); use assertThrows.
  • Sharing mutable state through static fields between tests.
  • Testing implementation details (private methods, call order) instead of behaviour, so every refactor breaks tests.
  • Using assertEquals(double, double) without a delta.

Version note

The examples use JUnit 5 (Jupiter) with the packages org.junit.jupiter.api and org.junit.jupiter.params. A newer major version, JUnit 6, was released in late 2025 and keeps the same annotations and packages for everyday use; check the project's dependency version before copying build settings, because the minimum Java version is higher. Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x set the JUnit version for you through their BOM.

Interview: "How do you unit-test a method? JUnit 4 vs 5?"

  • Arrange-Act-Assert; one behaviour per test; cover happy path, edge cases and exceptions (assertThrows).
  • Isolation: fresh object per test via @BeforeEach; mock external dependencies.
  • JUnit 5 has modular architecture (Platform, Jupiter, Vintage), @BeforeEach instead of @Before, @ParameterizedTest, @Nested, assertAll, lambdas in assertions, and extensions instead of runners.
  • Unit test vs integration test: speed, scope, and what is real (database, Spring context).

JDBC basics: connecting, PreparedStatement and SQL injection

JDBC is Java's standard API for relational databases: a driver implements it, DriverManager gives you a Connection, and you run SQL through a PreparedStatement with ? placeholders — never by concatenating user input.

JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is a set of interfaces in java.sql. Your code talks to the interfaces; a JDBC driver — a JAR provided by the database vendor — implements them for PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle and so on. Frameworks like Spring Data JPA, Hibernate and MyBatis all run on JDBC underneath, so understanding it explains what they do and why things go wrong.

The core types

TypeRole
DriverManagerFinds a registered driver and opens a connection from a URL
ConnectionOne session with the database; controls transactions; creates statements
StatementRuns a fixed SQL string
PreparedStatementPrecompiled SQL with ? parameters, safe and reusable
CallableStatementCalls stored procedures and functions
ResultSetThe rows returned by a query; a cursor you move with next()
SQLExceptionAnything that goes wrong (checked exception)

Setting up

Add the driver as a runtime dependency (see the pom.xml): org.postgresql:postgresql, or for MySQL com.mysql:mysql-connector-j. Since JDBC 4 (Java 6) the driver on the classpath registers itself, so the old line Class.forName("org.postgresql.Driver") is unnecessary. Create the table once:

CREATE TABLE customers (
    id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,          -- MySQL: BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY
    name    VARCHAR(100)  NOT NULL,
    email   VARCHAR(150)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    city    VARCHAR(60),
    balance NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
DatabaseURL pattern
PostgreSQLjdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
MySQLjdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/shop

The URL has the shape jdbc:<vendor>://host:port/database?options. The default ports are 5432 (PostgreSQL) and 3306 (MySQL).

Connect and run a query

import java.sql.*;

public class FirstQuery {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
        String url = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop";
        String user = System.getenv("DB_USER");            // never hard-code secrets
        String password = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD");

        String sql = "SELECT id, name, city FROM customers WHERE city = ?";

        try (Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password);
             PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {

            ps.setString(1, "Pune");                        // parameter index starts at 1

            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                while (rs.next()) {                         // move to the next row
                    long id = rs.getLong("id");
                    String name = rs.getString("name");
                    String city = rs.getString("city");
                    System.out.println(id + " " + name + " " + city);
                }
            }
        }                                                   // all three closed automatically
    }
}
1 Asha Rao Pune
4 Vikram Shah Pune

Three things to remember:

  • Use try-with-resources so ResultSet, PreparedStatement and Connection are always closed, even on exceptions. Closing the connection also closes its statements, but closing each one explicitly is good hygiene.
  • Parameter and column indexes start at 1, not 0. Prefer column names (rs.getString("name")) to numbers.
  • rs.next() returns false when there are no more rows; the cursor starts before the first row, so you must call next() before reading.

PreparedStatement methods

MethodUse for
executeQuery()SELECT; returns a ResultSet
executeUpdate()INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL; returns the number of affected rows
execute()Unknown or multiple results; returns true if the first result is a ResultSet
setString, setInt, setLong, setBigDecimal, setBooleanBind a parameter by position
setObject(i, localDate), setNull(i, Types.VARCHAR)Dates and times (java.time types work with JDBC 4.2 drivers); explicit NULL
addBatch() / executeBatch()Send many statements in one round trip

On ResultSet: getInt, getLong, getString, getBigDecimal, getBoolean, getObject("created", LocalDateTime.class). A SQL NULL becomes null for objects but 0/false for primitive getters; call rs.wasNull() straight after, or use getObject(col, Integer.class).

Statement vs PreparedStatement vs CallableStatement

PointStatementPreparedStatementCallableStatement
SQLComplete string each timeTemplate with ?, bound later{call proc(?, ?)}
SQL injectionVulnerable if you concatenate inputSafe for valuesSafe for parameters
PerformanceParsed every timeCan be pre-parsed and reusedRuns a stored routine
Use forFixed DDL with no inputAlmost everythingStored procedures and functions
 
try (CallableStatement cs = con.prepareCall("{call archive_orders(?)}")) {
    cs.setInt(1, 2024);
    cs.execute();
}

SQL injection: the attack

SQL injection happens when user input becomes part of the SQL text. The input can then change the meaning of the query. This code builds the query by concatenation:

static boolean login(Connection con, String email, String password) throws SQLException {
    String sql = "SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '" + email
               + "' AND password_hash = '" + password + "'";
    try (Statement st = con.createStatement();
         ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery(sql)) {
        return rs.next();                     // any row found = logged in
    }
}

With a normal input the SQL is ... WHERE email = 'asha@mail.in' AND password_hash = 'x'. Now an attacker types ' OR '1'='1 as both fields:

SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1' AND password_hash = '' OR '1'='1'

The condition is always true; the query returns rows and the attacker is "logged in" as the first user. Worse input like '; DROP TABLE users; -- can delete data on databases and drivers that accept several statements in one call. SQL injection has been in the OWASP Top 10 for years and remains a common cause of real data breaches.

The fix: PreparedStatement

static boolean login(Connection con, String email, String passwordHash) throws SQLException {
    String sql = "SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = ? AND password_hash = ?";
    try (PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
        ps.setString(1, email);               // the value can never become SQL
        ps.setString(2, passwordHash);
        try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
            return rs.next();
        }
    }
}

With a prepared statement the SQL text (with its ? placeholders) and the values travel separately. The database parses the structure first; later, the value ' OR '1'='1 is treated as one harmless string to compare with, not as code. (In real systems you also never store plain passwords: you hash them with BCrypt, covered in Spring Security.)

  • Placeholders work only for values, not for table names, column names or keywords like ORDER BY direction. If you must choose them from user input, validate against a fixed whitelist (Set.of("name", "city")) and build the text from your own constants.
  • For LIKE, put the wildcards in the value: ps.setString(1, "%" + term + "%");.
  • For IN (...) create as many ? as there are values.
  • ORMs are safe when you use their parameter features (JPQL :name, Spring Data derived queries), but string-concatenated JPQL or native SQL is just as vulnerable.

Rule: never build SQL by concatenating or formatting user input

Not with +, not with String.format, not with text blocks. Always bind values with PreparedStatement placeholders.

Conventions

  • Read the URL, user and password from environment variables or configuration, not from source code.
  • Open a connection late, close it early (try-with-resources); in real services get connections from a pool (next article).
  • Select only the columns you need instead of SELECT *; map rows into small objects (records) immediately.
  • Use BigDecimal for money (NUMERIC in the database), never double.

Errors you will meet

  • No suitable driver found for jdbc:… — driver JAR missing from the classpath (wrong Maven scope), or a typo in the URL.
  • Connection refused / connection timed out — database not running, wrong host or port, firewall.
  • password authentication failed (PostgreSQL) / Access denied (MySQL) — wrong credentials.
  • relation "customers" does not exist — wrong database or schema, table not created.
  • The column name x was not found in this ResultSet — the column is not in the SELECT list or is misspelled.
  • Operation not allowed after ResultSet closed — you used the ResultSet after closing its statement or connection.

Interview: "What is JDBC? Statement vs PreparedStatement? How do you prevent SQL injection?"

  • JDBC is the standard API; the driver implements it; steps: connection, statement, execute, process ResultSet, close (try-with-resources).
  • PreparedStatement is precompiled, parameterised, reusable, faster for repeated calls and — most importantly — prevents SQL injection because values are sent separately from the SQL.
  • Demo the attack (' OR '1'='1) and the fix; mention whitelisting for identifiers and hashing passwords.
  • Index start at 1; executeQuery vs executeUpdate; CallableStatement for stored procedures.

JDBC in practice: CRUD DAO, transactions, batches and connection pools

A DAO class hides all JDBC code behind simple methods; use try-with-resources for every call, setAutoCommit(false) with commit/rollback for multi-step changes, batches for bulk inserts, and a connection pool such as HikariCP in real applications.

The DAO pattern

A DAO (Data Access Object) is a class whose only job is to read and write one kind of data. The rest of the application calls customerDao.findById(7) and never sees SQL or Connection. When the database changes, only the DAO changes; in tests you can replace it with a fake. Spring Data repositories are an automatic version of the same idea. Mapping each row to a record keeps the data object short and immutable.

A complete CRUD DAO

public record Customer(long id, String name, String email, String city) {}
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

public class CustomerDao {
    private final String url;
    private final String user;
    private final String password;

    public CustomerDao(String url, String user, String password) {
        this.url = url;
        this.user = user;
        this.password = password;
    }

    private Connection connect() throws SQLException {
        return DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password);
    }

    // Row -> object. The ResultSet is already positioned on a row.
    private Customer map(ResultSet rs) throws SQLException {
        return new Customer(
                rs.getLong("id"),
                rs.getString("name"),
                rs.getString("email"),
                rs.getString("city"));              // may be null
    }

    // CREATE
    public Customer insert(String name, String email, String city) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
        try (Connection con = connect();
             PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)) {
            ps.setString(1, name);
            ps.setString(2, email);
            ps.setString(3, city);
            ps.executeUpdate();
            try (ResultSet keys = ps.getGeneratedKeys()) {
                keys.next();
                return new Customer(keys.getLong("id"), name, email, city);
            }
        }
    }

    // READ one
    public Optional<Customer> findById(long id) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "SELECT id, name, email, city FROM customers WHERE id = ?";
        try (Connection con = connect();
             PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setLong(1, id);
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                return rs.next() ? Optional.of(map(rs)) : Optional.empty();
            }
        }
    }

    // READ many
    public List<Customer> findByCity(String city) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "SELECT id, name, email, city FROM customers WHERE city = ? ORDER BY name";
        List<Customer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        try (Connection con = connect();
             PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setString(1, city);
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                while (rs.next()) {
                    result.add(map(rs));
                }
            }
        }
        return result;
    }

    // UPDATE
    public boolean updateCity(long id, String newCity) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "UPDATE customers SET city = ? WHERE id = ?";
        try (Connection con = connect();
             PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setString(1, newCity);
            ps.setLong(2, id);
            return ps.executeUpdate() == 1;           // rows affected
        }
    }

    // DELETE
    public boolean delete(long id) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection con = connect();
             PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = ?")) {
            ps.setLong(1, id);
            return ps.executeUpdate() == 1;
        }
    }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        CustomerDao dao = new CustomerDao("jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop",
                System.getenv("DB_USER"), System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));

        Customer saved = dao.insert("Asha Rao", "asha@mail.in", "Pune");
        System.out.println(saved);
        System.out.println(dao.findById(saved.id()).isPresent());
        System.out.println(dao.findByCity("Pune"));
        System.out.println(dao.updateCity(saved.id(), "Mumbai"));
        System.out.println(dao.findById(saved.id()).orElseThrow().city());
        System.out.println(dao.delete(saved.id()));
        System.out.println(dao.findById(saved.id()));
    }
}
Customer[id=1, name=Asha Rao, email=asha@mail.in, city=Pune]
true
[Customer[id=1, name=Asha Rao, email=asha@mail.in, city=Pune]]
true
Mumbai
true
Optional.empty

Notes: RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS asks the driver to return the database-generated id. In PostgreSQL you can also write INSERT ... RETURNING id and run it with executeQuery. This DAO opens a new connection per call, which is fine for learning but slow in real systems (see pools below).

Transactions

A transaction groups several statements so they either all succeed or none do (ACID, see SQL · Module 5). By default JDBC is in auto-commit mode: every statement is committed immediately. For a multi-step operation such as a money transfer, turn auto-commit off, then commit() on success and rollback() on failure.

public void transfer(long fromId, long toId, BigDecimal amount) throws SQLException {
    String debitSql = "UPDATE customers SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?";
    String creditSql = "UPDATE customers SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?";

    try (Connection con = connect()) {
        con.setAutoCommit(false);                              // start a transaction
        try (PreparedStatement debit = con.prepareStatement(debitSql);
             PreparedStatement credit = con.prepareStatement(creditSql)) {

            debit.setBigDecimal(1, amount);
            debit.setLong(2, fromId);
            debit.setBigDecimal(3, amount);
            if (debit.executeUpdate() != 1) {
                throw new SQLException("Insufficient balance or unknown account " + fromId);
            }

            credit.setBigDecimal(1, amount);
            credit.setLong(2, toId);
            if (credit.executeUpdate() != 1) {
                throw new SQLException("Unknown account " + toId);
            }

            con.commit();                                      // both changes become permanent
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            con.rollback();                                    // undo the debit if anything failed
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

If the credit fails after the debit succeeded, rollback() restores the sender's money. Without a transaction, the money would simply vanish. If the connection closes without commit(), uncommitted work is rolled back by most drivers, but do not rely on it. In Spring you replace all of this with @Transactional (Spring Boot · Module 3). Isolation levels can be set with con.setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED).

Batch inserts

Sending 10,000 inserts one by one costs 10,000 network round trips. A batch queues the statements and sends them together:

public void insertAll(List<Customer> customers) throws SQLException {
    String sql = "INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
    try (Connection con = connect();
         PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
        con.setAutoCommit(false);
        int count = 0;
        for (Customer c : customers) {
            ps.setString(1, c.name());
            ps.setString(2, c.email());
            ps.setString(3, c.city());
            ps.addBatch();                       // queue, do not run yet
            if (++count % 500 == 0) {
                ps.executeBatch();               // send every 500 rows
            }
        }
        ps.executeBatch();                       // send the remainder
        con.commit();
    }
}

executeBatch() returns an int[] of update counts. Some drivers need an option to really rewrite batches into fewer statements (reWriteBatchedInserts=true for PostgreSQL, rewriteBatchedStatements=true for MySQL, both added to the JDBC URL). Keep batches to a few hundred or thousand rows to limit memory.

Handling SQLException

try {
    dao.insert("Asha Rao", "asha@mail.in", "Pune");
} catch (SQLException e) {
    System.err.println("Message : " + e.getMessage());
    System.err.println("SQLState: " + e.getSQLState());     // standard 5-char code
    System.err.println("Vendor  : " + e.getErrorCode());    // database-specific code
    if ("23505".equals(e.getSQLState())) {                   // PostgreSQL unique violation
        throw new IllegalStateException("Email already registered", e);
    }
    throw new RuntimeException("Database error", e);          // keep the cause
}
  • SQLException is a checked exception. Do not swallow it with an empty catch; either handle it meaningfully or wrap it in your own unchecked exception with the original as the cause.
  • The SQLState is a five-character standard code whose first two characters give the class: 23xxx is an integrity-constraint violation (23505 is a duplicate key in PostgreSQL; MySQL reports duplicates with state 23000 and error code 1062), 08xxx is a connection problem, 42xxx is a syntax or access error.
  • Never show raw SQL errors to end users: they expose table names and structure. Log them, return a safe message.

Why connection pools exist

Opening a database connection is expensive: a TCP connection, authentication, and session setup on the server — typically many milliseconds, which dwarfs a fast query. Databases also limit the number of simultaneous connections. A connection pool opens a fixed set of connections once and lends them out: getConnection() returns a pooled connection quickly, and close() does not really close it, it returns it to the pool.

HikariCP is the fast, standard pool and the default in Spring Boot. Spring Boot creates a pooled DataSource from spring.datasource.url, username and password; HikariCP's default maximum pool size is 10 (spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size). If all connections are busy, new requests wait and may time out. Pool configuration and tuning are in Spring Boot · Module 3. Your DAO code stays the same: replace DriverManager.getConnection(...) by dataSource.getConnection() and keep closing the connection in try-with-resources — that is what returns it to the pool.

Rules

  • Always close Connection, PreparedStatement and ResultSet (try-with-resources). A connection leak exhausts the pool and freezes the application.
  • In a transaction, rollback() on failure, and use one Connection for all steps — separate connections are separate transactions.
  • Never share a Connection between threads.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving auto-commit on for a multi-statement business operation.
  • Forgetting to commit() after setAutoCommit(false): data seems saved in your session but vanishes.
  • Returning a ResultSet from a method after its connection was closed; map to objects inside the method.
  • Running one query per row in a loop (the N+1 problem); use a JOIN or IN, or batch.
  • Reading a nullable INT column with getInt and treating the returned 0 as real.
  • Catching SQLException and only calling e.printStackTrace().

Real projects

Few teams write raw JDBC for every query today: Spring Data JPA or JdbcTemplate remove the boilerplate. But everything above still runs underneath: a pooled DataSource, prepared statements, transactions, batches and SQLException translation. Raw JDBC remains common for bulk loads, reports and tools. When a framework misbehaves, turning on SQL logging (Logging) shows the exact statements JDBC receives.

Interview: "How do you handle transactions in JDBC? Why use a connection pool?"

  • setAutoCommit(false), do the steps on one connection, commit(), rollback() in the catch block, then close.
  • Pool: connection creation is expensive and databases limit connections; the pool reuses them; close() returns to the pool; HikariCP is the default in Spring Boot.
  • Batch: addBatch/executeBatch reduce round trips.
  • DAO pattern separates persistence from business logic. Mention try-with-resources and checked SQLException with getSQLState().

Logging with SLF4J and Logback instead of System.out.println

Write log messages through the SLF4J interface, let Logback (or Log4j2) decide where and how they appear, choose the right level, use {} placeholders, pass the exception as the last argument, and never log secrets.

Why not System.out.println?

A println is fine for a ten-line practice program. In an application running on a server it is a problem:

  • No levels. You cannot turn off debug chatter in production or turn it on for one package.
  • No context. No timestamp, thread name or class name, which you need to follow one request among thousands.
  • No control over the destination. You cannot send output to rolling files, to a log server (ELK, Loki, CloudWatch) or in JSON.
  • Slow and unsynchronised. Console output is slow and lines from different threads can interleave.
  • No stack-trace handling. e.printStackTrace() writes to System.err, outside your logging setup.

SLF4J facade and implementations

SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is only an API: Logger, LoggerFactory and MDC. The real work is done by an implementation found at runtime. This lets libraries log through SLF4J without forcing one logging library on you.

  • Logback — written by SLF4J's author; the default in Spring Boot (spring-boot-starter-logging). Add ch.qos.logback:logback-classic in a plain project; it brings slf4j-api with it.
  • Log4j2 — a powerful alternative (async loggers, many appenders). Keep it up to date: old 2.x versions had the serious Log4Shell vulnerability. In Spring Boot you can switch to it by excluding the logging starter and adding spring-boot-starter-log4j2.
  • If no implementation is on the classpath, SLF4J prints a warning that no providers were found and discards the messages. Having several implementations gives a warning about multiple providers.

Using a logger

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

public class OrderService {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class);

    public void placeOrder(long orderId, long customerId) {
        log.debug("Placing order {} for customer {}", orderId, customerId);
        try {
            charge(orderId);
            log.info("Order {} created for customer {}", orderId, customerId);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            log.error("Payment failed for order {}", orderId, e);   // exception LAST
            throw e;
        }
    }

    private void charge(long orderId) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Gateway timeout");
    }
}
10:15:32.118 [main] INFO  com.shop.OrderService - Order 1042 created for customer 7
10:15:32.121 [main] ERROR com.shop.OrderService - Payment failed for order 1042
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Gateway timeout
	at com.shop.OrderService.charge(OrderService.java:18)
	at com.shop.OrderService.placeOrder(OrderService.java:9)

(Only lines at INFO and above show with the default configuration, so the debug line is hidden until you lower the level.) One example run shows either the first or the second path; both are shown here to illustrate the format.

  • One logger per class, declared private static final, named after the class. The logger name is how you filter later (com.shop.OrderService, or everything under com.shop).
  • With Lombok, @Slf4j on the class generates a field named log.

Log levels

LevelUse it forExample
ERRORAn operation failed and needs attention; the system could not do what was askedPayment gateway unreachable, unexpected exception in a request
WARNSomething unexpected or risky happened, but the system recovered or continuesRetry succeeded on 3rd attempt, deprecated API used, cache miss rate high
INFOImportant business and lifecycle events; the "story" of the applicationApplication started, order created, scheduled job finished
DEBUGDetails useful to developers while diagnosingRequest parameters, SQL timing, decision branches
TRACEVery fine-grained flowMethod entry/exit, every loop iteration

Levels are ordered TRACE < DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR. Setting a logger to INFO shows INFO, WARN and ERROR. Production usually runs at INFO (or WARN for noisy libraries) and you temporarily lower one package to DEBUG when investigating. SLF4J has no FATAL level (Log4j2 does). Do not log expected, normal situations (like "user typed a wrong password") at ERROR, or the alerts become noise.

Parameterised messages

Wrong: concatenation

log.debug("Order " + order + " has " + items.size() + " items");
// builds the whole string even when DEBUG is off

Right: placeholders

log.debug("Order {} has {} items", order, items.size());
// string is built only if DEBUG is enabled

With {} the message is formatted only when the level is enabled, so disabled debug statements cost almost nothing. If computing an argument is itself expensive (for example serialising a big object to JSON), guard it: if (log.isDebugEnabled()) { log.debug("Payload: {}", toJson(payload)); }. SLF4J 2 also offers a fluent API (log.atDebug().setMessage(...).log()) with lambdas for lazy arguments.

Logging exceptions

Wrong: the stack trace is lost

catch (Exception e) {
    log.error("Failed: " + e.getMessage());
    // or: e.printStackTrace();
}

Right: pass the exception as the last argument

catch (Exception e) {
    log.error("Failed to place order {}", orderId, e);
}

When the last argument is a Throwable and there is no placeholder left for it, SLF4J prints its full stack trace and the chain of causes. Also:

  • Log an exception once. Either handle it (and log) or rethrow it; do not log.error and then throw at every layer, or one failure fills the log with the same stack trace five times. A common pattern: lower layers throw, and one place (a global exception handler in Spring, @ControllerAdvice) logs.
  • Include identifiers that make the message searchable (order id, user id, request id), not vague text like "error occurred".

Configuration basics

Logback reads logback.xml (or logback-test.xml for tests) from src/main/resources:

<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <logger name="com.shop" level="DEBUG"/>       <!-- our code: verbose -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.SQL" level="WARN"/>

    <root level="INFO">                           <!-- everything else -->
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
Logger
A named source of messages, arranged in a hierarchy by dots: com.shop.OrderService inherits the level of com.shop, which inherits from root.
Appender
A destination: console, a file, a rolling file (new file per day or size, old ones deleted), syslog, a network socket.
Encoder / layout / pattern
The format of each line: %d date, %thread, %-5level, %logger{36} abbreviated class name, %msg message, %n newline. JSON encoders exist for log-aggregation systems.

In Spring Boot you rarely write XML; use properties (add a logback-spring.xml only when you need more):

logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.shop=DEBUG
logging.level.org.springframework.web=WARN
logging.file.name=logs/app.log
logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} %-5level [%thread] %logger{20} - %msg%n

Setting logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG prints the SQL that Hibernate sends — handy when debugging JPA (Spring Boot · Module 3).

MDC — adding context to every line

The MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is a per-thread map of key-value pairs that Logback can print on every line. A filter puts a request id or user id in at the start of a request; every log line from that request, in any class, then carries it, which is how you follow one request through the logs.

import org.slf4j.MDC;

MDC.put("requestId", "req-8f21");
try {
    service.handle(request);          // every log line inside can show %X{requestId}
} finally {
    MDC.clear();                      // threads are reused: always clean up
}
// pattern: %d [%thread] %-5level %X{requestId} %logger{20} - %msg%n

MDC values live in the current thread; they do not automatically move to other threads (executors, async code), so copy them when you hand work over.

What never to log

  • Passwords, OTPs, API keys, JWTs, session ids and other secrets.
  • Card numbers, CVV, bank account numbers, Aadhaar, PAN and other government or financial identifiers; mask them (XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-4242).
  • Full personal data (address, phone, e-mail, health data) beyond what you need; privacy law (such as India's DPDP Act, GDPR) applies to log files too.
  • Whole request or response bodies by default; they hide secrets and fill disks.
  • Anything inside a tight loop at INFO or above.

Logs are copied, shipped to third-party tools and read by many people. Treat them as semi-public. Beware of logging a whole object whose toString() includes a password field; exclude sensitive fields from toString.

Rules

  • Depend on the SLF4J API in your code; keep exactly one implementation on the classpath.
  • Use placeholders, not concatenation; pass the exception as the last argument.
  • Never log secrets or full card/ID numbers.

Conventions

  • Messages are short sentences with identifiers: "Order {} shipped to {}". Start with the event, not "Entering method".
  • Log business events at INFO at service boundaries (request received, job finished) and details at DEBUG.
  • Never use System.out or e.printStackTrace() in application code. Replace tutorial code with log.info.
  • Add a correlation/request id through the MDC in services that call other services.

Common mistakes

  • Logging and rethrowing at every layer (duplicate stack traces).
  • log.info("Result: " + result) in a hot path — string building and I/O cost.
  • Using ERROR for validation failures caused by users.
  • Creating a new logger per call or logging with the wrong class (copy-pasted getLogger(OtherClass.class)).
  • A DEBUG level left on in production for a whole day, filling the disk.

Interview: "Why use a logging framework? What are the log levels?"

  • Levels, formatting, destinations, rolling files, performance and per-package configuration, all changeable without code changes.
  • SLF4J is a facade; Logback or Log4j2 implement it; Spring Boot uses Logback by default.
  • Levels: TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, with a one-line meaning each. Placeholders avoid string building; the exception goes last.
  • MDC for request ids; never log passwords, tokens or card numbers.

Javadoc and code style

Write Javadoc comments for public classes and methods (@param, @return, @throws), and follow one consistent style enforced by the IDE formatter and a style guide such as Google Java Style.

Javadoc

Javadoc is documentation written in special comments (/** ... */) directly above a class, method or field. The javadoc tool turns them into the HTML API pages you know from the JDK documentation, and IntelliJ shows them when you press Ctrl+Q over a name. The first sentence is the summary.

/**
 * A prepaid wallet that holds an amount in paise.
 *
 * <p>Instances are not thread-safe. Amounts are never negative.
 *
 * @author Asha Rao
 * @since 1.0
 */
public class Wallet {
    private long balancePaise;

    /**
     * Withdraws money from the wallet.
     *
     * @param amountPaise the amount to withdraw, in paise; must be positive
     * @return the balance after the withdrawal, in paise
     * @throws IllegalArgumentException if {@code amountPaise} is zero or negative
     * @throws InsufficientFundsException if the balance is lower than the amount
     * @see #deposit(long)
     */
    public long withdraw(long amountPaise) throws InsufficientFundsException {
        if (amountPaise <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        }
        if (amountPaise > balancePaise) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(balancePaise, amountPaise);
        }
        balancePaise -= amountPaise;
        return balancePaise;
    }
}
TagMeaning
@param nameDescribes a parameter (what it means, units, allowed values)
@returnDescribes the returned value (not for void)
@throws TypeWhen the method throws that exception
@see, {@link Type#method}Cross-reference to another class or method
{@code text}Inline code, with HTML characters shown literally
@since, @author, @deprecatedVersion, author, and a note about the replacement for old API

Generate the HTML with the JDK tool or Maven: javadoc -d docs src/main/java/com/shop/*.java or mvn javadoc:javadoc (output in target/site/apidocs); IntelliJ has Tools → Generate JavaDoc. Use <p> for new paragraphs inside a comment.

  • Document the contract, not the implementation: what the caller must pass, what comes back, what can go wrong.
  • Public APIs of libraries and shared modules need Javadoc; internal one-line helpers rarely do. Do not write comments that repeat the code (// increments i).
  • A comment that explains why (a business rule, a workaround, a link to a ticket) is worth more than one that explains what. If you need a comment to explain what a block does, consider renaming or extracting a method.
  • Keep documentation true: a wrong comment is worse than none.

Code style

Consistent formatting makes code reviews about logic, not about spaces, and makes diffs in Git small. Rules professionals follow:

  • Follow the Java naming conventions (Module 1): PascalCase classes, camelCase methods and variables, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants.
  • One style per codebase, applied by tools, not by arguing. The two common choices are the Google Java Style (2-space indent, 100-column limit, braces always) and IntelliJ's defaults (4-space indent, 120-column limit). Both are fine; the repository's choice wins.
  • Always use braces for if/for/while, one statement per line, one variable per declaration, no wildcard imports, no unused imports.
  • Keep methods short, with one purpose, and avoid deep nesting (use guard clauses).
  • Use meaningful names; avoid abbreviations and magic numbers (static final int MAX_RETRIES = 3;).
  • Declare variables as close as possible to first use; prefer final for fields that never change.
  • Order members consistently: constants, fields, constructors, public methods, private helpers.

Tools that enforce it:

  • IntelliJ formatter: Ctrl+Alt+L reformats, Ctrl+Alt+O optimises imports. Turn on Reformat code and Optimize imports in the commit dialog or "on save" actions.
  • .editorconfig: a small file in the repository root (indent size, line endings, final newline) understood by IntelliJ, VS Code and Eclipse.
  • Formatter plugins: google-java-format or Spotless (Maven/Gradle) can format or check formatting in the build; Checkstyle checks rules; SonarLint/SonarQube and the IDE inspections warn about bugs and smells.

Convention: make style automatic

Add an .editorconfig, share the IDE formatter settings (or use Spotless), and let CI fail when formatting is off. Then nobody discusses braces in a pull request.

Common mistakes

  • Javadoc that only repeats the method name ("Gets the name").
  • Forgetting to update a comment when the code changes.
  • Reformatting a whole file in an unrelated commit, which makes the real change impossible to review.
  • Leaving commented-out code in the file; Git remembers it for you.

Interview: "How do you keep code readable?"

  • Good names, small methods, consistent formatting through tools, comments for the why, Javadoc for public APIs.
  • Code reviews, linters (Checkstyle, SonarLint), and tests as living documentation.

Interview questions — Tools every Java developer uses

How do you debug a Java application in IntelliJ? Name the stepping options.

Set a breakpoint, start in Debug mode, and inspect variables, the frames (call stack) and watches. Step Over (F8) runs a line, Step Into (F7) enters the method on the line, Step Out (Shift+F8) finishes the current method, Run to Cursor (Alt+F9) jumps ahead, and Resume (F9) goes to the next breakpoint. Conditional breakpoints stop only when an expression is true, exception breakpoints stop where an exception is thrown, and Evaluate Expression runs code against the paused state.

What is remote debugging and how do you enable it?

It attaches the IDE to a JVM running elsewhere. Start that JVM with -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=*:5005, then create a Remote JVM Debug configuration in IntelliJ with the host and port. Use it only on protected environments, because an open debug port allows arbitrary code execution.

What is Maven and what does mvn clean install do?

Maven is a build and dependency-management tool configured by pom.xml. clean deletes target/; install runs the default lifecycle up to the install phase: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install. The result is a JAR in target/ that is also copied to the local repository ~/.m2.

Explain Maven coordinates and dependency scopes.

Coordinates are groupId (organisation), artifactId (module name) and version. Scopes: compile (default, everywhere), provided (needed to compile, supplied by the runtime, e.g. servlet API), runtime (not needed to compile, needed to run, e.g. JDBC driver) and test (only for tests, e.g. JUnit).

What are transitive dependencies and how do you resolve a version conflict?

A transitive dependency is a library required by a library you declared. When two paths need different versions, Maven keeps the nearest one in the dependency tree, and the first declared on a tie. Inspect with mvn dependency:tree, then pin a version in dependencyManagement, add an exclusion, or use a BOM such as Spring Boot's. Symptoms of a conflict are NoSuchMethodError and NoClassDefFoundError at runtime.

Maven vs Gradle?

Both use Maven Central. Maven has declarative XML, a fixed lifecycle and strong conventions, which makes projects uniform. Gradle uses a Kotlin or Groovy script, a task graph, incremental builds and a build cache, and is more flexible and often faster on large builds. Scope test corresponds to testImplementation, provided to compileOnly, and runtime to runtimeOnly. Both provide a wrapper (mvnw, gradlew).

What is a SNAPSHOT version? Why shouldn't you abuse -DskipTests?

A SNAPSHOT is a moving, in-development version; Maven checks for newer builds, so the same version string can mean different code. A release version is immutable. -DskipTests compiles tests but does not run them; using it to get a green build hides failures and ships bugs, so keep tests on in CI and release builds.

How do you write a unit test with JUnit 5? What are the lifecycle annotations?

Create a class in src/test/java, annotate methods with @Test, follow Arrange-Act-Assert and use Assertions (assertEquals(expected, actual), assertThrows, assertAll). @BeforeEach/@AfterEach run around every test; @BeforeAll/@AfterAll run once and are static. JUnit makes a new test-class instance per method, so tests are independent.

What is a parameterised test and when do you use it?

It runs one test method several times with different arguments, using @ParameterizedTest and a source such as @ValueSource, @CsvSource or @MethodSource. Use it for the same behaviour over many inputs (boundary values, valid and invalid cases) instead of copy-pasting tests.

Describe the steps of a JDBC query and why try-with-resources matters.

Get a Connection (from DriverManager or a pooled DataSource), create a PreparedStatement, bind parameters (index starts at 1), call executeQuery or executeUpdate, iterate the ResultSet with next(), and close everything. Try-with-resources closes the ResultSet, statement and connection even when an exception occurs; unclosed connections leak and exhaust the pool.

Statement vs PreparedStatement vs CallableStatement; what is SQL injection?

Statement runs a complete SQL string; PreparedStatement uses ? placeholders, is precompiled and reusable; CallableStatement calls stored procedures. SQL injection is an attack where user input concatenated into SQL changes the query (' OR '1'='1 turns a login into always-true). Prepared statements send values separately from the SQL text, so input cannot become code. Identifiers such as column names cannot be parameters and must be whitelisted.

How do transactions work in JDBC?

Auto-commit is on by default. For several dependent statements call con.setAutoCommit(false), run them on the same connection, call commit() if all succeed, and rollback() in the catch block if any fails. In Spring this becomes @Transactional.

Why use a connection pool such as HikariCP?

Opening a database connection is slow and databases limit how many they accept. A pool creates connections once and lends them to threads; closing a pooled connection just returns it. This improves latency and caps the load on the database. HikariCP is the default in Spring Boot, with a maximum pool size of 10 unless configured.

Why use SLF4J and Logback instead of System.out.println? What are the log levels and how do you log an exception?

Logging frameworks add levels, timestamps, thread and class names, configurable outputs (files, rolling, JSON) and per-package control, with better performance. SLF4J is the API; Logback or Log4j2 implement it. Levels are TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR. Use placeholders (log.info("User {} created", id)) and pass the exception last (log.error("Failed for {}", id, e)) so the stack trace is printed. Never log passwords, tokens or card numbers.

What is MDC and why do teams use it?

The Mapped Diagnostic Context is a per-thread map whose entries (request id, user id) can be printed on every log line. It lets you follow one request through all classes and, with a correlation id passed between services, across a microservice system. Clear it in a finally block because threads are reused.

Cheat sheet — Tools every Java developer uses

  • Debug keys Shift+F9 debug, F8 step over, F7 step into, Shift+F8 step out, Alt+F9 run to cursor, F9 resume, Alt+F8 evaluate.
  • Breakpoints line, conditional, logging, exception, method, field watchpoint.
  • Remote debug -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y,suspend=n,address=*:5005; never open it in production.
  • Maven layout src/main/java, src/main/resources, src/test/java, output in target/.
  • Coordinates groupId : artifactId : version.
  • Scopes compile (default), provided, runtime, test.
  • Lifecycle validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy; a phase runs all earlier ones.
  • Commands mvn clean install, mvn test -Dtest=Name, mvn dependency:tree, mvn -U, ./mvnw.
  • install vs deploy to ~/.m2 vs to a remote repository.
  • Conflicts nearest wins, then first declared; fix with dependencyManagement, exclusions or a BOM.
  • SNAPSHOT changing development version; release versions never change.
  • -DskipTests skips running tests; do not use it to hide failures.
  • Gradle implementation, runtimeOnly, compileOnly, testImplementation; ./gradlew build; useJUnitPlatform().
  • JUnit 5 @Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll (static), @DisplayName, @ParameterizedTest.
  • Assertions assertEquals(expected, actual), assertTrue, assertThrows, assertAll; doubles need a delta.
  • Test shape Arrange-Act-Assert; fast, isolated, repeatable; name the behaviour.
  • JDBC flow Connection → PreparedStatement → bind (from 1) → execute → ResultSet (next()) → close.
  • URLs jdbc:postgresql://host:5432/db, jdbc:mysql://host:3306/db.
  • Injection never concatenate input into SQL; use ? placeholders; whitelist identifiers.
  • Transactions setAutoCommit(false) → commit() / rollback().
  • Batch addBatch() + executeBatch(); commit once at the end.
  • SQLException checked; getSQLState(), 23505 = duplicate key in PostgreSQL.
  • Pool HikariCP reuses open connections; close() returns the connection to the pool.
  • Logging SLF4J API + Logback; levels TRACE < DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR.
  • Log calls log.info("Order {} created", id); log.error("msg {}", id, e); one private static final Logger per class.
  • Never log passwords, tokens, card or ID numbers; log an exception once.
  • Javadoc /** … */ with @param, @return, @throws; document the contract.
  • Style one formatter for the team (Ctrl+Alt+L), .editorconfig, no wildcard imports.

Practice — Tools every Java developer uses

  1. Debug the cart (easy). Copy the Cart program from the debugger article and use a breakpoint, the Variables panel and a watch on items.size() to find the off-by-one. Then add a conditional breakpoint that stops only when item.price() > 100. Done when you can find the bug without adding a single println.
  2. Exception breakpoint (easy). Write code that throws a NullPointerException three calls deep. Add a Java Exception Breakpoint for it and use the Frames panel to walk back to the line that passed the null. Done when you can state the cause from the debugger alone.
  3. Maven project from scratch (easy). Create a project with Spring Initializr or mvn archetype:generate, or hand-write the pom.xml from this module (Java 21, Logback, JUnit). Run mvn clean install and run the JAR with java -jar (set the mainClass in the manifest). Done when the build is green and the program prints a log line.
  4. Dependency conflicts (medium). Add two libraries that need different versions of one dependency, run mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose, identify the conflict, and fix it with dependencyManagement and an exclusion. Done when the tree shows only the version you chose.
  5. JUnit suite (medium). Test a PriceCalculator or your own class: at least one test per rule, edge cases, an assertThrows, one @ParameterizedTest with @CsvSource, and @BeforeEach. Done when a deliberately introduced bug makes exactly the right test fail, and the tests run with mvn test.
  6. JDBC DAO (medium). Create the customers table in PostgreSQL or MySQL and write a DAO with insert, findById, findAll, update and delete using records, try-with-resources and environment variables for credentials. Done when a main method exercises every method and the table matches what you expect.
  7. Break it, then fix it (medium). Write a login method using string concatenation, log in with ' OR '1'='1, then rewrite it with a PreparedStatement. Done when the attack succeeds on the first version and fails on the second.
  8. Transaction and batch (medium). Implement transfer(from, to, amount) with commit and rollback; prove that a failure after the debit leaves balances unchanged. Then insert 10,000 customers with a batch and compare the time with single inserts. Done when both results are shown with numbers.
  9. Replace println with logging (easy). Add SLF4J and Logback to an earlier practice program, write a logback.xml with a console appender, log at three levels, log an exception with its stack trace, and add a request id through MDC. Done when changing one level in the config shows or hides messages without code changes.
  10. Project 1 — Expense tracker or library manager (end of month 2). Build a console application with a menu. Requirements: OOP classes (for example Expense, Category, ExpenseService; or Book, Member, Loan), collections for in-memory work, data saved in MySQL or PostgreSQL through JDBC with a DAO layer and try-with-resources, custom exceptions (for example ExpenseNotFoundException, BookNotAvailableException), SLF4J logging, a few JUnit tests for the service layer, and a Maven build. Put it on GitHub with a README that has the description, setup steps (database script, environment variables, how to run), screenshots or sample output, and the features list. Done when someone else can clone it, follow the README and run it, and every commit message says what changed.
